Author
Rachel Thomas

Published
August 7, 2019

Over 225 police departments have partnered with Amazon to have access to Amazon’s video footage obtained as part of the “smart” doorbell product Ring, and in many cases these partnerships are heavily subsidized with taxpayer money. Police departments are allowing Amazon to stream 911 call information directly in real-time, and Amazon requires police departments to read pre-approved scripts when talking about the program. If a homeowner doesn’t want to share data from their video camera doorbell with police, an officer for the Fresno County Sheriff’s Office said they can just go directly to Amazon to obtain it. This creation of an extensive surveillance network, the murky private-public partnership surrounding it, and a lack of any sort of regulations or oversight is frightening. And this is just one of many examples related to surveillance technology that have recently come to light.

I frequently talk with people who are not that concerned about surveillance, or who feel that the positives outweigh the risks. Here, I want to share some important truths about surveillance:

Surveillance can facilitate human rights abuses and even genocide
Data is often used for different purposes than why it was collected
Data often contains errors
Surveillance typically operates with no accountability
Surveillance changes our behavior
Surveillance disproportionately impacts the marginalized
Data privacy is a public good
We don’t have to accept invasive surveillance
While I was writing this post, a number of investigative articles came out with disturbing new developments related to surveillance. I decided that rather than attempt to include everything in one post (which would make it too long and too dense), I would go ahead and share the above facts about surveillance, as they are just a relevant as ever.

Surveillance can facilitate human rights abuses and even genocide
There is a long history of data about sensitive attributes being misused, including the use of the 1940 USA Census to intern Japanese Americans, a system of identity cards introduced by the Belgian colonial government that were later used during the 1994 Rwandan genocide (in which nearly a million people were murdered), and the role of IBM in helping Nazi Germany use punchcard computers to identify and track the mass killing of millions of Jewish people. More recently, the mass internment of over one million people who are part of an ethnic minority in Western China was facilitated through the use of a surveillance network of cameras, biometric data (including images of people’s faces, audio of their voices, and blood samples), and phone monitoring.

Adolf Hitler meeting with IBM CEO Tom Watson Sr. in 1937. Source: Computer History
Pictured above is Adolf Hitler (far left) meeting with IBM CEO Tom Watson Sr. (2nd from left), shortly before Hitler awarded Watson a special “Service to the Reich” medal in 1937 (for a timeline of the Holocaust, see here). Watson returned the medal in 1940, although IBM continued to do business with the Nazis. IBM technology helped the Nazis conduct detailed censuses in countries they occupied, to thoroughly identify anyone of Jewish descent. Nazi concentration camps used IBM’s punchcard machines to tabulate prisoners, recording whether they were Jewish, gay, or Gypsies, and whether they died of “natural causes,” execution, suicide, or via “special treatment” in gas chambers. It is not the case that IBM sold the machines and then was done with it. Rather, IBM and its subsidiaries provided regular training and maintenance on-site at the concentration camps: printing off cards, configuring machines, and repairing them as they broke frequently.

Data is often used for different purposes than why it was collected
In the above examples, the data collection began before genocide was committed. IBM began selling to Nazi Germany well before the Holocaust (although continued for far too long), including helping with Germany’s 1933 census conducted by Adolf Hitler, which was effective at identifying far more Jewish people than had previously been recognized in Germany.

It is important to recognize how data and images gathered through surveillance can be weaponized later. Columbia professor Tim Wu wrote that “One [hard truth] is that data and surveillance networks created for one purpose can and will be used for others. You must assume that any personal data that Facebook or Android keeps are data that governments around the world will try to get or that thieves will try to steal.”

Plenty of data collection is not involved with such extreme abuse as genocide; however, in a time of global resurgence of white supremacist, ethno-nationalist, and authoritarian movements, it would be deeply irresponsible to not consider how data & surveillance can and will be weaponized against already vulnerable groups.

Data often has errors (and no mechanism for correcting them)
A database of suspected gang members maintained by California law enforcement officials was found to be full of errors, including 42 babies who had been added to the database when they were less than 1 year old (28 of whom were marked as “admitting to being gang members”). Even worse, there was no process in place for correcting mistakes or removing people once they’ve been added.

An
@NPR

  reporter recounts his experience of trying to rent an apartment and discovering that TransUnion, one of the 3 major credit bureaus, incorrectly reported him as having two felony firearms convictions. TransUnion only removed the mistakes after a dozen phone calls and notification that the story would be reported on. This is not an unusual story: the FTC’s large-scale study of credit reports in 2012 found 26% of consumers had at least one mistake in their files and 5% had errors that could be devastating. An even more opaque, unregulated “4th bureau” exists: a collection of companies buying and selling personal information about people on the margins of the banking system (such as immigrants, students, and people with low incomes), with no standards on what types of data are included, no way to opt out, and no system for identifying or correcting mistakes.

Surveillance typically operates with no accountability
What makes the examples in the previous section disturbing is not just that errors occurred, but that there was no way to identify or correct them, and no accountability for those profiting off the error-laden data. Often, even the existence of the systems being used is not publicly known (much less details of how these systems work), unless discovered by journalists or revealed by whistleblowers. The Detroit Police Dept used facial recognition technology for nearly two years without public input and in violation of a requirement that a policy be approved by the city’s Board of Police Commissioners, until a study from Georgetown Law’s Center for Privacy & Technology drew attention to the issue. Palantir, the defense startup founded by billionaire Peter Thiel, ran a program with New Orleans Police Department for 6 years which city council members did not even know about, much less have any oversight.

After two studies found that Amazon’s facial recognition software produced inaccurate and racially biased results, Amazon countered that the researchers should have changed the default parameters. However, it turned out that Amazon was not instructing police departments that use its software to do this either. Surveillance programs are operating with few regulations, no oversight, no accountability around accuracy or mistakes, and in many cases, no public knowledge of what is going on.

Surveillance changes our behavior
Hundreds of thousands of people in Hong Kong are protesting an unpopular new bill which would allow extradition to China. Typically, Hong Kong locals use their rechargeable smart cards to ride the subway. However, during the protests, long lines of people waited to use cash to buy paper tickets (usually something that only tourists do) concerned that they would be tracked for having attended the protests. Would fewer people protest if this was not an option?

In the United States, in 2015 the Baltimore Police Department used facial recognition technology to surveil people protesting the death of Freddie Grey, a young Black man who was killed in police custody, and arrested protesters with outstanding warrants. Mass surveillance could have a chilling impact on our rights to move about freely, to express ourselves, and to protest. “We act differently when we know we are ‘on the record.’ Mass privacy is the freedom to act without being watched and thus in a sense, to be who we really are,” Columbia professor Tim Wu wrote in the New York Times.

Flyer from the company Geofeedia Source
Surveillance disproportionately impacts those who are already marginalized
Surveillance is applied unevenly, causing the greatest harm to people who are already marginalized, including immigrants, people of color, and people living in poverty. These groups are more heavily policed and surveilled. The Perpetual Line-Up from the Georgetown Law Center on Privacy and Technology studied the unregulated use of facial recognition by police, with half of all Americans appearing in law enforcement databases, and the risks of errors, racial bias, misuses, and threats to civil liberties. The researchers pointed out that African Americans are more likely to appear in these databases (many of which are drawn from mug shots) since they are disproportionately likely to be stopped, interrogated, or arrested. For another example, consider the contrast between how easily people over 65 can apply for Medicare benefits by filling out an online form, with the invasive personal questions asked of a low-income mother on Medicaid about her lovers, hygiene, parental shortcomings, and personal habits.

In an article titled Trading privacy for survival is another tax on the poor, Ciara Byrne wrote, “Current public benefits programs ask applicants extremely detailed and personal questions and sometimes mandate home visits, drug tests, fingerprinting, and collection of biometric information… Employers of low-income workers listen to phone calls, conduct drug tests, monitor closed-circuit television, and require psychometric tests as conditions of employment. Prisoners in some states have to consent to be voiceprinted in order to make phone calls.”

Data privacy is a public good, like air quality or safe drinking water
Data is more revealing in aggregate. It can be nearly impossible to know what your individual data could reveal when combined with the data of others or with data from other sources, or when machine learning inference is performed on it. For instance, as Zeynep Tufekci wrote in the New York Times, individual Strava users could not have predicted how in aggregate their data could be used to identify the locations of US military bases. “Data privacy is not like a consumer good, where you click ‘I accept’ and all is well. Data privacy is more like air quality or safe drinking water, a public good that cannot be effectively regulated by trusting in the wisdom of millions of individual choices. A more collective response is needed.”

Unfortunately, this also means that you can’t fully safeguard your privacy on your own. You may choose not to purchase Amazon’s ring doorbell, yet you can still show up in the video footage collected by others. You might strengthen your online privacy practices, yet conclusions will still be inferred about you based on the behavior of others. As Professor Tufekci wrote, we need a collective response.

We don’t have to accept invasive surveillance
Many people are uncomfortable with surveillance, but feel like they have no say in the matter. While the threats surveillance poses are large, it is not too late to act. We are seeing success: in response to community organizing and an audit, Los Angeles Police Department scrapped a controversial program to predict who is most likely to commit violent crimes. Citizens, researchers, and activists in Detroit have been effective at drawing attention to the Detroit Police Department’s unregulated use of facial recognition and a bill calling for a 5-year moratorium has been introduced to the state legislature. Local governments in San Francisco, Oakland, and Somerville have banned the use of facial recognition by police.

For further resources, please check out: - Georgetown Law Center on Privacy and Technology - Digital Defense Playbook

Plenty of data collection is not involved with such extreme abuse as genocide; however, in a time of global resurgence of white supremacist, ethno-nationalist, and authoritarian movements, it would be deeply irresponsible to not consider how data & surveillance can and will be weaponized against already vulnerable groups.

Data often has errors (and no mechanism for correcting them)
A database of suspected gang members maintained by California law enforcement officials was found to be full of errors, including 42 babies who had been added to the database when they were less than 1 year old (28 of whom were marked as “admitting to being gang members”). Even worse, there was no process in place for correcting mistakes or removing people once they’ve been added.

An
@NPR
  reporter recounts his experience of trying to rent an apartment and discovering that TransUnion, one of the 3 major credit bureaus, incorrectly reported him as having two felony firearms convictions. TransUnion only removed the mistakes after a dozen phone calls and notification that the story would be reported on. This is not an unusual story: the FTC’s large-scale study of credit reports in 2012 found 26% of consumers had at least one mistake in their files and 5% had errors that could be devastating. An even more opaque, unregulated “4th bureau” exists: a collection of companies buying and selling personal information about people on the margins of the banking system (such as immigrants, students, and people with low incomes), with no standards on what types of data are included, no way to opt out, and no system for identifying or correcting mistakes.

Surveillance typically operates with no accountability
What makes the examples in the previous section disturbing is not just that errors occurred, but that there was no way to identify or correct them, and no accountability for those profiting off the error-laden data. Often, even the existence of the systems being used is not publicly known (much less details of how these systems work), unless discovered by journalists or revealed by whistleblowers. The Detroit Police Dept used facial recognition technology for nearly two years without public input and in violation of a requirement that a policy be approved by the city’s Board of Police Commissioners, until a study from Georgetown Law’s Center for Privacy & Technology drew attention to the issue. Palantir, the defense startup founded by billionaire Peter Thiel, ran a program with New Orleans Police Department for 6 years which city council members did not even know about, much less have any oversight.

After two studies found that Amazon’s facial recognition software produced inaccurate and racially biased results, Amazon countered that the researchers should have changed the default parameters. However, it turned out that Amazon was not instructing police departments that use its software to do this either. Surveillance programs are operating with few regulations, no oversight, no accountability around accuracy or mistakes, and in many cases, no public knowledge of what is going on.

Surveillance changes our behavior
Hundreds of thousands of people in Hong Kong are protesting an unpopular new bill which would allow extradition to China. Typically, Hong Kong locals use their rechargeable smart cards to ride the subway. However, during the protests, long lines of people waited to use cash to buy paper tickets (usually something that only tourists do) concerned that they would be tracked for having attended the protests. Would fewer people protest if this was not an option?

In the United States, in 2015 the Baltimore Police Department used facial recognition technology to surveil people protesting the death of Freddie Grey, a young Black man who was killed in police custody, and arrested protesters with outstanding warrants. Mass surveillance could have a chilling impact on our rights to move about freely, to express ourselves, and to protest. “We act differently when we know we are ‘on the record.’ Mass privacy is the freedom to act without being watched and thus in a sense, to be who we really are,” Columbia professor Tim Wu wrote in the New York Times.

Flyer from the company Geofeedia Source
Surveillance disproportionately impacts those who are already marginalized
Surveillance is applied unevenly, causing the greatest harm to people who are already marginalized, including immigrants, people of color, and people living in poverty. These groups are more heavily policed and surveilled. The Perpetual Line-Up from the Georgetown Law Center on Privacy and Technology studied the unregulated use of facial recognition by police, with half of all Americans appearing in law enforcement databases, and the risks of errors, racial bias, misuses, and threats to civil liberties. The researchers pointed out that African Americans are more likely to appear in these databases (many of which are drawn from mug shots) since they are disproportionately likely to be stopped, interrogated, or arrested. For another example, consider the contrast between how easily people over 65 can apply for Medicare benefits by filling out an online form, with the invasive personal questions asked of a low-income mother on Medicaid about her lovers, hygiene, parental shortcomings, and personal habits.

In an article titled Trading privacy for survival is another tax on the poor, Ciara Byrne wrote, “Current public benefits programs ask applicants extremely detailed and personal questions and sometimes mandate home visits, drug tests, fingerprinting, and collection of biometric information… Employers of low-income workers listen to phone calls, conduct drug tests, monitor closed-circuit television, and require psychometric tests as conditions of employment. Prisoners in some states have to consent to be voiceprinted in order to make phone calls.”

Data privacy is a public good, like air quality or safe drinking water
Data is more revealing in aggregate. It can be nearly impossible to know what your individual data could reveal when combined with the data of others or with data from other sources, or when machine learning inference is performed on it. For instance, as Zeynep Tufekci wrote in the New York Times, individual Strava users could not have predicted how in aggregate their data could be used to identify the locations of US military bases. “Data privacy is not like a consumer good, where you click ‘I accept’ and all is well. Data privacy is more like air quality or safe drinking water, a public good that cannot be effectively regulated by trusting in the wisdom of millions of individual choices. A more collective response is needed.”

Unfortunately, this also means that you can’t fully safeguard your privacy on your own. You may choose not to purchase Amazon’s ring doorbell, yet you can still show up in the video footage collected by others. You might strengthen your online privacy practices, yet conclusions will still be inferred about you based on the behavior of others. As Professor Tufekci wrote, we need a collective response.

We don’t have to accept invasive surveillance
Many people are uncomfortable with surveillance, but feel like they have no say in the matter. While the threats surveillance poses are large, it is not too late to act. We are seeing success: in response to community organizing and an audit, Los Angeles Police Department scrapped a controversial program to predict who is most likely to commit violent crimes. Citizens, researchers, and activists in Detroit have been effective at drawing attention to the Detroit Police Department’s unregulated use of facial recognition and a bill calling for a 5-year moratorium has been introduced to the state legislature. Local governments in San Francisco, Oakland, and Somerville have banned the use of facial recognition by police.

For further resources, please check out: - Georgetown Law Center on Privacy and Technology - Digital Defense Playbook

THE MAN WHO BOUGHT THE FUTURE

An NVIDIA Chip, a Village Called Borat’s — and the Most Expensive Promise in the World

THE NVIDIA FILES
A Continuing Series of Independent Investigations
In Borat's village, the future occupied the place of honour upon the dining-room table.

It was an NVIDIA chip: an object so extraordinary that it had become the envy of every neighbour, although not one of them could say with any confidence what it actually did.

Its owner had purchased it after watching a distinguished gentleman on television explain that this tiny marvel of engineering represented the future of mankind.

He possessed nothing into which it might be fitted. Nor had he bought it for that purpose.

He had bought the future itself, and there are few men who can claim to have done so.

The neighbours came to admire it. Some wanted to invest in it. Others offered to lend him money against its future value. One proposed building an enormous factory around it. Another suggested asking the government for a subsidy.

Nobody asked whether it worked.

That, they agreed, was a question for the past.

And somewhere far away, in the boardrooms of America and the corridors of Washington, the same remarkable conversation was taking place — only with better suits, larger numbers and considerably more expensive dining tables.

Who wins? Who loses? Who lies? Who cheats?

And perhaps the most important question of all:

Who is paying for a future that has already been sold?

text:
This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here.

If regulators don’t act now, the generative AI boom will concentrate Big Tech’s power even further. That’s the central argument of a new report from research institute AI Now. And it makes sense. To understand why, consider that the current AI boom depends on two things: large amounts of data, and enough computing power to process it.  

Both of these resources are only really available to big companies. And although some of the most exciting applications, such as OpenAI’s chatbot ChatGPT and https://t.co/G133p3BVPF’s image-generation AI Stable Diffusion, are created by startups, they rely on deals with Big Tech that gives them access to its vast data and computing resources. 

“A couple of big tech firms are poised to consolidate power through AI rather than democratize it,” says Sarah Myers West, managing director of the AI Now Institute, a research nonprofit. 

Right now, Big Tech has a chokehold on AI. But Myers West believes we’re actually at a watershed moment. It’s the start of a new tech hype cycle, and that means lawmakers and regulators have a unique opportunity to ensure that the next decade of AI technology is more democratic and fair. 

What separates this tech boom from previous ones is that we have a better understanding of all the catastrophic ways AI can go awry. And regulators everywhere are paying close attention. 

China just unveiled a draft bill on generative AI calling for more transparency and oversight, while the European Union is negotiating the AI Act, which will require tech companies to be more transparent about how generative AI systems work. It’s also planning  a bill to make them liable for AI harms.

The US has traditionally been reluctant to regulate its tech sector. But that’s changing. The Biden administration is seeking input on ways to oversee AI models such as ChatGPT—for example, by requiring tech companies to produce audits and impact assessments, or by mandating that AI systems meet certain standards before they are released. It’s one of the most concrete steps the administration has taken to curb AI harms.

Meanwhile, Federal Trade Commission chair Lina Khan has also highlighted Big Tech’s advantage in data and computing power and vowed to ensure competition in the AI industry. The agency has dangled the threat of antitrust investigations and crackdowns on deceptive business practices. 

This new focus on the AI sector is partly influenced by the fact that many members of the AI Now Institute, including Myers West, have spent time at the FTC. 

Myers West says her stint taught her that AI regulation doesn’t have to start from a blank slate. Instead of waiting for AI-specific regulations such as the EU’s AI Act, which will take years to put into place, regulators should ramp up enforcement of existing data protection and competition laws.

Because AI as we know it today is largely dependent on massive amounts of data, data policy is also artificial-intelligence policy, says Myers West. 

Case in point: ChatGPT has faced intense scrutiny from European and Canadian data protection authorities, and it has been blocked in Italy for allegedly scraping personal data off the web illegally and misusing personal data. 

The call for regulation is not just coming from government officials. Something interesting has happened. After decades of fighting regulation tooth and nail, today most tech companies, including OpenAI, claim they welcome it.  

The big question everyone’s still fighting over is how AI should be regulated. Though tech companies claim they support regulation, they’re still pursuing a “release first, ask question later” approach when it comes to launching AI-powered products. They are rushing to release image- and text-generating AI models as products even though these models have major flaws: they make up nonsense, perpetuate harmful biases, infringe copyright, and contain security vulnerabilities.

The White House’s proposal to tackle AI accountability with post-AI product launch measures such as algorithmic audits is not enough to mitigate AI harms, AI Now’s report argues. Stronger, swifter action is needed to ensure that companies first prove their models are fit for release, Myers West says.

“We should be very wary of approaches that do not put the burden on companies. There are a lot of approaches to regulation that essentially put the onus on the broader public and on regulators to root out AI-enabled harms,” she says. 

And importantly, Myers West says, regulators need to take action swiftly. 

“There need to be consequences for when [tech companies] violate the law.” 

Deeper Learning

How AI is helping historians better understand our past

This is cool. Historians have started using machine learning to examine historical documents smudged by centuries spent in mildewed archives. They’re using these techniques to restore ancient texts, and making significant discoveries along the way. 

Connecting the dots: Historians say the application of modern computer science to the distant past helps draw broader connections across the centuries than would otherwise be possible. But there is a risk that these computer programs introduce distortions of their own, slipping bias or outright falsifications into the historical record. Read more from Moira Donovan here.

Bits and bytes

Google is overhauling Search to compete with AI rivals  
Threatened by Microsoft’s relative success with AI-powered Bing search, Google is building a new search engine that uses large language models, and upgrading its existing search engine with AI features. It hopes the new search engine will offer users a more personalized experience. (The New York Times) 

Elon Musk has created a new AI company to rival OpenAI 
Over the past few months, Musk has been trying to hire researchers to join his new AI venture, https://t.co/sJHwd99urj. Musk was one of OpenAI’s cofounders, but he was ousted in 2018 after a power struggle with CEO Sam Altman. Musk has accused OpenAI’s chatbot ChatGPT of being politically biased and says he wants to create “truth-seeking” AI models. What does that mean? Your guess is as good as mine. (The Wall Street Journal) 

https://t.co/G133p3BVPF is at risk of going under
https://t.co/G133p3BVPF, the creator of the open-source image-generating AI model Stable Diffusion, just released a new version of the model whose results are slightly more photorealistic. But the business is in trouble. It’s burning through cash fast and struggling to generate revenue, and staff are losing faith in the CEO. (Semafor)

Meet the world’s worst AI program
The bot on https://t.co/sMVeSs5u7S, depicted  as a turtleneck-wearing Bulgarian man with bushy eyebrows, a thick beard, and a slightly receding hairline, is designed to be absolutely awful at chess. While other AI bots are programmed to dazzle, Martin is a reminder that even dumb AI systems can still surprise, delight, and teach us. (The Atlantic)

text:
SATIRE | By Kim Wojcinski, USA Best-Selling Author
The evidence will be presented. The verdict is yours.

DAYTON, OHIO — Wilbur and Orville Wright are at it again. This time, they took an old copper moonshine still, modified it in their garage, and figured out how to turn ordinary tap water into helium-3.

They invited the neighbors over for a demonstration at noon. The federal government arrived at eleven.

The Wright Flyer was parked out back. The agents walked right past it.

What comes out of the still?

Think of the helium in a party balloon. Almost all of it is helium-4. At the center of each atom are two protons and two neutrons. Helium-3 has two protons and just one neutron. That makes it a lighter form of the same element. It’s rare on Earth, useful in instruments that detect neutrons, and being studied as a possible fuel for certain types of nuclear fusion. A cheap way to make it would get the attention of researchers, investors, and, as the Wrights were about to learn, people who arrive in a van with no markings.

The still looked like something a sheriff would have dragged out of the woods a hundred years ago. It had a dented copper belly, a crooked coil, and a brass garden-hose fitting Wilbur had filed down by hand. Orville had hung a cardboard sign on it that read HELIUM-3. He’d learned from the airplane that people liked to know what they were looking at.

The man in charge glanced at the sign.

“Take that, too,” he told an agent.

First they took the still. Then they took the recipe.

“At first I thought you were here to do business,” Orville said. “Last time, the Army wanted to buy what we built.”

The man introduced himself as counsel for the department. He handed Orville a notice saying the still was being taken under emergency authority. The order itself was classified, along with the reasons for issuing it and the name of the official who signed it.

“What’s the emergency?” Wilbur asked.

“Someone could get hold of the process.”

“Who?”

“Anyone with access to the notebook.”

At that moment, an agent picked up the notebook.

The still itself had cost the brothers next to nothing. The notebook held six months of work. It recorded the changes they’d made, the trials that failed, and the one that finally worked. An agent thumbed past the first few pages and asked if they’d made copies.

“You’ve already got the still,” Wilbur said. “What do you need the notebook for?”

“Our scientists may need to reproduce your results.”

“Can we build another one?”

“You could be prosecuted.”

“Can you build another one?”

“The department will make that determination.”

Wilbur looked at Orville. “There’s your buyer.”

How much does the government owe you?

The lawyer said the brothers were free to file a claim. They would need to show what they’d invented, demonstrate that it worked, and provide an independent estimate of what it was worth.

“Can our appraiser see the still and the notebook?” Wilbur asked.

“He would need a clearance.”

“How does he get one?”

“He would need an official reason to see the materials.”

“He needs to see them to tell you what you owe us.”

“That’s a private reason.”

The agents spent another ten minutes in the garage looking for copies. One checked inside the coffee can where Wilbur kept spare washers. They never asked what the invention was worth. They asked three times whether anyone else had the recipe.

That afternoon, a government spokesman told reporters the Wright brothers had voluntarily made their equipment available for scientific evaluation. Orville read that statement at the kitchen table. Beside it was the notice warning him that interference with the removal could result in arrest.

“I did volunteer to stay out of jail,” he said.

The spokesman also assured reporters that the government had taken no intellectual property. The inventory, he said, listed a used copper vessel and a notebook.

The appeal

At the end of the driveway, Wilbur caught up with the lawyer.

“You could’ve knocked on the door and made us an offer,” he said. “We’d have heard you out.”

“An offer would have given you the right to say no.”

The lawyer got into the back seat. Orville called after him.

“Who do we appeal to?”

As the car pulled away, the lawyer raised his middle finger.

Orville went inside and wrote it down. He wanted a record of at least one answer.

Eighteen months later

The department unveiled a process for making helium-3 from tap water. At the press conference, the secretary called it a triumph of federal research and thanked the scientists whose years of painstaking work had made it possible.

The brothers watched on a television in the garage. The apparatus onstage was housed in a polished steel cabinet. When the secretary opened it for the cameras, Orville leaned forward.

“Look at the bottom of the coil, Will.”

The camera moved in. Behind the shiny new panel was their dented copper still. On the intake was the same brass fitting, with one side filed flat.

Wilbur turned off the television. On the workbench lay the government’s final response to their claim for compensation.

The brothers, it said, had furnished no evidence that they had ever built a working machine.

The evidence has been presented. The verdict is yours.

At the age of eleven, Delin’s home city was attacked by the Infusans. Her father, Arden, tried to escape with her through the old sewer tunnels below the city. As they fled, they were spotted by Infusan soldiers. Arden was gunned down while shielding his daughter. Delin fell into the river below with her father’s lifeless body. In that moment, she uncovered one of her signature shield spells. A magical body barrier that forms on her entire body protected her from the impact, saving her life.

She washed ashore alone and pulled herself out of the water. Nearby, she found the body of a fallen Vaelari warrior and a ceremonial dagger. Hearing tortured screams coming from a hut, she followed the sound and witnessed a nightmare. Inside were three Infusan soldiers tormenting three young Vaelari girls named Iris, Sky, and Rose, all around ten years old.

The Infusans had mutilated them. Iris’s fingers and toes had been severed. Sky’s teeth had been ripped out. Rose’s face had been doused in acid, leaving her blind in one eye and badly burned. The soldiers were laughing as they continued the torture. One of the men removed his helmet, revealing his skin.

All Vaelari females are born with a unique ability called Essence Drain, a racial trait that activates through direct skin contact. Delin used the opportunity to grab the unarmored Infusan and triggered her Essence Drain. Her eyes turned red as she absorbed his strength, overwhelming and killing all three soldiers with the dagger. The three girls were saved, and from that moment, they stuck together.

The four escaped the town and eventually reached a collapsing bridge with Infusan soldiers closing in. At the last moment, a man named Kade appeared, singlehandedly destroying the enemy squad. He led the girls to an abandoned castle deep in the wilderness. There, they began to recover and train.

Kade appeared as a savior but he harbored a dark secret. He had willingly submitted to a spirit walker, believing it would grant him the power to protect others. Instead, it took control of him. These spirit walkers require only verbal consent to possess a host, and they choose those with strong bodies and fragile minds.

Over time, the three girls named Sky, Rose, and Iris became hardened and vengeful. The trauma they endured warped them. Though still young, they began to embrace a darker path. Delin, however, remained committed to justice and compassion. She rejected vengeance, even while the others began to follow Kade’s twisted ideals.

Delin’s inner strength made her an outlier. She questioned Kade, stood her ground, and began to distance herself from him and the others. Her bond with her sisters grew strained. Though she understood their pain, she refused to let it consume her. She remained the only one among them to resist corruption.

At a later point in the story, Delin is mortally wounded by an Infusan sniper during a quest for the artifact. As she lays dying, a spiritual entity appears and offers her power in exchange for control. The player is given a choice: accept the deal and take the dark path, or resist. If Delin resists, her collected elemental relics awaken. The final two relics, light and dark, manifest and unlock her true artifact weapon, Despair’s Requiem.

Delin’s story is one of loss, endurance, and choice. She fights not for revenge, but to protect what little hope remains in a world scarred by suffering. Her strength was born from what she refused to become. Her debut arrives in late 2027-2028.

Combat Style

Delin has two combat specializations.

One focuses on shield-based defense, protection magic, and precise counterattacks. The other transforms her sword into a massive two-handed weapon, channeling absorbed essence into devastating strikes.

The Biggest Irony Of Human Psychology: We Ignore What Is Free And Respect What Is Expensive!

Charge ₹25,000 For A Service, And People Take It Seriously. Offer The Same Service For Free, And Suddenly Nobody Has Time!

Is It Really About Value, Or Is It Our Strange Human Mindset?

Three Friends Were Having Filter Coffee In Chennai.

The First Was An Employee.

His company provided a powerful CRM system free of cost. He hardly used it but was willing to spend ₹15,000 on a productivity course!

The Second Was A Mutual Fund Distributor.

He received a free digital platform to build his identity, publish articles and attract investors. He ignored it but was ready to spend ₹25,000 on digital marketing!

The Third Was An Investor.

He never attended free investor awareness programme but happily paid ₹10,000 for a wealth creation course!

An elderly gentleman listening to them smiled and said:

"When Something Is Free, We Think We Can Use It Tomorrow. When We Pay For It, We Want To Recover Every Rupee!"

In South Indian households, we are taught not to waste even a grain of rice. Yet we often waste valuable opportunities simply because they come without a price tag.

Free Does Not Mean Worthless.

Expensive Does Not Mean Valuable.

And Having Access Does Not Mean Taking Action!

Sometimes, the biggest loss is not the money we spend but the opportunities we ignore.

A Price Tag May Create Seriousness, But Only Action Creates Results!

My Question: If The Same Free Service Were Priced At ₹25,000, Would People Suddenly Start Valuing It?

OPEN HEAVENS DAILY DEVOTIONAL
 
DATE: SUNDAY, NOVEMBER 15TH, 2026
 
THEME: BAPTISED WITH FIRE
 
MEMORISE:
"I indeed baptise you with water unto repentance: but He that cometh after me is mightier than I, whose shoes I am not worthy to bear: He shall baptize you with the Holy Ghost, and with fire:" - Matthew 3:11 KJV
 
READ: Malachi 3:1-4 KJV
1 Behold, I will send my messenger, and he shall prepare the way before me: and the Lord, whom ye seek, shall suddenly come to his temple, even the messenger of the covenant, whom ye delight in: behold, he shall come, saith the LORD of hosts.

2 But who may abide the day of his coming? and who shall stand when he appeareth? for he is like a refiner's fire, and like fullers' soap:

3 And he shall sit as a refiner and purifier of silver: and he shall purify the sons of Levi, and purge them as gold and silver, that they may offer unto the LORD an offering in righteousness.

4 Then shall the offering of Judah and Jerusalem be pleasant unto the LORD, as in the days of old, and as in former years.
 
MESSAGE:
Anyone whom God wants to use as His vessel must be baptised, not only with the Holy Ghost, but also with fire. Fire has many functions, one of which is that it purifies. In Isaiah 6:5, after Isaiah realised how unclean he was, the angel of the Lord used a live coal to touch his lips and said, "This hath touched thy lips; and thine iniquity is taken away, and thy sin purged" (Isaiah 6:6-7). Isaiah received a baptism of fire that cleansed him and made him a useful and worthy vessel to carry out God's assignment.

Before the Apostles were sent out to proclaim the gospel of Christ around the world, Jesus instructed them to wait for the baptism of the Holy Ghost, as we see in Acts 1:4-5: "And, being assembled together with them, commanded them that they should not depart from Jerusalem, but wait for the promise of the Father, which, saith He, ye have heard of Me. For John truly baptised with water; but ye shall be baptised with the Holy Ghost not many days hence."

They obeyed this instruction, and they were baptised by the Holy Spirit and fire in Acts 2. This encounter marked the beginning of their exploits for Jesus, starting with Peter's sermon, which God used to save about 3,000 souls that same day. If you want to be a worthy vessel in God's hands, you must allow Him to set you apart and baptise you with the Holy Ghost and fire.

Beloved, God is still looking for vessels He can purify with fire and put to use in His vineyard. Today's Bible reading tells us that God is a Refiner and Purifier of those who will serve Him in righteousness. Until the Lord refines you with His fire, your offering cannot be pleasant to Him. Offering in this context means your life. Gold in its raw state is not beautiful, but after it has been purified by fire, it becomes precious. This is why it is called a precious metal. If you don't want to remain a common vessel in God's vineyard, ask Him to visit you with His fire. Allow His fire to take away any filth in your life that will not allow you to be useful and precious in His sight. If you really want to be a useful vessel for God, pray today's prayer point with all your heart.
 
PRAYER POINT:
Father, I am ready: please, let Your fire fall on me.

Ys World Magazine X Ancient Story Lalo’s opera Le roi d’Ys and Debussy’s La cathédrale engloutie are the two most influential musical works inspired by the legend of Ys, one dramatizing the city’s fall on stage and the other evoking its cathedral rising from the sea through impressionist harmony. Together they shaped how modern audiences imagine the myth. https://t.co/2SxPYGP4sm https://t.co/8LO5cxvkyP https://t.co/YRNHg4anoV’s Le roi d’Ys (1888) https://t.co/pXDMsHi3vg https://t.co/HGC439IwFd the Metropolitan Opera in New York, showing its international popularity before fading from modern repertory. https://t.co/dnibJz4l8Q classic 1957 recording conducted by André Cluytens remains a key reference, featuring Janine Micheau, Rita Gorr, and Henri Legay. https://t.co/YggWnc3F2t, the opera blends French Romantic lyricism with large choral scenes that depict the rising waters and the city’s destruction. https://t.co/5czrlD8LfN’s La cathédrale engloutie (1910) https://t.co/B12jWjLkft solo piano prelude from Book I of Debussy’s Préludes, directly inspired by the myth of the submerged cathedral of Ys. https://t.co/S5ADDmKkPm https://t.co/OyFTnbM2kF uses parallel fifths, open sonorities, and pentatonic scales to evoke bells, chant, and the slow emergence of the cathedral from the sea.  The piece is a hallmark of musical impressionism, depicting imagery rather than telling a narrative.  The rising dynamic waves and organ-like chords represent the cathedral appearing in sunlight before sinking again beneath the water.  How These Works Shape the Legend Today  Lalo’s opera gives Ys a dramatic, character-driven interpretation, emphasizing moral conflict and divine punishment.  Debussy’s prelude offers a symbolic, atmospheric vision, focusing on the mystical beauty of the myth rather than its tragedy.  Together, they helped popularize the legend beyond Brittany, influencing later adaptations in literature, art, and even modern fantasy media.  Ys in Modern Culture  The legend continues to appear in contemporary works, most notably the Ys video game series, which reimagines the lost civilization in a high‑fantasy setting (though not directly tied to the original Breton tale).  Debussy’s prelude remains one of the most performed impressionist piano works, and Lalo’s opera is still recorded and occasionally revived, keeping the myth alive in classical music circles.  Ys World Magazine X Ancient Story A closely related ancient story to the fall of Ys is the Greek myth of Deucalion and Pyrrha, another tale of divine punishment, a catastrophic flood, and the rebirth of humanity.  A Similar Ancient Story: Deucalion and Pyrrha (Greek Mythology)  Core Narrative  Zeus sends a great flood to destroy humanity because of its wickedness.  Prometheus warns his son Deucalion, who builds a boat with his wife Pyrrha.  They survive the deluge and land on Mount Parnassos after the waters recede.  Following divine instructions, they throw stones over their shoulders, which transform into humans—Deucalion’s stones become men, Pyrrha’s become women—thus repopulating the Earth.  Why It’s Similar to Ys  Both stories involve divine judgment and the destruction of a civilization.  Each myth ends with renewal: Ys becomes a cautionary tale of moral decline, while Deucalion and Pyrrha mark the rebirth of humankind.  Both myths are part of a broader global pattern of flood narratives, found in cultures from Mesopotamia to India and the Americas.  Other Ancient Flood Myths You Might Find Interesting  These stories share thematic DNA with Ys—catastrophe, divine intervention, and rebirth:  Epic of Gilgamesh (Mesopotamia) — Utnapishtim survives a god‑sent flood after building a boat, one of the oldest known flood stories. text:
🙏The President Who Stayed🙏

In January 2020, Markwayne Mullin’s 15-year-old son Jim — a world-class wrestler who’d competed all over the world since he was 12 — suffered a severe brain injury on the mat.

He nearly didn’t make it. 

When he woke up, he was a different kid. Couldn’t touch his nose. Couldn’t walk right. Short-term memory gone. Didn’t fully recognize his own parents. The only thing he still knew for sure was that Donald Trump was the President.

Trump called immediately. Offered his private plane to get Jim to a top rehab center in California. Then, in the middle of the toughest stretch of the 2020 campaign, he called almost every single day for two weeks just to check on him.

Later he went to see Jim in person. His team told him twice it was time to leave. Both times he said not yet. The third time he looked at them and told them the plane wasn’t leaving without him for at least another 15 minutes. 

He sat with the boy and just loved on him.

That visit helped Jim’s memory start coming back. Trump kept checking in afterward — no cameras, no statements, no credit. Just a President who cared about one injured kid and his family.

text:
The main problem with the Texas GOP is not that it doesn't support marijuana legalization (as Joe Rogan, noted pothead, seemingly claims). It's that it doesn't support working class people enough. 

Property taxes are important, I get it. I am a homeowner myself and each February stings. But it's not something to base a political party on. 

There are entire swathes of the Texas electorate who, either don't own a home and want to, or are barely hanging on to homes that they do own. A few hundred dollars of property tax relief is not going to do anything for them.

Those who rent are also a constituency that Texas Republicans have ignored. What are you doing for these people? How are you making their lives better? How are you helping them reach their potential?

Texas is making the same mistake as California, Colorado, Virginia, Arizona, and even Washington did: they attracted the industries they wanted to (mostly high-tech) but those industries are filled with people who are themselves Leftists. It's just the way it is: the more highly-educated you are, the more likely you are to be on the Left. I saw this everywhere at one of the big tech companies I worked at.

Texas also allowed its education system to be captured by Leftists. They were fairly restrained when the GOP was in control of the governorship, but that's about to change soon. The Teachers' Union is gonna go wild. They're gonna press all the buttons they can at once because this will be the first time they've been in control for a while. They'll be dancing in the end zone because they HAVEN'T been there before (or not for a long time, anyways). 

The Texas GOP can't just assume that 2028 means an automatic "Texas will return to being red" is going to happen. It absolutely will not happen if the Texas GOP just sits on its hands and does business as usual. 

Talk about what the ordinary working man is going through and what you're going to do to help him. Not with a handout, but with action that will save the state, save his children, and save the nation. Offer hope to the common man and ignore your corporate and rich landowner donors for just a solitary minute. You just might win bigly like someone else I know has by pushing that exact message.

It hasn't been delivered on or, at the very least, the working man is not FEELING it, whatever the "line go up" numbers say. So what are you going to do for him? That is what democracy is all about, right? Listening to the voters. Well... are you listening or are you lecturing?

Personal Harmeet story: she, my wife, and a woman I'll call "Candy" know each other from California politics. Candy takes a job at a DC-based organization in summer 2020, needs a place to stay, we offer our spare bedroom and the in-law suite we're going to add.

Anyway, Candy turns out to be a psycho to live with. Final straw was the puddle of her dog's piss that she left at the top of our stairs without cleaning or warning us ("luckily" it was me who discovered this by slipping and falling in it, and not my then-1-year-old son) and we kick her out after 2 weeks.

Candy goes to FB to post a sob story about how our actions were going to cost her the job (a lie: I put her up in a hotel for a week to get her out, and we think they may have already fired her by then), and unsurprisingly the replies were generally women offering sympathy and in some cases money to help her.

Except for one woman - Harmeet - who (not knowing our side of the story, FWIW) read through the facts and bluntly replied that Candy was badly overreacting to a minor housing hiccup. She gained more respect from me by being willing and able to call out that bullshit than anyone else has ever done.

I don't agree with some of the things she's saying since resigning, but I'm willing to believe her when she claims to have been bottling everything up during her time at the USDOJ.

text:
It’s nearly 8:00 pm EST, and I’m reading Brian Kilmeade’s recent NYT bestseller: “Uniting the States,” subtitled “Six Crucial Moments That Forged the American Miracle.” It’s fascinating, well written, and yet easy to digest.

There is no Introduction to this accounting other than the PREAMBLE to the Constitution. I reread it every time I pick up this book. 

“We the People of the United States of America, in order to form a more perfect union, ESTABLISH JUSTICE, INSURE DOMESTIC TRANQUILITY, provide for the common defense, promote the GENERAL WELFARE, and SECURE BLESSINGS of liberty to ourselves AND OUR POSTERITY, do ordain  and establish this Constitution for the United States of America.”

It gives me chills. This one paragraph is prescient. How wise our forefathers were to understand how precarious our Constitution is to offer a warning about its vulnerability. Yet, as Americans, we take little concern about waking one morning to an entirely different form of government. This was evident with the results of the midterm. I personally know two people who decided not to vote…each one of them knocked out someone else’s vote merely by staying home: my vote, their own votes and that of another.

I tried to explain how that stubbornness and their ONE NON-VOTE kills two votes. And how many others stayed home in droves? For what? Pettiness, revenge or laziness? They cut off their own noses and that of others as well, while undocumented voters, living or dead, stole our freedom from us on November 3, 2026.

We HAVE GOT TO BE SMARTER THAN THE DOORKNOB, folks, if we want to maintain our liberties. YES, our LIBERTIES…freedom from government control, and continue with capitalism and freedom of religion. I’m nearly 72, and not a day in those 72 years did I fear for my freedom. We won’t be toppled with guns and bombs, but by an invisible yet obvious cancer called socialism.

How careless and braindead we are to have allowed this to happen. Buckle up people, the road you voted for is about to get very uncertain and difficult, and some of us deserve it.

text:
🚨Cristiano Ronaldo on Portugal suffering the biggest defeat in their history after a 4-1 loss to Denmark:

🗣️ “After training, I went home and watched the game with my family.

We sat down and I watched Portugal from the first minute until the final whistle.

Honestly, I wasn’t impressed.

I wasn’t angry because they lost. I’ve lost plenty of games with Portugal.

But what I watched against Denmark was different.

I saw players wearing the Portugal shirt, but not enough fighting for it.

That bothered me.

People don’t always understand what that shirt represents. It carries generations of Portuguese football.

When I put that shirt on, I knew I was carrying something bigger than myself.

Against Denmark, I didn’t see it.

Denmark were winning duels, second balls, controlling possession and attacking with confidence.

Portugal weren’t making them uncomfortable.

When the first goal went in, I was waiting for somebody to stand up and say, ‘Come on, we are Portugal.’

I didn’t see enough of that.

Then another goal comes. Then another. Suddenly it’s 4-1.

And I’m thinking, ‘What happened to the mentality?’

Jorge told me I couldn’t offer the team more.

Some players also said it was time for me to step aside.

They said Portugal needed a younger generation.

They said others needed responsibility.

Fine, okay. I accepted it.

I stepped away.

I didn’t fight them or create problems.

I gave them exactly what they asked for.

I gave them the shirt.

And this is what happened.

Portugal suffered the biggest defeat in its history.

And we suffered it against Denmark.

That is difficult for me to accept.

If you tell me I am the problem, then when I leave, I expect the problem to disappear.

Instead, you remove me and the team looks like it doesn’t know how to fight.

So what was I supposed to be?

The problem?

Or the player carrying more responsibility than people wanted to admit?

You cannot say Portugal has moved beyond Cristiano Ronaldo, then lose 4-1 without anyone taking responsibility.

If you want the new generation, show me the new generation.

Don’t tell me about potential.

Don’t tell me about talent.

Don’t tell me about the future.

Show me now.

Fight now.

Compete now.

Because the Portugal shirt doesn’t wait for you to become ready.

When you put it on, you are ready.

I watched Denmark play with hunger.

They wanted every ball, attacked us and made Portugal uncomfortable.

And our players looked like they were waiting for someone to wake them up.

That is unacceptable.

I don’t expect every player to be Cristiano Ronaldo.

But I expect every player wearing Portugal to have courage when things become difficult.

When we were losing, I asked for the ball.

When I missed, I asked for another chance.

That is what representing Portugal meant to me.

Maybe people will say I’m angry because I’ve retired.

No. I’m angry because I care.

I gave more than twenty years to that shirt.

I sacrificed, suffered and celebrated for it.

And I never once believed I was doing Portugal a favour by playing.

So when Jorge says I couldn’t offer the team more, I accepted his decision.

When players said I should step aside, I stepped aside.

But now they have to accept their responsibility too.

You cannot push the old generation out and then complain when nobody takes responsibility for what comes next.

You asked for this team.

You wanted this team.

Now own it.

The biggest defeat in Portugal’s history isn’t just a result. It’s a warning.

The shirt is still there.

The history and expectations are still there.

I’m not.

So nobody can hide behind Cristiano Ronaldo anymore.

If Portugal wants to move forward without me, do it.

But don’t tell me you are ready for the future while playing like a team that has forgotten its past.

I stepped aside because they said I couldn’t offer more.

Now Portugal has suffered its biggest defeat in history.

Against Denmark.

I don’t need to say more.

The football answered the question.”

text:
This evening I received a text so long I thought a company had accidentally sent me its employee handbook, annual report, and the director’s cut of its unresolved feelings. 

It was from a company I mention often. The message, in essence: stop tagging our name, or else. OR ELSE? Sir, I write about hiring. I didn’t steal the Declaration of Independence. I read it twice. Not because I was intimidated, but because I was searching for the part where the author offered me a job. After all, if you have time to compose a novel about my LinkedIn posts, surely somebody has five minutes to reply to a candidate. Priorities, people. A text threatening consequences gets same day delivery; an applicant asking for an update gets sent into the Bermuda Triangle with a PDF resume.

Apparently, I have committed the unforgivable corporate sin of using the name of a company while discussing its hiring practices. I assumed that was how conversation worked. You mention a business, you discuss an experience, and everyone moves on. But somewhere, someone saw a tag and reacted like I’d launched a submarine in their conference room. I can picture the emergency meeting: legal on line one, communications on line two, and a VP whispering, “Has anyone tried making the process better?”

Let’s be clear: I don’t wake up plotting how to ruin somebody’s Tuesday. I wake up, drink coffee, and read stories from people who are exhausted by a system that treats their time like it’s free and their dignity like it’s optional. Then I write. Sometimes with jokes. Sometimes with anger. Sometimes with both, because apparently sarcasm is the only department still responding within 24 hours.

And yes, it stings. Not the warning itself. It’s realizing how quickly a company can find the words to tell someone to be quiet, while so many people wait weeks for a few words about whether they still have a shot at a job. Imagine the energy we could save if just a fraction of that urgency went into treating applicants like human beings instead of abandoned shopping carts.

Maybe speaking up costs opportunities. Maybe it makes people uncomfortable. I know the risks. There are nights when I wonder whether I should just post motivational quotes about synergy, compliment every CEO’s leadership journey, and call a four month hiring process an exciting adventure. It would probably be easier. I could even sell mugs: SILENCE IS GOLDEN, ESPECIALLY DURING RESTRUCTURING. But then another person writes to say, “Thank you. I thought I was the only one.” And that matters more than a corporate approved smile.

So to the company texting me tonight: I hear you. I won’t invent stories, and I don’t expect anyone to agree with every word I say. But asking questions and sharing opinions aren’t crimes against the quarterly earnings call.

And if your next message is another five page thriller, please include a plot twist, a decent ending, and an actual human response to the people applying for jobs. They’re still waiting.

Enjoying the California sunshine and a more relaxed lifestyle in Los Angeles is understandable at this stage of his career, but Son Heung-min still has plenty left to show. At 34–35 he is no longer the explosive player of his mid-20s, yet he remains a high-level technician with excellent finishing, movement, and football intelligence. The Bundesliga (or another top European league) would still allow him to operate at a competitive intensity that MLS simply does not provide on a consistent basis.
There is also unfinished business from a pure sporting perspective:
•  He has never won a major European club trophy beyond the 2024/25 Europa League with Tottenham.
•  A return to Germany — especially to a side that can challenge for the title or at least play in the Champions League — would give him another chance at meaningful silverware while he is still capable of contributing at a high level.
•  As South Korea’s captain, staying sharp in a demanding league matters. The national team still needs his leadership and quality for the next cycle, and playing regularly against better opposition helps maintain that edge.
The free-agent window opening in January 2027 makes the opportunity even cleaner. He could move without a transfer fee, which lowers the risk for any Bundesliga club and increases the chance of a meaningful role rather than a pure marketing signing.
So while the LA lifestyle is appealing, your assessment feels right: he still has more to offer on the pitch than simply enjoying the sun. Whether he actually chooses that path is another matter — he has been clear about wanting to stay focused on LAFC for now — but from a footballing standpoint, the argument for one more European chapter remains strong.

text:
How Did a Japanese Soy Sauce Company Conquer the World’s Kitchens Without Changing Their Recipes?

Imagine trying to sell Japanese soy sauce to American families in the 1950s, when most had little experience with Japanese cuisine.

You could tell them to start cooking Japanese food.

Or you could try something much more ambitious.

Show them how soy sauce could make their own food taste better.

That was the path Kikkoman chose.

Its roots stretch back to the soy sauce brewers of Noda, Japan, where families developed their craft over generations. But after World War II, Kikkoman began imagining a future far beyond Japan.

In 1957, the company established a sales operation in San Francisco. Instead of insisting that Americans adopt Japanese dishes, it demonstrated how soy sauce could enhance meat and other familiar ingredients.

The message was simple. You don’t have to abandon your food culture to enjoy something from Japan.

The strategy worked.

In 1973, Kikkoman began shipping soy sauce from its new factory in Wisconsin, bringing Japanese fermentation expertise into the American Midwest.

It also emphasized hiring locally, working with local businesses, and becoming part of the surrounding community.

The same philosophy shaped its expansion into Europe. In Düsseldorf, Kikkoman opened a teppanyaki restaurant where customers could discover how soy sauce complemented familiar foods.

Today, Kikkoman soy sauce is sold in more than 100 countries.

What impresses me most isn’t simply the company’s international success.

It’s the philosophy behind it.

Kikkoman didn’t need to convince the world that Japanese cuisine was superior. It recognized that every food culture had something worth preserving.

And then it found a way for Japanese tradition to contribute to those cultures.

I believe this offers a lesson that reaches far beyond business.

Cultural exchange doesn’t have to mean replacing one tradition with another. Sometimes, the most meaningful exchange happens when different traditions make each other richer.

A Japanese seasoning became part of kitchens around the world, not by demanding that everyone become Japanese, but by finding a place at their tables.

What ingredient from another country has become indispensable in your own kitchen?

LIVERPOOL FC MORNING BRIEFING: ARAUJO INJURY WORRY AHEAD OF MANCHESTER UNITED VISIT

Ronald Araujo finished Uruguay's win over Argentina on Friday night walking with difficulty, according to the Uruguayan newspaper El Observador, a week before Manchester United visit Anfield. Neither Liverpool nor the Uruguayan federation has commented.

Overnight, Mauricio Pochettino's United States beat Haiti 6-0 in his penultimate game before he takes charge at Old Trafford, and four Liverpool players are in squads for tonight's Nations League games.

ARAUJO FITNESS WATCH

Araujo played the full game in central defence as Uruguay won 2-1 at La Bombonera in Buenos Aires. In its player ratings, El Observador gave him five out of 10, said he won the header that led to Uruguay's opening goal, which went down as an own goal by Leonardo Balerdi, and said he finished the match walking with difficulty after a well-timed challenge on Julián Álvarez.

On Saturday the same paper listed Uruguay's confirmed absentees for Tuesday's friendly against the Dominican Republic in Maldonado as Giorgian de Arrascaeta, Guillermo Varela and Joaquín Piquerez, all released early at their clubs' request. Araujo was not named among the players released early.

Araujo, 27, is on loan from Barcelona. There has been no official word on his condition from Liverpool or from Uruguay.

POCHETTINO'S USA HIT SIX

The United States beat Haiti 6-0 at Nu Stadium in Miami in the first leg of their Concacaf Nations League quarter-final, with Christian Pulisic scoring twice. It was the biggest win of Pochettino's two years in charge.

The second leg in Cincinnati on Tuesday will be his last game as USA head coach. He officially becomes Manchester United head coach on Wednesday 18 November, and his first game in charge will be at Anfield next Sunday.

NO CHANGE ON SZOBOSZLAI

Liverpool have not issued a fresh update on Dominik Szoboszlai's knee following Hungary's 2-0 win in Georgia on Saturday. The midfielder played the full game but said afterwards that he came close to withdrawing during the warm-up. Hungary host Northern Ireland at the Puskás Aréna in Budapest on Tuesday at 7.45pm UK time.

REDS ON DUTY TONIGHT

Bradley Barcola and Jeremy Jacquet, who both started France's 3-1 defeat in Italy on Thursday, are in the France squad to face Turkiye in Bordeaux. Rio Ngumoha and Victor Muñoz could come up against each other when Spain host England in Madrid. Both games kick off at 7.45pm UK time.

TRANSFER TALK

Football Insider claims Liverpool have joined the race for Lens defender Ismaelo Ganiou. The claim has not been backed up by an established Liverpool reporter. Credibility: Low.

Sport Witness reported on Tuesday that Liverpool have made enquiries with Palmeiras about young attacking midfielder Erick Belé. The report has since been repeated by Brazilian websites, but the original source says no formal offer has been made. Credibility: Low.

Both stories were reproduced on the Media Watch page of Liverpool's official website, which is not club confirmation. There have been no credible new contract, ownership or senior staffing developments overnight.

text:
Washington, April 12, 1977.
Sale of Boeing Chinook Helicopters to Nigeria:

The Boeing Vertol Company has informed us that the Nigerian Air Force wishes to purchase seven Chinook helicopters (CH–47C’s). 

Since this prospective sale could change the nature of our military supply relationship with Nigeria, I am informing you about it at this early stage to obtain your views.

The total sale could amount to about $40 million. 

If approved, it would represent the first sale on a Foreign Military Sales (FMS) basis of U.S. military equipment to Nigeria since the Nigerian civil war. (The Nigerians already have six C–130 transport planes, but these were purchased commercially, not through FMS.) Boeing representatives have informed us that the Nigerian Federal Military Government (FMG) would like to send a 5–7 man team to the United States the week of April 17 to visit the Boeing production facility and U.S. Army installations to inspect and see CH–47 helicopters demonstrated. State Department permission would be required for a visit to the Boeing factory because it is a defense plant. Defense Department clearance is required to visit U.S. Army installations.

Our Ambassador to Nigeria strongly favors the sale of Chinooks, but he and Boeing are concerned that the Nigerians not be allowed to proceed too far if there is any chance the USG would turn down a subsequent request for a FMS Letter of Offer and Acceptance. Boeing has requested an advisory opinion on whether we would issue an export license.

Although your election and Ambassador Young’s trip to Nigeria have already strengthened our bilateral relations, we have an interest in further links to the FMG. The USG’s decision not to sell spare parts and ammunition during the Nigerian civil war was a basic reason for the decline in our relations. 

A Nigerian decision to proceed with the Chinook purchase could contribute to the further improvement of US-Nigerian relations.

With respect to arms transfer policy concerns, the Chinook is a heavy-lift helicopter which would improve the mobility of the Nigerian armed forces and would also be available for non-military roles such as civic action and infrastructure projects. 

It is unarmed, and we have sold non-lethal equipment to Nigeria in the past. For these reasons, Ambassador Young supports this sale. It cannot be air transported (except by the very largest cargo aircraft) and has limited range, so that it is unlikely to be used outside the immediate environs of Nigeria. 
Nigeria is already militarily much stronger than its neighbors, but this has not raised concerns among them. However, a Chinook sale could lead to further sales inquiries from the Nigerians.

Canada's ‘dystopian’ offer to American veteran sent her sprinting back to U.S. health care system

Nov. 14, 2026

Kristin Logan and Donovan James moved to Canada in chase of the free healthcare dream, and left after encountering a "dystopian" system offering death in place of treatment.

Kristin Logan and Donovan James say they moved to Canada with their sights set on the financial and medical benefits of publicly funded healthcare — but say they encountered a "dystopian" system that offered medically assisted death before cancer treatment, prompting them to return to the United States.

"Canada has been slowly sliding into an entire dystopian situation. The way they've expanded the MAID system is frightening. It was never supposed to be used this way, to be offered so easily and so upfront when a person gets sick. I think it's evil," James told Fox News Digital.

"It was the most heartbreaking experience, to basically be set up to die. And if I wanted to live, I had to take my life into my own hands and leave the country. It's pretty dystopian to think about now, to get information about ways that I can end my life and what the end of my life looks like before I'd even gotten an oncology appointment," Logan continued.

Kristin Logan and Donovan James say they moved to Canada hoping to benefit from its publicly funded healthcare system but returned to the United States after encountering what they described as a "dystopian" system that offered medically assisted death before cancer treatment. 

Logan said she was first diagnosed in September 2023, leaving Canada later that month to get initial treatment. She later had a bowel obstruction in March 2024. She had to leave the country again, and then returned in April 2024 before the cancer returned in December 2024.

The couple decided to leave Canada in January 2025 and officially moved back to the United States in May of that year.

MAID — Canada's medical assistance in dying program — is described by Health Canada as "a health service that allows eligible people to receive help from a medical practitioner in ending their life."

According to Kristin and Donovan, MAID was the best initial solution Canada offered to her upon her diagnosis. The Atlantic has reported that MAID now accounts for about one in 20 deaths in Canada, "surpassing countries where assisted dying has been legal for far longer," with some raising concerns the program has become too expansive.

"They should be focusing on treating people and helping people live, but instead they've expanded the system as a kind offer because they pretty much assume you're going to die," he continued.

James, a Canadian citizen living in the United States with a green card, is the husband of Kristin Logan, a U.S. Air Force veteran who has stage four ovarian cancer.

They moved to Canada to get ahead of potential financial difficulty in the case of a future medical crisis to avoid "ever going bankrupt" — a hypothetical that crashed into reality following Kristin’s three separate travels back to America in a desperate fight for her life due to high wait times and lack of resources available in the Canadian healthcare system.

Logan had multiple emergencies and hospital trips during her time in Canada when a second bowel obstruction shifted her and her family’s fight or flight into overdrive to find a plan to save her life.

Wall Street’s Trillion-Dollar Stress Test: Nvidia’s Post-Jensen Era, Anthropic’s Historic IPO, and a Hawkish Fed Collide Next Week
Buckle up. Next week isn’t just another earnings calendar—it is a high-stakes collision of Silicon Valley’s biggest leadership shakeup, a trillion-dollar AI debut, and a Federal Reserve suddenly back on the warpath.
With the 10-year Treasury yield surging toward 5.15% following hotter-than-expected October CPI and PPI prints, Wall Street’s margin for error has evaporated. According to market outlooks from CNBC and TradingKey, four massive catalysts will dictate whether the market rallies into the holidays or hits a wall.

1. AI’s Double Reckoning: Nvidia Without Jensen & Anthropic’s $1.4T Debut

The AI trade is facing its biggest reality check since the boom began, with two historic events unfolding within 48 hours of each other.
• Nvidia’s First Post-Jensen Earnings (Tuesday, Nov. 17, After the Bell): Following founder Jensen Huang’s shock resignation amid personal scandal, interim CEO and CFO Colette Kress steps into the spotlight for her first quarterly report at the helm. Wall Street isn't just looking at numbers; it’s hunting for strategic continuity and clues on a permanent successor. Expectations are sky-high: consensus calls for $108.99 billion in revenue (up ~91.2% YoY) and $2.49 in EPS. Options traders are bracing for fireworks, pricing in an implied post-earnings move of ±8.6%.
• Anthropic’s Blockbuster Nasdaq IPO (Pricing Wednesday, Nov. 18; Trading Thursday, Nov. 19): Generative AI powerhouse Anthropic is set to debut under the ticker ANT. Priced between $70 and $78 per share, the offering targets a staggering fully diluted valuation of $1.26 trillion to $1.4 trillion. Rumors on the Street suggest the book is already roughly 6x oversubscribed. This trillion-dollar listing will be the ultimate litmus test for public market appetite—and whether investors are still willing to pay stratospheric multiples for AI growth.

2. The Fed’s Hawkish Pivot & Crucial Macro Data

Inflation refuses to go quietly, and rate-cut hopes have rapidly flipped into fears of a December hike.
• October FOMC Minutes (Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2:00 PM ET): After voting 10–2 last month to hold the federal funds rate at 3.75%–4.00%, the minutes will pull back the curtain on the Fed's internal divide. Traders will dissect every word for clues on whether policymakers are leaning toward a 25 bps—or even a jumbo 50 bps—hike in December.
• Wall-to-Wall Fed Speak (Monday–Thursday): Prepare for headline whiplash. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh takes the podium on Monday, while New York Fed President John Williams speaks on both Monday and Wednesday. Any hawkish pushback on inflation or terminal rates will immediately pressure tech valuations.
• October Retail Sales (Tuesday, Nov. 17, 8:30 AM ET): Consensus expects a modest 0.2% to 0.3% month-over-month gain, cooling sharply from September's +0.8% surge. This print will reveal whether the American consumer is finally buckling under 5%+ yields.
• Other Key Prints: Watch the NY Empire State Manufacturing Index on Monday, Industrial Production on Tuesday, Initial Jobless Claims (est. 200K) on Thursday, and the final November University of Michigan Consumer Sentiment reading on Friday.

3. The Retail & Chinese Tech Earnings Gauntlet

Ahead of Thanksgiving and Black Friday, big-box retailers and Chinese tech giants will offer an unfiltered look at global consumer health:
• Monday, Nov. 16: Baidu (BIDU) and XPeng (XPEV) report before the open, spotlighting AI cloud monetization and EV delivery margins.
• Tuesday, Nov. 17: Home Depot (HD) and Disney (DIS) kick off the morning with updates on housing resilience and streaming profitability, followed by https://t.co/bqQB5Tp2Ko (JD) pre-market and Nvidia (NVDA) after the close.
• Wednesday, Nov. 18: Target (TGT), Lowe’s (LOW), and TJX Companies (TJX) report before the bell—keep an eye on inventory levels and holiday guidance. Palo Alto Networks (PANW) headlines after-hours cyber spending.
• Thursday, Nov. 19: The main event for consumer staples arrives pre-market with Walmart (WMT) and Alibaba (BABA), testing tariff impacts, pricing power, and e-commerce demand.

4. Geopolitics & Wildcards on the Radar

• APEC Leaders' Summit in Shenzhen (Nov. 18–19): As world leaders gather in China for the 33rd APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting, all eyes are on a potential face-to-face bilateral meeting between U.S. and Chinese leadership. Any fresh rhetoric on advanced semiconductor export controls or trade tariffs could trigger sharp swings across chipmakers and multinational industrials.
• Airline Grounding Fallout: Following Friday’s (Nov. 13) nationwide commercial aircraft grounding, expect lingering operational disruptions and choppy early-week trading across major U.S. carriers like United (UAL) and Delta (DAL).
