text:
The Frost nails its uncanny, disconcerting vibe in its first few shots. Vast icy mountains, a makeshift camp of military-style tents, a group of people huddled around a fire, barking dogs. It’s familiar stuff, yet weird enough to plant a growing seed of dread. There’s something wrong here.

“Pass me the tail,” someone says. Cut to a close-up of a man by the fire gnawing on a pink piece of jerky. It’s grotesque. The way his lips are moving isn’t quite right. For a beat it looks as if he’s chewing on his own frozen tongue.

Welcome to the unsettling world of AI moviemaking. “We kind of hit a point where we just stopped fighting the desire for photographic accuracy and started leaning into the weirdness that is DALL-E,” says Stephen Parker at Waymark, the Detroit-based video creation company behind The Frost.

The Frost is a 12-minute movie in which every shot is generated by an image-making AI. It’s one of the most impressive—and bizarre—examples yet of this strange new genre. You can watch the film below in an exclusive reveal from MIT Technology Review.

To make The Frost, Waymark took a script written by Josh Rubin, an executive producer at the company who directed the film, and fed it to OpenAI’s image-making model DALL-E 2. After some trial and error to get the model to produce images in a style they were happy with, the filmmakers used DALL-E 2 to generate every single shot. Then they used D-ID, an AI tool that can add movement to still images, to animate these shots, making eyes blink and lips move.

“We built a world out of what DALL-E was giving back to us,” says Rubin. “It’s a strange aesthetic, but we welcomed it with open arms. It became the look of the film.”

“This is certainly the first generative AI film I’ve seen where the style feels consistent,” says Souki Mehdaoui, an independent filmmaker and cofounder of Bell & Whistle, a consultancy specializing in creative technologies. “Generating still images and puppeteering them gives it a fun collaged vibe.” 

The Frost joins a string of short films made using various generative AI tools that have been released in the last few months. The best generative video models can still produce only a few seconds of video. So the current crop of films exhibit a wide range of styles and techniques, ranging from storyboard-like sequences of still images, as in  The Frost, to mash-ups of many different seconds-long video clips.  

In February and March, Runway, a firm that makes AI tools for video production, hosted an AI film festival in New York. Highlights include the otherworldly PLSTC by Laen Sanches, a dizzying sequence of odd, plastic-wrapped sea creatures generated by the image-making model Midjourney; the dreamlike Given Again by Jake Oleson, which uses a technology called NeRF (neural radiance fields) that turns 2D photos into 3D virtual objects; and the surreal nostalgia of Expanded Childhood by Sam Lawton, a slideshow of Lawton’s old family photos that he got DALL-E 2 to extend beyond their borders, letting him toy with the half-remembered details of old pictures. 

Lawton showed the images to his father and records his reaction in the film: “Something’s wrong. I don’t know what that is. Do I just not remember it?”

Fast and cheap

Artists are often the first to experiment with new technology. But the immediate future of generative video is being shaped by the advertising industry. Waymark made The Frost to explore how generative AI could be built into its products. The company makes video creation tools for businesses looking for a fast and cheap way to make commercials. Waymark is one of several startups, alongside firms such as Softcube and Vedia AI, that offer bespoke video ads for clients with just a few clicks.

Waymark’s current tech, launched at the start of the year, pulls together several different AI techniques, including large language models, image recognition, and speech synthesis, to generate a video ad on the fly. Waymark also drew on its large data set of non-AI-generated commercials created for previous customers. “We have hundreds of thousands of videos,” says CEO Alex Persky-Stern. “We’ve pulled the best of those and trained it on what a good video looks like.”

To use Waymark’s tool, which it offers as part of a tiered subscription service starting at $25 a month, users simply supply a business name and location. The tool starts by scraping that business’s websites and social media accounts for text and images. It then uses that data to generate a commercial, using OpenAI’s GPT-3 to write a script that is read aloud by a synthesized voice over selected images that highlight the business.

A slick minute-long commercial can be generated in seconds. Users can edit the result if they wish, tweaking the script, editing images, choosing a different voice, and so on. Waymark says that more than 100,000 people have used its tool so far. (You can watch one of Waymark’s AI-generated commercials here.)

The trouble is that not every business has a website or images to draw from, says Parker. “An accountant or a therapist might have no assets at all,” he says. 

Waymark’s next idea is to use generative AI to create images and video for businesses that don’t yet have any—or don’t want to use the ones they have. “That’s the thrust behind making The Frost,” says Parker. “Create a world, a vibe.”

The Frost has a vibe, for sure. But it is also janky. “It’s not a perfect medium yet by any means,” says Rubin. “It was a bit of a struggle to get certain things from DALL-E, like emotional responses in faces. But at other times, it delighted us. We’d be like, ‘Oh my God, this is magic happening before our eyes.’”

This hit-and-miss process will improve as the technology gets better. DALL-E 2, which Waymark used to make The Frost, was released just a year ago. Video generation tools that generate short clips have only been around for a few months.  

The most revolutionary aspect of the technology is being able to generate new shots whenever you want them, says Rubin: “With 15 minutes of trial and error, you get that shot you wanted that fits perfectly into a sequence.” He remembers cutting the film together and needing particular shots, like a close-up of a boot on a mountainside. With DALL-E, he could just call it up. “It’s mind-blowing,” he says. “That’s when it started to be a real eye-opening experience as a filmmaker.”

Chris Boyle, cofounder of Private Island, a London-based startup that makes short-form video, also recalls his first impressions of image-making models last year: “I had a moment of vertigo when I was like, ‘This is going to change everything.’”

Boyle and his team have made commercials for a range of global brands, including Bud Light, Nike, Uber, and Terry’s Chocolate, as well as short in-game videos for blockbuster titles such as Call of Duty.

Private Island has been using AI tools in postproduction for a few years but ramped up during the pandemic. “During lockdown we were very busy but couldn’t shoot in the same way we could before, so we started leaning a lot more into machine learning at that time,” says Boyle.

The company adopted a range of technologies that make postproduction and visual effects easier, such as creating 3D scenes from 2D images with NeRFs and using machine learning to rip motion-capture data from existing footage instead of collecting it from scratch.  

But generative AI is the new frontier. A couple of months ago, Private Island posted a spoof beer commercial on its Instagram account that was produced using Runway’s video-making model Gen-2 and Stability AI’s image-making model Stable Diffusion. It became a slow-burn viral hit. Called Synthetic Summer, the video shows a typical backyard party scene where young, carefree people kick back and sip their drinks in the sunshine. Except many of these people have gaping holes instead of mouths, their beer cans sink into their heads when they drink and the backyard is on fire. It’s a horror show.     

“You watch it initially—it’s just a very generic, middle-of-the-road Americana thing,” says Boyle. “But your hind brain or whatever is going, ‘Ugh all their faces are on backwards.’”

“We like to play around with using the medium itself to tell the story,” he says. “And I think ‘Synthetic Summer’ is a great example because the medium itself is so creepy. It kind of visualizes some of our fears about AI.”

Playing to its strengths

Is this the beginning of a new era of filmmaking? Current tools have a limited palette. The Frost and “Synthetic Summer” both play to the strengths of the tech that made them. The Frost is well suited to the creepy aesthetic of DALL-E 2. “Synthetic Summer” has many quick cuts, because video generation tools like Gen-2 produce only a few seconds of video at a time that then need to be stitched together. That works for a party scene where everything is chaotic, says Boyle. Private Island also looked at making a martial arts movie, where rapid cuts suit the subject.

This may mean that we will start to see generative video used in music videos and commercials. But beyond that, it’s not clear. Apart from experimental artists and a few brands, there aren’t many other people using it yet, says Mehdaoui.

The constant state of flux is also off-putting to potential clients. “I’ve spoken with many companies who seem interested but balk at putting resources into projects because the tech is changing so fast,” she says. Boyle says that many companies are also wary of the ongoing lawsuits around the use of copyrighted images in the data sets used to train models such as Stable Diffusion.  

Nobody knows for sure where this is headed, says Mehdaoui: “There are a lot of assumptions being thrown like darts right now, without a whole lot of nuanced consideration behind them.”

In the meantime, filmmakers are continuing to experiment with these new tools. Inspired by the work of Jake Olseon, who is a friend of hers, Mehdaoui is using generative AI tools to make a short documentary to help destigmatize opioid use disorder.

Waymark is planning a sequel to The Frost, but it is not sold on DALL-E 2. “I’d say it’s more of a ‘watch this space’ kind of thing,” says Persky-Stern. “When we do the next one, we’ll probably use some new tech and see what it can do.”

Private Island is experimenting with other films too. Earlier this year it made a video with a script produced by ChatGPT and images produced by Stable Diffusion. Now it is working on a film that’s a hybrid, with live-action performers wearing costumes designed by Stable Diffusion.

“We’re very into the aesthetic,” says Boyle, adding that it’s a change from the dominant imagery in digital culture, which has been reduced to the emoji and the glitch effect. “It’s very exciting to see where the new aesthetics will come from. Generative AI is like a broken mirror of us.”

From better agent coordination and local AI to interface building blocks and robotics: seven developments, what they change, and where the claims need caution.

TECH — November 14, 2026: corrections and clarifications

This edition covers announcements from November 11–14, not releases all made on November 14.

• Claude Projects: the announced workflow features are supported; the discussion's claims about precisely truncating or isolating internal context/state are not established by the announcement.
• Grok Bot: about 7% more usage, or up to about 15% on routine runs, are developer-reported expectations, not guarantees. The specific VRAM-management and KV-caching explanations in the discussion are unverified. The source identifies Sam Sokolin.
• Vercel UI SDK: accessibility primitives do not guarantee a flawless or compliant application. Complete applications still need testing. Broad claims about what AI coding models cannot do were commentary, not a measured evaluation.
• Magni/AllQuant: the tested reconstruction was slower than BF16 attention. This does not establish a universal rule that portable or quantized kernels are slower, nor verify the particular hardware explanation offered in the discussion.
• Yasakani: no 99% reduction in testing effort was measured. That percentage was an unsupported exaggeration.
• Praxis-1: the specific expert roles described were illustrative, not verified model internals. GPT-4's architecture was not publicly disclosed in the cited materials. Runway reported 46.2% success across 1,200 RoboLab-120 episodes; the discussion's detailed test characterization and zero-/few-shot claim were not established by our sources. Open robotics models predate this release. Training-cost estimates and claims of very cheap, fast adaptation were unverified, not measured results.

text:
On Father's Day weekend in 1969, the men of the Martin family went camping in the Great Smoky Mountains.

It was a family tradition. Grandfather, father, sons. They'd hike up from Cades Cove to a high, grassy bald called Spence Field, right on the Appalachian Trail.

This year, for the first time, six year old Dennis got to come along. He'd turn seven in less than a week. It was his first overnight trip.

On the afternoon of June 14, Dennis and some of the other boys came up with a plan. They'd sneak off into the brush and jump out to scare the grown ups.

The boys split up and hid.

Dennis was wearing a red shirt. His family watched him disappear behind the bushes.

The other boys popped out. Dennis didn't.

His father started calling his name. Then searching. Then running down the trail.

Within minutes, a little boy had vanished.

That night, about three inches of rain hammered the mountains. Wind wailed across the field. Fog rolled in for days.

What came next was the largest search in the history of the park.

Around 1,400 people. Park rangers. FBI agents. The National Guard. Bloodhounds. Army helicopters. Boy Scouts. Volunteers from all over.

And Green Berets.

Special Forces soldiers from Fort Bragg happened to be training nearby. At one point, 71 of them joined the hunt. They lived in the mountains, combing the steep, overgrown ridges, eating rattlesnakes they came across while they searched.

Spence Field turned into a military base camp. Landing zones were cut out of the forest for helicopters.

They covered more than 50 square miles.

They found nothing. Not a shoe. Not a scrap of red cloth.

By the end of June, the active search was called off. It officially closed that September.

His father offered a $5,000 reward. No one ever collected it.

In 1985, a ginseng hunter said he'd found a child size skeleton below Spence Field, near an uprooted tree. Searchers went back. They found nothing.

Over the years, the story attracted wild theories. Bears. Kidnappers. Even rumors that the Green Berets were really there hunting something else.

The truth is simpler, and somehow worse. With all those people, all those soldiers, all those dogs, nobody could find one little boy.

Dennis Martin would be 64 years old now.

What happened to him in those few minutes on that mountain?

text:
🌿 THE MANDRAKE: MACHIAVELLI'S COMEDY OF POWER (c. 1518) • Play Review 🎧
"One night in Florence, a fox's comedy, and the man behind The Prince."

"Di cosa nasce cosa, e il tempo la governa."
One thing leads to another, and time does the steering. 
— Callimaco, Act I, Scene 1

✍️ By 3 Star Media — The BX Files, on the author of The Prince and the Discourses on Livy 🏇💨
▸ ▸ ▸

Niccolò Machiavelli wrote a comedy about a lover, a lawyer, a mother, a friar and a fixer, and every one of them walks away with what they wanted. The only one whose no never counts is the woman the whole plan is about.

📍 SNAPSHOT

🇫🇷 Callimaco, a rich young Florentine who has spent most of his life in Paris, heard a friend there praise the beauty of Lucrezia, wife of the lawyer Messer Nicia. He came home to Florence to see her and found her lovelier than her reputation. A month later, when the play's single day begins, he is desperate.

🍷 Ligurio, a one-time marriage broker turned freeloader, takes the job. He sees the opening at once: Nicia and Lucrezia have been married six years with no child, and Nicia wants an heir more than he wants anything.

🧪 Callimaco poses as a famous doctor from Paris, studies a urine sample, and prescribes a potion of mandrake root. It is the plant Rachel bargains for in Genesis 30, with a fertility reputation as old as that story. Then he adds the catch he invented: the first man to lie with Lucrezia after the dose will die within eight days.

🪤 The "doctor" has the answer to his own catch. Grab some young nobody off the street, put him in Lucrezia's bed for one night, and let him carry the poison away. Nicia agrees.

⛪ Lucrezia, devout and faithful, refuses. Her mother, Sostrata, and her confessor, Fra Timoteo, take turns on her until she gives way.

🎸 That night Callimaco plays the nobody, in a short tunic with a lute and his face twisted out of shape. The friar dresses as the doctor. Nicia himself helps bundle the "stranger" into his wife's room.

🔑 By morning Lucrezia knows exactly who was in her bed and why. Nicia, delighted with everyone, hands Callimaco and Ligurio a key to his house, and the friar waves the whole company into church.

🧭 INTERESTING ANGLES

🗣️ THE SERMON THAT SELLS A SIN

Before Ligurio asks the friar for anything real, he tests him. In Act III he offers Fra Timoteo three hundred ducats of Nicia's alms and a story about a young woman in a convent, four months pregnant, who needs a potion to end it. The friar hesitates for a moment. Then he agrees, in five words:

"Sia, col nome di Dio."
So be it, in the name of God.
— Fra Timoteo, Act III, Scene 4

The pregnant girl never existed. The test did its job. Ligurio now knows the price of the man Lucrezia trusts most, and in Act III, Scene 11, Timoteo earns it. He tells her the act is not the sin, because sin lives in the will and not in the body, and her will is only to please her husband and fill a seat in paradise.

"Quanto allo atto, che sia peccato, questo è una favola, perché la volontà è quella che pecca, non el corpo."
As for the act being a sin, that's a fairy tale, because it's the will that sins, not the body.
— Fra Timoteo, Act III, Scene 11

He even reaches for the Bible: Lot's daughters slept with their father, he says, and because their intention was good, they did not sin. It is the funniest scene in the play, and the darkest. Machiavelli gives the friar one more detail that tells you what he is selling.

On the morning after, Timoteo grumbles that his shrine once held five hundred votive offerings and now holds fewer than twenty. Business is down, and the man of God has found a new line of work.

🕯️ THE WOMAN WHOSE ANSWER COMES SECONDHAND

Strip away the laughter and the plot is this: a woman maneuvered into bed by every person she trusts. Her husband signs off on it. Her mother pushes. Her priest absolves it in advance.

Her lover's fixer runs the whole operation. Early on, alone on stage, Ligurio calls her wise, well-mannered and fit to govern a kingdom. The play then spends four acts keeping her from governing anything, until the last scene, when she finally sets terms of her own.

Her biggest speech comes in Act V, and we never hear it from her mouth. Callimaco reports it to Ligurio, which means even her answer reaches us through the man who deceived her.

"Poiché l'astuzia tua, la sciocchezza del mio marito, la semplicità di mia madre e la tristizia del mio confessoro mi hanno condutto a fare quello che mai per me medesima arei fatto, io voglio iudicare che venga da una celeste disposizione."
Since your cunning, my husband's stupidity, my mother's simple-mindedness and my confessor's wickedness have led me to do what I would never have done on my own, I choose to judge that it comes from heaven's design.
— Lucrezia, as Callimaco reports her words, Act V, Scene 4

Read that sentence slowly. She names all four of them, one by one, and gives each a verdict. Then she takes Callimaco as her lord, master and guide, and arranges for the two of them to meet at any hour without suspicion.

Some readers hear a woman turning a trap into a choice. Others hear a woman with no exit left, calling it heaven's will because nothing else is on offer. The text supports both readings, and it never lets us ask her directly.

🎭 THE PROLOGUE IS A CONFESSION

Machiavelli opens the comedy by apologizing for it, in verse. If this light matter seems unworthy of a man who wants to look wise and serious, he says, excuse him:

"con questi van pensieri / fare el suo tristo tempo più suave, / perch'altrove non have / dove voltare el viso."
With these idle thoughts he tries to make his miserable days a little sweeter, because he has nowhere else to turn his face.
— Prologue, La Mandragola

The next lines say he has been cut off from showing his worth in other work, and that his labors earn no reward. It reads as more than the usual apology. It sounds like the voice of a man the state threw out.

The same prologue also sets up the night's last joke. Lucrezia was deceived, the speaker tells the ladies in the audience, and he would like them to be deceived just the way she was. From the first minute, the audience is the final mark.

🔗 TIES

🏛️ THE MAN WHO HAD NOWHERE ELSE TO TURN

On the evening of December 10, 1513, a former diplomat on a small farm outside Florence sat down to tell a friend how he spent his days. He had been snaring thrushes with his own hands. At night he went into his study, took off the clothes he had worn in the mud, and put on courtly ones. Then, he wrote to Francesco Vettori, he entered the ancient courts of ancient men, asked them why they did what they did, and for four hours forgot every trouble.

In that same letter he mentions a little work he had put together. He called it De principatibus. We call it The Prince.

Months earlier he had been in a cell. Born in Florence on May 3, 1469, Machiavelli emerged from obscurity at 29, days after the city hanged and burned the friar Savonarola in May 1498, to run the republic's second chancery and serve the Ten, the body that ran its wars. In fourteen years in office he carried Florence's business to kings and popes.

He talked the republic's leader, Piero Soderini, into raising a militia of its own instead of renting mercenaries. It was not enough. In 1512 a Spanish army raised by Pope Julius II brought the republic down and the Medici back.

On February 19, 1513, a town crier read the order for his arrest at fifty places across the city. His name had turned up on a list connected to a plot against the Medici. He was jailed and tortured on the strappado, the rope that hauls a prisoner up by wrists tied behind his back and drops him.

No evidence of his direct involvement came to light. When Giovanni de' Medici became Pope Leo X in March 1513, an amnesty opened the cell door, and Machiavelli went home to the farm and the thrushes.

The rest of his life is the work. He wrote The Prince and the Discourses on Livy in exile, and neither was printed while he lived. He wrote The Art of War, published in 1521, one of the few of his books to reach print in his lifetime.

In 1520 the Medici commissioned his Florentine Histories, and he presented them to Pope Clement VII in 1525. He wrote comedies too. In October 1525 he signed a letter to his friend Francesco Guicciardini "historico, comico et tragico," historian, comic writer, tragic writer, as if he were drafting his own epitaph.

He died in Florence on June 21, 1527. He was buried in his family's chapel in Santa Croce in a grave the basilica's own curators describe as "of no particular distinction." In 1559 the Church's Index of forbidden books condemned every one of his works, this comedy included.

His marble monument did not arrive until 1787, carved by Innocenzo Spinazzi, with a Latin line beneath it: TANTO NOMINI NULLUM PAR ELOGIUM. No praise is equal to so great a name.

📜 A COMEDY WITH A MYSTERY BIRTHDAY

Nobody knows exactly when the play was written. The historian Sergio Bertelli called its dating one of the most difficult problems in Machiavelli scholarship.

The surest fixed point is a manuscript in Florence's Laurenziana library whose copy opens with the year 1519 and the words "Comedia facta p. niccholo machiavegli," a comedy made by Niccolò Machiavelli, in a book that also holds 149 sonnets by Lorenzo the Magnificent. The biographer Roberto Ridolfi went further, arguing it was written in early 1518 for the wedding of Lorenzo di Piero de' Medici, a dating many scholars now doubt, though the name is worth holding on to: Lorenzo di Piero is the man Machiavelli finally dedicated The Prince to.

⚠️ When the play first reached a stage is disputed, and the sources disagree.

One account places the first performance at a Florentine carnival that ended in February 1520, and a letter of 26 April 1520 has a correspondent telling Machiavelli he had spoken about the comedy to Pope Leo X. Then came Venice, February 13, 1522, in the convent of the Crosechieri, a night the diarist Marin Sanudo recorded and historians treat as exceptional, though one study credits the crowd's delight mostly to the actors. A comedy about a corrupt friar, staged in a convent: Machiavelli could not have written it better.

For the carnival of 1526, Guicciardini planned his own staging in Faenza, with the singer Barbera Salutati performing songs between the acts that Machiavelli offered to write for her. Whether that night ever happened, the record does not settle.

👑 THE PRINCE, SCENE BY SCENE

Read the comedy next to The Prince and the two books start finishing each other's sentences. What follows is our reading, not the author's stated plan.

The strongest case against it deserves a hearing first. Read on its own terms, the play is a classic five-act comedy in the Roman manner of Terence, with a debt to a tale from Boccaccio. One writer on it sets out the common objection, that apart from a few stray references to the Italian wars and the Church it appears to have little to say about politics, before arguing against it.

Our answer is that Machiavelli's politics were never only about states. Before Ligurio trusts the friar with the real request, he tests his price with a false one, the move of an envoy sounding out an ally before a treaty, a job Machiavelli did for Florence again and again across fourteen years.

Chapter XV is where Machiavelli announces his method. He will go after the effectual truth of things, not the imagination of them:

"andare drieto alla verità effettuale della cosa, che alla imaginazione di essa."
To go after the effectual truth of the thing rather than the imagined version of it.
— The Prince, Chapter XV

The Mandragola is that sentence turned into a cast list. Nobody on that stage behaves the way a sermon says people should. They behave the way people do, and the play keeps score.

Chapter XVIII gives the treatise its most famous animals. A ruler must be a fox to recognize the traps and a lion to frighten off the wolves, and he must be a great pretender and dissembler, "gran simulatore e dissimulatore." Nobody in this comedy plays the lion.

It is foxes from the first scene to the last. Ligurio wins without one threat or one blade, only by reading what each person wants and fears. The friar plays piety while pricing a sin.

Chapter VII tells the story of men who rise by fortune and other people's strength, with Cesare Borgia as the case. Callimaco is that kind of winner. He has money and desire.

Most of the ideas that work belong to Ligurio, and the decisive push belongs to the friar and the mother. He gets the prize the way Borgia got his state: on loan.

Chapter XXV holds the line most readers remember, and the one this comedy forces us to look at hardest. Fortune, Machiavelli writes, governs about half of what we do, and he judges it better to be bold than cautious:

"perché la fortuna è donna, ed è necessario, volendola tenere sotto, batterla e urtarla."
Because fortune is a woman, and if you want to keep her down, you have to beat her and shove her around.
— The Prince, Chapter XXV

Here the comedy puts a real woman where the metaphor stands. Callimaco is the bold young man, Lucrezia is the fortune he "wins," and her last speech hands the whole thing to heaven, a celestial design she says she cannot refuse. The treatise uses the image to make a point about ambition. The play lets us see what the image costs the person on the other end of it.

One more bridge runs to the Discourses on Livy. Livy's Lucretia, raped by a king's son, took her own life, and Rome threw out its kings. Machiavelli, writing about that history, is coolly unsentimental: if her case had not come, he says, another would have produced the same result, because the tyrant had already broken the city's laws.

His comedy borrows her name and reverses her story. Livy's Lucretia ends a monarchy. Machiavelli's Lucrezia ends with her lover holding a key to her husband's house.

📚 HIS WORKS, RANKED

Our ranking, weighing influence, depth and craft together. It is a judgment, not a scholarly consensus.

1️⃣ THE PRINCE, written 1513, printed 1532. The most famous and the most influential. Its full story is told above.

2️⃣ DISCOURSES ON LIVY, written over several years in the 1510s, printed 1531. His deepest political book: why republics thrive, rot and fall, built on Rome's history. The historian J. G. A. Pocock traced Florentine republican ideas, the Discourses among them, into Civil War England and the American Revolution in The Machiavellian Moment (1975), though not every historian accepts his account.

3️⃣ LA MANDRAGOLA, about 1518, certainly by 1519. His literary masterpiece, and the place where his ideas stop explaining and start moving.

4️⃣ THE ART OF WAR, printed 1521. A dialogue arguing that a free state needs its own citizen soldiers, not hired ones.

5️⃣ FLORENTINE HISTORIES, commissioned 1520, presented 1525, printed 1532. His history of his own city, written for the very family whose rise it examines.

6️⃣ CLIZIA, staged at a party at a villa outside Florence on January 13, 1525. His other surviving original comedy, built on an old Roman model, about an old man's foolish desire and a household that outwits him.

7️⃣ THE LIFE OF CASTRUCCIO CASTRACANI, 1520. A heavily embellished biography of a fourteenth-century warlord, where history and storytelling blur on purpose.

Beyond the seven, there is a short story about a devil who marries, Belfagor, verse histories of his own times called the Decennali, and a translation of the Roman comedy Andria. The man never stopped writing.

🎥 CRITICS

✍️ Thomas Babington Macaulay — writing in the Edinburgh Review in March 1827, Macaulay defended Machiavelli's character and then turned to the comedies. His verdict on this one: it "is superior to the best of Goldoni, and inferior only to the best of Molière." From the young Macaulay, weighing it against two masters of the stage, that is a crown.

✍️ Ronald L. Martinez — in "The Pharmacy of Machiavelli: Roman Lucretia in Mandragola," Renaissance Drama, 1983, Martinez reads the play closely against Livy. Livy's Lucretia becomes the sacrifice that founds a republic, he argues; Machiavelli's comedy founds something too, a small new community built on calculated private advantage and the urge to acquire.

✍️ Susan Behuniak-Long — in The Review of Politics, 1989, she takes on the play's central puzzle: an intelligent, virtuous wife who by the end agrees not only to adultery but to a plan that was supposed to kill a stranger. Her answer is provocative: "the real deception is that Lucrezia does not undergo a conversion." In her reading, Lucrezia was never as innocent as the others believed, and free will proves no match for Fortune.

💛 WHY THIS FEELS SO SPECIAL

Machiavelli spent his treatises telling princes how power works. In this comedy he stopped telling and showed us. Nobody draws a sword and nobody raises an army.

A fixer reads the people around him and finds the want or the fear in each one. By morning the whole household has rearranged itself around a lie.

What makes it last is that he refused to look away. The laughs are real and so is the cost, and much of the cost lands on Lucrezia.

The play ends at a church door, with a husband beaming, a friar waving everyone inside, and a lover holding a key. One thing led to another, just as Callimaco promised in the first scene, and time did the steering. Five centuries later, the comedy Machiavelli apologized for is still one of the clearest pictures we have of the man who wrote The Prince, watching people exactly as they are.

🎧 PRESS PLAY

The Mandrake Root (2008) is Malachi Bogdanov's first feature film, adapted by Bogdanov himself and produced by Simon M. Woods, Rosanna Castangia and Carlo Dessi as the first release of the European Drama Network. A UK and Italian crew shot it in 14 days in Sassari, Sardinia, on a budget of about 200,000 pounds, moving Machiavelli's Florence to a Sardinian city of the same era.

By the production's own account it opens with the play's prologue. It was nominated for Best Drama at the 2008 Royal Television Society Midlands awards, and its distributor now offers it remastered in its original HD.

🎭 Watch for Jason Nicoli as Callimaco, Chara Jackson as Lucrezia, Geoffrey Bateman as Nicia, Mike Rogers as Ligurio and Jonathan Owen as Fra Timoteo. Look for the friar's sermon and for Lucrezia's last scene. In the play, those are the two moments everything turns on.

text:
The Mesopotamian myth of Adapa, preserved on ancient cuneiform tablets.

Adapa was a wise human associated with the god Ea (Enki), who gave him extraordinary knowledge.

According to the story:
Adapa possessed wisdom beyond ordinary humans.
He understood the workings of the world.
He broke the wing of the South Wind when it overturned his boat.
He was summoned before the sky god Anu to answer for his actions.
But here's the extraordinary part.

When Adapa appeared before Anu, he was offered the food and water of life.

That was potentially his opportunity to become immortal.

He refused.

Why?

Ea had warned him not to eat or drink anything offered in heaven because he believed it would bring death.

Adapa obeyed his teacher and unknowingly turned down immortality.

The mystery: Did humanity lose immortality because of disobedience, or because someone gave humanity incorrect information?

There is an interesting parallel with Genesis: knowledge, divine boundaries, and the loss of access to eternal life.

Hi there River to the sea dude...here's your kool aid:
📷📷📷20 sourcesArab states have largely refused full permanent integration or mass acceptance of Palestinian refugees for a combination of political, security, demographic, and historical reasons that have been consistent since 1948.Political leverage and the “right of return”
Most Arab governments have treated the refugee issue as a political instrument against Israel. Permanent resettlement or widespread citizenship would reduce pressure for the “right of return” to former homes inside Israel (a demand linked to UNGA Resolution 194). Host countries and the Palestinian leadership have long argued that integration would amount to abandoning that claim and accepting the outcome of the 1948 war. This stance has kept large numbers of Palestinians in a prolonged refugee status under UNRWA rather than resolving it through local absorption.⁠JnsSecurity and past experience
Palestinian armed groups have repeatedly created “states within states” that threatened host regimes:In Jordan, the PLO and fedayeen established autonomous control in refugee camps in the late 1960s. This culminated in Black September (1970–71), a civil conflict in which the Jordanian army fought the PLO, expelled most of its fighters, and killed thousands. The PLO then relocated to Lebanon.⁠Wikipedia
In Lebanon, the PLO’s presence contributed to the outbreak and dynamics of the Lebanese Civil War (1975–1990) and drew Israeli interventions.
Egypt and others have cited risks of militant infiltration (especially from Gaza) and the potential for radical groups to destabilize Sinai or other areas.
These experiences created lasting reluctance to accept large additional numbers of Palestinians who might bring armed factions or political challenges.Demographic and domestic political concerns
Lebanon: Citizenship is tightly restricted to preserve the delicate sectarian balance (Christian, Sunni, Shia, Druze). Granting citizenship to large numbers of (mostly Sunni) Palestinians would shift that balance, so most remain without citizenship despite decades of residence.⁠Jns
Jordan: It is the partial exception. It granted citizenship to most 1948 West Bank refugees and has a large population of Palestinian origin. However, it has limited further absorption, revoked some citizenships after its 1988 disengagement from the West Bank, and has firmly rejected proposals for mass relocation from Gaza.
Other states (Syria, Gulf countries, Egypt) have generally offered limited rights or temporary residence while avoiding full naturalization that would end the distinct Palestinian status.
Recent statements
Egypt and Jordan (among others) have repeatedly and publicly rejected proposals to take large numbers of Gazans, citing the same combination of security risks, demographic pressures, opposition to permanent displacement, and the desire to keep Palestinians “on their land” in the context of a two-state https://t.co/A2a6rcD1C4 short, the pattern is driven more by Arab states’ own political calculations, security interests, and internal stability concerns than by a simple failure of solidarity. Jordan’s partial integration is the main exception; most others have prioritized keeping the refugee issue open and avoiding the risks of full absorption.

The allocation of Springs and Stuhm farms raised eyebrows, resulting in a complaint being filed with ZACC.
“I write on behalf of the Stuhm Residents’ Association, of which I’m secretary and also a beneficiary of Stand Number 1332. We wish to formally report what we strongly believe to be a case of high-level public sector corruption involving the illegal allocation of large tracts of public land,” wrote the association’s secretary Trevor Saruwaka in a letter dated July 17, 2025, titled Report of Suspected Corruption – Irregular Allocation of 903.072 Hectares of Public Land by Minister Daniel Garwe to Marimba Residential Properties (Pvt) Ltd.
Circumstances around the Aspindale Park land that Rautenbach had attempted to seize are that the property was acquired by the State for housing cooperatives under the National Housing Delivery Programme. 
The government allocated the land to housing cooperatives, who were then surprised when Rautenbach emerged claiming he owned the land.
The cooperatives then approached the High Court, which ruled in their favour. 
The March 25, 2019 ruling therefore raises serious questions about the justification for compensating Rautenbach with alternative land, given the court’s findings concerning ownership of the Aspindale land.
The other bone of contention is the scale of the compensation, which has also attracted criticism.
Approximately 180 hectares of urban land in Aspindale were used as the basis for allocating more than 1,080 hectares at Springs and Stuhm farms, raising questions about the valuations and methodology used to determine the compensation.
The ruling therefore raised questions about the justification for compensating Rautenbach with alternative land, given the court’s findings concerning ownership of the Aspindale properties.
The scale of the proposed compensation has also attracted criticism.
Approximately 180 hectares of urban land in Aspindale were used as the basis for allocating more than 1,080 hectares at Springs and Stuhm farms, raising questions about the valuations and methodology used to determine the compensation.
The proposed reallocation threatens the interests of farmers and war veterans who have occupied, developed and relied on the properties for more than two decades. 
Some have argued that it goes against the principles of the war of liberation and the land reform programme.
In July 2025, Dembure also ruled against the withdrawal of offer letters, describing the minister’s decision as irrational and unreasonable.
Army welfare crisis highlights importance of Springs Farm project
This is against a background where Defence Minister Oppah Muchinguri-Kashiri has raised serious concerns over the welfare of soldiers, revealing that members of the military are borrowing ceremonial uniforms, facing an accommodation crisis and experiencing restricted access to water and electricity as Treasury fails to release funds on time.
She said the ministry is required to provide three sets of uniforms per soldier but has managed only two. 
The budget for uniforms stands at US$620 million against a bid of ZiG4 billion, representing approximately 25 percent of requirements.
“Currently the ministry is failing to meet the requirement for ceremonial uniforms. Many have to borrow. This does not give us the dignity we deserve,” Muchinguri-Kashiri said.
The minister also revealed that the flagship Manyame Hospital, which is approximately 97% complete and has a capacity of 149 beds, has remained uncommissioned for two years because the Army has been unable to equip it. 
The contractor has reportedly moved off site due to non-payment.
“This structure is ready and will not only cater for soldiers but our general public. We would save a lot of US dollars if we got this hospital operational,” she said, noting that military officers were currently being referred to India for treatment.

IFS (P) 2025–27 Course | Thematic Tour-III | 14 November 2026
Venue: Mudumalai Tiger Reserve

As part of Thematic Tour-III, Officer Trainees (OTs) visited the Theppakadu Elephant Camp, where they learned about the feeding, grazing routines, and management of captive kumki elephants. The session covered weight-based nutritional supplements, including ragi, horse gram, rice, jaggery, and sugarcane, along with the crucial role of mahouts and cavadies in elephant care and training.

A subsequent safari provided insights into the local landscape, forest types, flora, and fauna, highlighting their significance in effective habitat management.

In the afternoon, OTs interacted with the Deputy Director of Mudumalai Tiger Reserve on ground-level conservation practices, including the capture-recapture method for tiger and leopard identification. Discussions also covered initiatives such as highway plastic collection, dedicated patrol units, aerial bundled cables to prevent wildlife electrocution, carcass monitoring, and synchronised tri-state vulture population estimation.

The visit offered valuable field-level exposure to captive elephant management, tiger habitat conservation, wildlife-friendly infrastructure, responsible ecotourism, and the practical aspects of protected area administration.

RICE: India’s Price Advantage Is Becoming Increasingly Formidable

Global rice production remains unchanged, but lower consumption is pushing projected ending stocks higher. Global trade forecasts have been revised downward, with reduced exports from India.

Yet the biggest competitive advantage in the global rice market remains India’s pricing.

Export prices have surged across all major origins since the October WASDE:

🇺🇸 US: $680/ton (+$41)
🇺🇾 Uruguay: $610/ton (+$19)
🇹🇭 Thailand: $497/ton (+$31)
🇻🇳 Vietnam: $439/ton (+$24)
🇵🇰 Pakistan: $411/ton (+$15)
🇮🇳 India: $389/ton (+$5)

India is now cheaper than:
• US by $291/ton
• Uruguay by $221/ton
• Thailand by $108/ton
• Vietnam by $50/ton
• Pakistan by $22/ton

This is not a marginal pricing advantage. India is undercutting Thailand by nearly 22% and the US by 43%.

While competing origins are witnessing sharp price appreciation, Indian offers have risen just $5/ton.

The message for global buyers is clear: India remains the benchmark for competitive rice sourcing. Unless rival exporters significantly narrow this price gap, India will retain a powerful advantage in capturing price-sensitive demand.

text:
My uncle William is much younger than his wife, and for years, everyone in our family wondered why he stayed married to her.

Aunt Corinne treated him like a child.

At family lunches, she finished his sentences. If he offered an opinion, she sighed loudly. If he spent money on anything, she demanded the receipt and read it aloud to the table.

One Saturday, she looked at him over the rice and said, “You still think like a schoolboy, William. If I let you decide anything, we would be sleeping on the street.”

Nobody spoke.

My cousin Felix was the only one who stepped in.

 “Leave him alone, Auntie. He’s trying his best.”       ￼

OPEN HEAVENS DEVOTIONAL 

DATE: SUNDAY NOVEMBER 15TH 2026.

TOPIC: BAPTISED WITH FIRE

MEMORISE
I indeed baptize you with water unto repentance: but he that cometh after me is mightier than I, whose shoes I am not worthy to bear: he shall baptize you with the Holy Ghost, and with fire: - (Matthew 3:11)

BIBLE READING: MALACHI 3:1-4 (KJV)

1 Behold, I will send my messenger, and he shall prepare the way before me: and the Lord, whom ye seek, shall suddenly come to his temple, even the messenger of the covenant, whom ye delight in: behold, he shall come, saith the Lord of hosts.

2 But who may abide the day of his coming? and who shall stand when he appeareth? for he is like a refiner's fire, and like fullers' soap:

3 And he shall sit as a refiner and purifier of silver: and he shall purify the sons of Levi, and purge them as gold and silver, that they may offer unto the Lord an offering in righteousness.

4 Then shall the offering of Judah and Jerusalem be pleasant unto the Lord, as in the days of old, and as in former years.

MESSAGE

Anyone whom God wants to use as His vessel must be baptised, note not only with the Holy Ghost, but also with fire. Fire has many functions, one of which is that it purifies. In Isaiah 6:5, after Isaiah realised how unclean he was, the angel of the Lord used a live coal to touch his lips and said, "This hath touched thy lips; and thine iniquity is taken away, and thy sin purged" (Isaiah 6:6-7). Isaiah received a baptism of fire that cleansed him and made him a useful and worthy vessel to carry out God's assignment.

Before the apostles were sent out to proclaim the gospel of Christ around the world, Jesus instructed them to wait for the baptism of the Holy Ghost, as we see in Acts 1:4-5:

And, being assembled together with them, commanded them that they should not depart from Jerusalem, but wait for the promise of the Father, which, saith he, ye have heard of me. For John truly baptized with water; but ye shall be baptized with the Holy Ghost not many days hence.

They obeyed this instruction, and they were baptised by the Holy Spirit and fire in Acts 2. This encounter marked the beginning of their exploits for Jesus, starting with Peter's sermon, which God used to save about 3,000 souls that same day. If you want to be a worthy vessel in God's hands, you must allow Him to set you apart and baptise you with the Holy Ghost and fire.

Beloved, God is still looking for vessels He can purify with fire and put to use in His vineyard. Today's Bible reading tells us that God is a refiner and purifier of those who will serve Him in righteousness. Until the Lord refines you with His fire, your offering cannot be pleasant to Him. Offering in this context means your life. Gold in its raw state is not beautiful, but after it has been purified by fire, it becomes precious. This is why it is called a precious metal. If you don't want to remain a common vessel in God's vineyard, ask Him to visit you with His fire. Allow His fire to take away any filth in your life that will not allow you to be useful and precious in His sight. If you really want to be a useful vessel for God, pray today's prayer point with all your heart. 

PRAYER POINT
Father, I am ready; please, let Your fire fall on me.

text:
Here's a breakdown how the early Church Fathers and New Testament texts specifically framed the Church as the continuation of Israel.

From an Orthodox perspective, the Church is not a "Plan B" or a separate Gentile entity running parallel to Israel; it is the historical continuation, restoration, and fulfillment of Israel in the Messiah. Both the New Testament apostles and the earliest Church Fathers were unanimous on this point, arguing directly from the Hebrew Scriptures that covenant membership was always defined by faithfulness to God rather than mere physical descent.

1. The New Testament Foundation
The apostles systematically dismantled the idea of a dual-covenant system by redefining Israel around Christ Himself.

Christ as the True Israel:
In Matthew 2:15, the Evangelist applies Hosea 11:1 ("Out of Egypt I called my son") directly to Jesus. Throughout the Gospels, Jesus recapitulates Israel's history—passing through the waters (baptism), enduring forty days in the wilderness, and appointing twelve apostles (Luke 22:30) specifically to reconstitute the twelve tribes of Israel.

The Olive Tree (Romans 9–11):
St. Paul explicitly states that "not all who are descended from Israel belong to Israel" (Romans 9:6). In Romans 11, he uses the image of a single cultivated olive tree: unbelieving branches were broken off, and believing Gentiles were grafted into the existing root of Israel. There is only one tree, not two.

Children of Abraham by Faith (Galatians 3 & 6):
Paul argues that God's promises were made to Abraham and his singular "offspring"—Christ (Galatians 3:16). Therefore, "if you are Christ’s, then you are Abraham’s offspring, heirs according to promise" (Galatians 3:29), concluding his epistle by calling the Church "the Israel of God" (Galatians 6:16).

Old Covenant Titles Transferred (1 Peter 2:9):
St. Peter takes the exact covenant titles bestowed upon Israel at Mount Sinai in Exodus 19:5–6 and applies them directly to the Church: "a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for his own possession."

The Synagogue of Satan (Revelation 2:9 & 3:9):
St. John writes to the churches in Smyrna and Philadelphia regarding those "who say that they are Jews and are not," establishing that rejecting the Messiah forfeits the spiritual claim to the covenant name.

In St. Paul's agricultural metaphor, wild Gentile branches do not form a separate orchard; they draw their life directly from the ancient patriarchs' rootstock.

2. The Early Church Fathers
Within a single generation of the apostles, the Fathers defended this exact ecclesiology against both Roman pagans and non-Christian Jewish polemicists, leaving zero room for modern dispensationalist distinctions.

St. Justin Martyr c. 160 AD Dialogue with Trypho
Explicitly calls the Church "the true spiritual Israel" and descendants of Judah, Jacob, Isaac, and Abraham (Ch. 11).

St. Irenaeus of Lyons c. 180 AD Against Heresies
Teaches that the Church is the true seed of Abraham, inheriting the promises because the patriarchs rejoiced to see Christ's day (Book 4.8).

Tertullian c. 200 AD An Answer to the Jews Argues from Rebecca's twins (Esau and Jacob) that the "older" people (Israel according to the flesh) now serve the "younger" people (the Church).

St. Cyprian of Carthage c. 250 AD Three Books of Testimonies
Compiles dozens of Old Testament prophecies demonstrating that the Gentiles were foretold to inherit the vineyard and covenant of Israel.

Eusebius of Caesarea c. 324 AD Church History
Traces the Church back to Abraham and the righteous pre-Mosaic patriarchs, showing Christianity is the original religion of Israel restored.

St. John Chrysostom c. 387 AD Homilies on Galatians
Emphasizes that the "Israel of God" consists of those who walk by the rule of the Cross, whether Jew or Gentile by birth.

Key Patristic Arguments Against Sola Scriptura Proof-Texting
When modern Christian Zionists cite Old Testament land or blessing promises as unfulfilled guarantees for a modern secular state, they bypass how the Fathers read Scripture:

Typology and Fulfillment: The Fathers read the Old Testament Christologically. The earthly Jerusalem, the Temple, and the land of Canaan were types (foreshadowings) pointing toward the Heavenly Jerusalem (Hebrews 12:22), the Body of Christ as the true Temple (John 2:21), and the entire cosmos redeemed in the Resurrection.

The "Remnant" Theology:
Drawing on Isaiah 10:22 and Romans 11:5, the Fathers pointed out that Israel was never completely cast off; rather, the faithful remnant of Israel—the Virgin Mary, the Twelve Apostles, the 3,000 baptized at Pentecost—became the foundation stones of the Church, into which the nations were then gathered.

Eucharistic Continuity:
Even the earliest liturgical manuals, such as the Didache (late 1st century), apply Malachi 1:11's prophecy of a "pure sacrifice" offered by the Gentiles directly to the Christian Eucharist, demonstrating that the Church understood itself from day one as offering the true, fulfilled worship of Israel.

The Synagogue of Satan (Revelation 2:9 & 3:9):
St. John writes to the churches in Smyrna and Philadelphia regarding those "who say that they are Jews and are not," establishing that rejecting the Messiah forfeits the spiritual claim to the covenant name.

In St. Paul's agricultural metaphor, wild Gentile branches do not form a separate orchard; they draw their life directly from the ancient patriarchs' rootstock.

2. The Early Church Fathers
Within a single generation of the apostles, the Fathers defended this exact ecclesiology against both Roman pagans and non-Christian Jewish polemicists, leaving zero room for modern dispensationalist distinctions.

St. Justin Martyr c. 160 AD Dialogue with Trypho
Explicitly calls the Church "the true spiritual Israel" and descendants of Judah, Jacob, Isaac, and Abraham (Ch. 11).

St. Irenaeus of Lyons c. 180 AD Against Heresies
Teaches that the Church is the true seed of Abraham, inheriting the promises because the patriarchs rejoiced to see Christ's day (Book 4.8).

Tertullian c. 200 AD An Answer to the Jews 
Argues from Rebecca's twins (Esau and Jacob) that the "older" people (Israel according to the flesh) now serve the "younger" people (the Church).

St. Cyprian of Carthage c. 250 AD Three Books of Testimonies
Compiles dozens of Old Testament prophecies demonstrating that the Gentiles were foretold to inherit the vineyard and covenant of Israel.

Eusebius of Caesarea c. 324 AD Church History
Traces the Church back to Abraham and the righteous pre-Mosaic patriarchs, showing Christianity is the original religion of Israel restored.

St. John Chrysostom c. 387 AD Homilies on Galatians
Emphasizes that the "Israel of God" consists of those who walk by the rule of the Cross, whether Jew or Gentile by birth.

Key Patristic Arguments Against Sola Scriptura Proof-Texting

When modern Christian Zionists cite Old Testament land or blessing promises as unfulfilled guarantees for a modern secular state, they bypass how the Fathers read Scripture:

Typology and Fulfillment: The Fathers read the Old Testament Christologically. The earthly Jerusalem, the Temple, and the land of Canaan were types (foreshadowings) pointing toward the Heavenly Jerusalem (Hebrews 12:22), the Body of Christ as the true Temple (John 2:21), and the entire cosmos redeemed in the Resurrection.

The "Remnant" Theology:
Drawing on Isaiah 10:22 and Romans 11:5, the Fathers pointed out that Israel was never completely cast off; rather, the faithful remnant of Israel—the Virgin Mary, the Twelve Apostles, the 3,000 baptized at Pentecost—became the foundation stones of the Church, into which the nations were then gathered.

Eucharistic Continuity:
Even the earliest liturgical manuals, such as the Didache (late 1st century), apply Malachi 1:11's prophecy of a "pure sacrifice" offered by the Gentiles directly to the Christian Eucharist, demonstrating that the Church understood itself from day one as offering the true, fulfilled worship of Israel.

"Lol people still believe the Church is a physical building?!"

I get this response from "Churchless Christians" a lot, and it's such an odd departure from the faith.

It's almost always an excuse for loner Christianity.. Avoiding spiritual accountability, avoiding confession, and refusing to obey Hebrews 10:25 "not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together"

The Church is one, indivisible, theanthropic (divine-human) reality. Just like Jesus Christ Himself.. Think about the Incarnation as the exact model for the Church.

Christ is both fully God (invisible, spiritual) and fully Man (visible, physical flesh). To say "I believe in Jesus, just not His physical body" is the ancient heresy of Gnosticism/Docetism.

The Church is the Body of Christ. Just like Christ, the Church has an invisible, heavenly dimension (the Triumphant Church of the Saints and Angels, united by the Holy Spirit) ANDDDD a concrete, visible, physical dimension on earth (real baptized people, real ordained bishops and priests, real physical bread and wine, and consecrated temples where the Eucharist is offered).

The very Greek word for Church, Ekklesia, literally means "a physical assembly called out together". You can't obey Hebrews 10:25 by sitting alone on your phone claiming to be part of an "invisible" church. 

You cannot baptize someone invisibly, you need physical water and a priest. You cannot receive the Body and Blood of Christ invisibly, you need a physical altar, physical bread, and physical wine. And St. Paul explicitly warns in 1 Corinthians 11:29 that those who fail to discern the physical Body of the Lord in the Eucharist bring judgment on themselves.

In the Old Testament, God commanded the building of a physical Tabernacle and Temple filled with sacred vessels, incense, and liturgical worship, patterned directly after heaven. Early Christians immediately consecrated physical house churches (like the 3rd century Dura-Europos church, which already had a baptistery, an altar area, and icons painted on the walls) and built glorious temples the moment Roman persecution ended.

🇮🇷 Iranian Discombobulator!

Anthony Aguilar noticed something unusual about the way US Central Command described its latest strikes on Iran.

Normally, when CENTCOM reports striking a target on Qeshm Island, Bandar Abbas, Jask, or Sarik, its statements are quite specific. They refer to a missile launcher or a missile.

This time, however, CENTCOM used a different word: "device."

That caught Aguilar's attention. In military reporting, words matter, particularly when describing battle damage. If the target was a missile launcher, why not call it one? If it was a missile, why not say so? What exactly had the US military struck?

Aguilar believes the answer may lie in a capability Iran has been developing.

Iran operates small submarines, including the Ghadir and Fatah classes, under a shared area of responsibility between the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and the Iranian Navy. These submarines are much smaller than those operated by the United States, Israel, or NATO countries. But their size does not make them insignificant. They can carry ballistic missiles.

Operating these submarines throughout the Strait of Hormuz presents challenges. The narrow waterway is crowded with ships, mines, and US surveillance drones, leaving limited room to maneuver or remain concealed.

But the submarines offer Iran something else: a ballistic missile capability.

According to Aguilar, Iran has adapted that capability for use on land. Rather than relying on the submarines themselves to launch the missiles, Iran has modified the launch systems so they can operate from mobile land-based platforms.

He points to Russian equipment, including older K10 systems associated with the S-400 family, as part of the technology involved in these modifications. The idea is to adapt existing components so missiles can be launched through tube-based systems rather than conventional launch rails.

The result is a different way of deploying a capability Iran already possesses.

Aguilar says the missiles involved are JK-2 ballistic missiles, associated with the coastal port city of Jask. Iran originally configured these missiles for its Ghadir and Fatah mini-submarines.

Now, he believes Iran has adapted the same technology for mobile land-based use.

That may explain why the recent US strikes have attracted his attention.

When American forces struck targets on Qeshm Island, the objects visible in the available imagery appeared to resemble missile systems. But they did not look like conventional missile launchers.

And that brings us back to CENTCOM's choice of words.

Rather than identifying the targets as missiles or launchers, the US military described them as devices.

Aguilar's interpretation is that the United States may be encountering a configuration it has not previously seen in this form.

The technology itself is not necessarily new. Iran has combined existing systems and modified their configuration to create a different operational capability.

As Aguilar explains, it is like taking parts from an old Toyota and an old Nissan and combining them to build something that has never existed in quite that form before.

The underlying capability remains the same. The way it is deployed has changed.

And that could be what makes Iran's latest missile configuration particularly significant.

text:
Rats seem to feel regret.

In 2014, Adam Steiner and David Redish at the University of Minnesota built a maze called "Restaurant Row". Rats went past four "restaurants", each offering a different flavour of food. At each one, a tone told the rat how long it would have to wait.

Sometimes a rat skipped a good deal, then found a much worse one at the next restaurant. In those moments, the rats looked back at the restaurant they had passed. Brain recordings showed that their brains were replaying the option they had missed.

After these moments, the rats were more likely to accept the next offer, even a worse one, and ate faster.

The study was published in Nature Neuroscience. The researchers say it is the first time regret has been seen in rats, a feeling we thought only humans had.

text:
Launch costs are about to get absolutely insane.

Over the past couple of days at Starbase, watching Starship and talking with investors and space founders, I heard and read some fascinating perspectives. Here's a sum up:

@pronounced_kyle said, Starship, carrying 100 tons of payload, costs roughly $1 million in propellant per launch. With full reusability, that translates to a fuel cost of just $10/kg.

Suddenly, @elonmusk ’s target of $100/kg doesn’t sound particularly ambitious.

Fun fact: shipping a computer from California to Australia by air could eventually cost more than sending it into space.

@PhilipJohnston The founder of @Starcloud_ , the orbital data center company, said SpaceX charging a premium is not a big problem. As long as the price stays around $500/kg, or five times the target cost, he’s happy with it. Falcon 9 currently charges roughly three times its cost.

When I met the Starcloud team at the NYSE Space Summit in May, the company was valued at around $1 billion. Now it’s worth $2.3 billion.

He’s even considering paying extra to charter entire Falcon 9 launches next year. Launch capacity is becoming a serious bottleneck.

@zebulgar offered a very different perspective. He said that ever since he started working on Varda, Falcon 9’s commercial launch price hasn’t gone down. So whenever he sees people talking about how many times Starship will reduce launch costs, he finds it amusing.

In a market dominated by a single player, what makes you think you have any pricing power?

Cost is cost. Price is price.

@ycombinator approached it from another angle: What we should really be thinking about is what becomes commercially viable in space when launch costs fall by 100x.

And we should start building those companies today, rather than waiting for launch prices to come down.

In fact, this is the very first topic in YC’s latest Requests for Startups.

But launch economics are only half the story. The satellites themselves are getting dramatically better, too.

On this flight alone, Starship deployed 26 @Starlink V3 satellites, each with a design capacity of 1 Tbps, for a combined 26 Tbps.

And eventually, a fully loaded Starship could deploy 60 V3 satellites in one flight, delivering 60 Tbps of additional capacity.

Higher payload capacity.
Lower launch costs.
More powerful satellites.
Higher launch frequency.

These four variables don’t add up. They multiply.

When the cost of accessing space falls by 100x, it won’t just transform the aerospace industry. It will redefine the entire space economy.

text:
🏘️ EVER WONDER WHO HAMMOND AVENUE IN PRINCE GEORGE WAS NAMED AFTER?

There's a name on a Prince George street sign that comes with quite a story.

George J. Hammond was a land speculator who arrived on the local scene in 1909 with enormous ambitions for Fort George.

He envisioned a bustling metropolis that could rival Vancouver, Seattle and Winnipeg. Building lots were advertised for $100, with just $10 down and $10 a month.

But Hammond's past was considerably less impressive than his promises.

Before coming to British Columbia, he'd been involved in questionable stock-market operations in the United States, faced allegations of defrauding investors and had several encounters with the law.

Then came his battle with the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway.

Hammond desperately wanted the railway station near his Fort George development. He offered the railway $200,000 to build its station nearby, but the railway had other plans.

The dispute dragged on for years.

Meanwhile, the new Prince George townsite developed, businesses relocated and Hammond's grand ambitions gradually faded.

He eventually left British Columbia and died in California in 1950.

Yet his name remains part of Prince George.

Hammond Avenue is named after the man whose dream of building a great northern metropolis became tangled in land speculation, newspaper feuds and railway politics.

It's a reminder that the names on our streets don't always tell the whole story about the people behind them.

How many times have you travelled along Hammond Avenue without knowing the history behind the name?

📚 Sources: The Notorious Georges: Crime and Community in British Columbia's Northern Interior, 1909–25, Jonathan Swainger, UBC Press, 2023, and the local street-name history shown in the accompanying photograph.

text:
At seven in the morning on November 15, 1864, William Tecumseh Sherman paused on a hill just outside Atlanta and looked back at his city. Behind him lay "Atlanta, smouldering and in ruins, the black smoke rising high in air, and hanging like a pall over the ruined city." Ahead of him: three hundred miles of Georgia, no supply lines, and an army that had to eat its way through the South. Some band struck up "John Brown's Body" by accident; the men caught it up, and Sherman wrote later that he never heard "Glory, glory, hallelujah!" sung with more spirit — or in better harmony of time and place.

**THE SETUP:**

Atlanta had fallen on September 2. For two and a half months after that, Sherman sat inside the city deciding what to do next. His enemy made the choice for him: Confederate General Hood took most of Georgia's army north into Tennessee chasing him, and Sherman welcomed it — "If he will go to the Ohio River, I'll give him rations." What was left in his path never grew past 13,000 effective men: Wheeler's cavalry and a militia made up largely of boys and old men.

Sherman and Grant believed the war would end only if the Confederacy's strategic capacity for warfare could be decisively broken — so Sherman planned an operation that has been compared to the chevauchée of medieval European warfare, a raid deep into enemy country with no supply lines at all. March straight through Georgia to the coast at Savannah, living off the land. Lincoln had doubts about it; Grant had doubts too. On November 2, Grant sent a telegram with four words: "Go as you propose."

The army that left Atlanta numbered about 62,000 men — 55,000 infantry, 5,000 cavalry, and 2,000 artillerymen manning 64 guns. Eighty percent were veterans of the Western campaigns; doctors had examined every man and left behind one percent as too weak or sick. Sherman wanted only the "best fighting material." Each regiment carried one wagon and one ambulance; each company one pack mule for its officers' baggage. That was the whole supply train.

**THE ORDERS:**

The army would be out of touch with the North throughout the campaign, so Sherman issued Special Field Orders No. 120 — a short document that became famous: "The army will forage liberally on the country during the march." Each brigade organized its own foraging parties to gather corn, meat, vegetables, whatever was needed; wagons were to keep at least ten days' provisions and three days' forage. Soldiers must not enter the dwellings of the inhabitants — but they could take horses, mules, and wagons from "the rich."

The men carried twenty days of rations before that ran out and Georgia had to feed them. The foragers got a nickname: bummers. And Sherman had planned the route with something no general had used before — livestock and crop data from the 1860 United States census, so the army would march through the areas where he believed they could forage most effectively.

**THE MARCH:**

The two wings marched south in separate columns: Howard's Army of the Tennessee on the right, Slocum's Army of Georgia on the left, Kilpatrick's cavalry between them. The Confederates couldn't tell whether Sherman was heading for Macon, Augusta, or Savannah — and that uncertainty was part of the plan.

At Lovejoy's Station, Wheeler's militia attacked for hours — badly coordinated — and withdrew with about 1,100 casualties, including 600 prisoners, against Union losses of 100. On November 23, Slocum took Milledgeville, the state capital; Governor Joseph Brown and the legislature fled in a hurry, and Sherman's men held a mock legislative session in the capitol building, jokingly voting Georgia back into the Union.

Behind them, the army left its signature on the landscape: railroad rails heated over fires until red-hot, twisted around tree trunks, and abandoned. The South called them Sherman's neckties. In all, three hundred miles of railroad went down with bridges and telegraph lines.

Sherman rode at the head of his own column with a personal escort that was itself a statement: the 1st Alabama Cavalry — a regiment made up entirely of Southerners who had stayed loyal to the Union.

**WHAT THE MARCH LEFT BEHIND:**

The march was not only an army moving; it was a population following it. A Confederate officer estimated that about 10,000 liberated slaves followed Sherman's army — and hundreds died along the way of "hunger, disease, or exposure." North of Savannah, hundreds more drowned trying to cross at Ebenezer Creek while attempting to follow the army. In 2011, Georgia finally put a marker there for them.

Sherman kept his own ledger. He estimated the campaign had done $100 million in destruction — about one billion dollars today — and admitted that only about a fifth of it "inured to our advantage"; the rest, he wrote, was "simple waste and destruction." The army seized 5,000 horses, 4,000 mules, and 13,000 head of cattle; confiscated 9.5 million pounds of corn and 10.5 million pounds of fodder; destroyed uncounted cotton gins and mills.

**DID SHERMAN STARVE ANDERSONVILLE?:**

The story many Georgians grew up with is this: the march destroyed the supplies that would have fed Andersonville's prisoners, and Sherman could simply have swung south and liberated them — 30,000 captives. The National Park Service has a different timeline. Atlanta fell on September 2; word reached the prison immediately, and in just the week of September 7–13 nearly 17,000 prisoners were transferred to other prisons in Georgia and the Carolinas. By mid-September, Sherman and Hood had negotiated a special exchange that sent about 2,000 more out. When the march began on November 15, fewer than 200 men remained in the stockade — and by then around 12,100 had already died there. Virtually all of Andersonville's deaths occurred before Sherman destroyed anything in central Georgia.

**SAVANNAH:**

On December 10 the army reached the outskirts of Savannah — and found it was not going to be easy. Hardee had entrenched 10,000 men in strong positions and flooded the surrounding rice fields, leaving only narrow causeways for an approach. Sherman's plan to link up with the Navy was blocked, so he sent cavalry against Fort McAllister on the Ogeechee River. On December 13, Hazen's division stormed the fort and took it in fifteen minutes; 134 Union men were killed or wounded, some by torpedoes — crude land mines used only rarely in this war.

On December 17 Sherman sent Hardee a message: he had "guns that can cast heavy and destructive shot as far as the heart of your city," and if forced to assault, he would make "little effort to restrain my army." Hardee chose not to surrender — he chose to run. On December 20 he led his men across the Savannah River on a makeshift pontoon bridge.

The next morning, Savannah's mayor Richard Dennis Arnold rode out with a delegation of aldermen and ladies to offer terms: the city would surrender without resistance in exchange for protection of its citizens and property. Fleeing Confederate cavalry unhorsed some of them along the way. Arnold handed over the key to the city; Geary's division marched in on December 21.

**THE CHRISTMAS GIFT:**

Sherman telegraphed Lincoln: "I beg to present you as a Christmas gift the City of Savannah, with one hundred and fifty heavy guns and plenty of ammunition and about twenty-five thousand bales of cotton." On December 26 the president replied: "Many, many, thanks for your Christmas-gift—the capture of Savannah. When you were about leaving Atlanta for the Atlantic coast, I was anxious, if not fearful; but feeling that you were the better judge, and remembering that 'nothing risked, nothing gained' I did not interfere."

**WHY IT MATTERED:**

The march broke more than railroads. Historians Herman Hattaway and Archer Jones wrote that "Sherman's raid succeeded in 'knocking the Confederate war effort to pieces'." David J. Eicher: "He had defied military principles by operating deep within enemy territory and without lines of supply or communication." A 2022 study in the American Economic Journal found that the capital destruction induced by the march led to a contraction in agricultural investment, farm asset prices, and manufacturing — elements of which persisted through 1920.

The army itself became legend. Liddell Hart called it "probably the finest army of military 'workmen' the modern world has seen." When Johnston surrendered to Sherman four months later, he said: "there has been no such army since the days of Julius Caesar." The march set up the Carolinas campaign that followed — and on April 26, 1865, in North Carolina, Johnston's surrender ended the war.

**WHAT REMAINS:**

The name came from a prisoner of war. S. H. M. Byers, a Union captive at Camp Sorghum near Columbia, South Carolina, wrote a poem titled "Sherman's March to the Sea" in late 1864; his fellow prisoner W. O. Rockwell set it to music. When Byers was freed by the capture of Columbia, he handed Sherman a scrap of paper with the poem on it. Sherman promoted him to his staff; they became lifelong friends. The song became an instant hit with the army — and then there was another one: "Marching Through Georgia," written in 1865 by Henry Clay Work. It was played at almost every public appearance Sherman attended, and he came to dislike it.

Sixty-two thousand men left Atlanta with twenty days of rations and no supply lines — and ate their way to the sea. The South never fully recovered.

how much does it cost to get a session of psychedelic mushrooms in Oregon

A legal, supervised psilocybin session in Oregon typically costs between $850 and $3,500. While low-dose or group options start around $325 to $500, multi-day luxury retreats can exceed $5,000. [1, 2, 3, 4]
Because the Oregon Health Authority does not regulate pricing, individual service centers and facilitators set their own rates. [1]

Price Breakdown by Session Type
Pricing varies widely depending on the dosage, whether the session is private or in a group, and the amenities offered by the center. [1, 2]
•
•Low-Dose Sessions ($325 – $500). These shorter, two-hour sessions use smaller doses (around 10 mg) for mild effects without a full psychedelic trip. [1]
•
•Group Sessions ($500 – $2,000 per person). Clients share a facilitator and space with a few other participants, lowering the individual cost. [1, 2]
•
•Standard Private Sessions ($850 – $3,500). This is the most common option, offering one-on-one supervision for up to six or eight hours. [1, 2, 3]
•
•Multi-Day Retreats ($3,500 – $6,500+). Boutique centers offer all-inclusive packages that bundle lodging, meals, and multiple sessions. [1]
• 

What the Cost Covers
Under Oregon's Measure 109 framework, you cannot simply buy mushrooms to take home. Your total bill is bundled into three required phases and operational expenses: [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
•
•Preparation Session. A mandatory intake meeting with a licensed facilitator to review your health history, set goals, and create a safety and transportation plan.
•
•Administration Session. The supervised, on-site experience at a state-licensed service center, which lasts between four and eight hours depending on the dose.
•
•Integration Session. At least one follow-up meeting within 72 hours to help you process the experience.
•
•Psilocybin Product and Taxes. The actual mushrooms typically cost between $25 and $150 depending on the dosage, plus a 15% state retail tax. Some centers bundle this into their flat rate, while others bill it separately. [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]
• 

Insurance and Financial Assistance
•
•Out-of-Pocket Payment. Because psilocybin remains illegal at the federal level, health insurance, Medicare, Medicaid, HSA, and FSA funds cannot be used to pay for services. [1]
•
•Discounts and Scholarships. Many centers—such as Space Psychedelic Clinic in Portland or Satya Therapeutics in Ashland—offer sliding-scale rates, veteran discounts, or partial scholarships. You can also reduce costs by enrolling in state-approved observational research studies when booking. [1, 2, 3]
