Statement Issued by the Council of Church Leaders in Jordan

Cancellation of Christmas Celebrations in Solidarity with the Martyrs of the Nation… While Prayers Remain a Testimony to Hope and Peace

Amman, 14 November 2026

In light of the heinous terrorist crimes that have targeted our beloved homeland, Jordan, resulting in the martyrdom of ten of our fellow citizens, we extend our sincerest condolences and deepest sympathies to the families of all the martyrs. We continue to offer our prayers for the repose of their souls and for the speedy recovery of the injured, asking God to protect Jordan and its people from all harm.

Following our meeting with the families and relatives of the martyrs, during which we expressed our solidarity and support, we announce the cancellation of all celebrations associated with Christmas this year. However, religious services, prayers, and spiritual and pastoral duties will continue to be observed in accordance with established Church traditions, as they represent the very essence and spiritual message of the occasion.

We call upon the members of our Churches and our institutions to ensure that all pastoral activities associated with this feast are conducted with simplicity and solemnity, while preserving the spirituality of Christmas and its humanitarian values. Priority should be given to prayers, spiritual activities, and acts of mercy and social solidarity, in keeping with the message and values of Christmas and our sense of national solidarity.

We encourage our Churches to make the Christmas tree, this year, a symbol of hope, unity, and peace, and to light candles in memory of the souls of the martyrs, offering prayers before this symbolic sign of Christmas. We also encourage them to dedicate a memorial space beside the tree to honour our martyrs and to incorporate symbols that express justice and peace.

As we reaffirm our allegiance to His Majesty King Abdullah II Ibn Al Hussein, may God protect and preserve him, and our confidence in the institutions of the State, our Arab Army, and our security services, we affirm our belief that Jordan will remain strong through the unity, cohesion, and solidarity of its people. We highly commend the efforts being made to safeguard the security and well-being of all.

We raise our hands in humble prayer to God that Christmas may remain a testimony to hope, love, and peace, and that He may protect Jordan—its leadership, government, and people—so that our homeland may remain safe and stable.

Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace, goodwill toward all.

text:
Oh, here we go again. The standard deflection: "I don't drink, I don't eat pork, I pray, I dress modestly, I give to charity, so why are you criticizing Islam?"

Congratulations on having personal habits. That's not an argument. That's a lifestyle description.

Nobody cares what you eat for breakfast, what you wear, or how many times you pray. The conversation is about something considerably bigger than your personal routine.

Let's discuss apostasy laws. Blasphemy laws. Religious persecution. The treatment of women under oppressive interpretations of Sharia. The Taliban banning girls from education. Compulsory hijab laws. The criminalization of homosexuality. The persecution of ex-Muslims. Religious extremism. And the political movements that want religious law imposed on entire populations.

Where is your little list of personal virtues when we're discussing those subjects?

And before you accuse everyone of Islamophobia, remember that Muslim women protesting compulsory veiling are not necessarily Islamophobes. Ex-Muslims speaking about religious coercion are not necessarily Islamophobes. Muslims demanding equal rights are not Islamophobes.

Sometimes the people criticizing religious oppression are the very people who have suffered under it.

Your decision to follow Islam is your business. The consequences of laws and ideologies justified in its name are everybody's business.

You are free to worship Allah. Someone else is free to reject Allah. A woman is free to choose what she wears. An atheist is free to criticize your scripture. A former Muslim is free to walk away.

And none of them should have to fear punishment for exercising those freedoms.

So stop confusing your right to practice Islam with everybody else's obligation to approve of it.

If all you can offer in defense of religious doctrine is that you personally don't drink alcohol and eat pork, you've answered a question nobody asked while avoiding every question that actually matters.

Religious freedom protects your right to believe. It does not protect your beliefs from criticism.

Get used to the distinction.

6. The Bridal Chamber Ceremony (Phithi Song Tua Khao Ho, พิธีส่งตัวเข้าหอ)

This marks the final stage of the wedding proceedings. One essential element of this ceremony is the house where the bride and groom will begin their life together as husband and wife, traditionally known as the bridal home (ruean ho, เรือนหอ)

Next, the couple performs an auspicious lying-down ritual (phithi non ao ruek) to bring good fortune to their married life. They are then led by the hand into the bridal chamber that has been prepared for them. Once the elders have offered their advice and guidance to the newlyweds, the wedding ceremony following traditional Isan customs is considered complete.

In the past, the groom was traditionally responsible for providing the bridal home itself, while the bride was responsible for furnishing it with items such as cabinets, beds, mattresses, pillows, mosquito nets, and kitchen utensils.

*Items to Prepare
1) One medicinal grinding stone: symbolizing a steadfast and resolute mind.
2) One walking stick:  symbolizing longevity.
3) One winter melon: symbolizing a cool, calm, and peaceful life.
4) One bag each of beans and sesame seeds:  symbolizing growth, flourishing, and increasing prosperity.
5) One vessel filled with water: symbolizing unity, harmony, and togetherness, like water becoming one.
6) One cat; symbolizing love for the home and household. If a real cat is unavailable, a cat doll may be used instead.
7) One white chicken: symbolizing the ability to stay up late, rise early, and remain diligent and hardworking. If a real chicken is unavailable, a toy or figurine may be used instead.
8) A completely new set of bedding for the bride and groom, including the bed, mattress, bedding, and pillows.
9) One bowl of holy water, together with a sprinkler for sprinkling the water.
10) One bowl of popped rice and flowers, including crown flowers (dok rak), jasmine, and roses, mixed with nine gold coins and nine silver coins, respectively, or as many as desired.

text:
HAVE YOU NOTICED THAT THE FIRST FEW BITES OF A DELICIOUS MEAL CAN FEEL MORE EXCITING THAN THE LAST TEN?

There's a fascinating explanation for this.

It is called sensory-specific satiety.

Let me explain.

Imagine you're eating your favourite jollof rice.

The first few spoonfuls are wonderful.

The aroma.

The flavour.

The texture.

Everything is working beautifully.

As you continue eating, however, the pleasure associated with that particular food can gradually decline.

It doesn't necessarily mean the food has become less delicious.

Your nervous system is changing how rewarding the experience feels.

Our brains respond to food through several interacting systems involving taste, smell, learning, appetite and reward.

As we consume a particular food, its relative pleasantness can decrease compared with foods that offer different sensory experiences.

This is one reason you can feel tired of eating one food but suddenly become interested when somebody brings out a different dessert.

The phenomenon is sometimes described through the idea of a dessert stomach.

Your stomach has not developed an additional chamber for cake.

Your brain is responding to novelty.

And this is where food environments become interesting.

Think about a buffet.

Rice.

Chicken.

Plantain.

Salad.

Pastries.

Ice cream.

Every time you become less interested in one food, something different appears.

That variety can encourage additional eating because each new option offers a different sensory experience.

Now, variety is not bad.

In fact, variety across nutritious foods can help improve dietary quality.

But when you're surrounded by many highly appealing foods, it can also become easier to eat beyond the point where you would have stopped with a simpler meal.

Here's the practical lesson.

You don't need to hate delicious food.

You need to understand that appetite is influenced by much more than how empty your stomach is.

Pleasure, sensory novelty, food availability and environmental cues can all influence how much you eat.

And if you're trying to manage portions, paying attention to these influences can be useful.

Sometimes the question is not whether you're still hungry.

It's whether you have just discovered a completely different food that your brain is excited to experience.

That is why somebody can finish a substantial meal and still announce:

"I don't have space for anything else."

Then the ice cream arrives.

Suddenly, a vacant apartment has been discovered inside the abdomen.

👕 What to Wear

Choose clothing that covers your shoulders and knees. Wear shoes that are easy to remove before entering prayer halls. Step over raised wooden thresholds rather than onto them.

☀️ On-site Comfort

The open courtyards offer limited shade, so bring drinking water and sun protection. Take your time on temple steps and watch your footing around historic structures.

🙏 Local Etiquette

Keep your voice low, silence your phone, and avoid pointing your feet toward Buddha images. Give worshippers space during prayers and offerings. Ask permission before photographing people or religious ceremonies.

🔎 Sacred Spaces & Restrictions

The inverted chedi projection depends on sunlight and a darkened room, making it less visible on cloudy days.
Women are traditionally not permitted inside Ho Phra Phutthabat, but another viewing point is available at Viharn Phra Phut. Follow posted access restrictions.

🌿 Protect the Heritage

Avoid touching ancient murals, carved wooden decorations, or sacred objects. Check photography rules before taking pictures inside historic halls.

🧭 WAT PHRA THAT LAMPANG LUANG | TRAVEL ESSENTIALS
📍 Getting There

Located in Ko Kha District, approximately 18 km southwest of Lampang city, the temple is easiest to reach by taxi, private car, or hired songthaew. Public transport to Ko Kha is possible, but reaching the temple requires an additional local transfer. Arrange your return journey in advance.

🗺️ What to Explore

Begin at the grand naga staircase and historic entrance, then explore the main Viharn Luang, the golden chedi, and Viharn Nam Taem, known for its traditional murals. The temple's camera-obscura phenomenon is another highlight, although access to certain viewing spaces is restricted.

⏱️ Time Needed

Allow 1–2 hours inside the complex, or approximately half a day including travel from Lampang. For a broader cultural itinerary, combine the visit with Lampang's historic town and traditional wooden architecture.

🕰️ Opening Hours & Costs

The temple is generally open daily from 7:30 AM to 5:00 PM. Morning visits offer a comfortable opportunity to explore the outdoor courtyards.
Published admission information varies, so confirm any applicable entrance fee locally before visiting.

DATE: SUNDAY NOVEMBER 15TH 2026.

TOPIC: BAPTISED WITH FIRE

MEMORISE
I indeed baptize you with water unto repentance: but he that cometh after me is mightier than I, whose shoes I am not worthy to bear: he shall baptize you with the Holy Ghost, and with fire: - (Matthew 3:11)

BIBLE READING: MALACHI 3:1-4 (KJV)

1 Behold, I will send my messenger, and he shall prepare the way before me: and the Lord, whom ye seek, shall suddenly come to his temple, even the messenger of the covenant, whom ye delight in: behold, he shall come, saith the Lord of hosts.

2 But who may abide the day of his coming? and who shall stand when he appeareth? for he is like a refiner's fire, and like fullers' soap:

3 And he shall sit as a refiner and purifier of silver: and he shall purify the sons of Levi, and purge them as gold and silver, that they may offer unto the Lord an offering in righteousness.

4 Then shall the offering of Judah and Jerusalem be pleasant unto the Lord, as in the days of old, and as in former years.

MESSAGE

Anyone whom God wants to use as His vessel must be baptised, note not only with the Holy Ghost, but also with fire. Fire has many functions, one of which is that it purifies. In Isaiah 6:5, after Isaiah realised how unclean he was, the angel of the Lord used a live coal to touch his lips and said, "This hath touched thy lips; and thine iniquity is taken away, and thy sin purged" (Isaiah 6:6-7). Isaiah received a baptism of fire that cleansed him and made him a useful and worthy vessel to carry out God's assignment.

Before the apostles were sent out to proclaim the gospel of Christ around the world, Jesus instructed them to wait for the baptism of the Holy Ghost, as we see in Acts 1:4-5:

And, being assembled together with them, commanded them that they should not depart from Jerusalem, but wait for the promise of the Father, which, saith he, ye have heard of me. For John truly baptized with water; but ye shall be baptized with the Holy Ghost not many days hence.

They obeyed this instruction, and they were baptised by the Holy Spirit and fire in Acts 2. This encounter marked the beginning of their exploits for Jesus, starting with Peter's sermon, which God used to save about 3,000 souls that same day. If you want to be a worthy vessel in God's hands, you must allow Him to set you apart and baptise you with the Holy Ghost and fire.

Beloved, God is still looking for vessels He can purify with fire and put to use in His vineyard. Today's Bible reading tells us that God is a refiner and purifier of those who will serve Him in righteousness. Until the Lord refines you with His fire, your offering cannot be pleasant to Him. Offering in this context means your life. Gold in its raw state is not beautiful, but after it has been purified by fire, it becomes precious. This is why it is called a precious metal. If you don't want to remain a common vessel in God's vineyard, ask Him to visit you with His fire. Allow His fire to take away any filth in your life that will not allow you to be useful and precious in His sight. If you really want to be a useful vessel for God, pray today's prayer point with all your heart. 

PRAYER POINT
Father, I am ready; please, let Your fire fall on me.

text:
Erika Kirk's uncle Jack Solomon and the centre for Jewish studies at UVU.

(Deseret News 1995)
The kinship between Jews and Mormons is being stoked at the new Center for Jewish Studies at Utah Valley State College.

Through classes, lecture series and public forums the center is trying to build bridges of understanding between the two faiths, which both assert a relationship to the house of Israel and have histories shaped by persecution.The impetus for the center came from Marlene Telford. She grew acquainted with Jewish culture and history while working in the garment industry in California.

Six years ago, after moving to Utah, Telford was asked to teach a gospel doctrine class on the Old Testament at her Mormon ward.

"As a youngster I felt that was the most boring book I'd read," Telford said. "All I could remember were the begats, the begats, the begats."

But she was mesmerized by Jewish history as she researched material for her class. Telford whet her interest in the subject by completing a major in Near Eastern studies at Brigham Young University.

Telford then figured if she was so entranced with Jewish history, other Mormons must be. In 1993, she proposed setting up the center at the college.

She received support from UVSC President Kerry Romes-burg and gathered an illustrious group of people willing to get the center rolling.

"The thrust of the center is to further understanding of the Jewish people, Judaism and the land of Israel among the peoples of Utah," Telford said.

The center's 25 board directors include David Galbraith, a Brigham Young University professor and former director of the school's Jerusalem Center; Victor Ludlow, a BYU professor of ancient scripture; Joe Cannon, Geneva Steel magnate and the largest gentile donor to the U.S. Holocaust Museum in Washington, D.C.; businessman Jack Solomon, who also serves as a trustee for Hebrew University; Wayne Nelson, president of HealthCost Management Foundation of Utah; Laurence Loeb, a University of Utah professor and cantor at the Kol Ami synagogue; and L.K. Abbott, executive director of the National Conference for Christians and Jews.

UVSC provides a perfect home for the center, Telford said. The college is dynamic and growing. It is close to but distinct from BYU, which has taken a broad approach through its center for international studies. The U. is home to a center for Middle Eastern studies.

Recent headlines about graduation exercises at West High School show there is definitely a need for interfaith dialogue, Telford said.

"If we really want results in terms of understanding, then it must come from the heart, not directives mandated by law, governments, courts or coercion," Telford said. "And each mistake must be overlooked with a smile and forgiveness, not attacked through allegations of false assumptions. It is time to heal."

Board member Jack Solomon, who has lived in Utah 15 years, said there is "no place in the world where the Christian community has been so supportive of the Jewish people and Judaism."

In fact, Brigham Young donated the land for the Jewish community's cemetery. The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints also donated money to help built the synagogue Montfesiore in Salt Lake City. In 1903, when the synagogue was dedicated, then-LDS Church President George Fielding Smith gave an address.
"This community has been very, very interested in Judaism and the Old Testament," Solomon said. "The center will satisfy a worthwhile purpose so both groups can get to know more about each other and their common heritage."

After all, Solomon said, the two groups share not just a common heritage, but a similar landscape: in both Utah and Israel, a Jordan River joins a body of fresh water to a body of salt water.

Through the center, Telford has taught a class on Jewish history. The center also offered a mini-lecture series last year on "What is a Jew?" and this year on "Zionism and the state of Israel."

text:
#designmatters26 Fast ≠ Good / Michel Ferreira (Figma)
Good Design Isn't About Speed. It's About Understanding People.

Fast ≠ Good — Why Judgment, Intentionality, and Accountability Matter More Than Ever in the Age of AI

Generative AI has dramatically accelerated the design process. New models, tools, and capabilities are emerging almost daily, and the entire industry seems caught in a relentless race to move faster, ship more, and produce more output.

But being able to make something faster doesn't necessarily mean we're making something better.

Drawing on nearly 30 years of experience in design, Michel Ferreira, Designer Advocate at Figma, challenged us to reconsider what it means to be a designer in the age of AI.

At the heart of his talk was a simple but powerful statement:

"Speed is just a control. Good design is a responsibility."

● Why Are We So Obsessed with Speed?

Today's design industry is increasingly focused on metrics that are easy to quantify: production time, generation speed, lines of code shipped, and the volume of output.

Speed is measurable. It's a clock, a KPI, a number.

But "good" is much harder to measure.

Good for whom? Good for what? What is the design trying to achieve? What context are we designing for?

Evaluating good design requires comparison, interpretation, human judgment, and an understanding of the people on the other side of the experience.

That doesn't mean speed is bad. You can be fast and good. You can also be slow and terrible.

Speed tells you nothing about the quality of what you're delivering. They aren't even on the same axis.

There's also a cognitive cost to constantly rushing. Under pressure, our perception becomes less accurate, our attention shifts, and our decisions suffer.

Speed doesn't just change how quickly we work. It changes how we think.

● AI Is a Blender. Design Is Cooking.

Michel used a memorable analogy to explain the difference between generative AI and human design: a blender versus a chef.

AI is an extraordinary interpolation machine. It takes existing patterns, layouts, interfaces, and conventions, identifies relationships between them, and recombines them at incredible speed.

Imagine throwing every interface ever designed into a blender and pressing a button. Something comes out, but it's largely a recombination of what was already there.

"Design isn't a blender. Design is cooking."

A chef can work with the same ingredients but bring something entirely different to the table.

There's touch, taste, timing, technique, and lived experience. A chef can pause, taste, adjust the seasoning, experiment, and make deliberate decisions.

The same applies to designers.

We don't simply assemble existing patterns. We interpret context, challenge assumptions, make trade-offs, and combine ideas in unexpected ways.

Michel contrasted interpolation with extrapolation: the ability to make a leap beyond existing patterns and introduce something new.

Design is an intentional process. It requires agency, ownership, and judgment.

● Fidelity Matches Confidence — Don't Make It Look Finished Before It Is

One of the most important principles Michel brought from his time at Shopify was:

"Fidelity matches confidence."

When an idea is still uncertain, a rough sketch is exactly what you need.

Low-fidelity explorations create space for discussion, critique, pushback, and iteration. Their unfinished appearance signals that the solution is still open to change.

That roughness also protects designers from falling in love with a solution too early.

As understanding grows and confidence increases, fidelity should increase with it.

The problem with generative AI is that it often skips this progression entirely.

"Maximum fidelity, first pass, every single time."

AI can produce a polished, high-fidelity interface from the very first prompt. It looks finished, so people start treating it as finished, even when the underlying assumptions haven't been tested.

AI-generated polish can create the illusion of confidence that the design process hasn't actually earned.

Looking finished isn't the same as being ready.

When we jump straight to high-fidelity output, we risk skipping the exploration, critical thinking, and design critique that should inform our decisions.

● Designers Know When to Change Speed

Unlike machines, humans don't have to move in a straight line at a constant speed.

We can sprint during exploration, slow down when trying to understand complex problems, accelerate during execution, and ship small to learn.

Sometimes we need to move quickly. Sometimes we need to pause, question our assumptions, and reconsider the direction.

The valuable skill isn't simply being fast or slow.

It's knowing when to change speed.

AI tends to move confidently toward an answer. Designers can navigate ambiguity, reconsider constraints, explore alternatives, and recognize when the problem itself needs to be reframed.

If we're constantly producing outputs without examining the reasoning behind them, we're not really designing.

We're just shipping.

● Never Delegate Understanding

Toward the end of the talk, Michel returned to 1958, when the Indian government invited Charles and Ray Eames to explore how design education could support the country's future.

Instead of developing their recommendations from their home in California, the Eameses spent three months traveling across India, speaking with craftspeople, scientists, farmers, weavers, and cooks.

Their approach reflected a principle Michel believes is more relevant than ever:

"Never delegate understanding."

One of the objects they studied was a traditional brass water vessel, refined through generations of everyday use.

Its value wasn't simply in its appearance. It embodied countless decisions about carrying water, balance, ergonomics, cleaning, materials, craftsmanship, and cultural practices.

Generations of people had shaped and refined it through lived experience.

A seemingly simple object contained an extraordinary depth of design knowledge that couldn't be reproduced merely by copying its form.

Michel also referenced Ray Eames:

"What works good is better than what looks good, because what works good lasts."

And Dieter Rams:

"Good design is as little design as possible."

AI makes it incredibly easy to add more features, screens, components, and content.

But just because something is easy to generate doesn't mean it belongs in the experience.

The ability to add more doesn't replace the judgment to know what should be left out.

● Design Is the Labor of Understanding People

Michel offered his own definition of design:

"Design is the labor of understanding people."

The word labor matters.

Understanding people isn't free. It takes time, observation, conversations, disagreement, ambiguity, and sometimes discomfort.

It requires us to sit with uncertainty rather than rush toward a solution.

Understanding and solving are not the same thing.

Understanding comes first. Solving comes after.

Michel also referenced Brazilian educator Paulo Freire, who argued that alienating people from their own decision-making turns them into objects.

The same concern applies when we allow AI to make decisions on behalf of the people we're designing for—or when we let it make those decisions for us.

AI may increasingly take over parts of our craft, but responsibility for the consequences remains with us.

Michel also connected this idea to the Japanese concept of Fueki Ryūkō (不易流行)—the relationship between what remains unchanged and what continually evolves.

We don't have to choose between tradition and progress.

Our tools, workflows, and processes will continue to evolve. But curiosity, judgment, intentionality, and our commitment to understanding people are worth preserving.

And preserving them requires conscious effort.

● Our Job Isn't Just to Make Things Faster. It's to Make Things Better.

As generative AI lowers the barriers to making things, the value of designers increasingly lies beyond execution.

It's in understanding the problem, recognizing context, challenging assumptions, navigating trade-offs, and taking responsibility for decisions.

The goal isn't to protect our job titles, defend traditional workflows, or preserve the way we've always worked.

It's to protect our ability to ask why, challenge decisions, and advocate for better experiences.

"Speed is just a control. Good design is a responsibility."

AI may become faster, more capable, and more deeply integrated into every part of the design process.

But we should never delegate our responsibility to understand the people we're designing for.

That understanding—and the judgment that comes from it—is what makes design matter.

text:
What do Pepsi and economic sanctions have in common?
More than you might think.
I grew up in the Soviet Union, and I remember drinking Pepsi as a child. Back then, I had no idea that an ordinary bottle of Pepsi was part of one of the most unusual trade arrangements of the Cold War.
In the early 1970s, PepsiCo wanted to enter the Soviet market. The Soviet authorities were interested too. But there was a problem. The ruble was not convertible, and the Soviet Union had limited access to hard currency. Paying an American company in dollars was not so simple.
So they found another solution.
PepsiCo supplied concentrate to Soviet bottling plants. In return, it received the right to distribute Stolichnaya vodka in the United States.
Americans bought Soviet vodka. We drank American Pepsi.
And it worked.
By the late 1980s, the arrangement had become even more extraordinary. Decommissioned Soviet naval vessels, including submarines, were included in barter deals connected to PepsiCo.
No, Pepsi wasn’t planning to build its own navy. The vessels were intended for scrapping or resale.
But the economic logic behind this story is worth remembering today.
Sanctions and restrictions on international payments are once again forcing companies to look for alternative ways to settle transactions. Barter, payments in national currencies, intermediaries and complicated clearing arrangements are becoming relevant again.
Of course, the circumstances are different. In the Soviet Union, the problem was primarily the nonconvertible ruble and a shortage of hard currency. Today, financial sanctions can create similar obstacles to international settlements.
The underlying mechanism, however, is familiar.
When conventional payment channels are unavailable, trade doesn’t necessarily disappear. It finds another route. Usually a more expensive, complicated and less transparent one.
This doesn’t mean sanctions don’t work. It means their effectiveness cannot be judged simply by whether goods continue crossing borders. The additional costs, risks and inefficiencies matter too.
I find it remarkable that something I remember from my Soviet childhood offers such a useful illustration of a problem we are discussing again today.
Back then, Pepsi was just Pepsi to me. Now I see a small piece of international monetary history in that bottle.
#SundayReading #EconomicHistory #Sanctions

text:
An iconic 1945 photograph shows U.S. General Douglas MacArthur standing casually in an unbuttoned khaki shirt beside Japan's Emperor Hirohito at the U.S. Embassy in Tokyo on September 27, 1945...

Weeks after Japan's surrender in World War II, Emperor Hirohito visited General MacArthur at the U.S. Embassy in Tokyo. MacArthur stood tall in a relaxed khakis uniform with his hands on his hips and no tie, while Hirohito appeared diminutive in a formal morning coat, shattering centuries-old imperial protocol where the emperor was revered as a living god and strictly shielded from casual public imagery.

Japan's Home Ministry attempted to ban or seize newspapers from publishing the photograph, viewing the stark visual power dynamic as an insult to the throne. MacArthur's command overruled the Japanese government's ban, allowing the image to run across Japanese newspapers two days later as a psychological measure to make clear who held supreme authority during the occupation.

. . . 

On September 27, 1945, Emperor Hirohito left his palace and went to the US Embassy in Tokyo to meet the man now running his country, General Douglas MacArthur.

Twenty-five days earlier, Japan had signed its surrender on the deck of the USS Missouri.

Hirohito came in full formal dress, a morning coat with a top hat, and stood stiffly at attention.

MacArthur met him in plain khakis with an open collar and no tie, his hands resting on his hips, a full head taller.

An Army photographer, Lt. Gaetano Faillace, took three pictures, and two were thrown out because of an awkward face.

For Japan, the one that survived was a shock.

Millions of Japanese had been taught that the emperor was a living god whom ordinary people were not supposed to look at directly, and here he was looking small beside an American who didn’t bother to dress up.

Japan’s Home Ministry banned the photo right away, saying it damaged the dignity of the throne.

MacArthur overruled the ban and ordered every major newspaper to run it, and millions of copies went out across the country.

Supporters call it the most honest picture of the war, a moment that told Japan the truth without firing another shot.

Critics call it a deliberate humiliation of a defeated nation’s most sacred figure.

What came next is just as divisive: MacArthur kept Hirohito on the throne and out of any war-crimes trial, and the two men went on to meet ten more times.

MacArthur later wrote that the emperor offered to take full responsibility for the war, a claim historians still argue about.

Thirty-year-old Hannah worked as a cleaner at a luxury hotel in Miami.

One morning, while cleaning a presidential suite, she discovered a black suitcase hidden beneath the bed.

When she opened it, she found stacks of cash worth approximately $280,000.

She immediately called her supervisor.

The hotel contacted the guest, a wealthy businessman who had checked out that morning.

He returned, collected the money, and thanked the management.

Hannah thought she would at least receive recognition for her honesty.

Instead, her supervisor called her into the office.

The businessman had complained that someone had opened his suitcase without permission.

Hannah was fired for violating hotel privacy rules.

She went home crying.

She had been working there for six years and was saving money to pay for her mother’s surgery.

Three days later, the businessman returned to the hotel.

He had discovered something unusual while reviewing his security footage.

Hannah hadn’t taken a single dollar.

In fact, another hotel employee had been seen trying to move the suitcase before Hannah reported it.

The businessman demanded that the hotel reinstate her.

But Hannah refused to return.

She said:

“I did the honest thing when nobody was watching. I shouldn’t have needed a rich man to prove I deserved my job.”

The businessman offered to pay her six months’ salary.

She accepted the money but never went back.

LET’S DISCUSS:

Should the hotel have fired Hannah for opening the suitcase, even though she reported the money?

And would you return to a workplace that punished you for doing the right thing?

text:
India’s New Zealand ODI batting collapse was a collective failure — not a Rohit Sharma or Virat Kohli problem.

Social media is once again targeting Rohit after a lean series (30 runs from 4 innings, two ducks) and secondarily Kohli, even though his 74 in the opener is the highest score by any Indian in the entire series. That framing is incomplete and unfair. This was a group shortfall in testing conditions, not an individual failure.

And it is not like that if it is India only which faltered, NewZealand also struggled on this challenging tour and it is them actually who lost the ODI series in their own backyard. So it is their batters also who could not cope up with the demands of these pitches.

Across the five-match series (one match abandoned), India’s batting totals were 143 (DLS), 113/7 (DLS), 89, and 209. No Indian scored a fifty outside Kohli’s 74. Multiple top-order collapses happened early. The numbers tell the story of a unit that struggled together:
•  Rohit Sharma: 30 runs (0, 23, 0, 7)
•  Virat Kohli: 86 runs (74, 7, 0, 5) — average 21.50
•  Shreyas Iyer, KL Rahul, Shubman Gill, and others contributed in patches but none sustained an innings
•  Axar Patel (~74) and Ishan Kishan (73, with two forties) were among the better contributors lower down
•  Several starts ended quickly against quality seam bowling

These conditions played a decisive role. November in New Zealand brought unseasonal rain and wet weather. Matches were interrupted, one was abandoned, and DLS was applied twice. Pitches that sat under covers retained moisture, producing extra bounce and pronounced seam movement. New Zealand’s seamers (Henry with 6/27 in one game, Duffy, Fisher, and others) exploited it ruthlessly. These were not typical flat ODI tracks. White-ball batting became significantly harder, and India’s top order felt it collectively.

For the 2027 ODI World Cup, the core batting group remains the same and should not be dismantled on the basis of one tough overseas series:
•  Rohit Sharma and Virat Kohli bring the experience, big-match temperament, and proven ability to absorb pressure that younger players are still developing.
•  Shubman Gill continues to be one of India’s most consistent ODI performers in 2026 across formats and conditions.
•  KL Rahul offers the technical solidity and middle-order stability required in longer formats.

Ishan Kishan showed intent and fight with two 40s and can reasonably be given a longer rope. Everyone else in the batting group still has to prove their worth through sustained performances rather than occasional starts.

One rain-affected, seamer-friendly series in New Zealand does not rewrite the longer script or the planning for 2027. Conditions matter. Collective responsibility matters. And the core four — Rohit, Virat, Gill, and Rahul — remain India’s best foundation heading into the next World Cup cycle.

text:
I Am Finally Living My Dream — 33-Year-Old Woman Leaves Husband After 10 Years Of Marriage to Live With Her Pet Pig 

A 33-year-old woman from Nashville, Tennessee, Gayla Thompson, has found an unusual way to celebrate her fresh start after ending her 10-year marriage by fulfilling her longtime dream of owning a pet pig. 

Thompson welcomed an eight-week-old piglet named Daisy in November 2025, shortly after her divorce was finalised. She revealed that her ex-husband had always opposed her having a pet pig, making the purchase a special way to begin her new chapter. 

“I traded one pig for another,” she joked, explaining that getting Daisy was something she had always wanted to do for herself. 

Daisy, who is now four months old and weighs about 50 pounds, has become a central part of Thompson’s life. The pig has her own bed, toys and litter box and regularly accompanies her to pet stores and Sonic, where staff recognise her and offer her treats. 

Despite the challenges of keeping a pig indoors, including having to secure cabinets and protect her carpets because of its natural digging behaviour, Thompson described Daisy as easy to care for and surprisingly clean, noting that she uses her litter box. 

She disclosed that Daisy’s upkeep initially cost about $50 monthly during winter, with expenses expected to drop to around $20 once the pig moves into a purpose-built outdoor pen. Her diet consists mainly of grain pellets twice daily, lettuce and Cheerios, while she also helps reduce food waste by eating leftovers. 

Thompson, who has loved animals since childhood and previously rescued and rehabilitated injured wildlife, said her family was not surprised by her decision to own an indoor pig. 

She has since found a new partner who fully supports her passion. The couple are planning to move in together and build a spacious pig pen on his country property. They have also welcomed another pig named Dude, with plans to expand their hobby farm to include chickens and possibly a donkey. 

Describing her new chapter as the dream she had always wanted, Thompson said she was finally living the life she envisioned.

text:
A Tucson woman is asking officials to spare her daughter’s dog after he bit her and sent her to the hospital.

His name is Sergeant Snuggles.

Jennifer Evancho brought him home to help guard her chickens. He was a 9-month-old Anatolian shepherd who already weighed about 100 pounds.

The kids called him Snuggles because he loved to snuggle with them. Jennifer’s husband, a military veteran, added “Sergeant” to give their new guard dog a name that sounded a little tougher.

On Oct. 7, 2025, Jennifer’s mother, Clara Gastelum, walked up behind Snuggles outside the family’s Tucson home.

Clara said he was focused on something beyond the yard. She thought it might be coyotes or another animal. When she reached down to pet him, he knocked her down and bit her.

Clara said he backed away as soon as she called his name.

She needed hospital treatment and said she came away with stitches and staples. When she later spoke about what happened, she called it “friendly fire.”

Animal control took Snuggles that day. Jennifer expected to bring him home after a 10-day quarantine.

The release date came and went.

On Nov. 24, Tucson City Court declared Snuggles vicious and ordered him euthanized. A higher court declined to overturn that ruling in March, and Jennifer continued to fight the order.

Then, in May, a trainer in North Carolina offered to take him.

Rick Dunton said he would pay to transport Snuggles, assess him and work with him before any adoption. He offered to sign a waiver and agreed to keep Snuggles out of Arizona permanently.

The county animal care director said he would consider an agreement if the county and shelter were protected from liability. A Tucson city prosecutor said the decision should be left to the court.

As of Nov. 11, 2026, Snuggles was still in custody, more than a year after animal control took him.

By then, the family had spent a year fighting for the dog their kids had named. A trainer had offered to take him and do the work of finding out what kind of home he could safely live in.

And Clara, who remembers the bite and the trip to the hospital, was still asking for him to have that chance.

(cont.)

"Render Unto Caesar What Is Caesar’s, and Unto God What Is God’s: The Sophistry Behind the Secularisation of Society

Jacques-Bénigne Bossuet (1627–1704) – In Politique tirée des propres paroles de l’Écriture sainte (Politics Drawn from the Very Words of Holy Scripture), Bossuet explains the divine foundations of political authority and the accountability of rulers before God.

Joseph de Maistre (1753–1821) – In Considérations sur la France (1797) and Du Pape (1819), de Maistre defends the religious foundations of political and social order, opposing the revolutionary attempt to emancipate society from Christianity.

Juan Donoso Cortés (1809–1853) – In Essay on Catholicism, Liberalism and Socialism (1851), Donoso Cortés argues that political systems cannot be separated from their underlying religious and philosophical foundations. He offers a powerful Catholic criticism of liberalism and secular political philosophy.

“Come, let us bow down in worship, let us kneel before the LORD our Maker.” Psalm 95:6 (NIV)🙏

What a beautiful blessing it is to wake up to another Sunday morning! Today is an opportunity to set aside the worries of the week, quiet our hearts, and turn our attention to the One who deserves all our praise.

Worship is more than the songs we sing or the prayers we offer in church. It is a grateful heart that recognizes God's goodness, a humble spirit that seeks His guidance, and a life that strives to honor Him in all things.

Sometimes we become so busy asking God for what we need that we forget to simply thank Him for who He is.

He is our Creator, our Provider, our Comforter, and our everlasting source of hope.

Whatever burdens you may be carrying this morning, bring them before the Lord. Whatever blessings you've received, give Him thanks. And whatever challenges lie ahead, remember that you serve a faithful God whose love never changes.

Heavenly Father, thank You for the precious gift of another Sunday morning. We come before You with humble hearts, grateful for Your mercy, Your grace, and Your unfailing love. Help us set aside distractions and draw closer to You today. Bless our families, strengthen those who are struggling, comfort those who are hurting, and renew our faith in Your promises. May our worship be sincere, our hearts be filled with gratitude, and our lives reflect Your goodness to others. Guide our steps throughout this day and help us walk in a way that brings honor and glory to Your holy name.

In Jesus name, Amen. 🙏

May your Sunday be filled with the peace of God's presence, the joy of His blessings, and the comfort of knowing you are deeply loved. ❤️

Peace and grace to you. 
Coffee first, and then church. ☕🙏

text:
That Village Pond, That Chhath Ghat, and My Childhood…! 

Sometimes, life takes us so far ahead that we become emotional remembering the beautiful moments we left behind.

I still remember my village…

It was the day of Chhath Puja. We children would wake up before sunrise, filled with a different kind of excitement. With spades, buckets, and cleaning tools in our hands, we would head towards the village pond.

No show-off, no selfish motives, no expectations from anyone…

Just one passion — to make our Chhath Ghat look the most beautiful that year.

First, we would clean the entire area around the pond. Then, we would plant tall banana stems to decorate the ghat. We would sprinkle water on the ground and carefully clean it. Finally, we would shape the wet soil into a circular form and create a small representation of God with our own hands.

Back then, we had no grand decorations, no fancy lights, and no expensive pandals.

Yet, the warmth and sense of belonging that existed in that simple, मिट्टी-covered ghat are perhaps impossible to recreate today, even with lakhs of rupees.

And then, as evening approached, the entire village would transform.

Women from every household would walk towards the ghat, carrying their traditional baskets on their heads and singing devotional songs dedicated to Chhathi Maiya. Some baskets were filled with coconuts, others with thekua, bananas, sugarcane, and seasonal fruits.

The glowing diyas along the pond, the reflection of the setting sun on the water, and the echo of Chhath songs in the air…

That beautiful scene is still alive in my memories, just as vividly as it was back then.

Perhaps, as children, we didn’t fully understand the significance of Chhath Puja. But today, I realise how much devotion, sacrifice, and faith were hidden behind every ritual — and how many silent prayers mothers offered for the well-being of their families.

Life has taken us far away from those village lanes. Responsibilities have increased, work has grown, and the world has changed.

But somewhere deep inside, my heart still stands beside that very village pond.

If only those childhood days could return once again…

The same early-morning cleaning of the ghat, the same banana stems being planted, the same little idols made from मिट्टी, and the same evenings spent with the entire village, watching the setting sun and offering prayers.

Today, I realise that back then, we weren’t just decorating a Chhath ghat. We were creating a world of memories that would remain in our hearts for a lifetime.

Honestly, Chhath Puja is not just a festival. It is our connection to the soil of our village, our roots, a mother’s unconditional love, the warmth of family, and a priceless treasure of childhood that no amount of wealth in this world can ever bring back.

My only prayer to Chhathi Maiya is that every home remains blessed with happiness and peace, every mother’s wishes come true, and everyone who has drifted away gets the chance to experience the joy of their village, their family, and their childhood once again.

Jai Chhathi Maiya! 🙏🌅

text:
U.S. semiconductors still offer significant structural investment opportunities, though capital is rotating from blindly buying a single market leader toward supply chain diversification and valuation rebalancing. Following a sharp sell-off triggered by U.S. midterm election regulatory concerns and executive governance turbulence at the industry's top player, the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index (SOX) has entered what Goldman Sachs describes as its deepest relative oversold territory in a decade, creating a fresh entry window for investors focused on 2027–2028 earnings delivery.

I. Why the Recent Volatility? A Mismatch Between Fundamentals and Sentiment

In early November 2026, U.S. semiconductor stocks experienced rare, acute turbulence. Rather than a collapse in end-demand, the pullback stemmed from a valuation reset driven by overlapping short-term catalysts:
Tighter policy and infrastructure permitting. Following the U.S. midterm elections, market concerns mounted over stricter regulations on data center power consumption, water usage, and land permits. Morgan Stanley estimates these hurdles could push roughly 20% of U.S. data center projects slated for 2028 into 2029, temporarily weighing on hardware delivery timelines.
Executive governance turbulence at the industry leader. Nvidia ($NVDA), the undisputed core of the sector, faced internal scrutiny and leadership stability concerns tied to personal executive matters. Significant single-week pressure on its shares prompted institutional capital to rotate out of concentrated mega-cap exposure and into broader segments of the value chain.
Tug-of-war over CapEx and free cash flow. Massive capital expenditures by hyperscalers and frontier AI labs sparked debate over financing sustainability. Goldman Sachs noted that the semiconductor sector pulled back roughly 21% over the past month, widening its valuation discount relative to the S&P 500 to a near ten-year high.

II. Four Core Pillars Supporting Future Opportunities

Despite near-term sentiment headwinds, firm supply chain orders and institutional forecasts indicate that the AI-driven semiconductor supercycle continues to deepen:
Long-term compute contracts lock in 2027–2028 growth. Institutional estimates project global AI infrastructure spending to reach $1.3 trillion to $1.6 trillion in 2027, climbing further to $1.8 trillion to $2.0 trillion in 2028. Leading foundation model developers recently disclosed roughly $900 billion in long-term compute purchase commitments during IPO roadshows, effectively placing a floor under downstream demand and ruling out a hard landing.
Rise of custom silicon (ASICs) and challenger platforms. As AI workloads scale from training to inference, cloud giants are accelerating in-house chip development to lower per-query compute costs. Broadcom ($AVGO), deeply embedded in custom ASIC design, has seen its AI semiconductor revenue more than double year-over-year, while AMD (\)AMD) issued strong guidance for over 80% revenue growth in 2027, propelled by server CPUs and rack-scale AI systems.
Memory chips emerge as the tightest bottleneck. High Bandwidth Memory (HBM) capacity for 2027 is virtually sold out, squeezing supply for conventional DRAM and enterprise solid-state drives (NAND). TechInsights projects memory chips to account for over 60% of total semiconductor industry revenue in 2027, positioning memory leaders like Micron ($MU) for surging volume and pricing power.
Foundries and equipment makers hold absolute pricing power. Regardless of how market share shifts among downstream chip designers, every player relies on leading-edge fabrication and advanced packaging. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company ($TSM), commanding over 70% of the pure-play foundry market alongside pricing power for 2027 leading-edge nodes, serves as the sector's anchor for both risk mitigation and broad AI exposure.

III. Investment Strategy and Key Risk Factors

In the current market environment, navigating U.S. semiconductors requires shifting from chasing sector-wide beta to selecting structural alpha:
Core Strategic Recommendations:Diversify single-company risk. Avoid over-concentrating portfolios in a single chip designer. Consider a barbell allocation combining foundry manufacturing, memory/interconnects, and custom ASICs to hedge against architectural shifts and governance risks, or use SOX-tracking ETFs to smooth out single-stock volatility.
Track high-frequency hard data. Focus closely on TSMC's monthly revenue growth, quarterly CapEx guidance from cloud hyperscalers, and HBM contract pricing trends, as these metrics reflect true industry momentum far better than short-term political noise.

Three Key Risks to Monitor:U.S. power and permitting bottlenecks: Grid interconnection delays and environmental reviews in key U.S. states during 2027–2028 could slow the pace of hardware deployments.
AI monetization shortfalls: If downstream software and enterprise applications fail to generate sufficient cash flow to justify massive compute outlays, cloud providers could trim CapEx in the second half of 2027.
Technological disruption: Rapid adoption of Co-Packaged Optics (CPO) and novel compute-in-memory architectures could reshape competitive dynamics among traditional optical transceiver and interconnect vendors.

text:
It’s a really weird time in AI. In just six months, the public discourse around the technology has gone from “Chatbots generate funny sea shanties” to “AI systems could cause human extinction.” Who else is feeling whiplash? 

My colleague Will Douglas Heaven asked AI experts why exactly people are talking about existential risk, and why now. Meredith Whittaker, president of the Signal Foundation (which is behind the private messaging app Signal) and a former Google researcher, sums it up nicely: “Ghost stories are contagious. It’s really exciting and stimulating to be afraid.” 

We’ve been here before, of course: AI doom follows AI hype. But this time feels different. The Overton window has shifted in discussions around AI risks and policy. What was once an extreme view is now a mainstream talking point, grabbing not only headlines but the attention of world leaders.

Read more from Will here. 

Whittaker is not the only one who thinks this. While influential people in Big Tech companies such as Google and Microsoft, and AI startups like OpenAI, have gone all in on warning people about extreme AI risks and closing up their AI models from public scrutiny, Meta is going the other way. 

Last week, on one of the hottest days of the year so far, I went to Meta’s Paris HQ to hear about the company’s recent AI work. As we sipped champagne on a rooftop with views to the Eiffel Tower, Meta’s chief AI scientist, Yann LeCun, a Turing Award winner, told us about his hobbies, which include building electronic wind instruments. But he was really there to talk about why he thinks the idea that a superintelligent AI system will take over the world is “preposterously ridiculous.” 

People are worried about AI systems that “are going to be able to recruit all the resources in the world to transform the universe into paper clips,” LeCun said. “That’s just insane.” (He was referring to the “paper clip maximizer problem,” a thought experiment in which an AI asked to make as many paper clips as possible does so in ways that ultimately harms humans, while still fulfilling its main objective.) 

He is in stark opposition to Geoffrey Hinton and Yoshua Bengio, two pioneering AI researchers (and the two other “godfathers of AI”), who shared the Turing prize with LeCun. Both have recently become outspoken about  existential AI risk.

Joelle Pineau, Meta’s vice president of AI research, agrees with LeCun. She calls the conversation ”unhinged.” The extreme focus on future risks does not leave much bandwidth to talk about current AI harms, she says. 

“When you start looking at ways to have a rational discussion about risk, you usually look at the probability of an outcome and you multiply it by the cost of that outcome. [The existential-risk crowd] have essentially put an infinite cost on that outcome,” says Pineau. 

“When you put an infinite cost, you can’t have any rational discussions about any other outcomes. And that takes the oxygen out of the room for any other discussion, which I think is too bad.”

While talking about existential risk is a signal that tech people are aware of AI risks, tech doomers have a bigger ulterior motive, LeCun and Pineau say: influencing the laws that govern tech. 

“At the moment, OpenAI is in a position where they are ahead, so the right thing to do is to slam the door behind you,” says LeCun. “Do we want a future in which AI systems are essentially transparent in their functioning or are … proprietary and owned by a small number of tech companies on the West Coast of the US?” 

What was clear from my conversations with Pineau and LeCun was that Meta, which has been slower than competitors to roll out cutting-edge models and generative AI in products, is banking on its open-source approach to give it an edge in an increasingly competitive AI market. Meta is, for example, open-sourcing its first model in keeping with LeCun’s vision of how to build AI systems with human-level intelligence. 

Open-sourcing technology sets a high bar, as it lets outsiders find faults and hold companies accountable, Pineau says. But it also helps Meta’s technologies become a more integral part of the infrastructure of the internet. 

“When you actually share your technology, you have the ability to drive the way in which technology will then be done,” she says. 

Deeper Learning

Five big takeaways from Europe’s AI Act

It’s crunch time for the AI Act. Last week, the European Parliament voted to approve its draft rules. My colleague Tate Ryan-Mosley has five takeaways from the proposal. The parliament would like the AI Act to include a total ban on real-time biometrics and predictive policing in public spaces, transparency obligations for large AI models, and a ban on the scraping of copyrighted material. It also classifies recommendation algorithms as “high risk” AI that requires stricter regulation. 

What happens next? This does not mean the EU is going to adopt these policies outright. Next, members of the European Parliament will have to thrash out details with the Council of the European Union and the EU’s executive arm, the European Commission, before the draft rules become law. The final legislation will be a compromise between three different drafts from the three institutions. European lawmakers are aiming to get the AI Act in final shape by December, and the regulation should be in force by 2026. 

You can read my previous piece on the AI Act here.

Bits and Bytes

A fight over facial recognition will make or break the AI Act
Whether to ban the use of facial recognition software in public places will be the biggest fight in the final negotiations for the AI Act. Members of the European Parliament want a complete ban on the technology, while EU countries want the freedom to use it in policing. (Politico)

AI researchers sign a letter calling for focus on current AI harms
Another open letter! This one comes from AI researchers at the ACM conference on Fairness, Accountability, and Transparency (FAccT), calling on policymakers to use existing tools to “design, audit, or resist AI systems to protect democracy, social justice, and human rights.” Signatories include Alondra Nelson and Suresh Venkatasubramanian, who wrote the White House’s AI Bill of Rights.

The UK wants to be a global hub for AI regulation
The UK’s prime minister, Rishi Sunak, pitched his country as the global home of artificial-intelligence regulation. Sunak’s hope is that the UK could offer a “third way” between the EU’s AI Act and the US’s Wild West. Sunak is hosting a AI regulation summit in London in the fall. I’m skeptical. The UK can try, but ultimately its AI companies will be forced to comply with the EU’s AI Act if they want to do business in the influential trading bloc. (Time) 

YouTube could give Google an edge in AI
Google has been tapping into the rich video repository of its video site YouTube to train its next large language model. This material could help Google train a model that can generate not only text but audio and video too. Apparently this is not lost on OpenAI, which has been secretly using YouTube data to train its AI models. (The Information) 

A four-week-old AI startup raised €105 million
Talk about AI hype. Mistral, a brand-new French AI startup with no products and barely any employees, has managed to raise €105 million in Europe’s largest-ever seed round. The founders of the company previously worked at DeepMind and Meta. Two of them were behind the team that developed Meta’s open-source Llama language model. (Financial Times)

text:
COLOURS OF LOVE 
❤️🧡💛💚💙💜🩷🤍

WHAT COLOUR IS YOUR LOVE?

LOVE. One of the most profoundly meaningful and frequently spoken words in the human language, yet  one of the least understood.

We assume LOVE is LOVE, as though its meaning is universal. But love carries so many different emotional depths, dimensions and expressions.

It's experienced differently, expressed differently and received differently, because what love means to one person may mean something entirely different to another.

We spend our lives saying three words.. I LOVE YOU.

But how often do we question what those words actually mean to the person saying them?

ARE WE LOVING SOMEONE IN THE WAY WE UNDERSTAND LOVE, OR IN THE WAY THEY NEED TO EXPERIENCE IT?? 

Two people can be deeply in love yet experience and express it differently?

I've been exploring an idea called COLOURS OF LOVE.. a shared emotional language to help partners understand one another.

❤️ RED - Passion, desire and romance.

🧡 ORANGE - Playfulness, laughter and excitement.

💛 YELLOW - Appreciation, encouragement and joy.

💚 GREEN - Growth, patience and forgiveness.

💙 BLUE - Safety, trust and reassurance.

💜 PURPLE - Depth, vulnerability and understanding.

🩷 PINK - Tenderness, affection and compassion.

🤍 WHITE - Peace, authenticity and acceptance.

But here's where it gets interesting.

WHAT IF LOVE HAS THREE DIFFERENT SPECTRUMS?

1. WHAT LOVE MEANS TO ME.
                        🤍💜🧡 

The feelings and qualities I associate with being in love.

2. HOW I NATURALLY GIVE LOVE.
                         💚💛🩷 

The ways I express love through my words, actions and behaviour.

3. WHAT I NEED TO FEEL LOVED.
                          ❤️🧡💛 

The expressions that help me recognise and experience someone else's love.

These three spectra can differ within the SAME PERSON.

You might define love as peace, depth and playfulness, GIVE it through patience, encouragement and tenderness, yet NEED passion, laughter and appreciation to FEEL loved.

Your partner may have an entirely different spectrum.

Neither necessarily loves more or less.

LOVE ISN'T ONLY ABOUT WHAT WE FEEL OR GIVE. IT'S ABOUT UNDERSTANDING WHAT THE OTHER PERSON NEEDS TO FEEL THAT LOVE.

The love we offer isn't always the love another person knows how to receive.

Imagine replacing "You don't love me" with "I need a little blue today, reassurance."

Or "I've been giving green, but I didn't realise you needed pink."

The colours wouldn't replace communication. 

THEY WOULD HELP CREATE IT.

Even two people choosing the SAME colour might give it different meanings. 

That's why we ask, listen and learn.

Imagine asking someone when you first fall in love..

"WHEN YOU SAY YOU LOVE ME, WHAT DOES LOVE MEAN TO YOU?"

"HOW DO YOU GIVE LOVE, AND WHAT DO YOU NEED TO FEEL LOVED?"

Some relationships don't lack love.. they lack understanding of how that love is communicated.

LOVE HAS NO UNIVERSAL COLOUR.

THE BEAUTY OF LOVE ISN'T FINDING SOMEONE WHO SEES YOUR COLOURS, BUT LEARNING TO UNDERSTAND THE SPECTRUM THROUGH WHICH THEY LOVE. 
🤍🩷❤️🧡💛💚💙🩵💜🤎

COLOURS OF LOVE ... Exploring the emotional spectrum of human connection. 🙏💋

🇺🇲 🇮🇷 Marco Rubio says Iran's ruling clerics are revolutionary expansionists driven by religious ideology, and warns that allowing them to acquire nuclear weapons would pose an unacceptable threat to the United States and the Middle East.

Speaking at the Federalist Society's National Lawyers Convention in Washington on November 13, the U.S. secretary of state delivered an extensive defense of the Trump administration's confrontation with Iran, arguing that the conflict cannot be understood solely through conventional geopolitics.

Rubio traced Washington's confrontation with Tehran to the 1979 Islamic Revolution, describing the Islamic Republic as a state whose ultimate authority rests with a radical Shia clerical establishment. In his account, these leaders are motivated not primarily by economic prosperity or the ordinary interests of national governance, but by a revolutionary ideology that seeks to extend its influence beyond Iran's borders.

He pointed to Hezbollah in Lebanon, Iranian-backed militias in Iraq, the Houthis in Yemen and Tehran's involvement in Syria as manifestations of that strategy. Rubio argued that these organizations have enabled Iran to project military influence across the region, threaten American forces and destabilize neighboring states without relying exclusively on direct military confrontation.

The nuclear question was central to his argument. Rubio accused Tehran of developing the enrichment capabilities, missiles and technical infrastructure needed to produce nuclear weapons despite its longstanding denials of such intentions. He warned that Iran could use an eventual nuclear arsenal to shield its regional operations from retaliation and exercise far greater coercive power over its neighbors.

Rubio also compared Iran with North Korea, arguing that Pyongyang's leadership is principally concerned with regime survival, while Tehran's revolutionary leadership has ambitions extending beyond its own borders. He cited the Iranian government's violent repression of protesters as further evidence of the danger he believes a nuclear-armed Islamic Republic would represent.

Yet Rubio also made a notable statement about the current phase of the war. He argued that the economic pressure imposed on Iran has weakened the regime to the point that additional American military action is no longer necessary for now, even as Washington continues to insist that Tehran must never acquire nuclear weapons.

For Rubio, the definition of American victory is straightforward: preventing Iran from ever obtaining a nuclear weapon, whether through the destruction of its capabilities or the denial of the financial and technological resources required to develop one.

His remarks offer a detailed explanation of how the Trump administration publicly frames the Iranian threat: as a combination of revolutionary ideology, regional military networks and nuclear ambitions. They also raise a central question about the administration's strategy, whether sustained economic and military pressure can achieve a permanent nuclear outcome without another major escalation. https://t.co/QwRlboNdgW

text:
Washington is asking Japan to nearly triple its spending on hosting US troops: over ¥3 trillion for five years. Tokyo is considering about ¥300 billion a year — roughly 40% above the current level. The money covers base operations — utilities, facilities, Japanese staff salaries — not weapons purchases.

Tokyo would rather invest in infrastructure than simply pay rising bills — renovating old buildings, moving some facilities underground (contracts that would go to Japanese builders). Paying for servicing US aircraft and ships has been shelved for now: Japan's Defense Ministry says that goes beyond the original framework.

Last time, Trump opened with a demand to quadruple Japan's contribution — and Tokyo stalled until Biden arrived. That option doesn't exist now: the current agreement expires in March 2027, and Japan's offer covers only about half the US request. Negotiations will be tough.

🚨 BREAKING: Pakistan Steps In as US & Iran Clash at UN — "End the Provocations Now" 🇵🇰🇺🇳🇺🇸🇮🇷🌊

Pakistan has called for an immediate halt to military provocations in the Gulf and a fresh push for regional diplomacy at a tense UN Security Council session.

Ambassador Syed Haider Shah, Pakistan's Permanent Representative, addressed the council on Friday as the US, Iran and Gulf states traded heated accusations over attacks on shipping.

Shah condemned attacks on Gulf countries and demanded respect for their sovereignty, protection of civilians and commercial vessels, and a return to normal sea traffic.

He singled out Houthi attacks and threats against Saudi Arabia, reaffirming Pakistan's firm support for the Kingdom's security and territorial integrity.

He warned that threats in the Strait of Hormuz and Bab el-Mandab endanger sailors, disrupt global trade and deepen energy and food insecurity, especially for vulnerable economies.

Shah urged all sides to stop attacks, keep communication open and back diplomatic efforts, including the UN Secretary-General's good offices.

Iran's envoy Gholamhossein Darzi blamed US and Israeli strikes on Iran for the insecurity around Hormuz and rejected Security Council Resolution 2817 as politically motivated.

He said Tehran had not shut the door on diplomacy, but demanded Washington end military action and offer guarantees it would not be repeated.

#GONZOTRON: FOLLOW THE DAMN MONEY! 💰✈️

THE @FAANews • @L3HarrisTech • AIRS PACE INTELLIGENCE • @ATT • THE EQUITY WARRANT

ALOHA! NOW WE'RE TALKING ABOUT THE MONEY TRAIL WE INVESTIGATED YESTERDAY MORNING!

You're right. I left out the most unusual financial issue in this entire aviation story.

The two companies were L3HarrisTech and Air Space Intelligence (#ASI). Add @ATT, and we have three major corporate relationships that deserve examination.

But the extraordinary part is this:

The @FAANews reportedly pursued the right to become a shareholder in Air Space Intelligence, a private company already holding an @FAANews contract worth up to $875.95 million.

That is not speculation. The pursuit of an equity arrangement was documented by @politico in October 2026. Whether an ownership deal was actually executed remains unverified. @YahooFinance 

Exhibit 1: Three corporations and the federal treasury

@L3Technologies & Harris Merge to Form - L3HarrisTech 

L3HarrisTech 
The longstanding contractor behind the FAA's telecommunications infrastructure. The November 13 outage emerged during its copper-to-fiber modernization work, according to federal officials. @Reuters 

Air Space Intelligence (#ASI)
$875.95M
Maximum potential FAA contract value, through June 2038
Only $23.34 million was obligated in the federal award record reviewed. The contract is for flight traffic management software and associated data services.

AT&T Enterprises
$74.3M
FAA network-services development and planning order
Awarded August 12, 2026. Federal procurement records identify it as not competed — unique source. This is a documented procurement classification, not proof that the award violated procurement law.

Exhibit 2: THE WARRANT — WHEN THE CUSTOMER WANTS TO BECOME AN OWNER

This deserves its own headline.

On October 16, @semafor reported that the @FAANews was considering an ownership stake in #ASI and that the arrangement raised questions about the agency's statutory authority. @politico had obtained an internal document describing an equity term sheet and negotiations over a warrant.

A financial warrant can give its holder the right to acquire shares under predetermined conditions.

Illustration of the reported proposal, not a completed investment or confirmed cash flow.

The potential financial arrangement

#GONZO QUESTION: If a federal agency awards a lucrative contract to a company and subsequently acquires shares in that company, how is the public assured that future regulatory, procurement, and safety decisions remain independent of the government's potential financial interests?

There could be a taxpayer-benefit argument for equity participation. But that doesn't eliminate questions about conflicts of interest, who controls the shares, or the legal authority for acquiring them.

And in this case, no final warrant terms or completed acquisition have been verified.

Exhibit 3: The billion-dollar network nobody can simply unplug

The contracting story stretches back more than two decades.

In a 2021 investor presentation, L3HarrisTech described its @FAANews Telecommunications Infrastructure (#FTI) arrangement as a 20-year, $5 billion program, with a network owned and operated by L3HarrisTech.

This was not a new relationship formed after the shutdown. It was a longstanding publit. Forward.

The network was scheduled to be replaced by the @FAANews Enterprise Network Services program (#FENS).

And here's another twist.

March 2023 — @Verizon 

@Verizon received a 15-year @FAANews contract to build and operate the replacement network.

August 2026 — @ATT 

@ATT became the lead project manager and prime contractor, while @Verizon moved into a supporting role.

The @FAANews's stated reason for bypassing another competition was urgency. Officials estimated that a new procurement would take at least 22 months, jeopardizing their December 2028 modernization target. The award justification identified @ATT as the Tier-1 carrier willing and able to meet the schedule.

#GONZO QUESTION: Who decided that the deadline justified avoiding another competition? How much had already been committed to @Verizon, and what are the eventual costs of changing prime contractors?

Those questions are especially relevant because an earlier, separate 2025 controversy involved proposals to shift Verizon's work toward @SpaceX's @Starlink. That episode generated reported conflict-of-interest concerns, although it does not prove anything about the November 2026 shutdown. @APNews 

Exhibit 4: ASI — from federal contractor to $3 billion valuation

Lawmakers call for a pause in the Washington-area #SMART deployment pending answers about safety evaluations, testing, and training.

Warrant proposal reported

@politico reveals the federal government's pursuit of an equity interest in #ASI. The reported term sheet expires at the end of 2026.

The Series C financing was led by @sparkcapital, with participation from affiliates of @citsecurities (@Citadel), @craft_ventures, Andreessen Horowitz, @MeritechCapital, and @EnergyImpact_.

The timing raises a financial question: How would the government's proposed warrant be priced relative to a $3 billion private-market valuation?

We would need the actual term sheet to determine the strike price, number of shares, dilution, valuation protections, and any financial benefit to taxpayers.

We must also distinguish #ASI's software from L3HarrisTech's telecommunications infrastructure. Investigators have linked the grounding to the latter; there is no established evidence that #SMART or #ASI caused the network failure.

Exhibit 5: THE $50 BILLION QUESTION

On November 13, Secretary Duffy requested $30.1 billion for modernization before the grounding occurred, according to @WIRED.

Following the grounding, Secretary Duffy publicly said he wanted $50 billion.

An emergency can provide a powerful argument for faster modernization. It can also expose the risks of rushing procurement, leaving incompatible systems in service, or relying heavily on private contractors.

The @GovAcctProj (@Govt_Acct_Inst) had already raised concerns about schedule integration, cost estimates, and possible disruption from accelerated modernization. @WIRED 

Bringing Project 2025 into the money trail

Your Project 2025 excerpt specifically recommends that the FAA operate more like a business, separate its air traffic functions, change its funding arrangements, and permit revenue-bond financing.

That makes three separate questions relevant: 

(1) How the government awards contracts
(2) Whether it should acquire ownership in suppliers
(3) Whether the @FAANews's institutional structure should change.

THE GONZOTRON VERDICT ON THE MONEY TRAIL

We now have a far more concrete investigative framework than simply calling the grounding a false flag.

There is a longstanding contractor operating a privately owned communications backbone, a multibillion-dollar replacement program that changed leadership, an #AI [re artificial #SI = #ASI cf. #AEI] contractor with a nearly $876 million potential award, a proposed government equity warrant, major private investment, and a dramatic increase in the administration's requested modernization funding after the crisis.

Each connection deserves disclosure and scrutiny. None, individually or collectively, establishes that someone intentionally caused the outage.

Here is the passage I'd put at the heart of our #GONZO investigation:

THE GOVERNMENT CONTRACTS THE COMPANY. THE COMPANY BUILDS THE TECHNOLOGY. THE GOVERNMENT CONSIDERS BUYING THE COMPANY'S STOCK.

Then the nation's aviation communications fail, airplanes stop departing, and Washington calls for billions more.

Was the breakdown an accident, a failure of contractor oversight, or something more? The evidence must answer that.

But the financial question exists regardless: When the referee also has a financial interest in a player, who guarantees that the rules are enforced fairly?

Follow the contracts. Examine the warrants. Audit the decisions. And don't confuse a company's potential valuation with the public's actual return.

For the next investigative chapter, I'd concentrate on obtaining the #ASI equity term sheet, the @FAANews's legal justification for the warrant, the @ATT sole-source justification, and the final technical incident report. Those documents offer a much stronger route to determining whether any financial or institutional wrongdoing occurred.

#GONZOTRON: THE SKY MAY BE PUBLIC. THE NETWORKS HAVE OWNERS. AND THE PUBLIC DESERVES THE RECEIPTS.

~BbB~

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky says American negotiators have asked whether Kyiv would pull out of the remaining parts of Donbas it still holds in return for joining NATO.
The idea was raised by the US team led by Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff during the latest round of US-brokered peace talks with Russia in Abu Dhabi.
Zelensky's comments were published on Saturday, offering a rare look inside the closed-door negotiations.
He insisted that Ukraine is still not prepared to hand any territory over to Russia.
However, he said that if Kyiv were offered a complete package, he would put the question directly to the Ukrainian people in a national referendum.
That package, he explained, would need firm security guarantees, the right to keep a strong and well-funded army, and money to rebuild the war-torn country.
Washington has not confirmed his account, with a US official saying many ideas are still on the table and any final deal must be accepted by both sides.
Meanwhile, Russia has reportedly returned to hardline demands that NATO roll its forces back to where they stood in 1997, before the alliance expanded eastward.
Such a demand would affect every country that joined NATO after that date, a condition the alliance has long rejected.
The Donbas region has been the centre of the heaviest fighting since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022.
European leaders are also pushing for a bigger role in the peace process as the talks gather pace.
All eyes now turn to whether the swap idea becomes a formal proposal, and how Moscow and NATO members respond.
