text:
This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here.

I’m back from a wholesome week off picking blueberries in a forest. So this story we published last week about the messy ethics of AI in warfare is just the antidote, bringing my blood pressure right back up again. 

Arthur Holland Michel does a great job looking at the complicated and nuanced ethical questions around warfare and the military’s increasing use of artificial-intelligence tools. There are myriad ways AI could fail catastrophically or be abused in conflict situations, and there don’t seem to be any real rules constraining it yet. Holland Michel’s story illustrates how little there is to hold people accountable when things go wrong.  

Last year I wrote about how the war in Ukraine kick-started a new boom in business for defense AI startups. The latest hype cycle has only added to that, as companies—and now the military too—race to embed generative AI in products and services. 

Earlier this month, the US Department of Defense announced it is setting up a Generative AI Task Force, aimed at “analyzing and integrating” AI tools such as large language models across the department. 

The department sees tons of potential to “improve intelligence, operational planning, and administrative and business processes.” 

But Holland Michel’s story highlights why the first two use cases might be a bad idea. Generative AI tools, such as language models, are glitchy and unpredictable, and they make things up. They also have massive security vulnerabilities, privacy problems, and deeply ingrained biases.  

Applying these technologies in high-stakes settings could lead to deadly accidents where it’s unclear who or what should be held responsible, or even why the problem occurred. Everyone agrees that humans should make the final call, but that is made harder by technology that acts unpredictably, especially in fast-moving conflict situations. 

Some worry that the people lowest on the hierarchy will pay the highest price when things go wrong: “In the event of an accident—regardless of whether the human was wrong, the computer was wrong, or they were wrong together—the person who made the ‘decision’ will absorb the blame and protect everyone else along the chain of command from the full impact of accountability,” Holland Michel writes. 

The only ones who seem likely to face no consequences when AI fails in war are the companies supplying the technology.

It helps companies when the rules the US has set to govern AI in warfare are mere recommendations, not laws. That makes it really hard to hold anyone accountable. Even the AI Act, the EU’s sweeping upcoming regulation for high-risk AI systems, exempts military uses, which arguably are the highest-risk applications of them all. 

While everyone is looking for exciting new uses for generative AI, I personally can’t wait for it to become boring. 

Amid early signs that people are starting to lose interest in the technology, companies might find that these sorts of tools are better suited for mundane, low-risk applications than solving humanity’s biggest problems.

Applying AI in, for example, productivity software such as Excel, email, or word processing might not be the sexiest idea, but compared to warfare it’s a relatively low-stakes application, and simple enough to have the potential to actually work as advertised. It could help us do the tedious bits of our jobs faster and better.

Boring AI is unlikely to break as easily and, most important, won’t kill anyone. Hopefully, soon we’ll forget we’re interacting with AI at all. (It wasn’t that long ago when machine translation was an exciting new thing in AI. Now most people don’t even think about its role in powering Google Translate.) 

That’s why I’m more confident that organizations like the DoD will find success applying generative AI in administrative and business processes. 

Boring AI is not morally complex. It’s not magic. But it works. 

Deeper Learning

AI isn’t great at decoding human emotions. So why are regulators targeting the tech?

Amid all the chatter about ChatGPT, artificial general intelligence, and the prospect of robots taking people’s jobs, regulators in the EU and the US have been ramping up warnings against AI and emotion recognition. Emotion recognition is the attempt to identify a person’s feelings or state of mind using AI analysis of video, facial images, or audio recordings. 

But why is this a top concern? Western regulators are particularly concerned about China’s use of the technology, and its potential to enable social control. And there’s also evidence that it simply does not work properly. Tate Ryan-Mosley dissected the thorny questions around the technology in last week’s edition of The Technocrat, our weekly newsletter on tech policy.

Bits and Bytes

Meta is preparing to launch free code-generating software
A version of its new LLaMA 2 language model that is able to generate programming code will pose a stiff challenge to similar proprietary code-generating programs from rivals such as OpenAI, Microsoft, and Google. The open-source program is called Code Llama, and its launch is imminent, according to The Information. (The Information) 

OpenAI is testing GPT-4 for content moderation
Using the language model to moderate online content could really help alleviate the mental toll content moderation takes on humans. OpenAI says it’s seen some promising first results, although the tech does not outperform highly trained humans. A lot of big, open questions remain, such as whether the tool can be attuned to different cultures and pick up context and nuance. (OpenAI)

Google is working on an AI assistant that offers life advice
The generative AI tools could function as a life coach, offering up ideas, planning instructions, and tutoring tips. (The New York Times)

Two tech luminaries have quit their jobs to build AI systems inspired by bees
Sakana, a new AI research lab, draws inspiration from the animal kingdom. Founded by two prominent industry researchers and former Googlers, the company plans to make multiple smaller AI models that work together, the idea being that a “swarm” of programs could be as powerful as a single large AI model. (Bloomberg)

text:
"You work online? Ah! So you're into tech?" 😂

I've had this conversation more times than I can count.

And honestly, I understand why people think that way. Somehow, we've created this impression that the moment someone says they work online, they must be a software developer, programmer, cybersecurity expert or tech enthusiast.

But that's not entirely true.

Working online is NOT limited to working in tech.

Let me break it down.

People and businesses need services. And many of those services can be delivered remotely.

For example:

- Someone who can teach can become an online tutor.
- Someone who can write can work as a content writer.
- Someone who is organised can work as a virtual assistant.
- Someone who communicates well can work in customer support.
- Someone who understands social media can manage social media accounts.
- Someone who enjoys creating presentations can offer presentation design services.
- Someone who can research, type, organise documents or manage schedules can offer remote administrative support.

Do you see the connection?

These people don't necessarily need to become tech professionals before they can work online.

They are simply taking skills they already have and using digital platforms to deliver those services to people who need them.

And this is one of the misconceptions I want to address on this page.

You don't have to become a tech person before you can start working online.

You need to identify what you can do, understand who needs that service, learn how to position yourself and explore the platforms where opportunities exist.

I'm going to break these things down here, especially for those who are just starting out.

I won't assume you already know everything. We'll start from the basics.

And now I'm curious:

Have you ever told someone you work online and their immediate response was, "Oh, so you're into tech?" 😂

Or perhaps you are one of those people who still thinks online work is exclusively for tech professionals?

Let's talk in the comments. You might be surprised by how many opportunities exist outside tech.

There's more than one way to work online. ❤️

Existing users keep it. Reports say people who activated the offer before Oct 29 can use it for the rest of their subscription period. New prepaid users no longer get the benefit.

Users are reacting in two ways. Some say the Jio bundle mostly gave storage and no access to the newest models like Argon, so little was lost. Others say they only stayed on Jio for the Gemini plan. Resale of cheap Gemini deals has also dried up, according to one post.

There is a separate Antigravity wrinkle. Google's forum shows Hydrogen as usable by free, AI Plus and promotional Pro users. Jio-bundled users have complained it still shows as unavailable. Google support's fix is to update to Antigravity v2.31.2, then open Settings > Models.

Key numbers:
- Post date: Nov 15, 2026
- Post views: 263.8K
- Offer cutoff for keeping access: activated before Oct 29
- Hydrogen API price: $1.50 input, $7.50 output per million tokens

text:
Based on True Events:  We Were Something. We Are Nothing Now.

Siad Barre (AUN) is gone. In his place sit 
men who treat the state as a personal cash machine and the Somali people as raw material for foreign powers. The generation that replaced him was not raised for nation-building. It was raised on hatred ⭕️ clan hatred, personal hatred, and the cold calculation that a weak, broken Somalia is more useful to outsiders than a strong one.
Under Barre, for all the repression and the catastrophic mistakes of the Ogaden War, there was still a Somali state. There was a flag that meant something beyond clan, an army that could project force, a currency, a bureaucracy, and the idea 💡 however imperfectly enforced 💡 that a person was first Somali. The literacy campaigns, the infrastructure, the insistence on a single national identity were real. Somalis abroad carried passports that opened doors. The world knew who we were.

What replaced that is not reform. It is looting with better international PR. The men who now occupy Villa Somalia and the regional capitals have turned public office into a franchise. Ports, airports, fishing rights, oil blocks, and even the security of cities are traded to Gulf states, Turkey, Ethiopia, Kenya, and others in exchange for cash, protection, and personal immunity. These are not partners; they are patrons. The officials who serve them are not national leaders. They are local managers for foreign interests.

The hatred is the fuel. The 4.5 system, the clan conferences, the armed “administrations” that function as clan militias with flags!! these are not temporary compromises. They are the deliberate product of a political class that learned, after 1991, that power comes from mobilizing your own against everyone else. 

Children grow up hearing that the neighbor’s clan is the enemy, that the state is a prize to be captured, and that loyalty to outsiders who fund your faction is smarter than loyalty to a shared Somalia. The result is predictable: no functioning national army worthy of the name, no trusted judiciary, no serious revenue system, and a capital that remains a collection of armed enclaves.

We were something. We had the largest army in the Horn, a navy, an air force, and the ambition to speak for Somalis across borders. We are nothing now !! an open market for other countries’ strategic projects, a laboratory for clan experiments, and a place where young men join Al-Shabaab or foreign-backed militias because both offer clearer pay and purpose than the state.

This is not nostalgia for dictatorship. It is an accounting. A dictatorship that collapses into permanent clan fragmentation and foreign patronage is not progress. It is regression dressed up as “federalism” and “reconciliation.” The thieves who replaced Barre did not inherit a broken system and fail to fix it. They inherited the pieces and sold them, piece by piece, while teaching the next generation that hatred of the other Somali is the only reliable currency.

Until that changes !! until office is no longer a clan concession and a foreign contract !!the simple truth remains: we were something. We are nothing now.

text:
"Glory to the UPA" Slogans Appear on Polish Monuments After $500 Bounties Offered in Emigrant Chats

Police in the Polish capital are investigating two incidents in which the phrase was spray-painted in red: on the pedestal of the Monument to the Soldier of the 1st Polish Army on Anders Street and on the Monument to the Ghetto Heroes outside the POLIN Museum of the History of Polish Jews. One of the monuments is located roughly 150 meters from the Warsaw Metropolitan Police Headquarters, TVN Warszawa reports.

As early as November 10, the Belarusian media outlet MOST reported on efforts to recruit perpetrators for such tasks in a Telegram chat for migrants. A correspondent for the publication responded to an ad and was offered $500 to spray-paint the slogan onto monuments in Poznań and affix QR codes. The recruiter promised to cover travel expenses and claimed similar commissions were available for residents of Warsaw, Wrocław, and Lublin. "They'll blame it on a Russian provocation anyway," the client wrote.

On November 13, Polish police announced the detention of a 17-year-old Ukrainian citizen for painting similar slogans—not in the capital, however, but on monuments in Gdańsk and Gdynia. He has been charged with desecrating monuments, promoting fascist ideology, and inciting national hatred. The Ukrainian Embassy in Warsaw condemned the acts of vandalism as a Russian provocation and part of hybrid warfare.

In July, Polish prosecutors referred the case of another Ukrainian national, Ilya K., to court on charges of sabotage ordered by a foreign intelligence service. According to investigators, he was paid to paint UPA slogans and symbols onto various sites, including the Monument to the Ghetto Heroes, which was also targeted in this latest incident.

In Poland, the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA) is primarily viewed as the organization responsible for the mass killings of civilians in Volhynia and Eastern Galicia in 1943–1944. Warsaw classifies the atrocities as genocide, while Ukraine does not. Over the summer, Volodymyr Zelenskyy granted the "North" Separate Special Operations Center the honorary title "Named After the Heroes of the UPA," prompting Polish President Karol Nawrocki to strip Zelenskyy of the Order of the White Eagle, while several Ukrainian politicians voluntarily renounced their Polish state awards. Officials in Warsaw have even stated that the Volhynia massacre must be addressed when considering Ukraine's application to join the European Union.

text:
Democratic politicians, party officials, and progressive activists have repeatedly used racial epithets and “not really black” rhetoric against black conservatives and Republican candidates (especially Clarence Thomas, Tim Scott, and Byron Donalds). The goal has been to enforce political conformity by treating deviation from Democratic orthodoxy as racial betrayal.
Newsweek
Documented examples of other rhetoric
“Oreo” (black on the outside, white on the inside): Lamar County (Texas) Democratic Party chair Gary O’Connor posted that Sen. Tim Scott was “little more than an oreo with no real principles” after Scott’s 2021 response to Biden’s joint address. O’Connor apologized and offered to resign; local Democrats rejected the resignation.
The Hill
“Coon”: A Miami-Dade Democratic Party state committeewoman recorded a message played near polling places during Byron Donalds’ Florida gubernatorial campaign that said “Stay away from the coon. You know who it is.” This was reported by the Miami Herald and Bradenton Herald.
Miamiherald
“You ain’t black”: In a May 2020 Breakfast Club interview, Joe Biden told host Charlamagne tha God, “If you have a problem figuring out whether you’re for me or Trump, then you ain’t black.” Biden later called the remark “cavalier” and said it took the black vote for granted; it was widely criticized as gatekeeping black identity.
Politico
“All kinfolk ain’t skinfolk” / “skinfolk not kinfolk”: MS NOW (formerly MSNBC) host Symone Sanders Townsend used the phrase about newly elected Florida Gov. Byron Donalds, acknowledging the historic nature of his win while signaling he is not a true representative of black interests because of his politics.
Townhall
Additional recurring terms: “Sellout,” “race traitor,” “token,” “Uncle Tim” (a variant aimed at Tim Scott that trended), and “doesn’t like being black.” Democratic Rep. Bennie Thompson (D-MS) called Justice Clarence Thomas an “Uncle Tom” who “doesn’t like black people” and “doesn’t like being black” in a 2014 interview and stood by it. Georgia state Sen. Emanuel Jones (D) compared Thomas to someone who “sold his soul to the slave masters.” Rep. Jasmine Crockett (D-TX) referred to Byron Donalds as an “Uncle Tom” / “Uncle Ruckus.”
Nationalreview
These are not isolated online trolls. They come from elected Democrats, local party chairs, and prominent media figures. Black conservatives and candidates have described the pattern as an effort to keep minority voters aligned with the Democratic Party by punishing ideological independence with racial insults.
Washingtontimes
The same style of racial policing has occasionally appeared inside Democratic primaries (e.g., against black candidates seen as insufficiently progressive), but the highest-profile, sustained use has targeted black Republicans and conservatives. Both parties have histories of racially charged rhetoric; the specific “Uncle Tom” / “Oreo” / “coon” / “you ain’t black” cluster is overwhelmingly directed left-to-right against black candidates who reject Democratic policy orthodoxy.

text:
Sir Karl Popper (friend of Hayek) beautifully  in The Open Society and Its Enemies: democracy, properly understood as the open society with strong institutions, is the best practical option we have. 

Plato and Aristotle asked the wrong fundamental question, and their frameworks lead us astray. Here’s why I defend democracy using Popper’s powerful critique.
Plato’s Republic fascinates many, but Popper’s forensic takedown in Volume 1 (“The Spell of Plato”) reveals it as the original blueprint for a closed, totalitarian society. 

Plato asked “Who should rule?” and answered: philosopher-kings, an elite who grasp the eternal Forms and the true Good. He then engineered a rigid state to keep them in power forever—strict class hierarchy (guardians ruling over producers), censorship of art and ideas, the “noble lie” to pacify the masses, breeding controls, and the sacrifice of individuals to the collective “whole.”

Change is decay in Plato’s historicist view (ideal state degenerates through timocracy, oligarchy, democracy, into tyranny). His solution? Freeze society in perfection, suppress criticism, and treat the polis like a super-organism where holism trumps individualism. Popper shows this betrays Socrates’ critical spirit and paves the way for authoritarianism. Assuming infallible, wise rulers and designing institutions to entrench them leads to tyranny, not justice.

This is the foundational principle of Marxism. Marx's method was the revolutionary mechanism, a constant method essential to achieve revolutionary utopia.

Marxists' entire understanding is based on this constant cycle of revolution. That is why they ascribe any failure of communism to a flaw in the revolution. 

Such a flaw is often viewed as the resistance to their brutal methods, which calls for ever more brutality to overcome.  This explains the astonishing levels of cruelty and brutality we see in communist systems. 

That is why Marxism is such an incredibly dangerous ideology because the proponents believe they are doing good, which can excuse some of the most hideous crimes against humanity.  

Imagine sending a peasant farmer and his family to certain death for owning a sewing machine, as happened in the Soviet Union or torturing people on a metal bedstead through electrocution in 1970's Cambodia. Burying starving children alive for stealing rice in China.  

Aristotle, Plato’s student, offers a more empirical take in Politics with his classification of constitutions: rule by the one (monarchy/tyranny), the few (aristocracy/oligarchy), or the many (polity/democracy). 

He preferred mixed or moderate forms and saw “democracy” (deviant rule by the many, often the poor for their own interests) as unstable, prone to factionalism, mob rule, and degeneration. Aristotle’s essentialism and teleology still tie into cycles of rise and decay, assuming natural forms and purposes that history unfolds.

These are insightful observations, but they operate within the same flawed paradigm,

Popper rejects. Debating which number should rule best keeps us trapped in utopian blueprints or fatalistic cycles instead of practical solutions.

Popper’s revolutionary shift: Abandon “Who should rule?” entirely. The fundamental problem of politics is: “How can we so organise political institutions that bad or incompetent rulers can be prevented from doing too much damage?” (See Open Society, around the discussion of leadership and institutions.)

Democracy—constitutional, with rule of law, free speech, regular elections, opposition, and checks and balances—wins here. It doesn’t assume the many are inherently wise or virtuous (Popper rejects naive majoritarianism; “the people do not rule anywhere; governments rule”).

It provides peaceful, institutionalised ways to remove failing leaders without violence or revolution. It turns governance into an error-correcting process, like science: propose, criticise, test, reform.
This creates an open society: one that embraces individualism, criticism, change through piecemeal social engineering (fix specific problems incrementally, don’t impose grand utopias), and fallibility. No one has perfect knowledge of the Good. Open societies bear the “strain of civilization” but deliver real progress, freedom, and the ability to learn from mistakes.

I would say we all have self-interest and a deep anxiety about our future. Humans, like every other conscious creature, are concerned about their next meal and what comes after it. That is why the squirrel in my garden is burying nuts as winter approaches—it is a basic survival instinct that comes from being aware of an uncertain future. Anxiety is key here because it reveals how we experience temporality: we know the present will end and that we must prepare for what follows.

It is far better to build an economic system that recognises and works with that self-interest. Adam Smith saw this clearly. He understood that a productive society rests on incentivising and protecting the results of self-interested hard work. When people produce goods and services for voluntary exchange, the wider community’s needs are best satisfied—precisely because each person is motivated to make what others actually want and offer it at the most competitive price to earn a surplus (profit).

Thomas Burke and Adam Smith saw clearly the faults in the thinking of the French Revolution and why it led to terror.  They also saw the solution: property rights, democracy and the free exchange of goods and services.

text:
The Evolution of Matchless Amplifiers, 1989-2026

Founded in Hollywood, California, in 1989 by Mark Sampson and Rick Perrotta, Matchless helped establish the modern boutique amplifier industry. Its tube amplifiers combined vintage British circuit influences, hand-wired construction, premium transformers and heavy-duty components.

1989 - Matchless Founded

Sampson, an experienced amplifier technician familiar with vintage Vox designs, partnered with Perrotta to develop reliable professional amplifiers. Early prototypes were assembled in small workshops before commercial production began.

1991 - DC-30 Breakthrough

The DC-30 attracted national attention at the 1991 NAMM Show. Its 30-watt circuit employed four EL84 output tubes and two preamp channels, one using 12AX7 triodes and the other an EF86 pentode. The HC-30 offered the same basic architecture in head form.

1990s - Model Expansion

Matchless expanded beyond its original C-30 platform. The Clubman 35 employed two EL34 output tubes, delivering 35 watts. The Chieftain offered 40 watts from two EL34s, while the Lightning 15 used two EL84s for 15 watts. The Spitfire provided another compact EL84 design.

1994-1995 - Corporate Partnership

Matchless entered a business arrangement with U.S. Music Corporation, associated with Guild and Randall. The relationship ended in 1995, and Matchless continued independently.

1998-1999 - Financial Collapse

Despite its reputation, rising manufacturing costs and financial pressures undermined the original company. Matchless entered bankruptcy in 1998, with closure reported in 1999.

2000 - Matchless Revival

Matchless reopened in August 2000 under Phil Jamison, a veteran of the original operation. Manufacturing resumed in Los Angeles, retaining established circuit designs, hand wiring and robust construction.

2000s-2020s - New Designs

The Independence 35 introduced three channels and a 35-watt output stage using two EL34 tubes. The Laurel Canyon 20 employed two 6V6 output tubes, expanding Matchless beyond its traditional EL84 and EL34 configurations.

2025 - Mark Sampson

Co-founder Mark Sampson died February 27, 2025, aged 70. His engineering work helped establish boutique tube amplifiers as a significant category of professional guitar equipment.

2026 - Continuing Production

Matchless continues manufacturing tube amplifiers in Los Angeles, including established designs and newer models.

Collector Identification

Original C-30 series amplifiers carry M-prefix serial numbers; revival examples use A prefixes. Original Clubman and Chieftain models use C prefixes, changing to J after 2000. Lightning and Spitfire models use F prefixes originally and G prefixes following the revival.

Transformer date codes provide additional manufacturing evidence when components remain original.

Matchless demonstrated that small-scale American manufacturers could compete through circuit engineering, component selection and construction quality. Although the original company failed, its designs survived, establishing a continuous historical legacy from 1989 through 2026.

Here's a few other things her critics should know:

NYU awarded Taylor Swift an honorary Doctor of Fine Arts, a Ph.D, in recognition of her major cultural, artistic, and humanitarian achievements.  NYU’s reasoning was detailed at the graduation ceremony.  

Artistic & Commercial Impact: NYU described her as "one of the most prolific and celebrated artists of her generation".  The university specifically cited her historic milestones, including being the only female artist to win Album of the Year at the Grammys three times (she has since won a 4th, the only person ever to do so) and the only solo artist this century to have three albums reach No. 1 in a single year.  

Advocacy for Artists' Rights: During the ceremony, NYU praised her "commitment to speaking out forcefully, eloquently, and effectively on behalf of all artists".  This referred to her high-profile public battles over music ownership, streaming royalties, and re-recording her master catalog.  

Philanthropy & Anti-Discrimination Advocacy: The official citation recognized her work as a philanthropist and highlighted her "fierce advocacy for protection of those facing discrimination".  

Global Cultural Reach: Jason King noted that she "crossed genres, demographics, age groups, and borders of all kinds to touch lives around the globe".  

Beyond the formal citation, NYU already had an active academic tie to Swift’s career.  Just months before the ceremony, NYU’s Clive Davis Institute of Recorded Music launched an official college course dedicated to analyzing her songwriting, business strategy, and cultural influence.  

Her lyrics are also the subject of courses offered by prestigious universities such as Harvard, Duke, and Stanford.  

Haters:  You can refer to her as Dr. Swift in the future.  It's the proper honorific for someone who holds a Ph.D.

RT @velitesgear | Full Text Article: https://t.co/56qwg8qKDL | Author: @Helionbooks "The Most Disastrous of Defeats: Ramillies and the Campaign of 1706 

By Neil Litten

I have often asked myself how come the textbook triumph the Duke of Marlborough secured at Ramillies has received so little literary attention. In large part, this is due to the passive role assigned to the English contingent, which was only employed in a feint attack against the French left flank prior to its involvement in the ensuing pursuit. Although the presence of the feared redcoats crucially induced Marshal Villeroi’s flawed troop disposition, the isolated sector they operated in visually cut them off from the rest of the battlefield. Their determined assault there, only later recognised to be a ruse in Marlborough’s grand plan, critically ensured no French troops moved south during the afternoon, allowing the decisive breakthrough to come elsewhere. The subsequent collapse of the French centre was not personally witnessed by any of the letter writers or diarists whose unknowing participation in the deception assisted its success. This, in turn, led to a perception among the English scribes that the scale of the French defeat was less than the reality. As a result, Ramillies has lived long under the shadow of the battle of Blenheim fought two years earlier, despite being universally lauded as the more complete victory won with far fewer Allied casualties, and resulting in even greater consequences.

With the usually verbose commentators of other engagements either silent or writing in the most general of terms, I have only been able to answer the original question by making extensive use of the readily available Blenheim Papers housed in the British Library, and by widening out my research into foreign primary sources. Through the discovery, translation and inclusion of this material, in many cases for the first time in English, I have been able to offer a more balanced and nuanced sequence of events. Existing accounts of Ramillies, whether within biographies of Marlborough or as short studies of the engagement, have irritatingly continued to rehash errors and myths, and largely ignore new evidence. It is this frustration that I have attempted to address in my book. In order to give a clearer picture of the battle as it unfolded, and to present both sides of the story within an unbiased framework, I have trawled through libraries, museums, online resources, journals and periodicals to uncover much new material. For example, the long-held belief that Taviers was only taken after ferocious fighting, is dismissed by reference to the irrefutable evidence of the principal players present in that sector. Likewise, the French army’s limitations in a firefight are discussed, and its entire performance during the battle is analysed in the wake of the numerous reports and apologias send by officers and units to Louis XIV to justify their part in the disastrous day. Marshal Villeroi, though guilty of tactical mistakes once on the battlefield, becomes a convenient scapegoat in this process, notwithstanding that he was merely following the King’s instructions to march along a confrontational path.

In the later chapters I have sought to place the victory at Ramillies within the context of the campaign of 1706 and the war overall. The initial impact was extraordinary; the great towns of Brabant and Flanders viewed the Allies as liberators and opened their gates with token or no resistance. Similarly, the Italian theatre was transformed, culminating in the relief of Turin by Prince Eugène. However, as the threat of France dominating Europe receded, the common bonds that held the Grand Alliance together began to unravel, leaving the principal war aim of thwarting Bourbon dynastic aspirations in Spain unattainable.

Comprehensive appendices complement the narrative containing orders of battle, casualty lists, regimental breakdowns by nationality, notes on sources and a possible explanation to the strange story of the Kylemore flag.

The Most Disastrous of Defeats: Ramillies and the Campaign of 1706 is available to buy here.

text:
The Same AI That Could Stop the Next Pandemic Could Also Be Harming Your Health. Here’s How. | Darren Orf, Popular Mechanics

When CEOs and scientists wax poetic about the potential benefits of AI, the technology’s impact on human health often rises to the top—and in many ways, they’re not wrong. Artificial intelligence’s ability to sift through massive datasets makes these algorithms ideal for spotting early-stage cancer or discovering novel drugs. The United Nations even notes that AI-powered disease surveillance could detect potential outbreaks quickly and prevent crises from spiraling into global pandemics.

However, like any tool, artificial intelligence can also be used for nefarious purposes, and a new perspective published in the New England Journal of Medicine highlights a particularly insidious one and its potential impacts on human health: mass surveillance. Debates over how governments and companies collect our personal data are usually framed as civil liberties or national security issues. But experts from Massachusetts General Hospital, Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine, and Harvard Medical School say that being watched can make us sick, and in the age of AI, things could get much, much worse.

The authors identify at least three ways surveillance harms health. First, knowing (or even believing) that you’re constantly being monitored can lead to hypervigilance and chronic “anticipatory stress,” which takes a toll on both physical and mental health. Second, surveillance can scare vulnerable people away from essential health behaviors. This includes groups with a reasonable fear of persecution, such as undocumented immigrants or people seeking reproductive or gender-affirming care, who may avoid pharmacies and clinics, hold back details from their doctors, or even skip buying groceries. Third, surveillance data can be used to hand out things that shape our health, like insurance, housing, and jobs, unequally.

“Historically, mass surveillance programs in the United States have most often been organized by government agencies and subject to democratic oversight,” the authors write. “AI-enabled surveillance, however, relies on data ecosystems that are controlled primarily by private companies.”

That’s a big distinction. The Fourth Amendment’s protections are limited when people voluntarily share information with third parties, even if they don’t realize they’re doing so. HIPAA also generally doesn’t cover data collected by consumer-facing tech companies. As a result, AI companies and other private actors can access and analyze vast amounts of personal data, and they could share it with the government without your knowledge or permission. Traditional surveillance usually needed human oversight. AI, by contrast, can continuously comb through social media, search results, financial transactions, geolocation records, and camera footage, then combine it all into increasingly powerful predictions.

This concern isn’t without real-world precedent. The Denver-based Palantir Technologies, founded by billionaire Peter Thiel, developed AI-enabled tools for U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), including a system known as ImmigrationOS. ICE has used these tools to combine information from multiple government databases, including visa histories and Medicaid records, to target people for immigration enforcement. Another tool, called Enhanced Leads Identification and Targeting for Enforcement (ELITE), pulls names, photos, addresses, and race and ethnicity data from Medicaid records to map areas with people who could be detained, according to reporting in The BMJ. It can reportedly even generate a “confidence score” for whether someone might be at home.

For the authors, all this surveillance amounts to public health problem. When data collected for health care or social services can be repurposed for surveillance, trust erodes, and people may stop using vital programs. That’s why they argue that AI-enabled mass surveillance should be considered an emerging “structural determinant of health,” which they define as a social, political, environmental, or economic condition that shapes how health and illness are distributed across a population.

“We believe medicine has an urgent responsibility to confront these developments,” the authors write. “Decisions about AI-enabled mass surveillance are being made with limited input from health experts, even though these systems have clear consequences for population health.” Health care technologies can contribute to the problem, too. Clinicians increasingly recommend wearables and smartphone apps that continuously collect patient data, which means the medical system may be feeding the same data streams that could be used for surveillance.

Still, there are ways to fight back. The authors recommend that health care institutions push policymakers for stronger health data protections. They point to Washington state’s 2023 My Health My Data Act, which extended privacy protections to some consumer health data that HIPAA doesn’t cover, including information inferred by algorithms. Nevada and Connecticut have passed similar laws. But the authors warn that these protections are limited, differ from state to state, and don’t stop government agencies from getting and using that data.

The courts offer another option. More than 20 state attorneys general have sued the federal government for sharing Medicaid data with ICE and Palantir, and the authors say health care institutions can support these lawsuits by publicly opposing troubling data-sharing deals. Clinicians can also help by documenting patients’ fears about how their data is used and any resulting changes in whether they seek care, which gives litigators and policymakers evidence to work with.

AI surveillance could still be a boon to public health. The same ability to rapidly pull together data from different sources that makes it dangerous could also help health officials spot and respond to threats more effectively. In the end, AI is just a tool, and it’s up to us how we use it. But the authors warn that we may not have long to decide. By the time AI surveillance’s effects become fully apparent, its infrastructure “may already be deeply embedded in everyday life.” As they put it, “The norms established today could determine whether AI-enabled surveillance becomes a tool in service to population health or a driver of avoidable health inequities and structural harm.”

text:
In Japan, you end up in the newspaper when something has gone terribly wrong.

So it's strange that Michiru, who roomed with my wife in college, has a scrapbook of newspaper clippings about her family four inches thick.

In 2009, her husband's company sent them to a town in Nebraska. Population 1,140. One stoplight, which only blinks.

The town has a weekly paper. On page three, there's a column called "Around Town." A woman named Arvella has written it for forty-one years. Who visited their daughter in Lincoln. Whose tomatoes came in. Who is "doing much better, thank you."

The week they arrived, the Japanese family made Around Town.

They never left it.

Word for word:

"Welcome to Hiroki and Michiru Sugino and their daughter Honoka, 5, all the way from Japan, who have moved into the old Lindqvist place. Michiru says they do not need anything. We'll see about that."

"The Suginos received nine pies in their first week. Michiru reports they have 'eaten some.' Ladies, go get your pie plates. She is too polite to call. She is also too polite to stop eating them."

"Hiroki Sugino watched his first Husker game at Don and Gail's. He stood up for the kickoff. Nobody told him to. So the whole den stood up with him. We have decided to keep doing that."

"Honoka Sugino, 6, lost her first tooth at the Fourth of July picnic, in a caramel apple. If found, it is somewhere in the Johnsons' yard. The tooth fairy has been notified of the international situation."

"Michiru brought something called 'sushi' to the Methodist potluck. It was gone in eleven minutes. Pastor Lund had four. Pastor Lund has asked that we not print that. We are printing it."

"Hiroki's car went into the ditch on County Road 9 in the January storm. The Mueller boys pulled him out in twenty minutes. Hiroki offered them money. The Mueller boys are still laughing."

"Honoka Sugino played the smallest pumpkin in the Harvest Festival play. One line: 'I am a pumpkin.' She said it like she meant it. Standing ovation. Her father filmed the entire thing upside down."

Then there's one that isn't funny.

"Michiru Sugino's father passed away in Japan on Sunday. She could not get home in time. If you see her this week, you don't have to say anything. Just sit with her a while."

Michiru says she locked the door. In Japan, grief is private. You don't burden people.

Nobody in that town reads "locked door" that way.

The next week:

"Michiru reports that thirty-one people came and sat. Some brought their own lawn chairs. Nobody said much. She says it was more people than came to her father's funeral. She says thank you. She also says please, please stop bringing pies."

In 2012, the company called them home.

"The Suginos fly back to Japan on Thursday. Hiroki asked Around Town to print: 'Thank you, everyone. We were very happy here.' Michiru asked us to print nothing. We are printing both."

That should have been the last clipping.

It wasn't.

Arvella kept writing about them. Every few months, for fourteen years, from a town they no longer lived in.

"Word from Japan: Honoka has started school. She told her class she is from Nebraska. Nobody in Japan has argued with her."

"Word from Japan: Hiroki reports that every fall Saturday he still stands up for the Husker kickoff. In Osaka, that is one o'clock in the morning. His wife has asked us to ask him to stop. Hiroki, sit down."

Last month, an envelope came to Osaka.

Honoka got married in October. She is twenty-two.

She was on the front page.

Her wedding photo, in a white kimono. Above it, the biggest headline of the year:

OUR HONAKO GETS MARRIED

They spelled her name wrong. A correction ran the next week:

"The bride's name is Honoka. We knew that. We were excited."

Under the photo, Arvella had written one more line.

"The tooth has still not been found. The Johnsons have not stopped looking."

Then Michiru turned to page three.

It was Arvella's last Around Town. She's 86. After forty-one years, she had decided to retire. She said she wanted to go out on good news.

She chose Honoka.

Japan has more than 120 million people. No paper here printed that wedding.

A town of 1,140 put it on page one.

Michiru finally understands the difference.

In Japan, you're in the paper when something goes wrong.

In Nebraska, you're in the paper because you're theirs.

Stephen Speaks frontman Rockwell Ryan Ripperger is marveling at the nighttime view of Rockwell in Makati from his Manila balcony—even joking that the city bearing his name has grown almost as much as his band has.

In a Nov. 15 post via the band's official Facebook page, Ripperger shared a photo of Rockwell, clarifying that he has "no association" with the place despite having the same first name. He described the development as "just breathtaking."

He then recalled seeing the Milky Way for the first time while looking up at the skies over a pasture in Oklahoma, about 100 kilometers from any city lights. The experience, he said, was "absolutely breathtaking."

But for him, Manila offers a different kind of wonder.

"But cities like Manila take my breath away too. Places like this blow my mind equally," he wrote. "It is truly amazing what humans can build."

Ripperger also shared that the photo was taken using an iPhone 14 Pro Max with a cracked screen and was not edited.

The post also prompted a bit of Rockwell history. One commenter explained that the district was named after James Chapman Rockwell, the first president of Meralco. Its Power Plant Mall, meanwhile, takes its name from the thermal power station that once stood on the property and closed in 1994.

Ripperger then shared his own history with the place: His first performance in Manila was at the Rockwell Tent in 2003, when the development was still much smaller.

"Wow. Feels like yesterday," he wrote. "This city that has my name, has grown…. Ironically, so has Stephen Speaks. Or maybe slightly intentional."

The post came as Stephen Speaks prepares for a series of performances in the Philippines, including its Right on Time show on Nov. 27 at Teatrino Promenade in Greenhills, San Juan.

The band is set to kick off its Right on Time world tour in Dubai on Nov. 21, followed by the Manila show six days later. Ripperger is also scheduled to perform in Cebu on Dec. 13 at The Social Park Avenue. Stephen Speaks will join the lineup of Maskipaps: The Crossover 2026 on Dec. 19 at the UP Sunken Garden in Quezon City.

The band found a particularly devoted audience in the Philippines in the early 2000s, with crowd favorites such as "Passenger Seat" and "Out of My League."

Alabama Duck Hunters Gear Up for Promising Waterfowl Season

Alabama offers exceptional waterfowl hunting opportunities, particularly when local waterways and hunting grounds retain sufficient water. According to David Rainer, writer for the Alabama Department of Conservation and Natural Resources, having a decent amount of water on a property or hunting area is essential, as ducks traveling along the lower Central and Mississippi Flyways will continue flying until they locate suitable water sources.

LINK TO DETAILS:  https://t.co/QZ0uSyn1MG

With dry conditions affecting western Alabama and neighboring flyway states, duck hunters are happy to see rain in the state. Adequate rainfall ensures proper water coverage, making local habitats far more attractive to migrating waterfowl. Some of the most popular duck hunting areas across Alabama include the Mobile-Tensaw Delta, the Tennessee River lakes, the Tennessee-Tombigbee Waterway, and Guntersville.

For hunters planning their trips, Alabama's duck, coot, and merganser season is split into two segments:

First Segment: November 27–28
Second Segment: December 5 through January 31, 2027

In addition to hunting within state borders, many Alabama duck hunters travel out of state to hunt at Honey Brake Lodge in Louisiana. Situated on over 20,000 acres of the delta, Honey Brake is within easy driving distance and serves as a premier destination for waterfowl enthusiasts looking for expansive hunting grounds.

While Arkansas and Louisiana traditionally stand as the top states for duck hunting, Alabama could rise to a whole new level with an ample amount of rainfall this season. Those who wish for a hunting memory of a lifetime can always book a trip to the legendary Honey Brake Lodge for an unforgettable comparison.

In Alabama, hunting licenses can be conveniently purchased online through the official portal or via the Outdoor Alabama mobile app. Applicants can also obtain a license in person by visiting local county probate offices, License Commissioner locations, Wildlife & Freshwater Fisheries district offices, or authorized retail license agents statewide. Additionally, licenses can be ordered over the phone by calling 1-888-848-6887 or requested by mail through the Alabama Department of Conservation and Natural Resources.

While wet, dreary weather often leaves many residents, commuters, and weekend planners disappointed by canceled outdoor activities and soggy conditions, duck hunters across Alabama are widely rejoicing over the rainfall.

text:
Good morning from Virginia! 🇺🇸

In the late autumn of 1777, with the British army settled into Philadelphia and the fate of the Revolution still hanging by a thread, the Continental Congress gathered in the small Pennsylvania town of York. The delegates met in the courthouse on the square, a plain brick building that offered little comfort against the November chill. Many had traveled rough roads and river crossings to reach it. They were tired, short of money, and acutely aware that the war was going badly. It was in that modest setting, far from the drama of the battlefield, that they took up the unfinished business of creating a government.

The document before them had been in the making for more than a year. John Dickinson of Pennsylvania, a careful and thoughtful man who had earlier opposed independence, had produced the first draft in 1776. What emerged after months of argument was something quite different from his original plan. The Articles of Confederation established a “firm league of friendship” among thirteen sovereign states. Each state would keep its independence and its “sovereignty, freedom, and independence.” Congress was given authority over foreign affairs, war, and the western lands, but almost nothing else. There would be no national executive, no national courts, and no power to levy taxes. Every state, large or small, would have one vote. Any change to the Articles would require the agreement of all thirteen.

The debates had been long and sometimes sharp. Larger states wanted representation based on population or wealth. Smaller states insisted on equality. States with claims to western lands resisted any scheme that might force them to surrender those claims for the common good. Men who had only recently broken free of one distant power were determined not to create another. On November 15 they finally voted to adopt the Articles and send them to the states for ratification. It was not a moment of triumph so much as a hard-won compromise under the pressure of war.

The Articles would not take full effect until Maryland’s ratification in March 1781, nearly four years later. In the meantime they gave the struggling nation a single voice in dealing with France and Spain, a framework for raising armies, and a means of organizing the vast territory northwest of the Ohio River. They also revealed, in painful detail, the limits of a government that could request money but could not compel it, that could declare war but could not reliably pay the soldiers who fought it. By the time the Constitutional Convention met in Philadelphia a decade later, the lessons of those years in York and afterward were clear to nearly everyone who had lived through them.

The men who voted in the York courthouse that November day did not know they were writing a temporary constitution. They knew only that thirteen separate colonies had to act as one if they were to have any chance of surviving. In the plain language of the Articles and in the careful restraints they placed upon the central government, one can still hear the caution of a people who had just declared themselves free and were determined to remain so.

text:
Today in History 
November 15th
1887
Born on this Day 
Georgia O’Keeffe (Georgia Totto O'Keeffe) was born on November 15, 1887 in 
Sun Prairie, Wisconsin, U.S. She was an American painter whose bold flowers, towering cityscapes, and stark desert landscapes helped define American modernism. Born on a dairy farm near Sun Prairie, Wisconsin, she was the second of seven children. Encouraged to draw from an early age, she decided while still young to become an artist. She studied at the School of the Art Institute of Chicago in 1905–1906 and the Art Students League in New York in 1907–1908, winning a still-life prize. Yet she grew dissatisfied with traditional realism, which emphasized faithfully copying appearances.

Her artistic breakthrough emerged amid a wider revolution in art. The 1913 Armory Show had exposed American audiences to European modernism, while American artists were searching for new ways to express the modern world. Influenced by the design principles of Arthur Wesley Dow, O’Keeffe began exploring shape, color, rhythm, and personal feeling rather than literal representation. While teaching in South Carolina and Texas, she produced striking abstract charcoal drawings in 1915. Her friend Anita Pollitzer showed them to influential photographer and gallery owner Alfred Stieglitz, who exhibited them at his New York gallery, 291, in 1916. A solo exhibition followed in 1917.

In 1918 O’Keeffe moved to New York, where she and Stieglitz began a personal and professional partnership. They married in 1924. Stieglitz promoted her work through major exhibitions, but O’Keeffe developed a distinctive artistic identity of her own. During the 1920s she painted skyscrapers that captured the ambition of a rapidly modernizing city, alongside enormous close-up flowers whose curves and colors transformed familiar natural forms into powerful compositions. Critics sometimes interpreted the flowers sexually, an interpretation she resisted. Her 1927 retrospective at the Brooklyn Museum confirmed her growing prominence.

A decisive change came in 1929 when she began spending summers in New Mexico. Its open skies, adobe buildings, mountains, bleached animal bones, and dramatic light offered an alternative to crowded Manhattan. During the Great Depression, she endured emotional strain and a period of illness, including a breakdown in 1933, but resumed painting. Her Southwest imagery became central to her reputation. Rather than merely documenting the desert, she simplified its forms to communicate its scale, silence, and intensity. In 1939 she also visited Hawaii on a commercial commission, creating paintings inspired by its tropical plants.

Major museums increasingly recognized her achievement. The Art Institute of Chicago presented a retrospective in 1943, and in 1946 the Museum of Modern Art in New York organized its first retrospective devoted to a woman artist, featuring O’Keeffe. Stieglitz died that year. After settling his estate, she moved permanently to New Mexico in 1949, dividing her time between Ghost Ranch and her home in Abiquiú. She continued painting desert cliffs, doors, bones, and later aerial views inspired by airplane travel.

As her eyesight deteriorated in the 1970s, she adapted her working methods and received assistance. She died in Santa Fe, New Mexico, at 98. Her legacy extends beyond her unmistakable style: she challenged expectations of women in the art world, insisted on her independence, and showed how close observation of ordinary subjects could produce radically new art. The Georgia O’Keeffe Museum opened in Santa Fe in 1997, preserving and interpreting her work for later generations. #OTD

text:
Arkansas Gov. Sanders offers GOP a playbook after party’s midterm rout | Josh Christenson & Geoff Earle, New York Post

Shell-shocked Republicans are looking to Arkansas Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders for the blueprint on how to resurrect the party after the midterm blowout.

Sanders scored a double-digit win over her Democratic challenger Fred Love even as other GOP strongholds toppled — and did so even while maintaining her longstanding ties to President Trump.

“I had one of the largest margins of victory of any Republican in the country — won by 15 points — so a very clear, decisive win,” she told The Post in an interview this week.

Her explanation for the victory: a focus on kitchen-table issues that matter to her constituents, in a state that ranks 47th in the country in per capita income.

“We’ve cut taxes four times, knocked 25% off the state income tax, returned a billion and a half dollars back to the people of our state. And so I think it wasn’t just oh you’re in a red state but we delivered on things that make a difference in the day-to-day lives of the people in our state,” she said.

“We’ve really focused on not just talking about what we’ve done but showing it,” she said while visiting New York to promote her new book, “Unapologetic: Clarity and Conviction in a World Gone Crazy.”

The former White House press secretary, who has advised Trump on messaging, has used high-profile moments — including her 2023 response to President Joe Biden’s State of the Union address — to draw a contrast between what she calls “normal” ideas and Democratic policies she brands “crazy.”

It’s a message Trump has embraced — and one Republicans could revive as they prepare to take on a Democratic-controlled Congress.

“As Democrats step in, I think you’re about to see a lot of crazy. Just listen to what they’re saying … I could be wrong, but I think they’re going to give us a reason to say, ‘Yeah, they’re crazy.'”

Sanders said her administration has focused on education and access to health care and has promised not to surrender to the “radical left.” She touts state investments in paid maternity leave, incentive bonuses for teachers, rising test scores and school choice — and still calls the Iran war the “right decision,” even though she concedes it affected the election.

Her pitch extends beyond steering money to teachers.

“We have to remember that we’re the party that wants to remove regulation, remove barriers. That we are the party that pushes for individual freedom and individual responsibility. Those two things go hand in hand and it can’t be one or the other,” she said.

Sanders also defended her campaign’s decision to run a TV ad about a welfare “Brad.” It shows a gaming Gen-Zer goofing off while on the dole while touting welfare work requirements – an issue that another famous Arkansan — Bill Clinton — embraced in the 1990s.

She called the GOP criticism “manufactured outrage” and said that “if you are young, able-bodied, and capable of working, you should.”

Sanders reported spending $1.4 million in September – compared with just $24,000 by Love, an Arkansas state senator. Sanders won 54-39%, with Libertarian Colt Shelby drawing 8% of the vote.

Asked about the electoral losses elsewhere in the country, Sanders said Texas Senate candidate Ken Paxton hurt candidates down the ballot. In her own state, Sanders and Sen. Tom Cotton (R-Ark.) were both reelected. Cotton defeated Democrat Hallie Shoffner, 51% to 42%.

“When you have such a divided top of the ticket, it impacts everything else,” she said.

She defended the president’s decision to attack Iran, even though polls showed it contributed to the Republican shellacking.

“I think the president is right to stand up for our allies, to stop Iran from having a nuclear weapon, and to punch the bully in the mouth,” said Sanders, who has been mentioned as both a presidential and a vice presidential contender.

Sanders, whose term runs until 2030, said Vice President JD Vance was the Republican front-runner “without a question.”

She was less direct when asked whether she has plans to return to the White House she used to serve by running for president.

“I just won re-election. I think that it is a mistake to immediately rush to what’s next,” she said.

“I love my job, I like what I do, and I think we’re doing really good work in my state and I’m hopeful that I get to keep it for four years. So I want to keep doing what I’m doing and continue to lead in places and on things I think we’re making a big difference.”

text:
Martin Luther: The contradiction between Christian freedom and religious intolerance.

There is something deeply contradictory about how Martin Luther is celebrated as the great liberator of individual conscience, while so much of his own writing reveals an extraordinarily authoritarian, judgemental, and intolerant disposition.

His response to the German Peasants' War in 1524–25 is particularly revealing. Many of the peasants were motivated by demands for justice, freedom from oppressive feudal obligations and a Christian understanding of human dignity. 

Yet Luther, who had initially helped create an atmosphere of religious challenge to established authority, turned decisively against them. In 'Against the Murderous, Thieving Hordes of Peasants' (1525), he urged the princes to slaughter the rebels without mercy. His later antisemitic tract, 'On the Jews and Their Lies' (1543), advocated burning synagogues, destroying Jewish homes, confiscating property and suppressing Jewish religious teaching.

These were not minor inconsistencies. They expose a profound problem in Luther's understanding of Christian liberty. He challenged the authority of Rome but appeared quite prepared to endorse the coercive authority of German princes when it suited his religious and political position.

I would go further, however, and question the philosophical and theological foundations of his rebellion.

Luther's attack on indulgences needs to be understood in its historical context. There were genuine abuses in the way indulgences were promoted and monetised. But that was different from the merciless exploitation of the princes that Luther so readily excused.

The Church's relationship with money and the financing of religious institutions deserved scrutiny. The Catholic Church was not frozen in dogma but quite the opposite. 

The money financed the Renaissance, and the great changes it funded are often overlooked.  The Church was granting greater freedoms, and Luther filled that space with his ideas. Like Mao, he abused the freedoms to overthrow an institution that was evolving. 

Protestants have deliberately misrepresented the Roman Church. This is the negative projection of the other and the heart of Protestantism.  

One might draw an analogy with the way modern governments impose financial penalties or taxes on particular behaviours: the existence of an institutional mechanism does not, in itself, invalidate the underlying moral or philosophical principle. The abuses of indulgence preaching should not automatically be confused with the entire theological understanding of penance, forgiveness, temporal consequences and reconciliation that had developed within Catholic theology.

More fundamentally, Luther narrowed the question of redemption around *sola fide* — justification by faith alone. It is important to acknowledge that he did not simply advocate abandoning good works. He regarded them as the natural fruits of genuine faith. But he fundamentally altered their theological significance.

The Catholic tradition, particularly through St Thomas Aquinas, offers a more integrated understanding of the relationship between faith, grace, human nature, virtue and good works. Human beings are not simply passive objects awaiting a declaration of justification. They are moral beings, capable of participating in the life of grace, developing virtue, exercising responsibility and being transformed through their relationship with God.

This brings us to a much deeper philosophical distinction.

Aquinas understood existence, or being, through a profound metaphysical framework. God is not simply an object within the universe, nor one explanatory force alongside other forces. God is the ground of being itself — ipsum esse subsistens, subsistent being itself. The mystery of God therefore transcends the categories through which human beings attempt to understand existence.

I worry that aspects of Luther's theology reduce this profound mystery to a much narrower argument about the mechanics of salvation, faith, divine judgement and human sin. His treatment of providence, the human will and the relationship between God and humanity raises difficult questions about time, eternity, freedom and moral responsibility.

There is a danger here of turning God into an object of theological argument, rather than recognising the transcendent mystery from which all existence derives.

I also find Luther's psychological and moral disposition troubling. Rather than consistently confronting the complexity of sin within human nature, he repeatedly directed his polemics against external enemies: Rome, the peasants, the Jews and those who disagreed with him. There is an uncomfortable sense of projection here. The sinner becomes identified with the opposing group, rather than the universal human condition that Christianity asks us to confront within ourselves.

His writing frequently displays a punitive and judgemental understanding of other people. It is difficult not to see in this a dark strain of Puritanism, subsequently developed in different ways within Protestant traditions, and particularly in some interpretations of Calvinist theology.

Christianity, however, should surely be about humility, self-examination, compassion and the recognition that every human being stands in need of grace.

The Catholic intellectual tradition was not simply an oppressive structure of dogma waiting to be liberated by Luther. It represented centuries of philosophical development, debate and theological refinement, from Augustine to Aquinas and beyond. Its understanding of ontology, natural law, virtue, reason, grace and the mystery of existence is considerably more sophisticated than the caricature of medieval Catholicism that has sometimes become embedded in the popular account of the Reformation.

None of this denies the corruption and abuses within the medieval Church. Reform was happening. But reform and intellectual destruction are not the same thing.

Luther deserves recognition for his historical influence, his contribution to biblical translation and his challenge to ecclesiastical abuses. But historical influence should not be confused with moral greatness, and religious rebellion should not automatically be equated with spiritual enlightenment.

Perhaps the greatest irony is that a man celebrated for liberating Christian conscience could be so merciless in judging the consciences of others.

The Christian challenge is not simply to identify the sinner outside ourselves, but to understand the nature of sin within ourselves. That is a considerably more demanding theological and philosophical undertaking than denouncing one's opponents and claiming certainty about God's judgement of them.

text:
Christophe Barraud (@C_Barraud) led his Top 10 Macro/Financial Charts of the Week with ZeroHedge’s “Bank of Nvidia” chart, which links to a detailed piece on the state of the Nvidia investing flywheel now that Jensen Huang is out and CFO Colette Kress is running Nvidia as interim CEO (while keeping the CFO job).

ZH’s argument: per the WSJ, Reuters and The Information, Kress was the one executive who kept asking what Nvidia’s guarantees were actually worth and, in at least one case, pushed back on how big they got.

That one case was the OpenAI Ohio backstop, which she cut from a reported $250B to the $105B that was eventually filed. ZH says that’s probably good for $NVDA shareholders but bad for the long list of AI companies counting on Nvidia’s balance sheet to fund 2027. Their bottom line: the circular AI funding machine “just lost its accelerator.”

Some numbers:

▪️ Nvidia’s 10-Q for the quarter ended Jul 26 showed $530.5B of commitments and guarantees, including $108.5B of guarantees and $36B of agreements to buy back capacity from AI cloud providers.

▪️ The next leg was supposed to be a $500B GPU financing platform that Huang launched in August with Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman and KKR. The aim was to turn AI chips into collateral that lenders could fund, with Nvidia pledging to backstop up to 25% ($125B). Bloomberg reports it hasn’t closed a single deal in three months, partly because lenders want more than 25%, and Broadcom has been offering far more: it backstopped $30B of a $35B Anthropic TPU deal (86%) and $43B of a second $63B deal (about 68%). If Nvidia wouldn’t offer more under Huang, it seems unlikely it will under Kress.

▪️ Existing deals should survive, though. Goldman’s James Schneider expects every announced commitment to be honored. The next round of deals is what gets harder, he says.

The fallout from an Nvidia pullback in financing:

▪️ UBS’s Tim Arcuri estimates Nvidia generates about $50 - 60B of free cash flow a quarter, much of it recycled back into the AI ecosystem. For scale, the 10-Q IOUs alone already equal roughly 9-11 quarters of that FCF.

▪️ Investment-grade corporate spreads are just 0.89%, near the tightest since at least 2013, while the ICE BofA CCC & Lower spread hit 13.56% on Oct 23, its widest since summer 2020 and above even the 2022 peak. Most of Nvidia’s borrowers sit somewhere between those two extremes, and Nvidia’s guarantee is what turns debt backed by a cash-burning AI lab or a junk-rated neocloud into an investment-grade loan. Take it away and some deals just get more expensive, while others may not get done at all. CoreWeave fell 11% on news of Huang’s exit on the same day it was marketing a $4B+ investment-grade loan where Nvidia is presumably the guarantor.

We probably won’t learn much from Nvidia’s Q3 earnings call on Tuesday (Nov 17). Kress has been in the job less than a week, and a CFO-turned-interim-CEO with a board search underway has every reason to say “existing commitments will be honored” and nothing more.

The more useful read will come from the Q3 10-Q, which updates the footnotes behind that $530.5B for the quarter ended in late October. According to the WSJ, that’s the stretch when Nvidia was already pulling back. In late August it paused some of its credit-support deals with cloud providers (guarantees given in exchange for a cut of their revenue) and started requiring executive-team and board sign-off on each one. By October, the WSJ reports, it had begun turning off the tap. If guarantees and cloud buy-back commitments flattened or fell from July’s $108.5B and $36B, the “Bank of Nvidia” was already cutting back even before Huang left.

RT @velitesgear | Full Text Article: https://t.co/DzCtxCsBPP | Author: @militarnyi B-21 Raider Begins Weapons Testing 
The U.S. B-21 Raider stealth strategic bomber has conducted its first in-flight weapons-release tests as part of its flight-testing program.

Northrop Grumman announced this.

The company said the aircraft, which its representatives describe as “the world’s first sixth-generation aircraft,” offers exceptional payload flexibility.

The B-21 will be capable of performing a wide range of missions, from long-range strikes to operations in airspace protected by advanced air defense systems. Its design also allows integration of new weapons and expansion of the aircraft’s capabilities.

 B-21 Raider refuels in flight from a KC-135 Stratotanker. Photo credits: Northrop Grumman

The company says the B-21 is being developed as the backbone of future long-range strikes designed to penetrate enemy defenses. Its range will allow it to threaten any target anywhere in the world.

B-21 Raider

The B-21 Raider is the latest U.S. stealth strategic bomber, developed by Northrop Grumman. The program officially began in 2011 under the name Long Range Strike Bomber (LRS-B).

After a lengthy competition, the Pentagon selected Northrop Grumman as the project’s prime contractor on October 27, 2015. By 2018, the developers had completed the critical design review, paving the way for construction of the first prototypes at Plant 42 in California.

The first aircraft was officially presented on December 2, 2022, marking the first public rollout of a new U.S. bomber in three decades. On November 10, 2023, the aircraft, bearing tail number 001, made its maiden flight and was relocated to Edwards Air Force Base for further testing.

Ground and flight testing are ongoing as part of the program. These tests assess the aircraft’s reliability and cover weapons loading, data collection, and maintenance between sorties.

Northrop Grumman said it has completed structural fatigue testing equivalent to several full service lives of the aircraft.

The bombers are expected to replace the aging B-1 Lancer and B-2 Spirit fleets in the 2030s. The first production B-21 Raider is expected to arrive at Ellsworth Air Force Base in South Dakota in 2027.

 Northrop Grumman’s B-21 Raider during testing, accompanied by an F-16. Photo credits: U.S. Air Force

Northrop Grumman has already opened a B-21 production facility in Layton, Utah, covering approximately 24,600 square meters. The company has also begun construction of a new final assembly facility covering approximately 92,900 square meters at Plant 42 in Palmdale, California.

The infrastructure expansion is part of an agreement between the U.S. Department of Defense and Northrop Grumman that calls for a 25% increase in annual B-21 Raider production capacity.

To accelerate production of the planned fleet of at least 100 aircraft, the U.S. Air Force is seeking an additional $4.5 billion in funding. Meanwhile, U.S. Strategic Command chief Adm. Richard Correll believes the planned B-21 fleet should be increased to 145 aircraft.

text:
Scientists find a simple daily routine linked to less pain and depression | University of Missouri-Columbia, ScienceDaily

University of Missouri researchers found that older adults who followed consistent daily schedules reported less physical pain and fewer symptoms of depression, even when they struggled with insomnia. Keeping regular times for sleeping, eating, and other activities may help regulate the body's internal clock, which influences mood, sleep, and overall health.

---

A consistent daily routine may do more for your health than you realize. Researchers at the University of Missouri have found that older adults who follow regular daily schedules tend to experience less physical pain and fewer symptoms of depression, even when they struggle to get a good night's sleep.

The findings suggest that everyday habits, such as waking up, eating meals, socializing, and going to bed at consistent times, may play an important role in physical and mental well-being. By helping the body maintain its natural internal clock, a predictable routine could offer health benefits that extend beyond improved sleep.

The discovery could be especially important for older adults, who frequently experience sleep difficulties. According to the National Council on Aging, roughly half of adults age 60 and older report symptoms of insomnia, a condition that can make it difficult to fall asleep, stay asleep, or get restful sleep.

Daily Routines Linked to Less Pain and Depression

To investigate the relationship between sleep, daily habits, and overall health, Eunjin Tracy, an assistant professor in the College of Education and Human Development at the University of Missouri, examined survey responses from 67 older adults. Among the participants, 37 reported experiencing insomnia.

As researchers expected, those with insomnia generally reported more physical pain and higher levels of depression than participants without the condition. However, another pattern emerged when Tracy examined their daily routines.

Participants who maintained more consistent schedules tended to report less pain and fewer depressive symptoms, regardless of their sleep quality. This suggests that keeping regular daily habits may be associated with better health even when sleep problems persist.

"Regardless of sleep quality, those who reported having a regular daily routine had lower levels of physical pain and less depression compared to those without a daily routine," Tracy said. "If we are consistent with when we wake up, eat, work or study, interact with others and go to bed, those time cues help synchronize our internal body clocks. Over the long term, that seems to be linked with improved health outcomes."

Why Your Body's Internal Clock Matters

One possible explanation involves the circadian rhythm, the body's natural 24-hour timing system. This internal clock helps coordinate when we feel awake or sleepy and influences numerous biological processes, including hormone activity, metabolism, and mood.

Rather than operating independently of our surroundings, the circadian system responds to signals that help it keep time. Light and darkness are especially important, but regular activities such as eating, working, interacting with others, and sleeping can also provide timing cues.

When these signals follow a predictable pattern, they help keep the body's biological rhythms aligned. Irregular schedules, on the other hand, can interfere with that coordination.

"When we regulate our circadian rhythm well, our bodies function well, but if it gets too distracted, our bodies don't function as well," Tracy said.

Although the study did not establish that regular routines directly reduce pain or depression, the findings point to circadian regulation as one possible explanation for the connection.

The Hidden Effects of Social Jet Lag

Even relatively small changes in daily schedules may disrupt the body's internal clock. One common example is social jet lag, which occurs when a person's sleep schedule shifts between workdays and days off.

Someone who wakes up early throughout the week but stays up late and sleeps in on weekends may experience this mismatch. The resulting disruption resembles some of the effects of traveling across time zones, even though the person has never left home.

Tracy suggests that maintaining reasonably consistent schedules throughout the entire week, including weekends, may help limit these disruptions and support healthier circadian rhythms.

"As someone who wakes up and goes to bed at the same time every day, I think a daily routine can be helpful for people of all ages across their lifespan," Tracy said. "There is growing awareness about the concept of social jet lag -- waking up and going to bed at different times on weekends compared to weekdays -- and the disruptions it causes to our circadian rhythm, so hopefully this research helps more people consider the health benefits of a daily routine. Since one-third of our lives will be spent sleeping, I think health and well-being research should be looked at holistically from a 24-hour perspective and not just focus on when we are awake."

A Simple Habit With Potential Health Benefits

The research highlights an aspect of healthy living that can be easy to overlook. While getting enough quality sleep remains important, the consistency of activities throughout the day may also be connected to how people feel physically and emotionally.

Because the study relied on survey data from a relatively small group of older adults, it cannot prove that adopting a regular routine will relieve pain or depression. Larger studies would be needed to establish whether changing daily schedules directly improves these outcomes.

Still, the findings suggest that a predictable daily routine may be a useful component of a broader approach to health, particularly for people experiencing insomnia.

For older adults and potentially people of other ages, simple habits such as maintaining regular waking times, eating meals on a consistent schedule, and limiting major changes in weekend sleep patterns may help support the body's natural rhythms.

The study, "Behavioral-social rhythms and insomnia symptoms: associations with pain, body mass index, and depressive symptoms among older adults," was published in the Journal of Behavioral Medicine.
