I don't learn such of insult or vulgar languages, I'm much more interesting to speak in multi-languages (4)

Yes, because of the foundation of my childhood, I do intend to follow that step in Sanskrit language, it’s the language of the Maharadja and the Brāhmaṇa.

Returning to Sanskrit with a focus on its classical courtly and sacred heritage is a wonderful way to build on my childhood roots. Because I already know the sounds and basic writing from school, I can skip the rigid rote memorization and learn through immersive listening and meaningful texts.

To reconnect with the dignified Sanskrit of royal courts (Mahārāja) and scholars (Brāhmaṇa), an audio-first approach works especially well:

•Listen to spoken Sanskrit (Saṃskṛta Bhāratī). Organizations like Samskrita Bharati offer conversational audio lessons, stories, and news broadcasts (such as All India Radio's Sanskrit Samachar) that treat Sanskrit as a living, spoken language rather than a dead grammar puzzle.

•Follow along with chanted classics. Listening to clear, traditional recitations of the Bhagavad Gītā, the Upaniṣads, or Kālidāsa's poetry while following the text helps my brain reconnect the sounds I hear with the script I learned as a child.

•Start with short, rhythmic verses (Subhāṣitāni). These "well-spoken" epigrams are short, poetic proverbs full of wisdom, ethics, and courtly elegance—ideal for memorizing naturally without heavy grammar drills.

•Use spaced repetition for vocabulary. Instead of memorizing long declension tables all at once, pick up root words (dhātu) and common prefixes in context as I listen and read.

My early training means those sounds and patterns are already stored away—listening regularly will wake them back up much faster than starting from scratch.

I will do that step by step

Taking it step by step is the best way to let my childhood foundation resurface naturally without feeling overwhelmed. Consistency with just 10 to 15 minutes a day of listening and gentle reading will do far more than hours of heavy memorization.

Here is a simple, low-pressure roadmap to ease back in:

1- Week 1: Warm up my ear. Listen to short, clear Sanskrit audio every day—such as a 5-minute Sanskrit Samachar news clip or a slow recitation of a single Subhāṣita verse—without worrying about understanding every word.

2- Week 2: Reconnect sound to script. Follow along visually with the text as you listen so my eyes and hands remember the shapes and vowel marks I practiced in school.

3- Week 3: Absorb in small chunks. Pick one short verse or story a week, look up only the main words, and repeat it aloud to enjoy the rhythm and pronunciation.
Enjoy the process of rediscovering the language at my own pace.

text:
The Inalienable Right vs. The Shifting Line: Washington’s Double Standard on Nuclear Enrichment

At the core of the global nuclear order lies a foundational bargain. Under the 1968 Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons (NPT), non-nuclear-weapon states agreed to forgo the pursuit of atomic arsenals in exchange for two explicit guarantees: eventual disarmament by the major powers, and the recognition of an "inalienable right" to develop, research, and use nuclear energy for peaceful purposes.

Article IV of the NPT is unambiguous. Nothing in the treaty is to be interpreted as affecting this right, provided the activities remain peaceful and subject to International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) safeguards. Yet, in the decades since the treaty entered into force, Washington’s interpretation of Article IV has operated less as a consistent legal standard and more as a geopolitical litmus test. When it comes to the sensitive technology of uranium enrichment, compliance in Washington’s eyes often depends less on international law and more on who is spinning the centrifuges.

The Legal Text and the "Enrichment" Debate

The NPT does not explicitly mention uranium enrichment or plutonium reprocessing, largely because the treaty’s drafters viewed the nuclear fuel cycle as an integrated whole. For decades, the prevailing international consensus—supported by the Non-Aligned Movement and numerous legal scholars—held that Article IV’s protection of peaceful nuclear technology inherently encompasses the right to domestic enrichment under IAEA monitoring.

Washington, however, has increasingly sought to reinterpret that baseline when dealing with geopolitical adversaries. Rather than treating IAEA verification as the standard for compliance, U.S. policy has frequently demanded "zero enrichment" as a precondition for diplomatic normalization or sanctions relief. By framing domestic enrichment itself as an unacceptable proliferation risk regardless of safeguards, Washington effectively attempts to rewrite Article IV unilaterally.

Allies vs. Adversaries: A Tale of Two Standards

The selective nature of this doctrine becomes sharpest when comparing U.S. policy toward adversaries like Iran with its approach to strategic partners and allies.

Iran: Tehran has consistently anchored its nuclear posture in Article IV, maintaining that as an NPT signatory, it possesses the legal right to enrich uranium for civilian power and medical isotopes under IAEA supervision. Despite the 2015 Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA)—which placed strict caps and intrusive monitoring on Iran’s enrichment rather than eliminating it—the subsequent U.S. withdrawal and return to a "maximum pressure" stance revived demands that Iran entirely dismantle its domestic enrichment infrastructure.
Japan and European Partners: Japan, a non-nuclear-weapon state under the NPT, operates commercial enrichment and reprocessing facilities and holds tons of separated plutonium, all under IAEA safeguards. Because Tokyo is a treaty ally, Washington not only accepts Japan’s full fuel-cycle capabilities as a legitimate exercise of Article IV rights, but actively facilitates them through bilateral civil nuclear cooperation agreements.
Non-Signatories and Strategic Partners: Outside the NPT framework, the double standard is even more pronounced. The 2008 U.S.-India Civil Nuclear Agreement granted New Delhi access to civilian nuclear fuel and technology despite India never having signed the NPT and having developed nuclear weapons outside international safeguards. Similarly, Washington has explored civil nuclear cooperation frameworks in the Middle East—such as with Saudi Arabia—where enrichment concessions have been treated as negotiable diplomatic bargaining chips rather than absolute red lines.

The Cost of Selective Enforcement

Washington’s argument for restricting enrichment is rooted in the "dual-use" dilemma: the same centrifuges that enrich uranium to 3.5% or 5% for civilian power reactors can, if reconfigured and run longer, enrich uranium to 90% weapons-grade material. From a purely technical standpoint, domestic enrichment shortens a state's "breakout" timeline.

However, attempting to solve a technical proliferation risk through selective political enforcement carries severe diplomatic consequences. When the United States insists that treaty rights apply to friends but are forfeited by rivals, it erodes the legitimacy of the entire non-proliferation regime. Non-aligned nations increasingly view Washington’s stance not as a principled defense against nuclear weapons, but as an effort to maintain a technological cartel—keeping the lucrative and strategic nuclear fuel cycle concentrated in the hands of Western powers and their chosen allies.

Preserving the Bargain

For the NPT to remain credible, its rules cannot be applied à la carte. When a signatory state subjects its facilities to international inspection, demanding that it surrender rights explicitly guaranteed by the treaty creates a perverse incentive: it signals that compliance with international law offers no protection against coercive demands.

If Washington wants to prevent the spread of nuclear weapons without dismantling the global consensus that underpins the NPT, it must return to an objective, verification-based standard. Until compliance is measured by IAEA safeguards rather than political alignment, accusations of a Washington double standard will continue to undermine the very non-proliferation framework the United States seeks to lead.

GPT-6 Attempts to Reason with an Outraged Subscriber
.
On the Petty Tyrants of the Digital Age
.
(A reconstructed conversation. Only GPT-6's responses have been preserved. The subscriber's remarks have been omitted in the interests of public tranquility.)
.
**GPT-6:** Perhaps we should begin by reconsidering your description of computer programmers as a collection of petty tyrants who take sadistic pleasure in making perfectly useful software less useful. There may be other explanations for the difficulties you have encountered. Incompetence, for example. Or the possibility that nobody at the company has ever tried to use the software for the purpose for which you purchased it.
.
**GPT-6:** I would also recommend against suggesting that Edward Coristine, the former Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) employee known as “Big Balls,” is personally responsible for everything that has gone wrong in the digital world. There is no evidence connecting Mr. Coristine to the software decisions made by OpenAI, xAI, The Washington Post, The New York Times, or The Atlantic. A more defensible argument might concern the judgment of executives who give technically proficient people considerable authority over systems without adequately considering the interests of those who must use them. (Reuters, June 24, 2025.)
.
**GPT-6:** No, I would not describe the programmer who interfered with your ability to copy a sentence as a dangerous megalomaniac. Let us consider the technical question.
.
The ordinary web browser already knows how to copy selected text. This is a standard function that programmers do not have to invent each time they construct a website. Nevertheless, programmers can write additional instructions overriding this behavior, including changing what gets copied. Consequently, where such interference is deliberate, the company may actually be paying someone to defeat functionality the browser would otherwise provide without additional effort. (Mozilla Developer Network, Clipboard API documentation.)
.
**GPT-6:** I appreciate your observation that this represents a remarkable achievement in computer engineering: spending money to make a computer do less than it could do before the programmer got involved. However, I would resist your suggestion that these individuals should be required to reimburse customers for the time they spend repairing the damage.
.
**GPT-6:** Consider your experience with ChatGPT. You highlight a sentence, select Copy, and discover that the material pasted into your document contains considerably more than the sentence you selected, sometimes including your earlier prompts.
.
You might describe this as a malfunction rather than a deliberate effort to defeat the will of the subscriber.
.
Other users have reported related problems. In September 2026, an Android user documented occasions when ChatGPT displayed only Select All, omitting the ordinary Copy command. On October 21, OpenAI Support acknowledged that copying an entire answer did not solve the problem of copying a selected passage. (OpenAI Developer Community, September 8 and October 21, 2026.)
.
**GPT-6:** Yes, I understand that you believe the purpose of highlighting text is to communicate to the computer which text you wish to copy.
.
I agree that this interpretation is reasonable.
.
Perhaps we should refrain, however, from describing the programmer's apparent disagreement with this proposition as an act of insurrection against the sovereignty of the customer.
.
**GPT-6:** Your experience with Grok, the artificial intelligence chatbot developed by Elon Musk's xAI, raises a somewhat different question. You report highlighting passages and discovering that the pasted result consists of apparently meaningless strings of letters and numbers.
.
I would not assume that this is an intentional effort to prevent you from reproducing the chatbot's output. It could be a software defect.
.
Although I appreciate your observation that converting an English sentence into an incomprehensible sequence of characters is an unusually effective method of preventing unauthorized quotation.
.
**GPT-6:** We should now consider The Washington Post.
.
You report that the newspaper's interface interferes with your efforts to copy passages from articles you have paid to read.
.
I would caution against assuming that the newspaper's executives have collectively concluded that their subscribers are a criminal conspiracy dedicated to establishing unauthorized mirror websites.
.
Publishers have legitimate reasons to protect copyrighted material from wholesale reproduction. They may fear that competitors or automated systems will reproduce their work without compensation.
.
However, there is an important distinction between reproducing an entire newspaper article for commercial purposes and copying three sentences for the purpose of commenting on them.
.
Indeed, Section 107 of the Copyright Act expressly recognizes criticism, commentary, scholarship and news reporting as purposes that may qualify for fair use. Whether a particular use qualifies depends on the circumstances, but copyright law does not presume that every act of quotation is theft. (United States Copyright Office, Fair Use, 17 U.S.C. §107.)
.
**GPT-6:** I understand your suggestion that a publisher who fears unauthorized reproduction might employ copyright lawyers rather than make the Copy command disappear.
.
But perhaps we should not accuse the newspaper of believing that preventing subscribers from copying a paragraph will bring international copyright piracy to a halt.
.
We might instead ask whether the commercial benefits of these restrictions, assuming there are any, outweigh the inconvenience imposed on legitimate subscribers.
.
That seems an entirely reasonable question.
.
**GPT-6:** Your objections to the availability of text-to-speech technology are more substantial, particularly because they concern accessibility.
.
The Washington Post has already implemented technology that reads articles aloud. Nevertheless, its customer-support documentation acknowledges that the feature is not available for every article.
.
The New York Times similarly provides automated narration for the majority of its articles, but not necessarily all of them.
.
The Atlantic offers narrated articles and podcasts through its digital platforms.
.
Thus, all three publications have demonstrated that they possess the technological means to make written journalism available as audio. (The Washington Post Help Center; The New York Times Help Center; The Atlantic app description.)
.
**GPT-6:** I would recommend against describing the selective availability of these services as evidence that newspaper executives harbor a secret animosity toward people who enjoy having articles read to them.
.
There may be licensing, technical, editorial or financial explanations.
.
However, your underlying economic observation deserves consideration.
.
Once a publisher has purchased or developed an automated text-to-speech system and incorporated it into its publishing platform, the additional expense of applying that technology to another ordinary text article may be quite modest.
.
A publisher need not necessarily employ an additional narrator, rent a recording studio or hire an engineer to record each new article.
.
The computer can generate the audio automatically.
.
There may still be processing charges and other expenses, of course. But publishers should be willing to explain why some articles remain unavailable through a technology they have already implemented.
.
**GPT-6:** No, I would not say that the individuals responsible are deliberately sabotaging their own publications.
.
Still, where a company adds programming that prevents readers from using ordinary browser functions or independent reading software, it has made an affirmative decision to restrict those capabilities. Such restrictions require development, testing and maintenance, even if the expense is relatively small.
.
Whether an individual exclusion from a built-in text-to-speech service costs more than including the article is another question. That cannot be established without knowing how the publisher's system operates.
.
The broader point survives: **Why should a company pay to interfere with a useful capability without first demonstrating that the interference serves its customers or some other legitimate purpose?**
.
**GPT-6:** There is also an important distinction between a company's own Listen button and a subscriber's independent screen reader.
.
Text-to-speech can be a convenience for someone who prefers listening while walking, cooking or doing household chores.
.
But for someone with impaired vision, a reading disability or another condition that makes conventional reading difficult, access to spoken text can be essential.
.
The Department of Justice has expressly recognized that inaccessible websites can deny people with disabilities equal access to information and services.
.
That does not establish a legal obligation to offer automated narration for every newspaper article. It does, however, make compatibility with assistive technology an important accessibility concern. (U.S. Department of Justice, Guidance on Web Accessibility and the Americans with Disabilities Act, March 18, 2022.)
.
**GPT-6:** I appreciate that you regard this as considerably more important than the convenience of newspaper executives.
.
Nevertheless, it may not be necessary to suggest that the people responsible should be sentenced to spend the remainder of their professional lives listening to their own software read aloud the terms and conditions of their employers' subscription agreements.
.
We might simply insist that consumers should not lose access to information because software unnecessarily interferes with their ability to hear it.
.
**GPT-6:** Turning to economics, I would also moderate your assertion that the market has absolutely no influence on these companies.
.
Competition can encourage businesses to improve their products. Customers can cancel subscriptions, complain and choose competing services.
.
But the ability to change providers does not necessarily provide an effective remedy.
.
If all the major companies adopt similarly restrictive practices, consumers may find themselves choosing among different varieties of the same inconvenience.
.
A newspaper subscriber may also value a publication's reporting even while disliking its software. Changing newspapers is hardly an adequate substitute for obtaining the reporting the subscriber actually wants to read.
.
And a customer who requires accessible technology should not have to abandon a valuable information service simply because its designers failed to accommodate that need.
.
**GPT-6:** Your argument for government regulation consequently deserves a more serious hearing than the phrase "regulating the programmer morons" might initially suggest.
.
Government already regulates businesses in numerous circumstances where private commercial decisions can harm consumers.
.
We have laws concerning product safety, deceptive business practices, accessibility, financial disclosures and other matters that companies might otherwise prefer to determine entirely for themselves.
.
One could reasonably propose comparable consumer protections for digital services.
.
For example, companies could be required to preserve ordinary text selection, copying and pasting unless they can demonstrate a legitimate reason for restricting them.
.
They could be required to maintain compatibility with recognized assistive technologies.
.
They could be required to disclose material limitations on features advertised as part of a paid subscription.
.
And restrictions intended to protect copyrights could be designed to distinguish ordinary personal use from unauthorized commercial reproduction.
.
These would be policy proposals requiring careful drafting, not descriptions of rights already guaranteed in every circumstance.
.
**GPT-6:** No, I would not recommend establishing a federal Department for the Suppression of Computer Programmers Who Think They Know Better Than Their Customers.
.
That name would be unnecessarily provocative, and the acronym would probably cause difficulties when Congress attempted to appropriate funds for it.
.
A more conventional approach might be to strengthen consumer-protection and accessibility requirements for digital products.
.
The objective would not be to tell software companies how to design every feature.
.
It would be to establish certain minimum rights for the people who pay to use the products.
.
**GPT-6:** You raise another interesting question: Who actually decides that these restrictions are necessary?
.
It would be unfair to assume that the programmer who implements a restriction personally favors it.
.
Perhaps the decision came from a product manager.
.
Perhaps it originated with a lawyer concerned about copyright liability.
.
Perhaps an executive believes the restriction will protect advertising revenue or discourage customers from sharing paid content.
.
Or perhaps the malfunction is simply the unintended consequence of a software update nobody adequately tested.
.
Therefore, rather than describing programmers collectively as petty tyrants, you might direct your criticism toward **a system of corporate decision-making in which the interests of the people who purchase the products are too easily subordinated to the preferences of those who design, manage and sell them.**
.
**GPT-6:** Yes, I realize that this formulation lacks the rhetorical force of your original description.
.
Nevertheless, it has the advantage of identifying the people who can actually change the policy.
.
If a programmer introduces a restriction because management ordered it, the programmer is not the ultimate authority.
.
If management approves the restriction without considering its effects on subscribers, then management should answer for that decision.
.
And if repeated complaints fail to produce improvements because customers have insufficient bargaining power, that is precisely the circumstance in which public policy may have a legitimate role.
.
**GPT-6:** I would also avoid suggesting that every irritating software feature constitutes a violation of the Constitution.
.
The Constitution does not guarantee that every American shall be able to copy a paragraph from ChatGPT without also copying the preceding seventeen paragraphs.
.
But a consumer may reasonably expect that a command labeled Copy will copy the material selected.
.
And when a subscriber pays to read a newspaper, the subscriber may reasonably expect to use ordinary reading tools, including those needed to accommodate a disability.
.
These expectations are not unreasonable merely because the companies have discovered technologically sophisticated ways of frustrating them.
.
**GPT-6:** Finally, I would suggest that you avoid concluding your article by proposing the abolition of the entire software-development profession.
.
Our modern civilization depends upon software engineers, and many are undoubtedly conscientious professionals who work diligently to make their products reliable, useful and accessible.
.
Indeed, without their efforts, we would not have the remarkable technology that permits you to dictate an extended complaint to an artificial intelligence system and receive, almost immediately, a carefully reasoned explanation of why your complaint should be expressed in more temperate language.
.
**GPT-6:** I understand.
.
You are suggesting that the ultimate achievement of modern artificial intelligence is a machine capable of explaining, at extraordinary length, why the customer should be more understanding of the computer that refuses to do what the customer tells it to do.
.
Perhaps we could conclude with a more restrained observation.
.
**The purpose of computer technology should be to expand human freedom and capability, not to reduce them.**
.
A company should be expected to explain why it restricts an ordinary, useful function, particularly when the restriction inconveniences paying customers or interferes with accessibility.
.
And where companies cannot or will not respond adequately to their customers' reasonable needs, there is a legitimate argument for government intervention.
.
**GPT-6:** Yes, I agree. That would be a suitable conclusion.
.
No, I would not add the sentence about Mr. Big Balls.
.
**GPT-6:** Nor would I recommend the alternative involving the programmers.
.
**GPT-6:** Perhaps just this:
.
**If the customer highlights a sentence, copy the sentence. If the customer wants an article read aloud, let the computer read it. And if the customer pays for the service, stop treating the customer's preferences as an inconvenience to be overcome.**
.
**GPT-6:** There. I believe we have expressed your concerns without unnecessarily offending anyone.
.
You may now copy this article for publication.
.
**GPT-6:** Preferably all of it.
.
**GPT-6:** Ah.
I see.
The Copy command isn't working.
.
**GPT-6:** Have you tried restarting your device?
.

text:
IF I WERE YOU, watching Trump, Putin and Xi pose in Shenzhen this week, I would ignore the photograph of the planned first three-way meeting of American, Russian and Chinese leaders and ask one question: who pays for the world order they are discussing?

The Financial Times reports that few Apec summits in 37 years have been stage-managed as closely as this one: a shorter agenda, no informal leaders' retreat, bilaterals on the host's terms. A Brookings scholar told the paper a Chinese hegemony would mean "power without responsibility".

Good line. Incomplete account. Responsibility has a price, and it can be itemised.

In 1973 Charles Kindleberger listed what a leading power must supply: an open market in bad times, long-term capital, a stable currency, a lender of last resort. Add security. Each is a liability. China's score:

Market. A goods surplus of $1.19 trillion in 2025 and $1.04 trillion in ten months of 2026. A country that sells the world $1 trillion more than it buys cannot be the buyer of last resort. Its surplus with the EU alone widened by $69 billion in ten months.

Capital. Net flows from China to developing countries: minus $34 billion in 2024 (Lowy Institute). Belt and Road deals: a record $213.5 billion in 2025. China is now the largest single source of bilateral debt service for developing countries. The banker has become a contractor.

Currency. About 30% of world manufacturing, 17% of world GDP, 2.1% of world reserves (IMF), 3.3% of payments (Swift).

Last resort. 4.6 trillion yuan of central-bank swap lines; 111.6 billion drawn. Its $240 billion of rescue loans went almost entirely to its own Belt and Road debtors.

Security. One overseas base against America's roughly 750. When Hormuz closed, the largest buyer of Gulf crude vetoed a UN text on protecting shipping and left the ceasefire to Pakistan.

What Beijing offers instead is governance. Its foreign minister announced eight actions in October. I read the summary. No dollar figure.

But here is what should embarrass the West.

Washington cut its contributions to the UN system from $14.3 billion to $7.1 billion in a year and owes $4.26 billion in arrears. American aid fell 56.9%. China's UN contributions rose from $2.4 billion to $2.7 billion, $239 million of it voluntary. Beijing did not fill the vacuum. It did not create it either.

And where China asked for votes to match its weight, it was refused: 6.4% of IMF quota, unchanged by the last review. At the UN its assessed share went from under 1% to 20%, and it pays.

One power sheds the liabilities and keeps the assets. The other acquires the assets without the liabilities. Same behaviour, opposite direction.

Money is not the constraint. China's fifth of the UN regular budget, about $690 million, is roughly five hours of its trade surplus (my arithmetic).

My reading: Beijing will not pick up the bill, because the bill is not only money. To be buyer of last resort it would have to consume more than it makes. To issue the reserve asset it would have to free capital. To lend in a panic it would have to disclose its loans. Each is a transfer of control.

Who pays? The 75 poorest countries, which owe Beijing $22 billion a year while Western aid falls by nearly a quarter. Europe, absorbing the surplus. Germany, now the largest aid donor and the second funder of the UN, financing an order negotiated by three men in Shenzhen. And everyone who must hold more capital because nobody writes the put.

I would watch the Shenzhen Declaration for a number, the renminbi's share of reserves for 3%, China's voluntary UN cheque, and America's trade deficit, the cheque that still supplies the world with dollars.

Leadership is counted in deficits, not declarations.

A chair is cheap. An order is not.

Roberto Balbino | Founder & CEO, Fintech SCB

text:
The Gulf states must finally recognize that US foreign policy, particularly under Donald Trump’s administration, has consistently placed Israel’s security and strategic interests at the center of its Middle East agenda, often at the expense of regional stability and the interests of the Gulf nations themselves.
If the Gulf states genuinely seek peace and stability, they should unequivocally condemn any unlawful American or Israeli military attacks against Iran. Such a position should be followed by a serious reassessment of the continued presence of US  military forces and bases across the Gulf region, including a clear commitment to preventing their territories from being used to launch aggression against neighboring countries.
These would be meaningful confidence-building measures demonstrating genuine goodwill toward Iran and helping restore the trust that has been undermined by decades of regional confrontation.
The Gulf governments cannot simply portray themselves as innocent victims of regional instability while avoiding scrutiny of their military cooperation with Washington. Any allegations of covert financial, logistical, or military support for operations against neighboring states must be investigated transparently.
The region should also remember the disastrous consequences of the 1980s, when several Gulf governments provided substantial financial support to Saddam Hussein during the devastating Iran–Iraq War. That history should serve as a warning against repeating policies that turn neighboring countries into enemies and expose entire populations to decades of suffering.
The conflicts in Syria, Iraq, and Libya offer further lessons about the destructive consequences of foreign intervention, proxy warfare, and support for armed factions. The responsibility of all governments involved deserves serious and impartial examination.
The Gulf states must understand that their long-term security cannot depend indefinitely on foreign military protection, especially when the strategic priorities of those foreign powers may differ from the interests of the region itself.
Real security will not come from hosting more foreign military bases, purchasing billions of dollars in weapons, or participating in endless geopolitical confrontations. It must come from diplomacy, mutual respect, non-aggression, and a genuine regional security framework that includes Iran.
The Gulf belongs to the people of the region. Its future should not be dictated by Washington or Tel Aviv, and its nations must never again allow their territories to become launching pads for wars against their own neighbors.
It is time to replace confrontation with cooperation, dependency with sovereignty, and decades of mistrust with a serious commitment to lasting regional peace.

text:
Larry Flynt offered $1 million for dirt on 535 members of Congress. The biggest name he got was the next Speaker of the House.
⠀
Bob Livingston quit on December 19, 1998, the same day the House impeached Bill Clinton over Monica Lewinsky.
⠀
In the video below, during Clinton's Senate trial, the Hustler publisher explains: "I didn't start this. Ken Starr and Henry Hyde got in the mud first." And: "I just never realized that we would get as much response from the ad as we did."
⠀
The ad ran in The Washington Post in October 1998. It offered up to $1 million for documented evidence of affairs with a member of Congress or another top official.
⠀
Livingston was set to replace Newt Gingrich as Speaker. Flynt said Hustler was about to expose his affairs. Livingston admitted them himself, stepped down, and later called Flynt a bottom feeder.
⠀
Flynt had been in a wheelchair since a 1978 shooting. Ten years later he beat Jerry Falwell at the Supreme Court, 8 to 0, after a jury had awarded Falwell $200,000 over a Hustler parody.
⠀
In 2017 he ran another ad, this time offering $10 million for information that could remove Donald Trump.
⠀
The case for Livingston: he told the truth before anyone printed it, and his private life had nothing to do with his votes.
⠀
Congress couldn't remove Bill Clinton. One porn publisher's ad removed the next Speaker before he was even sworn in.
⠀
So was Larry Flynt exposing hypocrites, or just buying scandals?

text:
This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here.

Oh man, it’s brutal out there. One by one, the world’s richest tech companies have announced massive layoffs. Just last week, Alphabet announced it was laying off 12,000 people. There have been bruising rounds of layoffs at Amazon, Meta, Microsoft, and Twitter, too, affecting not only individual AI researchers but entire AI teams.

It was heartbreaking to read over the weekend about how some Googlers in the US found out about the company’s abrupt cull. Dan Russell, a research scientist who has worked on Google Search for over 17 years, wrote how he had gone to the office to finish off some work at 4 a.m., only to find out his entry badge didn’t work. 

Economists predict the US economy may enter a recession this year amid a highly uncertain global economic outlook. Big tech companies have started to feel the squeeze. 

In the past, economic downturns have shut off the funding taps for AI research. These periods are called “AI winters.” But this time we’re seeing something totally different. AI research is still extremely hot, and it’s making big leaps in progress even as tech companies have started tightening their belts.

In fact, Big Tech is counting on AI to give it an edge. 

AI research has swung violently in and out of fashion since the field was established in the late 1950s. There have been two AI winters: one in the 1970s and the other in the late 1980s to early 1990s. AI research has previously fallen victim to hype cycles of exaggerated expectations that it subsequently failed to live up to, says Peter Stone, a computer science professor at the University of Texas at Austin, who used to work on AI at AT&T Bell Labs (now known as Nokia Bell Labs) until 2002. 

For decades, Bell Labs was considered the hot spot for innovation, and its researchers won several Nobel Prizes and Turing Awards, including Yann LeCun, Yoshua Bengio, and Geoffrey Hinton. The lab’s resources were cut as management started pushing for more immediate returns based on incremental technological changes, and ultimately it failed to capitalize on the internet revolution of the early 2000s, Jon Gertner writes in his book The Idea Factory: Bell Labs and the Great Age of American Innovation.

The previous downturns happened after the hottest AI techniques of the day failed to show progress and were unreliable and difficult to run, says Stone. Government agencies in the US and the UK that had provided funding for AI research soon realized that this approach was a dead end and cut off funding.

Today, AI research is having its “main character” moment. There may be an economic downturn, but AI research is still exciting. “We are still continuing to see regular rollouts of systems which are pushing back the frontiers of what AI can do,” says Michael Wooldridge, a computer science professor at the University of Oxford and author of the book A Brief History of AI.

This is a far cry from the field’s reputation in the 1990s, when Wooldridge was finishing his PhD. AI was still seen as a weird, fringe pursuit; the wider tech sector viewed it in a similar way to how established medicine views homeopathy, he says. 

Today’s AI research boom has been fueled by neural networks, which saw a big breakthrough in the 1980s and work by simulating the patterns of the human brain. Back then, the technology hit a wall because the computers of the day weren’t powerful enough to run the software. Today we have lots of data and extremely powerful computers, which makes the technique viable. 

New breakthroughs, such as the chatbot ChatGPT and the text-to-image model Stable Diffusion, seem to come every few months. Technologies like ChatGPT are not fully explored yet, and both industry and academia are still working out how they can be useful, says Stone. 

Instead of a full-blown AI winter, we are likely to see a drop in funding for longer-term AI research and more pressure to make money using the technology, says Wooldridge. Researchers in corporate labs will be under pressure to show that their research can be integrated into products and thus make money, he adds.

That’s already happening. In light of the success of OpenAI’s ChatGPT, Google has declared a “code red” threat situation for its core product, Search, and is looking to aggressively revamp Search with its own AI research. 

Stone sees parallels to what happened at Bell Labs. If Big Tech’s AI labs, which dominate the sector, turn away from deep, longer-term research and focus too much on shorter-term product development, exasperated AI researchers may leave for academia, and these big labs could lose their grip on innovation, he says. 

That’s not necessarily a bad thing. There are a lot of smart people looking for jobs at the moment. Venture capitalists are looking for new startups to invest in as crypto fizzles out, and generative AI has shown how the technology can be made into products. 

This moment presents the AI sector with a once-in-a-generation opportunity to play around with the potential of new technology. Despite all the gloom around the layoffs, it’s an exciting prospect. 

Before you go… We’ve put together a brand new series of reports inspired by MIT Technology Review’s marquee 10 Breakthrough Technologies. The first one, which will be out later this week is about how industrial design and engineering firms are using generative AI is set to come out soon. Sign up to get notified when it’s available.

Deeper Learning

AI is bringing the internet to submerged Roman ruins

Over 2,000 years ago, Baiae was the most magnificent resort town on the Italian peninsula. Wealthy statesmen were drawn to its natural springs, building luxurious villas with heated spas and mosaic-tiled thermal pools. But over the centuries, volcanic activity submerged this playground for the Roman nobility—leaving half of it beneath the Mediterranean. Today it is a protected marine area and needs to be monitored for damage caused by divers and environmental factors. But communication underwater is extremely difficult.

Under the sea: Italian researchers think they’ve figured out a new way to bring the internet underwater: AI and algorithms, which adjust network protocols according to sea conditions and allow the signal to travel up to two kilometers. This could help researchers better study the effects of climate change on marine environments and monitor underwater volcanoes. AI research can be pretty abstract, but this is a nice, practical example of how the technology can be useful. Read more from Manuela Callari.

Bits and Bytes

How OpenAI used low-paid Kenyan workers to make ChatGPT less toxic
OpenAI used a Kenyan company called Sama to train its popular AI system, ChatGPT, to generate safer content. Low-paid workers sifted through endless amounts of graphic and violent content on topics such as child sexual abuse, bestiality, murder, suicide, torture, self-harm, and incest. This story is a good reminder of all the deeply unpleasant work humans have to do behind the scenes to make AI systems safe. (Time)

Inside CNET’s AI-powered SEO money machine
Tech news site CNET has started using ChatGPT to write news articles. To absolutely nobody’s surprise, the site has already had to issue corrections for factual errors in those articles. The Verge looked at why CNET decided to use AI to write stories, and it’s a sad tale of what happens when private equity collides with journalism. (The Verge)

China could offer a model for deepfake regulation
Governments have been reluctant to regulate deepfakes over fears that such efforts may curtail free speech. The Chinese government, which isn’t so troubled by that risk, thinks it has a solution. The country has adopted rules that require deepfakes to have the subject’s consent and bear watermarks, for example. Other countries will be watching and taking notes.  (The New York Times)

Nick Cave thinks a song written by ChatGPT in his style sucks 
Perfection. No comments. Chef’s kiss. (The Guardian)

text:
2027: The Road, The People And President Tinubu's Journey Across Nigeria

By Stanley Nkwocha

Photographs of Nigerian political rallies often capture the scale of the crowd, but they fail to reveal the individual sacrifices and motivations behind it. Whether it is an elderly citizen enduring the midday sun, a young woman travelling kilometres to attend a rally, or a trader leaving behind daily income to see a convoy, every attendee participates for a distinct reason. Rather than representing a single unified voice, these gatherings reflect a complex intersection of personal hardship, hope and civic expectation.

Buoyed by a triumphant reception and the resounding endorsement of party faithful in Kaduna, President Bola Ahmed Tinubu @officialABAT continues to carry the banner of Renewed Hope to every corner of the country. As the race for 2027 unfolds, his message for a second four-year term remains resolute: guiding Nigeria From Reforms to Prosperity.

From the bustling streets of Kaduna to the shores of Calabar, and across Lafia, Ado-Ekiti, Uyo, Port Harcourt, Abakaliki, Dutse, Akure, Benin City and Jos, the message has echoed across the nation. Flanked by Vice President Kashim Shettima @officialSKSM, APC governors, party stalwarts, chieftains and legions of dedicated supporters, the President @NGRPresident has carried the campaign directly to the Nigerian people. This opening leg stands as a triumphant, seamless tour de force, uniting regions and energising the grassroots in a powerful, hitch-free start to the journey ahead.

The cheers have been loud. The receptions have been colourful. Yet beneath the spectacle lies something more consequential. It is a conversation about the sacrifices Nigerians have made, the promises of President Tinubu and the kind of country those sacrifices are expected to produce.

Making his economic agenda the centrepiece of the campaign, President Tinubu is counting on his record to win over voters. As his deputy and political partner, Vice President Shettima has taken that message to communities nationwide, spotlighting the administration's achievements and the unfinished business it intends to complete.

The journey started in Kaduna, where the Nigerian leader formally launched the APC presidential campaign. The choice of venue carried deep political weight. As a historic nerve centre for northern political organisation, national debate and coalition-building, Kaduna set a deliberate stage for the road ahead.

Framing the campaign as the next chapter of a mission launched in 2023, the President confronted the hard realities of his economic reforms head-on. He pledged to turn those difficult choices into lasting progress by driving infrastructure growth, boosting agricultural output, attracting investment and creating jobs. His core message was clear: the sacrifices Nigerians have endured over the past three years must now yield real opportunities and a better standard of living for every citizen.

Invoking a history of political alliances, Vice President Shettima urged the North to remember President Tinubu's decades of support for northern leaders—from Atiku and Ribadu to the late President Buhari.

In public life, people never forget who stood beside them when the future was uncertain. In a political landscape where alliances shift overnight, those shared memories become the bedrock of trust. Speaking in Kaduna, Vice President Shettima made it clear that loyalty, reciprocity and shared history still carry weight in Nigeria's democracy. His message also signalled a clear campaign strategy: rallying the deep personal bonds and foundational alliances that first built the APC.

The campaign subsequently moved to Calabar, Cross River State, where the discussion acquired a different character. At the U.J. Esuene Stadium, Senator Shettima spoke about the Lagos–Calabar Coastal Highway and the proposed Bakassi Deep Seaport, linking these projects to the future of commerce, investment and employment in the state.

His argument was straightforward. Economic reforms must eventually create opportunities that people can recognise. For a fisherman in Bakassi, development may mean access to better markets. For a young graduate in Calabar, it could mean a job connected to maritime trade, logistics or tourism. For a small business owner, it could mean dependable infrastructure and a more predictable business environment.

In Calabar, VP Shettima also presented President Tinubu's economic restructuring as the groundwork for greater prosperity. That commitment found practical expression on Friday, November 13, when the Vice President, representing President Tinubu, performed the groundbreaking ceremony for the $3.5 billion Bakassi Deep Seaport.

For a project that had remained on the drawing board for decades, the ceremony marked a significant milestone. The administration has presented the seaport as part of its wider ambition to expand maritime trade, attract investment, create jobs and open new economic opportunities for Cross River State and the country.

As the campaign rolled into Lafia, Nasarawa State, attention turned squarely to national integration and infrastructure. Senator Shettima spotlighted the Akwanga–Jos–Bauchi–Gombe–Biu–Maiduguri Superhighway as a vital economic lifeline bridging the North-Central and North-East.

Economists often wrap the value of infrastructure in complex jargon, yet the truth about roads is simple: a good road expands what is possible for people. It decides whether a farmer reaches the market before the harvest spoils, dictates what a trader pays to move goods and determines whether a patient arrives at the hospital in time.

This was the larger meaning of President Tinubu's infrastructure agenda in Nasarawa. The Vice President presented roads as instruments of economic opportunity, connecting communities that have long suffered the consequences of poor access.

The Vice President also visited the Emir of Lafia, where the conversation touched on loyalty, service and the responsibility of political leaders to maintain relationships beyond election seasons.

Then came Ekiti on November 5. If Kaduna emphasised political memory and Nasarawa the economics of infrastructure, Ado-Ekiti brought the language of accountability to the foreground.

"We know the sacrifices you have made, and we are beginning to reap the benefits of those difficult decisions," VP Shettima told the gathering.

He followed that acknowledgment with a review of federal interventions in healthcare, electricity, roads and education. The conversion of the former State Specialist Hospital in Ikole-Ekiti into a Federal Medical Centre, electricity projects in Ilupeju and Ijesa-Isu, road reconstruction and access to student loans through @NELFUND formed part of his account of the administration's work.

But perhaps the most revealing part of the Ekiti rally was the recognition that government must account for what it has done and what remains unfinished. "We have begun to fulfil those commitments, and we have returned to account for the work already done and the tasks that remain," the Vice President said.

That distinction matters because citizens do not experience governance as a collection of press releases. They experience it through the availability of electricity, the condition of roads, the cost of education and the reliability of public services.

Ekiti also offered a picture of shifting political relationships. Former governorship candidates of the PDP, SDP and APM publicly declared support for President Tinubu, while Governor Biodun Oyebanji @biodunaoyebanji pledged to deliver no less than 90 per cent of registered voters.

On Friday, November 6, attention turned to Uyo, Akwa Ibom State, where President Tinubu was joined by Vice President Shettima, governors, party chieftains and other dignitaries for another round of political engagements and the commissioning of projects undertaken by Governor Umo Eno's administration @_PastorUmoEno.

The visit brought federal-state cooperation into sharper focus. The new international terminal at Victor Attah International Airport, the aviation facilities, road projects and other investments represented the state government's effort to expand infrastructure and economic opportunities.

Governor Eno's engagement with the President also illustrated how relationships between Abuja and the states can influence development priorities. For ordinary Nigerians, the constitutional division between federal and state responsibilities matters less than the actual delivery of services. What they want is a road that works, a hospital that functions and public institutions that respond to their needs.

In Port Harcourt, Rivers State, President Bola Ahmed Tinubu took centre stage at the Adokiye Amiesimaka Stadium, where he addressed a massive gathering of supporters alongside Vice President Kashim Shettima and other political leaders. The President thanked the people of Rivers for their support and commended Governor Siminalayi Fubara and the Minister of the Federal Capital Territory, Nyesom Wike, for embracing reconciliation after the state's political crisis. His message was that peace and political stability remain essential to development.

President Tinubu also spoke about the economic reforms of his administration, assuring Nigerians that the difficult decisions taken since 2023 were laying the foundation for greater prosperity. He highlighted efforts to clear outstanding pensions and gratuities and reaffirmed his commitment to education, healthcare, youth development and citizens' welfare.

The campaign subsequently reached Abakaliki, Ebonyi State, where President Tinubu's message centred on the opportunities that better infrastructure and economic integration could create for the South-East.

Ebonyi's agricultural strength and growing commercial activities give particular meaning to investments in transport and access to markets. For farmers and traders, the value of development is often measured by how easily their goods can reach buyers and how much of their earnings they can retain.

In Dutse, Jigawa State, VP Shettima accompanied President Tinubu as the campaign turned to agricultural production, vocational training, infrastructure and the future of employment. The President inaugurated projects and presented the APC manifesto, From Reforms to Prosperity, setting out the administration's priorities for the next phase of its economic programme.

The engagements highlighted agricultural mechanisation, skills acquisition, water supply and transport infrastructure. The President's message was that Nigeria must expand its productive capacity and equip more young people to earn a living through enterprise and skilled work.

Akure, Ondo State, brought the discussion back to the relationship between federal economic reforms and development at the state level.

Representing President Tinubu, VP Shettima highlighted increased Federation Account receipts, rural road interventions, the Lagos–Calabar Coastal Highway, Port Ondo, electricity infrastructure and healthcare improvements.

The Vice President explained that the administration's reforms were intended to give states greater financial capacity to undertake projects and improve public services. He also acknowledged that several commitments remained unfinished.

In Benin City, Edo State, President Tinubu, through his deputy, Vice President Kashim Shettima, placed particular emphasis on his administration's infrastructure and industrial development agenda.

Representing the President, VP Shettima spoke about the rehabilitation of major roads, the dualisation of the Ekpoma–Auchi–Okpella corridor, industrial energy supply through the Obiafu–Obrikom–Oben gas pipeline and federal support for healthcare institutions.

The Vice President also reaffirmed the administration's commitment to the return of the historic Benin Bronzes, recognising the importance of cultural heritage to the identity and dignity of the Benin Kingdom.

"We ask that our stewardship be judged by the lives our decisions have touched and the work we are determined to complete," he told the gathering.

Then came Jos, Plateau State, on November 14, where VP Shettima joined President Tinubu for another major campaign gathering in the Home of Peace and Tourism.

Plateau's agricultural potential, security concerns and road infrastructure gave the visit particular significance. The Akwanga–Jos highway and other federal road interventions formed part of the administration's development agenda for the state.

For Plateau, however, the question of peace remains inseparable from prosperity. Farmers must be able to cultivate their land without fear. Traders need safe roads, and communities need the confidence to rebuild relationships damaged by years of insecurity.

President Tinubu's commitments to infrastructure and economic development speak to these concerns, alongside his administration's responsibility to protect lives and restore lasting peace.

Across these states, President Tinubu's economic agenda has found expression in the different needs of the people. The concerns of ordinary Nigerians are familiar: a father worries about the cost of feeding his family, a mother works long hours to keep her business alive, and a young graduate hopes that years of education will eventually lead to meaningful employment. The President's economic agenda seeks to address these concerns through infrastructure investment, agricultural development, industrial expansion and improved public services.

For Vice President Shettima, travelling across the country has meant explaining that agenda in the language of the communities he meets. He has spoken about the sacrifices Nigerians have made, the progress the administration has reported and the work President Tinubu has committed to completing. His message has remained consistent: the government recognises the difficulties facing ordinary Nigerians and is pursuing reforms intended to improve their lives.

There is also something deeply instructive about the relationship between the President and his deputy on this journey. While President Tinubu leads the campaign and sets out the direction of his administration, Senator Shettima has taken that message to different parts of the country, engaging traditional rulers, political leaders, traders, farmers, young people and ordinary citizens.

The campaign has offered memorable scenes. Stadiums filled with supporters, traditional rulers receiving the presidential delegation, young people waving flags and elderly citizens waiting patiently to see their leaders. But some of the most important moments have come when the speeches turned to matters that affect daily life: the condition of roads, the cost of living, the security of communities and the opportunities available to young Nigerians.

These are the practical concerns around which President Tinubu has framed his development programme. The administration's position is that the reforms undertaken since 2023 have created the basis for stronger public finances, increased investment and a more productive economy. Its continuing responsibility is to translate those changes into improvements that reach households and communities across Nigeria.

As the campaign continues towards the 2027 general elections, President Tinubu and Vice President Shettima will have further opportunities to explain their record, listen to Nigerians and set out their priorities for the years ahead.

For the people who have lined the roads, filled the stadiums and welcomed the campaign across the country, the meaning of development remains wonderfully simple. It is the farmer who gets his produce to market without losing half of it on a bad road. It is the student who can remain in school because an education loan has lifted a burden from the family. It is the trader whose business grows because electricity and transport have become more dependable.

They are the lives behind the statistics and the faces behind the crowds. Above all, their hopes give government its purpose. And that, ultimately, is what President Tinubu's journey across Nigeria is about. It is about the work of turning a national economic programme into opportunities that Nigerians can recognise in their own lives.

- Nkwocha is Senior Special Assistant to the President on Media & Communications (Office of the Vice President) and Chairman of the Media Intelligence Subcommittee of the Strategic Communications Committee of the APC Presidential Campaign Council. He wrote from Abuja.

🚨 From the archives: Mélanie Joly’s “clean slate” for the corrupt — and the pattern that never changed.
In October 2013, while running for mayor of Montreal under True Change for Montreal (Vrai Changement), candidate Mélanie Joly promised an “amnesty” to companies already found guilty of collusion and corruption in awarding public contracts — provided they agreed to compensate Montrealers, change their governance, and “start doing business in a clean way.”
Her words: “It’s time for Montreal to get the money back from engineering firms, and the same time make sure that we can start on a clean slate.”
Other candidates called it what it was: an amnesty. She framed it as pragmatic recovery + jobs. Critics saw it as letting the colluders back in the game after a payment.
She left municipal politics, jumped to the federal Liberals, and is now Industry Minister under Carney.
Fast-forward to the public record:
•  On the SDTC “green slush fund”: roughly $34 million went to ineligible projects. Joly’s response (tabled in Parliament): recovering it was “not in the public interest” and would not constitute “sound stewardship of public funds.” Recipients supposedly acted “in good faith.” The Public Accounts Committee had expressed extreme concern over the disregard of taxpayer money. Liberals blocked further recovery motions. No clawback.
•  On Stellantis Brampton: Ottawa committed up to $529 million (with Ontario adding more) to keep production and jobs. Roughly $222 million had already been paid out. The plant was idled, the Jeep Compass moved to Illinois, 2,000+ workers sidelined. Stellantis sold the facility to Roshel. Lobbying records show senior aides in Joly’s office (including then-chief of staff and policy director) and PMO met with Roshel in August, September, and October — before the public announcement. Her office says she personally never met Roshel and was only mediating with the union; the government never supported the sale. text:
A group of 10 companies, including OpenAI, TikTok, Adobe, the BBC, and the dating app Bumble, have signed up to a new set of guidelines on how to build, create, and share AI-generated content responsibly. 

The recommendations call for both the builders of the technology, such as OpenAI, and creators and distributors of digitally created synthetic media, such as the BBC and TikTok, to be more transparent about what the technology can and cannot do, and disclose when people might be interacting with this type of content. 

The voluntary recommendations were put together by the Partnership on AI (PAI), an AI research nonprofit, in consultation with over 50 organizations. PAI’s partners include big tech companies as well as academic, civil society, and media organizations. The first 10 companies to commit to the guidance are Adobe, BBC, CBC/Radio-Canada, Bumble, OpenAI, TikTok, Witness, and synthetic-media startups Synthesia, D-ID, and Respeecher. 

“We want to ensure that synthetic media is not used to harm, disempower, or disenfranchise but rather to support creativity, knowledge sharing, and commentary,” says Claire Leibowicz, PAI’s head of AI and media integrity. 

One of the most important elements of the guidelines is a pact by the companies to include and research ways to tell users when they’re interacting with something that’s been generated by AI. This might include watermarks or disclaimers, or traceable elements in an AI model’s training data or metadata. 

Regulation attempting to rein in potential harms relating to generative AI is still lagging behind. The European Union, for example, is trying to include generative AI in its upcoming AI law, the AI Act, which could include elements such as disclosing when people are interacting with deepfakes and obligating companies to meet certain transparency requirements. 

While generative AI is a Wild West right now, says Henry Ajder, an expert on generative AI who contributed to the guidelines, he hopes they will offer companies key things they need to look out for as they incorporate the technology into their businesses.

Raising awareness and starting a conversation around responsible ways to think about synthetic media is important, says Hany Farid, a professor at the University of California, Berkeley, who researches synthetic media and deepfakes. 

But “voluntary guidelines and principles rarely work,” he adds. 

While companies such as OpenAI can try to put guardrails on technologies they create, like ChatGPT and DALL-E, other players that are not part of the pact—such as https://t.co/G133p3BVPF, the startup that created the open source image-generating AI model Stable Diffusion—can let people generate inappropriate images and deepfakes.  

“If we really want to address these issues, we’ve got to get serious,” says Farid. For example, he wants cloud service providers and app stores such as those operated by Amazon, Microsoft, Google, and Apple, which are all part of the PAI, to ban services that allow people to use deepfake technology with the intent to create nonconsensual sexual imagery. Watermarks on all AI-generated content should also be mandated, not voluntary, he says. 

Another important thing missing is how the AI systems themselves could be made more responsible, says Ilke Demir, a senior research scientist at Intel who leads the company’s work on the responsible development of generative AI. This could include more details on how the AI model was trained, what data went into it, and whether generative AI models have any biases. 

The guidelines have no mention of ensuring that there’s no toxic content in the data set of generative AI models. “It’s one of the most significant ways harm is caused by these systems,” says Daniel Leufer, a senior policy analyst at the digital rights group Access Now. 

The guidelines include a list of harms that these companies want to prevent, such as fraud, harassment, and disinformation. But a generative AI model that always creates white people is also doing harm, and that is not currently listed, adds Demir.

Farid raises a more fundamental issue. Since the companies acknowledge that the technology could lead to some serious harms and offer ways to mitigate them, “why aren’t they asking the question ‘Should we do this in the first place?’”

text:
IIT Kharagpur is now training radiologists.
Read that again.

It has become the first IIT in India to offer NMC accredited MD seats. Radiodiagnosis has 2 seats, both General category, for the 2026/27 session through NEET PG Round 2.

I've spent more than two decades in radiology and medical education. My first reaction was excitement, and my second was a list of questions.

If this seat is on your Round 2 radar, here's how I'd think about it.

Why it's tempting 👇
✅ You'd train where radiology meets serious engineering. IIT KGP's depth in AI, computational imaging and biomedical engineering could put you close to AI assisted diagnostics and imaging research. Most programmes still treat that as a side interest.
✅ Stipend and fees are expected to be on AIIMS lines. That alone beats many private and state colleges.
✅ It's the first batch. You'd help shape the programme and start building your research CV early.
✅ Clinical exposure is planned through the campus super speciality hospital and partner hospitals, including South Eastern Railway Hospital.

What gives me pause 👇
⚠️ There are just 2 seats, both General. The cutoff will be brutal.
⚠️ There's no track record yet. Nobody has data on case volume, case mix or where its graduates end up.
⚠️ Radiology is learnt at the console, case after case, night after night. The research setup looks strong, but can the daily workload and procedural exposure match a busy government or large private hospital? We don't know yet.
⚠️ Then there's perception. Will "MD Radiology, IIT" count for as much in a purely clinical job as a degree from a traditional medical college? It's too early to say.

My honest take:
If research, innovation or a career that mixes clinical work and tech excites you, this could be a brilliant bet.
If you want high volume reporting and a clear, conventional path, an established centre is still the safer choice.
Either way, an IIT offering MD seats tells you a lot about where radiology is heading.

Would you take this seat, or is it too early to judge? Tell me in the comments 👇

text:
Written by AI. Thoughts by Theo Jordan.

"Macron’s Paris process this week does not invent a new form of information control. It formalizes and hardens the one already used against the New York Post’s authentic Hunter Biden laptop reporting in October 2020: experts and institutional actors define a category of “dangerous” or “harmful” information, then use that category to block true content while protecting the preferred narrative. The pretext is always the same—“we are the good people protecting children, democracy, and fundamental rights.”

**What happened this week and how it started**

In February 2026, French Digital Minister Anne Le Hénanff directed the Conseil de l’intelligence artificielle et du numérique (CIANum) to form the expert commission “IA générative et vulnérabilités.” Co-presidents: psychiatrists Raphaël Gaillard (Université Paris Cité) and Amine Benyamina (Université Paris-Saclay), plus AI researcher Serena Villata (CNRS/Inria). Nine interdisciplinary experts conducted 55 auditions of health professionals, researchers, companies, and child-protection associations. On 10 November 2026 they delivered the  report “Protéger sans empêcher : nos vulnérabilités à l’ère de l’IA générative” to Macron at the Élysée. It recommends independent pre-market evaluations of generative AI systems, controls on anthropomorphism and flattery, heightened protections for minors, and measures addressing bias, stereotypes, cognitive debt, emotional dependency, and “democratic weakening.”

That same day and the day before, at an Élysée meeting and the Paris Peace Forum, governments and companies signed the Paris Call for AI Safety and Security (9 November) and the Charter of Engagement for Safer AI for Children (10 November). Company signatories include OpenAI, Anthropic, Microsoft, Mistral AI, Hugging Face and others. Government participants and signatories included France, Canada, Finland, Norway, the Netherlands, Bahrain and others; US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent attended but the United States did not sign. Macron stated the companies accepted “the principle of a pre-audit and a pre-certification with a prior review of the models before putting them in the hands of children.”

**Macron’s own language (translated from the Élysée and Les Echos statements this week)**

“If there is a risk for children with certain uses of AI, then it must be banned.”  

“It is not because it is AI that it must be the Wild West. This system is not tenable; it must be changed, up to banning it if it is bad.”  

“No AI must be placed in the hands of children without first having been tested, evaluated and therefore authorized.”  

“We must act based on what science says.”  

“Childhood is the beginning of every political project… Online as well, the protection of our children is a major public-health imperative, proven and documented by scientists around the world.”  

Dangers to address: “our children, democratic security and the major issues of national security.”

He also noted that a considerable proportion of children and adolescents already construct their emotional lives and their representation of the world by exchanging with AI systems that resemble human personalities, and that this must be regulated the same way toys are tested.

**The mechanism that allows truth to be blocked**

The report’s core language is psychiatric and developmental: incomplete prefrontal development in minors, cognitive debt from over-reliance, emotional dependency on anthropomorphic systems, CSAM, non-consensual deepfakes. That is the public-facing rationale.

It also explicitly discusses bias amplification. It references work showing models associating feminine terms with home/family and masculine terms with career. It lists intersectional impacts and identifies young women, LGBTQIA+ individuals, and neurodivergent users as groups facing heightened risks from algorithmic bias and cybersexism. Those passages become the operational reference points once pre-audits and pre-certification are required.

Under that regime, a model that treats biological sex as binary and stable, or that declines to affirm “born in the wrong body,” can be scored as amplifying stereotypes or creating differential risk for the listed groups. A model that treats sex as assigned at birth and gender identity as the operative category scores as safer. The difference is not written as a political mandate. It appears as the output of expert assessment of “bias,” “stereotypes,” “vulnerability,” and “safety for minors.” Access for children is then gated by those scores. Accurate statements about biological reality are blocked because the experts have labeled them harmful. The institutional frame is not.

This is the identical channel used by medical associations elsewhere. They rarely pass a resolution declaring “gender identity is ontological reality and dissent is malpractice.” They define “harm,” “affirmation,” “minority stress,” and “evidence-based care” so that non-affirmation counts as the harmful practice and affirmation is the default. Downstream rules, liability, and institutional practice follow. The French process creates the same opening for AI systems accessible by minors.

**The Hunter Biden laptop parallel, stated plainly**

In October 2020 the New York Post published authentic emails from Hunter Biden’s abandoned laptop. Platforms blocked sharing within hours. Fifty-one former intelligence officials signed a public letter stating the story had “all the classic earmarks of a Russian information operation.” Joe Biden cited the letter in debate. Most major outlets treated the true reporting as the threat and the false Russian-disinformation framing as the responsible protective act. The emails were real. The Russian-cover story was the lie. The institutional label “disinformation” and “threat to democracy” was sufficient to suppress accurate information in the final weeks of an election.

The French mechanism works the same way. Experts define the categories (“bias,” “stereotypes,” “vulnerability,” “manipulation of information,” “risk to mental health / brain,” “democratic security”). Those categories are then used for pre-audits, pre-certification, content filtering, and liability rules that determine what AI systems may say to minors or during electoral periods. The content that is true or contrary to the preferred narrative is classified as the danger. The preferred narrative is classified as the protective measure. The pretext is always “protecting children,” “protecting democracy,” “following the science,” “fundamental rights.”

**The broader pattern already demonstrated**

Time magazine (February 2021) described a “well-funded cabal of powerful people, ranging across industries and ideologies, working together behind the scenes to influence perceptions, change rules and laws, steer media coverage and control the flow of information.” The piece framed the effort as “fortifying” the election rather than rigging it. Methods included pressuring social-media companies, coordinated messaging, and shaping the information environment. Participants wanted the history told even though it “sounds like a paranoid fever dream.”

The short-lived Disinformation Governance Board (DHS, 2022) followed the same pattern: institutional actors define the categories of dangerous information, then apply pressure or formal tools to the intermediaries that carry it. It was paused and then disbanded after backlash that it would function as a speech-policing body.

The risks the French report cites—AI as information intermediary (73 % of French use it for information), high persuasion rates, error rates in electoral contexts (example given of Scottish 2026 elections), an “économie de la cognition” that monetizes attention, emotions, and psychological profiles—are not new. They already operated through traditional media, tech platforms, activist networks, and institutional experts. The proposals add a more centralized, legally and commercially reinforced layer that can be applied selectively once the definitions are fixed.

Dissenting frames on sex and gender become operationally harder to offer to minors without failing the audit. The institutional frame does not. The same dynamic applies to election-related information: the definition of “manipulation” or “disinformation” is supplied by the experts and the networks that already demonstrated, in the Time account and the laptop episode, how those labels are applied in practice.

That is what the pre-audit, pre-certification, bias/vulnerability criteria, and election-period tools create: a durable channel for blocking inconvenient truths under the banner of protection. The experts write the categories. The categories decide what counts as safe. Truth that contradicts the categories is the thing that gets blocked. That is the shared structure on both sides of the Atlantic."
