text:
—And from that time onward an absurd problem offered itself: “how could God allow it!” To which the deranged reason of the little community formulated an answer that was terrifying in its absurdity: God gave his son as a sacrifice for the forgiveness of sins. At once there was an end of the gospels! Sacrifice for sin, and in its most obnoxious and barbarous form: sacrifice of the innocent for the sins of the guilty! What appalling paganism!—Jesus him self had done away with the very concept of “guilt,” he denied that there was any gulf fixed between God and man; he lived this unity between God and man, and that was precisely his “glad tidings”.... And not as a mere privilege!—From this time forward the type of the Saviour was corrupted, bit by bit, by the doctrine of judgment and of the second coming, the doctrine of death as a sacrifice, the doctrine of the resurrection, by means of which the entire concept of “blessedness,” the whole and only reality of the gospels, is juggled away—in favour of a state of existence after death!... St. Paul, with that rabbinical impudence which shows itself in all his doings, gave a logical quality to that conception, that indecentconception, in this way: “If Christ did not rise from the dead, then all our faith is in vain!”—And at once there sprang from the Gospels the most contemptible of all unfulfillable promises, the shameless doctrine of personal immortality.... Paul even preached it as a reward....
42.

One now begins to see just what it was that came to an end with the death on the cross: a  new and thoroughly original effort to found a Buddhistic peace movement, and so establish happiness on earth—real, not merely promised. For this remains—as I have already pointed out—the essential difference between the two religions of décadence: Buddhism promises nothing, but actually fulfils; Christianity promises everything, but fulfils nothing.—Hard upon the heels of the “glad tidings” came the worst imaginable: those of Paul. In Paul is incarnated the very opposite of the “bearer of glad tidings”; he represents the genius for hatred, the vision of hatred, the relentless logic of hatred. What, indeed, has not this dysangelist sacrificed to hatred! Above all, the Saviour: he nailed him to his own cross. The life, the example, the teaching, the death of Christ, the meaning and the law of the whole gospels—nothing was left of all this after that counterfeiter in hatred had reduced it to his uses. Surely not reality; surely not historical truth!... Once more the priestly instinct of the Jew perpetrated the same old master crime against history—he simply struck out the yesterday and the day before yesterday of Christianity, and invented his own history of Christian beginnings. Going  further, he treated the history of Israel to another falsification, so that it became a mere prologue to his achievement: all the prophets, it now appeared, had referred to his “Saviour.”... Later on the church even falsified the history of man in order to make it a prologue to Christianity.... The figure of the Saviour, his teaching, his way of life, his death, the meaning of his death, even the consequences of his death—nothing remained untouched, nothing remained in even remote contact with reality. Paul simply shifted the centre of gravity of that whole life to a place behind this existence—in the lie of the “risen” Jesus. At bottom, he had no use for the life of the Saviour—what he needed was the death on the cross, andsomething more. To see anything honest in such a man as Paul, whose home was at the centre of the Stoical enlightenment, when he converts an hallucination into a proofof the resurrection of the Saviour, or even to believe his tale that he suffered from this hallucination himself—this would be a genuine niaiserie in a psychologist. Paul willed the end; therefore he also willed the means.... What he himself didn’t believe was swallowed readily enough by the idiots among whom he  spread his teaching.—What he wanted was power; in Paul the priest once more reached out for power—he had use only for such concepts, teachings and symbols as served the purpose of tyrannizing over the masses and organizing mobs. What was the only part of Christianity that Mohammed borrowed later on? Paul’s invention, his device for establishing priestly tyranny and organizing the mob: the belief in the immortality of the soul—that is to say, the doctrine of “judgment”....

text:
I like the energy and ambition of Andhra Pradesh Chief Minister Chandrababu Naidu. He is one of the few leaders who can sell his state to the world. But I feel this model of centrally-planned development, where the Chief Minister decides which town will make drones, which will make chips and which will make quantum computers, has a basic problem.

Industries do not grow because a government marks a place on a map. They grow where the talent, the suppliers and the customers are, and where it is easy to do business. I think no one sitting in a state capital, however capable, can know this better than the thousands of entrepreneurs who are risking their own money.

It also makes development depend on one leader. Amaravati itself was largely stalled for five years when the government changed. If a plan can stop when one person loses an election, how can any investor plan for twenty years?

And the land given away for these projects is not free. It comes from farmers, and if the project does not come, the land and the money are locked up with no one accountable for the promise.

I feel there is a deeper reason why we cheer for such plans. For decades, the license raj held us back. Even after 1991, our reforms were half-hearted, and the government is still deeply involved in planning the economy. Our entrepreneurs and innovators still fight red tape at every step, and many of our brightest have simply left the country.

So we Indians are desperate for someone to show us the way, and when a rare politician offers us some government-driven industrialization, we start worshipping him. I think we should not fall for that. In such plans, it is often the well-connected who benefit the most. Most government-driven economic planning favours a few, many a time undeserving, at the expense of others who are more deserving.

Only a truly competitive economy, where the government does not pick winners and losers, can be efficient and reward those who truly deserve it.

That is why what we should fight for instead is our right to be economically free. An ultra-minimal government and bureaucracy, with clear land titles, fast and simple approvals, reliable power, good roads, law and order, and courts that enforce contracts quickly. The government as a referee, not as the player.

Then every town can compete in a decentralized and natural way, and every one of us can plan our own economic lives, in a way that is more efficient, more sustainable and more fair. That kind of development does not depend on any one leader, and no change of government can stop it.

text:
During World War II, romantic and intimate relationships between German soldiers and women in occupied territories often referred to broadly as horizontal collaboration or fraternization—were common, complex, and heavily stigmatized. The romance stories involving German soldiers during World War II span real-life wartime relationships, historical biographies, and popular fiction that explore forbidden connections across enemy lines, moral ambiguities, and survival... 

On the British Channel Islands (occupied by German forces for five years), local young women—derogatorily nicknamed "Jerrybags" by some townspeople—formed romantic relationships with stationed German soldiers who had access to scarce food, gifts, and a semblance of normal life.

One notable documented account from War History Online is the story of Dolly Edwards, a local woman who survived harsh conditions and forced labor on Guernsey and fell in love with a German signalman named Willi Joanknecht. After the 1945 liberation and Willi's time as a prisoner of war (POW), the couple reunited, married in 1946, and remained together for nearly seven decades.

In neutral-turned-occupied Norway, roughly 30,000 to 50,000 women (tyskerpiker or "German girls") entered into relationships or had children with the approximately 300,000 stationed German troops. After the war, these women faced severe societal and legal reprisals, including job losses, internment, and forced exile, though the Norwegian government officially apologized for these human rights violations decades later in 2018 as reported by The Guardian.

In countries like France, the Netherlands, and Belgium, relationships ranged from forced or transactional prostitution to genuine romantic attachments. For many women, alignment or affection with a Wehrmacht soldier offered survival, food rations, and protection against the bleakness or danger of daily occupation. Conversely, when liberation came, women accused of such ties (known in France as les tondues) were frequently subjected to public shaming, head-shaving, and mob violence. While some relationships were born of genuine emotional connection or mutual loneliness, they unfolded within an extreme power imbalance where the occupier held military dominance over the occupied population.

. . . 

The German soldiers who occupied the Netherlands from 1940-45 found love, affairs or just sex in the Netherlands. Historian Laura Fahnenbruck (studied archives from the German army and the Dutch police together with court reports. She also used dairies, letters, photos and personal ads. As an academic she is interested in the history of everyday life). She spent eight years studying the everyday sexuality of the Wehrmacht soldier in the years of occupation, and thus the sexuality of Dutch women during the WWII. 

The German supreme command looked favourably upon contact between German soldiers and Dutch women. The Netherlands was considered to be a more or less German area, and the German administration was keen to prove that the occupation was a necessary evil. Contact between soldiers and Dutch women was thought to make a valuable contribution to the propaganda effort. This was handy for soldiers, because they could show the home front how good they had it in the Netherlands and it gave them the opportunity to conform to the image of the macho soldier.

This often went further than having your photo taken together. German soldiers turned their backs on traditional authority in Dutch society, which made them interesting to young women. Fahnenbruck: ‘You saw this immediately in May 1940. There are already reports of girls rejecting authority. They had found a strong new group, and contact with it had its advantages.’ Although fraternization with soldiers was widely disapproved of, it gave young women a real chance to have sexual experiences.

text:
Chapter IV: Off to Vienna.
.
In this way Stanislaus went on until he was nearly fourteen years old and his brother Paul was approaching fifteen. Then the Lord John Kostka thought his boys had better continue their studies, not at home, but at a regular school. He picked out John Bilinski, a young man who had lately completed his college course, as tutor for them. He gave them a couple of servants, mounted them all on good horses, and sent them off six hundred miles or more on horseback to Vienna.
You may be sure Stanislaus enjoyed the long ride. It would be strange if he, a nobleman of the finest cavalry nation in the world, were not a good horseman. He loved the smell of the open fields, he loved the boisterous song of the mountain torrent. The hills and the plains were his home, for the hills and the plains were nearer to God than the houses of men.
In those days all travel was on foot or on horseback. The wealthy and noble rode, the poor footed it. Great highways cut Europe from end to end; though there were tracts in Stanislaus’ country where the roadway was only the broad steppe, where the grasses waved and tossed like the sea, where men were few and their dwellings scattered far apart.
They crossed great rivers, they climbed the foothills of the Carpathian mountains. Many a night Paul and Stanislaus, with their people, slept under the stars. Many a wild, rough border town they passed. Many a great forest they penetrated, the home of the wild boar and the aurochs.
And the tar burners in the forests looked up from under their matted brows at the fair oval face of the Polish boy, and said:
“He is like a wild flower blown by the wind. He is like the violets that laugh in spring at the sun.”
And the shaggy fighting-men of the frontier villages watched him ride through their streets, and thought:
“This is an angel. He looks toward heaven because he sees his Brothers there.”
They crossed themselves piously as he passed. And some of the light and laughter of his face glowed ‘for a moment in their dark lives, as a gloomy glen in the forest is brightened up by a darting ray of sunlight.
He was wonderful, but he was always a boy. He was glad to feel the good horse under him, to grip the Tartar saddle with his knees, to feel the air rush by his cheek.
Sometimes they met poor people staggering wearily afoot along the road. Often Stanislaus checked his horse and lightly dismounted.
“Get up, get up, old father!” he would cry. “My legs are stiff from the saddle. I want to walk.”
And though a peasant might often be afraid to accept the favor from a noble, or be surly and churlish, the folk never were so with Stanislaus. Up climbed the old father into the saddle, and Stanislaus stepped out by his side.
“God give your grace long years!” said the thankful old man.
“Long years!” cried Stanislaus. I want more than that. I want eternity. I was born for greater things than long years.”
And the old man would understand; for he was of the poor, and the poor know more of this longing for heaven than do the rich. But he looked almost with awe at this richly dressed noble boy who had learned even now to value life so justly. Then it was easy for Stanislaus to talk of heaven to the old man.
“Old father, in the barony of the Lord Jesus there is no poverty or old age or weariness. Nor is there any difference of rank there as here, for we shall all be great lords and castellans in heaven.”
“Aye, but your grace will be a hetman surely in the army of the Lord Jesus,” said the old man.
“Who knows!” cried Stanislaus. “I should love that dearly. Though the generals in His kingdom are not always from amongst the nobles. It may be that you will be hetman, and I a common soldier. But it is good to be even a common soldier with Him.”
“I went against the Tartars in my youth,” said the old man. “Perhaps we shall have a campaign against that dog-brother Lucifer, and Saint Michael and Saint Wenceslaus will lead us under the Lord Jesus; and our Lady of Yasna Gora will look on when we come back victorious!”
And so they talked on until it was time to set the old man down, and Stanislaus mounted again to catch up with his party, which had gone ahead.
“With God!” cried the old man.
“With God!” echoed Stanislaus. ‘And if you go to heaven before me, father, do not forget to plead for me with the Lord Jesus and with His Mother.”
Then he clattered along the road, and shortly came up with Bilinski and Paul.
Sometimes they came to districts infested by robbers, and waited to join themselves to some larger party for protection. Sometimes they made long stretches of many hours in the saddle, when the inns were far apart and they could get no food on the road. Sometimes they tarried a day or two in a little town to rest their horses.
But everywhere Stanislaus thought of God, and prayed, and when occasion offered spoke of holy things as only he could speak. Bilinski and Paul often laughed at him, for they were of a different stamp. But he did not mind their ridicule, and he bore them no grudge for it. And so, after. many days, they came at length to Vienna, on July 26, 1564...

text:
Sometimes research throws out something really interesting, and this paper is one of them:

Enhancing maternity healthcare workers' wellbeing using insider participatory action research by Wood, Chambers and Marshall's (2025). 

Their HEARS study explored what makes maternity staff feel good at work, looking at emotional, professional and physical nourishment. 

The findings: 

-Culture shifted to be more compassionate and inclusive
-morale, positivity, and atmosphere improved
-Ways of working changed
-Colleagues more proactively cared for each other, worked well together in teams, expressed thanks and feedback, and instigated interventions for colleagues' and women's welfare.

What really struck me was that these improvements happened despite staffing numbers and working conditions remaining unchanged.

The authors also suggested introducing Colleague Support Volunteers (CSVs). What might this might look like in practice?

Could we involve retired midwives, former healthcare professionals or others with relevant experience to spend time in maternity areas, offering a friendly face, a listening ear, a cup of tea or simply someone to talk to? Not to replace staff or undertake clinical work, but to offer a little extra support when it is needed.

It also makes me think about Power to the Middle, everyday leadership and therapeutic presence. We all know people who can lift the atmosphere simply by being there. People who notice, listen, encourage and make others feel valued. You don't need a job title to have that influence.

Of course, volunteers won't fix staffing shortages or compensate for the investment maternity services need. 

But perhaps we shouldn't underestimate what a little additional support and human connection could achieve while the bigger changes are being worked through. 

What could we do now, with what we already have, to make the experience of working in maternity services a little better?

This can’t be a government initiative but it could be government supported. 

Because what helps the maternity team helps women and their families. 

Wood CM, Chambers M, Marshall JE (2025). BMC Health Services Research, 25, 188.

text:
Why SpaceX Catch Was Cheered In Gulf Shores

When SpaceX achieved the historic midair capture of its Starship spacecraft, the milestone resonated far beyond the launch pad in Texas. For Alabamians, and particularly the residents of Huntsville, the accomplishment strikes a deep emotional and professional chord. Known globally as "Rocket City," Huntsville has been the bedrock of American rocketry for decades, and SpaceX’s breakthrough serves as a powerful validation of the region’s enduring aerospace legacy.

Huntsville’s identity as the center of rocket technology began with the development of the Saturn V rocket at NASA’s Marshall Space Flight Center, located on the U.S. Army’s Redstone Arsenal. Today, that propulsion and engineering heritage remains directly intertwined with commercial space exploration.

SpaceX’s Starship architecture is a cornerstone of NASA’s Artemis program, which aims to return human crews to the lunar surface. The complex engineering, testing, and defense support networks centered at Redstone Arsenal provide crucial expertise, infrastructure, and contract oversight that make ambitious commercial endeavors possible. When SpaceX successfully catches and reuses massive rocket hardware, it reflects the culmination of decades of research, testing, and innovation pioneered by North Alabama’s world-class scientific workforce.

Bridging Rocket City and Alabama's Coast:

The technological and economic energy of Huntsville is increasingly connected to the rest of the state, particularly Coastal Alabama. Allegiant Air offers a direct, nonstop flight connecting Huntsville International Airport (HSV) to Gulf Shores International Airport (GUF).

As the state’s only intrastate commercial airline route, this flight allows passengers to travel between North Alabama and the beach in approximately one hour, bypassing a long driving trip.

The connection between Huntsville and Gulf Shores extends well beyond weekend getaways. Aerospace engineers, defense researchers, and space support personnel are not only visiting Alabama's white-sand beaches but are actively investing in coastal real estate and local businesses. The influx of capital and high-earning professionals from North Alabama is driving year-round economic growth along the coast, creating a strong economic link between Huntsville’s tech corridor and the Gulf region.

Alabama’s Fastest-Growing Economic Engine

Huntsville continues to hold its position as the fastest-growing economy in Alabama. The city’s high quality of life, skilled workforce, and robust infrastructure have attracted major industrial projects and corporate expansions across aerospace, defense, biotechnology, and advanced manufacturing:

Eli Lilly and Company: Building a $6 billion pharmaceutical manufacturing facility at I-565 and Greenbrier Parkway—representing the largest private industrial investment in Alabama history. The 260-acre campus will produce small molecule synthetic and peptide medicines using advanced automation and AI, creating approximately 450 jobs through 2032.
U.S. Space Command HQ: Relocating its permanent headquarters to Redstone Arsenal, bringing more than 1,400 high-value defense and aerospace jobs to the region.
Blue Origin & Redwire: Expanding aerospace and defense operations tied to North Alabama's rocket infrastructure .
L3Harris Technologies: Expanding its solid rocket motor manufacturing and defense production facilities.
Performance Drone Works: Constructing a 90,000-square-foot facility backed by a $9.1 million investment, creating over 500 jobs.
Parsons Corporation: Expanding its Huntsville footprint with a $5 million-plus investment, adding nearly 200 jobs.
Glaukos Corporation & SPX Enterprises: Establishing new operational footprints and facilities in North Alabama.

SEE VIDEO:  https://t.co/ZQmFtOiFVR

SpaceX’s rocket catch symbolizes more than an engineering triumph; it mirrors the momentum of Alabama itself. From the defense innovations at Redstone Arsenal to the shores of the Gulf Coast, Gulf Shores has rapidly become the premier playground and investment destination for the new wave of high-tech professionals relocating to Huntsville. Ultimately, the state is demonstrating how aerospace achievement, economic expansion, and quality of life go hand in hand.

text:
𝐒𝐭𝐞𝐯𝐞 𝐍𝐚𝐥𝐥𝐨𝐧’𝐬 𝐟𝐢𝐥𝐦 𝐭𝐚𝐥𝐤 𝐨𝐧 ‘𝑪𝒊𝒏𝒆𝒎𝒂 𝑨𝒃𝒐𝒖𝒕 𝑻𝒆𝒍𝒆𝒗𝒊𝒔𝒊𝒐𝒏’ 

Steve Nallon, in this talk on cinema about television (with the focal example being PLEASANTVILLE), looks at those movies that are about the television industry, the making of television, and, more particularly, the viewers’ experience of watching television and the ethos of the programmes shown.  
Steve begins by considering Marshall McLuhan’s famous remark from his book UNDERSTANDING MEDIA (1964) where he says, “the medium is the message”. The questions raised are: first, to what extent does the medium shape the message it transmits; and, second, in these days of so-called post-post-modernism, are we way too knowing of the nature of the medium itself? Picking up on this last point, the lecture suggests that, far from being a recent innovation, creators have for centuries had an awareness of the media they are working in. For example, in the prose fiction, there is Sterne’s TRISTRAM SHANDY, and in the theatre there is Aristophanes’s THE POET AND THE WOMEN. In cinema history, there is the early example of the nature of the medium being aware of itself in Buster Keaton’s SHERLOCK JR.. The question is then asked: ‘When a medium explores its own nature, or that of another medium, what aspect of that medium is being represented: its form, the creative process, or the audience response to it?’ 
Before considering how cinema represents the medium of television, the lecture sets out some of the differences between the two media, including time (specifically duration and frequency) and space (particularly the use of fictional spaces). The presentation then notes that, although there are differences, the two media do have one thing in common that is not to be found in any other medium – and that is editing. However, Steve does point out that the two media have different editing styles. Here, the lecture specifically discusses the television editing style of the 1950s American sitcom and its relationship to PLEASANTVILLE. The choice for the film director when making PLEASANTVILLE was to decide between the presentational style of the sitcom form of the 1950s and the movie editing style of the modern era. The basic point is that PLEASANTVILLE looks like a film, not a film that reproduces a television-style visual form. Also, on the subject of presentational style, the talk observes that television in the 1950s was in black and white, adding that, since it is in the nature of black and white not to be realistic, the medium is always a ‘representation’ of reality and never a simple reproduction of reality. This may seem an obvious, and even unimportant observation, but for younger cinemagoers and television viewers, who are almost exclusively brought up on colour images in both media, it is a major presentational difference. More importantly, the change from black and white to colour is a key visual conceit in the film.
The talk then moves on to consider several key terms in academia that are often used to discuss film and media, namely ‘reflexivity’, ‘intertextuality’, and ‘metatextuality’. Reflexivity comes from the idea of the reflexive pronoun; for example, ‘himself’ – as in ‘This lecturer thinks very highly of himself.’ Essentially, reflexivity in a narrative work is when the medium turns back on itself to remind its audience or readership that they are watching/reading a constructed piece of fiction. An example of reflexivity in film would be THE PLAYER, which ends with the plot of THE PLAYER being offered to the main character of the Player in the film (Griffin Mill) as an idea for a movie. Intertextuality occurs when another film (or text) is brought into the world of a film. For example, WAYNE’S WORLD has a scene where the policeman from TERMINATOR II asks, “Have you seen this boy?” Metatextuality occurs when the film draws attention to its own filmic nature. In GEORGE OF THE JUNGLE, for example, the voice-over narrator observes, “Meanwhile, back at the big and expensive jungle set.” The talk suggests that although such terms can be useful in introducing ideas, there are other less ‘jargony’ words that are equally useful when considering film referencing – and these include evoke, parody, and homage. 
The lecture then lists a few of the cultural references made in PLEASANTVILLE. The set design, for example, has a look of THE DONNA REED SHOW, and Don Knotts, famous as Barney Fife in the 1960s series THE ANDY GRIFFITH SHOW, is cast as the TV repair man. Both clearly refer back to another era. As well as television references, there are nods to movies, especially PATTON and CITIZEN KANE, in the portrayal of the mayor. Also, the whole fantasy plot is Capraesque in that it draws from IT’S A WONDERFUL LIFE in both its structure and its setting. Indeed, a strong aspect of the film’s referencing comes from its use of 1950s iconographic images of small-town America, such as the pebbles at the girl’s window and the soda cafe. Towards the end of the movie, the allusions are brought up to date with a reference to the town of Springfield, the home of the Simpson family. There are also visual references to the Bible, specifically Eden and the apple of knowledge. The question the lecture is asking is, ‘Can the complexity and range of the referencing that is in PLEASANTVILLE be accommodated by film studies jargon and, more importantly, do such references conflict and so potentially confuse the viewer?’ What certainly can be said is that the multiplicity of references, ‘Easter Eggs’, and nods in PLEASANTVILLE is not just concerned with television and a focus on the medium of television alone. Such a limitation would be a disservice to the film.
The lecture then moves on to briefly discuss some films about films. These include movies about the film business (GET SHORTY), filmmaking (SHADOW OF A VAMPIRE), stardom (A STAR IS BORN), and the audience (PLAY IT AGAIN, SAM). Steve notes that some are affectionate portrayals, while others are more satirical. Next, Steve’s presentation considers some films about television, including BROADCAST NEWS, CAPRICORN ONE, TO DIE FOR, and THE KING OF COMEDY. Following on from this, the question is asked: ‘In the cinema’s portrayal of the media of film and television, which medium is presented as telling the biggest lie?’ To answer this, the lecture compares SINGIN’ IN THE RAIN to QUIZ SHOW and THE TRUMAN SHOW. Lies are told, for each movie has characters speaking words that are not their own, but, arguably QUIZ SHOW and THE TRUMAN SHOW tell the bigger lie. The lecture develops this theme with numerous examples, and then briefly compares films about the watching of television (POLTERGEIST and VIDEODROME) with films about the watching of movies (CINEMA PARADISO, THE PURPLE ROSE OF CAIRO, and THE LONG DAY CLOSES). 
The point of all these examples and observations is that, unlike most representations of television in the movies, the representation of television in PLEASANTVILLE is hardly clear-cut. Is the fictional sitcom PLEASANTVILLE a good or bad programme? Is it advisable to watch such television? In a way, though, suggests the talk, these are the wrong questions. Gary Ross, the writer and director of PLEASANTVILLE, claims in the DVD commentary that the movie is about the failure of people to connect with the world. Both David and Jennifer fail to connect with the world around them, but when they do finally connect, that is the moment when they change colour. Likewise, the world of the town of Pleasantville, as presented in the film, has failed to connect with the real world of the 1950s, and it is only when jazz and Picasso arrive in Pleasantville that it finally changes colour. The talk makes the point that television in the 1950s did not lie directly, but it did lie through omission. Steve then notes that, in more recent years, movies have taken a more positive view, in general, towards the power and influence of television, and here he cites examples such was FROST/NIXON, and GOODNIGHT, AND GOOD LUCK, and, more recently, I SAW THE TV GLOW. 
Steve’s presentation moves to a conclusion by observing that when film represents television, the representation of television might not be what the film is actually about. If that is the only consideration, then one might be missing the entire point of the film. THE TRUMAN SHOW might be regarded as being about television, but it also rejects the traditional Hollywood notion of ‘The Grand Narrative’, where every action has a reason, every cause has an effect, and every event has a purpose. Indeed, the talk observes, the name of the guide or god-like overseer is Christof. Steve suggests that PLEASANTVILLE is not really about television, even though its representation of television is complex and challenging. Instead, he offers the idea that the real focus of PLEASANTVILLE is America coming to terms with its so-called Utopian era of the 1950s being a false dream. Steve argues that PLEASANTVILLE is setting out a third way of living with the past in the present. It seems to be suggesting not an attitude of outright rejection of the past, as Jennifer at first seems to represent, nor an outright rejection of the present, as David seems to want in the early section of the movie, but instead a coming to terms with both.
Presentations are available for literary festivals, cultural societies, schools, colleges, libraries, museums, cruises, and film clubs.

text:
【Confessing to Witchcraft Could Save Your Life】The Salem Witch Trials

At Salem, admitting you served the devil could help you escape the gallows. Insisting you were innocent could end with a rope around your neck.

In 1692, in colonial Massachusetts, magistrates offered the accused a way out: confess, repent, and name others.

Every new name could put another person in danger.

The court accepted “spectral evidence”—claims that an accused person’s spirit had appeared and tormented someone. Your body could be elsewhere. Your supposed ghost could still be used against you.

Then there was Giles Corey.

He refused to enter a plea. To force him to answer, officials laid weights on his body. He died under them on September 19. Three days later, his wife Martha was hanged.

By the end of the crisis, nineteen people had been hanged, Corey had been crushed to death, and at least five others had died in jail.

These were not killings by a mob outside the law. Arrest warrants were issued. Witnesses testified. Courts condemned people.

In October, the governor dissolved the special court. In 1697, one of its judges, Samuel Sewall, publicly acknowledged his guilt and asked forgiveness for his part in the trials.

The court had offered some of its victims a terrible bargain: admit to an imaginary crime and help it find the next accused.

If telling the truth could get you killed, while naming someone else could help you survive, what kind of testimony was that court producing?

ㄴ 이들은 저주받은 자에게는 땅에 묻힐 자격도 없다며 태워 죽이고, 이미 묻힌 경우에는 파내어 시신을 훼손하기까지 하는데요.

“죽은 자를 땅에 묻는 걸 허락하지 않는 것은 차르 표토르의 궁정에서도 잔혹한 벌에 속했다.” — 81p

마을에서는 사람이 계속 죽고, 붉은 비가 내리고, 나무에는 새빨간 물도 기름도 아닌 무언가가 섞여 있고…

이 기이한 현상들을 모두 저주라는 한마디로 설명해도 되는 걸까요?

“믿음이 죽으려면 얼마나 긴 시간이 흘러야 하나?” — 241p

물론! 이 이야기는 소설이지만, 실제 마녀사냥의 사례로 자주 언급되는 세일럼 사건을 함께 떠올려볼 만한데요. 1692년 세일럼에서는 “저 사람의 영혼이 나를 공격했다”는 검증할 수 없는 주장까지 법정에서 증거로 받아들여졌습니다. 이 마녀재판으로 19명이 교수형을 당했고, 다른 1명은 무거운 돌로 몸을 압박하는 고문 끝에 사망했어요.

𝐀 𝐌𝐈𝐂𝐇𝐈𝐆𝐀𝐍 𝐆𝐔𝐀𝐑𝐃𝐈𝐀𝐍 𝐈𝐌𝐏𝐑𝐈𝐒𝐎𝐍𝐄𝐃 𝐁𝐀𝐑𝐁 𝐀𝐍𝐃 𝐁𝐎𝐁 𝐀𝐓 𝐇𝐎𝐌𝐄 — 𝐏𝐎𝐋𝐈𝐂𝐄 𝐂𝐀𝐌𝐄 𝟏𝟑 𝐓𝐈𝐌𝐄𝐒

Barb Elbridge, 70, and her husband Bob Mitchell, 72, spent a lifetime building a $2.7 million estate in Utica, Michigan. Today a stranger controls every dollar of it, and their own daughter can’t get past a six-foot fence to see them. “𝘐 𝘫𝘶𝘴𝘵 𝘸𝘢𝘯𝘵 𝘮𝘺 𝘱𝘢𝘳𝘦𝘯𝘵𝘴 𝘣𝘢𝘤𝘬,” Marcie Mitchell told WXYZ-TV Detroit’s 7 Investigators.

Macomb County Probate Judge Kathryn George appointed 𝐂𝐚𝐫𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐇𝐞𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐬 𝐌𝐢𝐜𝐡𝐢𝐠𝐚𝐧, owned by Catherine “Cathy” Kirk, as guardian and conservator over the couple. Kirk’s other company, Executive Care, now supplies their 24-hour caregivers — and bills the estate for the privilege. The money only moves one direction: into Kirk’s companies, out of a couple who never got a vote.

Since the takeover, the family says Barb and Bob’s landline was cut, their cell phones confiscated, and their own cars towed out of their own driveway. Caregivers put up a six-foot privacy fence between the couple’s house and the relatives next door. The family says Bob has tried to escape more than once, and recent photos they shared show 𝐛𝐫𝐮𝐢𝐬𝐞𝐬 𝐮𝐩 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐝𝐨𝐰𝐧 𝐡𝐢𝐬 𝐚𝐫𝐦𝐬. Utica police have been called to the home 𝟏𝟑 𝐭𝐢𝐦𝐞𝐬 since Caring Hearts moved in — and when WXYZ’s reporter came to ask questions, caregivers called police on the family instead, claiming they were leaning over the fence. The family denies it.

The company’s attorney, Michael Taylor — who also happens to be the mayor of Sterling Heights — told the court Executive Care was state-licensed. It isn’t. State officials confirmed Kirk’s companies 𝐝𝐨𝐧’𝐭 𝐚𝐩𝐩𝐞𝐚𝐫 𝐨𝐧 𝐌𝐢𝐜𝐡𝐢𝐠𝐚𝐧’𝐬 𝐨𝐰𝐧 𝐥𝐢𝐬𝐭 𝐨𝐟 𝐚𝐩𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐝 𝐡𝐨𝐦𝐞-𝐜𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝐚𝐠𝐞𝐧𝐜𝐢𝐞𝐬. Caring Hearts claims the couple was malnourished and living in unsanitary, dangerous conditions before it stepped in; the family calls that a lie invented to justify taking their parents and their money. The Michigan Attorney General has now opened an investigation.

Only after WXYZ started asking Judge George hard questions did Caring Hearts suddenly offer the family a visit. Everyone is due back in court next month — but for now, a couple worth $2.7 million sits behind a fence a judge put up, guarded by a company that lied about its license to get the keys.

𝐓𝐡𝐢𝐬 𝐢𝐬 𝐰𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐌𝐢𝐜𝐡𝐢𝐠𝐚𝐧 𝐜𝐚𝐥𝐥𝐬 𝐞𝐥𝐝𝐞𝐫 𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐭𝐞𝐜𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧: 𝐚 $𝟐.𝟕 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐭𝐞 𝐥𝐨𝐜𝐤𝐞𝐝 𝐛𝐞𝐡𝐢𝐧𝐝 𝐚 𝐟𝐞𝐧𝐜𝐞, 𝐚 𝐟𝐚𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐲 𝐥𝐨𝐜𝐤𝐞𝐝 𝐨𝐮𝐭, 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐚 𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐩𝐚𝐧𝐲 𝐭𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐥𝐢𝐞𝐝 𝐚𝐛𝐨𝐮𝐭 𝐢𝐭𝐬 𝐥𝐢𝐜𝐞𝐧𝐬𝐞 𝐭𝐨 𝐠𝐞𝐭 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐤𝐞𝐲𝐬.

text:
🕹️ The History of Video Games in 300 Moments

🔬 THE LAB ERA (1947–1971)

𝟏. 1947: Goldsmith and Mann patent a "cathode-ray tube amusement device", often called the first electronic game.

𝟐. 1950: Bertie the Brain, a 4 m tall tic-tac-toe computer, wows visitors in Toronto 🇨🇦.

𝟑. 1951: The Nimrod computer plays the game Nim at the Festival of Britain 🇬🇧.

𝟒. 1952: A.S. Douglas writes OXO, a noughts-and-crosses game, on Cambridge's EDSAC computer.

𝟓. 1958: William Higinbotham shows Tennis for Two on an oscilloscope in New York 🇺🇸.

𝟔. 1962: Steve Russell and friends at MIT create Spacewar! on a PDP-1 computer.

𝟕. 1962: Spacewar! spreads from lab to lab and inspires a generation of programmers.

𝟖. 1966: Engineer Ralph Baer writes down his idea of playing games on a home TV.

𝟗. 1968: Baer's "Brown Box" prototype, the ancestor of every home console, is up and running.

𝟏𝟎. 1971: Galaxy Game, a coin-operated Spacewar!, is installed at Stanford University.

𝟏𝟏. 1971: Nolan Bushnell and Ted Dabney release Computer Space, the first commercial arcade video game.

𝟏𝟐. 1971: Computer Space reportedly sells only about 1,500 units: too complex for bar customers.

𝟏𝟑. 1971: Three student teachers in Minnesota write the first version of The Oregon Trail.

🕹️ PONG & THE FIRST CONSOLES (1972–1977)

𝟏𝟒. 1972: Baer's design becomes the Magnavox Odyssey, the first home video game console.

𝟏𝟓. 1972: The Odyssey has no sound and uses plastic overlays on the TV screen.

𝟏𝟔. 1972: Bushnell and Dabney found Atari in California.

𝟏𝟕. 1972: Allan Alcorn builds Pong, originally as a training exercise.

𝟏𝟖. 1972: Legend says the first Pong test machine broke because its coin box overflowed.

𝟏𝟗. 1973: Maze War, one of the first first-person shooters, appears at NASA.

𝟐𝟎. 1974: Atari's Gran Trak 10 is among the first arcade racing games.

𝟐𝟏. 1975: Home Pong is sold through the US retailer Sears and becomes a Christmas hit.

𝟐𝟐. 1975: Gun Fight is one of the first arcade games to use a microprocessor.

𝟐𝟑. 1976: Atari settles Magnavox's lawsuit over Pong's similarity to the Odyssey's table tennis.

𝟐𝟒. 1976: The Fairchild Channel F is the first console with swappable ROM cartridges.

𝟐𝟓. 1976: Its cartridge team is led by Jerry Lawson, a pioneering Black engineer.

𝟐𝟔. 1976: Will Crowther's Colossal Cave Adventure starts the adventure genre.

𝟐𝟕. 1976: The arcade game Death Race sparks the first big public outcry over video game violence.

𝟐𝟖. 1976: Warner Communications buys Atari for about $28 million.

𝟐𝟗. 1976: Atari releases Breakout; Steve Wozniak and Steve Jobs worked on its prototype.

𝟑𝟎. 1977: The Atari VCS, later called the 2600, launches with joysticks and cartridges.

𝟑𝟏. 1977: The 2600 goes on to sell about 30 million units.

𝟑𝟐. 1977: Nintendo enters home video games in Japan 🇯🇵 with the Color TV-Game 6.

👾 THE GOLDEN AGE OF ARCADES (1978–1982)

𝟑𝟑. 1978: Tomohiro Nishikado creates Space Invaders for Taito.

𝟑𝟒. 1978: Space Invaders is said to have caused a 100-yen coin shortage in Japan, a disputed claim.

𝟑𝟓. 1978: Roy Trubshaw and Richard Bartle create MUD1 in England 🇬🇧, the first multi-user dungeon.

𝟑𝟔. 1979: Asteroids becomes Atari's best-selling arcade machine.

𝟑𝟕. 1979: Four former Atari programmers found Activision, the first third-party console game developer.

𝟑𝟖. 1979: Namco's Galaxian brings full-colour graphics to the arcade.

𝟑𝟗. 1979: Milton Bradley's Microvision is the first handheld with interchangeable cartridges.

𝟒𝟎. 1980: Toru Iwatani's Pac-Man arrives in arcades.

𝟒𝟏. 1980: Iwatani said Pac-Man's shape was inspired by a pizza with a slice missing.

𝟒𝟐. 1980: In Japan the game was called Puck Man; the name was changed abroad.

𝟒𝟑. 1980: Blinky, Pinky, Inky and Clyde each chase Pac-Man in a different way.

𝟒𝟒. 1980: The US Army reportedly commissions a training version of Battlezone.

𝟒𝟓. 1980: Space Invaders on the Atari 2600 is the first licensed arcade port.

𝟒𝟔. 1980: Warren Robinett hides his name in Atari's Adventure, one of the first known Easter eggs.

𝟒𝟕. 1980: Rogue's random dungeons give the "roguelike" genre its name.

𝟒𝟖. 1980: Infocom releases Zork I, a landmark of text adventures.

𝟒𝟗. 1980: Gunpei Yokoi's Game & Watch handhelds launch at Nintendo.

𝟓𝟎. 1980: Missile Command puts players in charge of defending cities from nuclear attack.

𝟓𝟏. 1981: Shigeru Miyamoto's Donkey Kong introduces Jumpman, soon renamed Mario.

𝟓𝟐. 1981: Mario was reportedly named after Mario Segale, Nintendo of America's landlord.

𝟓𝟑. 1981: Williams' Defender scrolls across a world bigger than the screen.

𝟓𝟒. 1981: Konami's Frogger and Namco's Galaga become arcade staples.

𝟓𝟓. 1981: Ultima and Wizardry lay the foundations of computer role-playing games.

𝟓𝟔. 1982: Ms. Pac-Man, born as an unofficial upgrade kit, becomes a US arcade smash.

𝟓𝟕. 1982: The Commodore 64 launches; estimates of its sales run from 12 to 17 million.

𝟓𝟖. 1982: The ZX Spectrum kicks off the bedroom-coding scene in the UK 🇬🇧.

𝟓𝟗. 1982: Electronic Arts is founded by Trip Hawkins.

𝟔𝟎. 1982: David Crane's Pitfall! for Activision is one of the first side-scrolling platform games.

𝟔𝟏. 1982: ColecoVision launches with Donkey Kong as its pack-in game.

𝟔𝟐. 1982: Namco's Pole Position becomes the top-earning arcade game in North America in 1983.

𝟔𝟑. 1982: Atari's rushed Pac-Man port for the 2600 sells millions but disappoints players.

𝟔𝟒. 1982: Howard Scott Warshaw makes the E.T. game in about five weeks.

💥 THE CRASH & THE COMEBACK (1983–1988)

𝟔𝟓. 1983: Dragon's Lair, animated by Don Bluth on laserdisc, costs 50 cents a play.

𝟔𝟔. 1983: The North American video game market crashes; revenues fall by about 97% by 1985.

𝟔𝟕. 1983: Atari buries unsold cartridges in a landfill in Alamogordo, New Mexico 🇺🇸.

𝟔𝟖. 1983: Nintendo releases the Famicom in Japan 🇯🇵 on 15 July.

𝟔𝟗. 1983: Sega's first home console, the SG-1000, launches the very same day.

𝟕𝟎. 1983: Mario Bros. introduces his brother Luigi.

𝟕𝟏. 1983: Microsoft and ASCII announce the MSX home computer standard.

𝟕𝟐. 1984: Alexey Pajitnov creates Tetris at a Soviet computing centre in Moscow.

𝟕𝟑. 1984: The name Tetris combines "tetra" (four) and tennis, Pajitnov's favourite sport.

𝟕𝟒. 1984: David Braben and Ian Bell's Elite squeezes a 3D space universe into a BBC Micro.

𝟕𝟓. 1984: Roberta Williams' King's Quest brings animated graphics to adventure games.

𝟕𝟔. 1985: The Nintendo Entertainment System test-launches in New York 🇺🇸.

𝟕𝟕. 1985: Nintendo bundles R.O.B. the robot so shops will treat the NES as a toy.

𝟕𝟖. 1985: Nintendo's Seal of Quality limits shovelware, which had helped cause the crash.

𝟕𝟗. 1985: Super Mario Bros. arrives and goes on to sell over 40 million copies.

𝟖𝟎. 1985: Atari Games' Gauntlet lets four players fight side by side in the arcade.

𝟖𝟏. 1985: The Commodore Amiga launches with advanced graphics and sound.

𝟖𝟐. 1986: The Legend of Zelda debuts, inspired by Miyamoto's childhood explorations around Kyoto.

𝟖𝟑. 1986: Yuji Horii's Dragon Quest, with art by Akira Toriyama, makes RPGs a craze in Japan.

𝟖𝟒. 1986: Metroid surprises players by revealing hero Samus Aran as a woman.

𝟖𝟓. 1986: Yu Suzuki's Out Run lets players choose the music on the car radio.

𝟖𝟔. 1987: Square releases Final Fantasy; legend says it was named as a possible last game.

𝟖𝟕. 1987: Hideo Kojima's Metal Gear launches stealth action on the MSX2.

𝟖𝟖. 1987: Capcom releases Street Fighter and Mega Man.

𝟖𝟗. 1987: NEC's PC Engine, known as the TurboGrafx-16 in the West, launches in Japan.

𝟗𝟎. 1987: Maniac Mansion debuts the SCUMM engine behind many LucasArts adventures.

𝟗𝟏. 1988: Sega launches the Mega Drive in Japan.

𝟗𝟐. 1988: Super Mario Bros. 3 is released in Japan and later sells over 17 million copies.

𝟗𝟑. 1988: Nintendo Power magazine launches in the US.

𝟗𝟒. 1988: John Madden Football (1988) starts a sports series that still runs every year.

🦔 THE 16-BIT WARS (1989–1995)

𝟗𝟓. 1989: Gunpei Yokoi's Game Boy launches in Japan.

𝟗𝟔. 1989: Tetris is bundled with the Game Boy in North America and becomes a global obsession.

𝟗𝟕. 1989: The Game Boy line, including the Color, sells about 119 million units.

𝟗𝟖. 1989: The Atari Lynx is the first handheld with a colour LCD.

𝟗𝟗. 1989: Will Wright's SimCity creates a game you cannot really win.

𝟏𝟎𝟎. 1989: Jordan Mechner animates Prince of Persia by filming his brother running and jumping.

𝟏𝟎𝟏. 1989: The Sega Genesis arrives in North America.

𝟏𝟎𝟐. 1990: Nintendo releases the Super Famicom in Japan.

𝟏𝟎𝟑. 1990: Launch title Super Mario World introduces Yoshi.

𝟏𝟎𝟒. 1990: id Software's Commander Keen shows smooth scrolling on PCs.

𝟏𝟎𝟓. 1990: SNK launches the Neo Geo, with arcade-quality games at home.

𝟏𝟎𝟔. 1991: Sonic the Hedgehog gives Sega a fast, cool mascot to rival Mario.

𝟏𝟎𝟕. 1991: Sega's slogan "Genesis does what Nintendon't" fuels the console war.

𝟏𝟎𝟖. 1991: Street Fighter II sets off a worldwide fighting game boom.

𝟏𝟎𝟗. 1991: Its combos reportedly began as a happy programming accident.

𝟏𝟏𝟎. 1991: Sid Meier's Civilization launches the "one more turn" genre.

𝟏𝟏𝟏. 1991: Nintendo's SNES arrives in North America.

𝟏𝟏𝟐. 1991: The Legend of Zelda: A Link to the Past arrives on the Super Famicom.

𝟏𝟏𝟑. 1991: DMA Design in Scotland 🇬🇧 releases Lemmings.

𝟏𝟏𝟒. 1992: Mortal Kombat's digitised actors and gory "fatalities" cause outrage.

𝟏𝟏𝟓. 1992: Wolfenstein 3D popularises the first-person shooter.

𝟏𝟏𝟔. 1992: Alone in the Dark lays the groundwork for 3D survival horror.

𝟏𝟏𝟕. 1992: Super Mario Kart popularises the kart racing genre.

𝟏𝟏𝟖. 1992: Westwood's Dune II sets the template for real-time strategy.

𝟏𝟏𝟗. 1992: Sega launches Sonic 2 worldwide on "Sonic 2sday", a Tuesday in November.

𝟏𝟐𝟎. 1993: id Software releases Doom on 10 December.

𝟏𝟐𝟏. 1993: Doom's first episode is free as shareware and spreads everywhere.

𝟏𝟐𝟐. 1993: Doom popularises the word "deathmatch".

𝟏𝟐𝟑. 1993: US Senate hearings on video game violence follow Mortal Kombat and Night Trap.

𝟏𝟐𝟒. 1993: Myst becomes a CD-ROM phenomenon and is long the best-selling PC game.

𝟏𝟐𝟓. 1993: Star Fox uses the Super FX chip to bring 3D polygons to the SNES.

𝟏𝟐𝟔. 1993: The Atari Jaguar is marketed as the first "64-bit" console.

𝟏𝟐𝟕. 1993: Sega's Virtua Fighter is the first 3D fighting game.

𝟏𝟐𝟖. 1994: The ESRB age rating system is founded in North America.

𝟏𝟐𝟗. 1994: Sony launches the PlayStation in Japan 🇯🇵 on 3 December.

𝟏𝟑𝟎. 1994: The PlayStation grew out of a failed CD add-on deal between Sony and Nintendo.

𝟏𝟑𝟏. 1994: Sega launches the Saturn in Japan.

𝟏𝟑𝟐. 1994: Rare's Donkey Kong Country stuns players with pre-rendered 3D graphics.

𝟏𝟑𝟑. 1994: Blizzard releases Warcraft: Orcs & Humans.

𝟏𝟑𝟒. 1994: Super Metroid perfects the exploration style later called "Metroidvania".

𝟏𝟑𝟓. 1995: The first E3 expo is held in Los Angeles.

𝟏𝟑𝟔. 1995: At E3 Sega surprise-launches the Saturn at $399; Sony answers with one word on stage: "$299".

𝟏𝟑𝟕. 1995: Square's "Dream Team" releases Chrono Trigger.

𝟏𝟑𝟖. 1995: Nintendo's Virtual Boy flops and is discontinued within about a year.

𝟏𝟑𝟗. 1995: Microsoft's DirectX helps turn Windows into a gaming platform.

𝟏𝟒𝟎. 1995: Command & Conquer popularises RTS online and over local networks.

💿 THE 3D REVOLUTION (1996–1999)

𝟏𝟒𝟏. 1996: The Nintendo 64 launches in Japan.

𝟏𝟒𝟐. 1996: Super Mario 64 shows how to move in 3D with an analogue stick.

𝟏𝟒𝟑. 1996: Pokémon Red and Green are released in Japan on 27 February.

𝟏𝟒𝟒. 1996: Creator Satoshi Tajiri was inspired by his childhood hobby of collecting insects.

𝟏𝟒𝟓. 1996: Core Design's Tomb Raider introduces Lara Croft.

𝟏𝟒𝟔. 1996: Capcom's Resident Evil popularises the term "survival horror".

𝟏𝟒𝟕. 1996: Quake brings true 3D worlds and online multiplayer to PCs.

𝟏𝟒𝟖. 1996: Blizzard releases Diablo along with its free online service, https://t.co/HRjdI4HaQs.

𝟏𝟒𝟗. 1996: Bandai's Tamagotchi virtual pet becomes a global craze.

𝟏𝟓𝟎. 1996: Naughty Dog's Crash Bandicoot becomes an early PlayStation mascot.

𝟏𝟓𝟏. 1997: Final Fantasy VII becomes a worldwide hit and makes JRPGs mainstream in the West.

𝟏𝟓𝟐. 1997: Rare's GoldenEye 007 makes split-screen multiplayer a sleepover ritual.

𝟏𝟓𝟑. 1997: Ultima Online popularises the massively multiplayer online game.

𝟏𝟓𝟒. 1997: In a test, a player kills Lord British, creator Richard Garriott's usually invulnerable character.

𝟏𝟓𝟓. 1997: Nokia's 6110 phone comes with Snake, a mobile game for millions 🇫🇮.

𝟏𝟓𝟔. 1997: DMA Design releases the first Grand Theft Auto.

𝟏𝟓𝟕. 1997: Gran Turismo sets a new bar for realistic racing.

𝟏𝟓𝟖. 1997: Sony's DualShock brings two analogue sticks and rumble to the PlayStation.

𝟏𝟓𝟗. 1997: Microsoft releases Age of Empires.

𝟏𝟔𝟎. 1997: Interplay's Fallout drops players into a post-nuclear wasteland.

𝟏𝟔𝟏. 1998: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time introduces Z-targeting.

𝟏𝟔𝟐. 1998: Valve's Half-Life tells its story without cutscenes.

𝟏𝟔𝟑. 1998: StarCraft is released and becomes a TV sport in South Korea 🇰🇷.

𝟏𝟔𝟒. 1998: Metal Gear Solid brings cinematic stealth to the PlayStation.

𝟏𝟔𝟓. 1998: Sega's Dreamcast launches in Japan with a built-in modem.

𝟏𝟔𝟔. 1998: Nintendo releases the Game Boy Color.

𝟏𝟔𝟕. 1998: Pokémon reaches North America and the anime spreads worldwide.

𝟏𝟔𝟖. 1998: Konami's Dance Dance Revolution puts a dance floor in the arcade.

𝟏𝟔𝟗. 1999: EverQuest hooks so many players it is nicknamed "EverCrack".

𝟏𝟕𝟎. 1999: Counter-Strike starts as a fan-made mod for Half-Life.

𝟏𝟕𝟏. 1999: The Dreamcast launches in North America on 9/9/99.

𝟏𝟕𝟐. 1999: Sega's Shenmue is reportedly among the most expensive games made up to that time.

𝟏𝟕𝟑. 1999: Unreal Tournament and Quake III Arena push online arena shooters.

🌐 ONLINE & THE SIXTH GENERATION (2000–2005)

𝟏𝟕𝟒. 2000: The PlayStation 2 launches in Japan and doubles as a cheap DVD player.

𝟏𝟕𝟓. 2000: The PS2 becomes the best-selling console ever, at more than 160 million units.

𝟏𝟕𝟔. 2000: Will Wright's The Sims becomes one of PC's biggest hits.

𝟏𝟕𝟕. 2000: Blizzard's Diablo II becomes a huge online action-RPG hit.

𝟏𝟕𝟖. 2000: Deus Ex shows how player choice can shape a story.

𝟏𝟕𝟗. 2001: Microsoft enters the market with the Xbox.

𝟏𝟖𝟎. 2001: Halo: Combat Evolved shows that shooters can work on a gamepad.

𝟏𝟖𝟏. 2001: Nintendo launches the GameCube and the Game Boy Advance.

𝟏𝟖𝟐. 2001: Sega stops making consoles and becomes a third-party publisher.

𝟏𝟖𝟑. 2001: Grand Theft Auto III creates the modern open-world 3D city.

𝟏𝟖𝟒. 2002: Xbox Live brings online multiplayer and voice chat to consoles.

𝟏𝟖𝟓. 2002: Kingdom Hearts unites Disney and Final Fantasy characters.

𝟏𝟖𝟔. 2002: The US Army releases America's Army, a free game used as a recruiting tool.

𝟏𝟖𝟕. 2002: The Sims passes Myst as the best-selling PC game of its time.

𝟏𝟖𝟖. 2003: Valve launches Steam, now the world's largest PC game store.

𝟏𝟖𝟗. 2003: EVE Online begins in Iceland 🇮🇸, famous for vast player-run wars.

𝟏𝟗𝟎. 2003: Nokia's N-Gage tries to combine a phone with a game console.

𝟏𝟗𝟏. 2004: World of Warcraft launches; it later peaks at about 12 million subscribers.

𝟏𝟗𝟐. 2004: The dual-screen, touch-screen Nintendo DS launches.

𝟏𝟗𝟑. 2004: Sony enters handhelds with the PSP.

𝟏𝟗𝟒. 2004: Half-Life 2 puts realistic physics and the Gravity Gun in players' hands.

𝟏𝟗𝟓. 2004: Halo 2 sets an entertainment record with $125 million in first-day sales.

𝟏𝟗𝟔. 2005: The Xbox 360 launches and popularises Achievements.

text:
At 9 years old, Jensen Huang was cleaning toilets in a boarding school in Kentucky.
Today, he leads NVIDIA, one of the most valuable companies in human history.
But the journey between those two points is far more interesting than the money, the black leather jacket, or the billions of dollars.
Because NVIDIA almost died before the world knew what it was.
And the decisions that saved it were not always popular.
Let's go back to the beginning.
Jensen was born in Taiwan in 1963. When he was about five, his family moved to Thailand.
His parents eventually became concerned about the safety and future of their children. So they made a difficult decision.
They sent Jensen and his older brother to America ahead of them.
Jensen was only nine.
Imagine being that young, leaving your parents behind, travelling to another country, and trying to find your place in a world you barely understand.
But things became even more difficult.
His uncle wanted the boys to receive a good education, so he enrolled them in a boarding school in Kentucky.
There was just one problem.
It wasn't the kind of school he thought it was.
The school was actually a religious reform school for troubled teenagers.
Jensen was one of the youngest students there. He struggled with English, had a strong accent, and was one of the few Asian children.
Some of the older students were violent. His roommate was 17 and had scars from being stabbed.
And what was Jensen's daily responsibility?
Cleaning toilets.
Every single day.
But something interesting happened.
His roommate couldn't read, while Jensen could.
So they made a deal.
Jensen would teach him how to read, and in return, the older boy would teach him how to become stronger.
They became friends.
Think about that for a moment.
A nine-year-old boy, thousands of miles away from his parents, found a way to survive by identifying what someone else needed and offering something in return.
Years later, Jensen and his wife would donate $2 million to that same school to help build a dormitory and classroom building for girls.
He didn't forget where he came from.
When his parents eventually joined him in America, the family settled in Oregon.
Jensen attended Aloha High School, skipped two grades, and graduated at just 16.
He was interested in mathematics, computers, and engineering.
But he also needed money.
At 15, he got a job at Denny's, an American restaurant chain.
He started as a dishwasher.
Then he became a busboy, clearing tables, and eventually a waiter.
He worked overnight shifts while going to school.
Years later, he would say that the job helped him overcome his shyness and taught him how to work under pressure.
Interestingly, those restaurant jobs are still part of his professional story.
But nobody working alongside that teenager could have imagined what he would eventually build.
Jensen went on to study electrical engineering at Oregon State University.
After graduating, he worked as a chip designer at AMD and later joined LSI Logic.
He also attended Stanford at night, eventually earning a master's degree in electrical engineering.
By his late twenties, he had a stable career and a comfortable future.
He could have stayed there.
But he didn't.
In 1993, three engineers walked into a Denny's restaurant in San Jose, California.
Their names were Jensen Huang, Chris Malachowsky, and Curtis Priem.
They sat in a booth, drank cheap coffee, and discussed an idea.
They wanted to build computer chips that would make video games look better.
That was the original idea behind NVIDIA.
Not artificial intelligence.
Not ChatGPT.
Not the technology powering the world's biggest data centres.
Just better graphics for video games.
They believed computers would eventually need special chips to handle increasingly realistic graphics.
Many people weren't convinced.
But the three founders took the risk.
They raised money, hired engineers, and started building.
Then came their first major mistake.
Their first graphics chip, the NV1, used a different approach from what most of the industry was adopting.
It was an intelligent idea on paper, but the rest of the industry was moving in another direction.
Game developers were building around triangles, while NVIDIA had chosen curved surfaces.
The result?
Their chip struggled to work with the software developers were already using.
Sales were disappointing.
The next product was also built around the same flawed approach.
Money started disappearing.
And the company was running out of time.
At one point, NVIDIA was roughly 30 days away from going out of business.
Let that sink in.
The company that would eventually become a multi-trillion-dollar business was once struggling to survive another month.
Jensen had a difficult decision to make.
He could continue pretending everything was fine, or admit that the technology they had built wasn't going to work.
He chose to admit the mistake.
But there was another problem.
NVIDIA had a contract with Sega, the Japanese video game company.
Jensen knew they couldn't deliver the product as originally promised.
So he travelled to Japan to meet a Sega executive named Shoichiro Irimajiri.
He explained the situation honestly.
He told him that NVIDIA couldn't deliver the chip in the way they had planned.
Then he made an unusual request.
He asked Sega to pay the remaining $5 million anyway.
Not because NVIDIA had delivered everything perfectly, but because the company needed the money to survive.
Sega could have walked away.
Instead, the executive agreed.
That $5 million gave NVIDIA the time it desperately needed.
Think about it.
Sometimes, the difference between a business that survives and one that disappears isn't a perfect business plan.
Sometimes, it's one person willing to trust you when you have very little left to offer.
But the money wasn't enough on its own.
NVIDIA had to change direction.
The company abandoned its original graphics approach and focused on the technology the wider industry was adopting.
It developed the RIVA 128 graphics chip.
The product was a success.
NVIDIA reportedly sold around a million units within its first four months.
The company that had nearly disappeared was back in the game.
In 1999, NVIDIA went public.
That same year, it introduced the GeForce 256 and helped establish the term GPU, short for Graphics Processing Unit.
At the time, these chips were mainly associated with gaming.
But Jensen noticed something other people were overlooking.
Scientists and researchers were beginning to use graphics chips for work that had nothing to do with video games.
And that observation would lead to the biggest decision in NVIDIA's history.
In 2006, NVIDIA introduced CUDA.
To understand why this mattered, imagine two kitchens.
The first has one extremely talented chef who can prepare almost any meal, but can only prepare one dish at a time.
The second has thousands of cooks, each handling a small part of the work at the same time.
The first kitchen is similar to a CPU.
The second is similar to a GPU.
A GPU can perform thousands of smaller calculations at once.
This makes it incredibly useful for certain types of scientific research, simulations, and artificial intelligence.
But there was a problem.
Using graphics chips for these other tasks was difficult.
So NVIDIA created CUDA, a system that allowed developers to write software that could use the power of its GPUs for much more than graphics.
Here is where Jensen made another unpopular decision.
He didn't reserve this technology for expensive, specialised chips.
He invested in making it available across NVIDIA's product range, including gaming graphics cards.
It cost money.
Investors questioned the decision.
For years, the investment affected profits, and many people wondered why a company known for gaming was spending so much on software that most of its customers barely used.
Jensen continued anyway.
NVIDIA made the tools available, supported universities, and helped train developers to use them.
He was building something that might not pay off immediately.
And that is what makes this decision so important.
He wasn't just selling computer chips anymore.
He was building an entire ecosystem around them.
Years later, researchers at the University of Toronto used two NVIDIA gaming graphics cards to train a system called AlexNet.
In 2012, that system achieved a remarkable result in a major image-recognition competition.
It showed the research world just how powerful GPUs could be for deep learning.
Suddenly, the same type of chips people bought to play video games could help computers learn to recognise images.
NVIDIA had spent years preparing for a market that was only beginning to emerge.
And it wasn't finished.
In 2016, Jensen personally delivered NVIDIA's first DGX-1 supercomputer to a young research organisation called OpenAI.
At the time, very few people understood just how important artificial intelligence would become.
Then came November 2022.
OpenAI released ChatGPT.
Millions of people started interacting with AI in a completely new way.
Businesses wanted their own AI systems.
Researchers wanted more computing power.
Technology companies began building enormous data centres.
And almost everyone needed the same thing:
NVIDIA's chips.
The H100 became one of the most sought-after pieces of technology in the world.
The company that started by making graphics cards for video games had become central to the artificial intelligence revolution.
Its market value climbed from $1 trillion in 2023 to $2 trillion, then $3 trillion, and eventually reached $5 trillion in 2025.
Jensen became a global celebrity.
The black leather jacket became his signature.
World leaders wanted meetings with him. People lined up for pictures and autographs.
But there is something important about this story that people often overlook.
NVIDIA didn't become what it is today because of one lucky moment.
It was built through decades of decisions.
Some worked.
Some failed.
The company struggled with product mistakes, competition, financial crises, failed market entries, and missed opportunities.
It also made major investments that looked questionable at the time.
One of the most important was CUDA.
Without years of investment in that software ecosystem, NVIDIA's position in the AI industry could look very different today.
And that brings us to another lesson.
Sometimes, the biggest opportunities are hidden inside things that other people don't take seriously.
But success doesn't mean the journey is always upward.
Even today, NVIDIA faces serious questions.
There are concerns about the enormous spending on artificial intelligence, whether the current AI boom can justify its cost, competition from other chipmakers, and restrictions on selling advanced chips to China.
There are also questions about the way money moves between NVIDIA and some of the companies buying its technology.
Supporters point to its revenue and profits.
Critics worry that parts of the AI industry may be growing too quickly.
Both sides have arguments worth examining.
And then, in November 2026, another story put Jensen himself under the spotlight.
Reports raised questions about his relationship with a Chinese executive linked to a Singapore-based data centre company.
Some reports described that executive as a suspected spy, but those allegations have not been established as facts.
NVIDIA's board announced an independent investigation into reports that Jensen had been targeted by a foreign intelligence effort.
The board said it had no reason to believe company secrets or national security information had been compromised.
Jensen also committed to cooperating with the review.
A lawsuit was subsequently filed by a law firm, making claims about what the company and its CEO disclosed to investors. Those claims have not been tested in court.
The investigation is ongoing.
And that is important because a story involving allegations, a major company, investors, and national security deserves facts, not assumptions.
For now, there are still questions that need answers.
But regardless of how that situation develops, the larger story of NVIDIA remains remarkable.
Go back to where we started.
A nine-year-old boy in a Kentucky boarding school, cleaning toilets and trying to find his place in a country far from home.
A teenager washing dishes at Denny's.
A young engineer sitting in a restaurant booth with two friends, dreaming about better computer graphics.
A founder admitting to a major mistake and asking a business partner for $5 million when his company had barely 30 days left.
An executive continuing to invest in technology that Wall Street didn't understand.
And eventually, a man leading a company at the centre of one of the biggest technological shifts in history.
There is one lesson I think is worth taking from all of this.
You don't have to be the smartest person in the room. You don't have to get everything right the first time. And you certainly don't have to start with everything figured out.
What matters is your ability to keep learning, recognise when you're wrong, make difficult decisions, and continue building when the results are not yet visible.
Jensen Huang didn't build NVIDIA in a day.
He built it over more than three decades.
The $5 million that saved the company.
The decision to abandon a failing chip.
The investment in CUDA that few people understood.
The years of building before the AI boom arrived.
None of those moments looked like the beginning of a multi-trillion-dollar company at the time.
But they mattered.
And perhaps that's the biggest takeaway:
Don't underestimate what years of doing the difficult, unglamorous work can eventually become.
Sometimes, the thing you're building today won't make sense to the world until years later.

Jensen attended Aloha High School, skipped two grades, and graduated at just 16.
He was interested in mathematics, computers, and engineering.
But he also needed money.
At 15, he got a job at Denny's, an American restaurant chain.
He started as a dishwasher.
Then he became a busboy, clearing tables, and eventually a waiter.
He worked overnight shifts while going to school.
Years later, he would say that the job helped him overcome his shyness and taught him how to work under pressure.
Interestingly, those restaurant jobs are still part of his professional story.
But nobody working alongside that teenager could have imagined what he would eventually build.
Jensen went on to study electrical engineering at Oregon State University.
After graduating, he worked as a chip designer at AMD and later joined LSI Logic.
He also attended Stanford at night, eventually earning a master's degree in electrical engineering.
By his late twenties, he had a stable career and a comfortable future.
He could have stayed there.
But he didn't.
In 1993, three engineers walked into a Denny's restaurant in San Jose, California.
Their names were Jensen Huang, Chris Malachowsky, and Curtis Priem.
They sat in a booth, drank cheap coffee, and discussed an idea.
They wanted to build computer chips that would make video games look better.
That was the original idea behind NVIDIA.
Not artificial intelligence.
Not ChatGPT.
Not the technology powering the world's biggest data centres.
Just better graphics for video games.
They believed computers would eventually need special chips to handle increasingly realistic graphics.
Many people weren't convinced.
But the three founders took the risk.
They raised money, hired engineers, and started building.
Then came their first major mistake.
Their first graphics chip, the NV1, used a different approach from what most of the industry was adopting.
It was an intelligent idea on paper, but the rest of the industry was moving in another direction.
Game developers were building around triangles, while NVIDIA had chosen curved surfaces.
The result?
Their chip struggled to work with the software developers were already using.
Sales were disappointing.
The next product was also built around the same flawed approach.
Money started disappearing.
And the company was running out of time.
At one point, NVIDIA was roughly 30 days away from going out of business.
Let that sink in.
The company that would eventually become a multi-trillion-dollar business was once struggling to survive another month.
Jensen had a difficult decision to make.
He could continue pretending everything was fine, or admit that the technology they had built wasn't going to work.
He chose to admit the mistake.
But there was another problem.
NVIDIA had a contract with Sega, the Japanese video game company.
Jensen knew they couldn't deliver the product as originally promised.
So he travelled to Japan to meet a Sega executive named Shoichiro Irimajiri.
He explained the situation honestly.
He told him that NVIDIA couldn't deliver the chip in the way they had planned.
Then he made an unusual request.
He asked Sega to pay the remaining $5 million anyway.
Not because NVIDIA had delivered everything perfectly, but because the company needed the money to survive.
Sega could have walked away.
Instead, the executive agreed.
That $5 million gave NVIDIA the time it desperately needed.
Think about it.
Sometimes, the difference between a business that survives and one that disappears isn't a perfect business plan.
Sometimes, it's one person willing to trust you when you have very little left to offer.
But the money wasn't enough on its own.
NVIDIA had to change direction.
The company abandoned its original graphics approach and focused on the technology the wider industry was adopting.
It developed the RIVA 128 graphics chip.
The product was a success.
NVIDIA reportedly sold around a million units within its first four months.
The company that had nearly disappeared was back in the game.
In 1999, NVIDIA went public.
That same year, it introduced the GeForce 256 and helped establish the term GPU, short for Graphics Processing Unit.
At the time, these chips were mainly associated with gaming.
But Jensen noticed something other people were overlooking.
Scientists and researchers were beginning to use graphics chips for work that had nothing to do with video games.
And that observation would lead to the biggest decision in NVIDIA's history.
In 2006, NVIDIA introduced CUDA.
To understand why this mattered, imagine two kitchens.
The first has one extremely talented chef who can prepare almost any meal, but can only prepare one dish at a time.
The second has thousands of cooks, each handling a small part of the work at the same time.
The first kitchen is similar to a CPU.
The second is similar to a GPU.
A GPU can perform thousands of smaller calculations at once.
This makes it incredibly useful for certain types of scientific research, simulations, and artificial intelligence.
But there was a problem.
Using graphics chips for these other tasks was difficult.
So NVIDIA created CUDA, a system that allowed developers to write software that could use the power of its GPUs for much more than graphics.
Here is where Jensen made another unpopular decision.
He didn't reserve this technology for expensive, specialised chips.
He invested in making it available across NVIDIA's product range, including gaming graphics cards.
It cost money.
Investors questioned the decision.
For years, the investment affected profits, and many people wondered why a company known for gaming was spending so much on software that most of its customers barely used.
Jensen continued anyway.
NVIDIA made the tools available, supported universities, and helped train developers to use them.
He was building something that might not pay off immediately.
And that is what makes this decision so important.
He wasn't just selling computer chips anymore.
He was building an entire ecosystem around them.
Years later, researchers at the University of Toronto used two NVIDIA gaming graphics cards to train a system called AlexNet.
In 2012, that system achieved a remarkable result in a major image-recognition competition.
It showed the research world just how powerful GPUs could be for deep learning.
Suddenly, the same type of chips people bought to play video games could help computers learn to recognise images.
NVIDIA had spent years preparing for a market that was only beginning to emerge.
And it wasn't finished.
In 2016, Jensen personally delivered NVIDIA's first DGX-1 supercomputer to a young research organisation called OpenAI.
At the time, very few people understood just how important artificial intelligence would become.
Then came November 2022.
OpenAI released ChatGPT.
Millions of people started interacting with AI in a completely new way.
Businesses wanted their own AI systems.
Researchers wanted more computing power.
Technology companies began building enormous data centres.
And almost everyone needed the same thing:
NVIDIA's chips.
The H100 became one of the most sought-after pieces of technology in the world.
The company that started by making graphics cards for video games had become central to the artificial intelligence revolution.
Its market value climbed from $1 trillion in 2023 to $2 trillion, then $3 trillion, and eventually reached $5 trillion in 2025.
Jensen became a global celebrity.
The black leather jacket became his signature.
World leaders wanted meetings with him. People lined up for pictures and autographs.
But there is something important about this story that people often overlook.
NVIDIA didn't become what it is today because of one lucky moment.
It was built through decades of decisions.
Some worked.
Some failed.
The company struggled with product mistakes, competition, financial crises, failed market entries, and missed opportunities.
It also made major investments that looked questionable at the time.
One of the most important was CUDA.
Without years of investment in that software ecosystem, NVIDIA's position in the AI industry could look very different today.
And that brings us to another lesson.
Sometimes, the biggest opportunities are hidden inside things that other people don't take seriously.
But success doesn't mean the journey is always upward.
Even today, NVIDIA faces serious questions.
There are concerns about the enormous spending on artificial intelligence, whether the current AI boom can justify its cost, competition from other chipmakers, and restrictions on selling advanced chips to China.
There are also questions about the way money moves between NVIDIA and some of the companies buying its technology.
Supporters point to its revenue and profits.
Critics worry that parts of the AI industry may be growing too quickly.
Both sides have arguments worth examining.
And then, in November 2026, another story put Jensen himself under the spotlight.
Reports raised questions about his relationship with a Chinese executive linked to a Singapore-based data centre company.
Some reports described that executive as a suspected spy, but those allegations have not been established as facts.
NVIDIA's board announced an independent investigation into reports that Jensen had been targeted by a foreign intelligence effort.
The board said it had no reason to believe company secrets or national security information had been compromised.
Jensen also committed to cooperating with the review.
A lawsuit was subsequently filed by a law firm, making claims about what the company and its CEO disclosed to investors. Those claims have not been tested in court.
The investigation is ongoing.
And that is important because a story involving allegations, a major company, investors, and national security deserves facts, not assumptions.
For now, there are still questions that need answers.
But regardless of how that situation develops, the larger story of NVIDIA remains remarkable.
Go back to where we started.
A nine-year-old boy in a Kentucky boarding school, cleaning toilets and trying to find his place in a country far from home.
A teenager washing dishes at Denny's.
A young engineer sitting in a restaurant booth with two friends, dreaming about better computer graphics.
A founder admitting to a major mistake and asking a business partner for $5 million when his company had barely 30 days left.
An executive continuing to invest in technology that Wall Street didn't understand.
And eventually, a man leading a company at the centre of one of the biggest technological shifts in history.
There is one lesson I think is worth taking from all of this.
You don't have to be the smartest person in the room. You don't have to get everything right the first time. And you certainly don't have to start with everything figured out.
What matters is your ability to keep learning, recognise when you're wrong, make difficult decisions, and continue building when the results are not yet visible.
Jensen Huang didn't build NVIDIA in a day.
He built it over more than three decades.
The $5 million that saved the company.
The decision to abandon a failing chip.
The investment in CUDA that few people understood.
The years of building before the AI boom arrived.
None of those moments looked like the beginning of a multi-trillion-dollar company at the time.
But they mattered.
And perhaps that's the biggest takeaway:
Don't underestimate what years of doing the difficult, unglamorous work can eventually become.
Sometimes, the thing you're building today won't make sense to the world until years later.

His younger brother, Cody Walker, shared these words in November 2014, as the first anniversary of the actor's death approached. In an interview with E! News, he was asked what he hoped people would learn from Paul’s life, and he offered a lesson that reflects the values ​​his brother had instilled in him: "Live life to the fullest. Laugh a lot, love, and find your true happiness. No matter how 'tough' you think you are, you’re never so tough that you can look down on anyone else—never."

Paul Walker, best known for his role as Brian O'Conner in the *Fast & Furious* franchise, left a mark that extended well beyond the screen. In 2010, he founded Reach Out Worldwide, an organization that brings together volunteers and professionals to assist communities affected by natural disasters. The actor lost his life on November 30, 2013, at the age of 40, in a car accident in California while on his way to a charity event. 

Following his passing, his family has continued to support the organization. His story serves as a reminder that success and recognition do not make us superior to others. True greatness is also revealed through humility, respect, and the way we treat people—regardless of who they are or what they possess.
