WRAL News Says Climate Action Should Be a Priority; Voters Are More Worried About Affordability | Linnea Lueken, ClimateREALISM

A recent article from WRAL News, a North Carolina NBC affiliate, titled “Climate change takes a back seat in campaigns, but research suggests voters still care,” claims: climate change is making storms worse and life more expensive; that people want climate action; and suggests that green policy offers cost savings on energy bills. Each of these points is false. Climate change has not make extreme weather like hurricanes worse. Rather, green policies have caused rising energy bills, not climate change itself. Additionally, people may say that they want climate action, but repeated polls show they are not willing to pay or sacrifice much for it. Climate change ranks way down the list of concerns.

WRAL opines that affordability was a main area of discussion for Democrat candidates this year, rather than climate change, which they assert “remains a concern for many voters.”

They look at the North Carolina Senate race as an example of the “disconnect,” where Democrat Governor Roy Cooper seemed to have dropped or limited talking about climate change on the campaign trail, while he discussed it often during his governorship, including blaming Hurricane Helene on climate change.

Hurricane Helene was not caused or worsened by climate change, despite what biased attribution groups claimed at the time. We at Climate Realism covered that in depth here, here, and here. Later in the article, WRAL tries to connect climate change to rising insurance costs, but this is another red herring, which Climate Realism has addressed on numerous occasions. Extreme weather is not becoming more frequent, so it cannot be to blame for rising insurance costs, even if insurance companies try to shift that blame away from themselves.

Gov. Cooper focused this year’s campaign on affordability instead, which WRAL says is a shift in how politicians discuss energy policy. The implication is that this is a bad thing, that climate is taking a backseat in these discussions. WRAL and those they interview for this piece couldn’t be more wrong. If Democrats are serious about designing energy policy based on what is most affordable, then that is good, a positive shift in their policy focus, However, it’s doubtful that Democrats have genuinely shifted their priorities. Much more likely, climate change dropped from public campaigns because voters know that climate policy means higher costs.

WRAL cites polling research that found “messaging focused on cost savings can increase support for renewable energy across party lines, suggesting affordability and climate action do not have to be competing campaign priorities.”

Except, renewables are directly responsible for higher rates across the country. Recent studies have found that high penetration of renewables is directly correlated to the fastest rising energy costs in the country, like in places like California. If Democrats are claiming otherwise, they are misleading their voters, possibly outright knowingly lying.

The reason they lie about this, is because while polling shows if you ask people if they are concerned about climate change, they say “yes,” it also shows that the associated increased cost of living that comes with various policies proposed to fight climate change are very unpopular, and not just in the United States either.

For instance, a YouGov poll from 2023 found that while Europeans said they were worried about climate change, most were unwilling to make the kinds of lifestyle changes that green activists and politicians say are necessary to stop global warming. Those would be changes such as giving up or even limiting meat consumption, limiting the number of children they have, or paying extra fuel taxes.

The Yale study that WRAL cites is unsurprising. It found that a majority of people claim that they are “worried” about global warming, and that they want candidates who will “support action to address” it. But this support means little if voters don’t want the policies that will supposedly address it. A poll from the Energy Policy Institute at the University of Chicago and the Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research (UC/AP) in 2023 also found that the majority of people are unwilling to do something as simple as pay a single dollar per month to fight climate change.

Climate policy is meant to limit the use of products like gasoline and affordable energy like natural gas, necessitating that those things become much more expensive. Proponents of net zero and climate action are aware of this fact.

Another survey WRAL looked at said that “that roughly two-thirds of registered voters believe global warming is contributing to higher utility bills. That finding measures voters’ perceptions, and does not establish any factual connection between climate change and what individual energy users pay for transportation fuel and electricity.

Voters have been misled to believe that global warming is causing higher bills, when it is actually climate policy itself. This is one of the most deceitful narratives promoted by politicians and the mainstream media. Renewables like wind and solar raise utility bills and reduce the reliability of the grid itself, especially when the policy is paired with reliable coal plants being prematurely shuttered — even some natural gas plants have been closed before their official retirement.

Again, people might claim they want to tackle climate change, but it ranks extremely low (and lower every year) on their concerns list, and they are unwilling to pay more to do so. Democrats like Cooper, and media like WRAL, are misleading voters by claiming falsely that renewables are less expensive. Democrats ran on affordability. If the past is any guide, the policies they promote to fix it will only make the problem worse.

text:
Chapter XII: The Road to Rome.
.
Canisius kept Stanislaus at his work in the kitchen and about the house for a couple of weeks. He noted his cheerfulness, his love of prayer, his readiness to do any sort of work, and best of all, his simplicity, his entire lack of pose. He saw that this Senator’s son made no virtue of taking on himself such lowly tasks, and he knew, therefore, that he was really humble.
Then he called the boy to him. He said:
“If I admit you into the Society here, your father may still annoy you. It is better you should go to Rome and become a novice there. I shall give you a letter to the Father General, Francis Borgia. In a few days two of ours are to go to Rome. You can go with them.”
Stanislaus was delighted. He was come into quiet waters at last. But Canisius spoke further:
“First, however, you must get some decent clothes. Your old tunic,” he said, with a twinkle in his eye, “might do well enough for a noble, but not for a future Jesuit.”
So the college tailor made Stanislaus a simple, neat suit of clothes. And about September 20th he set out for Rome. He went on foot, of course; in the company of Jacopo Levanzio, a Genoese, and Fabricius Reiner, of Liége.
They struck south through Bavaria to the Tyrolese Alps. By what pass they crossed the Alps we do not know. But Stanislaus saw first from afar the white peaks, with their everlasting snows, shining in the sun. Then he went up and up, into cooler and rarer air, where one’s lungs expand and one’s step is light and buoyant, but where one gets tired more easily than in the plains. High up in the passes he felt the cold of Winter, although it was as yet early Autumn.
Then he came down the southern slopes of the great mountain-wall that locks in Italy, and with him came the headwaters of great rivers. He came down through bare rocks, then through twisted mountain-pines, then through green and lovely valleys, and so into the plains of northern Italy. He saw the mountain torrents leap and flash, and grow always bigger and stronger. He saw them slack their speed and widen their beds in the upland valleys. He saw them grow sluggish, tawny with mud, in the plain.
He saw the many spires of Milan’s wonderful cathedral as they drew near the city. And when they tarried there a little while for rest, he saw the famous armor made there, hung up for show in little shop windows. He passed great cavalcades of nobles and soldiers, and marveled at their straight, slim rapiers, so different from the heavy Polish saber. He heard Italian speech for the first time, and tried to get at its meaning through his Latin.
But he and his companions had not over-much time for observing. They were traveling pretty swiftly. From Dillingen to Rome is a matter of about eight hundred miles. They left Dillingen September 20th; they reached Rome October 25th. That figures out to an average of about twenty-two miles each day. Then, if you remember that they had to climb mountains the first part of the way, that there were delays entering towns, delays of devotion when they came to great churches, you can see that many a day they must have equaled or surpassed Stanislaus’ thirty miles a day from Vienna.
But it was pleasanter. for Stanislaus than his first great tramp. Now he had two good companions, with whom he could speak easily and familiarly of the things nearest his heart. He had none of the uncertainty about the result of this journey which he had had about his former journey. He found shelter and friendship in many Jesuit houses on the way.
As the three went on they lightened the road with pious songs, they heard Mass and received Holy Communion whenever occasion offered, they knelt by many a wayside shrine, a crucifix, or statue of our Lady, scattered everywhere through Catholic Italy.
It did not take the two Jesuits long to appreciate Stanislaus and delight in his company. He was so light-hearted, so merry in all the discomforts and hardships of the long road, so thoroughly and simply good. They wondered at his physical endurance, at the ease and buoyancy with which the lad of seventeen kept up that hard march, day after day.
The grasses of the Campagna were brown and brittle, the trees sere and yellow in the Autumn, when they came to the Eternal City, the center of the world then as now. The saintly General Francis Borgia, busy as he was with the cares of the widespread Society, found time to welcome the three travelers, and to hear Stanislaus’ wonderful story in full.
And this time there was no hesitation or delay. Stanislaus entered his name in the book containing the register of the novices, on October 25, 1567. Three days later he received his cassock and entered at once upon his noviceship.
There were so many novices in Rome then that no single house of the Jesuits there could hold them all. So they were scattered through three houses, each one spending a part of his two years’ noviceship successively in each house. Stanislaus went first to the Professed House, then called Santa Maria della Strada, and afterward the site of the famous Gesu, one of the notable churches of Rome. From there he passed in time to the Roman College, then to the Noviciate proper at Sant’ Andrea.
The Society of Jesus was then in its early youth, in the midst of that first brilliant charge against the ranks of heresy without, and against the huge sluggish inertia so striking within the Church itself.
He was fellow-novice with Claude Acquaviva, son of the Duke of Atri, and afterwards one of the greatest Generals of the Society, which he ruled for thirty years. With him were also Claude’s nephew, Rudolph Acquaviva, who died a martyr; Torres, a great theologian; Prando, the first philosopher at the University of Bologna; Fabio de’ Fabii, who traced his descent from the great Roman family of that name; the Pole, Warscewiski, formerly ambassador to the Sultan and Secretary of State in Poland, who first wrote a life of Stanislaus; and many more, distinguished for birth, learning, holiness.
Most of these were a great deal older, too, than Stanislaus. Many of them had already made their names familiar to men. Yet the boy of seventeen, who came quietly and modestly amongst them, was somehow soon looked up to by all. They felt the force of something in him which made him their superior. Heaven was wonderfully near him. He was not old-fashioned; he was always a boy, unconscious of anything unusual in himself; not solemn nor impressive nor austere in manner. All that he did, he did with perfect naturalness; for to him the supernatural had become almost natural.
.
Chapter XIII: The Noviceship.
.
Most of us, perhaps, think of the saints as men and women who accomplished visibly great things. Saint Paul, Saint Augustine, Saint Patrick, Saint Theresa, Saint Philip Neri, Saint Francis Xavier: such names as these come first to our minds when we think of “a saint.” Yet the fact is that the greater number of saints are men and women who never did anything that the world would consider great or striking. Saint Joseph was of that sort. Even the Blessed Virgin lived and died in obscurity, made no stir in the world.
Sanctity is measured not so much by what one does as by how one does all things. Externally a saint may not differ at all from other people. It is his soul that is different.
And so, a visitor to the Professed House in Rome in 1567, meeting Stanislaus Kostka, would see a handsome, pleasant-looking Polish boy of seventeen, with his sleeves rolled up above his elbows, with an apron over his cassock, carrying wood for the kitchen fires, washing dishes, serving at table, sweeping corridors and rooms.
He got up at half past four, or five o’clock, every morning. He spent half an hour in meditation, in thinking over some incident in our Lord’s life or some great truth, as that death is near to each of us, that this life is only the vestibule of eternity, that our whole business in life is to do what God wants us to do, or the like.
After that came Mass and, once or twice a week, Holy Communion and his thanksgiving. Then breakfast, taken in silence. He read in a spiritual book for half an hour or so after breakfast, then went to the kitchen or the dining hall or the scullery, where he set to work under the orders of the cook.
In the course of the morning there might be a talk or instruction from the priest in charge of the novices. There surely would be one or more visits to the chapel. When the hour for dinner came, Stanislaus probably served at table, taking his own meal later. After dinner there was an hour for recreation, when the novices walked and chatted in the garden or about the house.
The afternoon, like the morning, was taken up with lowly work, with prayer, and a little reading or instruction. Toward evening, he again spent half an hour in meditation. Then came the evening meal, another hour of recreation, a little reading in preparation for next morning’s meditation, and examination of conscience as to how the day had been spent, and then bed.
Two or three days a week, this routine was broken. Sometimes the novices walked out into the country to a villa, where they had games and ate their dinner. At other times they left their work to go with one of the Fathers to some church or other, upon business.
It was a quiet, humble life, full of peace, near to God, hidden away from men. In this life the novices had to continue for two years, before they took upon themselves the obligation of vows, and before they began the long studies that prepare a Jesuit for his work. During those two years they tested their vocation, making sure that God really called them to that life; and they tested their own wills to see if they were ready to endure what such a life demanded of them.
Stanislaus did just what the other novices did, did nothing out of the ordinary. Yet, of course, he was different from the others; he was a saint. What was the difference? Just this: they did things more or less well; he did things perfectly. If he prayed, he put his whole mind and soul into his prayer. If he worked, he obeyed orders absolutely, because in doing so he was obeying God.
There is in the Jesuit noviciate at Angers a series of paintings portraying incidents in the life of Stanislaus. In one he is shown carrying on his arm two or three bits of wood towards the kitchen. Underneath is written, “He will err if he carry more.”
The painting commemorates an occasion when Stanislaus and Claude Acquaviva were put by the cook to carry wood and told to carry only two or three pieces at a time. Acquaviva, when the two came to the wood-pile, said laughingly:
“Does the cook think we are babies? Why, we can each carry twenty or thirty of such little pieces of wood.”
“To be sure we can,” Stanislaus answered. “But do you think God wants us to carry twenty or thirty pieces now? The cook said two or three, and the cook just at present takes the place of God to command us.”
And so it was in everything. He studied singly to see what would please God most, and no matter how trifling seemed the command he did just that, with all his heart.
No one ever heard a sharp word from him, or saw him take offense at anything, or act in the least way out of vanity or selfishness.
And, of course, he was entirely unconscious that he was different from the rest. He knew he was trying to do his best in everything, but he supposed every one else was doing the same. And with all his earnestness and exactness, he was as simple and boyish as he had ever been.
One day Cardinal Commendoni, the Legate to Vienna, and a great friend of Stanislaus, came to Rome and hurried over to the Roman College to call upon Stanislaus. Stanislaus, as soon as he heard of his arrival, ran off to meet him just as he was, sleeves rolled up, apron on, straight from the scullery – just as any boy would do.
He was in everything perfectly at ease; content in his little round of little tasks; going ahead toward heaven without any show or heroics. He was doing just exactly the little things that God wants us to do, and he was entirely happy in so doing.
It is true he had never been really unhappy in his whole life. People who keep close to God never are. They have hard things to put up with; they may be poor, or fall sick, or lose their relatives or friends by death; they may have to fight very strong temptations. They feel all these things as keenly as others feel them. But they do not become unhappy. We may say they have a world of their own to live in, that their inmost lives are spent in that world, very little touched by the changes and accidents of the outer world. They see that there is an outer world, but they choose deliberately to ignore it; they will not go into it.
You know that if you go down deep into the sea, as men go in submarines, you find calm there always, even though a storm be raging up above and the waves toss with angry violence. So if you once get inside your life, under the surface, in the heart of life where God is, you will find calm there also and a certain peace which is as near as we can come to entire happiness in this world.
But though Stanislaus had learned this secret, and had therefore always kept his soul merry, he was happiest of all during the time of his noviceship. The very air around him breathed of God and heaven. His life there was really an unbroken prayer. He was like a swimmer who has been fighting his way through nasty, choppy, little waves, going ahead surely, but with great difficulty, and who comes at last into long, quiet, rolling swells, where his progress is delightful, where he can make long, easy strokes and feel pleasure in the very effort.
And as he was young and ardent, he was in danger of overdoing things. Prayer, even when it is a joy, is always hard work for us poor mortals. Stanislaus gave himself so heartily now to praying that he ran risk of losing his strength and health. So his superiors, being sensible men, stepped in and moderated his energy. He was made to work more and pray less, told to be prudent, to husband his strength for future work. And, of course, he did as he was told.
But God had special designs on Stanislaus. He was never to use his health and energy in work as a priest or teacher. Indeed, his work was nearly over, though it had been so brief. He had no long career before him on this earth; he was going home, and going soon...

Gotham FC has won two of the last three NWSL titles and never hosted a semifinal until today, when it plays Kansas City at 3pm ET on ESPN in a 5,000-seat track stadium on Randall's Island.

The pitch at Sports Illustrated Stadium, the 25,000-seat venue owned by MLS's New York Red Bulls, was already worn before an Oct. 30 rugby doubleheader finished it off, Gotham COO Kari Fleischauer told Front Office Sports. The NWSL fined Gotham $10,000 over the field at its Nov. 1 match.

Gotham offered to pay to re-sod, re-stitch, add grow lights or lay turf. Fleischauer says she trusts the Red Bulls' ground crew and the venue was overscheduled.

The Red Bulls say the pitch was cleared for every match this season, and that the experts and the league couldn't guarantee the extra work in time.

Gotham is chartering ferries for about 3,000 fans and refunding the difference on pricier seats. "The revenue hit we will take is not small," Fleischauer said.

Its quarterfinal drew 11,328, so today's cap shuts out 6,328 of that crowd.

text:
By: Selina Nyarko Prah (Sis.)
Pastor Joseph Owusu-Boateng, Resident Minister of PIWC Winneba, has urged Christians to develop a genuine concern for the glory of God, emphasising that believers must be willing to defend His name, uphold His honour and place His purposes above their personal interests. Delivering a sermon titled “Concerns for the Glory of God” during the climax of the District Week, dubbed Grace Convocation, at PIWC Winneba, Pastor Owusu-Boateng explained that a defining characteristic of people who walk closely with God is their concern for His glory.

Drawing from 2 Samuel 7:1–4, he examined the lives of three biblical figures, David, Elijah and Nehemiah, whose devotion to God was reflected in their commitment to His honour and purposes. He began with the story of David, who, despite living in a magnificent palace, became concerned that the Ark of God remained in a tent. According to the Resident Minister, David's desire to build a house for God demonstrated a heart that placed God's glory above personal comfort.

Although David was not permitted to build the temple, he did not abandon his concern for God's house. Instead, he deliberately made extensive preparations and provided resources for its construction. Pastor Owusu-Boateng explained that David's response revealed the depth of his commitment to God. 

He challenged the congregation to consider how they would react if someone rejected an offer they had made with good intentions. He observed that many people would simply withdraw their support after such a response. David, however, continued making provisions for the temple, ensuring that the resources needed for its construction would be available.

Pastor Owusu-Boateng emphasised that genuine concern for God's glory does not disappear when personal expectations are not met. Rather, it motivates believers to remain committed to God's purposes even when they are not the ones chosen to carry out a particular assignment. He further referred to 1 Samuel 17:26, where David questioned the audacity of Goliath, the uncircumcised Philistine, who had defied the armies of the living God.

According to Pastor Owusu-Boateng, David's response was motivated by his concern for God's reputation rather than a desire for personal recognition. While others saw Goliath as a terrifying opponent, David recognised that the honour of the living God was being challenged. His willingness to confront the Philistine demonstrated a determination to defend God's name when others were afraid to act.

Turning to the life of Elijah, Pastor Owusu-Boateng referred to 1 Kings 18:21, where the prophet confronted the Israelites over their divided allegiance between God and Baal. He explained that Elijah could not tolerate the people's continued wavering between two opinions. The prophet was determined to demonstrate that the Lord alone was worthy of their worship.

Referring also to 1 Kings 18:24, he highlighted Elijah's challenge on Mount Carmel, where the God who answered by fire would be acknowledged as the true God. Pastor Owusu-Boateng explained that Elijah's actions were not intended to promote himself but to restore the people's recognition of God's supremacy. He emphasised that when a believer's motives are genuinely directed towards God's glory, God is able to demonstrate His power in defence of His name.

Pastor Owusu-Boateng also identified Nehemiah among the biblical examples of individuals whose lives reflected a deep concern for God's honour and purposes.

Drawing lessons from these examples, Pastor Owusu-Boateng outlined the characteristics of people who are genuinely concerned about the glory of God. First, he explained that such individuals are grieved whenever God is dishonoured. They do not remain indifferent when God's name is treated with contempt or when conduct within the Church brings dishonour to Him.

He further stressed that believers who genuinely love God's glory do not celebrate the failures of the Church. According to him, rather than laughing when the Church experiences difficulties or setbacks, they are moved with concern and seek its restoration and progress. He challenged Christians to examine their reactions when they hear negative reports about the Church, explaining that their responses often reveal whether their concern is for God's glory or their personal interests.

Pastor Owusu-Boateng also emphasised that people who seek God's glory live for His pleasure rather than their own. Referring to 1 Corinthians 10:31, he reminded the congregation that whether Christians eat, drink or engage in any other activity, everything should be done to the glory of God. He explained that genuine devotion to God must influence everyday decisions, personal conduct and the motives behind one's actions.

Another characteristic he highlighted was the willingness to defend the name of the Lord. He explained that believers who are concerned about God's glory do not remain silent when His name is dishonoured. Like David and Elijah, they are willing to take a stand for God even when others are unwilling to do so.

Pastor Owusu-Boateng further emphasised the responsibility of Christians to proclaim God's name and make Him known to others. He noted that concern for God's glory should not remain a private conviction but must find expression in a believer's willingness to speak about God and make His greatness known.

Pastor Owusu-Boateng explained that genuine concern for God's glory also purifies a person's motives and transforms their mindset. According to him, when God's honour becomes the primary motivation behind a believer's actions, personal ambition and the desire for recognition begin to give way to a sincere commitment to pleasing Him.

He encouraged Christians to evaluate the reasons behind their service, sacrifices and involvement in church activities, emphasising that the desire to glorify God must remain central. He further noted that those who consistently seek God's glory develop a relationship with Him marked by His favour and approval.

Concluding his message, Pastor Owusu-Boateng challenged the congregation to follow the examples of David and Elijah by demonstrating a genuine concern for God's honour in every area of life. His message reinforced the need for Christians to move beyond merely professing love for God and demonstrate that love through their willingness to defend His name, support His work, proclaim His greatness and live according to His purposes.

text:
🧭 HUNG KINGS TEMPLE | TRAVEL ESSENTIALS
📍 Getting There

Located on Nghia Linh Mountain in Phu Tho Province, approximately 90 km from Hanoi. A private car or arranged transfer makes a day trip practical. Alternatively, travel by bus to Viet Tri and take a local taxi to the temple complex.

🗺️ What to Explore

Follow the traditional pilgrimage route: Lower Temple and Thien Quang Pagoda → Middle Temple → Upper Temple and the Hung King Mausoleum → Gieng Temple.

For a more extensive visit, include the separate shrines dedicated to Lac Long Quan and Au Co.

⏱️ Time Needed

Allow approximately 2–3 hours for the main temple route, including its stone stairways. Set aside most of a day if exploring the wider complex and returning to Hanoi.

🌤️ When to Visit

The Hung Kings Commemoration on the 10th day of the third lunar month offers a remarkable festival atmosphere but attracts large crowds. Ordinary weekdays are better for a quieter visit.

💰 Costs & Booking

Phu Tho's tourism portal lists free admission. Transport, parking and optional services may incur additional charges. Confirm arrangements before visiting, especially during major festivals.

🇨🇳 五国：受邀参加不熟悉的宗教活动前，值得了解的礼仪 TOP10

🇺🇸 Five Countries: What to Ask Before Attending an Unfamiliar Religious Ceremony TOP10
🇨🇳 中国
朋友说周末带你去寺院听经。到了门口，才想起还有一句没问：“我是跟你一起坐，还是先去找接待的人？”
1）到哪里报到 | どこで受付するか | 어디에서 접수하는지 | Đến đâu để báo danh | Where to check in
如果寺院设有知客处，可以先去说明自己受谁邀请、来参加哪一场活动。
2）这场活动对谁开放 | 誰が参加できる行事か | 누구에게 열린 행사인지 | Buổi lễ mở cho những ai | Who the event is open to
平日能进院参访，具体法会仍值得单独问一句：第一次来的人可以入殿旁听吗？
3）穿什么去合适 | どんな服装がふさわしいか | 어떤 옷차림이 적절한지 | Mặc gì cho phù hợp | What to wear
约好时间时顺便问一句。要是同一天还安排了爬山，出门前就知道要不要多带一件衣服。

4）哪些地方可以进 | どの場所に入れるか | 어디까지 들어갈 수 있는지 | Được vào những khu vực nào | Which areas are open to guests
殿门开着，有可能是给参加仪式的人出入。想进去之前，先看门口的提示，或问带你来的人。
5）礼佛时站在哪里 | 礼拝のときどこに立つか | 예불 때 어디에 서는지 | Đứng ở đâu khi lễ Phật | Where to stand during worship
不熟悉动作，可以先问有没有适合旁观的位置，也给正在礼佛的人留出空间。

6）清香放哪儿 | 線香をどこに供えるか | 향을 어디에 올리는지 | Thắp hương ở đâu | Where to offer incense
朋友若准备敬香，先看寺院指定了哪个地方。进了大殿再找香炉，可能已经走过了。
7）怎样称呼接待的法师 | 案内してくれる僧侶をどう呼ぶか | 안내하는 스님을 어떻게 부르는지 | Xưng hô với vị hướng dẫn thế nào | How to address the monastic host
朋友和对方熟悉，可能直接喊平时的称呼。你第一次见，可以先问朋友一句：“我怎么称呼合适？”
8）什么时候可以拍照 | いつ写真を撮ってよいか | 언제 사진을 찍어도 되는지 | Khi nào được chụp ảnh | When photos are allowed
院里能拍的地方，到了殿内或仪式开始后可能就有别的要求。想拍人，也先问对方愿不愿意入镜。
9）带去的水果交给谁 | 持参した果物を誰に渡すか | 가져온 과일을 누구에게 드리는지 | Trái cây mang theo gửi cho ai | Who should receive the fruit you brought
想带一点供品，先问活动方是否接收、应该放在哪里。到了现场就不用端着一袋水果往前找人。
10）需要早走从哪里出去 | 途中で帰るならどこから出るか | 먼저 나갈 때 어느 문을 쓰는지 | Cần về sớm thì ra bằng cửa nào | Which exit to use if you leave early
如果只能待到一半，入场前问好什么时候方便离席、坐哪边进出更顺。
第一次陪朋友去听经，你最想在进门前问清哪一点：能坐哪里，还是中途能不能离开？

🇯🇵 日本
友人に神社の祭典へ誘われた。普段の参拝なら知っているけれど、今日は受付があるらしい。待ち合わせの連絡で、服装と集合場所も聞いておく。

1）拝殿に入る行事か | 是否要进入拜殿 | 배전에 들어가는 행사인지 | Buổi lễ có vào điện thờ không | Whether the ceremony goes inside the worship hall
普段は外からお参りする神社でも、招かれた祭典では拝殿に上がることがある。当日の受付と入口を聞いておく。
2）鳥居の前でどうするか | 经过鸟居前怎么做 | 도리이 앞에서 어떻게 하는지 | Làm gì trước cổng torii | What to do at the torii
一礼してからくぐる人もいる。連れと話しながら歩いてきたなら、鳥居の手前でいったん足を止めれば落ち着いて入れる。
3）手水の使い方 | 手水的用法 | 데미즈 사용법 | Cách dùng nước thanh tẩy | How to use the purification basin
手水舎が使えるときは、現地の案内に沿って手を清める。柄杓がある場合も、口は柄杓に直接つけない。
4）参拝の拍手の回数 | 参拜时拍几次手 | 참배할 때 박수 치는 횟수 | Vỗ tay mấy lần khi lễ | How many times to clap during worship
二拝二拍手一拝が基本とされるが、作法が異なる神社もある。初めてなら、その神社の案内を見てから進む。
5）玉串を奉る役があるか | 是否要献玉串 | 다마구시를 올리는 순서가 있는지 | Có đến lượt mình dâng cành tamagushi không | Whether you’ll be asked to offer a tamagushi branch
案内に玉串奉奠とあっても、参列者全員が前に出るとは限らない。自分にも出番があるか、招いてくれた人に聞く。
6）初穂料の用意がいるか | 是否需要准备初穗料 | 하쓰호료를 준비해야 하는지 | Có cần chuẩn bị lễ phí hatsuhoryō không | Whether to prepare a ceremonial offering
祈祷を申し込む人と付き添いの人では用意が違うことがある。封筒まで必要か、受付の案内を確かめる。

7）どの席に座るか | 入场后坐哪里 | 어느 자리에 앉는지 | Vào lễ thì ngồi chỗ nào | Where to sit
家族や関係者の席が決まっている行事なら、空いて見える席でも先に係の人に尋ねる。
8）立つのが難しいとき | 不方便起立时怎么办 | 일어서기 어려울 때 어떻게 하는지 | Làm gì nếu khó đứng lên | What to do if standing is difficult
長く立つのが難しければ、始まる前に椅子の有無や、座ったまま参列できる場所を聞いておく。
9）撮影できる時間と場所 | 可以拍摄的时间和地点 | 촬영 가능한 시간과 장소 | Giờ và chỗ được chụp ảnh | When and where photography is allowed
境内の記念写真と、祭典中の撮影は分けて確認する。終わってから集合写真を撮る時間があるかもしれない。
10）終わったらどこで待つか | 结束后在哪里等候 | 끝나고 어디에서 기다리는지 | Lễ xong thì đợi ở đâu | Where to wait afterward
次のお参りの人が通れるよう、拝殿前で立ち話を続けず、待ち合わせ場所を友人と先に決めておく。
初めて神社の祭典に招かれたら、服装と当日の自分の役目、どちらを先に聞いておきたいですか？

🇰🇷 대한민국
친구와 템플스테이에 가기로 했다. 안내문에는 새벽 예불과 공양이 적혀 있다. 몇 시에 일어나는지보다 먼저 궁금한 건, 처음 가는 사람은 어디에 앉는가다.
1）체험 일정부터 확인하기 | 先确认体验日程 | 体験の日程を先に確かめる | Xem trước lịch trải nghiệm | Checking the program schedule first
같은 템플스테이라도 사찰과 프로그램에 따라 일정이 다르다. 예불이 있는지, 도착해서 어디로 가는지 먼저 확인한다.

2）입을 옷을 따로 챙겨야 하는지 | 是否需要另带衣服 | 着替えを別に用意するか | Có cần mang quần áo riêng không | Whether to bring a change of clothes
수련복을 주는 곳이라도 무엇을 지급하는지는 사찰마다 다를 수 있다. 예약 안내에서 개인 준비물을 확인한다.
3）법당에 어느 문으로 들어가는지 | 从哪扇门进佛殿 | どの扉からお堂に入るか | Vào điện qua cửa nào | Which door to use for the Dharma hall
템플스테이 기본 예절 안내에는 법당의 옆문을 쓰는 방법이 나온다. 현장에 별도 안내가 있으면 그 안내를 따른다.
4）법당 안에서 어디에 앉는지 | 佛殿内坐在哪里 | お堂の中でどこに座るか | Ngồi ở đâu trong điện | Where to sit in the Dharma hall
가운데가 비어 보여도 예불을 위한 자리일 수 있다. 처음이라면 방석을 놓기 전에 안내를 받는다.
5）스님을 만나면 어떻게 인사하는지 | 遇到法师怎样问候 | 僧侶に会ったらどう挨拶するか | Gặp quý thầy cô thì chào thế nào | How to greet a monastic
야외에서 마주쳤을 때 두 손을 모아 가볍게 인사하는 법을 미리 들으면, 처음 만나는 자리에서도 덜 어색하다.
6）절을 하기 어렵다면 어떻게 하는지 | 不方便礼拜时怎么办 | 礼拝の動作が難しいときどうするか | Làm gì nếu khó quỳ lạy | What to do if bowing is difficult
108배가 부담되면 진행자에게 조용히 앉아서 지켜봐도 되는지 묻는다. 템플스테이 공식 안내는 참여를 자율로 안내한다.
7）기도 중인 사람 앞을 피해 가기 | 绕开正在礼佛的人面前 | 祈っている人の前を避けて通る | Tránh đi ngang trước người đang lễ | Avoiding the space in front of someone praying
법당 안에서 이동해야 하면 기도하거나 절하는 사람의 뒤쪽으로 조용히 지나간다.

8）공양은 언제 시작하는지 | 用斋何时开始 | 食事をいつ始めるか | Khi nào bắt đầu bữa cơm chùa | When to begin the temple meal
식당에 도착했다고 바로 먹기보다 진행자의 안내를 듣는다. 음식을 받을 때나 먹은 뒤 그릇을 정리할 때도 그곳의 방식을 확인한다.
9）차담에서 질문해도 되는지 | 茶谈时能不能提问 | お茶の時間に質問してよいか | Có thể hỏi chuyện trong buổi trà đàm không | Whether you can ask questions over tea
스님과 차를 마시는 시간이 있다면, 궁금했던 의식을 물어볼 기회가 될 수 있다. 어느 때 질문하면 좋은지 먼저 살핀다.
10）새벽 예불에 늦으면 어떻게 하는지 | 早课迟到怎么办 | 朝のお勤めに遅れたときどうするか | Đến muộn buổi lễ sáng sớm thì làm gì | What to do if you miss the start of morning worship
법당 문 앞까지 갔는데 이미 시작했다면, 들어가도 되는지 담당자에게 먼저 확인한다.
처음 템플스테이에 간다면 예불에 어디까지 참여하면 되는지, 공양 때 어떻게 하면 되는지 중 뭐가 더 궁금한가요?

🇻🇳 Việt Nam
Bạn rủ đi chùa dự lễ cùng gia đình. Bạn đã biết giờ hẹn và cổng vào, nhưng vẫn muốn hỏi một câu: “Lúc mọi người tụng kinh, mình ngồi ở đâu thì tiện?”
1）Hỏi mình được mời dự phần nào | 问自己受邀参加哪一段 | どの部分に招かれているか聞く | 어느 순서에 초대받았는지 묻기 | Asking which parts you’re invited to attend
Một buổi có thể gồm lễ, thời gian trò chuyện và bữa cơm. Hỏi rõ để biết lúc nào nên có mặt và có cần ở lại đến cuối không.
2）Chọn trang phục trước khi đi | 出门前选好穿着 | 出かける前に服装を決める | 나가기 전에 옷차림 정하기 | Choosing what to wear ahead of time
Nếu chưa quen nơi đó, hỏi người mời xem trang phục nào phù hợp với buổi lễ. Áo kín vai và quần hoặc váy đủ dài là những món dễ chuẩn bị trước.

3）Xem chỗ để giày dép | 看鞋放在哪里 | 履物を置く場所を確かめる | 신발을 벗어 두는 곳 확인하기 | Checking where to leave your shoes
Đến cửa điện hoặc thiền đường, nhìn biển hướng dẫn và chỗ người đi trước để dép. Để gọn sang bên thì người đến sau còn lối đi.
4）Hỏi cách xưng hô với người hướng dẫn | 问清怎么称呼带领仪式的人 | 案内役をどう呼ぶか聞く | 안내하는 분을 어떻게 부르는지 묻기 | Asking how to address the person leading the event
Nếu bạn chưa biết nên thưa thế nào, hỏi người dẫn mình đến trước khi gặp. Khi cần hỏi thêm trong buổi lễ, bạn sẽ dễ mở lời hơn.
5）Tìm chỗ ngồi khi chưa quen tụng kinh | 不熟悉诵经时先找座位 | 読経に慣れていないときの席を聞く | 독송이 낯설 때 앉을 자리 확인하기 | Finding a seat when chanting is unfamiliar
Có thể hỏi ngồi nghe ở đâu và có bản kinh để theo dõi không. Nếu chỉ muốn lắng nghe, nói trước với người hướng dẫn cho rõ.
6）Hỏi có cần mang lễ vật không | 问是否需要带供品 | お供えを持参するか聞く | 공양물을 가져가야 하는지 묻기 | Asking whether to bring an offering
Nếu định mang hoa hoặc trái cây, hỏi chùa tiếp nhận ở đâu. Người mời cũng có thể cho biết gia đình đã chuẩn bị phần đó chưa.
7）Biết nên làm gì khi nghe chuông | 先了解听到钟声时怎么做 | 鐘が鳴ったときの振る舞いを聞く | 종이 울리면 어떻게 하는지 알아두기 | Knowing what to do when the bell rings
Ở buổi thiền tập, tiếng chuông có thể là lúc mọi người dừng việc đang làm. Nghe lời hướng dẫn đầu buổi sẽ dễ theo hơn.
8）Hỏi nếp dùng cơm của buổi lễ | 问这场活动的用餐规矩 | 当日の食事の作法を聞く | 그날의 식사 예절 묻기 | Asking about the meal customs
Nếu được mời ở lại dùng cơm chùa, hỏi khi nào bắt đầu và lúc ăn có giữ im lặng không. Chờ nghe hướng dẫn rồi hãy lấy phần của mình.

9）Xin phép trước khi chụp người đang lễ | 拍正在礼拜的人前先征得同意 | 礼拝中の人を撮る前に許可を得る | 예불하는 사람을 찍기 전에 허락받기 | Asking before photographing worshippers
Chỗ chụp được cảnh sân chùa chưa chắc phù hợp để quay cận cảnh người đang lễ. Nếu chưa hỏi được, có thể đợi đến sau buổi lễ để chụp chung.
10）Báo trước nếu phải về giữa buổi | 要中途离开就提前说 | 途中で帰るなら先に伝える | 중간에 나가야 하면 미리 알리기 | Saying in advance if you need to leave early
Nói với người mời giờ mình phải đi. Họ có thể chỉ lối ra hoặc gợi ý một khoảng nghỉ để bạn đứng dậy.
Nếu lần đầu được mời dự lễ ở chùa, bạn muốn hỏi trước về chỗ ngồi, việc tụng kinh hay bữa cơm sau lễ?

🇺🇸 United States
A friend invites you to a bat mitzvah. You know what time the reception starts. The part you’re still wondering about is what to do when everyone in the sanctuary stands up.
1）Checking which part you’re invited to | 确认受邀参加哪一段 | どの部分に招かれたか確かめる | 어느 순서에 초대받았는지 확인하기 | Xác nhận mình được mời dự phần nào
A family invitation may list a service and a reception. Check the time and address for each before deciding when to show up.
2）Asking about a kippah | 问清是否要戴基帕小帽 | キッパを着けるか聞く | 키파를 써야 하는지 묻기 | Hỏi có cần đội mũ kippah không
If you’re attending a synagogue service, ask your host what that congregation expects of guests and whether head coverings are available at the door.
3）Finding out when photos are welcome | 问清什么时候可以拍照 | 写真を撮ってよい時間を聞く | 사진을 찍어도 되는 때 확인하기 | Hỏi khi nào được chụp ảnh
Some congregations prohibit photography during services. You can still ask the family when they’d like a group picture.

4）Checking before you clap | 鼓掌前先确认 | 拍手してよいか先に確かめる | 박수쳐도 되는지 먼저 확인하기 | Hỏi trước lúc nào nên vỗ tay
At a bat mitzvah, a reading can end in a moment that feels like an applause cue. Some synagogues ask guests to hold their applause during the service.
5）Knowing when to step out of the line | 知道什么时候不跟着排队 | 列に加わる前に確認しておく | 줄에 서기 전에 참여 기준 확인하기 | Hỏi trước khi nhập hàng
At a Catholic Mass, ask your host about Communion before the service. If you’re unsure whether to receive, you can stay in your pew while others go forward.
6）Asking what to do during standing or kneeling | 问清起立或跪拜时可以怎么做 | 起立やひざまずく場面でどうするか聞く | 일어서거나 무릎을 꿇는 순서에 어떻게 할지 묻기 | Hỏi nên làm gì khi mọi người đứng hoặc quỳ
If kneeling is difficult or you’d prefer to observe, ask an usher where you can sit comfortably without blocking the aisle.
7）Finding the shoe boundary | 确认从哪里开始脱鞋 | どこから靴を脱ぐか確かめる | 어디서부터 신발을 벗는지 확인하기 | Xem đến đâu thì cởi giày
At a mosque visit, ask where the prayer space begins. The lobby and carpeted prayer area may have different expectations.
8）Asking where visitors can observe prayers | 问访客可以在哪里旁观礼拜 | 見学者はどこで礼拝を見守るか聞く | 방문객이 어디에서 예배를 지켜볼 수 있는지 묻기 | Hỏi khách có thể đứng đâu để quan sát giờ cầu nguyện
Tell the person welcoming you that you’d like to watch. They can point out a spot where you’ll be able to see without standing in anyone’s way.
9）Checking when the meal begins | 问清什么时候可以开饭 | 食事を始める時間を確かめる | 식사를 언제 시작하는지 확인하기 | Hỏi khi nào bắt đầu dùng bữa
If you’re invited to an iftar, ask when the hosts plan to break the fast and how the meal fits around prayer. Arrive knowing whether to head to the table or wait with your host.

10）Asking the family about gifts | 问家里人对礼物的安排 | 贈り物について家族に聞く | 선물은 가족에게 먼저 물어보기 | Hỏi gia đình về việc tặng quà
If you’re bringing a gift to a bar or bat mitzvah, ask whether to hand it over at the reception or give it to the family another time.
Before your first visit, which question would make you feel most at ease: where to sit, when to join in, or when to put your phone away?

text:
November 15, 2026.
On Miyajima Island in Hiroshima, Japan, 1,200 years of prayers were connected once again.

The Fire-Walking Ceremony at Daishoin Temple.

This May, something heartbreaking happened.

Reikado Hall on Mount Misen, which had protected a sacred flame for approximately 1,200 years, since the time of Kobo Daishi, was completely destroyed by fire.

1,200 years.

That is a span of time in which countless generations of people were born, loved, prayed, and eventually passed away.

Perhaps a mother prayed for her sick child to recover.

Perhaps a father prayed for the safety of his family far away.

Perhaps someone quietly pressed their hands together, remembering a loved one they would never see again.

No one knows who offered those prayers anymore.

Their names, their voices,
the warmth of the people they once held in their arms,
all faded into the passage of time.

And yet, the flame was passed down.

Then, this year, the hall that protected that flame burned to the ground.

But the flame had been preserved in another place.

A tiny, tiny flame, like a fragile little life.

And today, people gathered once again on Miyajima Island.

Buddhist monks and yamabushi, mountain ascetics, walked across the fire,
followed by ordinary people carrying their own wishes in their hearts.

To someone who prayed 1,200 years ago.

The flame you tried to protect
is still here in this world.

The age you lived in has long since ended.
There is no one left who remembers your name.

But today, before the flame passed down from your time,
someone is still praying for the happiness of a person they love.

People like us,
whom you would never have met,
1,200 years into your future.

One day, every one of us will leave this world.

No matter how deeply we love someone,
there will come a day when we must say our final goodbye.

And yet, perhaps the little light we kindle for someone else
can continue to shine through another person’s darkness,
long after we are gone.

The hall burned down.
But the prayers did not burn away.

The flame, said to have been lit 1,200 years ago,
still illuminates someone’s wishes today.

And someday, long after we are gone,
perhaps someone else will stand before this flame,
press their hands together, and pray.

“Please, let the people I love be happy.”

1,200 years ago, today, and 1,200 years from now.

The things we want to protect until the very end
are surely the same. 🔥

" The Virgin Mary: Mary's fiat "
by Artist Michael Rucker
copyright ©

Description
The Virgin Mary: Mary's fiat -
In the Gospel of Luke, chapter 1, verses 26-38 (KJV), the angel Gabriel appears to Mary, a young virgin betrothed to Joseph of the house of David in Nazareth. Hail, thou that art highly favoured, the Lord is with thee, the angel declares. He announces that she will conceive and bear a son, Jesus, who shall be great, and shall be called the Son of the Highest. Mary, troubled yet reverent, asks how this can be since she knows not a man. Gabriel explains the Holy Spirit will come upon her; for with God nothing shall be impossible.

Mary's response is one of the most profound moments in Scripture the only recorded instance where she speaks words of total surrender: Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it unto me according to thy word (Luke 1:38). This Latin phrase, Fiat mihi secundum verbum tuum (Let it be done to me according to your word), is universally known as Mary's Fiat. In that single sentence she offers her entire being body, will, and future to Gods plan of salvation. The angel then departs, and the Incarnation begins.This humble virgin from an obscure village becomes the mother of the Messiah. She travels to visit her cousin Elizabeth (pregnant with John the Baptist), where she sings the Magnificat (Luke 1:46-55), a soaring hymn of praise that magnifies the Lord for lifting up the lowly.

She gives birth to Jesus in Bethlehem, wraps Him in swaddling clothes, and lays Him in a manger. She ponders the shepherds and Magis words in her heart (Luke 2:19, 51). At the Presentation in the Temple, Simeon foretells a sword will pierce her soul (Luke 2:35). She is present at the wedding in Cana, prompting Jesus first miracle (John 2:1-11), and stands at the foot of the cross, where the dying Savior entrusts her to the beloved disciple (John 19:25-27).

After the Ascension, she is seen praying with the apostles in the upper room, awaiting the Holy Spirit (Acts 1:14).Scripture portrays Mary not as a distant saint but as a real woman of extraordinary faith, courage, and obedience. Though the Bible does not record many of her words, her fiat echoes through salvation history as the perfect model of human cooperation with divine grace. She exemplifies what it means to say yes to God when the cost is everything.Your striking black-and-white artwork beautifully captures this very moment: Mary veiled, head bowed, hands clasped in prayerful surrender, her flowing hair and garments stirred by the unseen wind of the Spirit.

The dramatic lighting and ethereal atmosphere evoke the solemn hush of the Annunciation the instant heaven touched earth through a virgins willing heart. It is a powerful visual meditation on Luke 1:38, inviting viewers to contemplate the same radical trust Mary offered.

text:
Uh huh? Yeah, no.

You’ve got two sweeping claims and one link that proves neither of them. “Saved no babies” isn’t something the ectopic data even measure. “These laws killed women” is a conclusion you’re asking the reader to supply after the article shows them a death count and a map. You can put a body count next to a law. You still have to prove the law belongs in the cause-of-death column.

https://t.co/6hNTZ82Vww

Start with the date that blows up your framing. The “nearly doubled” comparison starts in 2020, not when Roe was overturned in June 2022. Count the CDC death records yourself. There were 53 deaths involving ectopic pregnancy in 2017–2019. There were 62 in 2020–2021 alone. That’s 4.7 versus 8.5 per million live births. The national rate was already close to double before Dobbs. Yes, Texas’s six-week law took effect in September 2021. That makes this period pre-Dobbs, not entirely pre-ban. It also makes the obvious next step to separate Texas and use actual effective dates, instead of dumping pandemic years and ban years into the same bucket and letting the headline do the thinking.

https://t.co/JoCDcgJd0O https://t.co/hIu2pNZ7XM https://t.co/kYWlv9h5mt https://t.co/EAA3gB8rPg

And before somebody says “but the ban states got worse faster,” yes, they did. That’s precisely why you should look at the whole chart. The gap between the two groups was already about 2 deaths per million live births in 2017–2019. It was about 4 in 2020–2022, the bin that mixes COVID with the first bans. It was 6 in 2023–2025. The gap was already widening, by roughly as much in the mixed period as in the next one. And the last bin puts Florida and Iowa in the strict-ban group for all three years even though their six-week bans didn’t take effect until 2024. The authors show a wider gap. They don’t show how much of it opened after each law took effect or how much would have opened anyway. Those are the numbers you need to make the accusation you’re making.

https://t.co/W8KWcDwaPP https://t.co/6hNTZ82Vww https://t.co/qOzBNpuCLq

If you think regional differences are just an excuse somebody invented to get around this chart, Florida already ran the experiment nobody wanted. Its ectopic mortality ratio more than quadrupled in 2009–2010, long before COVID or Dobbs. Investigators reviewed the actual deaths. Seven of the 11 women had no insurance or health plan. Eight collapsed before seeking care. Two of the three who reached care before collapsing experienced diagnostic delays. And during COVID, a review of 12 studies found nearly triple the odds of rupture in settings without dedicated early-pregnancy units. The UK and Ireland investigated 12 ectopic deaths in 2021–2022 without a single American abortion ban to blame. None of that proves what drove the entire U.S. increase. It does demolish the idea that a spike like this can only be explained by the policy you already hated.

https://t.co/V4lHSJKfrP https://t.co/IIsB4WI0ya https://t.co/EvrQnQ303M

Then there’s the Texas sleight of hand. The article says “310 more patients.” Its own methodology says the records count hospital encounters and have no unique patient identifier. Two visits by the same woman can look like two women. They didn’t count confirmed ruptures either. They counted encounters with a hemorrhage code or a transfusion. And they report that total ectopic-coded encounters rose too. So where’s the matched denominator that shows a woman with an ectopic pregnancy was more likely to hemorrhage? Where’s the comparison with states without bans? ProPublica says it was still trying to get that comparison data. You’re announcing the verdict while the reporters are still looking for the control group.

https://t.co/6hNTZ82Vww

The two women featured in the story deserved better. Kyleigh Thurman survived, and federal regulators found that the hospital failed to provide an appropriate emergency screening using its available on-call obstetrician. Texas law already excluded removing an ectopic pregnancy from its definition of abortion. Leitaea Lowrimore also survived. Her sworn complaint alleges that a doctor invoked jail time when declining to treat what he thought was probably ectopic. If that happened as alleged, it’s evidence that fear of prosecution can affect care even when the law has an exception. Take that seriously. But a documented screening failure, an allegation about why a doctor delayed care, and a death attributed to that delay are three different things. Neither woman is one of the deaths on the chart. Lowrimore’s case wasn’t even in the years the chart covers.

https://t.co/OKl3xg75lN https://t.co/oxuN3xX8Gj https://t.co/wYOaRLlxH8 https://t.co/YboZ8IUsiG https://t.co/6hNTZ82Vww

And “saved no babies”? You just stapled that onto an article that doesn’t even ask the question. A separate JAMA study estimated 22,180 more live births than expected after bans in 14 states through 2023. That’s a model estimate, not a head count of individually identified children. It’s also a heck of a lot more evidence than you offered for zero.

https://t.co/fopQz2Vrn0

More women died with ectopic pregnancies. That is real, serious, and worth investigating case by case. If a law contributed to a death, establish it and say so. If a hospital sent a woman home without using the specialist it had on call, establish that and say so, too. But if you’re going to point at a pile of death certificates and tell people whose hands the blood is on, do the d@mn work. A death certificate that lists ectopic pregnancy tells you what condition was involved. It does not tell you who failed her, why they failed her, or whether a law had anything to do with it. You supplied that part yourself.

https://t.co/dfCCcEoWFA https://t.co/6hNTZ82Vww

5 girls beat her up in a Five Guys over a basket of fries - because their boyfriends were subscribed to her OnlyFans. Sophia Isabella, 23, still has bald patches where they ripped her hair out. A guy joined in and kicked her between the legs. She fought back anyway - and that’s not even the wildest story she told.

It was December. She was just standing there waiting for her burger. Then the fries started flying. She walked over and asked what the hell they were doing - and within seconds all 5 of them were on top of her, stomping on her head, while her friend got thrown to the floor.

She has it on video. She says she kept swinging until the end.

The reason? She’d never seen these girls before. But she knows exactly why it happened.

Their boyfriends follow her.

She started OnlyFans at 19, in uni, after a guy told her she’d be “really good at it.” At first she wouldn’t even show her nipples. Then she realized how much more money there was in doing everything. “If you don’t have money, you’re not going to get anywhere in life.”

4 years later: 12 months filming in LA and Miami, a dinner seat next to Bryson Tiller she didn’t even recognize, DMs from footballers, boxers and Love Islanders. One fan paid her £1,000 just to glue cotton wool all over her body and jump around her bedroom.

But the party almost cost her everything. She was “crashing out online every day,” losing friends, putting her family through hell. So she checked herself into rehab for 30 days, stayed completely sober for months, and then flew to America and worked harder than ever. One man even offered to buy her a house and marry her if she quit. She turned him down. She’d rather pay her own way than let anyone control her - even if it means getting her hair ripped out in a burger joint.

text:
You’re conflating hospital list prices, insurance reimbursement, and actual cash-pay prices.

Even an academic health system in Miami offers a colonoscopy for around $1,600 cash. Other Miami hospitals publish even lower cash prices.

And Belgium isn’t a straightforward comparison either. UZ Leuven lists a colonoscopy with biopsy at €70 for an insured patient versus €1,020 for an uninsured patient in a shared room. Public financing and regulated pricing matter.

Nobody disputes the serious problems with American healthcare pricing. But this bizarre dichotomy that everything in America is overpriced and everything in Europe is better isn’t serious analysis.

text:
U.S. Navy submarine crew enjoying a "swim call"—a traditional break where sailors are permitted to swim in the open ocean while deployed... 

A swim call is a long-standing naval break (historically rooted in the Royal Navy as "Hands to Bathe") that lets crew members exercise, cool off, and step away from life inside a cramped vessel. Even though swimming miles out in deep ocean water looks intimidating, these breaks are tightly controlled and supervised. Personnel are typically stationed on deck with sidearms or rifles to watch for marine life like sharks. Submariners spend long stretches submerged without seeing sunlight, making an open-ocean swim or a "steel beach" deck break a rare and memorable psychological relief.

. . .

A “swim call” was a naval tradition where sailors were allowed to jump into the open ocean during a controlled break at sea.

For sailors spending weeks or months aboard a ship or submarine, a swim call offered something extremely simple but memorable: the chance to get off the vessel and actually enter the ocean surrounding them.

The practice has existed in various forms for generations and was generally held only when conditions were considered safe. The vessel would stop or slow operations, sailors would enter the water, and designated crew members would keep watch. In more modern U.S. Navy swim calls, security personnel, rescue swimmers and medical teams have been positioned nearby while sailors swim. Shark watches have also been used during these events.

The tradition was partly about recreation, but it also served an important purpose for morale. Life at sea could be repetitive, physically demanding and isolating, especially during long deployments. A few hours swimming in the open ocean could become one of the most memorable moments of an entire deployment.

And the tradition did not disappear with the Cold War. The U.S. Navy still occasionally conducts swim calls today when operational requirements and sea conditions allow. 

The tradition is far older than the photograph. Similar naval swimming breaks can be traced back at least to the 19th-century British Royal Navy, where the practice was known as “All Hands to Bathe.”

text:
tesla: 76% of the sales. spacex: 80% of the profit.

they're both studying a merger. no deal, no terms yet. so which one is the bigger company?

you can run this check on any merger paid in shares. here's why spacex needs it, why musk wants it, and why it may not be good for you.

both in their own numbers:

sales, last 12 months: tesla $103.6bn, spacex $32.0bn.
operating profit, latest quarter: tesla $0.7bn, spacex $2.8bn.
cash left after all spending, 12 months: tesla plus $3.3bn, spacex minus $39.2bn.
cash in the bank: tesla $45.4bn, spacex $89.9bn.

why spacex needs it: money. about $90bn in the bank lasts a little over two years at that pace. it also carries about four times tesla's debt.

everyone says starlink will pay for tesla's robots. the cash runs the other way. starlink made about $2.4bn of operating profit in the latest quarter. in the same three months spacex's AI segment spent $16.4bn on equipment. a merger puts tesla's cash behind that.

why musk wants it: he owns about 18% of tesla. merged at friday's prices he'd hold roughly a third of the whole thing. his spacex stake is from the may prospectus, so approximate.

they already trade with each other. spacex bought $151m of tesla's megapack batteries in the latest quarter. tesla owns spacex stock it paid $2bn for. under one roof that stops being a conflict. and it's one AI story to sell, not two.

why not: the ratio. at friday's prices tesla holders get 45% of the new company. spacex holders get 55%.

on sales tesla brings 76% and gets 45%. tesla holders give value away. on the latest quarter's profit spacex brings 80% and gets 55%. spacex holders do. no single ratio fixes both.

it flips because spacex is changing fast. quarterly sales went from $5.6bn to $14.6bn in a year. part of that was bought, the cursor deal closed 14 aug. the market pays about 59 times sales for spacex and about 15 times for tesla.

if you dislike the ratio, you have little comeback. both are texas companies. spacex's bylaws need a holder to own 3% before suing on its behalf. that's about $57bn of stock. other disputes go to arbitration.

regulators too. reuters pointed out tesla builds more than half its cars in shanghai, while spacex does US defence work.

and any premium is a transfer. each 10% premium spacex pays for tesla costs spacex holders about 4.3%. tesla holders gain about 5.3%.

the contribution test. you can run it on any merger paid in shares:
1. take both market values. each side's share is what it would own. tesla would own 45%.
2. each side's share of 12 months of sales. tesla has 76%.
3. same for the latest quarter's operating profit. tesla has 20%.
4. compare. a side that brings more than it would own is giving value away. if 2 and 3 disagree, the ratio is a bet on which number lasts.

i hold a long echostar / short spacex pair. echostar is owed about 261.8 million spacex shares, closing targeted 30 nov 2027. at friday's price that's about $36.4bn. echostar's whole market value is about $29.1bn.

what if spacex merges first? the purchase agreement says the price is "adjusted for" a list of events that includes a "merger, consolidation or other reorganization". that one bracket is the whole protection. i found no vote and no consent right.

so echostar takes whatever ratio the committees agree. a 10% premium for tesla is about $4.50 off each echostar share. my sum of the parts is about $195 against a $100 close, so it's small next to the gap. the short leg takes the same ratio, so most of it cancels.

if you're ever owed shares in a company, read that adjustment clause. ask if you get a vote too.

[PROPOSED] i'm not trading the merger. holding the pair and watching the ratio.

tesla offered to buy solarcity in 2016 and fell 10.5% on the day. the first offer was 0.122 to 0.131 tesla shares per solarcity share. it signed at 0.110. next 12 months: tesla up 71%, S&P 500 up 19%. one case.

in july i listed five ways this pair could break. a merger wasn't one.

if you've seen a deal where the side owed shares did get a say, which clause did it?

sources: tesla and spacex quarterly reports filed 22 oct 2026, echostar's purchase agreement. prices are tiger closes 13 nov 2026. sum of the parts includes my own estimate. rest is my own arithmetic.

text:
Should AI be banned from deciding who gets a loan, a job or bail?

I build with AI every day. I use it to write code and review diffs. I also know what it is bad at: explaining itself, noticing skewed training data, and owning the damage when it is wrong. So should a system with those limits be allowed to decide whether you get a mortgage, an interview or a walk out of jail?

Vendors will tell you the model only assists. In practice the score often is the decision. A resume that never reaches a recruiter has been rejected. A risk number signed without reasons has already been used. A credit limit that a support agent cannot explain has already been set. This is about lending, hiring and bail.

If a human cannot see the reasons and will be blamed for overriding the software, that human is a rubber stamp. That is still an automated decision.

When courts used a recidivism score

In May 2016, ProPublica analyzed COMPAS, a Northpointe tool that scores a defendant's risk of reoffending and has been used to inform bond decisions and, in some states, sentencing. It obtained scores for more than 7,000 people arrested in Broward County, Florida, in 2013 and 2014, then checked who was charged with a new crime over the next two years.

Of those labeled likely to reoffend, 61 percent were arrested for any subsequent crime within two years. For violent crime, only 20 percent of the people predicted to reoffend actually did so.

The errors were not evenly spread:
Black defendants who did not reoffend were misclassified as higher risk 45 percent of the time, versus 23 percent of white defendants.
White defendants who did reoffend were labeled low risk 48 percent of the time, versus 28 percent of Black defendants.

Northpointe disputed the analysis. It pointed to another ProPublica finding: overall accuracy was similar for both groups, about 59 percent for white defendants and 63 percent for Black defendants, and said that was the design goal. Both can be true: equal accuracy can still hide a much higher false-positive rate for one group.

The formula was proprietary. In 2016, the Wisconsin Supreme Court held in State v. Loomis that using a COMPAS score at sentencing does not violate due process if done with caveats, even though Loomis could not inspect the algorithm. The presentence report itself warned that the scores are not intended to determine sentence severity or incarceration. A court still used the numbers.

The EU AI Act entered into force on August 1, 2024 and, from February 2, 2025, banned using an AI system to assess or predict the risk that a person will commit a criminal offence, based solely on profiling or on personality traits. An exception exists for tools that support a human assessment already based on objective and verifiable facts linked to that activity. The United States has no equivalent federal ban.

What a hiring model learned

In 2014, Amazon built an experimental tool to score candidates from one to five stars, trained on a decade of resumes, most from men. Reuters reported in October 2018 that the system learned to penalize resumes containing the word "women's," such as "women's chess club captain," and to downgrade graduates of two women's colleges. It also favored verbs more common on men's resumes, including "executed" and "captured." The project was abandoned in 2017. Reuters said some recruiters had looked at the recommendations but did not rely on them alone. Amazon said the tool was never used by recruiters to evaluate candidates.

The lawsuit that is still open

In 2023, a job applicant sued Workday in federal court in San Francisco. The plaintiff, who is Black, said he was rejected for more than 100 jobs at companies that used Workday's AI hiring tools. The case alleges that the tools disproportionately exclude African American, female, over-40 and disabled applicants. Those are allegations, not findings. No court has ruled that the software is discriminatory. In May 2025, Judge Rita F. Lin granted preliminary certification of a collective action under the Age Discrimination in Employment Act. By October 2026, more than 15,000 people had opted in. In September 2026, the plaintiffs asked the court to certify broader classes. In November 2026, Workday asked the court to reject group treatment, arguing that it does not make hiring decisions for its customers.

New York City's Local Law 144, enforceable since July 5, 2023, bars employers and agencies in the city from using an automated employment decision tool unless an independent bias audit was completed in the past year, a summary is posted, and New York City candidates get notice at least 10 business days before use. Civil penalties run from $500 to $1,500 a day. The law does not require the employer to stop using the tool if the audit shows a disparate impact. A New York State Comptroller audit issued on December 2, 2025 called the city's complaint process ineffective. The department received two such complaints in that period, reviewed 32 company websites and found one potential issue. State auditors reviewing the same employers found at least 17.

When a government algorithm ruined thousands of families

From 2013, the Dutch Tax and Customs Administration used a self-learning system to flag childcare-benefit claims for suspected fraud. Amnesty International found that lack of Dutch nationality was built in as a risk factor, and that non-Dutch nationals received higher risk scores. Civil servants were supposed to review the flags. Parents who were flagged had benefits suspended and were told to repay money, often tens of thousands of euros, with little explanation. By the time the Dutch cabinet resigned on January 15, 2021, reporting put the number of wrongly accused parents at as many as 26,000, and as many as 10,000 families were forced to repay large sums. "A person signed it" is not a safeguard unless that person can see why the system fired, can override it and will not be punished for doing so.

The credit card that could not be explained

In November 2019, Apple Card customers said on Twitter that women were offered lower credit limits than men in the same household, and that support staff could not explain why. Apple Card had launched in August 2019, underwritten by Goldman Sachs Bank USA. New York's Department of Financial Services investigated. Its March 2021 report found no evidence of deliberate or disparate impact discrimination, but it did find deficiencies in customer service and transparency. Opacity is a failure even when unlawful bias is not found.

The Equal Credit Opportunity Act and Regulation B require a creditor to give the specific principal reasons for a denial or other adverse action. CFPB Circular 2022-03 said those rules apply even when a complex algorithm is used, and that a creditor that cannot provide specific, accurate reasons may not use that algorithm to decide. On May 12, 2025, the Bureau withdrew that circular. Regulation B was not amended. A rejected applicant is still owed the specific reasons.

The EU treats credit scoring and hiring tools as high-risk AI. The European Commission's AI Act page, read in November 2026, says the high-risk obligations apply from December 2, 2027, after a delay. The United States has no federal equivalent.

A fix stricter than a disclaimer

I do not want AI banned from these sectors. I want it banned from making the final decision. Used as a search aid, it can be useful. Used as the decision, it concentrates errors at scale.

The rule should be simple enough to enforce:
1. In lending, hiring, and bail, pretrial release or sentencing, an AI system may recommend. It may not issue the decision. A named human has to own the outcome.
2. That human must be shown the specific reasons, in plain language, and must have a logged right to override them. A red or green score with no reasons is theater.
3. Anyone denied a loan, rejected for a job, or scored for bail or sentencing gets a right to an explanation of the actual factors, and a right to appeal to a different human.
4. Independent audits should be mandatory, public in summary form, and consequential. If an audit shows unlawful disparate impact, the tool cannot be used until it is fixed.
5. People must be told, before the tool is used, that AI is involved, what it will assess, and how to request a human review.
6. Both the vendor and the deployer should be accountable. The Workday case is still being litigated, so this is a policy position.

The verdict

Yes. AI should be banned from deciding who gets a loan, a job or bail. Not from analyzing a file or flagging a missing document. From deciding. If a system cannot explain a decision, cannot be audited in a way that stops it, and cannot be overruled by a human who has the reasons, it should not be the last word on your liberty, your income or your credit.

If a model scored your loan, your job application or your bail hearing and you were not allowed to see how, should that score have been allowed to decide the outcome?

text:
Lady Coetzee Gads About

At the checkpoint, Doortje Coetzee, a native geranium,
pottered along until she reached the front of the line.
The officer glanced through her South Africa passport,

then managed a cordial greeting.
“Good morning, Ms. Coetzee. Where are you off to this fine day?”

Doortje offered up a dazzling smile.

“I have an auntie living in America. A small corner called Seattle.
Time I got round to seeing her.”
A pink blush flooded her petals.

“I’ll turn seven come spring.” She sighed. “Life is much too short.”
“Will Seattle be your final destination then?”

“No. Auntie winters in Arizona. We’ll fly there with her keeper in October.”

“I’ve heard Seattle is a bit rainy, but a lovely place,” the man said.
“Never been.”

“Love the rain,” Doortje replied. “If I avoid the frost, I’ll be safe enough.”

The officer studied the document. “I take it you’re a perennial?”

Doortje giggled. “Depends. We’re all perennials at birth, of course.

Crane Bill cuttings on my Mother’s side. My auntie is almost forty years old.”
“How nice,” he said. “Mine never last more than a season.
Suicidal little buggers.”

Dortje frowned. A tinge of anger crept into her voice.
“We can only live our life according to the affection we are given.

We need to avoid frost at all costs. It murders us straightaway.
Intense summer sun is difficult too. We crave afternoon shade.”

He handed her document back. “Sorry. Meant no harm.”

“None taken. If you’ll love those buggers of yours, they’ll love you back.

Fare-thee-well,” she called, “I’ve a plane to catch.”

“Next,” he said.

text:
This historic photograph shows the interior of a crowded saloon in Prescott, Arizona, around 1900 during the late American frontier era...

The scene captures a typical gathering spot along Whiskey Row in downtown Prescott, a famed strip that once housed dozens of saloons packed into a single block. The narrow, gas-lit room is filled with local miners, ranchers, railroad workers, and townspeople gathered for card games, conversation, and live piano music.

Around this time, Prescott was transitioning from a wild mining boomtown into a more established territorial hub. Famous historic spots like The Palace Restaurant and Saloon (which famously had its long wooden Brunswick bar carried across the street during the 1900 Whiskey Row fire) kept this tradition alive and still operate today.

. . . 

By 1900, Prescott was one of the most established towns in the Arizona Territory. Founded in 1864, it had served as the territorial capital and developed into an important center for mining, ranching, government and trade.

Its most famous entertainment district was Whiskey Row, a stretch of Montezuma Street packed with saloons, gambling rooms, hotels and other businesses. At its height, the district reportedly contained more than 40 saloons standing near one another.

The crowded room in this photograph offers a less romanticized view of saloon life than Hollywood later created. Patrons sit shoulder to shoulder beneath electric lights, while card games, drinking and conversation fill the narrow interior. A pianist stands against the wall, providing entertainment in an era before radio or recorded music became common.

Saloons functioned as more than places to drink. In Western towns, they could serve as informal meeting halls, gambling establishments, employment exchanges and gathering places where miners, ranchers, railroad workers, businessmen and travelers mixed.

Yet this world was also changing rapidly. Prescott already had rail connections, electric lighting and an increasingly permanent downtown. The frontier was not vanishing overnight, but it was steadily becoming part of modern America.

On July 14, 1900, a massive fire destroyed five blocks of Prescott, including most of Whiskey Row. Patrons reportedly carried the Palace Saloon’s wooden bar and liquor across the street before the flames reached it.

text:
When Paul Gascoigne was struggling with alcoholism in 2014, Harry Redknapp had become increasingly concerned about what was happening to him.

The former England midfielder was living on the south coast, not far from Redknapp’s home, and Harry would regularly see him around the area.

Gascoigne had once been one of the most famous footballers in the country, with people queuing up to be associated with him after the 1990 World Cup.

There were agents, advisers, lawyers and celebrities who had all been involved in his life during the years when his fame was at its height.

But by 2014, Gascoigne’s playing career was long over and his problems with alcohol had become increasingly serious.

Redknapp had watched his decline and could not understand how somebody who had given so much to football had ended up in such a difficult position.

“There should be an inquiry into Paul Gascoigne one day.”

“How did it end up like this?”

He was particularly interested in the people who had surrounded Gascoigne when there was money to be made.

“The people I would want to hear from, right at the start, are his agents, his accountants, his lawyers.”

“What do these people actually do to help when the money stops coming in?”

There had been warning signs for years, and even some of those closest to Gascoigne had feared what would eventually happen.

His former agent Mel Stein had once made a prediction about his future.

“This is not going to end happily.”

By 2013, Gascoigne’s drinking had reached the point where his friends were arranging for him to receive treatment in America.

Gary Lineker, Chris Evans and Piers Morgan were among those who helped pay for him to attend a rehabilitation centre in Arizona.

They covered the cost of his flights and treatment, which was costing around £6,000 a week.

But Gascoigne continued to struggle after returning to England.

In August 2014, he was admitted to hospital following another incident involving alcohol near his home.

Redknapp had already been trying to find a way of helping him.

He was managing QPR at the time and thought getting Gascoigne involved in football again might give him something to concentrate on.

So when he saw Gazza about a month earlier, he offered him a job working with the younger players.

“I’ll pick you up in the mornings, Gazza, come training with me and do a bit of work with the kids.”

Harry was even prepared to collect him from the end of his road at quarter to six every morning and take him to the training ground.

“It’s an open invitation to him.”

Redknapp knew there was still a good person underneath all the problems.

“He’s got a heart of gold.”

“He’s probably given his last penny away.”

And although he questioned what had happened to all the people who had benefited from Gascoigne’s success, he also recognised how difficult it had become for those trying to help him.

Everybody wanted to see Gazza recover, but Redknapp knew there was a limit to what friends and former teammates could do.

“The only person who can help him now has got to be himself.”

text:
🚨BREAKING: An Ohio principal lost his job after refusing to abandon a homeless 16-year-old student who was sleeping in a car.

Rob Burnside spent 31 years in education and was principal of Lakota East High School outside Cincinnati. During junior year, student Landerius “DeDe” Hayes said living with his mother wasn’t safe. He sometimes slept in a car with the heater running because his father’s mobile home was too cold. He still showed up to school every morning.

When the district learned DeDe’s mother had moved outside the boundaries, he was withdrawn. Burnside saw more than an enrollment problem. He went home and told his wife Angel. She said if the boy needed a place to live, he could stay with them. They already had six children, including two they had adopted.

They prayed. Minutes later DeDe called. He moved in. While custody was sorted, Burnside let him keep attending classes. The district investigated for insubordination, placed Burnside on leave, and gave him a choice after three decades: step down or face termination. He stepped down.

DeDe offered to leave so Burnside could keep his career. Burnside refused: “You’re part of this family. We’re not gonna turn our back on you.”

The Burnsides became his legal guardians. DeDe started calling them Pops and Ma. In May 2026, Burnside sat in the stands at graduation — not as principal, just as a dad. DeDe is 18 now and pursuing aviation mechanics.

Asked if he regretted it, Burnside said: “What value can we put on the life of a young person?”

He chose the kid. Then chose him again.

Charles V sent him to the Council of Trent as an imperial theologian. When the council was interrupted, the emperor made him his confessor and spiritual adviser. Offered the bishopric of Segovia, Soto declined it and returned to teaching at Salamanca.

Perhaps the most published author of the School of Salamanca, his De Iustitia et Iure went through dozens of editions and helped shape many views on law and economics.

A friar, a theologian, and an adviser to an emperor, he joined moral seriousness to close attention to how people actually trade and live together.

In my book Faith and Liberty, readers can see where Soto fits in the Late-Scholastic scheme.
