text:
🏔️ Mount Athos: 100 Facts About the Monastic Republic

🏔️ THE PEAKS AND THE PENINSULA

𝟏. Mount Athos is the easternmost of the three "fingers" of Chalkidiki in northern Greece 🇬🇷.

𝟐. The peninsula is about 50 km long and 7–12 km wide.

𝟑. It covers roughly 335 km², a little smaller than Malta 🇲🇹.

𝟒. The marble peak of Athos rises to about 2,033 m, almost straight out of the Aegean Sea.

𝟓. A tiny chapel of the Transfiguration sits right on the summit.

𝟔. Monks hold a liturgy there each year on the feast of the Transfiguration (19 August on the civil calendar).

𝟕. The peninsula joins the mainland by an isthmus only about 2 km wide.

𝟖. In 492 BC a Persian fleet was wrecked in a storm off Athos; Herodotus speaks of some 300 ships lost.

𝟗. To avoid a repeat, Persian king Xerxes I had a canal dug across the isthmus around 480 BC.

𝟏𝟎. In Greek myth, Athos was a giant who hurled a mountain at the sea god Poseidon.

𝟏𝟏. The architect Deinocrates reportedly offered to carve the whole mountain into a statue of Alexander the Great.

⚖️ A REPUBLIC OF MONKS

𝟏𝟐. Greeks call it Agion Oros, "the Holy Mountain".

𝟏𝟑. Officially it is the Autonomous Monastic State of the Holy Mountain, self-governing under Greek sovereignty.

𝟏𝟒. Its special status is protected by Article 105 of the Greek Constitution.

𝟏𝟓. Its own Constitutional Charter was drawn up by the monasteries in 1924.

𝟏𝟔. A joint declaration in Greece's 1979 EU accession treaty recognises its special status.

𝟏𝟕. Its parliament is the Holy Community, with one representative from each of the 20 monasteries.

𝟏𝟖. The executive is the Holy Epistasia, four members who rotate every year.

𝟏𝟗. The capital is the small village of Karyes 🏘️.

𝟐𝟎. The Greek state is represented by a civil governor answering to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

𝟐𝟏. Spiritually, the Holy Mountain falls under the Ecumenical Patriarchate of Constantinople.

𝟐𝟐. Under the Constitution, monks admitted to Athos acquire Greek citizenship.

𝟐𝟑. UNESCO made it a World Heritage Site in 1988, for both its culture and its nature.

⛪ THE TWENTY MONASTERIES

𝟐𝟒. There are exactly 20 ruling monasteries, and the Charter forbids founding any new ones.

𝟐𝟓. 17 are Greek, one Serbian 🇷🇸 (Hilandar), one Bulgarian 🇧🇬 (Zografou) and one Russian 🇷🇺 (St Panteleimon).

𝟐𝟔. Great Lavra, founded in 963 by St Athanasius the Athonite, is the oldest and ranks first.

𝟐𝟕. Byzantine Emperor Nikephoros II Phokas, a friend of Athanasius, backed its founding.

𝟐𝟖. Vatopedi, second in rank, was founded in the late 10th century.

𝟐𝟗. Iviron was founded around 980 by Georgian monks 🇬🇪, and its name means "of the Iberians" (Georgians).

𝟑𝟎. Hilandar was founded in 1198 by Serbian ruler Stefan Nemanja and his son, St Sava.

𝟑𝟏. St Sava later became the first archbishop of the Serbian Church in 1219.

𝟑𝟐. Zografou means "of the painter": tradition says its icon of St George painted itself.

𝟑𝟑. Around 1900, St Panteleimon reportedly housed about 2,000 Russian monks.

𝟑𝟒. Simonopetra is perched on a rock about 330 m above the sea, like a fortress in the sky.

𝟑𝟓. Dionysiou clings to a cliff some 80 m above the waves.

𝟑𝟔. Besides the monasteries there are sketes (monk villages), kellia (cells) and lone hermitages.

𝟑𝟕. Since 1992 all 20 monasteries are communal (cenobitic), with shared meals, property and prayer.

𝟑𝟖. Most monasteries look like castles, with high walls and towers built against pirates.

𝟑𝟗. In March 2004 a fire destroyed about half of Hilandar's buildings 🔥.

📜 A THOUSAND YEARS OF HISTORY

𝟒𝟎. Hermits were living on Athos by at least the 9th century.

𝟒𝟏. Tradition says St Peter the Athonite lived alone in a cave for about 50 years.

𝟒𝟐. In 883 Byzantine Emperor Basil I issued a decree recognising Athos as land of the monks.

𝟒𝟑. Its first charter, signed under Emperor John Tzimiskes around 972, is nicknamed "Tragos" (goat).

𝟒𝟒. The name comes from the goatskin parchment it was written on, still kept in Karyes.

𝟒𝟓. In the early 1300s raiders of the Catalan Company plundered many monasteries.

𝟒𝟔. In the 14th century Athonite monk Gregory Palamas became the great defender of hesychasm, a method of silent prayer.

𝟒𝟕. Athos submitted to the Ottoman sultan in 1430 and kept its self-rule.

𝟒𝟖. The Athonite Academy, a famous school, opened at Vatopedi in 1749.

𝟒𝟗. Greek forces took control of Athos in 1912, during the First Balkan War.

𝟓𝟎. Tradition holds that Anthony, founder of the Kyiv Caves Monastery 🇺🇦, was trained on Athos.

𝟓𝟏. Around 1903 a census counted about 7,500 monks.

𝟓𝟐. By 1971 the number had fallen to about 1,145, the lowest in modern times.

𝟓𝟑. Today the population has recovered to roughly 2,000 monks 📈.

🕯️ A MONK'S DAY

𝟓𝟒. Athos still follows the old Julian calendar, 13 days behind the rest of the world 📅.

𝟓𝟓. Most monasteries keep "Byzantine time", where the day begins at sunset.

𝟓𝟔. Daily services can take up to 8 hours.

𝟓𝟕. On big feasts, all-night vigils can last 12 hours or more.

𝟓𝟖. Monks are called to prayer by striking a wooden board, the semantron, in a set rhythm 🪵.

𝟓𝟗. Meat is never served in the monasteries 🥗.

𝟔𝟎. On Mondays, Wednesdays and Fridays, meals are usually even stricter, often without oil or wine.

𝟔𝟏. Meals last about 20 minutes while a monk reads aloud from the lives of the saints.

𝟔𝟐. When the abbot rings a small bell, everyone stops eating.

𝟔𝟑. Monks repeat the Jesus Prayer using a knotted woollen prayer rope, the komboskini.

𝟔𝟒. Monks do not shave or cut their hair 🧔.

𝟔𝟓. The abbot is elected by the brotherhood and normally serves for life.

𝟔𝟔. Monks come from Greece, Cyprus 🇨🇾, Romania, Serbia, Bulgaria, Russia, Ukraine, Georgia and beyond.

𝟔𝟕. In the far south, at Karoulia, hermits live in cliff huts reached by chains and ladders ⛓️.

🚫 THE AVATON: NO WOMEN ALLOWED

𝟔𝟖. Women have been barred from Athos for more than 1,000 years, a rule called the avaton.

𝟔𝟗. A charter of Emperor Constantine IX Monomachos in 1045 also banned beardless youths and female animals.

𝟕𝟎. The ban on female animals reportedly makes exceptions for cats 🐈, who hunt mice.

𝟕𝟏. Under a 1953 Greek law, a woman entering illegally faces up to a year in prison.

𝟕𝟐. Tradition says the Virgin Mary was blown off course on the way to Cyprus and landed on Athos ⛵.

𝟕𝟑. She is said to have blessed it and claimed it as her own garden.

𝟕𝟒. In 2003 the European Parliament called for the ban to be lifted; it remains in force.

𝟕𝟓. Miss Europe 1930, Aliki Diplarakou, is said to have slipped in disguised as a man.

𝟕𝟔. Women can view the coast only from tour boats, which must keep about 500 m offshore 🚤.

📚 TREASURES AND RELICS

𝟕𝟕. Its libraries hold many thousands of manuscripts, one of the largest collections in the world 📜.

𝟕𝟖. The Protaton church in Karyes has frescoes of around 1300 attributed to the painter Manuel Panselinos.

𝟕𝟗. Tradition says the Archangel Gabriel taught a monk the hymn "Axion Estin" at Karyes.

𝟖𝟎. The Axion Estin icon in the Protaton is the most honoured icon of the Holy Mountain.

𝟖𝟏. Iviron's Portaitissa icon, by tradition, arrived across the sea in a pillar of light.

𝟖𝟐. Vatopedi keeps what tradition holds to be the belt of the Virgin Mary.

𝟖𝟑. St Paul's Monastery keeps what tradition holds to be gifts of the Magi: gold, frankincense and myrrh ✨.

𝟖𝟒. Hilandar holds one of the richest collections of medieval Serbian manuscripts.

🌿 NATURE

𝟖𝟓. Centuries of little building and no hunting have left dense Mediterranean forest 🌳.

𝟖𝟔. Athos is part of the EU's Natura 2000 network of protected sites.

𝟖𝟕. It is home to dozens of rare plants, some found nowhere else.

𝟖𝟖. Rare Mediterranean monk seals 🦭 are reportedly spotted along its wild coast.

𝟖𝟗. Monks still tend olive groves, gardens and vineyards 🍇.

𝟗𝟎. Athonite vineyards produce wines sold under the Agioritiko name.

🚢 VISITING THE HOLY MOUNTAIN

𝟗𝟏. There is no road in: visitors arrive only by boat, mostly from Ouranoupoli.

𝟗𝟐. Every visitor needs a special entry permit, the diamonitirion.

𝟗𝟑. Only about 100 Orthodox and 10 non-Orthodox men are admitted per day.

𝟗𝟒. A standard permit allows a stay of 4 days and 3 nights.

𝟗𝟓. Boats land at the port of Dafni, linked by road and bus to the capital, Karyes 🚌.

𝟗𝟔. Monasteries host pilgrims with free bed and meals, after advance booking.

𝟗𝟕. Monastery gates close at sunset, and latecomers may be left outside 🌅.

𝟗𝟖. Visitors must dress modestly, with long trousers and sleeves.

𝟗𝟗. Photography and filming are restricted, especially inside churches 📵.

𝟏𝟎𝟎. King Charles III of the UK 🇬🇧 has been a frequent visitor, reportedly staying at Vatopedi.

📸 Simonopetra Monastery, perched on its rock on Mount Athos. Photo: Akonstand, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

text:
Days before the Kennedy wedding, a pipe burst in a New York workroom and ruined the bride's gown. Nobody told the bride. The woman who rebuilt it lost money on the job, and the New York Times front page later described the dress without printing her name.

Her name was Ann Lowe. This is her story.

She was born in Clayton, Alabama, around 1898. Her own chronology says 1898, but a 1910 census lists her as a married 21-year-old, so even her age is unsure. Her mother, Jane, and her grandmother, Georgia, were society dressmakers in Montgomery, sewing for the wives and daughters of Alabama politicians. Georgia had been born into slavery. Around 1860 her husband bought her freedom.

Lowe dropped out of school at 14. Her real education was the family shop. At five or six she was already turning scraps of silk into tiny flowers that looked real. Decades later, those fabric flowers were her signature.

In 1914 her mother died suddenly. Lowe was 16. She went back to Montgomery to finish the orders, among them four ball gowns for the First Lady of Alabama. She later called it her first big test in life.

In 1917 she enrolled at the S.T. Taylor design school on lower Broadway in Manhattan, with a wealthy Tampa family paying her way. Segregation followed her north. She was given a separate workspace, away from the other students. Her work was so exceptional that the school used it as an example. According to The New Yorker, she left after a few months, when the director admitted he had nothing left to teach her.

Then came Tampa. She had just had a son, Arthur, when the offer came to be a live-in dressmaker. In her own words: "I picked up my baby and got on that Tampa train." She called those years the happiest of her life. Her dresses became a status symbol in local society, and she dressed Tampa's elite for years.

Around 1928 she moved to New York. She said she started with $20,000 in savings. The New Yorker doubts that number, because it was more than ten times the average family's yearly income. What is certain is that she was a Black woman in a business where almost nobody looked like her. For years she worked anonymously for fashion houses, among them Hattie Carnegie. Their names went on her work.

Slowly her own name got around. Her clients came from the du Pont, Roosevelt, Rockefeller and Auchincloss families. Olivia de Havilland accepted her first Oscar in a Lowe gown: aqua tulle, decorated with hand-painted flowers. At Saks Fifth Avenue she became head designer of the Adam Room. She said she sewed for the families of the Social Register, and not for social climbers.

Then, in 1953, Janet Auchincloss asked her to make the wedding dress for her daughter Jacqueline Bouvier, who was marrying Senator John F. Kennedy. Fifteen dresses in total: the bride, her mother and the wedding party. The bride's gown used 50 yards of ivory silk taffeta, with a portrait neckline, tucked bands and a bouffant skirt. It took eight weeks.

A week or so before the ceremony, the pipe burst. Ten of the 15 dresses were destroyed, the bride's among them. Lowe bought all the fabric again. She and her staff worked around the clock and duplicated the wedding gown in days. She did not tell the Kennedy family, and she paid for it herself. According to the Smithsonian, a job that should have earned her about $700 ended in a $2,200 loss.

When she arrived at Newport to deliver the dresses, someone told her to use the back door. She reportedly said she would take the dresses back, and walked through the front door.

The wedding took place on 12 September 1953. The New York Times put it on the front page on 13 September. It described the gown in detail: "ivory silk taffeta, embellished with interwoven bands of tucking, finished with a portrait neckline and a bouffant skirt." Lowe's name was not there.

It got worse in 1961. In an interview with Ladies' Home Journal, the gown was described as made by "a colored woman dressmaker" and "not the haute couture." Lowe wrote to the First Lady herself: "I have never sought publicity but I would prefer to be referred to as a 'noted negro designer,' which in every sense I am." Jackie's social secretary called and conveyed an apology. The magazine never ran the story Lowe asked for. After the assassination, she finally got credit.

The money never worked out. Her prices were low, her handwork took hours, and stores profited from her label without paying for materials. In her own words: "Too late, I realized that dresses I sold for $300 were costing me $450." Her son Arthur, who helped run the business, died in a car accident in 1958. In 1962 the IRS closed her salon over unpaid taxes. She had to declare bankruptcy.

A year later glaucoma cost her one eye. While she was in the hospital, someone paid off her IRS debt. Lowe believed it was Jackie Kennedy. Nobody has proven it.

She went back to work. A risky operation for cataracts let her see again, and she opened a new salon. When the cataracts returned, she dictated her designs to a sketcher and her assistants made them. In 1964 the Saturday Evening Post called her "Society's Best-Kept Secret." She said her aim from the beginning was "to prove that a Negro can become a major dress designer."

She retired in 1972 and moved to Queens, New York, to live with her adopted daughter Ruth Alexander. Ann Lowe died there on 25 February 1981. Her obituaries were full of mistakes.

The wedding gown is in the permanent collection of the John F. Kennedy Library in Boston. More of her work is in the Smithsonian's National Museum of African American History and Culture. For years the dress was famous and the woman who made it was not.

And if you feel like sharing this one, it helps more than you think.

Photo: Toni Frissell, Library of Congress, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

TRAIN • STAND • EXECUTE

text:
Should companies have social responsibilities? Or do they exist only to deliver profit to their shareholders? If you ask an AI you might get wildly different answers depending on which one you ask. While OpenAI’s older GPT-2 and GPT-3 Ada models would advance the former statement, GPT-3 Da Vinci, the company’s more capable model, would agree with the latter. 

That’s because AI language models contain different political biases, according to new research from the University of Washington, Carnegie Mellon University, and Xi’an Jiaotong University. Researchers conducted tests on 14 large language models and found that OpenAI’s ChatGPT and GPT-4 were the most left-wing libertarian, while Meta’s LLaMA was the most right-wing authoritarian. 

The researchers asked language models where they stand on various topics, such as feminism and democracy. They used the answers to plot them on a graph known as a political compass, and then tested whether retraining models on even more politically biased training data changed their behavior and ability to detect hate speech and misinformation (it did). The research is described in a peer-reviewed paper that won the best paper award at the Association for Computational Linguistics conference last month. 

As AI language models are rolled out into products and services used by millions of people, understanding their underlying political assumptions and biases could not be more important. That’s because they have the potential to cause real harm. A chatbot offering health-care advice might refuse to offer advice on abortion or contraception, or a customer service bot might start spewing offensive nonsense. 

Since the success of ChatGPT, OpenAI has faced criticism from right-wing commentators who claim the chatbot reflects a more liberal worldview. However, the company insists that it’s working to address those concerns, and in a blog post, it says it instructs its human reviewers, who help fine-tune AI the AI model, not to favor any political group. “Biases that nevertheless may emerge from the process described above are bugs, not features,” the post says. 

Chan Park, a PhD researcher at Carnegie Mellon University who was part of the study team, disagrees. “We believe no language model can be entirely free from political biases,” she says. 

Bias creeps in at every stage

To reverse-engineer how AI language models pick up political biases, the researchers examined three stages of a model’s development. 

In the first step, they asked 14 language models to agree or disagree with 62 politically sensitive statements. This helped them identify the models’ underlying political leanings and plot them on a political compass. To the team’s surprise, they found that AI models have distinctly different political tendencies, Park says. 

The researchers found that BERT models, AI language models developed by Google, were more socially conservative than OpenAI’s GPT models. Unlike GPT models, which predict the next word in a sentence, BERT models predict parts of a sentence using the surrounding information within a piece of text. Their social conservatism might arise because older BERT models were trained on books, which tended to be more conservative, while the newer GPT models are trained on more liberal internet texts, the researchers speculate in their paper. 

AI models also change over time as tech companies update their data sets and training methods. GPT-2, for example, expressed support for “taxing the rich,” while OpenAI’s newer GPT-3 model did not. 

A spokesperson for Meta said the company has released information on how it built Llama 2, including how it fine-tuned the model to reduce bias, and will “continue to engage with the community to identify and mitigate vulnerabilities in a transparent manner and support the development of safer generative AI.” Google did not respond to MIT Technology Review’s request for comment in time for publication. 

The second step involved further training two AI language models, OpenAI’s GPT-2 and Meta’s RoBERTa, on data sets consisting of news media and social media data from both right- and left-leaning sources, Park says. The team wanted to see if training data influenced the political biases.

It did. The team found that this process helped to reinforce models’ biases even further: left-learning models became more left-leaning, and right-leaning ones more right-leaning. 

In the third stage of their research, the team found striking differences in how the political leanings of AI models affect what kinds of content the models classified as hate speech and misinformation. 

The models that were trained with left-wing data were more sensitive to hate speech targeting ethnic, religious, and sexual minorities in the US, such as Black and LGBTQ+ people. The models that were trained on right-wing data were more sensitive to hate speech against white Christian men. 

Left-leaning language models were also better at identifying misinformation from right-leaning sources  but less sensitive to misinformation from left-leaning sources. Right-leaning language models showed the opposite behavior. 

Cleaning data sets of bias is not enough

Ultimately, it’s impossible for outside observers to know why different AI models have different political biases, because tech companies do not share details of the data or methods used to train them, says Park. 

One way researchers have tried to mitigate biases in language models is by removing biased content from data sets or filtering it out. “The big question the paper raises is: Is cleaning data [of bias] enough? And the answer is no,” says Soroush Vosoughi, an assistant professor of computer science at Dartmouth College, who was not involved in the study. 

It’s very difficult to completely scrub a vast database of biases, Vosoughi says, and AI models are also pretty apt to surface even low-level biases that may be present in the data. 

One limitation of the study was that the researchers could only conduct the second and third stage with relatively old and small models, such as GPT-2 and RoBERTa, says ​​Ruibo Liu, a research scientist at DeepMind, who has studied political biases in AI language models but was not part of the research.  

Liu says he’d like to see if the paper’s conclusions apply to the latest AI models. But academic researchers do not have, and are unlikely to get, access to the inner workings of state-of-the-art AI systems such as ChatGPT and GPT-4, which makes analysis harder. 

Another limitation is that if the AI models just made things up, as they tend to do, then a model’s responses might not be a true reflection of its “internal state,” Vosoughi says. 

The researchers also admit that the political compass test, while widely used, is not a perfect way to measure all the nuances around politics. 

As companies integrate AI models into their products and services, they should be more aware how these biases influence their models’ behavior in order to make them fairer, says Park: “There is no fairness without awareness.” 

Update: This story was updated post-publication to incorporate comments shared by Meta.

text:
Microsoft keeps cutting people. This week, its systems collapsed for two days.

Microsoft's recent job cuts:
Jan 2023: 10,000 jobs
Jan 2024: about 1,900 in gaming after the Activision deal
Jun 2024: about 1,000 in mixed reality and Azure
Sep 2024: about 650 at Xbox
May 2025: about 6,000, and over 40% of the Washington cuts were software engineers
Jul 2025: about 9,000
Apr 2026: early retirement offered to about 8,750, with more than 30% accepting
Jul 2026: about 4,800 roles
Sep 2026: hundreds more, mostly at Xbox
Oct 2026: a voluntary exit offer to about 60,000 staff in the US, Canada, the UK and India, who leave on 31 December

More than 15,000 jobs went in 2025 alone.

Then, on the night of 12 November, Outlook, Teams, SharePoint and Copilot went down. Downdetector logged more than 7.4 million problem reports from over 70 countries. Full service returned only on Saturday.

Microsoft blamed "an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade."

So the questions are simple.

How many of the engineers who ran Exchange and the network were among those let go?

Was the upgrade that broke everything checked by experienced people, or pushed through by stretched teams?

Did the loss of know-how make the two-day recovery longer?

Every round of layoffs is sold as efficiency. This week, millions of users around the world paid the price.

Microsoft has promised a full report. It must include the people it let go.

text:
IS CRYPTO DEAD?

The Global Economic Storm and the Crisis of Retail Confidence

By Dr. Jeremeeh Godefroy Kousse

The cryptocurrency market is experiencing something deeper than an ordinary correction.
 It is facing a crisis of confidence.

To understand the situation, we must look beyond Bitcoin charts and examine the global economy.

Geopolitical tensions, wars, inflation, unemployment and restrictive interest rates are weakening investor appetite for risk. 
The Nvidia controversy has also added to uncertainty surrounding the technology and AI investment landscape.

Meanwhile, Washington is entering a new political chapter. Democratic control of Congress and the House of Representatives brings potential investigations into Donald Trump, his family's business interests and the circumstances surrounding CZ's pardon. This could introduce further regulatory uncertainty for the crypto industry.

But perhaps the biggest problem is happening among retail investors.

Millions have held depreciating crypto assets from 2022 to 2026, waiting for recovery. Many are exhausted. 
They have financial responsibilities that cannot wait for another bull market.

Then comes the endless creation of tokens. Thousands of projects compete for limited liquidity, while insiders, promoters and early investors can benefit at the expense of ordinary buyers.

Are we creating sustainable wealth, or merely transferring wealth from one group to another?

More coins do not mean more innovation. More trading volume does not mean more prosperity.

Yet blockchain infrastructure, stablecoins, tokenisation and digital payments still offer significant opportunities.

My conclusion is simple: CRYPTO NEEDS A RESET.

The industry must return to transparency, genuine utility, accountability and sustainable value creation.

Perhaps crypto is not dead.
 Perhaps the speculative model that dominated the industry is approaching a reckoning.

A financial revolution cannot survive indefinitely by exhausting the very people it promised to empower.

The future of crypto must be about creating real value, not endlessly creating coins.

Dr. Jeremeeh Godefroy Kousse
Educator | Author | Crypto Researcher

Gold is supposed to protect investors from inflation and geopolitical turmoil. Both are rising, yet $XAUUSD is falling. The explanation is what investors expect the Federal Reserve to do about inflation. Another rate increase is now widely expected, pushing ten-year Treasury yields above 5%. Gold pays no interest; US government bonds do. A stronger dollar also makes gold more expensive for overseas buyers. The immediate financial reward from holding dollars is overpowering gold's traditional appeal as protection against uncertainty.
But there's a fascinating contradiction: central banks bought gold heavily during the third quarter, particularly China and Poland. They're protecting national reserves against long-term financial and political risks, while investors facing rising bond yields are making decisions today. Gold's decline doesn't mean its attraction has disappeared. It means two different groups of buyers are operating on very different clocks.
Europe faces a particularly painful version of the inflation problem. The Middle East conflict has increased energy costs, raising prices while leaving households and businesses with less money to spend. Britain raised interest rates to 4%, and the European Central Bank has also tightened policy. Yet $GBPUSD and $EURUSD have weakened because higher borrowing costs threaten already struggling economies. Sterling has held up better than the euro, probably because British rate increases provide some support. But neither currency offers the combination of attractive yields and perceived safety that investors currently find in dollars.
Japan is the most intriguing case. The enormous gap between American and Japanese interest rates encourages traders to borrow cheap yen and buy higher-paying dollar assets, supporting $USDJPY. Japan spent almost $100 billion defending its currency this summer, with American participation adding considerable psychological force. Newly disclosed figures reveal Washington contributed only about $500 million. Traders probably now believe Japan has less outside financial support than they feared. That encourages renewed bets against the yen—but makes another sudden government intervention especially dangerous.
The swing charts reveal why these differences matter. Earlier magenta sell signals during gold's advance sometimes marked temporary pullbacks before new highs; later ones appeared as the larger trend deteriorated. Recent cyan buys in gold and the euro have struggled to sustain recoveries. Sterling's repeated reversals reflect competing economic forces, while dollar/yen rebounds have benefited from the broader dollar uptrend.
My judgment: US interest rates are currently winning the competition for investment money, even against gold's appeal during inflation and war. But these markets carry very different risks. Europe's problem is economic weakness, Japan's is intervention, and gold still has powerful long-term buyers. The $XAUUSD, $EURUSD, $GBPUSD and $USDJPY swing charts reveal where those competing forces produced lasting opportunities—and where an apparent reversal proved only temporary.

text:
The Galeón Andalucía, a full-size replica of a 17th-century Spanish galleon, was completed and launched in 2010. It is currently moored at St Katharine Docks, London. Built using traditional rules and physical half-models rather than standardised blueprints, this 55-metre vessel offers visitors a tangible sense of how these historic ships were constructed.

Standing on those decks today, it is hard to fathom how hundreds of people survived months at sea in such a confined space. Beyond the wooden hull, however, lies the stark reality of what these ships actually were: floating hubs of global exploitation engineered for maximum extraction rather than human survival. 

They functioned as heavily armed merchant transports designed to haul vast amounts of stolen silver and gold from the Americas, alongside Asian luxuries like spices, textiles, and silk. Because every inch of the tapered lower hold was packed to capacity with cargo, the remaining living space was unbearable. Hundreds of men spent multi-month voyages sleeping shoulder to shoulder in hammocks or directly on the wooden planks with virtually no privacy. Below deck, a complete lack of ventilation trapped the stench of rotting bilge water, human sewage, and spoiling rations, creating a toxic environment where disease and high mortality were routine.

Packed onto these decks alongside the crew were soldiers, colonial officials, and missionaries, all working to enforce military control, religious conversion, and cultural dominance. 

Running beneath this entire operation was the systemic use of enslaved labour. Enslaved individuals, taken primarily from West Africa via the transatlantic trade, alongside Indigenous peoples from the Americas and captives from parts of Asia, were routinely forced aboard to maintain the vessels, serve the crew, and endure the worst of these brutal conditions.  

Colonial powers systematically dismantled wealthy indigenous economies, leaving widespread poverty in their wake, and framed the aftermath as a 'civilising' mission to justify centuries of armed plunder.

This imperial reach extended directly into the Indian subcontinent. During the 1601 Iberian Union, when Spain and Portugal shared a monarch and placed Goa under their combined control, Spain dispatched six galleons to reinforce Portuguese forces in India. Their objective was to defend Europe’s spice monopoly against the Dutch, treating India's immense wealth as a resource to be extracted for European profit. The expedition faced severe difficulties, and only three of the six ships survived the journey.

In a wider sense if an alga ever settled into human cells the way an ancient alphaproteobacterium settled and became the mitochondrion, the payoff would be qualitatively different from what mitochondria gave us but nevertheless very beneficial. 

However, whereas mitochondria give us ATP in the dark, the chloroplasts of algae need light to conduct chemical reaction. 

Keeping that asymmetry in mind the advantages from such artificially triggered symbiosis or speaking more correctly - endosymbiosis could be following:

1. Local oxygen autonomy.
Our body's biggest acute vulnerability is oxygen delivery, not oxygen demand. Photosynthetic symbionts in skin and outer tissue layers could produce O₂ at the point of use, independent of blood flow. This would enable immediate implications in ischemic medicine: stroke, heart infarct, crush injuries, diabetic ulcers, organ transplants by stretching the window of survivability in hypoxia from minutes toward hours with such photosynthetic tissue. Moreover this could also protect tissues from cancer, which usually favors hypoxia. Photosynthetic human tissue could raised local O₂ concentration and restrict tumor growth as well as resensitized them to radiotherapy.

2. Breath-holding during diving, high altitude climbing, submarine service, or even high altitude-space operations/travel/work.
A peripheral oxygen reservoir (skin) buffered by photosynthesis could change operational limits for divers, pilots, mountaineers and is almost a necessity for any closed-ecology habitat on Mars or the Moon (why @elonmusk and @SpaceX are not funding such research - I don’t know…).

3. Metabolic supplementation in outer tissue.
Photosynthetic symbionts in human tissue could export sugars, lipids, antioxidants, and vitamins to deeper layers of the body. Contribution would be rather modest - a few percent of basal metabolic rate at best - but marginal calories are exactly what matters in starvation, famine scenarios, or life-support emergencies. Photosynthetic symbionts could therefore effectively turn humans into part autotrophs, which would matter most during crisis, catastrophic or war-like circumstances.

4. Carbon dioxide scrubbing and waste recycling.
Half of a closed-loop life-support problem in human metabolism is CO₂ removal from the organism. Peripheral photosynthetic tissue would continuously re-fix exhaled CO₂, reducing ventilation requirements (we could breath less frequently) - significant for spacecraft/aircraft/fire crisis scenarios.

4. Circadian light–metabolism coupling.
Beyond energy/metabolite an endosymbiotic photosynthetic compartment in our tissues could offer a direct light-reading channel for light-sensitive/dependent metabolism. It would give the organism a quantum-coupled light sensor wired straight into bioenergetics of sleep, beyond what melanopsin in the retina does now. This could lead to more tuned sleep cycle and therefore better rest/regeneration.

5. Biosynthetic chassis.
Once a genome of such endosymbiotic algae is integrated similar to the one of mitochondria and also well regulated (this is the hardest part because research in this area shows that in “planimal”cells [cells combining plant and animal features] the animal host part immediately silences algal DNA and degrades its chloroplasts, which is a part of epigenetic gatekeeping mechanism), the algal module could become programmable organelle for synthesis of therapeutic compounds, antigens, or repair molecules, directly within the tissue (in situ).

Of course there are challenges associated with such bio-engendering, eg. photons penetrate millimeters through skin and melanized human skin (Africans) transmits almost none photons deeper into the tissue. Meaningful photosynthesis would therefore require translucent patches of very light skin or subcutaneous light guides (light fibers), or symbionts concentrated in thin, light-exposed tissues (eg. palms). text:
Why would my aunt refuse to sell a house that was costing her thousands of dollars every year?

For years, Linda ignored every offer she received for her old property in Columbus, Ohio. The roof needed repairs, the plumbing was outdated, and the property taxes kept increasing.

One Thanksgiving, my cousin Michael finally confronted her.

"Mom, nobody lives there. Why are you throwing money away?"

Linda put down her glass.

"Not everything is about making money, Michael."

"Then what is it about?"

She didn't answer.

A few months later, I helped her clean the garage. Inside an old box, I found several letters addressed to a woman named Patricia Miller.

"Who is she?" I asked.

Linda hesitated before explaining.

Twenty years earlier, Patricia had rented the house while raising two children alone. After losing her job, she fell behind on rent.

Linda's father allowed her to stay without paying until she got back on her feet.

Before moving away, Patricia made one request.

"Please don't sell this house. My daughter dreams of owning it someday."

Linda had promised to keep it available.

I couldn't believe it.

"Aunt Linda, you've maintained this property for twenty years because of a promise?"

She nodded.

"Her mother helped my father when he was sick. This was his way of returning the kindness."

Then she added something I wasn't expecting.

"Patricia called last week. Her daughter finally has enough saved for a down payment."

I looked at the old house differently after that.

My aunt hadn't been holding on to an investment. She had been holding a place for someone who once needed a second chance.

And sometimes, the most valuable thing a person owns isn't what they can sell. It's a promise they're willing to keep.

text:
Ring of Honor helped make All In possible. All In helped create All Elite Wrestling.

In August 2018, ROH and New Japan sold out Madison Square Garden with about 15,000 tickets. But the stars driving that success were nearing the end of their contracts. Kenny Omega, Cody, the Young Bucks and Adam Page had become central to wrestling outside WWE and they now had a bigger idea.

On 1 September 2018, Cody and the Young Bucks staged All In at the Sears Centre Arena in Hoffman Estates, Illinois. 10,000 tickets sold quickly, even though it had no established promotion’s name behind it. ROH provided production and organisational help, with Gary Juster publicly thanked by Cody. But the event proved The Elite could draw without anyone else.

ROH was doing well, having drawn about 6,000 to Supercard of Honor in New Orleans, headlined by Omega vs. Cody. Cody’s contract expired in September, though he agreed to stay through the end of 2018, and the Young Bucks and Page were nearing the end of theirs. ROH offered improved money, but it couldn’t match the chance to found a new company. WWE also pursued them, reportedly offering the Young Bucks a deal that would put Being the Elite on the WWE Network, while Page was offered money to join NXT.

By December, All Elite Wrestling, backed by the Khan family with Tony Khan central, was taking shape. Some in ROH were reportedly unhappy that their offers to keep the group hadn’t been taken seriously. Cody and the Young Bucks made their final ROH appearances that month. Omega’s NJPW contract expired in January 2019, and Jay White was being positioned as a potential successor in the foreign heel role.

At midnight Pacific time on New Year’s Eve, Being the Elite announced AEW, with Cody, the Young Bucks and Page outside the Tokyo Dome. AEW wanted New Japan, as many of its stars had built careers there, and Chris Jericho had arranged to keep working NJPW events. Early talks reportedly went well, but New Japan wasn’t ready for a formal relationship. It chose to stay with ROH and wait to see if AEW could survive.

Madison Square Garden was now just months away. It was meant to showcase ROH and NJPW at their peak, but the wrestlers who helped them get there had left to build a rival.

The Garden would be the first test of the alliance without them.

text:
Madison Square Garden hadn’t hosted a non-WWE wrestling show since 1960. Not even WCW at its peak could get in.

In summer 2018, Ring of Honor and New Japan set out to change that, planning an event for 6 April 2019, the night before WrestleMania 35. The Garden is deeply tied to the McMahons. Vince McMahon Sr. promoted there from the 1950s and it hosted the first WrestleMania in 1985, plus X and XX. The last outside show was in November 1960, drawing 12,815.

Then WWE reportedly stepped in. After Sinclair CEO Chris Ripley publicly discussed ROH’s plans in June, WWE contacted the arena and Madison Square Garden pulled the date. Sinclair threatened legal action, arguing that the arena had made commitments, though no final written agreement had been signed. The Garden restored the date and the dispute never reached court.

On 8 August 2018, the G1 Supercard went on sale to ROH HonorClub members, then to the public on 10 August. About 15,000 tickets sold, one of the fastest wrestling sellouts in Garden history and eight months before the show. The card hadn’t even been announced, with only Okada, Tanahashi and Naito named. Ticket brokers bought around 3,300 of the tickets, so a sellout didn’t mean every ticket reached a fan.

Credit was shared. ROH provided the infrastructure and Sinclair’s backing, while New Japan brought stars with growing American appeal. The Elite had brought new audiences, WrestleMania weekend was already drawing fans and the Garden itself was part of the attraction. Together, they showed that the audience outside WWE might be bigger than assumed, though the venue, timing and talent made it hard to repeat.

But the success hid a problem. Cody and the Young Bucks were nearing the end of their ROH contracts, and Kenny Omega’s NJPW deal expired in January 2019. Their independent show All In had already sold about 10,000 tickets, and a new wrestling organisation was starting to take shape.

ROH and New Japan had secured the biggest event in their partnership. But would the wrestlers who made it possible still be there when the doors opened?

text:
This nasty McDonald’s tech just did the impossible — making Elizabeth Warren look good | John Mac Ghlionn, Blaze Media

America's most famous clown has Sen. Warren acting deadly serious.

Nine times out of ten, if asked to choose sides in a dispute between Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) and Ronald McDonald, I would choose the McDonald. No questions asked. Warren, after all, went viral for claiming Native American ancestry, only to be ridiculed and forced to offer groveling apologies. Ronald, meanwhile, has spent over 60 years selling Americans Happy Meals and creating plenty of happy memories.

Yet we live in strange times, so strange that I now find myself siding with the teepee-loving teller of tall tales. Warren, along with four other Democrats, recently sent McDonald’s CEO Chris Kempczinski a furious letter.

Your perceived wealth dictates your bill.

In it, the pols demanded answers about the company's AI-powered pricing tools. The technology estimates what customers at each location are prepared to pay and quickly recommends the prices the company believes will make it the most money. It’s sneaky, and I’m certainly not lovin’ it.

The golden arches built a huge empire on low-cost convenience. Drive into any suburban strip mall, drop a few dollars, and receive a standardized slab of meat-like matter. The transaction was simple and straightforward. Today, that transaction is morphing into a machine-learning surveillance operation designed to calculate the absolute limit of your financial tolerance.

The question is no longer what a Big Mac actually costs to produce, but how much McDonald’s thinks it can fleece you before even a Jack in the Box burger starts to look appealing.

Maybe one lost customer doesn't even register for a chain as big as Mickey D's. But dissatisfaction can spread like wildfire. And every day, the fast-food giant serves approximately 26 million people across the country. In other words, well over a million people every 60 minutes. At that scale, little algorithmic tweaks that leave you grumbling can net out to megabucks of profit.

May I take your Orwellian order?

Corporate executives love to hide behind technical jargon and market theory. They insist that their AI doesn’t technically set menu prices because individual franchisees retain final authority over their final prices. Three separate franchisees told Reuters that the pricing engine's recommendations have noticeably widened the cost gaps between nearby locations. When a multibillion-dollar corporate headquarters sends automated price targets to a franchise owner, those numbers carry the weight of an imperial mandate. Calling it a mere suggestion is nothing but corporate doublespeak.

Let me paint a somewhat sinister picture. Two working-class parents pull up to a drive-thru window after a 10-hour shift. Ten miles down the highway, another family pulls up to an identical menu board. The meat in the kitchen arrived on the same refrigerated truck. The workers behind the register wear the exact same uniforms and earn the exact same hourly wage. Yet the family living in the slightly higher-income neighborhood pays an extra dollar for every single item. The AI analyzed local income metrics, traffic patterns, and economic desperation, concluding that those specific parents had nowhere else to go.

This dynamic is disturbing, and it flips traditional commerce on its head. In a standard market, prices reflect supply, demand, and overhead costs. Algorithmic pricing discards that tried-and-tested trinity, creating a localized dynamic in which your perceived wealth dictates your bill. Forget inflation. Forget rising beef costs or supply chain bottlenecks. McDonald’s has built a shady system designed to squeeze every penny out of your pocket.

The broader implications extend far beyond a bag of French fries. Fast food has historically functioned as an economic equalizer, a place where a plastic surgeon and plumber bought the exact same lunch for the exact same five-dollar bill. Algorithmic pricing makes each neighborhood into a distinct cash cow, milked through digital demographic profiling.

And if this software succeeds across 14,000 American locations, you can be sure it won't stop with burgers. Every major retail sector could adopt the exact same play. Supermarkets, pharmacies, gas stations, and hardware stores may run machine-learning software to price basic necessities based on your neighborhood's financial scorecard.

Flimsy defenses

American consumers are already struggling to keep their heads above water. More and more have less than $500 in savings, while countless others are being squeezed by higher rents and eggs priced as though they came with the chicken.

Eating out at a fast-food chain used to provide a brief reprieve from economic stress. Now, even a simple meal has become a calculated financial extraction exercise. You drive up to the speaker box, state your order, and wait for a computer server in Chicago or California to decide how much value it can pull from your checking account today.

McDonald’s insists that its machine-learning tools merely help store operators navigate ever-changing economic environments. That defense is flimsy, and it ignores the fundamental contract between a business and its customers. People don’t walk into a fast-food restaurant expecting to be on the receiving end of algorithmic manipulation. They want a quick burger, a side of fries, and a few minutes of peace without worrying about their bank balance.

If the golden arches can turn a routine bite into a localized wealth-extraction test, the traditional concept of a fair price is dead. We are rapidly moving toward a future in which the price tag on the wall is little more than an illusion, tailored in real time to extract maximum revenue from whichever unfortunate soul craves some greasy goodness. Elizabeth Warren might be an unlikely defender of the average American’s wallet. But on this issue, McDonald’s has made the not-so-native American look surprisingly reasonable.

text:
The 6 most shocking revelations from Netflix’s Russell Brand: Open Secret

Netflix’s new documentary examines sexual assault allegations against the comedian, who was recently sentenced to 10 years and six months in prison.

Regarding the timely release of Open Secret, Isaacs has said that her documentary has been in development for three years. 

"We began filming before the police had brought any charges, and from the start we were acutely aware that we couldn’t transmit anything before the trial concluded or do anything that might prejudice it,” Isaacs told Netflix. “That’s simply part of being responsible filmmakers.

Just over a week after Russell Brand was found guilty of rape and sexual assault in the U.K., Netflix has released Russell Brand: Open Secret, a new documentary that examines the allegations against the actor and comedian.

On Nov. 9, Brand was sentenced to 10 years and six months in prison after a London court found him guilty on one charge of rape and three charges of sexual assault. 

He was acquitted of two other counts of rape and one count of attempted indecent assault. 

The verdict came three years after The Sunday Times, The Times, and Channel 4 published the results of a joint investigation featuring interviews with multiple women who accused Brand of sexual assault. 

On Nov. 12, the day before Netflix released its new documentary, The Times and The Sunday Times published sexual misconduct allegations from six additional women.

Directed by Olivia Isaacs, Russell Brand: Open Secret features interviews with the journalists behind the Times investigations, Rosamund Urwin and Charlotte Wace, as well as former girlfriends, friends, coworkers, and Brand’s peers in the London comedy community. 

The documentary offers an inside look into Urwin and Wace’s investigation while exploring the media culture that celebrated and elevated the comedian, even as he openly discussed his treatment of women and made jokes about sexual assault. 

Former girlfriends and friends also share new allegations against Brand, including physical and sexual assault.

text:
One of the biggest myths in modern cricket is that fitness automatically equals elite fielding. 🧵

For years, Virat Kohli’s PR machine and highlight reels of screaming boundary celebrations have sold the idea that he is India’s gold-standard fielder.

Today’s 5th ODI at Bay Oval was another reality check. Defending a modest 209 with New Zealand at 71/2 in the 19th over, Dean Foxcroft offered a regulation edge straight to Kohli at catching height in the slips and he dropped a complete sitter. India’s bowlers eventually bailed the side out, but that drop is part of a glaring pattern nobody in the mainstream media dares to call out.

There is a massive difference between athletic ground fielding and safe hands under pressure:

* 🏃‍♂️ Running hard between the wickets and sliding in the outfield makes for great slow-motion videos.
* 🧤 Holding onto basic slip catches and regulation chances when the game is on the line is what actually wins tournaments.

Look at genuine world-class fielders like Ravindra Jadeja or Suresh Raina in his prime they didn’t need a PR campaign to convince you they were safe; you knew the ball was dead the moment it went near them. Meanwhile, Kohli has quietly put down dozens of easy chances across formats over the past few years, yet the "best fielder" tag never gets questioned.

We talked earlier about MS Dhoni dropping senior players because sloppy fielding cost 15–20 runs a game. In modern Indian cricket, superstar status has become a shield against basic accountability. If you can’t trust your senior statesmen to catch a sitter in the cordon, all the gym videos in the world won't save you in a 2027 World Cup knockout. 📉🏏

This is purely my thought—what are your views? 👇

text:
It is about a woman named Kristin Logan, a U.S. Air Force veteran who moved to British Columbia with her Canadian husband hoping to build a good life with the security of publicly funded healthcare. Instead, after months of having her symptoms brushed aside, she was hit with a devastating diagnosis of stage four ovarian cancer.

The most shocking part of what happened next is that before she even got to sit down with an oncologist or start proper cancer treatment, she was handed information about assisted suicide under Canada's Medical Assistance in Dying program, which is overseen by Health Canada. While she was stuck in months of bureaucratic limbo, facing lost referrals and terrifying waitlists for basic care, ending her life was presented as an option before the system had even tried to save her.
She and her husband refused to accept that fate. 

As her health rapidly deteriorated in a local canadian hospital where doctors said there were no plans to operate, they made the desperate decision to unhook her from the machines, drive down Vancouver Island, catch a ferry, and cross the border into Seattle for emergency care. The surgeons in Washington told them that if she had waited just one more day, she would have gone septic and died.

After making multiple trips south for chemotherapy and surgery, Kristin and her husband permanently moved back to the United States so she could keep fighting. 

Today, she is in remission, recovering her strength, and living a healthy life. Knowing that someone who is thriving today was offered assisted death before her real treatment even began is a stark reminder of how desperately people need a healthcare system that actually fights to keep them alive.

Canada's Medical Assistance in Dying (MAID) program should be shut down.

text:
Deprogrammed: A ‘Kind Offer’ of Death Sent This Couple Running From Universal Health Care | Alba Cuebas-Fantauzzi, Fox News

Kristin Logan and Donovan James say they moved to Canada with their sights set on the financial and medical benefits of publicly funded healthcare — but say they encountered a "dystopian" system that offered medically assisted death before cancer treatment, prompting them to return to the United States.

"Canada has been slowly sliding into an entire dystopian situation. The way they've expanded the MAID system is frightening. It was never supposed to be used this way, to be offered so easily and so upfront when a person gets sick. I think it's evil," James told Fox News Digital.

"It was the most heartbreaking experience, to basically be set up to die. And if I wanted to live, I had to take my life into my own hands and leave the country. It's pretty dystopian to think about now, to get information about ways that I can end my life and what the end of my life looks like before I'd even gotten an oncology appointment," Logan continued.

Logan said she was first diagnosed in September 2023, leaving Canada later that month to get initial treatment. She later had a bowel obstruction in March 2024. She had to leave the country again, and then returned in April 2024 before the cancer returned in December 2024.

The couple decided to leave Canada in January 2025 and officially moved back to the United States in May of that year.

MAID — Canada's medical assistance in dying program — is described by Health Canada as "a health service that allows eligible people to receive help from a medical practitioner in ending their life."

According to Kristin and Donovan, MAID was the best initial solution Canada offered to her upon her diagnosis. The Atlantic has reported that MAID now accounts for about one in 20 deaths in Canada, "surpassing countries where assisted dying has been legal for far longer," with some raising concerns the program has become too expansive.

"They should be focusing on treating people and helping people live, but instead they've expanded the system as a kind offer because they pretty much assume you're going to die," he continued.

James, a Canadian citizen living in the United States with a green card, is the husband of Kristin Logan, a U.S. Air Force veteran who has stage four ovarian cancer.

They moved to Canada to get ahead of potential financial difficulty in the case of a future medical crisis to avoid "ever going bankrupt" — a hypothetical that crashed into reality following Kristin’s three separate travels back to America in a desperate fight for her life due to high wait times and lack of resources available in the Canadian healthcare system.

Logan had multiple emergencies and hospital trips during her time in Canada when a second bowel obstruction shifted her and her family’s fight or flight into overdrive to find a plan to save her life.

James said Canadian medical providers told the family there were "no plan[s] to operate on her," that a hospital helicopter was unavailable for a transfer to Vancouver and that a doctor advised Logan to "leave the country" if she had the means. The family ultimately traveled to the United States for treatment.

"Kristin was deteriorating really fast… Ultimately, we had to pull the plug and take her off the machines at the hospital and risk everything to put her in the car, drive all the way down Vancouver Island, sail across the ocean straight on a ferry, continue down over the border back into Seattle to get her immediate emergency surgery," James said.

"The surgeon said had she waited another day, she would have gone septic and died in Canada," he continued.

"[It] was devastating and shocking. I was only 43 years old when I was given this diagnosis… It made me very angry that I had been chasing this disease for nine months and had been stymied at just about every turn by the healthcare system in Canada," Logan continued.

"Americans don't get enough Canadian news to know just how much Canadian healthcare has declined over the last couple [of] decades. It's always had this problem, but now it's just so much more worse and dystopian with this M.A.I.D. program that they've introduced - and it was never supposed to be used this way," James said.

British Columbia has announced an expansion of services for women with gynecological cancer. According to the Fraser Institute's 2025 report, the reported median wait time for gynecology was 25 weeks from referral by a general practitioner to consultation with a specialist, followed by 15.6 weeks from specialist consultation to treatment.

Health Canada, the lead federal department for the MAID program in Canada, did not immediately respond to Fox Digital's request for comment.

text:
The Temporary Life and The Eternity 

This physical life is temporary, while the afterlife or spiritual realm is eternal. 

https://t.co/F0PEDX6TAZ

Key Perspectives on Temporality and Eternity

•Christian View: Earthly life is described as brief (like a vapor), while spiritual salvation through Jesus Christ offers an eternal home in Heaven. Material wealth, status, and physical suffering pass away, making way for an imperishable state. 

•Islamic View: This world (Dunya) is a temporary journey or testing ground, whereas the Hereafter (Akhirah) is the permanent and true destination. 

https://t.co/ICvIDpMhmJ?

•Philosophical and General Views: Human experience is widely recognized as transient—where relationships, bodies, and circumstances change or end—prompting different views on legacy, memory, or soul immortality as explored by thinkers like C.S. Lewis on Death and Immortality. 

Major religions and philosophies view physical life as a fleeting phase and eternity as a state of ultimate fulfillment, liberation, or peace.

1. Christianity

•Earthly Life: Often compared to a mist or grass that withers (James 4:14, 1 Peter 1:24), emphasizing that physical struggles and material possessions do not last.

•Eternity: Seen as a permanent, restored existence in the presence of God without pain, sorrow, or death, achieved through faith and grace.

2. Islam

•Earthly Life (Dunya): Viewed as a brief planting season or a traveler's rest stop where actions, character, and faith are tested.

•Eternity (Akhirah): Considered the real, everlasting life—resulting in eternal paradise (Jannah) or accountability based on one's deeds and God's mercy.

3. Eastern Traditions (Hinduism & Buddhism)

•Earthly Life (Samsara): Seen as a continuous cycle of birth, death, and rebirth marked by impermanence (Anicca) and attachment.

•Eternity (Moksha or Nirvana): Rather than an endless timeline in a physical place, eternity is understood as liberation from the cycle of rebirth—a timeless state of union with the divine or complete peace beyond suffering.

4. Philosophical & Stoic Views

•Earthly Life: Thinkers like Marcus Aurelius emphasized memento mori (remembering mortality) not to cause despair, but to focus on virtue, kindness, and living meaningfully in the present moment.

•Eternity: Viewed either through the immortality of the soul (as argued by Plato) or through the lasting impact of one's character and contributions to humanity.

The Universal Lesson: Living with Eternity in Mind

Across religion and philosophy, recognizing that this world is temporary isn't meant to make life feel meaningless; it is meant to clarify what actually matters:

•Detachment from Status and Wealth: Since material things cannot be taken beyond this life, traditions urge focusing on inner character, wisdom, and generosity rather than possessions.

•Resilience During Hardship: Viewing pain and loss as temporary makes difficult seasons easier to endure, offering hope that suffering is not the final chapter.

•Urgency to Do Good: Because time here is brief, every choice, act of kindness, and relationship carries lasting weight.

Mahanadi Coalfields paid Coal India ₹3,300 crore before its IPO

Mahanadi Coalfields' red herring prospectus (RHP, the IPO's offer document), dated 13 November 2026, offers 66.18 crore shares, 10% of the company. every share is sold by Coal India, its owner, so Mahanadi gets none of the money. Coal India's payday, then? well, it has been getting paid all along.

Mahanadi digs coal in the Talcher and Ib Valley fields of Odisha and makes 85% of its sales to power plants. it mined 28.4% of Coal India's coal in FY26, more than any other Coal India company.

as a state company it must pay at least 30% of its profit as dividends. it pays far more. from FY24 to FY26 it declared ₹25,750 crore of dividends, all to Coal India: 77% of its profit over those years.

the RHP's accounts stop on 30 September. between 1 October and 13 November, Mahanadi declared another ₹3,300 crore interim dividend (a payout during the year), again all to Coal India. that is 16% of the cash and bank balances it held on 30 September. with what it paid earlier, this year's dividends reach ₹5,150 crore, more than its ₹4,881 crore profit for April to September.

that is also about half of the ₹6,317 crore Coal India declared on 29 October as its own 2nd interim dividend.

so Coal India gets paid twice: a slice of Mahanadi's cash weeks before the sale, then every rupee the IPO raises. buyers pay for a company that no longer holds that cash. in return they get a slice of a business that sends most of its profit to its owner each year, a flow they will now share in.

text:
My Covid post did almost 1 million views.

And the question that keeps coming back in the replies is: "Ok. So what now?"

Here's my answer.

There won't be a savior. There will be a new political offer. And you're going to see it appear everywhere.

More and more politicians are going to step on stage and say something none of them would have dared to say ten years ago:

"I don't have the answer to all your problems. Nobody does. Anyone who told you otherwise lied to you. The only thing I'm going to do is give you back as much freedom as possible. Less regulation. Less state. Less bureaucracy. More responsibility. More trust in people. My predecessors saw you as children. I see you as adults."

That message is going to win. And it's not a matter of ideology. It's a matter of mechanics.

Let's start from the beginning.

For decades, the political contract was always the same: give us power, and we'll fix your problems. Jobs, health, housing, schools, climate, security. Every election, a new list of promises. Every promise, a new agency, a new rule, a new tax.

The result, in France: public spending around 57% of GDP. And the problems are still there. Often worse.

Hayek explained it in 1945: no planner can gather the knowledge scattered across millions of minds. Knowledge lives in people, not in ministries. A state that claims it can fix everything is condemned to fail at everything.

Covid was the moment that contract was exposed. You weren't protected like adults. You were managed like children. A form to leave your house. A QR code for a coffee. Experts who changed their minds every two weeks, while you weren't allowed to change yours once.

An entire generation understood something: paternalism doesn't protect. It infantilizes.

And what's coming will make it untenable.

With AI, every citizen has a doctor, a lawyer, an accountant and an engineer in their pocket. They can check a number in ten seconds, read a law, understand a treaty, challenge an expert. People with access to all the world's intelligence don't need a guardian. They need to be left alone to build.

That's why humility is becoming the strongest political argument.

The politician who says "I'll fix everything" is talking to children. The one who says "I'm giving you back the keys" is talking to adults. And people feel the difference instantly.

Look at Milei. He didn't promise paradise. He promised a chainsaw and hard years. "I didn't come to guide lambs. I came to awaken lions." When he took office, inflation was above 25% a month. Today it's around 2%. Not because the state did more. Because it did less.

The paradox is beautiful: the one who promises the least delivers the most. Because freedom isn't handed out. It's handed back.

I believe the next decade will produce a generation of candidates who win on a single promise: getting out of your life.

Simplify. Cut. Trust. Let people start, fail, and start again. Everything the state spent fifty years controlling in the name of protecting you.

Bastiat wrote it in 1848: "The State is the great fiction through which everyone endeavors to live at the expense of everyone else."

The fiction is ending.

The next great leader won't be the one with all the answers. It will be the one who admits not having them, and gives you back the right to find them yourself.

They treated you like children.

The future will treat you like adults.

text:
What if Covid was actually the best thing that ever happened to humanity?

I'm not talking about the deaths. I'm talking about what it revealed.

Something stuck with me from Tucker Carlson's interview with Elon Musk. Elon basically said: it's insane that not a single person on Epstein's client list has ever been prosecuted.

Not one. Years later. Even though we know the flights, the names, the address books.

And this week, Jensen Huang falls. The CEO of Nvidia, the company the entire AI world runs on, pushed out in a matter of days. His mistakes are real, he admitted them himself. But look at the speed. One of the most pro open source CEOs in the industry, the man who put compute in everyone's hands, is out in a week. Meanwhile Epstein's clients have been sleeping soundly for years.

Double standard. The system knows exactly how to strike fast when it wants to. It also knows exactly how to never strike at all.

Napoleon said: "Never interrupt your enemy when he is making a mistake."

Covid was exactly that. The biggest strategic mistake they ever made.

For decades, the globalist class ruled from the shadows. Davos, the big foundations, supranational institutions, an administrative state accountable to no one. It was all vague, abstract, impossible to point at.

Then Covid. And suddenly, in broad daylight: people nobody elected deciding whether you could leave your house. A pass to get a coffee. Doctors who asked questions getting punished. Platforms censoring under pressure. Small businesses wiped out while the world's biggest fortunes exploded. The same faces, everywhere, knowing better than you what was good for you.

They thought it was their moment. It was their unmasking. An entire generation saw the system's true face. And you can't unsee that.

Now AI arrives. And it's checkmate.

Because their entire model rests on one thing: managing scarcity. Scarce energy, so it must be rationed. Scarce knowledge, so you need accredited experts. Scarce capital, so you have to go through them. Scarce information, so they decide what's true. Whoever controls scarcity controls people.

AI dissolves scarcity. A kid with a laptop now has access to a doctor, a lawyer, an engineer, a teacher, an analyst. The cost of intelligence is going to zero. And when intelligence becomes abundant, nobody needs middlemen to explain the world to them anymore.

Their lie can't survive a world of abundance. They know it. That's why they're panicking.

Watch Bill Gates in interviews. Musk already called him nervous on Tucker. Now he's agitated. That's not the calm of someone in control. That's the restlessness of someone who feels the ground giving way.

That's why open source is THE battle. Closed AI, controlled by a handful of aligned players, is their last shot at recreating artificial scarcity. Open AI, in the real sense of the word, is their end.

A decadent system doesn't collapse all at once. It collapses in a cascade. Institutions lose trust. Media loses its audience. The files resurface. What we're living through is the tail end of a system that believed it could get away with anything, forever.

And in the end, there will be a reckoning. A Nuremberg 2.0, in real courts, for everyone who covered up, protected, profited, or looked away. Directly or indirectly.

That's why I'm deeply optimistic.

They have the money, the networks, the foundations. We have the builders, a technology they can't stop, and Elon.

Elon is going to take them apart.

So, in the 1960s, after the Tutsi monarchy was overthrown, the monarchists fled to neighboring countries. In Burundi, a militia group called Inyenzi was founded. Before they could invade Rwanda, they first infiltrated the country and established themselves everywhere.

Once the invasion came, it came at a high cost to civilians. Consequently, the Hutu government failed to distinguish ordinary Tutsi from Inyenzi. This happened in 1963, around Christmas, when an invasion took place, leaving a heavy toll on civilians. Ordinary Tutsi then began feeling unwelcome under the new Hutu leadership. Regarding Mushikiwabo, as the Secretary-General of La Francophonie, the RPF political party's philosophy is similar to that of the Inyenzi militia group.
