By: Selina Nyarko Prah (Sis.)
Pastor Joseph Owusu-Boateng, Resident Minister of PIWC Winneba, has urged Christians to develop a genuine concern for the glory of God, emphasising that believers must be willing to defend His name, uphold His honour and place His purposes above their personal interests. Delivering a sermon titled “Concern for the Glory of God” during the climax of the District Week, dubbed Grace Convocation, at PIWC Winneba, Pastor Owusu-Boateng explained that a defining characteristic of people who walk closely with God is their concern for His glory.

Drawing from 2 Samuel 7:1–4, he examined the lives of three biblical figures, David, Elijah and Nehemiah, whose devotion to God was reflected in their commitment to His honour and purposes. He began with the story of David, who, despite living in a magnificent palace, became concerned that the Ark of God remained in a tent. According to the Resident Minister, David's desire to build a house for God demonstrated a heart that placed God's glory above personal comfort.

Although David was not permitted to build the temple, he did not abandon his concern for God's house. Instead, he deliberately made extensive preparations and provided resources for its construction. Pastor Owusu-Boateng explained that David's response revealed the depth of his commitment to God. 

He challenged the congregation to consider how they would react if someone rejected an offer they had made with good intentions. He observed that many people would simply withdraw their support after such a response. David, however, continued making provisions for the temple, ensuring that the resources needed for its construction would be available.

Pastor Owusu-Boateng emphasised that genuine concern for God's glory does not disappear when personal expectations are not met. Rather, it motivates believers to remain committed to God's purposes even when they are not the ones chosen to carry out a particular assignment. He further referred to 1 Samuel 17:26, where David questioned the audacity of Goliath, the uncircumcised Philistine, who had defied the armies of the living God.

According to Pastor Owusu-Boateng, David's response was motivated by his concern for God's reputation rather than a desire for personal recognition. While others saw Goliath as a terrifying opponent, David recognised that the honour of the living God was being challenged. His willingness to confront the Philistine demonstrated a determination to defend God's name when others were afraid to act.

Turning to the life of Elijah, Pastor Owusu-Boateng referred to 1 Kings 18:21, where the prophet confronted the Israelites over their divided allegiance between God and Baal. He explained that Elijah could not tolerate the people's continued wavering between two opinions. The prophet was determined to demonstrate that the Lord alone was worthy of their worship.

Referring also to 1 Kings 18:24, he highlighted Elijah's challenge on Mount Carmel, where the God who answered by fire would be acknowledged as the true God. Pastor Owusu-Boateng explained that Elijah's actions were not intended to promote himself but to restore the people's recognition of God's supremacy. He emphasised that when a believer's motives are genuinely directed towards God's glory, God is able to demonstrate His power in defence of His name.

Pastor Owusu-Boateng also identified Nehemiah among the biblical examples of individuals whose lives reflected a deep concern for God's honour and purposes.

Drawing lessons from these examples, Pastor Owusu-Boateng outlined the characteristics of people who are genuinely concerned about the glory of God. First, he explained that such individuals are grieved whenever God is dishonoured. They do not remain indifferent when God's name is treated with contempt or when conduct within the Church brings dishonour to Him.

He further stressed that believers who genuinely love God's glory do not celebrate the failures of the Church. According to him, rather than laughing when the Church experiences difficulties or setbacks, they are moved with concern and seek its restoration and progress. He challenged Christians to examine their reactions when they hear negative reports about the Church, explaining that their responses often reveal whether their concern is for God's glory or their personal interests.

Pastor Owusu-Boateng also emphasised that people who seek God's glory live for His pleasure rather than their own. Referring to 1 Corinthians 10:31, he reminded the congregation that whether Christians eat, drink or engage in any other activity, everything should be done to the glory of God. He explained that genuine devotion to God must influence everyday decisions, personal conduct and the motives behind one's actions.

Another characteristic he highlighted was the willingness to defend the name of the Lord. He explained that believers who are concerned about God's glory do not remain silent when His name is dishonoured. Like David and Elijah, they are willing to take a stand for God even when others are unwilling to do so.

Pastor Owusu-Boateng further emphasised the responsibility of Christians to proclaim God's name and make Him known to others. He noted that concern for God's glory should not remain a private conviction but must find expression in a believer's willingness to speak about God and make His greatness known.

Pastor Owusu-Boateng explained that genuine concern for God's glory also purifies a person's motives and transforms their mindset. According to him, when God's honour becomes the primary motivation behind a believer's actions, personal ambition and the desire for recognition begin to give way to a sincere commitment to pleasing Him.

He encouraged Christians to evaluate the reasons behind their service, sacrifices and involvement in church activities, emphasising that the desire to glorify God must remain central. He further noted that those who consistently seek God's glory develop a relationship with Him marked by His favour and approval.

Concluding his message, Pastor Owusu-Boateng challenged the congregation to follow the examples of David and Elijah by demonstrating a genuine concern for God's honour in every area of life. His message reinforced the need for Christians to move beyond merely professing love for God and demonstrate that love through their willingness to defend His name, support His work, proclaim His greatness and live according to His purposes.

In October 2016, she pleaded guilty to solicitation of capital murder and was sentenced to 20 years in prison.

. . . 

A wife hired a hitman to kill her husband while they were going through a divorce. She was willing to offer money, his truck and other valuables to make sure he was murdered. Unfortunately for her, she had approached the wrong person. The man she hired to kill her husband was actually helping the police bring her plan to light.

The story happened in Montgomery County, Texas, in 2015.

Maria De Lourdes Sosa and her husband, Ramon Sosa, were going through a bitter divorce. Ramon was a boxer and the owner of Woodlands Boxing and Fitness, a business the couple had been involved in together.

As their marriage fell apart, they were also dealing with disagreements over their finances and the division of their assets.

But Maria apparently had something much more disturbing in mind than simply ending the marriage.

In June 2015, she approached a man known as Gustavo, a mutual friend of both her and Ramon. She reportedly began talking about wanting her husband to disappear.

During a conversation with ABC13 Houston, Gustavo explained that Maria had made it clear she wanted Ramon dead. He told her he could help find someone to carry out the murder.

What Maria apparently did not realise was that Gustavo was also friends with the husband she wanted killed.

Instead of helping her arrange the murder, Gustavo contacted the police and then informed Ramon about what his wife had been discussing.

Ramon initially struggled to believe what he was hearing. The woman he had shared a home and marriage with was apparently making plans to have him murdered.

Gustavo and Ramon began cooperating with investigators. Gustavo secretly recorded conversations with Maria as she continued discussing the plan and confirming that she wanted her husband killed.

The authorities eventually arranged an undercover operation. A Texas Department of Public Safety officer posed as a hitman and began communicating directly with Maria.

On July 20, 2015, Maria met the undercover officer in a vehicle at a parking lot along Rayford Road.

During their conversation, she offered him $2,000, her husband's truck and other valuables in exchange for killing Ramon.

At one point, the undercover officer asked whether she wanted her husband beaten up instead.

Her reported response was chilling: "No, I want him dead."

Two days later, on July 22, the undercover officer contacted Maria and told her that the murder had been carried out.

He arranged another meeting and presented her with photographs showing what appeared to be her husband's dead body.

But Ramon was not dead.

He had actually cooperated with investigators and agreed to participate in staging his own murder. Texas Rangers applied makeup to his head to make it look as though he had been shot, and he posed in a shallow grave for the photographs.

The pictures were then given to Maria as supposed proof that the job had been completed.

According to the arrest affidavit, she smiled, shook the undercover officer's hand and paid him an additional $1,000.

She had just celebrated what she believed was her husband's murder, completely unaware that he was alive and that the entire operation had been designed to expose her.

Maria was arrested and initially charged with solicitation of capital murder.

text:
Advance Scouting Report on Fernando Mendoza

By: Former New York Jets Pro Scout Daniel Kelly

@Seahawks @Broncos @Browns @chargers @Titans @AZCardinals @Chiefs 

Background: Indiana carried Fernando Mendoza with their run game and their National Championship roster, and he’s coming off a rough preseason for the Raiders. He had one appearance during the regular season for Las Vegas vs. New England where he threw mostly short passes in one drive.

In the preseason, Mendoza played in three games and completed 55.6% of his passes, 1 TD, 2 INT, 4 Sacks (Fox Sports). 

Per Pro Football Focus (PFF) Mendoza preseason: 

4/5 (behind the line of scrimmage) 80.0%

17/23 (0-9 yards) 73.9%

5/10 (10-19 yards) 50.0%

0/2 (20+ yards) 0%

Per PFF:

During the preseason, Mendoza’s time to throw was 3.02 seconds (ranked No. 79/108) in the NFL, and he had a 21.1% Pressure to sack P2S% (ranked No. 67/108) in the NFL.

Completion percentages (PFF):

Kept clean: 65.6%
Under pressure: 35.7%
Not blitzed: 55.3%
When blitzed: 62.5%

Preseason summary: Mendoza was conservative, had a slow time to throw, and a below 60% completion percentage vs. vanilla defensive schemes. He also struggled vs. pressure. 

Mendoza showed at Indiana and in his NFL experience to date that he is an elementary and limited game manager. 

He has the skillset of a third string quarterback in the NFL. 

He has a conservative and calculated nature.

Mendoza is a sequential hardcore rigid linear thinker. He needs to have everything lined up for him just so and he needs everything to go as planned. He does not have a mind that can quickly and successfully adapt to change.

He is not a dual-threat. He looks stiff and awkward as a runner and he lacks bend. When he runs, he looks like a first baseman trying to steal second.

He wants to work from the pocket and he likes the highest percentage throws that offer him the most throwing leverage.

At Indiana, Mendoza either handed the ball off or he repetitively kept throwing the same 3-4 pass routes that offered him the most throwing leverage. Mendoza was very repetitive. Indiana’s No. 13 (Team Rankings) rushing attack propped him up. Indiana averaged 207.3 rushing yards per game. They averaged 33.8 rushing attempts per game (Team Rankings). 

*Mendoza depended on the run game at Indiana.

At Indiana, his completion percentage dropped to 53.2% when he was forced to move (ESPN) and 51.2% (PFF) when he was under pressure last season. 

https://t.co/pbP2dhAnVY

Last season at Indiana vs. Purdue, he completed 53.3% of his passes. That was his lowest completion percentage of the season. Purdue did that by showing him a lot of different defensive looks as talked about in this video clip: https://t.co/xqAaUlUzof

Mendoza loves to throw high percentage passes to the outside to the sidelines. 

When the University of Miami tightened up their outside pass coverage in the second half of the National Championship Game, Mendoza’s completion percentage dropped to 40.0% https://t.co/rz3LW2ARx3

Raiders unit rankings (PFF)

Rushing: No. 25 (65.7)
Pass blocking: No. 28 (58.0)
Defense: No. 32 (50.5)
Special Teams: No. 22 (78.0)

How to defeat Mendoza: 

• Play 8 in the box and dare him to throw it. He’s going to try to lean heavily on the run game the way he did at Indiana. They are going to try to run to set up the pass. Take away the run. Put the game on Mendoza’s shoulders. 

• Show him a lot of different looks defensively pre-snap. Then switch it up on him post-snap. Make his mind attempt to adapt.

• Flush him out of the pocket. 

• Focus on taking away the short passing game and outside passing game (sidelines). That’s his bread and butter. 

• Play tight man coverage.

• Cornerbacks should sit on his trademark sideline routes as seen in this video clip: https://t.co/f63IssFnM6

Key to victory: 

Get Mendoza down on the scoreboard early.

text:
They Can't Sign It Tomorrow. They're Building It for 2029.

Democrats just took the House 254–167 and the Senate by a working majority. They flipped Texas. They have a governor-elect in Austin who has already told The Washington Post she will tear down a terrorism designation. And they have a two-year problem named Donald Trump, who can veto almost anything they send him until January 20, 2029.
That last sentence is not a lullaby. It is a countdown.

They do not have the votes to override him. A veto dies unless two-thirds of both chambers say otherwise — 290 in the House and 67 in the Senate. They have 254 and about 54. So no, they cannot enact Medicare for All, a national amnesty, or a 13-justice Court in February. Anyone who tells you they can is selling panic, not a bill. The honest danger is different: they will spend the next two years investigating, defunding, legislating for the record, and changing the rules of the Senate so that the first Democrat who takes the White House can sign the stack.
Chuck Schumer already admitted the wall is there. "Will Trump sign all of it into law? Knowing Trump's and Republicans' intransigence, of course not," he said after the election. Then he promised to fight "bill by bill, brick by brick, for as long as it takes."

They will not say "open borders." Watch what they fund.

No serious Democratic leader ran around the country shouting "open borders." Hakeem Jeffries, the next speaker, says the system is "broken" and should be "fixed in a bipartisan way." Fine. Then listen to the rest of the sentence. House Democrats, he told reporters, will not give "a dime" to what he calls the administration's "violent mass deportation machine." He wants to redirect $75 billion previously provided to Immigration and Customs Enforcement through 2029. ICE, in his words, got a "slush fund so that masked agents could brutalize and kill American citizens, and violently target law-abiding immigrant communities."
That is a promise to starve the agency that enforces the law we have.

The bill they are actually waving is the American Dream and Promise Act, from Rep. Sylvia Garcia of Texas. It would offer permanent-resident status — a green card, with a path beyond it — to immigrants brought here as children and to people whose temporary protected status was revoked, if they have been in the country since 2021 and meet education, military, or work tests and a background check. Republicans call that amnesty. Trump has said, "There is no amnesty." The text is a legalization program, and legalization is the point.

Some Democrats talked this fall about abolishing or gutting ICE. After the election, a Capitol press conference of progressives and moderates declined to offer a plan to abolish it. They talked instead about "legal pathways for long-term immigrants." Do not confuse a change in tone with a change in destination. The destination is less enforcement and more status for people who entered or stayed illegally. The people who benefit first are not the citizens who waited in line.

Medicare for All is not a vibe. It is a bill, and the bill is enormous.

Leadership's first-hundred-days health talk is more incremental: restore Affordable Care Act subsidies, reverse Medicaid cuts. Jeffries and Schumer have not even sponsored the current Medicare for All bill. The progressive wing will not stay quiet, and some new members ran on the real thing.
The real thing is on paper. The Medicare for All Act introduced in April 2025 by Rep. Pramila Jayapal would entitle "every individual who is a resident of the United States" to benefits, bar discrimination on the basis of "citizenship status," and let the Health and Human Services secretary extend eligibility to other people "to ensure that every person in the United States has access to health care." It would also prohibit private insurers from selling coverage that "duplicates the benefits" of the program, and prohibit employers from offering duplicate coverage.

🎯🤡That didn’t take long. Fresh off their statehouse victories around the country, Democrats are promising to use their power to eviscerate school voucher and education scholarship programs.

“We will work tirelessly to repair the damage of the Texas voucher scam,” the state’s Democratic Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa declared after her victory last week. She’s referring to the education savings accounts that GOP Gov. Greg Abbott tirelessly championed.

The program provides parents an average of roughly $10,500 for private school tuition—roughly half as much as the state spends per pupil on public schools. Parents can also receive as much as $2,000 to home school their child. ESA spending is capped at $1 billion, which is less than 1% of K-12 public school spending in the state.

Democrats oppose the program because it offers parents a choice other than a failing neighborhood public school. Sarah Eckhardt, a Democratic state senator who was elected comptroller, voted against the ESAs and will oversee the program. She has called for more accountability and transparency, which is union code for using regulation to strangle the program.

Democrats also gained control of the Texas state house, which will give them more leverage to squeeze ESAs. Diego Bernal, the Democratic vice chair of the House education committee, told the progressive website ProPublica that “I guarantee that program is not going to be untouched, and it will be probably unrecognizable, if not extinct, by the time we’re done with it.” Is obliterating ESAs really what Texans voted for on Election Day?

Mr. Bernal also said that some Republicans who showed lukewarm support for ESAs may be willing to join Democrats and kill the program. Let’s hope not. Mr. Abbott backed primary challenges in 2024 to GOP lawmakers who opposed ESAs. Most of the challengers won, which suggests high levels of support among rank-and-file Republicans.

A Texas Southern University poll from February 2025 also showed broad electoral support for ESAs, including among 57% of black Democrats. But elected Democrats answer first to the teachers union that funds their campaigns than to black parents.

Arizona Democratic Gov. Katie Hobbs also vowed on election night to “crack down on the waste, fraud and abuse in the out-of-control ESA entitlement program while delivering $1 billion to our public schools.” Translation: She plans to starve ESAs to boost funding for union-controlled public schools that are failing children.

The teachers unions have long sought to abolish Arizona’s universal ESA program, and they now may have the power. Democrats will have total control of Arizona’s government for the first time in 60 years, including a 20-10 supermajority in the Senate and a 37-23 advantage in the House.

Some 1.5 million children participate in private-school choice programs nationwide. text:
I spotted this wreck some years back while enjoying a Sunday lusting after cars at a show in Leander, Texas. 

I am not clear if it was wind and weather that did the damage, or a demolition contractor that left for one reason or another, or no reason at all. Either way…

The House That Couldn't Make Up Its Mind

A Sunday Afternoon in Leander, Texas — May 2015

I found a house one Sunday noon,
Beneath a bright and cloudless June.
Though May was young, the house was old,
Its story waiting to be told.

Its roof had suffered quite a fright,
Perhaps a storm one windy night.
The shingles scattered, rafters bent,
And several boards had clearly went.

The chimney stood, a faithful friend,
Still hoping this might not be the end.
The walls remained, though somewhat bare,
With half a house still standing there.

The front door opened to the breeze,
No longer bothered by locks or keys.
The windows offered quite a view,
Of everything the neighbors do.

The roof beams pointed every way,
As if they'd tried to fly away.
A few still clung to their old place,
With stubborn pride upon their face.

The bushes gathered at the side,
As though the house had something to hide.
They crept beneath the broken wall,
And whispered, "Nature gets it all."

Was this the work of Texas wind,
Or demolition poorly pinned?
Had some contractor called it quits,
Deciding he'd had quite enough of it?

Perhaps the owner gave the word,
"Take down the house, but leave the bird..."
Then somebody misplaced the plan,
And left the job to finish when they can.

I stood there with my camera eye,
Beneath that brilliant Texas sky.
A car show waited down the street,
With polished chrome and tires neat.

But here was something quite unique,
A house too stubborn to look weak.
It hadn't fallen, hadn't fled,
Just lost its roof and most its head.

I took my picture, then moved along,
But houses like this inspire a song.
For even ruins have tales to tell,
Of better days when all was well.

And should that house have one last wish,
Beyond a roof and perhaps a dish,
It might request, before the next big blow:
"Either tear me down...
Or finish the job, for heaven's sake, and let me go!"

text:
When Paul Gascoigne was battling alcoholism in 2014, Harry Redknapp was becoming increasingly worried about what was happening to him.

The former England midfielder lived near Redknapp on the south coast, and Harry regularly saw him around the area.

Gascoigne had once been one of the country's biggest football stars. After the 1990 World Cup, agents, advisers, lawyers and celebrities had all wanted to be part of his life.

But by 2014, his playing career was over and his alcohol problems had become increasingly serious.

Redknapp could not understand how someone who had given so much to football had ended up in such a difficult situation.

“There should be an inquiry into Paul Gascoigne one day.”

“How did it end up like this?”

He questioned the people who had surrounded Gazza when he was famous and making money.

“The people I would want to hear from, right at the start, are his agents, his accountants, his lawyers.”

“What do these people actually do to help when the money stops coming in?”

His former agent, Mel Stein, had even predicted the situation years earlier.

“This is not going to end happily.”

In 2013, Gary Lineker, Chris Evans and Piers Morgan helped fund Gascoigne's rehabilitation in Arizona, covering his flights and treatment, which cost around £6,000 a week.

But his struggles continued after returning to England, and in August 2014, he was admitted to hospital following another alcohol-related incident near his home.

Redknapp had already tried to offer him a way back.

Managing QPR at the time, he believed getting Gazza involved in football again could give him some purpose.

He offered him a job working with the younger players.

“I’ll pick you up in the mornings, Gazza, come training with me and do a bit of work with the kids.”

Harry was even willing to collect him at 5:45 every morning and take him to the training ground.

“It’s an open invitation to him.”

Redknapp still saw the good person beneath the struggles.

“He’s got a heart of gold.”

“He’s probably given his last penny away.”

But he also understood that no matter how much friends and former teammates wanted to help, there was one person who ultimately had to make the decision to fight for recovery.

“The only person who can help him now has got to be himself.”

text:
A baby pigeon has no concept of tomorrow. It has a crop, and the crop is either full or it isn't.

That is the entire drama of its night. For a bird this young, nothing else on earth matters as much as one small pouch at the base of its throat, and whether somebody remembered to fill it before the light went out.

There is a short video about exactly that question. It runs about twenty-six seconds. It is not loud. It does not announce itself as the most emotional thing you will see today. But it is built around the oldest unit of care there is: making sure the smallest, most dependent creature in the room goes to sleep fed.

I want to explain why a bird most people walk past without seeing can carry a story this heavy. Because once you understand what a baby pigeon actually is, and what it needs from the world at the end of every single day, you cannot watch that clip casually again.

Start with something you have probably never noticed.

You have seen thousands of pigeons. Pigeons on rooftops, on train platforms, on the edge of fountains, on statues of men who were important a long time ago. Now try to remember a baby one. Not a young one. A baby. Pink, sparse, oversized feet, a head that seems too heavy for the neck holding it.

You can't. Almost nobody can.

Pigeons are one of the most visible birds on the planet, and yet their babies are one of the most hidden sights in the city. They stay in the nest, out of view, until they are nearly as large as their parents. The earliest chapter of a pigeon's life happens in a place we never look, in a state we never see, and it is a chapter that depends completely on someone showing up.

That word matters. Showing up.

A newly hatched pigeon cannot walk to food. It cannot peck at seeds, because it has no way to find or manage them yet. It cannot keep itself warm the way an adult does. Biologists have a word for this kind of beginning: altricial. It means born unfinished, born needing. Born with a very large number of requirements and almost no ability to meet any of them.

So the entire survival strategy of a baby pigeon comes down to one bet: that a larger creature will keep returning.

Hold onto that, because it is the emotional engine of everything that follows. The bet is not made once. It is made again at every feeding, every dusk, every night. A baby pigeon is placing that wager over and over, with no way of knowing the odds.

And here is where the story gets stranger than most people expect.

What a baby pigeon eats at the very start of its life is not seed, not insects, not anything you would find on the ground.

It is milk.

Real milk, in a sense that surprises people. Pigeons and doves produce what is known as crop milk, a thick, nutrient-dense secretion made in the lining of the crop. It is rich in protein and fat. It is produced under the influence of the same kind of hormone that drives lactation in mammals. And here is the part that quietly overturns a lot of assumptions: both parents make it. The father produces it too.

Think about how unusual that is. In the animal kingdom, feeding the young from your own body is a rare thing, and sharing that duty equally between the sexes is rarer still. Flamingos do something similar. So do emperor penguins, in their own way. But among all the birds you might see on an ordinary street, the pigeon is the quiet masterclass in it.

The people who call pigeons dirty, stupid, or disposable have never been told this. A creature they step around on the way to work spends the first days of its children's lives converting its own body into food, taking shifts, and doing it with a patience that would exhaust most of us.

Then the menu begins to change. Over the following days, the parents gradually mix in more solid food. The milk fades. The seeds arrive. The baby is being slowly negotiated out of total dependence and into a bigger world, one feeding at a time.

This is where care gets technical and where it gets tender at the same time.

The crop is a storage organ. It works a bit like a pantry attached to the throat, a place where food can wait before being passed along for digestion. For an adult bird, it is convenient. For a baby, it is closer to a lifeline. A baby that goes to sleep with a full crop has something to draw on through the dark hours. A baby that goes to sleep with an empty one has nothing but hope.

That is why the phrase on that video matters so much. The idea of making sure a baby pigeon is full before sleep is not a cute caption. It is the whole logic of the night. Sleep is the longest stretch without a feeding, and a baby this young does not get to negotiate for a snack at three in the morning.

Parents in the wild solve this by timing. They feed, they feed again, they settle in, and the nest becomes quiet. Pigeons typically lay two eggs, incubate them for roughly seventeen to nineteen days, and the work is shared: the male commonly takes the daytime hours, the female commonly takes the night. Two adults, two shifts, one fragile project.

Now ask yourself what happens when that arrangement is replaced by a single person.

No second shift. No partner to cover the dusk. No instinct tuned over millions of years to know exactly when the crop is full enough. Just one human being, a lot of attention, and the full weight of a very small question: is this baby ready for the night?

That question is not dramatic. That is exactly why it is powerful.

Let's talk about speed, because speed is the hidden pressure behind every feeding.

A baby pigeon grows at a pace that makes other young animals look unhurried. In roughly a month, it goes from a hatchling you could lose in the palm of your hand to a bird that is close to adult size and ready to leave the nest. Pin feathers break through. The skin that looked bare and pink disappears under a new coat. The head that looked too large settles into proportion. The legs that could barely hold it learn to carry it.

All of that is built out of food.

Every feather is made of what was eaten days earlier. Every bit of muscle that will one day power a wing for hours was assembled from meals. There is no shortcut in that process and no way to catch up afterward by doing extra later. The growth is happening now, on a schedule the baby cannot slow down, and the fuel has to arrive on time.

This is why people who work with young birds talk about routine with a seriousness that can sound almost obsessive to outsiders. Same hours. Same attention. Same care about how much, how fast, and when to stop. Not because they enjoy rules, but because a baby bird's body has no patience for improvisation.

And yet, from the outside, it all looks gentle.

That is the paradox I find hardest to stop thinking about. The most consequential work often looks the least dramatic. A person, a small creature, a quiet moment, a task so ordinary that it does not seem to deserve attention. Meanwhile the thing at stake is not small at all. It is a living animal's entire next stretch of time.

There is a reason these moments are so hard to scroll past. We are wired to respond to dependence. Show a human being something that is soft, unfinished, and completely reliant on another creature's attention, and something in the brain slows down. It is the same mechanism that makes a person lower their voice around a sleeping infant without being told to.

But I think there is something more specific happening with this particular subject.

A baby pigeon does not look like what we have been taught to find adorable. It is not fluffy in the way a duckling is. It is not round-eyed and cartoonish. It is an odd, bare, slightly prehistoric little creature with a long neck and a lot of unfinished edges. Nobody designed it to win hearts.

And that is precisely what makes caring for it feel so honest.

There is no reward built into the arrangement. No applause. No audience. Nothing that makes the work easy to justify except the plain fact that a living being needs it. When someone does that carefully, patiently, and at the right hour, it tells you something about them that a thousand statements about kindness never could.

So the real subject of that clip is not the bird.

Or rather, it is not only the bird.

It is the person on the other side of the bet. The one who got the question right.

Now let me complicate the picture, because the pigeon deserves better than sentiment. It deserves the truth, and the truth about pigeons is stranger and more impressive than their reputation.

For thousands of years, humans have lived alongside pigeons by choice. They were among the earliest birds people kept, bred for food, for flight, for beauty and for messages. Charles Darwin was so fascinated by fancy pigeon breeds that he kept them himself and leaned on them heavily as evidence while building the argument of On the Origin of Species. Look at the extravagant varieties people produced over generations, he said in effect, and you can see how much change is possible when selection does its work.

That is a serious place in the history of ideas for a bird the modern world treats as scenery.

Then there is the thing pigeons became famous for: finding their way home. Scientists are still debating the exact toolkit, which seems to involve some blend of the sun, landmarks, smell and the planet's magnetic field. What nobody debates is the result. Racing and homing pigeons have returned to their lofts across distances of hundreds of miles. A bird that began its life in a nest, unable to do anything for itself, grows into an animal capable of crossing a landscape and arriving at one precise address.

Think about the distance between those two points. Helpless on one end. Navigating continents on the other. And somewhere in between is a period of rapid growth that depends entirely on being fed, kept warm, and looked after.

War history makes the same point in a harder register. In the First World War, a pigeon named Cher Ami carried a message that helped bring relief to a trapped American battalion in France, reaching her destination badly wounded. By the usual telling, roughly two hundred men were saved. She was honored with the French Croix de Guerre.

In the Second World War, a pigeon named G.I. Joe delivered a message in Italy that is credited with preventing an air strike on a village already held by Allied troops, with some accounts putting the number of lives spared close to a thousand. The Dickin Medal, created to honor animals that showed gallantry in wartime service, has been awarded to thirty-two pigeons in total.

Thirty-two. Remember that number the next time someone calls a pigeon a nuisance.

And these were not only flying machines. They were animals that once had to be fed in the dark by something bigger than themselves, in a nest nobody was watching, in a week nobody would remember.

That is the thread I want you to hold. Every extraordinary pigeon story begins in the least extraordinary place: a very small bird, a very large need, and an ordinary evening.

If you still think of a pigeon as a simple creature, the research is going to be uncomfortable.

In a well-known experiment from 1981, pigeons were trained to use a mirror to locate a mark on their own bodies, behavior that researchers had long treated as a hallmark of a more sophisticated mind. The result is still argued over, as these things should be, but it forced people to rethink what they had assumed about a bird they considered ordinary.

In the 1990s, a team in Japan showed that pigeons could be trained to distinguish paintings by Monet from paintings by Picasso, and could often carry that distinction over to artists they had never been shown. Later work found that pigeons can learn to tell individual human faces apart, which means the person who walks past a flock every day may be recognized by animals they have never noticed noticing them.

Other studies have shown that pigeons can learn to rank symbols by order and can pick up rules that were once thought to belong mainly to primates. None of this makes a pigeon a person. It makes a pigeon something more interesting: a mind we have been underestimating for a very long time.

Which brings me back to the baby, and to a question I cannot stop turning over.

If an adult pigeon can remember a face, if it can learn a pattern, if it can cross a continent and come home, then what is being built during those first weeks in the nest? Not just a body. Something is also being shaped in the way the young bird meets the world. In every species that raises dependent young, the earliest experiences of food, warmth and being responded to leave marks that no later chapter fully erases.

I am careful here, because I do not want to claim more than anyone knows. Nobody can tell you what a baby pigeon feels at the end of a feeding. I will not pretend that I can. Science has not given us a verdict on that, and an honest post should not fake one.

But we do not need to read a bird's thoughts to understand what is at stake. The stakes are physical and plain. A small animal with a large future needs to be full, warm and safe when the dark arrives. And the quality of the person standing between that animal and the night shows up in a very specific way: in details.

How patient is the pace? How steady are the hands? Does the person notice when the baby has had enough, or only when the baby makes it obvious? How many times has this been done, and does it still get the same attention as the first?

Details are the language of care. They are how you tell love from obligation, even when no one is speaking.

There is another side to pigeon life that rarely appears in the jokes, and it is the part that made me rethink what I was looking at.

Pigeons are typically devoted partners. Many pairs stay together across seasons, return to the same nesting spot, and divide the labor of raising their young with a steadiness that would put many human households to shame. The shifts at the nest, the swapped duties, the shared milk. It is a partnership built around one purpose: keeping something small alive long enough to become something strong.

When that arrangement works, nobody notices. That is the nature of reliable care. You only see how much it mattered when it is missing.

Pigeons have also known loss on a scale that is hard to hold in the mind. Not long ago, the passenger pigeon, a close cousin of the birds on our streets, filled North American skies in flocks so large that observers wrote of daylight dimming. Estimates run into the billions. And then, within a human lifetime, they were gone. The last one, a female named Martha, lived in a zoo in Cincinnati until 1914.

Billions, and then a single bird in a cage, and then nothing.

I mention this not to darken the mood but to adjust the scale. A species can be so common that nobody feels responsible for it, and the moment you stop feeling responsible is exactly the moment it becomes fragile. Abundance makes us careless. Familiarity makes us blind.

Today's pigeons are not endangered. Rock pigeons are everywhere, and I am not trying to tell you they are on the edge. But the lesson of the passenger pigeon is less about numbers and more about attention: how quickly a living thing can become invisible to the people sharing a sky with it, and how much it can cost to look away.

So when I watch someone give a baby pigeon their full, undivided attention, I do not see a sentimental hobby. I see the opposite of the habit that has cost this planet so much. I see a person looking at one small life as if it were the only one in the room.

And that is a rarer sight than it should be.

Because here is the uncomfortable truth about compassion. It is easy at a distance and easy on a scale. It is easy when the animal is photogenic, when the cause is trending, when the audience is watching. It is much harder when the creature is plain, the hour is late and the only witness is the one being cared for.

That is the test. Not whether you can care loudly, but whether you can care quietly, on time, again tomorrow.

Let's go back to the night, because the night is where this whole story lives.

Every living thing that depends on someone else has a version of the same fear, even if we cannot prove what it feels like from the inside. The fear is not of the dark. It is of the gap. The long stretch between one feeding and the next, between one presence and the next, during which you must carry yourself on whatever was given before.

Human beings know this gap intimately. Every parent has stood in a quiet hallway at an unreasonable hour, listening for a sound. Every caregiver of any kind knows the particular weight of the last task of the day, the one that decides whether the next hours are peaceful or anxious. We do not call it heroic. We call it getting them settled.

But "settled" is a deceptively soft word. Behind it is a decision. Did we do enough? Did we do it right? Is there anything we missed that will matter at three in the morning, when it is too late to fix?

That is the quiet tension at the center of the phrase on that video. Making sure a baby is full before sleep is not a single action. It is a judgment. Too little leaves the baby short for the long hours ahead. Too much is its own kind of problem, and experienced bird keepers will tell you that over-eagerness is one of the most common mistakes in the field. The skill is in the middle, in the pause, in knowing when to stop.

And you cannot learn that from a caption. You can only learn it from watching someone who already knows.

This is, I think, the real reason care videos like this one hold people so tightly. They are not entertainment in the usual sense. They are a rare chance to watch expertise that is invisible everywhere else. Most skilled work happens out of sight: in kitchens, in nurseries, in barns, in quiet rooms. When a camera happens to catch it, the effect is hypnotic, because we are seeing competence performed without performance.

There is no script, no showmanship, no need to impress. Just attention, applied at the correct moment, to the correct creature, in the correct amount.

Try to remember the last time you saw anything online that did not want something from you. Not a click, not a reaction, not an opinion. Something that simply existed because a task needed doing.

That quality is rarer every year. And it is a large part of why these twenty-six seconds feel longer than they are.

Now, a few honest words, because a post like this should leave people better informed, not just moved.

Raising a baby bird is not a casual project, and it is not something to try on instinct or on the strength of a short clip. Young birds have exacting needs, their health can change quickly, and well-meaning mistakes in feeding, temperature or technique can do real harm. The people who do this work well tend to learn from experienced keepers, rehabilitators and avian veterinarians, and they are often the first to say how much there is still to learn.

If you ever come across a baby bird outdoors, the kindest first move is usually not to take over. Many young birds that look abandoned are being watched by parents nearby, and in many places the right call is to contact a licensed wildlife rehabilitator or a local vet before doing anything else. Care is not the same as intervention. Sometimes the most loving act is knowing who to call.

I say this because the best version of compassion is informed compassion. The kind that checks, asks and learns. The kind that is willing to be corrected. Not the kind that needs to be the hero of the story.

That distinction is, in a strange way, part of what makes this subject so compelling. The people most devoted to the welfare of animals are very often the ones who talk the most about their own limits.

They say: I am not the parent. I am the stand-in. And a stand-in has to be better prepared than the original, because nature spent a very long time perfecting the original.

Think about what that means. A pigeon pair, equipped with hormones, instinct and shared shifts, has a system refined across enormous stretches of time. A human replacing that system has to learn it consciously, imitate it faithfully and make up for everything the birds would have done automatically. That is an enormous act of humility dressed as an ordinary chore.

It is also, quietly, one of the most honest things a person can do. To say: this life is not mine, but for now it is in my hands, and I am going to take that seriously.

There is no ego in that sentence. There is only responsibility.

And responsibility, offered gently, at the right hour, to a creature that cannot thank you, may be the purest form of kindness we have.

So why does a clip about a bird's bedtime deserve to travel?

Not because it is cute, though it may be. Not because it is rare, because plenty of people feed animals. It deserves to travel because it asks a question most of us avoid: what do we owe to the small, the plain and the dependent when nobody is keeping score?

We are surrounded by creatures and people whose needs are real and undramatic. They do not trend. They do not make good headlines. They are simply there, requiring someone to notice at the right moment, again and again, for as long as it takes. The work of looking after them is mostly invisible, mostly unpaid in attention, and mostly unthanked.

And yet entire lives are built on it.

I think that is why so many people send this kind of video to a friend with no explanation. No caption, no argument. Just the link, and maybe a single line. Because some things are easier to share than to say. Some feelings arrive in the gap between a quiet scene and a quiet thought, and the only honest way to pass them on is to hand over the scene itself.

Ask yourself who in your own life stayed up when you could not. Who made sure you were fed before the night, who checked, who adjusted, who got the amount right. Most of us can name someone. Most of us never told them what it meant.

Maybe that is the unexpected gift hiding inside twenty-six seconds about a bird. It reaches past the animal and lands somewhere closer to home.

There is also a gentler question underneath, one worth asking without turning it into a lecture. How many small lives pass in front of us every day that we never learn to see? Not only pigeons. Neighbors, strangers, creatures at the edge of the road, people at the edge of a conversation. Each of them is somebody's whole world, or the whole world of somebody who has not yet found a way to say so.

You do not have to rescue all of them. Nobody can. But there is a difference between a world where care is a rare event and a world where it is a habit, and habits are built exactly the way this clip suggests: one ordinary evening at a time, done properly, with attention.

Maybe the lesson is not to do something grand. Maybe it is to do the small thing well, and to do it tonight.

One more detail worth knowing. Baby pigeons are fed by an unusual method: the chick reaches inside the parent's beak to take the meal, a close, almost intimate exchange repeated across countless generations of nests. It hints that for this bird, feeding has never been only about food. It has always involved contact, too. Remember that the next time you pass a pigeon.

Everything above is context. None of it is the point. The point is the clip itself, and the particular quiet it holds.

I have deliberately not told you what happens in it, because telling would flatten it. Some experiences lose their power when summarized. You can read a hundred paragraphs about patience and still feel nothing, then watch a few seconds of it and feel something shift in your chest. That is not a flaw in language. It is the reason video exists.

So I will tell you only what I can say without spoiling it. It is short. It is gentle. It is about the thing every young creature needs and almost none of us think to appreciate: the assurance that someone is paying attention to the end of the day.

Watch it once for the bird. Watch it again for the person.

And notice what you feel in between. Whether it is warmth, or a flicker of envy at being cared for that carefully, or a sudden memory of your own, or a small, stubborn urge to be a little more patient with the living things in your own life.

Whatever shows up, do not rush past it. That feeling is information. It is telling you what you value.

The internet is full of noise. Most of it asks you to be angry, to be afraid, to be certain. Very little of it asks you to be gentle. When something does, and does it without raising its voice, it deserves a moment of your time.

Twenty-six seconds. One small bird. One question that was settled before the night began.

Press play.

Then tell me: when was the last time you made sure something small went to sleep full, safe and unafraid?

Some bedtimes are the biggest thing a day contains.

text:
On Saturday mornings in a lot of mountain county seats, the most important business in town was not happening at the bank or the courthouse. It was happening on a row of plank tables along the curb, and nearly every one of them was run by a farm woman.

You might remember being lifted into the truck before daylight, wedged between baskets of eggs, pounds of butter wrapped in damp cloth, jars of beans, bunches of greens, a dressed hen or two and a cake under a dish towel. Mama had been up since three. By the time the town ladies came down the sidewalk with their shopping baskets, her table was set out neat as a church dinner. 

These were curb markets, and in the 1920s and 1930s home demonstration agents helped farm women set them up in towns across North Carolina and other Southern states. The idea was simple and powerful. Instead of trading her goods at the store for whatever credit the storekeeper offered, a woman could sell straight to town families for cash, set her own prices and build her own regular customers.

And that cash was hers. In the hard years of the Depression, a good Saturday at the curb market could pay for school shoes, the doctor, a sack of flour, the light bill in town or the taxes on the farm. Some women kept careful books at the kitchen table. Some quietly paid off debts their husbands never fully knew about. 

More than a few families held on to their land because a mother sold butter and pound cake by the pound every week. Nobody called it a business. It was just Mama going to market. But it was a business, with stock, customers, prices, profit and a reputation she guarded like gold. Plenty of us grew up eating off money that came from those plank tables.

text:
The price of yarn obfuscates how your crafting skill is valued, so let's ignore the cost of wool. We'll assume I gave you some wool I picked up at Shetland, so it cost you nothing.

We can then focus on your crafting it into a blanket and assume 100% of the sale value is from your skill.

How much is that skill worth?

You offer to sell it to me for $125, but I think that is too much. The value of your skill is indeterminate.

I offer you $75, but you think that is too low. Again, the value of your skill is indeterminate.

Finally, we decide on $100. Without a doubt, we can say that making that piece was worth $100.

It started as merely a ball of yarn. You applied your skill and turned it into a beautiful blanket.

In that moment, for that blanket, your skill was worth $100. We know it wasn't worth $125, and we know it wasn't $75, but we know for sure it was worth $100.

text:
Ammianus Marcellinus' The Later Roman Empire (354-378 AD) - Review - 1 of 2

Ammianus - The Historian of Julian the Apostate

Ammianus quotes Cicero
“Although the state most to be desired is the permanent continuance of undisturbed good fortune, nevertheless such a smooth course of life does not provide so piquant a sensation as a change to better things from misery and disaster.”

Ammianus Marcellinus (AD 330–390) was the last of the great Roman historians, making his The Chronicles of Events the last of the ancient classics. He originally titled his work Rerum gestarum libri, and it was comprised of 31 books. Ammianus declares his purpose is to continue Tacitus’ Histories, just as Xenophon picked up the history of Thucydides’ Peloponnesian Wars, another great work that breaks off abruptly. Both authors took on the challenging burden of following the greatest writers of their milieu. Thucydides is known as the “historian’s historian” due to his unflinching focus on the evidence of events, and the flaws of human nature, that he diagnosed as the drivers of wars. Tacitus is ranked among the greatest of Latin history writers, along with Sallust and Livy, and his works are acknowledged as literary masterpieces. Though a less known author, his achievements put Ammianus in the league of the historians Livy and Tacitus. 
Ammianus was born in AD 330 to a noble Greek family in Antioch. He served in the Roman army in numerous campaigns in Gaul and Persia. His military career spanned the reigns of Constantius II (AD 337-361) through Julian (AD 361-363) and Jovian (AD 363-364). His writing shows him to be a well-educated scholar who frequently references his expansive readings in the classics from the ancient Greeks back to Homer and famous Romans such as Cicero. His writing is vividly colorful, and he includes all the elements we find in the great historians starting with Herodotus. In addition to his meticulous recording of events, he includes rich rhetorical exercises in speeches, informative digressions on natural science, geography and sociology, and lofty philosophical observations.
We rely in this chapter on the Penguin Classics edition of Ammianus Marcellinus’ The Later Roman Empire (354-378 AD), first published in 1986. The material was selected and translated by Walter Hamilton (1908-1988), who was an Honorary Fellow at Magdalene College, Cambridge, and Master from 1967 to 1978. The Introduction and Notes were written by Andrew Wallace-Hadrill, currently Professor of Roman Studies and Director of Research in the Faculty of Classics at the University of Cambridge.
Of the 31 original books that Ammianus wrote, this volume includes those that we have, 14-31. Sources document that the earlier books were lost by the sixth century. Wallace-Hadrill provides the full perspective on the original scope of this history in the opening of his Introduction.

"In his closing words Ammianus indicates the starting-point of his work: the accession of Nerva in 96. In some ways this is a surprising revelation. The books that survive (14-31) cover events within the author’s own lifetime. … The figure of Julian is in fact the heart of this history; the period from his appointment as Caesar to his death forms the core – Books 15-25. What precedes Book 15 is in a sense prelude; what follows Book 25 is marked off as postlude, an afterthought."

Some preliminary information helps to understand the terms Ammianus uses frequently. “Caesar” is the title or rank just below the ruler, and denotes the heir and likely successor to the Emperor, who is formally known as the “Augustus”. And the central figure in Ammianus’ history is the Augustus Julian, a nephew of the great Constantine I. He is sometimes referred to as Julian the Apostate, who fashioned himself a philosopher like Marcus Aurelius, and although he tolerated Christianity which had been raised to the state religion of Rome by Constantine, Julian was determined to revive paganism. Ammianus refers to these developments in his history.
As we have seen in so many editions from fine publishers like Penguin, Oxford, Landmark and others, the front matter and back matter of these books add not only to our understanding but also to our enjoyment of the ancient works. Later in the Introduction (p. 24-25), Wallace-Hadrill comments on Ammianus’ extensive digressions, which along with the vivid combat descriptions, add to the reader’s fascination.
The digression was another traditional feature of ancient historical writing, but Ammianus uses it on a scale unparalleled since the father of history, Herodotus. For his digressions may seem bewildering – in number, length and diversity of subject matter … siege engines (23.4), the obelisk (17.4), the calendar (26.1), the plague (19.4), the causes of earthquakes (17.7), the eclipse (20.3), or the rainbow (20.3). There are delights in these digressions, like the picture of the Gallic wife who enters the fray on her husband’s behalf with arms flailing like a catapult (15.12). 
Ammianus provides a whirlwind review of the entire history of Rome with his own colorful characterizations of each stage at 14.6. In these few sentences he reprises the history of the Roman Republic that Livy covers in his first few books where the Romans go to war with their closest neighbors, beginning with the Sabines. He continues in the fewest words to many wars, including the three Punic Wars reported by Polybius and Caesar’s 10 years of Gallic Wars “beyond the Alps”. He surveys the centuries into the Roman Empire and the civilization it establishes.

"From its first infancy to the end of its childhood, a period comprising some three hundred years, the Roman people were engaged in wars close to its walls; next, in its adolescence, after various grievous struggles, it penetrated beyond the Alps and the sea; in its early and its mature manhood it won laurels of victory in every part of the great globe; finally, when it verged on old age and owed its occasional victories only to reputation, it gave itself over to a more peaceful way of life. The venerable city, having set its foot on the proud necks of savage peoples and given them laws to serve as the eternal foundation and guarantee of liberty, took over the course which a thrifty, wise and rich parent does with his children, and handed over to the Caesars the administration of its heritage."

In 355, a powerful general, the “stout rebel Silvanus” had allowed his troops to declare him Augustus, threatening the emperor Constantius. It is resolved to relieve this rebel officer by sending a representative in the person of a recently disgraced but very experienced general who in this role “now became the wisest of generals, the great comrade-in-arms of the emperor Constantine” in Ammianus’ ironic phrasing. In the next sentence, he reveals the other side of this rehabilitation of Ursicinus. “Great efforts were certainly to be made … but if they failed … Ursicinus … would be utterly destroyed, and a very formidable stumbling block removed.” Insights like this, boldly stated about the emperor himself, demonstrate Ammianus’ courageous emulation of the great Tacitus in speaking freely. The author describes his own participation in this delegation, and provides us with a sense of his high rank in the military at 15.5.

"When this was settled Ursicinus received orders to set out. He was accompanied, at his own request, by some tribunes and ten officers of the general staff to help in meeting the needs of the situation. Among the latter were my colleague Verinian and myself; all the rest were chosen by the emperor. … each of us preoccupied solely by fear for his own safety. We were like condemned criminals thrown before fierce wild beasts.”

After this confession of understandable fear, Ammianus takes a philosophical stance, and quotes his most frequently referred authority, Cicero.

“Although the state most to be desired is the permanent continuance of undisturbed good fortune, nevertheless such a smooth course of life does not provide so piquant a sensation as a change to better things from misery and disaster.”

Ammianus offers a tremendous amount of combat reporting, always vivid and voluminous, written from the point of view of cavalry and infantry fighting the enemy face to face in deadly contests. At 16.12 we read of the Battle of Strasbourg in 357, where the Romans are barely surviving the onslaught of the Germans. He puts us in the battle: “Obstinately they struggled, hand to hand and shield to shield; the welkin rang with the shouts of the victors and the screams of the wounded.” At one point the Roman calvary is driven back upon the infantry lines and Ammianus treats us to a strangely elevated exhortation amid such turmoil. This incident reminds us that from most ancient times the greatest battle leaders, from the Spartan Brasidas to the Macedonian Alexander to the Roman Julius Caesar, always put themselves at the front in the most intense fighting. And we see again how Ammianus aims for and often achieves grandeur in his writing.

"The Caesar, seeing from a distance his cavalry turning to flight, put spurs to his horse and threw himself into their path. He was recognized by the purple dragon attached to the tip of a long lance and streaming on the wind like the cast skin of a snake, and the tribune of the squadron turned back, pale and trembling, to renew the fight. The Caesar took the course usual in moments of crisis, and addressed the men in terms of mild reproach: “Where are we off to, my brave fellows? Don’t you know that flight never saved anyone? It is simply the proof of the folly of a vain enterprise. Let us return to our comrades, and at least have a share in their glory, even though we have thoughtlessly abandoned them in their fight for our country.” This tactful speech brought them all back to their duty."

Ammianus makes frequent references to ancient history, so we must assume not only that he was extremely well-read, but he was also writing for a sophisticated and educated audience who will appreciate these learned references. In this case, at 17.11, just after we have read of the great successes of Julian, the hero of this entire work, in defeating and subjugating the Alamanni and other Germanic tribes, the courtiers and confidantes of the emperor Constantius are mocking and belittling him. Ammianus offers an amusing array of specific insults, including “His victories are becoming a bore” “Babbling mole,” “ape in purple,” and “Greek dilettante.” He compares this treatment of great heroes in history and teaches us new lessons of famous men whom we have read about in earlier accounts.

"Cimon, son of Militiades … destroyed a countless host of Persians … was accused of drunkenness. … Scipio Aemilianus, whose unerring alertness brought about the destruction of two powerful cities bent on the ruin of Rome, was represented … as a sleepy-head. … Pompey’s distractors … Such was the futile argument employed by those who barked at the heels of a man whom we have the clearest proof to have had no equal as a hero and a patriot."

Ammianus displays more of his knowledge of the classics in a story about the value of circumspect silence in desperate circumstances, and after citing ancient history, he carries his lesson on to an entertaining illustration in the natural world. In this case, he begins with Aristotle’s advice to his great-nephew Callisthenes who accompanied Alexander on his expeditions as an historian. Ammianus must assume his readers know this advice was tragically disregarded. He is describing the self-induced downfall of a man named Barbatio caused by his own malicious gossip. At the end of 18.3 we read this fascinating dissertation on the sensibility of silence.

"He cannot have known the wise saying of old Aristotle, who, when he sent his pupil and kinsman on a mission to king Alexander, repeatedly enjoined him to speak as little as possible in the presence of a man in whose tongue lay the power of life and death, and then only in pleasant terms. … even irrational animals protect themselves at times by observing dead silence. … When wild geese … approach the Taurus mountains, where eagles are common, their fear of these formidable birds leads them to stop up their beaks with small stones, to prevent a cry escaping them, however hard-pressed. But when they have passed over these hills in rapid flight they let the stones fall, and so pursue their way free from fear."

text:
Ladies and gentlemen,

We are living through one of the most consequential moments in modern history.

And I fear that many in the free world have yet to understand the magnitude of what is unfolding before their eyes.

For decades, the Western world believed that history was moving in one direction.

Toward greater freedom.
Toward greater prosperity.
Toward democracy.
Toward the triumph of reason over fanaticism.

The Berlin Wall fell. The Soviet Union collapsed. Millions of people who had lived under tyranny embraced the promise of freedom.

Many concluded that the great ideological struggles of history were behind us.

But history did not end.

It changed its battlefield.

And today, a different ideological challenge confronts the free world.

It is radical Islamism.

Let me be precise.

This is not a war against Islam. Islam is a major world religion, followed by diverse societies and individuals, and millions of Muslims themselves are victims of Islamist extremism.

This is a struggle against a totalitarian political ideology that seeks to subordinate individual freedom, religious pluralism and national sovereignty to an absolutist religious-political doctrine.

An ideology that glorifies martyrdom through murder.
That celebrates the destruction of those who disagree with it.
That views pluralism not as a strength, but as a weakness to be exploited.

And that is not merely a Middle Eastern problem.

It is a challenge to the foundations of the modern international order.

---

I. THE NATURE OF THE THREAT

We have seen what happens when this ideology acquires political power.

We have seen it in the atrocities of ISIS.

We have seen it in the Iranian regime's revolutionary project and its support for armed organizations across the Middle East.

We have seen it in the actions of Al-Qaeda.

And we have seen it in Hamas's October 7 massacre.

These are different organizations, with different structures, objectives and histories. They should not be treated as identical.

But they demonstrate a broader danger: political movements that reject the legitimacy of coexistence and use terror to advance their ambitions.

Their victims are not only Jews.

Their victims include Muslims who reject their extremism, Christians, Yazidis, Kurds, secular intellectuals and anyone who refuses to submit to their authority.

Consider the contradiction.

The very people who claim to defend a religious civilization often begin by persecuting members of that same civilization who disagree with them.

This is the nature of totalitarianism.

It cannot tolerate independent thought.

It cannot tolerate competing loyalties.

And ultimately, it cannot tolerate freedom.

---

II. THE WESTERN ILLUSION

But I want to speak about something even more troubling.

The danger does not come exclusively from outside the West.

It also comes from the West's inability to understand itself.

A civilization cannot defend principles it no longer believes in.

For generations, Western democracies understood that freedom was not free.

They understood that democratic institutions required courage, discipline, historical memory and a willingness to defend the conditions that made freedom possible.

Today, too many political leaders appear to have forgotten this.

They confuse tolerance with surrender.

They confuse pluralism with the obligation to accept movements that seek to abolish pluralism.

They confuse freedom of expression with immunity from criticism.

And they sometimes mistake the absence of confrontation for peace.

But peace and the absence of resistance are not the same thing.

Democracy must be tolerant.

But it must not be suicidal.

A democratic society has the right, and indeed the responsibility, to defend its constitutional order against movements that seek to destroy it.

And it must do so through the rule of law, equal citizenship and the protection of fundamental rights.

---

III. HOW DEMOCRACIES COLLAPSE

Ladies and gentlemen,

Democracies rarely collapse in a single dramatic moment.

Sometimes they collapse through military conquest.

But more often, their institutions weaken gradually.

Trust disappears.

National identity fragments.

Political leaders lose the ability to distinguish between legitimate disagreement and attacks on the constitutional order.

Institutions become instruments of partisan warfare.

Citizens stop believing that their governments can protect them.

And external adversaries learn to exploit these divisions.

This is the danger facing the Western world.

I am not predicting that Western democracy will inevitably collapse.

I am warning that its survival cannot be taken for granted.

Consider the historical lesson of the Weimar Republic.

Germany possessed universities, a sophisticated intellectual culture, advanced industry and democratic institutions.

Yet those achievements did not prevent the destruction of its democracy.

Economic crisis, political polarization, institutional weakness and the rise of an extremist movement combined to undermine the republic.

History does not repeat itself mechanically.

But it does offer warnings.

The lesson is that civilization is not protected by its achievements alone.

It must be defended by the generations that inherit it.

---

IV. THE STRATEGIC BLINDNESS OF THE WEST

There is another mistake.

For too long, many Western policymakers believed that economic integration would automatically moderate ideological extremism.

That trade would overcome hostility.

That technological modernization would inevitably produce liberal political values.

But history has demonstrated otherwise.

A society can possess advanced technology and still embrace authoritarianism.

A regime can participate in international markets while financing terrorism.

A movement can use social media, modern communications and sophisticated financial networks while promoting an ideology fundamentally hostile to individual freedom.

Modern technology does not necessarily produce modern political values.

That is one of the central strategic lessons of our time.

The West must therefore abandon the illusion that every adversary can be transformed through economic incentives alone.

Diplomacy is essential.

Economic cooperation is essential.

But deterrence, credible institutions and the willingness to defend democratic principles are equally essential.

---

V. ISRAEL AND THE FUTURE OF THE WEST

Israel understands something that the West is in danger of forgetting.

Freedom is precious precisely because it is vulnerable.

We are a small country.

We have faced wars, terrorism, international pressure and existential threats.

Yet we have built a democratic society with an independent judiciary, a free press, competitive elections, universities, scientific institutions and extraordinary technological capabilities.

Our democracy is not perfect. No democracy is.

But its existence in a region marked by authoritarianism and political instability demonstrates that democratic institutions can take root in the Middle East.

And we have learned a difficult lesson:

A democracy must be capable of defending itself.

A country that cannot protect its citizens cannot guarantee their freedom.

A society that cannot maintain its security cannot sustain its political independence.

This is why the alliance between Israel and the United States is so important.

It is not simply an alliance of military interests.

It is a partnership built on shared democratic institutions, strategic cooperation and historical experience.

But I would say something more.

America must not defend Israel because Israel is dependent on America.

America should recognize that a strong, democratic Israel is a strategic partner in a dangerous region.

And Israel must never forget that its security ultimately rests on its own national strength.

---

VI. THE GREAT QUESTION: WHAT HAPPENS IF THE WEST LOSES ITS WILL?

Let me pose a question.

What happens if the world's most powerful democracies become so divided internally that they can no longer recognize a common strategic threat?

What happens when their political systems reward short-term popularity over long-term security?

What happens when their institutions become incapable of enforcing their own laws?

What happens when the enemies of democracy understand its freedoms better than its defenders understand their responsibilities?

This is not a theoretical question.

It is a question of the future.

The greatest danger is not necessarily that an external adversary will defeat the West militarily.

It is that the West may gradually lose the political, intellectual and moral confidence necessary to defend itself.

That is how a civilization becomes vulnerable.

Not because it lacks resources.

Not because it lacks knowledge.

But because it loses the conviction that what it has built is worth defending.

---

VII. THE WORLD IN 2050

What will the world look like in 2050?

There are two possible directions.

In one, democratic societies renew themselves.

They rebuild public trust.

They strengthen their institutions.

They protect freedom of religion and expression.

They integrate newcomers without abandoning the principles that make their societies democratic.

They develop new technological capabilities while preserving human dignity.

They establish partnerships with countries that share an interest in stability and international security.

In that world, the United States remains a leading democratic power. Europe rediscovers its strategic confidence. Israel becomes an increasingly important center of innovation and regional cooperation. And moderate Muslim-majority societies participate in a more prosperous and stable international order.

But there is another possibility.

A world in which democratic institutions become increasingly fragile.

Where political polarization destroys public trust.

Where authoritarian powers exploit Western divisions.

Where extremist movements gain influence by exploiting democratic freedoms while rejecting the principles that sustain them.

Where the international order becomes more fragmented, and the protection of individual liberty is increasingly subordinated to the ambitions of states and ideological movements.

That is the world we must prevent.

And preventing it requires more than speeches.

It requires leadership.

It requires education.

It requires economic strength.

It requires national security.

And above all, it requires moral clarity.

---

VIII. A FINAL MESSAGE TO THE FREE WORLD

Ladies and gentlemen,

The Jewish people have experienced the consequences of a world in which civilization failed to confront barbarism in time.

We know what happens when hatred is normalized.

We know what happens when threats are dismissed as exaggerations.

We know what happens when the defenders of freedom convince themselves that somebody else will deal with the danger.

We have paid an extraordinary price for those lessons.

We do not seek a world divided between religions.

We seek a world in which people of different religions can live together in peace.

We do not seek a war between civilizations.

We seek cooperation between civilizations that respect the right of others to exist.

But cooperation cannot mean surrendering the principles that make coexistence possible.

The answer to radical Islamism is not hostility toward Muslims.

The answer is the defense of freedom, the rule of law, religious pluralism and the dignity of every human being.

And the answer to the enemies of democracy is not to abandon democracy.

It is to make democracy stronger.

Let us remember:

Barbarism is not defeated by pretending it does not exist.

Tyranny is not defeated by appeasement.

And freedom is not preserved by those who take it for granted.

The future of Western democracy is not predetermined.

It will be decided by what its citizens believe, what its leaders are prepared to defend, and what its institutions are capable of sustaining.

The question before us is not whether the challenges are serious.

They are.

The question is whether we possess the courage and wisdom to meet them.

I believe we do.

But belief alone is not enough.

We must act.

We must stand together.

And we must ensure that the next generation inherits not a civilization that has forgotten how to defend its freedom, but one that has rediscovered why freedom is worth defending.

Thank you.
