I'd have to think of a way to steelman a case against that, with Grok's help I guess. It doesn't specify what a regime of property rights looks like - does current IP law match the ideal? - and so it might be considered too abstract a statement to qualify as steelmanning. But it does correctly state in concise, essentialized, and strong terms what the point of Rand's advocacy for capitalism is, tied to philosophical fundamentals as much as a 280-character statement can be: something about the creative intellect as a or the defining characteristic of something desirable such as human civilization or advanced-civilization ethics such as respect for individual achievement and autonomy. Why on earth should the state be allowed to treat man as a sacrificial animal, Rand asked, especially given that free creative intellectual activity is the root of progress and flourishing? (Throw in something about how Rand supplies an economic corollary to the principle of JS Mill's On Liberty concerning how the free market of ideas leads to progress/flourishing, and you've got something pretty steelmannable here? We're not selling 'utopia' or a revolution in human culture here, just some common sense cause-and-effect recognizing about the relation between freedom of the creative intellect on the one hand and progress/flourishing on the other. OTOH it took how many centuries between Plato/Aristotle on the one hand and Mises/Rand on the other for the 'common sense' arc of history to bend toward laissez-faire capitalism or more broadly private property / free markets?)

(Thoughts that come to me as I ponder the ~4 hour podcast interview between Papola (Dad Saves America) and a Marxist History Prof. I wish there were many more conversations at that level and while the Marxist guy raised many of what I'd call interesting points, they just don't seem to come to grips with a steelmanned case for capitalism like the Randian one. A dog not barking is that there's hardly any mention of Rand in the whole interview, I think Papola brings her up once, even though there's never been any decent rebuttal to the essence of her theme/thesis in Atlas and elsewhere re the mind, freedom and flourishing. Nothing whatsoever in all of Marxist Professor Guy's verbal outpourings really touched upon how under capitalism those using their creative intellects best will tend to accumulate greater power in the marketplace - what Rand called economic power, which is the power to command the direction of economic resources based on the will expressed by the customers re one's products (of one's intellect). What Marxist Professor Guy and his ilk would need to plausibly show is how confiscating the physical capital owned by Musk to the tune of so much percentage and handing it over to other people is a better way - applying the Millian & Randian observations concerning the relation between freedom and progress in this or that marketplace, no less -  to steward economic resources and improve living standards. Somehow Marxist Professor Guy thinks there's compelling evidence in favor of confiscating Musk's wealth and letting Democrats (who ruin institutions & create legitimacy crises) decide instead how those funds are best used? I think his more plausible critiques of society are focused elsewhere, and I notice a dog not barking is that hardly anywhere in the whole ~4 hours of podcast are the Aristotelian criteria for actual praxis and flourishing touched upon. Marx Guy just keeps going on about the social conditions for flourishing. Isn't this the same basic problem with liberalism as conservatives often frame it - that it peddles freedom as a condition for living a good life but then has so little to say or offer in the way of the best uses of that freedom in a virtuous life? For Marxism it seems like all of 'ethics' is embedded in what it takes to bring about the communist end-goal. History has shown what this mentality has done, to the tune of ~100M killed by Marxist lunatics with power. And yet in ~4 hours that kinda-central point hardly gets touched upon, it's mostly stuff about political economy. It's almost surely and by a good margin the best engagement I'v ever seen from a Marxist and yet Rand & ethics (or, heck, epistemological methods if not metaphysical fundamentals) hardly get brought up? I'll just mention that Marxism is quite the minority viewpoint in Philosophy despite taking over so much of the humanities and social sciences (Econ excepted - parallels with Philosophy here?). Marx shows up around #20 in polls of philosophers when it comes to influence, with Plato-Aristotle-Kant holding well onto the Big Three. Is the complaint from Marxists about something like this, that their ideas just haven't been steelmanned hard enough, that the 70 bloody years of commie experimenting were some kind of fluke? And what f'ing right do Marxists of all people have to complain about ideas not being steelmanned hard enough? Marx Guy should have known well, and volunteered to bring up and refute the steelmanned Rand, if he were really up to the task. Again, that was the *very best* engagement I've *ever* seen from a Marxist over a matter of decades, and by Drill Instructor standards it still sucks.)

text:
💸 Telesat’s $1.7B GEO debt hits Dec 6 wall. Lightspeed delayed to mid-2028 with zero sats up and still needs SpaceX launches. Taxpayer and pension money already deep in the bet. 

Telesat is a Canadian satellite company. It runs older satellites that sit high above Earth and make most of its current money. That older part of the business is shrinking. Customers are leaving and revenue is down.

On December 6 a big chunk of debt on that older part comes due. The amount is about 1.7 billion US dollars. Telesat has told investors its cash and expected money coming in will not cover what it owes. Lenders have offered rescue deals that would bring in new money from shareholders and more loans. Those deals could give creditors a stronger claim on the company’s new satellite project if things go wrong.

The new project is called Lightspeed. It is a set of satellites closer to Earth meant to provide internet and communications. The Canadian government has put a lot of public money and contracts behind Lightspeed. That includes a large deal to give the military better coverage in the Arctic.

Officials talk about it as a Canadian controlled system so the country is less dependent on foreign services like Starlink. None of the Lightspeed satellites are flying yet for customers. The start of full service has been pushed back to the middle of 2028. The company still plans to put the satellites on SpaceX rockets.

Taxpayers and people whose pensions are managed by a big public fund could feel the pain if the debt problem gets worse or if more public support is needed. The company is still talking to its lenders. Nothing has been settled. The deadline is close.

text:
Remember when the Biden administration, DOJ, and FBI repeatedly declared white supremacy the greatest terrorist threat facing America?

While Americans were being told whom to fear, the country was undergoing profound changes to its borders, culture, institutions, and national identity.

The question is no longer simply what government called a threat. It's who will be allowed to challenge what is happening without being branded one.

THE NARRATIVE

The statements were unmistakable.

In April 2021, Biden declared white-supremacist terrorism the most lethal terrorist threat to the homeland. In June, at Tulsa, he doubled down: "Not ISIS, not al Qaeda—white supremacists."

Attorney General Merrick Garland and FBI Director Christopher Wray also repeatedly identified racially motivated violent extremism as a major domestic security concern.

These were declarations from the highest levels of government. Their political consequences deserve serious scrutiny.

THE DANGEROUS DISTINCTION

There is a fundamental difference between violent extremism and defending America's borders, sovereignty, traditions, constitutional principles, and national interests.

Yet the progressive left increasingly blurs that distinction.

Question immigration policy? Far-right.

Demand assimilation? Xenophobic.

Defend traditional values? Extremist.

Prioritize American citizens? Nationalist—as though that were an accusation.

When political labels replace arguments, dissent itself becomes the target.

EUROPE'S WARNING

Look across the Atlantic. Britain, Ireland, and France offer important warnings about growing tensions surrounding immigration, national identity, cultural integration, and political dissent.

Different countries, different circumstances—but a common concern: expanding government discretion over protest and public expression.

When peaceful dissent becomes subject to increasingly broad restrictions, ordinary citizens have reason to be vigilant.

THE LABELING MACHINE

As Americans resist policies they believe threaten their culture, institutions, economic security, and national sovereignty, expect the familiar labels:

Racist. Xenophobic. White supremacist. Far-right. Domestic extremist.

The political objective is straightforward: portray resistance as intolerance rather than confront legitimate grievances. Discredit opposition, intimidate dissent, and make citizens think twice before speaking.

AMERICA FIRST IS NOT RACISM

American nationalism is a civic principle, not a racial test.

Our Constitution, laws, institutions, and shared national identity form the foundation of the Republic. Americans of every race and background have an equal stake in preserving them.

Citizenship carries responsibilities: loyalty to our constitutional order, respect for the rule of law, and commitment to the country we share.

Religious freedom is protected by the Constitution. The oath of public office is to the Constitution, not a particular religious book. Our founding framework is the standard, regardless of faith.

THE LINE AMERICANS MUST NOT CROSS

The greatest danger is a country where citizens become afraid to defend their own national identity.

A government that treats peaceful opposition as extremism, patriotism as suspicion, and accountability as a threat ultimately undermines the freedoms it claims to protect.

America should recognize Europe's warning before it becomes our reality.

The right to disagree is protected by our Constitution, not granted by political parties, government agencies, or ideological movements.

America belongs to its citizens. Its future should be determined by them. No political movement has the authority to redefine patriotism as extremism simply because Americans refuse to surrender their country without a fight.

text:
Burt Reynolds went bankrupt owing his toupee maker $122,000.

Three years earlier, on national TV, he offered his wife everything he owned if she'd take a truth serum test.

She didn't take it. She took a reported $2 million instead.

Then came $11.2 million in debts, his Golden Globe sold at auction for $21,250, and a judge ordering him to pay her another $154,520.98, twenty years after the divorce.

In the video below, he makes the truth serum challenge on camera in 1993. Then, at 76, Piers Morgan asks him how much he spent.

1988. He marries Loni Anderson, the WKRP star. They adopt a son, Quinton.

June 1993. He files for divorce. She says she was served at their Florida home with no warning.

August 1993. On ABC he accuses her of affairs and dares her to take a sodium pentothal test. If she wins, she gets everything, "including my ranch, my house." If he wins, he gets Quinton. She denies the accusations.

September 1993. His lawyer says she asked for $5 million cash, half of everything above that, and $50,000 a month for Quinton until he turned 21.

January 1994. They settle. Reported terms: $2 million and a $500,000 house for her, plus $11,000 a month in alimony through 1994. He keeps his $4 million Florida ranch.

His version, on NBC: "I'm paying the third-highest alimony and child support in the world. And the only two ahead of me are sheiks."

December 1996. Chapter 11. $11.2 million in debts. Among his 49 creditors: CBS and his toupee maker.

2014. A judge orders him to pay Loni the $97,000 he still owed. With interest: $154,520.98.

That December he auctions his Golden Globe, his Emmy and the Smokey and the Bandit Trans Am.

Piers asks how much he spent: "I have no idea how much. Let me just tell you all, I had a hell of a good time."

$2 million. $122,000 for toupees. $154,520.98 twenty years later.

Did Loni take him to the cleaners, or did Burt spend himself broke?

text:
Billionaire Kevin O'Leary told Florida farmer Johnny Georges to triple his $4.50 price on Shark Tank, leaving Georges in tears minutes later when billionaire John Paul DeJoria gave him $150,000 on his original terms.

Georges invented the Tree-T-Pee, a recycled plastic cone that wraps around young citrus trees and cuts water usage from 25,000 gallons per year down to 800 gallons.

Before appearing on television, Georges tested the product by sneaking onto a local grove during a freezing night and placing five cones on random trees. The owner caught him and threatened to call the police for trespassing.

A week later, that same woman called him back. Those five protected trees were the only ones in her entire grove that survived the freeze, and she ordered 4,995 more units on the spot.

On Shark Tank, Georges laid out his exact unit economics. Each cone cost $2.95 to manufacture, and he sold them directly to struggling farmers for $4.50, keeping just $1.55 in profit per unit.

Kevin O'Leary told him the margins were too thin for retail distribution and demanded a massive price hike before dropping out. "I need to be able to sell it for $12 at least so that I can make some profit," O'Leary said.

When Georges refused to gouge his neighbors, John Paul DeJoria stepped in and matched the exact offer. "I'm going to give you everything you're asking for, your $150,000 for 20 percent," DeJoria said. "What you're doing is right, and you deserve the chance to make it big."

After shaking hands, DeJoria praised his character and said, "Tell your dad he's a great man." Georges broke down in tears on camera and replied, "He died 12 years ago. He's still a great man. He made me who I am."

Within days of the episode airing, Tree-T-Pee pulled in over $1 million in direct orders, and Home Depot put the cones on shelves across Florida at the original $4.50 price.

text:
for months one of mantras in Georgia has been that what is missing is a 'credible alternative'. 

Today, at least beginning of one became visible, as the Movement for Social Democracy @Movement_for_SD had its founding event in Tbilisi. This felt new &  different. 

Genuine enthusiasm and cheers as people stepped forward for the party's council, and -- a party that felt like it is actually owned by the people who were there. 

Sure, an emphasis on more social & economic justice makes a lot of sense right now to most, even if you otherwise are center-right, when so many families across Georgia are struggling while rich cronies celebrate opening of the next Lamborghini showroom. The system is mostly rigged towards a tiny clique. 

But next to offering a specific answer, the crew also did really well. 

The big charisma in the room? It was how they worked together, how different people (& different type of people) all had a place. Vakhushti Menabde and @sophoverdzeuli moderated well & various speakers delivered. Levan Lortkipanidze, one of speakers, quoted Willi Brandt (in German): "Wir wollen mehr Demokratie wagen." / Let's dare more for democracy!

600+ people supporting this foundational event today. Social Democracy has proud history in Georgia (and Guria) and they appealed to this too. 

Mzia Amaghlobeli and Zviad Ratiani were mentioned. They paid attention to details, too -- guests were not really supposed to be there, as they pointed out to me, but then v kindly let me stay. As previously mentioned, they have thought-through program. Posting the rough clips here, so that you can get a sense of the real energy. (Final photo was when many already out in lobby, but still.)

Even if Social Democracy isn't your thing, if you care about Georgia, this was a truly good day, with people -- some of them also exposed to quite the repressions, such as Gota Chanturia -- stepping forward. Also an invitation for others who have quibbles to step up and offer their vision of the future. Great to see many friends there, too. 

Well done, everyone who contributed to this.

text:
The Communist Priest, High Priest of the Anti-Israel Narrative

When warnings about Iran’s partition become a defense of the status quo

In his latest interview, Ervand Abrahamian claims that Israel wants to break Iran apart—not merely change its government, but dismantle the country. It is a grave accusation. Yet instead of presenting a document, a concrete plan, or direct evidence, Abrahamian offers a conjecture. He says he is not sure anyone in the White House has even considered the idea, but that he thinks it was Israel’s agenda.

That is not proof of a plan. It is a political interpretation presented in the language of historical analysis.

First concern: A hypothesis becomes a headline

Abrahamian moves from comparisons with Iraq, Syria, and Libya to a claim about Israel’s intentions. But analogy is not evidence. The fact that a state’s collapse can lead to civil war or fragmentation does not prove that Israel has such an objective for Iran.

His wording invites audiences to hear a settled fact where he has offered a personal inference. That is where analysis leaves the ground of evidence and becomes political narrative.

Second concern: The external threat grows as the regime’s responsibility shrinks

In Abrahamian’s account, the central threat comes from Washington and Tel Aviv. Iran’s government recedes from the center of the story, appearing instead as a state under pressure from foreign enemies. That shift serves the Islamic Republic well: it can present repression as “defending Iran” and cast dissent as serving the enemy.

But who brought the country to this point? The Islamic Republic has deepened the crisis through repression, discrimination, the destruction of independent institutions, and its own regional policies. Warnings about foreign intervention should not erase the regime’s responsibility.

Third concern: Iranians disappear from the political story

In this narrative, Iranians are less often treated as people with political agency and more often as a population at risk of being manipulated, drawn into war, or swept into collapse. Their demand to end the Islamic Republic is overshadowed by the specter of partition.

That echoes the regime’s familiar message: if the Islamic Republic falls, Iran will fall with it. But opposing the Islamic Republic is not opposing Iran. Millions of Iranians want freedom and also support the country’s territorial integrity.

Fourth concern: Fear of tomorrow replaces scrutiny of today

Abrahamian emphasizes the danger of civil war, but gives less weight to the danger of the regime’s continued rule. What has weakened society, isolated the country, and widened its fractures? Which government has answered peaceful protest with bullets and turned politics into an instrument of repression?

When an analyst stresses only the dangers of change and minimizes the dangers of the status quo, the warning is no longer neutral. It becomes an argument for preserving the existing order.

Fifth concern: Anti-Israel polemic displaces an analysis of Iran

Abrahamian’s framework repeatedly places hostility toward the United States and Israel at the center of his interpretation of Iranian history. It reflects a long-standing habit in parts of the left: first view the world through the lens of imperialism and anti-Israel politics, then—if space remains—ask what Iranians themselves want.

Within that framework, the Islamic Republic can be recast as a force of “resistance,” despite its repression and failures, while Iranian protesters become unwitting pieces in a foreign power’s game. The regime benefits from this narrative because it redirects attention from its own abuses and failures.

Sixth concern: Recasting a failed revolution

One interview cannot establish Abrahamian’s inner motives. But this latest narrative bears the imprint of a Tudeh-influenced, anti-Israel left that once interpreted the 1979 revolution through the struggle against imperialism.

text:
It’s yet another summer of extreme weather, with unprecedented heat waves, wildfires, and floods battering countries around the world. In response to the challenge of accurately predicting such extremes, semiconductor giant Nvidia is building an AI-powered “digital twin” for the entire planet. 

This digital twin, called Earth-2, will use predictions from FourCastNet, an AI model that uses tens of terabytes of Earth system data and can predict the next two weeks of weather tens of thousands of times faster and more accurately than current forecasting methods. 

Usual weather prediction systems have the capacity to generate around 50 predictions for the week ahead. FourCastNet can instead predict thousands of possibilities, accurately capturing the risk of rare but deadly disasters and thereby giving vulnerable populations valuable time to prepare and evacuate. 

The hoped-for revolution in climate modeling is just the beginning. With the advent of AI, science is about to become much more exciting—and in some ways unrecognizable. The reverberations of this shift will be felt far outside the lab; they will affect us all. 

If we play our cards right, with sensible regulation and proper support for innovative uses of AI to address science’s most pressing issues, AI can rewrite the scientific process. We can build a future where AI-powered tools will both save us from mindless and time-consuming labor and also lead us to creative inventions and discoveries, encouraging breakthroughs that would otherwise take decades.

AI in recent months has become almost synonymous with large language models, or LLMs, but in science there are a multitude of different model architectures that may have even bigger impacts. In the past decade, most progress in science has come through smaller, “classical” models focused on specific questions. These models have already brought about profound advances. More recently, larger deep-learning models that are beginning to incorporate cross-domain knowledge and generative AI have expanded what is possible.

Scientists at McMaster and MIT, for example, used an AI model to identify an antibiotic to combat a pathogen that the World Health Organization labeled one of the world’s most dangerous antibiotic-resistant bacteria for hospital patients. A Google DeepMind model can control plasma in nuclear fusion reactions, bringing us closer to a clean-energy revolution. Within health care, the US Food and Drug Administration has already cleared 523 devices that use AI—75% of them for use in radiology.

Reimagining science

At its core, the scientific process we all learned in elementary school will remain the same: conduct background research, identify a hypothesis, test it through experimentation, analyze the collected data, and reach a conclusion. But AI has the potential to revolutionize how each of these components looks in the future. 

Artificial intelligence is already transforming how some scientists conduct literature reviews. Tools like PaperQA and Elicit harness LLMs to scan databases of articles and produce succinct and accurate summaries of the existing literature—citations included.

Once the literature review is complete, scientists form a hypothesis to be tested. LLMs at their core work by predicting the next word in a sentence, building up to entire sentences and paragraphs. This technique makes LLMs uniquely suited to scaled problems intrinsic to science’s hierarchical structure and could enable them to predict the next big discovery in physics or biology. 

AI can also spread the search net for hypotheses wider and narrow the net more quickly. As a result, AI tools can help formulate stronger hypotheses, such as models that spit out more promising candidates for new drugs. We’re already seeing simulations running multiple orders of magnitude faster than just a few years ago, allowing scientists to try more design options in simulation before carrying out real-world experiments. 

Scientists at Caltech, for example, used an AI fluid simulation model to automatically design a better catheter that prevents bacteria from swimming upstream and causing infections. This kind of ability will fundamentally shift the incremental process of scientific discovery, allowing researchers to design for the optimal solution from the outset rather than progress through a long line of progressively better designs, as we saw in years of innovation on filaments in lightbulb design.

Moving on to the experimentation step, AI will be able to conduct experiments faster, cheaper, and at greater scale. For example, we can build AI-powered machines with hundreds of micropipettes running day and night to create samples at a rate no human could match. Instead of limiting themselves to just six experiments, scientists can use AI tools to run a thousand.

Scientists who are worried about their next grant, publication, or tenure process will no longer be bound to safe experiments with the highest odds of success; they will be free to pursue bolder and more interdisciplinary hypotheses. When evaluating new molecules, for example, researchers tend to stick to candidates similar in structure to those we already know, but AI models do not have to have the same biases and constraints. 

Eventually, much of science will be conducted at “self-driving labs”—automated robotic platforms combined with artificial intelligence. Here, we can bring AI prowess from the digital realm into the physical world. Such self-driving labs are already emerging at companies like Emerald Cloud Lab and Artificial and even at Argonne National Laboratory. 

Finally, at the stage of analysis and conclusion, self-driving labs will move beyond automation and, informed by experimental results they produced, use LLMs to interpret the results and recommend the next experiment to run. Then, as partners in the research process, the AI lab assistant could order supplies to replace those used in earlier experiments and set up and run the next recommended experiments overnight, with results ready to deliver in the morning—all while the experimenter is home sleeping.

Possibilities and limitations

Young researchers might be shifting nervously in their seats at the prospect. Luckily, the new jobs that emerge from this revolution are likely to be more creative and less mindless than most current lab work. 

AI tools can lower the barrier to entry for new scientists and open up opportunities to those traditionally excluded from the field. With LLMs able to assist in building code, STEM students will no longer have to master obscure coding languages, opening the doors of the ivory tower to new, nontraditional talent and making it easier for scientists to engage with fields beyond their own. Soon, specifically trained LLMs might move beyond offering first drafts of written work like grant proposals and might be developed to offer “peer” reviews of new papers alongside human reviewers. 

AI tools have incredible potential, but we must recognize where the human touch is still important and avoid running before we can walk. For example, successfully melding AI and robotics through self-driving labs will not be easy. There is a lot of tacit knowledge that scientists learn in labs that is difficult to pass to AI-powered robotics. Similarly, we should be cognizant of the limitations—and even hallucinations—of current LLMs before we offload much of our paperwork, research, and analysis to them. 

Companies like OpenAI and DeepMind are still leading the way in new breakthroughs, models, and research papers, but the current dominance of industry won’t last forever. DeepMind has so far excelled by focusing on well-defined problems with clear objectives and metrics. One of its most famous successes came at the Critical Assessment of Structure Prediction, a biennial competition where research teams predict a protein’s exact shape from the order of its amino acids. 

From 2006 to 2016, the average score in the hardest category ranged from around 30 to 40 on CASP’s scale of 1 to 100. Suddenly, in 2018, DeepMind’s AlphaFold model scored a whopping 58. An updated version called AlphaFold2 scored 87 two years later, leaving its human competitors even further in the dust.

Thanks to open-source resources, we’re beginning to see a pattern where industry hits certain benchmarks and then academia steps in to refine the model. After DeepMind’s release of AlphaFold, Minkyung Baek and David Baker at the University of Washington released RoseTTAFold, which uses DeepMind’s framework to predict the structures of protein complexes instead of only the single protein structures that AlphaFold could originally handle. More important, academics are more shielded from the competitive pressures of the market, so they can venture beyond the well-defined problems and measurable successes that attract DeepMind. 

In addition to reaching new heights, AI can help verify what we already know by addressing science’s replicability crisis. Around 70% of scientists report having been unable to reproduce another scientist’s experiment—a disheartening figure. As AI lowers the cost and effort of running experiments, it will in some cases be easier to replicate results or conclude that they can’t be replicated, contributing to a greater trust in science.

The key to replicability and trust is transparency. In an ideal world, everything in science would be open access, from articles without paywalls to open-source data, code, and models. Sadly, with the dangers that such models are able to unleash, it isn’t always realistic to make all models open source. In many cases, the risks of being completely transparent outweigh the benefits of trust and equity. Nevertheless, to the extent that we can be transparent with models—especially classical AI models with more limited uses—we should be. 

The importance of regulation

With all these areas, it’s essential to remember the inherent limitations and risks of artificial intelligence. AI is such a powerful tool because it allows humans to accomplish more with less: less time, less education, less equipment. But these capabilities make it a dangerous weapon in the wrong hands. Andrew White, a professor at the University of Rochester, was contracted by OpenAI to participate in a “red team” that could expose GPT-4’s risks before it was released. Using the language model and giving it access to tools, White found it could propose dangerous compounds and even order them from a chemical supplier. To test the process, he had a (safe) test compound shipped to his house the next week. OpenAI says it used his findings to tweak GPT-4 before it was released.

Even humans with entirely good intentions can still prompt AIs to produce bad outcomes. We should worry less about creating the Terminator and, as computer scientist Stuart Russell has put it, more about becoming King Midas, who wished for everything he touched to turn to gold and thereby accidentally killed his daughter with a hug. 

We have no mechanism to prompt an AI to change its goal, even when it reacts to its goal in a way we don’t anticipate. One oft-cited hypothetical asks you to imagine telling an AI to produce as many paper clips as possible. Determined to accomplish its goal, the model hijacks the electrical grid and kills any human who tries to stop it as the paper clips keep piling up. The world is left in shambles. The AI pats itself on the back; it has done its job. (In a wink to this famous thought experiment, many OpenAI employees carry around branded paper clips.)

OpenAI has managed to implement an impressive array of safeguards, but these will only remain in place as long as GPT-4 is housed on OpenAI’s servers. The day will likely soon come when someone manages to copy the model and house it on their own servers. Such frontier models need to be protected to prevent thieves from removing the AI safety guardrails so carefully added by their original developers.

To address both intentional and unintentional bad uses of AI, we need smart, well-informed regulation—on both tech giants and open-source models—that doesn’t keep us from using AI in ways that can be beneficial to science. Although tech companies have made strides in AI safety, government regulators are currently woefully underprepared to enact proper laws and should take greater steps to educate themselves on the latest developments.

Beyond regulation, governments—along with philanthropy—can support scientific projects with a high social return but little financial return or academic incentive. Several areas are especially urgent, including climate change, biosecurity, and pandemic preparedness. It is in these areas where we most need the speed and scale that AI simulations and self-driving labs offer. 

Government can also help develop large, high-quality data sets such as those on which AlphaFold relied—insofar as safety concerns allow. Open data sets are public goods: they benefit many researchers, but researchers have little incentive to create them themselves. Government and philanthropic organizations can work with universities and companies to pinpoint seminal challenges in science that would benefit from access to powerful databases. 

Chemistry, for example, has one language that unites the field, which would seem to lend itself to easy analysis by AI models. But no one has properly aggregated data on molecular properties stored across dozens of databases, which keeps us from accessing insights into the field that would be within reach of AI models if we had a single source. Biology, meanwhile, lacks the known and calculable data that underlies physics or chemistry, with subfields like intrinsically disordered proteins that are still mysterious to us. It will therefore require a more concerted effort to understand—and even record—the data for an aggregated database.

The road ahead to broad AI adoption in the sciences is long, with a lot that we must get right, from building the right databases to implementing the right regulations, mitigating biases in AI algorithms to ensuring equal access to computing resources across borders. 

Nevertheless, this is a profoundly optimistic moment. Previous paradigm shifts in science, like the emergence of the scientific process or big data, have been inwardly focused—making science more precise, accurate, and methodical. AI, meanwhile, is expansive, allowing us to combine information in novel ways and bring creativity and progress in the sciences to new heights.

Eric Schmidt was the CEO of Google from 2001 to 2011. He is currently cofounder of Schmidt Futures, a philanthropic initiative that bets early on exceptional people making the world better, applying science and technology, and bringing people together across fields.

text: Canada has once again expanded its Russia sanctions program, and the breadth of the latest round deserves careful attention from any business with cross-border exposure. On November 9, 2026, on the margins of the Group of Seven Foreign Ministers' Meeting in Paris, the Government of Canada announced the designation of 38 entities and 24 individuals under the Special Economic Measures (Russia) Regulations. The announcement describes the targets in general terms, spanning defence manufacturing, cyber activities and financial intermediaries, yet the list itself reaches well beyond weapons production to include consumer-facing banks, payment platforms, cryptocurrency exchanges and long-established scientific and research institutions, many of which serve ordinary commercial and civilian customers. As with prior rounds, the published listings identify names but offer no individualized reasons for each designation, leaving affected parties, and the businesses that deal with them, to infer the basis for the measures and to absorb the consequences in the meantime. Canada reports that, since 2014, it has sanctioned more than 3,500 individuals and entities and more than 700 vessels, and it has stated that it acts in concert with its allies and partners, which suggests that parallel measures from the United States, the United Kingdom and the European Union may follow. Each successive round widens the circle of companies and individuals who may find themselves exposed, not because of their own conduct, but because of a counterparty, a shareholder, a payment route or a supply chain several steps removed. The practical consequences of a designation rarely end with the announcement: assets may be frozen, transactions blocked midstream, contractual counterparties may invoke force majeure or termination rights, and authorities in several jurisdictions may open parallel inquiries. Companies and individuals affected by these measures, whether directly listed, linked through ownership or caught in a disrupted transaction, often face questions that require coordinated answers across Ottawa, Washington, London and Brussels, including whether a delisting petition is viable, whether a specific license can release a frozen payment, how to recover assets held by an intermediary, and how to respond to an inquiry from an enforcement authority, and those questions are best addressed early, with a clear record and a strategy that accounts for every jurisdiction involved. The full announcement from Global Affairs Canada is available here: https://t.co/TIRK7c0NDf #Sanctions #Russia #Canada #AssetRecovery #InternationalDisputes

text:
To receive The Algorithm in your inbox every Monday, sign up here.

Welcome to the Algorithm! 

Some technologists hope that one day we will develop a superintelligent AI system that people will be able to have conversations with. Ask it a question, and it will offer an answer that sounds like something composed by a human expert. You could use it to ask for medical advice, or to help plan a holiday. Well, that’s the idea, at least. 

In reality, we’re still a long way away from that. Even the most sophisticated systems of today are pretty dumb. I once got Meta’s AI chatbot BlenderBot to tell me that a prominent Dutch politician was a terrorist. In experiments where AI-powered chatbots were used to offer medical advice, they told pretend patients to kill themselves. Doesn’t fill you with a lot of optimism, does it? 

That’s why AI labs are working hard to make their conversational AIs safer and more helpful before turning them loose in the real world. I just published a story about Alphabet-owned AI lab DeepMind’s latest effort: a new chatbot called Sparrow.

DeepMind’s new trick to making a good AI-powered chatbot was to have humans tell it how to behave—and force it to back up its claims using Google search. Human participants were then asked to evaluate how plausible the AI system’s answers were. The idea is to keep training the AI using dialogue between humans and machines. 

In reporting the story, I spoke to Sara Hooker, who leads Cohere for AI, a nonprofit AI research lab.

She told me that one of the biggest hurdles in safely deploying conversational AI systems is their brittleness, meaning they perform brilliantly until they are taken to unfamiliar territory, which makes them behave unpredictably.

“It is also a difficult problem to solve because any two people might disagree on whether a conversation is inappropriate. And even if we agree that something is appropriate right now, this may change over time, or rely on shared context that can be subjective,” Hooker says. 

Despite that, DeepMind’s findings underline that AI safety is not just a technical fix. You need humans in the loop. 

In the long term, DeepMind hopes, having people steer the chatbot through dialogue could be a helpful tool for supervising machines. 

“We might have a discussion about what a machine is doing in a way that allows us to communicate what we actually want and not miss subtle things,” says Geoffrey Irving, a safety researcher at DeepMind. 

DeepMind’s model combines a lot of different strands of safety research into one model, with impressive results. You can read about it here. 

But let’s be real. Nobody is building these systems purely because they want customer service bots to have better tools to help you rebook your canceled flight. 

AI chatbots are powered by large language models, which produce human-sounding text by scraping vast amounts of writing from the internet. They could be a powerful tool for an entire new form of online search. 

There’s a lot of money to be made in improving search, which has really lost its mojo. Google search has become overpersonalized and overcommercialized. It’s also riddled with hidden scams and malware. 

Google is extremely anxious, too, about new competitors such as TikTok, which has quickly become Gen Z’s go-to source of information. That company is already offering a kind of search that the Googles of the world are trying to build: type in a question, and you’ll get tons of engaging content featuring actual humans. 

But there are legitimate questions about whether AI can ever compete with this, as my colleague Will Heaven wrote last March. 

Or as Emily Bender of the University of Washington, who studies computational linguistics and ethical issues in natural-language processing, put it in Will’s story: “The Star Trek fantasy—where you have this all-knowing computer that you can ask questions and it just gives you the answer—is not what we can provide and not what we need.” 

“It is infantilizing to say that the way we get information is to ask an expert and have them just give it to us,” Bender said.

Deeper Learning

This startup’s AI is smart enough to drive different types of vehicles

Wayve, a driverless car startup based in London, has made a single machine-learning model that can drive two different types of vehicles, a passenger car and a delivery truck—a first for the industry.

Watch out, Tesla: The breakthrough suggests that Wayve’s approach to autonomous vehicles might just scale up faster than the technology of mainstream companies like Cruise, Waymo, and Tesla. My colleague Will Heaven visited Wayve’s offices in London to check out the company’s new vehicle. Read more here. 

Bits and Bytes

How colleges use AI to monitor student protests. 
Colleges in the US are using Social Sentinel, a tool pitched as a way to help save students’ lives. Quelle surprise: it was used to surveil students. Following this investigation, one college has announced it is dropping the tool. (The Dallas Morning News) 

Clearview AI, used by police to find criminals, is now in public defenders’ hands.
The lawyer for a man accused of vehicular homicide used the controversial facial recognition software to prove his client’s innocence. (The New York Times)

Hated that video? YouTube’s algorithm might push you another just like it.
New research from Mozilla shows that user controls have little effect on which videos YouTube’s influential AI recommends. (MIT Technology Review)

The YouTube baker fighting back against deadly “craft hacks.”
More on moderation: Ann Reardon spends her time debunking dangerous activities that go viral on the platform—but the craze shows no signs of abating. (MIT Technology Review)

ISIS executions and nonconsensual porn are powering AI art.
The data sets behind AI art tools are full of problematic content, as I reportedin last week’s edition. Getty images has also ​​banned AI-generated images over fears of lawsuits. (Vice)

How AI art sees Los Angeles.
A lovely piece about what AI art generator Midjourney produces when descriptions of LA from literature are used as prompts. (LA Times)

That’s it from me. Catch you next week! 

Melissa

text:
Nvidia fought harder for China to get AI chips than China did, and Congress is finally shutting it down.

Jensen Huang's scandal ended the most successful lobbying run in tech, and Nvidia's own track record shows exactly why Washington stopped trusting it:

In May 2025, Jensen told a tech forum in Taipei that America's export controls were a failure. He said Nvidia's share of China's AI chip market had fallen from 95% to 50%.

Then came the lobbying:

Last year, the Senate passed the GAIN AI Act as part of the annual defense bill. It would've forced Nvidia and AMD to offer their best chips to American customers before selling to China.

Nvidia argued it would restrict global competition. On December 3, Jensen was on Capitol Hill, and that same day Bloomberg reported the bill had been left out of the final defense bill. Bloomberg's headline called it a lobbying win for Nvidia.

Then the China sales came back. Washington cleared Nvidia's H200 for China with the US government taking a 25% cut, and by May about 10 Chinese companies had been cleared to buy it, according to Reuters.

And then there's the part that should've ended the debate:

In August 2025, Nvidia's top lawyer emailed the Commerce Department agents investigating Megaspeed, a Singapore company suspected of helping move restricted chips into China, according to the New York Times. The agents refused to meet. Some officials saw the contact as a breach that could taint the case.

Megaspeed's Malaysian sister company bought at least $4.8 billion of Nvidia-based AI equipment between mid-2024 and early 2026. Alice Huang, the woman US intelligence reportedly believes was working for China, was an executive at Megaspeed.

And according to the classified memo the Times reported on, part of China's plan for her was to push Nvidia to lobby for China to get its most advanced chips.

That's the line I can't get past.

China's spy agency reportedly wanted Nvidia lobbying Washington on China's behalf. Nvidia was already doing it, in public, for its own reasons.

Nobody has shown that Jensen knew who she reportedly was, and he reportedly told the President he didn't.

But Congress has seen enough:

Both parties are backing a package of chip bills that could ride on the must-pass defense bill. That's the same kind of bill Nvidia got the GAIN AI Act cut from last year.

One would let Congress review and block advanced chip sales to adversaries the way it reviews arms sales, including sales the White House already approved.

Another would close the loophole that lets Chinese labs rent Nvidia's best chips in data centers outside China. The House passed that one 369 to 22 in January, and it's been stuck in the Senate ever since.

Nvidia spent a record $2.15 million on federal lobbying last quarter, and its filing lists both of those bills by name.

This time, Jensen isn't there to work the halls.

Jensen has argued for years that cutting China off just pushes it to build its own chips, and Huawei is trying to do exactly that. A company fighting for its biggest overseas market is doing what companies do. And punishing a company for its former CEO's personal life sets an ugly precedent.

My problem is what Nvidia was fighting to sell:

These are the chips that decide who leads in AI. Nvidia pushed to sell them to the country America's own intelligence officials worry about most, while its CEO was reportedly a target of that country's spy agency.

Nvidia reports earnings on Tuesday, its first report without Jensen as CEO.

So should a company that fought this hard to sell AI chips to China get ANY say in the rules from here?

text:
TWELVE HOURS IN THE JENSEN HUANG CASE FROM 10PM TO 10AM on 11/15/26

In this window the channel record widened again: the Wall Street Journal reported records showing Megaspeed arranged to send nearly $12 billion of top Nvidia chips to companies in China, a fifth chip figure with its own window, and reported an unwritten Nvidia rule capping partners' Chinese customers and a new channel node, Aolani Cloud. Megaspeed answered publicly for the first time on Alice Huang, saying she left the company effective August 30, 2025 and that it has retained outside counsel for an internal investigation. The Washington Post reported Huang is quietly helping pick his own successor, and Elon Musk said many of Nvidia's supply deals were a handshake with Huang personally.

A FIFTH CHIP FIGURE

• The Wall Street Journal reported that records it reviewed show Megaspeed arranged to send nearly $12 billion worth of top-of-the-line Nvidia chips to companies in China between March 2024 and June 2025, the shipment records showing orders for several hundred thousand chips. The records do not show how much of the hardware was actually delivered or where it originated.
• This is a fifth chip figure in the case, owned by the Journal with its own window. It is not merged or summed with the other four: the customs figure of at least $4.6 billion and at least 136,000 GPUs from 2023 to November 2025, the Speedmatrix reconstruction of $4.606 billion from December 2024 to January 2026, the $4.8 billion figure from June 2024 to February 2026, or the network figure of at least $7.5 billion and about 240,000 chips since 2023. The Journal's reporting rests on records it reviewed; the records themselves were not seen in the case record.

THE RULES NVIDIA SET, UNWRITTEN

• The Journal also reported that beginning last year Nvidia required many of its cloud partners outside China to keep their Chinese customers below a certain level, which has shifted between 30% and 49%, though the rule was not written into any contracts, people familiar with the matter said.
• Per the same reporting, Nvidia also urged some cloud partners to weed out Chinese nationals from top management and push out Chinese investors, the people said.

A NEW CHANNEL NODE

• The Journal reported that Aolani Cloud, a Singapore cloud-computing provider and Nvidia partner, courted investors last year saying the geopolitical situation provided a unique opportunity for companies that could connect Chinese customers with advanced chips, explaining in an investor presentation viewed by the Journal that top Chinese internet companies had to rent the chips they were blocked from buying.
• Per the Journal, Aolani's investors helped it fund some $2.5 billion in hardware in Malaysia by the beginning of this year, and its anchor customer is ByteDance. Aolani says it has systems in place to strictly adhere to U.S. regulations and has been focused on building a global customer base.

MEGASPEED ANSWERS

• Megaspeed told CNBC on Sunday, November 15, in an emailed statement: "Ms. Alice Huang officially left Megaspeed effective August 30, 2025 and currently has no role with the Company," adding "Megaspeed does not comment on Ms. Huang's personal and private matters." The August 30, 2025 date places her exit before the affair reporting broke in late October 2026.
• In the same statement, Megaspeed said media reports about its business, supply chain and global operations are not supported by verifiable evidence and that it has retained external legal counsel, no firm named, to conduct a "thorough internal investigation". It stated that it "designs and maintains its global operational and supply-chain control frameworks to comply with all applicable laws and regulatory regimes, including United States export control requirements", and added that it will review the reporting and communicate further with stakeholders as appropriate.
• The Journal separately reported that Megaspeed said this past week that it retained a U.S. law firm to lead a census of its graphics processing units, and that Megaspeed told the Journal it takes compliance seriously and is committed to following U.S. law, while Nvidia told the Journal it works to prevent smuggling. Whether the census engagement and the internal investigation are the same retention is not established by either report. This is Megaspeed's first statement announcing an internal investigation.

HUANG IN THE SUCCESSOR SEARCH

• The Washington Post reported on November 14 that Jensen Huang is quietly helping pick his own successor at Nvidia: he has kept a low profile since resigning on November 12, but he is involved in Nvidia's CEO search and has personally called at least one potential candidate. CFO Colette Kress serves as interim CEO.
• The Post report rests on a person familiar with the matter. The Post original is paywalled and was not read firsthand in the case record; the report was read through detailed carriages that agree verbatim on the load-bearing points. Huang's personal participation, if the Post's account is right, sits alongside the board's November 13 statement that it was still selecting a search firm and had not formally engaged any candidate.

MUSK ON THE HANDSHAKE DEALS

• Elon Musk posted on X on November 14: "Jensen drove supply chain brilliantly at Nvidia, but many of those deals were a handshake with Jensen, not a written contract. Without Jensen, at least some of those critical deals will be lost."
• That is Musk's assertion and prediction, stated as a directly involved market party and Huang supporter. No document or counterparty corroboration is offered, and the contract form of any Nvidia supply deal has not been verified in the case record. It lands against South Korea's statement in the prior window that Nvidia has reconfirmed its 260,000 GPU supply plan at the corporate level after the resignation.

THE CHECKPOINTS

• November 15: House Select Committee Chair John Moolenaar appears on Face the Nation at 10:30 a.m. ET on the Nvidia scandal and the AI chip war.
• November 17: Nvidia earnings, and the Warren and Coons records preservation confirmation is due.
• November 24: Bennet's answers due.
• December 1: Huang's requested closed door transcribed interview before the three House committees, and the House Foreign Affairs Democrats' answers due.
• December 2: Teter's requested closed door transcribed interview.
• December 3: Scott's requested public Senate Banking hearing with Huang, and the Foreign Affairs hearing with Under Secretary Kessler at 10 a.m.
• December 10: Scott's requested public Senate Banking hearing with Lutnick.

Yes, Mr @JhaSanjay , comparing @narendramodi with Jawaharlal Nehru is indeed an exercise in absurdity.

Nehru’s fascination with women and his romantic relationships have been extensively discussed by historians and biographers. His deeply affectionate relationship with Lady Edwina Mountbatten is well documented. His alleged romantic associations with Padmaja Naidu, Mridula Sarabhai, Devika Rani and Eslanda Robeson have also figured in various biographical accounts.

Books such as Stanley Wolpert’s Nehru: A Tryst with Destiny, Alex von Tunzelmann’s Indian Summer and Andrew Lownie’s The Mountbattens: Their Lives and Loves offer insights into Nehru’s personal life.

Narendra Modi and Jawaharlal Nehru had distinctly different priorities and personalities. While Modi remains focused on his national agenda, Nehru’s fascination with women has been a recurring subject of discussion among historians and biographers.

Nehru’s interactions with Jacqueline Kennedy and her daughter, was embarrassing for India. I believe you must also be aware of the remark attributed to John F. Kennedy that Nehru’s visit to Washington was the worst state visit of his presidency.

Therefore, Mr Jha, perhaps you are quite right in comparing Donald Trump with Jawaharlal Nehru, given the controversies surrounding their fondness for  women. Comparing Narendra Modi with Nehru rightly absurd.

text:
LATEST: Anthropic told the US Securities and Exchange Commission it expects to price its initial public offering (IPO) at $70 to $78 a share. A contract tracking the same shares trades at $101.65 on TradeXYZ, a venue built on Hyperliquid. That is 30% above the top of the range.

The contract is not a share. 

TradeXYZ's own documents say it carries no ownership, no IPO allocation and no claim on Anthropic. It settles in cash, allows up to 10x leverage, and its funding moves between traders. 

None of it goes to Anthropic.

The bigger change is funding. Before the listing, TradeXYZ runs the funding formula at a multiplier of 0.005. After the contract converts to Nasdaq pricing, the multiplier becomes 0.5. That is 100 times.

At today's base rate, a $10,000 long pays about 1.5 cents a day. After conversion, the same long pays about $1.50 a day. In an example where the contract trades 1% above its price feed, the daily bill goes from about $1.43 to about $142.50.

Anthropic expects to set its price on 18 November and start trading on 19th November, US Eastern time. TradeXYZ lists 20 November as its anticipated listing date.

The filing has Anthropic selling 801,351,354 shares and existing holders selling 23,648,646. 7 companies, including Google, Nvidia and Microsoft, have agreed to buy $26 billion more in a private placement at the IPO price.

There is a precedent on the same venue. In June, its Quantinuum contract fell from $97.43 to $59.64 in 1 day. Quantinuum priced at $60.

My call is Anthropic prices its IPO at $78 or higher, the top of its filed range. About 75%. I am wrong if the final prospectus on the SEC's EDGAR system shows a price below $78, or if no price is filed by 25th November 2026.

text:
Some landing pages ask for a decision before they've earned it. A bold headline, one line of copy, and a "Start your free trial" button.

If that one line doesn't show why the offer is worth trying, the page has skipped Desire.

In AIDA (Attention, Interest, Desire, Action), Desire is where "interesting" turns into "I want that." You get there by showing what the reader's day or business looks like with your offer in it, like a Monday morning when last week's invoices already went out.

Before you blame the button, run it through a three-question test called RAD:
• Require: Does the visitor have all the information they need to click?
• Acquire: Is the button easy to find and click?
• Desire: Do they actually want what the button promises?

If the answer to the first one is no, new button copy won't help. Go back to the page above it and fill in what's missing.

A new button colour won't answer a question the page never covered.

1 | Wise now operates 80 regulatory licenses and continues to add more, adding Chile and Thailand recently.

We're already operating 80 regulatory licenses and adding more, recently started operating in Chile and Thailand. We built technical connections to local interbank clearing systems. In this period, we went live as a member in the Malaysian real-time DuitNow system. That follows Japan and Brazil from the previous period.

We launched transfers for people in Thailand earlier this year. And now in September, we also gave our Thai customers access to the multi-currency Wise account along with the Wise Card. In Chile, we're rolling out services starting with transfers.

2 | Went live with Malaysia’ DuitNow and able to better service the customer base.

I share your excitement about Malaysia, I love the country and our -- and we've actually built up a nice, substantial customer base in Malaysia over the years, our direct customer base. We have Wise Platform partners, banks in Malaysia. So it is within Asia, Malaysia is a good -- quite meaningful substantial country that we serve. So connecting to their direct payment system, their QR code system is very good and interesting.

3 | 78% of transactions arrived <20 seconds, and average price is 0.49%, 3bps lower YoY.

Investing in this infrastructure means transfers are getting faster and cheaper for our customers and for our Wise Platform clients alike. In the last quarter, 78% of transactions arrived instantly in under 20 seconds in the recipient's bank account on the other side of the world. Such speed was unimaginable even a few years ago. Thanks to the efficiency and scale of our infrastructure, we brought our average price down to just 0.49% last quarter. That's down 3 basis points compared to a year earlier.

4 | Wise Platform  (B2B) continues to grow the fastest, +50% YoY and now is 6% of volumes vs 4% 18 months ago.

Wise Platform was also a highlight that it continued to be our fastest growing offering. In H1 '27, Wise Platform represents circa 6% of crossborder volume and delivered growth of nearly 50% YoY.

5 | Wise added new Wise platform partners and 2 large undisclosed North American banks in Q2, in addition to Morgan Stanley.

That's both adding new Wise platform partners, including Raiffeisen Bank, Standard Chartered, and Capitec on top of large partners increasing in their scale, likes of Morgan Stanley and Itau.

Further, in this period, we've added 2 large North American banks, including Morgan Stanley. This brings our coverage to 3 out of the top 20 North American banks live on platform.

For the 2 specific banks that you are mentioning, this is legacy banks that are joining the multitude of partners that we're having today.

6 | Added FX Forward hedging (up to 6 months) for business customers in the UK, approval tools for German businesses and accounting tools for Dutch and Belgian customers.

We are on the journey of making Wise Business more and more useful for larger, small businesses. This means supporting more sophisticated use cases, more accounting and approval flows. For example, we started rolling out the FX forwards feature in the U.K., which lets business customers lock an exchange rate up to 6 months ahead. An important threat for our business customers is how their international business banking on Wise is integrated to their local tooling. Accounting tools, for example. This quarter, we enabled syncing with DATEV for our German businesses and the local accounting tools for our Dutch and Belgian customers.

7 | Enabling FX forward hedging for UK business customers because they are getting bigger, and have more complicated cash flows and want to hedge their FX exposures, and because Wise already actively hedges for themselves, enabling this for their clients is easy.

I think I'd say you could try out the FX forward if you're a U.K. business customer. It is, like all of our features, we felt really simple. But it is indicative that our small business customers that we're serving are all getting bigger themselves, but also we're onboarding bigger and bigger small and medium businesses. And their cash flows are slightly more complicated, and they want to do slightly more sophisticated things with their -- with managing their cash flows. One is just having certainty on exchange rates so that they don't expose themselves into volatility and have more certainty in their business. So this is something that is easy for us to support them with. If we have probably one of the more sophisticated treasury operations of the world regarding to FX and the risk management features that we're using for ourselves, for our Wise Platform and our own client flows are very sophisticated already. So taking on the FX forwards thoughtfully is a small -- in some ways, a small step for our treasury team, but a big step for our customers.

8 | When Wise customers use it for cross-border payments, they tend to send and convert more, and become stickier.

our customers are using Wise for so much more. In H1 '27, for each $1 of cross-border volume sent or convert by Personal customers, they use Wise twice as much for all other activities, such as domestic transfers, cash payments, holding of assets or balances. And this is even more relevant for Business customers where from each $1 of cross-border volume, they use Wise 5x as much for all the activities, showing a strong adoption of our products.

9 | Wise incurred higher OPEX due to larger regulatory and compliance operations, and automation.

In H1 '27, servicing spent $251 million, up 15% versus H2 '26. A significant portion of this investment was related to regulatory and compliance operations as we build trusted compliance systems. We also focus on delivering an excellent experience to our customers. For this, we follow a hybrid approach supported by automation. In H1, circa 50% of customer service chatbot replies were automated. Our colleagues also leverage AI tools to increase the efficiency in their interactions with customers. In H1, 75% of inquiries received initial response within 60 seconds on live channels and 60 minutes on e-mail. And we resolved 95% of supported case within 12 hours, a 25% YoY increase.

10 | Wise Belgium subsidiary has agreed to a non-material settlement with the Brussel prosecutors with no admission of fault or wrongdoing.

Here, we announced today that we've been engaging -- Wise Belgium subsidiary have been engaging with our Brussels prosecutors in response to inquiries about our business. And an agreement has been reached to fully resolve and settle this matter with no admission of wrongdoing. So that's what we announced today.

Actually, the settlement, we agree with both parties that we will not disclose, but it was not material because, as you know, otherwise, we will have to disclose it to the market. So it's not material compared to the rest of our results today. The fact is we settled and we achieved an agreement with no admission of fault, which of wrongdoing, which is very important to us.

11 | Wise sees OPEX as an investment and want to be very efficient around it.

And on OpEx there, I really like the question because basically, it's also part of our philosophy and culture. We want to be e cient. We want to be disciplined. And OpEx is for us an investment. And as such, we really look at the return that we generate. And we think that in H1, we've been investing in a very ROI manner, and we want to continue to do so.

12 | Wise sees the elasticity on price reduction as long term, and don’t think they can do this in a sustainable manner, will consider cutting prices when they can.

The price reduction, as you know, the elasticity on price reduction is usually very long term. So I don't think that -- we always do this in a sustainable manner. So once we get the efficiency gain, when we are a clear view that these price adjustments are justified because of our cost structure and our discipline in terms of margin -- cost plus margin. So I will not put this directly in relation, but we will continue to consider price reduction where we -- when we see that we have the room to do this. I think this discipline is through the entire structure of our P&L. This is true for price adjustments. This is true for OpEx. So I don't -- I will not see this too critical.

13 | Wise invested more in R&D, with over 1,300 engineers, and deployments grew 57%. Added a second cloud hosting location to increase redundancy.

In H1 '27, we invested $292 million in tech development. We now have over 1,300 engineers deploying code. We are not just only growing our tech team, we are also implementing AI tools to increase the efficiency. In H1, our teams complete 45,000 deployments, an increase of 57% YoY. We also increased the redundancy of our infrastructure in H1 by adding a second cloud hosting location. We achieved this while still delivering efficiency in our transactional unit cost.

14 | Wise focused much more making its products safer with Wise Call, improving onboarding flow and costs

Our teams work to manage our risk profile, building tools that allow us to improve the resilience of our products and make our products even safer for customers. A couple of examples include financial crime detection with more targeted personal and business scams models and Wise Call Status, an update which allow customers to know if it is Wise who's speaking to them on the phone with the aim to reduce scams. Our teams also work really hard to drive scale and efficiency. For example, we recently deployed products to improve the onboarding flow for customers in Japan and in the U.S., significantly reducing the time it takes them to join Wise and the onboarding costs associated to -- with this. And very importantly, the aim of some of these is to drive growth. Kristo has already covered some examples in this section, but these would include the work needed to launch in Chile, our direct integrations in Malaysia, the launch of our products in Thailand, our [ Asian ] offering and many others. Lastly, we are continuing to invest in our core functions.

15 | Expect 2027 revenue growth to be 20%, and EBT margins at the high end of the 2025 range.

Before we conclude, I'd like to cover our margins and outlook. Income before tax was $335 million in H1 '27 with a margin of 22% as we seek to deliver margins in line with our medium-term targets. This margin demonstrates that it is possible to offer customers the best prices while investing into building a high pro table business. Our investment framework is evident in our financial projections. For 2027, we expect net revenue growth to be at the upper half of our medium-term guidance of 15% to 20%, and we continue to aim for full year margins around the high end of the 2025 range.

➡️ Key Takeaways on Wise $WISE 

Wise continues to grow its business of B2C with personal and business strongly across customers, volumes, spend, balances. Lower prices and take-rates are strategic to win more new, drive higher retention, and usage. Higher near-term reinvestment re-normalizes profitability back to long-term levels that are highly strategic to strengthening its growing cross-border payments infrastructure moat of over 70 licenses and soon to be 8 direct instant payment connections that is increasingly becoming difficult to replicate and compete against, with the strength in on/off ramps. B2B platforms are growing faster and Wise becomes the lowest cost provider powering the 2nd/3rd tier FIs and gradually extending that to the more dominant ones. Wise is almost the “Costco/Shopify” of Cross-Border Payments” building the cross-border payments infrastructure moat of a great enduring generational business.

She said the seventh thing customers should change is how they use vision insurance, because the allowance can quietly push prices up.

Most customers see a frame allowance and pick frames that use all of it. She said that's often a trap.

"Vision insurance plans often give you an allowance for frames and cover basic lenses, with extra costs for upgrades. People treat the allowance like free money and choose frames priced right at or above it, then pay extra for coatings."

She said here's what to do: ask for the store's cash price and compare it with your insurance price. Check whether your plan offers reimbursement for out-of-network or online purchases, and how to submit receipts.

"Sometimes the cash price at an online retailer was lower than the insured price at the store, even after insurance. Customers almost never asked."

She said read your plan.

"Every plan is different. Look up your plan's allowances, copays and out-of-network rules before you shop."

text:
She said the sixth thing customers should change is where they buy progressive lenses, because fit matters more than price.

Many people with progressives try to save money online. She said that's riskier.

"Progressive lenses have different zones for distance, middle and reading vision. They need precise measurements, including where your eyes sit in the frame. If the measurement is off, the lenses can feel uncomfortable or hard to use."

She said here's the safer approach: buy progressives from a store or retailer that takes in-person fitting measurements, or make sure the online retailer offers a strong remake guarantee.

"Progressives were the most common online purchase people came back to us to fix. Single-vision lenses online are usually easy. Progressives are trickier."

She said try warehouse clubs.

"Costco Optical and similar warehouse clubs often offer progressives at lower prices with in-person fittings. It can be a good middle ground."

text:
She said the fifth thing customers should change is choosing lens material by price alone, because the right material matters for some prescriptions.

Most customers don't know there are different lens materials. She said it's worth asking.

"Higher prescriptions can mean thick, heavy lenses. High-index lenses are thinner and lighter, which helps for strong prescriptions. Polycarbonate and Trivex are impact-resistant and commonly recommended for kids and sports."

She said here's when to spend more: if your prescription is strong, ask about high-index lenses. For children or active lifestyles, ask for impact-resistant materials.

"For mild prescriptions, I often told customers they didn't need the most expensive high-index lenses. For strong prescriptions, it made a big difference in comfort."

She said online stores offer these too.

"Many online retailers offer high-index and polycarbonate lenses at lower prices than stores. Compare the same material, not just the same frame."

text:
Traditional Zangbeto Ceremony Showcases Libation Ritual and Spinning Raffia Guardian in West Africa

A traditional West African spiritual ceremony featuring a Vodún priest spraying libation over a sacred red-robed figure before a tall, conical straw structure spins rapidly across an open sandy ground highlights the centuries-old cultural practices of the Zangbeto guardians.

During the ritual, a traditional priest takes a mouthful of local spirit from a glass bottle and sprays it over a red-robed shrine figure to invoke ancestral and spiritual forces. Moments after the libation is offered, a towering haystack-like figure constructed entirely of dried raffia strands begins to rotate at high speed across the sand without any visible human limbs or support.

Known as Zangbeto—a term in the Gun language that translates to "men of the night" or "night watchmen"—the figures hold a prominent place in the traditional governance and spiritual life of the Ogu (Egun) people across Benin, Togo, and southwestern Nigeria.

Among practitioners and local believers, the Zangbeto is revered not as a costumed performer, but as a physical vessel inhabited by nocturnal guardian spirits. Adherents maintain that there is no human being inside the dense raffia structure during its rapid, trance-like spinning dances.

To demonstrate this belief during public ceremonies, attendants frequently lift or overturn the spinning raffia cones, revealing an empty interior—or occasionally small symbolic objects, animals, or miniature statues—before the structure resumes its movement.

The act of spraying alcohol from the mouth over a red-robed figure serves as a traditional Vodún libation. In West African spiritual customs, liquid offerings such as locally distilled palm gin (sodabi or ogogoro) are used to purify the ritual space, awaken spiritual entities, and secure their protection for the community.

Historically, the Zangbeto society functioned as an indigenous night-watch and law-enforcement institution before the establishment of modern police forces. Today, the Zangbeto continues to operate alongside local authorities in many coastal communities, maintaining nocturnal order, deterring theft, settling disputes, and preserving ancestral heritage through public festivals and ceremonial displays.

text:
Ethiopia was Offered a Port at Tadjourah.  It Wanted More!

November 14, 2026

The Rejection that Exposed Ethiopia’s Red Sea Hallucination

By Ghidewon Abay Asmerom
@RedSeaBeacon 

An Offer that Exposed an Agenda

Imagine a government telling the world that its country’s economic survival depends on securing access to the sea. It repeatedly invokes its enormous population, growing economy, historical grievances, and national security needs. It warns that remaining landlocked is intolerable and portrays access to a neighboring country’s coastline as an existential necessity. Then, when a coastal neighbor offers it majority commercial participation in a modern port, supported by an established transport corridor, that government declines the proposal and reportedly demands additional territorial privileges.
This is not a hypothetical scenario. It is the contradiction exposed by Ethiopia’s response to Djibouti’s offer of the Port of Tadjourah.
Since October 2023, Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed and members of his government have increasingly presented maritime access as a matter of national survival, get or die. What began as an argument about the economic disadvantages of landlocked geography has evolved into a campaign involving pseudo-historical claims, demands for sovereign access, proposals for special corridors, and ambitions for a naval presence on the Red Sea. Ethiopia’s commercial interests have become entangled with a far more contentious proposition: that its economic and strategic needs justify exercising authority over territory belonging to its neighbors.
Djibouti’s offer of Tadjourah provided an opportunity to distinguish between these objectives. In August 2024, as Ethiopia’s controversial memorandum of understanding with Somaliland threatened to destabilize relations with Somalia, Djibouti proposed granting Ethiopia extensive management rights over Tadjourah, a modern port on the Gulf of Tadjourah. The proposal included access to an existing transport corridor toward the Ethiopian border and was intended to reduce transportation costs, diversify Ethiopia’s maritime gateways, and ease regional tensions (Maruf 2024; The Maritime Executive 2024).
Djibouti subsequently went further. According to statements made in April 2026 by Aboubakar Omar Hadi, chairman of the Djibouti Ports and Free Zones Authority, Ethiopia was offered a 60 percent stake in Tadjourah. Yet Addis Ababa declined the proposal, reportedly seeking additional corridor arrangements (Sheikh 2026). Subsequent reporting in September 2026 described an Ethiopian request for an extraterritorial corridor and a naval base, both of which Djibouti rejected (Diarra 2026).
Here, at last, was a practical test of Ethiopia’s repeated declarations. A neighboring country had offered substantial commercial participation in an existing port, yet the proposal was reportedly insufficient because Ethiopia wanted rights extending beyond the port itself.
The question is no longer whether Ethiopia needs access to the sea. The question is why access, even accompanied by majority commercial participation, was apparently not enough.
