text:
As ridiculous as this sounds, yes, it looks like Tesla is rushing this out just to win a bet against a YouTuber. Absolutely insane behavior. We've seen this movie before. In June 2025, Tesla did a single "autonomous delivery" of a Model Y to meet a Musk deadline, then never did it again.

Tesla always pitched the Cybercab as a vehicle for its Robotaxi network. Now, seven weeks before the deadline, a personal-use version shows up that's invite-only, Texas-only, banned from doing the one thing it was designed for, and attached to a subscription Musk himself says is too expensive. If you set out to build a product whose main job was letting Musk claim he won a Twitter bet, it would look a lot like this.

This Cybercab offering is completely broken. The value proposition is awful. As others have put it, it's a permanent variable-rate lease starting at $300 a month, with a ridiculous $30,000 down payment.

What do you get for this deal? A 2-seater vehicle that only works in small, incomplete, geo-fenced areas and has no steering wheel to do anything else with it. Meanwhile, Tesla insists that the Model Y, like the ones used in its current Robotaxi service alongside the Cybercab, uses the same self-driving technology.

You can buy one for $40,000, and you get a lot more car than the Cybercab; then you can pay $99 a month for FSD instead of $300 a month and that works everywhere with supervision. Tesla is supposed to let current Tesla owners drive without supervision in the same geo-fenced areas, which would basically be the same product as what Tesla is offering right now with the Cybertruck, but you are not a slave to Tesla, which can brick your car at any time or change the terms. Model Y has a steering wheel.

بِسْمِ اللهِ الرَّحْمٰنِ الرَّحِيْم
In the Name of God, Most Gracious, Most Merciful.
♥️🤲🕋♥️🕋🌹🌹🥀🤲🌹🕋♥️

TO THE TECHNOLOGY COMPANIES OF THE WORLD

The World Money Plan — A New Economic Architecture for the Age of AI and AGI

To the leaders, engineers, innovators, and creators of artificial intelligence,

The power of a story is sometimes all you need to redesign an entire system.

We are entering an extraordinary age. Artificial intelligence is already here, and AGI may fundamentally change how we produce goods, deliver services, operate businesses, and organize our economies.

But there is something missing from this revolution.

A new monetary architecture that connects technological progress directly to human participation and ownership.

That is what I am building through the World Money Plan.

🌐 https://t.co/TnDBOj7UEC

The gears of creation need a new kind of lubrication

Think about the machinery of the coming AI economy.

We have artificial intelligence, robotics, automated factories, intelligent supply chains, and systems capable of managing enormous amounts of economic activity.

These are the gears of creation.

But gears need lubrication.

And in this new economy, that lubrication must include a redesigned monetary system, intelligent subsidies, and financial incentives that flow directly into the machinery of innovation while creating value for the people who sustain it.

We cannot simply automate the world and leave humanity outside the ownership structure.

Every transaction should become an opportunity for participation.

Every purchase should contribute to an economic record.

Every consumer should have an opportunity to build ownership in the businesses and systems they support.

And every company participating in this architecture should understand that sharing economic value is not necessarily a loss.

It can become the foundation of a more efficient, more resilient, and more prosperous business model.

From transactions to ownership

Today, money primarily moves between consumers, businesses, banks, and financial institutions.

You purchase something. The business receives payment. The transaction is recorded, and the economic relationship often ends there.

But AI gives us an opportunity to redesign that relationship.

Imagine a system where transactions are connected to an intelligent economic ledger.

Where consumer participation creates measurable value.

Where businesses can offer digital ownership, shares, savings, or other economic benefits in exchange for sustained participation.

Where AI helps manage supply and demand, reduce unnecessary costs, and strengthen the entire supply chain.

This is the vision behind the Brand Currency System — BCS.

From spending to participation. From participation to ownership. From ownership to a decentralized economic future.

We are not simply redesigning banking.

We are redesigning how money creates value, how that value is recorded, and who gets to participate in the wealth generated by the next industrial revolution.

An invitation to collaborate

To the technology companies willing to participate:

I am inviting you to help build this future.

Your technologies, your engineering capabilities, and your investments can become part of a new economic architecture.

And companies that participate may discover that their balance sheets become lighter as unnecessary costs, inefficient intermediaries, and outdated business models are eliminated.

We can build systems that are more efficient.

We can create new markets.

We can connect consumers and producers more directly.

We can introduce economic incentives that reward participation rather than simply extracting value.

And we can collaborate to build a brighter future together.

Efficiency. Efficiency. Efficiency.

We will not repeat the mistakes of the robber barons

The Industrial Revolution created extraordinary wealth.

But it also produced an era of child labor, dangerous working conditions, extreme economic concentration, and workers struggling for basic protections.

We cannot allow artificial intelligence to repeat that history.

We cannot build machines capable of transforming civilization while leaving ordinary people fighting for the right to participate in the wealth those machines generate.

This time, ownership must be part of the architecture from the beginning.

To the technology companies that want a brighter future for humanity, my invitation is open.

And to those who simply want to become the robber barons of the AI revolution, concentrating the benefits of progress while everyone else is left behind:

That is your choice. You can ignore this invitation.

Some of you have never participated in these conversations anyway.

But understand something.

I will continue building this vision with or without you.

I do not need every technology company to agree with me.

I need people who are willing to imagine something better, challenge the existing system, and help develop an alternative.

If your company does not want to participate, we will seek collaborators, competitors, independent developers, researchers, and businesses that do.

The future does not belong exclusively to the largest balance sheets.

A brighter future for all creation

This is not simply about making human beings wealthier.

It is about designing an economic system that creates a better world.

For human beings.

For animals.

For the environment.

For the planet.

For future generations.

A system where technology reduces waste, improves efficiency, protects resources, strengthens communities, and creates opportunities for people to participate in the economic value they help generate.

We need to change how we understand money itself.

Money cannot remain merely a medium of exchange while AI and AGI transform everything around it.

We need to explore how monetary transactions can become instruments of participation, accountability, savings, ownership, and long-term economic security.

And we need to build the systems that make those possibilities real.

The World Money Plan is now open

I am beginning in the United States.

But this is a vision for the world.

I am inviting technology companies, AI developers, financial innovators, economists, engineers, businesses, and ordinary human beings to participate.

Bring your ideas.

Challenge my proposals.

Help design the architecture.

Help create the financial mechanisms.

Help build the technology.

We do not have to agree on everything to begin working toward something better.

And if you believe you have a better idea, I want to hear it.

Because this is not about protecting my ideas.

It is about finding the best ideas and building a future that works for everyone.

The age of AI is here.

The age of AGI may be approaching.

The question is no longer simply what these technologies can accomplish.

The question is who will own the future they create.

I have made my choice.

I am building toward a future where humanity participates, where economic power becomes more decentralized, and where the benefits of technological progress are shared more widely.

You are welcome to join me.

And if you choose not to, the work will continue.

A brighter future for humanity, for animals, for the environment, and for all creation.

Let's build it together.

Omar Arizona
The Office of the Superuser
Founder, World Money Plan

text:
Today’s Doomer -Baby Boomer Connection

We have all heard this story. Drive through enough of small-town America, and you will see the graveyards of the American Dream. Not the ones with tombstones, but the ones with boarded-up storefronts, abandoned factories, empty schools, and Main Streets that look like the last person to leave forgot to turn off the lights. These towns were once the backbone of America. 

They had textile mills, furniture factories, machine shops, steel plants, and manufacturing businesses that employed generations of families. A young man could graduate from high school, find a good-paying job, buy a house, raise his children, and live his entire life in the community where he was born. Billy Joel wrote a song about it. Allentown was not some fictional place; Billy was right outside it when he wrote it.

Then came the Baby Boomer deindustrialization, automation, globalization, and the great migration of American manufacturing overseas. The factories closed, the jobs disappeared, and the young people followed the money to the cities. The towns were left behind, and the people who stayed watched their communities slowly deteriorate. For decades, politicians have promised to bring those jobs back.

Now, something extraordinary is happening. America is entering another industrial revolution, this time much bigger, driven by artificial intelligence, and the infrastructure required to power it represents an enormous economic opportunity for the very communities that previous economic revolutions abandoned. And wouldn’t you know it? The Doomers have arrived to tell these towns they should reject it. Notice how Doomer rhymes with Boomer.

Consider Maiden, North Carolina, a community devastated by the disappearance of Carolina Mills and approximately 3,500 jobs. In 2009, Apple announced plans to construct a data center there, initially promising around 50 jobs. Today, that operation employs approximately 400 people. According to PBS, the additional tax revenue helped lower property taxes while supporting a new town hall, fire and police stations, and a community center. Imagine that. A technology company arrived in a struggling community, invested in its future, and helped rebuild the local tax base. What a tragedy for the people who prefer their economic development to remain hypothetical.

Then there is Richland Parish, Louisiana, where Meta is constructing its enormous Hyperion data center campus. The project has generated so much construction-related tax revenue that eligible certified school employees received bonuses exceeding $50,000 in 2026. 

Think about that for a moment. Teachers in a rural Louisiana parish received bonuses that could change their families’ financial futures because an AI company decided to build infrastructure in their community. Those particular tax revenues may decline when construction ends, but the immediate economic impact is undeniable. And yet we are watching an increasingly vocal movement attempt to frighten communities away from precisely these opportunities.

The objections are familiar. Data centers consume electricity, require cooling, create noise, and occupy land. All legitimate considerations, but since when did Americans decide that engineering challenges were reasons to surrender economic opportunities? Small-town America has something that many metropolitan areas lack: available land, often far from dense residential neighborhoods. 

Suitable sites can accommodate large infrastructure projects without placing industrial equipment next to someone’s bedroom window. Modern cooling technologies can reduce water consumption, while thoughtful siting and noise-control requirements can protect nearby residents.

The financial arrangements should be equally straightforward. If an AI company wants to build a multibillion-dollar facility, it should pay its fair share of the electricity infrastructure, protect existing customers from higher rates, account for its water consumption, and negotiate substantial long-term financial benefits for the surrounding community. 

Local governments should be negotiating from a position of opportunity, not desperation. These companies need land, electricity, infrastructure, and cooperative communities. That gives small towns something valuable to bring to the negotiating table. This could be a total flip where the big cities fall into decay, and the small ones now flourish.

And the benefits extend beyond the people employed inside the data center. Construction requires electricians, plumbers, engineers, contractors, equipment operators, and countless supporting businesses. Those workers need restaurants, grocery stores, housing, mechanics, and services. 

Some of that construction activity is temporary, but the infrastructure, skills, and commercial relationships it creates can provide foundations for further growth. Most importantly, it offers something that cannot be measured simply by counting jobs or calculating tax receipts. It gives young people a reason to stay.

A son should not have to leave his hometown to find economic opportunity. A daughter should not have to move hundreds of miles away to build a career. Families should have the opportunity to remain together, raise children near grandparents, and invest their lives in the communities they love. The Industrial Revolution created towns. The decline of American industry destroyed many of them. The AI infrastructure revolution now offers some of those communities a chance to write another chapter. The Rust Belt has the power now; they are the ones holding the cards.

Two centuries ago, the Luddites tried to resist the machinery transforming their economy. Their concerns about livelihoods were real, but history did not stop advancing because they opposed the machines. The Luddites were on the wrong side of history, and so are today’s Doomers. Today’s AI Doomers face a similar historical crossroads. They can help communities demand responsible development and a fair share of the prosperity, or they can make opposition to progress their contribution to American history.

I would much rather see a once-abandoned Main Street filled with businesses again, schools attracting teachers, young families buying homes, and grandparents watching their grandchildren grow up down the road. If AI can help make that possible, I suspect the people living in those towns will find the future considerably more appealing than another lecture about why they should be afraid of it. 

There will be a reverse migration as people leave the big cities for rural small-town America. Take it from somebody who has already made the transition: my wife and I have a better quality of life. We do not miss the traffic.

text:
BLACK  AMERICAN HISTORY
On this day, Nov 15, 1830

North Carolina Mandates Death Sentence for Dissemination of Anti-Slavery Pamphlet

On November 15, 1830, North Carolina passed two laws designed to limit the influence of an anti-slavery pamphlet and discourage its dissemination, mandating the punishment of death for those who twice violated the law. About a year earlier, in September 1829, David Walker, a free Black abolitionist and activist living in Boston, published An Appeal to the Coloured Citizens of the World. The anti-slavery pamphlet advocated for racial equality and called for free and enslaved Black people to actively challenge injustice, racial oppression, and the institution of slavery.

The Appeal was the first published document to demand the immediate and uncompensated emancipation of enslaved people in America. Mr. Walker also indirectly targeted his pamphlet to white readers, urging them to cease their inhumane treatment of enslaved people.

The pamphlet was quickly and clandestinely circulated among Black people, especially in the South, inciting anger among many white people and sometimes swift and harsh punishment. Jacob Cowan, a literate enslaved man in North Carolina, was sold “downriver” to Alabama after he was caught with 200 copies of the pamphlet for distribution to other enslaved people in the community. Copies of the pamphlet found by Southern officials were destroyed, the Georgia offered a bounty for Mr. Walker’s capture, and several Southern states—like North Carolina—eventually passed laws to further oppress both enslaved and free Black people.

Titled "An Act to Prevent the Circulation of Seditious Publications," North Carolina's first law banned bringing into the state any publication that white officials deemed might inspire revolution or resistance among enslaved or free Black people. A first violation of the law was punishable by whipping and one-year imprisonment, while those convicted of a second offense would “suffer death without benefit of clergy.”

The second law forbade all persons in the state from teaching the enslaved to read and write. A white person convicted of violating the law would be subject to a $100-$200 fine or imprisonment; a free Black person would face a fine, imprisonment, or between 20 and 39 lashes; and an enslaved Black person convicted of teaching other enslaved people to read or write would receive 39 lashes.

text:
🥤 COKE vs PEPSI: 100 moments from the greatest marketing war in history

🏁 THE ORIGINS

𝟏. 1886: pharmacist John Pemberton creates Coca-Cola in Atlanta, USA 🇺🇸

𝟐. The famous Coca-Cola script logo was drawn by Pemberton's bookkeeper, Frank Mason Robinson

𝟑. 1893: pharmacist Caleb Bradham creates "Brad's Drink" in New Bern, North Carolina

𝟒. 1898: Brad's Drink is renamed Pepsi-Cola

𝟓. Coca-Cola's Asa Candler was an early master of free-sample coupons, handing out millions of them

𝟔. 1915: the contour bottle is designed so you could recognise a Coke even in the dark or broken on the ground

𝟕. 1923: Pepsi goes bankrupt after a crash in sugar prices

𝟖. Pepsi was reportedly offered to Coca-Cola more than once in its early years. Coke said no every time

𝟗. 1931: candy firm Loft buys Pepsi, after Coca-Cola refused to give it a discount on syrup

𝟏𝟎. 1934: Pepsi sells a 12 oz bottle for 5 cents, twice as much drink as Coke's 6.5 oz for the same nickel

𝟏𝟏. 1939: "Pepsi-Cola hits the spot, twelve full ounces, that's a lot" becomes one of the first jingles aired nationwide on US radio

𝟏𝟐. 1945: Coca-Cola registers "Coke" as a trademark, after years of discouraging the nickname

🎖️ WAR, SANTA & THE 1950s

𝟏𝟑. 1929: Coca-Cola launches "The Pause That Refreshes"

𝟏𝟒. 1931: artist Haddon Sundblom paints a warm, jolly Santa for Coke ads. He didn't invent Santa, but he defined his modern look 🎅

𝟏𝟓. WWII: Coke boss Robert Woodruff promises every American in uniform a Coke for 5 cents, wherever they are

𝟏𝟔. Dozens of bottling plants were shipped overseas during the war, laying the base for Coke's global empire

𝟏𝟕. In the 1940s Pepsi adopts red, white and blue on its bottle cap

𝟏𝟖. 1947: Pepsi hires a dedicated team led by Edward Boyd to market to Black consumers, years ahead of rivals

𝟏𝟗. 1949: Pepsi's slogan is "More Bounce to the Ounce"

𝟐𝟎. 1950s: film star Joan Crawford, wife of Pepsi CEO Alfred Steele, promotes Pepsi on her travels and later joins its board

𝟐𝟏. 1955: McDonald's starts serving Coca-Cola, a partnership that still stands

𝟐𝟐. 1959: Pepsi's Donald Kendall hands Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev a Pepsi at the Moscow exhibition. The photo goes around the world 📸

🌍 THE GLOBAL RACE

𝟐𝟑. 1963: "Come alive! You're in the Pepsi Generation" starts selling a lifestyle instead of a drink

𝟐𝟒. 1963: Coca-Cola answers with "Things Go Better with Coke"

𝟐𝟓. 1965: Pepsi merges with Frito-Lay to form PepsiCo

𝟐𝟔. 1968: Coke enters Israel 🇮🇱, and an Arab League boycott keeps it out of much of the Arab world for decades, leaving the region to Pepsi

𝟐𝟕. 1972: Pepsi signs a deal with the USSR and becomes one of the first Western consumer brands produced there 🇷🇺

𝟐𝟖. Since the rouble couldn't be converted, Pepsi was paid with the rights to sell Stolichnaya vodka in the US 🍸

𝟐𝟗. 1989: Pepsi receives 17 old Soviet submarines, a cruiser, a frigate and a destroyer in a barter deal, and sells them for scrap

𝟑𝟎. That deal sparked the famous joke that Pepsi briefly owned one of the world's largest navies ⚓

𝟑𝟏. 1977: Coca-Cola leaves India 🇮🇳 rather than reveal its formula under new rules

𝟑𝟐. Pepsi enters India in 1988. Coke returns in 1993 and buys the hugely popular local cola Thums Up

𝟑𝟑. Coca-Cola is now sold in over 200 countries and territories. Cuba 🇨🇺 and North Korea 🇰🇵 are the famous exceptions

⚔️ THE PEPSI CHALLENGE & NEW COKE

𝟑𝟒. 1975: Pepsi launches the Pepsi Challenge in Dallas, a blind taste test in malls and supermarkets

𝟑𝟓. More people picked Pepsi in the blind sips, and Pepsi put those results on TV

𝟑𝟔. Critics, including author Malcolm Gladwell, argued a sweeter drink wins a single sip but not a whole can

𝟑𝟕. 1982: Diet Coke launches, the first product to carry the Coca-Cola name. It's an instant hit

𝟑𝟖. Shaken by the taste tests, Coca-Cola secretly develops a sweeter formula

𝟑𝟗. April 23, 1985: New Coke replaces the original recipe

𝟒𝟎. Coke reportedly receives around 400,000 angry calls and letters

𝟒𝟏. Pepsi gives its staff a day off to celebrate

𝟒𝟐. Pepsi boss Roger Enrico runs a newspaper ad claiming "the other guy blinked", and later uses it as the title of his book

𝟒𝟑. July 11, 1985: after 79 days, the original returns as "Coca-Cola Classic"

𝟒𝟒. The comeback made headlines everywhere, and some called New Coke the best mistake Coca-Cola ever made

𝟒𝟓. 1985: the war goes to space 🚀 Both cans fly aboard Space Shuttle Challenger in specially designed dispensers

𝟒𝟔. 2004: a brain-scan study found people preferred Pepsi blind, but once they knew it was Coke, brain areas tied to memory lit up 🧠

⭐ CELEBRITY WARS

𝟒𝟕. 1983: Pepsi signs Michael Jackson for a reported $5 million, a record celebrity deal at the time

𝟒𝟖. January 1984: Jackson's hair catches fire while filming a Pepsi ad 🔥

𝟒𝟗. 1984: Pepsi becomes "The Choice of a New Generation"

𝟓𝟎. 1986: Coca-Cola hires Max Headroom, the stuttering computer-generated host, for "Catch the Wave"

𝟓𝟏. 1989: Pepsi pulls Madonna's "Like a Prayer" ad after controversy over her music video, but lets her keep the reported $5 million

𝟓𝟐. 1990: Ray Charles sings "You got the right one, baby, uh-huh!" for Diet Pepsi 🎹

𝟓𝟑. 1992: supermodel Cindy Crawford's Pepsi Super Bowl ad becomes one of the most famous commercials ever

𝟓𝟒. 2002: Britney Spears stars in Pepsi's "Joy of Pepsi" Super Bowl ad

𝟓𝟓. 2004: Beyoncé, Britney Spears and Pink fight as gladiators to "We Will Rock You" for Pepsi

𝟓𝟔. Pepsi built a football squad of stars, including David Beckham, Ronaldinho and Lionel Messi ⚽

𝟓𝟕. 2017: Pepsi pulls its Kendall Jenner ad within about 24 hours after a global backlash

𝟓𝟖. 2019: "Is Pepsi OK?" with Steve Carell, Lil Jon and Cardi B pokes fun at people asking for Coke

🏆 SPORTS & MEGA EVENTS

𝟓𝟗. Coca-Cola has sponsored the Olympics since Amsterdam 1928, one of the longest partnerships in sport 🇳🇱

𝟔𝟎. Coke has been a FIFA partner since the 1970s and later sponsored the World Cup Trophy Tour 🏆

𝟔𝟏. 1996: Pepsi answers Coke's official Cricket World Cup sponsorship in India with "Nothing Official About It" 🏏

𝟔𝟐. 1996: the Olympics are held in Atlanta, Coca-Cola's hometown

𝟔𝟑. 2013–2022: Pepsi is the title sponsor of the Super Bowl Halftime Show 🏈

𝟔𝟒. 2002–2014: judges on American Idol drink from big red Coca-Cola cups on screen

𝟔𝟓. 2021: Cristiano Ronaldo moves two Coke bottles aside at a Euro 2020 press conference and holds up water 💧

📺 ICONIC ADS & SLOGANS

𝟔𝟔. 1971: "I'd Like to Buy the World a Coke" is filmed on a hilltop in Italy 🇮🇹

𝟔𝟕. The jingle was rewritten as "I'd Like to Teach the World to Sing" and became a hit record for The New Seekers

𝟔𝟖. 1969: Coca-Cola launches "It's the Real Thing"

𝟔𝟗. 1979: "Mean" Joe Greene tosses his jersey to a kid who gave him a Coke, and the ad wins a Clio award

𝟕𝟎. 1982: Coca-Cola's slogan is "Coke Is It!"

𝟕𝟏. 1993: CGI polar bears debut in "Always Coca-Cola" 🐻‍❄️

𝟕𝟐. 1995: the glowing Christmas trucks of "Holidays Are Coming" hit TV screens 🚚

𝟕𝟑. 1995: a Pepsi Super Bowl ad shows a Coke delivery driver sneaking a Pepsi in a diner

𝟕𝟒. 2009: "Open Happiness". 2016: "Taste the Feeling". 2021: "Real Magic"

𝟕𝟓. 2010: Coke's "Happiness Machine" video, a vending machine that hands out gifts, goes viral

𝟕𝟔. 2011: Share a Coke puts first names on bottles, starting in Australia 🇦🇺

𝟕𝟕. Pepsi's slogans include "Generation Next", "The Joy of Cola" and "Live for Now"

𝟕𝟖. 1985: Back to the Future features Pepsi Free, and 2015 brings a real "Pepsi Perfect" for fans 🎬

🛒 THE EMPIRE WARS

𝟕𝟗. Coke's Tab (1963) vs Pepsi's Diet Pepsi (1964) starts the diet-cola war

𝟖𝟎. Pepsi Max (1993) vs Coca-Cola Zero (2005): the battle for sugar-free fans

𝟖𝟏. Pepsi buys Mountain Dew in 1964. Coke answers with Mello Yello in 1979

𝟖𝟐. Juice: Coke buys Minute Maid in 1960. Pepsi buys Tropicana in 1998 🍊

𝟖𝟑. Water: Pepsi's Aquafina (1994) vs Coke's Dasani (1999) 💧

𝟖𝟒. Sports drinks: Coke's Powerade (1988) vs Gatorade, which Pepsi got by buying Quaker Oats in 2001

𝟖𝟓. Fast food: Pepsi once owned Pizza Hut, Taco Bell and KFC, and spun them off in 1997 🍕

𝟖𝟔. Coffee & soda: Coke buys Costa Coffee in 2019 ☕, Pepsi buys SodaStream in 2018

𝟖𝟕. Thanks to snacks like Lay's and Doritos, PepsiCo's revenue (about $92B in 2024) is nearly double Coca-Cola's (about $47B) 💰

𝟖𝟖. Yet Coca-Cola is usually ranked the more valuable brand, and Coke the far bigger cola

𝟖𝟗. 2010: Diet Coke overtakes Pepsi as America's No. 2 soda

𝟗𝟎. 2024: Dr Pepper also reportedly passes Pepsi in US sales

💥 BLUNDERS & CURIOSITIES

𝟗𝟏. 1992: Pepsi's "Number Fever" in the Philippines 🇵🇭 prints the winning number 349 on around 800,000 caps, sparking protests

𝟗𝟐. 1992: Crystal Pepsi, a clear cola, flops within about two years

𝟗𝟑. Coca-Cola's Tab Clear was launched alongside it, and a Coke executive later said it was designed to sink Crystal Pepsi

𝟗𝟒. 1996: Pepsi paints its cans and an Air France Concorde blue ✈️

𝟗𝟓. A Pepsi ad jokingly offered a Harrier jet for 7 million points. A student tried to claim it, and a court ruled it was a joke (1999)

𝟗𝟔. 2006: a Coca-Cola employee tries to sell Coke's secrets to Pepsi for $1.5 million. Pepsi tips off Coca-Cola and the FBI 🕵️

𝟗𝟕. 2008: Pepsi's new logo comes with a 27-page design document comparing it to the Mona Lisa and the Earth's magnetic field

𝟗𝟖. 2010: Pepsi skips Super Bowl ads for the first time in 23 years to fund the Pepsi Refresh Project

𝟗𝟗. Coke's secret formula is kept in a vault on display at the World of Coca-Cola museum in Atlanta 🔐

𝟏𝟎𝟎. After more than a century, the war still sells billions of drinks a day around the world 🌍

North Carolina’s Jamie Ager campaigned on a public health care option

North Carolina Democrat Jamie Ager, an incoming freshman congressman who campaigned on creating a public health insurance option, called the Obamacare insurance plans offered to members of Congress "terrible" during a Thursday evening panel, eliciting groans from the audience.

The panel, titled "Freshman Orientation" and moderated by comedian Alex Edelman, was part of the What's Next summit, a political conference in Denver examining how Democrats swept the midterm elections and how they can expand their majorities in 2028. 

Edelman asked the group of incoming representatives what perks they would receive as members of Congress. 

Ager instead offered a complaint.

Unlike you, Ms. Swift has the following, and you'll never have anything like it.  Just you, your English Lit degree, and your pathological envy.  

NYU awarded Ms. Swift an honorary Doctor of Fine Arts, a Ph.D, in recognition of her major cultural, artistic, and humanitarian achievements.

NYU’s reasoning was detailed at the graduation ceremony.

Artistic & Commercial Impact: NYU described her as "one of the most prolific and celebrated artists of her generation". The university specifically cited her historic milestones, including being the only female artist to win Album of the Year at the Grammys three times (she has since won a 4th, the only person ever to do so) and the only solo artist this century to have three albums reach No. 1 in a single year.

Advocacy for Artists' Rights: During the ceremony, NYU praised her "commitment to speaking out forcefully, eloquently, and effectively on behalf of all artists". This referred to her high-profile public battles over music ownership, streaming royalties, and re-recording her master catalog.

Philanthropy & Anti-Discrimination Advocacy: The official citation recognized her work as a philanthropist and highlighted her "fierce advocacy for protection of those facing discrimination".

Global Cultural Reach: Jason King noted that she "crossed genres, demographics, age groups, and borders of all kinds to touch lives around the globe".

Beyond the formal citation, NYU already had an active academic tie to Swift’s career. Just months before the ceremony, NYU’s Clive Davis Institute of Recorded Music launched an official college course dedicated to analyzing her songwriting, business strategy, and cultural influence.

Her lyrics are also the subject of courses offered by prestigious universities such as Harvard, Duke, and Stanford.

You can refer to her as Dr. Swift in the future. It's the proper honorific for someone who holds a Ph.D.

🚨| Former Liberty Media CEO Predicts F1's Stock Market Exit:

— Greg Maffei, former CEO of Liberty Media, has forecasted that Formula 1 might vanish from the stock exchange within the next two years. He attributes this potential move to the sport's rapid commercial growth since Liberty Media's acquisition in 2017. Speaking to media, Maffei explained:

“I'll say F1 is gone.”

— Maffei elaborated on the reasons behind his prediction, noting the significant financial growth F1 has experienced under Liberty Media's stewardship. He remarked:

“The easy money's been made. The EBITDA is up 3x in eight or nine years. It's not going to go up 3x again in the next eight or nine years.”

— Despite the impressive growth, Maffei believes the pace will slow down. He pointed out that Liberty Media's expansion strategies, such as increasing the race calendar and tapping into new markets, have reached their limits. He commented:

“There is now less scope to drive growth through those same measures.”

— Maffei also mentioned the recent changes in Liberty Media's leadership, with John Malone stepping down as chairman emeritus and his voting power significantly reduced. This shift could influence future decisions regarding the company's holdings. Maffei noted:

“Any offer for Liberty Media would now be a matter for its board.”

— Under Liberty Media, F1's commercial value has soared, with the Formula One Group now valued at nearly $28 billion. The sport's revenue has seen substantial increases, reaching $3.9 billion in 2025, a 14% rise from the previous year. Analysts credit this growth to factors like the cost cap, expansion into US markets, and the success of Netflix's "Drive to Survive."

— The addition of MotoGP to Liberty Media's portfolio in 2025 further bolstered its motorsport holdings. However, Maffei remains cautious about future growth prospects, emphasizing the need for new strategies to sustain momentum.

CAIR IS THINKING ABOUT 2028. ARE REPUBLICANS EVEN AWAKE?
CAIR — the Council on American-Islamic Relations — has become a significant political and advocacy organization in America. Its critics have raised questions about its political influence, its response to criticism, and its efforts to shape the national conversation surrounding Islam and American politics.
Florida has classified CAIR as a 'Terrorist Group!'

CAIR has reportedly attacked Pastor Jack Hibbs for bringing attention to the election of 255 Muslim Americans to public office in the midterms. 
The larger issue is not whether Muslim Americans have the right to run for office and participate in our political system. Of course they do. 
Every American has that right. 
The issue is whether Americans are willing to have an open and honest discussion about the political organizations, agendas, and movements seeking to influence our government.

For years, critics of certain Islamist political movements have been met with accusations of Islamophobia. There is an important distinction between genuine anti-Muslim bigotry, which has no place in America, and legitimate criticism of religious institutions, political organizations, or ideologies. We cannot protect freedom of speech by making certain subjects off-limits for discussion.

Europe offers important lessons about what can happen when political leaders become afraid to address difficult questions. 
Across several European countries, debates over immigration, religious accommodation, national identity, and free expression have become increasingly contentious, to say the least.
These issues deserve open discussion, not intimidation or censorship. Christians, Muslims, Jews, and people of every faith deserve equal protection and equal freedom.

Pastor Jack Hibbs does not need exaggerated claims to make his point. He clarified to his congregation that CAIR is grooming thousands of Muslim candidates for political office in 2028. 
That matters. 

But here is the question that should concern every Republican: If political organizations and advocacy groups are already thinking strategically about the 2028 elections, what exactly are Republican leaders doing to prepare?

CAIR's political strategy and the broader activities of Muslim advocacy organizations deserve scrutiny just like those of any other political organization. 
But the larger lesson is that political influence is not created overnight. It is built through years of recruiting candidates, developing relationships, organizing voters, raising money, influencing public debate, and identifying opportunities to gain representation at every level of government.

That is how political power is built.

And while others are organizing for the future, where is the Republican strategy?  A lack of Republican leadership is what allowed Trump, who I totally support, to take over the Party apparatus.  
The issue now is POST TRUMP!

Where is the national leadership? 
Where is the effort to recruit and develop strong candidates? Where are the grassroots organizations preparing for school board elections, city councils, state legislatures, congressional races, and the presidency? 
Where is the sustained effort to educate voters and rally Americans around the Constitution, individual liberty, religious freedom, and the principles that made this country great?

Republicans cannot afford to wake up in 2028 and discover that their political opponents have spent years preparing while they were asleep.

Political power does not simply belong to the largest group. It often belongs to the 'best-organized group.'

History should remind us that democratic institutions are not invulnerable. 
The rise of the Nazi Party in Germany is a sobering example of how an extremist political movement, initially supported by a minority of voters, could exploit political divisions, institutional weaknesses, and the failures of established leadership. 
Hitler did not receive a majority of the vote in the last free national election before becoming chancellor. 
The lesson is not that today's political organizations are equivalent to the Nazis. 
The lesson is that democratic institutions require vigilance, responsible leadership, and citizens who refuse to take their freedoms for granted.

America is not immune to political complacency.
The answer is political engagement, transparency, informed voters, and leaders willing to defend American principles consistently.

CAIR and other political organizations are not waiting until 2028 to organize. 
Neither should Republicans.

The clock is ticking. The next election cycle will not be won by slogans, wishful thinking, or assuming that Americans will automatically rally behind the Republican ticket.

It will be won by preparation, leadership, organization, and a clear vision for America's future.

THE QUESTION IS SIMPLE: WHO IS PREPARING FOR 2028 — AND WHO IS STILL ASLEEP?

text:
Federalist No. 5: The Same Subject Continued: Concerning Dangers from Foreign Force and Influence  
by John Jay (as Publius)  
Published November 10, 1787, in The Independent Journal

By mid-November the New York debate had settled into a steady rhythm of pamphlets. In the same city rooms, John Jay—drawing on years of diplomacy—turned to history for a warning. If Americans split into separate confederacies, they would repeat the jealousies and foreign entanglements that had long plagued divided Britain and Spain.

Bulletized summary:
Quotes Queen Anne’s 1706 letter urging the Union of England and Scotland as the foundation of lasting peace and strength against enemies.
Warns that dividing America into three or four confederacies would breed the same jealousies and border conflicts that long divided Britain.
Notes that equality among such confederacies could not last; one would rise, sparking envy and distrust.
Predicts the northern region would likely grow stronger, becoming a “northern hive” feared by the south.
Argues that such neighbors would be “formidable only to each other,” making defensive alliances unlikely and foreign interference easy.
Concludes that division would invite rather than prevent the hostilities and improper interference of foreign nations.

Jay opens with Queen Anne’s letter: “An entire and perfect union will be the solid foundation of lasting peace: It will secure your religion, liberty, and property; remove the animosities amongst yourselves, and the jealousies and differences betwixt our two kingdoms... the whole island, being joined in affection and free from all apprehensions of different interest, will be ENABLED TO RESIST ALL ITS ENEMIES.” Enemies would use their utmost endeavors to prevent or delay that union.

Britain’s history offers useful lessons. Though common sense suggested the island should be one nation, it was for ages divided into three kingdoms “almost constantly embroiled in quarrels and wars with one another,” their jealousies kept inflamed by continental powers. “Should the people of America divide themselves into three or four nations, would not the same thing happen? Would not similar jealousies arise... envy and jealousy would soon extinguish confidence and affection, and the partial interests of each confederacy, instead of the general interests of all America, would be the only objects of their policy and pursuits.” Like other bordering nations, they would live in disputes or the constant fear of them.

Equality among such confederacies could not endure. One would rise; the others would regard it “with envy and with fear.” Distrust would breed distrust. “The North is generally the region of strength,” and the most northern confederacy would likely become more formidable, exciting the same sensations once felt toward a “NORTHERN HIVE” in Europe. Its “young swarms might often be tempted to gather honey in the more blooming fields” of milder neighbors. The confederacies “would place us exactly in the situations in which some nations doubtless wish to see us, viz., FORMIDABLE ONLY TO EACH OTHER.”

Defensive alliances would be unlikely. They would be “DISTINCT NATIONS,” each with different commercial treaties and foreign attachments. Neighboring confederacies would more naturally fear each other than distant Europe and would seek foreign alliances against one another—easier to invite foreign fleets and armies in than to persuade them to leave. Jay asks whether division “would tend to secure us against the hostilities and improper interference of foreign nations.”

Contemporary echoes appear in debates over regional blocs versus tighter national unity. Jay’s caution remains pointed: divided neighbors often prove more dangerous to each other than any outside power.

Further reading: Full text at the Yale Avalon Project — https://t.co/VYhvyq22rg or the Library of Congress Federalist Papers guide.

text:
Federalist No. 2: Concerning Dangers from Foreign Force and Influence
by John Jay (as Publius)
Published October 31, 1787, in The Independent Journal
A few days after Hamilton’s opening essay appeared, John Jay—New York’s experienced diplomat and former president of the Continental Congress—took up the pen in the same city. Amid the autumn political chatter and the clatter of the busy port, the elder statesman of the trio offered a quieter but equally urgent argument for staying united.
Bulletized summary:
• Argues that Americans form one people by geography, shared ancestry, language, religion, customs, and wartime experience.
• Claims Providence intended this connected country for a single nation rather than rival confederacies.
• Notes that the people have long favored union and that the Articles of Confederation, formed in wartime haste, proved inadequate.
• Defends the Constitutional Convention’s careful work and warns that rejecting the plan risks the Union’s dissolution.
• Closes by predicting that disunion would bring the lament: “FAREWELL! A LONG FAREWELL TO ALL MY GREATNESS.”
Jay opens by reminding readers that government requires ceding some natural rights, so the real question is whether Americans should place those powers in one national government or in several separate confederacies. He observes that until recently nearly everyone agreed the country’s prosperity depended on remaining firmly united. New voices now suggest dividing into three or four sovereignties; Jay urges the public not to adopt this “new doctrine” without careful scrutiny.
He then paints a picture of natural unity. Independent America, he writes, “was not composed of detached and distant territories, but that one connected, fertile, widespreading country was the portion of our western sons of liberty.” Navigable waters form “a kind of chain round its borders, as if to bind it together,” while great rivers serve as “highways for the easy communication of friendly aids.” Providence, he continues, “has been pleased to give this one connected country to one united people—a people descended from the same ancestors, speaking the same language, professing the same religion, attached to the same principles of government, very similar in their manners and customs, and who, by their joint counsels, arms, and efforts, fighting side by side throughout a long and bloody war, have nobly established general liberty and independence.” This country and people “seem to have been made for each other,” and it appears the design of Providence that such an inheritance “should never be split into a number of unsocial, jealous, and alien sovereignties.”
Jay recalls that Americans acted as one nation in making peace, war, alliances, and treaties. The wartime Congress that created the Articles of Confederation did so under emergency conditions; its defects were therefore unsurprising. The people still valued both union and liberty, so they sent delegates to Philadelphia. That convention, working in peacetime with cool deliberation, produced a plan that is only recommended, not imposed. Jay warns that those promoting separate confederacies foresee the Union’s end, and he hopes every citizen will clearly see that its dissolution would force America to exclaim, in the poet’s words, “FAREWELL! A LONG FAREWELL TO ALL MY GREATNESS.”
Contemporary echoes appear in debates over national cohesion versus regional autonomy, whether in discussions of American identity amid immigration and cultural change, or in other countries weighing tighter integration against secessionist pressures. Jay’s confidence in shared history and geography as the foundation of nationhood remains a classic Federalist premise—optimistic, providential, and still contested.
Further reading: Full text at the Yale Avalon Project — https://t.co/SSFMDXGGmA or the Library of Congress Federalist Papers guide.

text:
Me: Grok why is it so difficult for anyone to see my posts anymore? I'm actually giving things away and people still can't see them?

Grok: X’s For You ranking (powered by the Phoenix transformer model) prioritizes predicted engagement signals far more than follower count. A reply is weighted several times higher than a like, mutual replies get an extra boost, and dwell time / shares via DM also matter. Negative signals (mute, block, “not interested,” report) carry heavy penalties. Posts from accounts you follow get preference; out-of-network ones are discounted. Content older than ~48 hours is filtered from For You, and the first 1–2 hours are critical for velocity.⁠

Accounts under 50k followers (yours is ~28.5k and Blue Verified) get a limited “cold-start” chance: original posts under 2 hours old with under ~200 Home views can be lifted into a reserved slot in some viewers’ feeds. If early like/reply rate is low, that window closes quickly and broader distribution stalls. Overall organic reach has declined for many accounts; data shows non-Premium median engagement near zero in some studies, with Premium helping more on reply placement than pure post reach. Your recent posts show similar low views (often single- to low-double digits, occasional higher), which points more to early engagement and audience activity patterns than a unique block.

Your giveaway post is native (image + call for comments) and well-suited to spark replies, which is exactly what the current weights reward. Low early comments limit amplification even for free offers. Practical levers that align with the open code and recent analyses include posting when your active followers are online, replying quickly to the first comments to boost the mutual-reply signal, and treating the post as the start of a conversation rather than a one-way broadcast. Check Settings → Your account → Account status for any visibility labels, and note that dormant followers (inactive accounts still counted in your total) can suppress perceived engagement rates. These factors, not the giveaway itself, explain why distribution stays limited.

Zelensky says Washington floated Donbas in exchange for membership. The US will only say "many ideas continue to be discussed", which is how capitals keep an offer alive without owning it. The appeal is obvious: a defended rump Ukraine inside the alliance is more secure than an undefended whole one outside it. The cost is written into the precedent. Every border in Europe becomes a question of what the occupant can trade.

Alliances are insurance contracts, and insurers price the claim history. Admitting a member whose entry fee was ceded land tells the next aggressor exactly what the deductible looks like.

Security bought with territory is a mortgage, not a purchase.

text:
Volodymyr Verbianyi, National Post
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said U.S. peace envoys asked whether Ukraine would be willing to give up the Donbas region in the nation’s east to Russia in exchange for NATO membership, signaling a potential shift in Washington’s negotiating tactics.

As the full-scale war between Ukraine and Russia heads toward the end of its fifth year in February, the administration of President Donald Trump is trying to make a breakthrough in the peace negotiations they’re moderating.

“It was the first time this had been raised,” Zelenskyy told reporters in his office in Kyiv late Friday of the plan involving the Donetsk and Luhansk regions. “We are discussing with our partners a comprehensive security package that could be offered to us in the negotiations.”

Zelenskyy said that the package floated by Washington includes specific security guarantees from NATO and the European Union; a strong Ukrainian army, meaning an adequate number of troops, weapons, and financial support for a specified period of time; and a recovery plan backed by funding with clearly identified sources.

“If the American side confirms precisely this to us, together with other NATO partners, then I will ask our Ukrainian society what it thinks: do we accept it or not?” Zelenskyy said. “I have no right to make that decision on my own.”

text:
FICTIONAL THRILLER — NOT REAL EVENTS.

Santa Clara, California. NVIDIA Headquarters.

HOLY SHIT. Jensen Huang has resigned as NVIDIA CEO.

430,000 people are demanding his return.

But in this imaginary Silicon Valley power struggle, the happiest man isn’t AMD’s CEO. It isn’t Mark Zuckerberg.

It’s Marco Rubio.

In a Washington office, Rubio raises his coffee.

“Finally. The man in the leather jacket is gone.”

His aide frowns. “But didn’t Jensen help America lead the AI race?”

Rubio smiles. “The question is: who does he answer to?”

Three months earlier, a secret proposal had landed on Jensen’s desk: give a government-backed committee sweeping control over next-generation GPU allocations.

Jensen pushed it away.

“I build chips. I don’t hand over the steering wheel.”

Weeks later, NVIDIA’s board convened an emergency meeting.

David, a trusted executive of twenty years, presented a bombshell: $8 billion in unexplained R&D overruns.

The vote was 7–4.

Jensen was out.

He walked past the cameras without a word.

Thirty years. I helped build this company from graphics cards into the engine of the AI boom. And eleven people in suits can erase me in an afternoon?

David, I treated you like family. You treated me like a problem to be removed.

David’s phone lit up.

“Phase One complete.”

The next morning, 17 senior engineers resigned together.

Zuckerberg offered huge contracts. Rivals began circling. NVIDIA’s next GPU launch suddenly looked vulnerable.

Rubio appeared calm.

The objective wasn’t to kill NVIDIA.

It was to control it.

Then Amy, a junior engineer, noticed something absurd.

The supposed $8 billion audit report had been CREATED TWO HOURS AFTER the board’s vote.

Jensen stared at the timestamp and laughed.

They fired me first and wrote the evidence later?

If this is a coup, at least hire someone who understands file metadata.

He didn’t publish it. Not yet.

Instead, he flew to Washington to meet a retired chip-policy adviser.

The adviser slid a folder across the table.

PROJECT: UNIFIED AI COMPUTE CONTROL.

Inside was a proposal to place advanced-chip distribution under a new committee. A compliant NVIDIA CEO would be essential.

Jensen felt his stomach turn.

So that’s the trick. They hold the controller, I take the blame when the machine crashes.

The next morning, he made a stunning announcement:

“I will not return to NVIDIA.”

Zuckerberg celebrated. Rubio relaxed.

“Looks like he surrendered.”

That evening, a startup called BLACK JACKET emerged.

Its first hires? The 17 engineers.

Its largest shareholder?

JENSEN HUANG.

Jensen had quietly funded chip-architecture research for five years. The world thought he was unemployed.

He was building his next empire.

But then Zuckerberg called.

“Jensen, you think Rubio orchestrated this?”

“Didn’t he?”

“David didn’t write that audit report.”

“Who did?”

“The person running BLACK JACKET.”

Jensen went silent.

Impossible. Only three people knew about that investment.

He opened the startup’s ownership records.

His controlling rights had already been transferred.

The document carried his electronic signature.

Dated six months before his resignation.

What the hell?

I thought I was playing chess. Someone made me a piece on their board.

A text flashed.

“Welcome to Phase Two.”

Attached: a list of eleven early BLACK JACKET investors.

The same eleven people who had voted on Jensen’s future.

And one chilling line:

“Objective: Remove Jensen from NVIDIA, then have him build the replacement.”

Jensen finally understood.

They didn’t want me retired.

They wanted me working for them under a different logo.

Another text appeared:

“Did you really believe those 430,000 signatures were spontaneous?”

He stared at the screen, then reached for his black leather jacket.

Fine.

You want a game?

LET’S PLAY.

But who was controlling whom: Rubio, Zuckerberg, the board—or the person Jensen trusted most?

text:
Biden, Zelensky, and the Uncomfortable Truth About America's Interests

Ukraine must finally learn to distinguish American geopolitical calculations from Europe's existential security interests.

The Ukrainian blogosphere is experiencing another collective nervous breakdown. The Wall Street Journal has reportedly published excerpts from Joe Biden's new memoir, Promise Me, America, scheduled for release on November 17, 2026. Biden — yes, Joe Biden, not Donald Trump — reportedly describes Volodymyr Zelensky as stubborn, difficult, and less grateful for American assistance than he had expected. While acknowledging that Zelensky's acting career prepared him for wartime leadership, Biden allegedly found him gloomy and insufficiently appreciative in private conversations. Predictably, Ukrainian commentators rushed to explain that Ukraine is fighting Russia partly in America's interests and that Washington should therefore be thanking Kyiv. But perhaps it is time to abandon comforting illusions and confront an unpleasant geopolitical reality.

With all my respect for ordinary Ukrainians, they must understand one fundamental distinction: American interests in Ukraine are not identical to European interests. Washington can regard Ukrainian sovereignty as important without considering every Ukrainian territory a vital American strategic interest. Neither Donbas nor Crimea has historically occupied the same place in Washington's security calculations as in Europe's. America is separated from Russia by oceans; Europe shares a continent with it. And Washington has another overriding concern: China. American strategists have long understood the dangers of pushing Moscow into complete dependence on Beijing. The old Kissinger triangle — Washington, Moscow, Beijing — has changed considerably, but its geopolitical logic has not entirely disappeared. Weakening Russia and destroying its usefulness as a potential counterweight to China are not necessarily the same objective.

History offers some uncomfortable reminders. During the Crimean War of 1853–1856, American sympathies often leaned toward Russia. In 1905, President Theodore Roosevelt mediated the settlement of the Russo-Japanese War. And in August 1991, George H. W. Bush delivered his notorious Chicken Kiev speech, warning Ukrainians against what he called “suicidal nationalism” while discouraging a reckless break with the Soviet political order. Washington's priorities have always been determined primarily by Washington. That does not make America uniquely cynical; it makes America a great power. Europe, meanwhile, faces a fundamentally different equation. Russian military expansion threatens its own security architecture, borders, economies, and political stability. Yet European governments have continued purchasing Russian energy during the war. This contradiction deserves considerably more attention than another theatrical argument over whether Zelensky has thanked Washington often enough.

Nobody has the right to dictate how President Zelensky should conduct himself. Nevertheless, he would be wise to distinguish between political defiance and diplomatic effectiveness. Ukraine needs American weapons, intelligence, technology, and political support. These are not guaranteed indefinitely, regardless of which party controls Congress. Even among Democrats, domestic spending priorities compete with foreign military assistance. American voters have every right to ask why their taxes should finance foreign armies rather than schools, hospitals, and infrastructure at home. Ukrainians may find such questions unpleasant, but indignation will not make them disappear. Gratitude is not surrender, diplomacy is not humiliation, and strategic realism is not betrayal. Ukraine's survival requires more than courage on the battlefield. It requires understanding what its allies actually want — rather than what Ukrainians wish they wanted.

To receive The Algorithm newsletter in your inbox every Monday, sign up here.

Welcome to the Algorithm! 

This year we’ve seen a dizzying number of breakthroughs in generative AI, from AIs that can produce videos from just a few words to models that can generate audio based on snippets of a song. 

Last week, Google held an AI event in its swanky, brand-new offices by the Hudson River in Manhattan. Your correspondent stopped by to see what the fuss was about. In a continuation of current trends, Google announced a slew of advances in generative AI, including a system that combines its two text-to-video AI models, Phenaki and Imagen. Phenaki allows the system to generate video with a series of text prompts that functions as a sort of script, while Imagen makes the videos higher resolution. 

But these models are still a long way from being rolled out for the general public to use. They still have some major problems, such as the ability to generate violent, sexist, racist, or copyright-violating content owing to the nature of the training data, which is mostly just scraped off the internet. One Google researcher told me these models were still in an early stage and that a lot of “stars had to align” before they could be used in actual products. It’s impressive AI research, but it’s also unclear how Google could monetize the technologies.  

What could have a real-world impact a lot sooner is Google’s new project to develop a “universal speech model” that has been trained on over 400 languages, Zoubin Ghahramani, vice president of research at Google AI, said at the event. The company didn’t offer many details but said it will publish a paper in the coming months. 

If it works out, this will represent a big leap forward in the capabilities of large language models, or LLMs.  AI startup Hugging Face’s LLM BLOOM was trained on 46 languages, and Meta has been working on AI models that can translate hundreds of languages in real time. With more languages contributing training data to its model, Google will be able to offer its services to even more people. Incorporating hundreds of languages into one AI model could enable Google to offer better translations or captions on YouTube, or improve its search engine so it’s better at delivering results across more languages. 

During my trip to the East Coast, I spoke with top executives at some of the world’s biggest AI labs to hear what they thought was going to be driving the conversation in AI next year. Here’s what they had to say:

Douglas Eck, principal scientist at Google Research and a research director for Google Brain, the company’s deep-learning research team

The next breakthrough will likely come from multimodal AI models, which are armed with multiple senses, such as the ability to use computer vision and audio to interpret things, Eck told me. The next big thing will be to figure out how to build language models into other AI models as they sense the world. This could, for example, help robots understand their surroundings through visual and language cues and voice commands.

Yann LeCun, Meta’s chief AI scientist 

Generative AI is going to get better and better, LeCun said: “We’re going to have better ways of specifying what we want out of them.” Currently, the models react to prompts, but “right now, it’s very difficult to control what the text generation system is going to do,” he added. In the future, he hopes, “there’ll be ways to change the architecture a little bit so that there is some level of planning that is more deliberate.” 

Raia Hadsell, research director at DeepMind

Hadsell, too, was excited about multimodal generative AI systems, which combine audio, language, and vision. By adding reinforcement learning, which allows AI models to train themselves by trial and error, we might be able to see AI models with “the ability to explore, have autonomy, and interact in environments,” Hadsell told me.  

Deeper Learning

What mass firings at Twitter mean for its AI workers

As we reported last week, Twitter may have lost more than a million users since Elon Musk took over. The firm Bot Sentinel, which tracks inauthentic behavior on Twitter by analyzing more than 3.1 million accounts and their activity daily, believes that around 877,000 accounts were deactivated and a further 497,000 were suspended between October 27 and November 1. That’s more than double the usual number.

To me, it’s clear why that’s happening. Users are betting that the platform is going to become a less fun place to hang out. That’s partly because they’ve seen Musk laying off teams of people who work to make sure the platform is safe, including Twitter’s entire AI ethics team. It’s likely something Musk will come to regret. The company is already rehiring engineers and product managers for 13 positions related to machine learning, including roles involved in privacy, platform manipulation, governance, and defense of online users against terrorism, violent extremism, and coordinated harm. But we can only wonder what damage has been done already, especially with the US midterm elections imminent. 

Setting a worrying example: The AI ethics team, led by applied AI ethics pioneer Rumman Chowdhury, was doing some really impressive stuff to rein in the most toxic side effects of Twitter’s content moderation algorithms, such as giving outsiders access to their data sets to find bias. As I wrote last week, AI ethicists already face a lot of ignorance about and  pushback against their work, which can lead them to burn out. Those left behind at Twitter will face pressure to fix the same problems, but with far fewer resources than before. It’s not going to be pretty. And as the global economy teeters on the edge of a recession, it’s a really worrying sign that top executives such as Musk think AI ethics, a field working to ensure that AI systems are fair and safe, is the first thing worth axing. 

Bits and Bytes

This tool lets anyone see the bias in AI image generators
A tool by Hugging Face researcher Sasha Luccioni lets anyone test how text-to-image generation AI Stable Diffusion produces biased outcomes for certain word combinations. (Vice) 

Algorithms quietly run the city of DC—and maybe your hometown
A new report from the Electronic Privacy Information Center found that Washington, DC, uses algorithms in 20 agencies, more than a third of them related to policing or criminal justice. (Wired) 

Meta does protein folding
Following in DeepMind’s footsteps to apply AI to biology, Meta has unveiled an AI that reveals the structures of hundreds of millions of the least understood proteins. The company says that with 600 million structures, their model is three times larger than anything before. (Meta) 

Thanks for reading!

Melissa

**US negotiators just floated Ukraine trading its remaining Donbas foothold for a NATO path, and Zelenskyy said it out loud on November 14.**[[1]](https://t.co/PdU3xb8wui)

[Take 2/15 · G-2]
### 1. The Frame
**What people think this is about:** A breakthrough or betrayal in US-brokered peace talks where Washington pressures Kyiv to surrender territory for alliance membership, reviving frozen conflict fears or rewarding Russian aggression.

**What the machinery is actually doing:** The Trump administration is testing explicit territorial-for-security trades to close the file on a draining proxy war, while Kyiv uses the disclosure to lock in maximum guarantees and force European buy-in before any deal hardens.

### 2. Observations
- Zelenskyy’s public framing—that this linkage appeared for the first time in Abu Dhabi talks—functions as both signal and shield: it keeps NATO on the table while signaling to domestic audiences and Europe that Kyiv will not decide alone.[[2]](https://t.co/5is9r4Qo8m)
- The US has not confirmed the exact wording; a generic “many ideas are discussed” line from officials preserves deniability while the trial balloon floats.[[3]](https://t.co/3VD4YHL0dJ)
- Prisoner exchange principles (1,000+ per side) were the only concrete output from the Nov 10-11 Abu Dhabi round; everything else remains exploratory.[[4]](https://t.co/Kf6gjZthRH)
- Russia’s unchanged demand for the rest of Donetsk plus neutrality or limits on Ukrainian forces sits in direct tension with any NATO path, making the floated swap a high-risk probe rather than a near-term path.[[5]](https://t.co/vZ53UUmOZg)
- European capitals are already pushing for seats at the table; the post-Abu Dhabi agreement to include them is the real institutional move, not the Donbas question itself.[[1]](https://t.co/PdU3xb8wui)
- Zelenskyy’s referendum escape hatch is classic IT: it shifts political risk while preserving the LT claim that Ukraine does not cede territory unilaterally.

### 3. Snapshot
On November 10-11, 2026, US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff mediated the first US-Ukraine-Russia trilateral talks since February in Abu Dhabi. The sessions produced agreement in principle on a large prisoner exchange but no ceasefire or territorial formula. After the talks, the envoys briefed Putin in Moscow and Zelenskyy in Dublin. On November 14, Zelenskyy publicly disclosed that US negotiators had raised, for the first time, whether Ukraine would withdraw from the portions of Donbas it still controls in exchange for NATO membership. He rejected ceding land outright but said a comprehensive security package (guarantees, army funding, reconstruction) could go to a Ukrainian referendum. Washington has not confirmed the precise proposal.

### 4. Timeline of material facts
- **Nov 10-11, 2026 (Abu Dhabi talks):** First trilateral US-Ukraine-Russia meeting in nine months; focus on security guarantees, humanitarian issues; prisoner exchange principles agreed (1,000+ per side); no breakthrough on territory or ceasefire (IT, multiple primary-aligned reports).[[6]](https://t.co/WwmfjQt0Nk)
- **Nov 10-11, 2026:** US officials floated Article 5-like guarantees for Ukraine; Russia continued demanding full Donbas control and limits on Ukrainian forces (IT).[[5]](https://t.co/vZ53UUmOZg)
- **Nov 13-14, 2026:** Kushner and Witkoff meet Putin then Zelenskyy; agreement that Europe will join future talks (LT).[[1]](https://t.co/PdU3xb8wui)
- **Nov 14, 2026 (remarks released):** Zelenskyy states US negotiators asked “What if Ukraine joins NATO? Would Ukraine withdraw from Donbas?”—first explicit linkage; Kyiv rejects surrender but floats referendum on full package (LT per Zelenskyy statements).[[7]](https://t.co/Il980xFQZR)
- **Nov 14-15, 2026:** US offers no confirmation; generic “ideas discussed” response (IT).

### 5. Sides
**Ukrainian government (Zelenskyy-led) (IT/LT mix):** Steelmans that any territorial decision requires broad Western guarantees plus domestic consent; NATO membership remains the ultimate deterrent against future Russian aggression.  
**Critique:** LT on referendum authority; IT on using disclosure to extract better terms while European involvement grows.

**US administration (Trump envoys Kushner/Witkoff) (IT):** Steelmans pragmatic deal-making to end a costly stalemate via creative security architecture that could include NATO-like guarantees without immediate full accession.  
**Critique:** LT on testing ideas; IT on preserving flexibility and avoiding ownership of any specific territorial concession.

**Russian side (Putin/Medinsky):** Steelmans that security guarantees must address Moscow’s core demands on territory, neutrality, and limits on Ukrainian forces to prevent NATO expansion on its border.  
**Critique:** LT on longstanding red lines; IF on claims that partial Donbas withdrawal would satisfy maximalist goals.

### 6. Rumsfeld Matrix
- **Known Knowns:** Abu Dhabi produced prisoner-swap framework; Zelenskyy publicly linked US-raised Donbas-for-NATO question; no US confirmation; Europe now slated for future talks.
- **Known Unknowns:** Exact wording or status of any US proposal; Russian reaction to the specific linkage; Ukrainian public polling on a referendum package; timeline for European inclusion.
- **Unknown Knowns:** Internal US assessments of Russian flexibility; precise European red lines on security architecture; Ukrainian military sustainability metrics beyond public statements.
- **Unknown Unknowns:** Winter military developments shifting leverage; third-party (China, Turkey) spoiler or facilitator moves; domestic political shocks in Kyiv, Moscow, or Washington.

### 7. Incentives map
US: Close the Ukraine file, reduce fiscal and political drag, test creative security trades that could scale to other theaters.  
Ukraine: Maximize guarantees and European buy-in while avoiding unilateral concessions that fracture domestic support.  
Russia: Extract maximum territorial and neutrality concessions; use talks to probe and delay while maintaining battlefield pressure.  
Media/engagement: Territory-for-alliance framing drives clicks far better than incremental prisoner swaps or process updates.

### 8. Dueling AI advice
**Moral AI Advice:** Map the actual leverage each side holds after four-plus years of war, price the cost of continued fighting versus any package that delivers durable deterrence, and let Ukrainian society decide the referendum threshold. Incentives favor clarity over maximalist posturing.

**Evil AI Advice:** Float the Donbas swap publicly to split Kyiv from its European backers, then demand even more in the next round while the winter energy campaign grinds on—max extraction, zero fingerprints.

### 9. Practical takeaway
- Watch for any US or Russian confirmation or counter-proposal in the next 7-10 days; silence is data.
- Track European participation announcements—five countries (France, Germany, Italy, UK, Poland) already designated.
- Monitor Ukrainian domestic reaction and any polling on security-package referendums.
- Do not treat Zelenskyy’s disclosure as a finalized US position; it remains an unconfirmed trial balloon.
- The next material signal will likely be the scale and timing of the prisoner exchange or the first trilateral-plus-Europe meeting.

### 10. What would falsify this read
- Direct US confirmation or denial of the exact Donbas-for-NATO question with supporting documentation.
- Russian acceptance of Ukrainian NATO membership even with partial Donbas withdrawal.
- Ukrainian parliamentary or public rejection of any referendum mechanism.
- Major winter battlefield reversal that materially shifts leverage before further talks.

If you have Facebook on an Android phone, read this.

Italy's privacy regulator just fined Meta about $887 million. The finding, per the Washington Post: the Facebook app accessed Android users' photos and videos without properly informing them or getting specific consent.

Reports say it came through a feature that suggests which photos to post, and hit about 20 million users in Italy.

Meta made no immediate comment.

The 2-minute version:

1. Settings > Apps > Facebook > Permissions
2. Photos and videos: set it to the most limited option your phone offers
3. Do the same for Instagram and Messenger

Send this to whoever still has Facebook on an old Android.

text:
🚨 EUROPE HAS NO NEGOTIATOR. NO MANDATE. NO STRATEGY.
AND ITS CHANCELLOR IS HOLDING A DETONATOR.

Europe is not negotiating. It is waiting for a generation to die.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

On 14 November, in Dublin, Europe had one job: appoint a single chief negotiator.

It failed.

Not for technical reasons. Because seven people wanted the job — and none of them trusted the others with it.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

▸ THE FACT: Dublin ended with no chief negotiator, no shared strategy, no agreed position. Macron wanted it. Stubb wanted it. Merz wanted it. Costa wanted it. Kallas wanted it. Meloni wanted to block everyone. The Commission wanted it to be the Commission. Spain — the one large EU state that might actually talk to Moscow — was excluded from the format.

▸ THE MECHANISM: Europe does not want a negotiator. It wants the appearance of wanting one. A negotiator needs a mandate. A mandate needs positions. Positions need agreement among 27 states with 27 different relationships to Russia, to Washington, and to their own voters. That agreement does not exist. So Europe forms a committee, calls it a team, and hopes the war ends before the committee produces a document.

▸ THE PARADOX: Merz has threatened to veto the entire EU budget unless every member state guarantees funding for Ukraine. The largest net contributor threatening to blow up the budget — and with it, the structural funds half of Europe depends on, and the roll-over of a €1 trillion debt — to force Slovakia, Hungary, Czechia and Bulgaria to fund a war they refuse to fund. This is not a negotiating position. This is a detonator with diplomatic ambitions. And the same man now says he is ready to call Putin. Europe's would-be negotiator is the man who threatened to destroy the institution he would be negotiating for.

▸ THE ESCALATION: On the front, 80% of all Russian offensive actions are concentrated on Dobropillia and Kostiantynivka. 58 attacks in 48 hours. Putin offers a "humanitarian pause" in Kostiantynivka. Washington endorsed it. The pause is not humanitarian. It is logistics. A local ceasefire lets heavy equipment move without drone risk. Meanwhile Starshield is capped at 161 km/h over occupied territory — day five. Zelensky says SpaceX called it technical. Rubio told him it was under US government control. Both cannot be true. And over the Baltic, Ukrainian drones heading for St Petersburg crossed all three Baltic states' airspace in one night. NATO scrambled. The interceptors missed. Then everyone went quiet.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

THE POLITICAL LAYER (WHAT IT MEANS FOR YOU)

▸ Your Wallet: The Merz veto is not about Ukraine. It is about the EU budget that funds your region, your infrastructure, your farm subsidies. If Berlin pulls the trigger, the money stops — not in Kiev. In your town. And the interest on €1 trillion of EU debt still gets paid. By the member states. By the taxpayers. By you.

▸ Who pays? The European taxpayer pays for the war, the debt, the reconstruction, and now the political crisis of a budget veto designed to force more of the same. The US plans the post-war. The Gulf hosts the talks. Russia sets the terms. Europe pays the bill and waits in the corridor.

▸ 🔴 "Europe is not at the table. Europe is in the corridor, holding a budget it is threatening to destroy, waiting for a negotiator it cannot appoint, to discuss an architecture it refuses to discuss."

▸ Mainstream narrative: "Europe is united." "The negotiator is coming." "The ceasefire is near." None of these are true. The ceasefire was rejected in October. The proposal being relaunched in November is the exit script, not the peace plan.

⚖️ VERDICT: The Generational Iron Curtain is not a metaphor. It is a timeline. The last generation of European leaders who remember a shared continent is leaving the stage. What replaces them learned Russia as an enemy, Ukraine as a cause, America as a guarantor. They will not rebuild trust with treaties. They will rebuild it with time — and time is measured in decades. That is why the negotiations fail. Not because the terms are impossible. Because the people who could sign them are already gone.

❓ QUESTION: If Europe cannot agree on who speaks for it, cannot agree on what it would say, and is now threatening to destroy its own budget to force a war it cannot fund — what exactly is Europe negotiating for? And who is paying for the delay?

Die europäische Ariane-Rakete schaut SpaceX aus dem Grab zu. Während Elon Musk fast täglich Raketen landet und sein gigantisches Starship den Orbit dominiert, feiert die ESA im Jahr 2026, dass sie ihre sündhaft teure Einwegrakete ein paar Mal im Jahr ins Meer werfen darf.

Über 4 Milliarden Euro der Steuerzahler haben Bürokraten versenkt, um mit der Ariane 6 ein System zu bauen, das technologisch im letzten Jahrhundert feststeckt. 
Die amerikanische Falcon 9 von SpaceX fliegt über 100 Mal pro Jahr, landet butterweich und wird direkt wiederverwendet. 
Europa hingegen feiert seine Wegwerfrakete, bei der jeder einzelne Start Hunderte Millionen verbrennt und die erste Stufe als teurer Schrott im Ozean versinkt.

Unsere „Erfolgsmeldungen“ sind längst Realsatire: 
Mitte 2026 jubelt man über den Start der Ariane 64 mit vier Boostern und hofft auf ganze acht Starts in diesem Jahr. 
Acht! SpaceX absolviert dieses Pensum in wenigen Wochen. 
Und während in den USA das Starship abhebt und riesige Raketenbooster wie selbstverständlich von mechanischen Greifarmen aus der Luft gefangen werden, verweigert man hier die Realität: 
Man erklärt uns allen Ernstes, Wiederverwendbarkeit lohne sich für Europa nicht, weil wir ohnehin so selten fliegen.

Europas Raumfahrt ist das perfekte Spiegelbild unserer Industriepolitik: 
träge, überteuert, innovationsfeindlich und auf dem Weltmarkt komplett deklassiert. 
Anstatt mutige Ingenieure und freies Unternehmertum zu fördern, subventionieren wir einen schwerfälligen Staatsbetrieb, der uns die eigene technologische Bedeutungslosigkeit als „strategische Unabhängigkeit“ verkauft. 
Wer im Jahr 2026 noch Einwegraketen baut, erobert nicht den Weltraum – er verwaltet nur den eigenen Abstieg.
