text:
The Fourth Sector: The Rise of the Automated Economy

Imagine machines growing wheat, baking bread, selling it and delivering it, with almost no human labor. Who earns the income?

In his Nov. 1, 2026 video, David Shapiro calls this a “fourth sector”: a framework for automated output across agriculture, manufacturing and services. The distinction is who does the work, rather than what gets sold.

The traditional three-sector model groups resources, manufacturing and services. Earlier technologies moved workers from farms to factories and then services. People remained essential. AI and robots could change that pattern by letting equipment perform more of the labor itself.

A genuinely driverless Robotaxi could take another fare without another hour of a driver's work. Cleaning, charging, maintenance and remote support still need people; profitability depends on reliability, cost and scale. Optimus could extend the idea across tasks and industries. Robots helping build more robots would take it further—a future possibility.

SpaceX offers another angle: reusable rockets, automated satellite production and the Starlink network let capital equipment keep delivering communications. Engineers and maintenance teams remain essential, while service capacity can grow without headcount rising at the same rate.

The chain is AI making decisions, robots acting, energy and computing supporting production, and automated systems delivering goods and services. Revenue buys more equipment for the next round. Capital begins to perform work once supplied by labor.

That could shift returns toward whoever owns the machines. Picture two households: one depends on wages; the other holds stakes in fleets, robotics companies and networks through shares or retirement accounts. More automation could intensify competition for the first household's work while increasing the second's asset income.

Human connection and experiences may retain a premium: live concerts, a chef's own cooking, companionship. Shapiro calls this the “last human industry.”

Cheaper output also raises a demand question: if many people lose wages, how do they pay? Wider asset ownership, public services and sharing productivity gains become part of the discussion.

I think the key shift may be from labor constraints toward energy, compute, resources and equipment. Tesla and SpaceX point toward that possibility. How can ordinary people share in wealth increasingly produced by machines?

text:
Sumner Welles (b. 14 October 1892) had everything a Washington power broker could desire—blue blood, old money, presidential connections, three marriages, two sons, and a diplomatic career that placed him within whispering distance of the most powerful man on earth. Unfortunately, the polished prince also had a weakness for gentlemen—and in wartime Washington, that was the sort of entanglement that could get a fellow permanently cancelled.

Born into New York aristocracy, Benjamin Sumner Welles attended Groton and Harvard, cultivated a lifelong friendship with Franklin D. Roosevelt, and entered the diplomatic service in 1915. Handsome, impeccably connected, and formidably ambitious, he rose through the ranks to become Under Secretary of State in 1937. He helped engineer Roosevelt's Latin America Good Neighbor Policy, influenced America's approach to World War II, and championed the international cooperation that would eventually produce the United Nations. His influence was enormous—his discretion, sadly, less reliable.

Behind the elegant suits, society marriages, and diplomatic niceties lurked a private life that Washington's gossip merchants would have paid handsomely to expose. Welles was sexually attracted to men—a fact that might have remained an open secret among the capital's well-connected set had it not been for one spectacularly indiscreet episode.

In September 1940, Welles accompanied President Roosevelt to Huntsville, Alabama, for the funeral of House Speaker William Bankhead (the father of that notorious actress and libertine, Tallulah). On the return trip to D.C., Sumner became heavily intoxicated, took barbiturates, and “under the influence”, made unwanted sexual advances toward several Black Pullman porters.

The incident began when porter John Stone, dressed in the standard Pullman uniform of a midnight-blue suit buttoned to the neck, answered Welles's summoning bell around 4:00 a.m. When Stone brought coffee to Welles's compartment—located directly next to the president's car—Sumner offered him money for sex. Stone tactfully declined and returned to the dining car. Undeterred, Welles repeatedly rang for other porters throughout the early morning hours, propositioning one after another, and even locking one inside his compartment while attempting to undress him. In keeping with Porter etiquette, the refusals were polite but firm. Not unlike Sumner—less the polite part—who pawed at the Porters in his futile and increasingly willful attempts at sexual fulfillment. The incident was duly reported by railroad officials and the Secret Service. And like all scandalous secrets too delicious to contain, the resulting whispers traveled through Washington faster than a highly classified diplomatic cable. Welles’ archrival, Secretary of State Cordell Hull, who already despised Sumner for enjoying FDR's confidence, was hardly inclined to let such damning ammunition go to waste. Now he was armed with something considerably more explosive than bureaucratic jealousy.

As the scandal sprouted legs and began to run, Roosevelt initially stood by his favorite diplomat. But even presidential friendship had its limits. With political enemies circling like ravenous buzzards, rumors multiplying, and the threat of public exposure hanging over his carefully coiffed head, Welles resigned in September 1943. Behind its smirks and winks, official Washington maintained its customary dignified silence—and privately savored every sordid detail.

Disgraced but hardly destitute, Welles retired to the more forgiving world of lectures and international affairs. His influential book, The Time for Decision, appeared in 1944, and he continued his advocacy for international cooperation until his death in 1961.

The Sumner Welles story is rich with irony. Here was a man who helped shape American diplomacy, advised a president, envisioned a new world order, and could navigate an international crisis with consummate skill yet couldn't survive his whispered salacious propositions aboard a presidential train.

In Washington, apparently, a gentleman could negotiate with dictators, maneuver around enemies, and help redesign the world—but heaven help him if he made a pass at the porter. All aboard! Next stop—political oblivion. 🏳️‍🌈

$𝟭𝟯 𝗠𝗶𝗹𝗹𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗮 𝗧𝗶𝗻𝘆 𝗕𝗿𝘂𝘀𝗵: 𝗪𝗵𝗲𝗻 𝗨𝗻𝗶𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘀𝗶𝘁𝘆 𝗣𝗥 𝗢𝘂𝘁𝗽𝗮𝗰𝗲𝘀 𝗖𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗶𝗰𝗮𝗹 𝗘𝘃𝗶𝗱𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗲

𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗗𝗶𝗱 𝘁𝗵𝗲 “𝗗𝗿𝗶𝗹𝗹-𝗙𝗿𝗲𝗲” 𝗧𝗿𝗶𝗮𝗹 𝗔𝗰𝘁𝘂𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘆 𝗦𝗵𝗼𝘄?

𝘈 𝘵𝘪𝘯𝘺 𝘣𝘳𝘶𝘴𝘩 𝘢𝘯𝘥 𝘢 𝘧𝘦𝘸 𝘴𝘦𝘤𝘰𝘯𝘥𝘴 𝘰𝘧 𝘢𝘱𝘱𝘭𝘪𝘤𝘢𝘵𝘪𝘰𝘯 𝘮𝘢𝘬𝘦 𝘧𝘰𝘳 𝘢 𝘤𝘰𝘮𝘱𝘦𝘭𝘭𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘴𝘵𝘰𝘳𝘺.

A recent 𝗨𝗻𝗶𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘀𝗶𝘁𝘆 𝗼𝗳 𝗠𝗶𝗰𝗵𝗶𝗴𝗮𝗻–𝗹𝗲𝗱 𝘁𝗿𝗶𝗮𝗹—conducted in collaboration with New York University, the University of Iowa, Indiana University, the University of Minnesota, and Marquette University—provides important, but already well-known, evidence. Among 830 young children with severe early childhood caries, 𝘀𝗶𝗹𝘃𝗲𝗿 𝗱𝗶𝗮𝗺𝗶𝗻𝗲 𝗳𝗹𝘂𝗼𝗿𝗶𝗱𝗲 (𝗦𝗗𝗙) arrested more cavitated lesions than water:

• 𝗔𝘁 𝟲 𝗺𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗵𝘀: Estimated arrest rates were 𝟱𝟰.𝟬% with SDF vs. 𝟮𝟮.𝟱% with placebo.

• 𝗔𝘁 𝟴 𝗺𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗵𝘀 (𝗮𝗳𝘁𝗲𝗿 𝗮 𝘀𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗻𝗱 𝗮𝗽𝗽𝗹𝗶𝗰𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻): Arrest rates dropped to 𝟱𝟬.𝟮% with SDF vs. 𝟭𝟳.𝟰% with placebo.

While notable, these are lesion-level results over a short follow-up period. Furthermore, the treatment was applied to an average of 𝗼𝗻𝗹𝘆 𝟮.𝟰 𝗰𝗮𝘃𝗶𝘁𝗶𝗲𝘀 𝗼𝘂𝘁 𝗼𝗳 𝟭𝟮 𝗱𝗺𝗳𝘁, leaving the remaining lesions in the same child in clinical limbo (the article didn't report the "d" value, but given the very young age of the children, it is not unexpected that the whole 12 is the "d" value).

𝗪𝗵𝗲𝗿𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗛𝗲𝗮𝗱𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗲 𝗗𝗿𝗶𝗳𝘁𝘀 𝗳𝗿𝗼𝗺 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗗𝗮𝘁𝗮

The university’s public-facing headline moves well beyond these findings, suggesting the treatment could prevent cavities from leading to pain, infections, emergency visits, and surgery.

𝙏𝙝𝙚 𝙩𝙧𝙞𝙖𝙡 𝙙𝙞𝙙 𝙣𝙤𝙩 𝙙𝙚𝙢𝙤𝙣𝙨𝙩𝙧𝙖𝙩𝙚 𝙩𝙝𝙖𝙩.

• 𝗡𝗼 𝗱𝗶𝗳𝗳𝗲𝗿𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗲 𝗶𝗻 𝗽𝗮𝗶𝗻: The study found no statistically significant difference in pain between the SDF and placebo groups.

• 𝗨𝗻𝗺𝗲𝗮𝘀𝘂𝗿𝗲𝗱 𝗰𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗶𝗰𝗮𝗹 𝗼𝘂𝘁𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗲𝘀: It did not measure whether SDF reduced emergency room visits or the eventual need for surgery under general anesthesia.

• 𝗔𝗯𝘀𝗰𝗲𝘀𝘀𝗲𝘀 𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗹𝗹 𝗼𝗰𝗰𝘂𝗿𝗿𝗲𝗱: Despite excluding lesions from the start that might compromise the targeted arrest rate, 𝟴.𝟱% 𝗼𝗳 𝗦𝗗𝗙-𝗽𝗮𝗶𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗱 𝘁𝗲𝗲𝘁𝗵 𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗹𝗹 𝗱𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗹𝗼𝗽𝗲𝗱 𝗱𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗮𝗹 𝗮𝗯𝘀𝗰𝗲𝘀𝘀𝗲𝘀—even within the pristine, tightly controlled environment of a clinical trial that rarely mirrors everyday, community, or general pediatric practice.

𝗪𝗵𝘆 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝘀 𝗱𝗶𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗺𝗮𝘁𝘁𝗲𝗿𝘀: Arresting a lesion by a study’s criteria is not the same as restoring a tooth’s form, function, or appearance, nor does it establish that a child will avoid later definitive treatment.

This trial offers repetitive evidence that SDF can arrest 𝘴𝘰𝘮𝘦 lesions for a 𝘭𝘪𝘮𝘪𝘵𝘦𝘥 period. It also documented efficacy fade with time despite the second application. It does not establish SDF as a "drill-free" substitute for comprehensive dental care.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗖𝗼𝘀𝘁 𝗼𝗳 𝗢𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘀𝘁𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗖𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗶𝗰𝗮𝗹 𝗘𝘃𝗶𝗱𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗲

𝗔 𝗿𝗲𝗽𝘂𝘁𝗮𝗯𝗹𝗲 𝘂𝗻𝗶𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘀𝗶𝘁𝘆 𝗰𝗮𝗻 𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗹𝗹 𝗱𝗿𝗶𝗳𝘁 𝗳𝗿𝗼𝗺 𝘄𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗶𝘁𝘀 𝗱𝗮𝘁𝗮 𝘀𝘂𝗽𝗽𝗼𝗿𝘁.

The trial’s roughly $𝟭𝟯 𝗺𝗶𝗹𝗹𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗶𝗻 𝗽𝘂𝗯𝗹𝗶𝗰 𝗿𝗲𝘀𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗰𝗵 𝗳𝘂𝗻𝗱𝗶𝗻𝗴 makes the evidence worth careful scrutiny, but a high price tag does not make broader claims true. Here, the data support a narrow conclusion about short-term lesion arrest—a mechanism documented many years ago. Claims about preventing pain, infection, emergency visits, or surgery require hard evidence that those specific patient outcomes actually improved.

𝘞𝘦 𝘸𝘪𝘴𝘩 𝘵𝘩𝘪𝘴 𝘴𝘵𝘶𝘥𝘺 𝘩𝘢𝘥 𝘣𝘦𝘦𝘯 𝘥𝘦𝘴𝘪𝘨𝘯𝘦𝘥 𝘵𝘰 𝘥𝘦𝘮𝘰𝘯𝘴𝘵𝘳𝘢𝘵𝘦 𝘵𝘩𝘰𝘴𝘦 𝘰𝘶𝘵𝘤𝘰𝘮𝘦𝘴 𝘵𝘰 𝘫𝘶𝘴𝘵𝘪𝘧𝘺 𝘪𝘵𝘴 𝘴𝘶𝘣𝘴𝘵𝘢𝘯𝘵𝘪𝘢𝘭 𝘤𝘰𝘴𝘵 and to resolve the clinical uncertainties that children, families, and front-line dentists have long awaited answers to.

The trial was halted early after a planned interim analysis of roughly half the enrolled cohort (680 of 1,144 planned children) met the primary efficacy threshold. In clinical trial statistics, stopping early for efficacy can overestimate true treatment effects and leave secondary endpoints underpowered. Halting a trial at an interim analysis (after ~59% of planned enrollment) for early efficacy is a known statistical phenomenon that tends to overestimate the true magnitude of an intervention's benefit ("random high" bias) and leaves secondary safety and patient-reported outcomes underpowered. Elite institutions, major funding bodies (like the NIH/NIDCR), and top-tier journals (like JAMA Pediatrics) are lowering scientific expectations by celebrating regulatory box-checking as landmark science and dropping what matters to children and families. 

𝗟𝗼𝗼𝗸𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗮𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗰𝘂𝗿𝗿𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝘀𝗰𝗶𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗳𝗶𝗰 𝗹𝗮𝗻𝗱𝘀𝗰𝗮𝗽𝗲 𝗶𝗻 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗨𝗦—𝘀𝗽𝗮𝗻𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗮𝗰𝗮𝗱𝗲𝗺𝗶𝗰 𝗶𝗻𝘀𝘁𝗶𝘁𝘂𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀, 𝗳𝘂𝗻𝗱𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗯𝗼𝗱𝗶𝗲𝘀, 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗼𝗿𝗴𝗮𝗻𝗶𝘇𝗲𝗱 𝗱𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗶𝘀𝘁𝗿𝘆—𝘁𝗵𝗶𝘀 𝗱𝗶𝘀𝗰𝗼𝗻𝗻𝗲𝗰𝘁 𝗯𝗲𝘁𝘄𝗲𝗲𝗻 𝗿𝗲𝘀𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗰𝗵 𝗱𝗮𝘁𝗮 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗽𝘂𝗯𝗹𝗶𝗰 𝗺𝗲𝘀𝘀𝗮𝗴𝗶𝗻𝗴, 𝗽𝗼𝗹𝗶𝗰𝘆 𝗱𝗿𝗮𝗳𝘁𝘀, 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗮𝗻𝗻𝘂𝗮𝗹 𝗴𝘂𝗶𝗱𝗲𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗲𝘀 𝗶𝘀 𝗱𝗲𝗲𝗽𝗹𝘆 𝘁𝗿𝗼𝘂𝗯𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗴.

text:
Anthropic's IPO lands Thursday with more than 900 billion dollars in spending commitments riding on it. The biggest tech IPO in years now carries the weight of much of the AI industry.

Anthropic is expected to price its shares on Wednesday and begin trading on Nasdaq under the ticker ANT on Thursday, at an expected 70 to 78 dollars a share. CNBC reports the stakes reach almost every major tech company. AMD, Broadcom, Google, Micron, Microsoft, Nvidia and TSMC are collectively investing 26 billion dollars at the IPO price.

The bigger exposure is what Anthropic has promised to spend. According to its prospectus, the Claude maker has outstanding spending commitments of more than 900 billion dollars. Those are commitments, not money spent or cash in hand. They include at least 110 billion dollars with Amazon over a decade, and, per filings and partner disclosures cited by CNBC, another 400 billion dollars with other cloud providers and 300 billion dollars with data center and chip partners.

The losses are just as large. Anthropic recorded a net loss of 104 billion dollars in the first nine months of 2026, CNBC reports. The IPO could yield more than 90 billion dollars on top of 132 billion dollars in existing cash and short-term investments. "In the past, we have significantly underestimated our compute requirements," the company says in its prospectus.

Partners are already carrying some of the risk. Google, set to own about 13 percent of Anthropic after the IPO, is backstopping 19 billion dollars in lease commitments to data center firm TeraWulf, according to TeraWulf. Bank of America, Blackstone, Citigroup and Morgan Stanley have offered 63 billion dollars to buy racks of Broadcom AI chips that Anthropic will rent, with Broadcom backstopping up to 43 billion dollars.

The timing is rough. The Nasdaq fell 5.3 percent in October. Nvidia shares dropped 13 percent last week after Jensen Huang's ouster, and interim CEO Colette Kress reports quarterly results on Tuesday, two days before Anthropic debuts.

"The numbers are just staggering," Eclipse partner Joe Fath told CNBC. For American investors and the companies building America's AI capacity, Thursday is a referendum on whether those numbers can be financed.

text:
On Christmas Eve, a boy filled his little brother and sister’s stockings with potatoes, coal, and sagebrush. They had no presents, and it was all he could give them.

Then a big automobile stopped outside.

The driver was Gilbert Hilman, a prosperous farmer in Nephi Anderson’s 1916 story “How the Spirit of Christmas Came.” Gilbert had spent the day avoiding his neighbors. 

He offered a worn-out horse to a neighbor who needed one, then filled two boys’ collection baskets with heavy carrots after they mentioned that apples were plentiful and cheap. He laughed as they struggled away.

Next came Willie Stanger, collecting for Sunday School. Gilbert had already given a nickel, but Willie insisted it was more blessed to give than receive. Then he asked whether Gilbert was lonely, living without any family.

Gilbert gave him two nickels. He wanted to be “twice blessed,” he said.

That evening, Gilbert sat alone with a book as snow fell outside. He’d inherited a farm and built up plenty of money, but lost touch with his neighbors. When he heard voices at the gate, he turned out the light.

It was Constance Davies, president of the ward Relief Society. Years before, Gilbert had wanted to marry her. She chose another man, and Gilbert avoided her afterward. Her husband had since died.

She needed Gilbert to drive her to Stringtown. Several poor families had been missed during Christmas deliveries, and their packages still needed to reach them. Gilbert never took his car out at night, he protested.

Constance said Christmas was a time to do good things, even when you didn’t want to. Gilbert asked whether she ever did something she disliked. She paused. “Coming here and asking for your automobile.”

She said the hard part wasn’t leaving without the car. It was staying when she knew he didn’t want her there. Gilbert apologized, brought the car around, and drove Constance and Mary Hill to the meetinghouse for their packages.

The storm had cleared, and moonlight shone on the snow. Gilbert waited in the car as the women delivered packages from house to house. 

At their last stop, Constance asked him to come inside. The children’s father might be home, and Constance didn’t want to approach the house without Gilbert. They knocked twice before a boy answered.

A boy named Frank let them into a dimly lit room with a bare floor, a rusty stove, and a box of chopped sagebrush for fuel. His younger brother and sister slept beneath a patched quilt. 

Beside the stove hung two pairs of ragged stockings, strangely full.

Constance felt inside one and pulled out a potato, then a lump of coal and a piece of sagebrush. Frank admitted he’d put them there himself. “They, the kids, would hang up their stockin’s, an’ that’s all I had.”

Gilbert remembered growing up in a room much like this one. One Christmas, his older brother had filled his stockings with coal and potatoes. 

When Gilbert woke and saw them bulging, he eagerly carried them back to bed, only to discover what was inside. He remembered crying alone that Christmas morning.

He stepped toward the sleeping children and gently stroked the little girl’s hair. He asked Constance whether she had a doll for the girl or any toy for the boy. She had neither.

“They shall not wake to the misery which I once did,” Gilbert said. He was determined to do something about it.

Gilbert checked his watch and drove into town. Thirty minutes later he returned with a doll, a train, a trumpet, and a bag of nuts. They filled the stockings until the doll’s feet and the train’s nose barely fit. Frank got presents, too.

Anderson published this story in the Juvenile Instructor in December 1916. It’s fiction, and one of the readings I included in Pioneer Christmas. 

He ended it with a hint about Gilbert’s future: “What more came back to him, beginning from that Christmas Eve, is quite another story.”

text:
She’d gone out for a quiet walk. Before she knew it, Susa Young Gates had been “crushed between two fighting women” arguing over a cheap trinket in a store.

That’s how Gates described an encounter with Christmas shoppers in an essay published in December 1906. Writing as “Aunt Su” in The Young Woman’s Journal, she complained about the packed streets, glittering shop windows, and exhausted girls working behind the counters. 

She wondered what king could be coming that people were willing to shove and wear themselves out getting ready for him.

The King of Kings, her imaginary listener answered. They were preparing to celebrate the birth of Christ.

Gates wasn’t convinced that people were celebrating him at all. Christ had been born in a stable, she pointed out. What did that have to do with extravagant gifts, debt, and weeks of worry?

“The modern Christmas ideal has become a Juggernaut,” she wrote, leaving “a trail of broken bodies and shattered nerves in its wake.”

And the shopping was only part of it. There were elaborate dinners, fancy table decorations, Christmas trees at home and school, social gatherings, and Church festivals for the poor. 

Gates thought all these obligations were making Christmas a season many wives and mothers dreaded.

Consider the gift list of a young Latter-day Saint woman. Gates pictured someone with a dozen brothers and sisters, another dozen aunts and uncles, and enough cousins, nieces, and nephews to bring the total to a hundred relatives. 

Then she was expected to keep up with gift ideas in the women’s magazines.

Gates had some thoughts about those magazines, too. She told readers that the elaborate holiday projects were often dreamed up by writers who didn’t have homes and children to care for. 

Their business was coming up with something novel for the next issue. “Anything to sell the magazine,” she complained.

Her answer had a familiar name among Latter-day Saints: “retrenchment.” Brigham Young had used that word when organizing women’s associations, urging them to cut back on extravagance in dress, food, speech, and daily living. 

Gates thought it was time to remember what he’d meant.

For a start, she said, stop feeling obligated to give gifts to every relative. And stop making social visits you dread just because you think you ought to. She repeated one woman’s advice to her sister about dreaded social calls: “don’t call … if you don’t want to.”

Another woman had resolved to give up Christmas presents altogether, apart from her usual five-dollar contribution to the Relief Society and some candy and nuts for the children. She could remember friends and family on birthdays instead.

Gates wasn’t proposing that families give up Christmas. She described an older kind of celebration with stockings over the fireplace, knitted mufflers, rag dolls, wooden swords, and perhaps a little store-bought candy. 

A simple dinner, some time together, and a reading of the story of Christ’s birth seemed a better way to spend the day.

She even had reservations about the Christmas tree. If the older children wanted to string popcorn and make decorations, fine. But if mother had to trim the tree, fill stockings, make her Relief Society visits on Christmas Eve, and prepare a huge dinner, she might be exhausted and irritable before anyone sat down to eat. 

In that case, Gates said, the tree was “a snare and a delusion.”

The essay was called “Simplicity: The Simple Holiday,” and it’s one of the readings I included in Pioneer Christmas. After several pages of scolding her readers, Gates admitted she was guilty of some of the same habits.

“Now, friend, I’ve said some harsh and bitter things,” she wrote. “And I am fool, or foolish, just as you and all the rest.”

text:
This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here.

This year millions of people have tried—and been wowed by— artificial-intelligence systems. That’s in no small part thanks to OpenAI’s chatbot ChatGPT. 

When it launched last November, the chatbot became an instant hit among students, many of whom embraced it as a tool to write essays and finish homework. Some media outlets went as far as to declare that the college essay is dead. 

Alarmed by an influx of AI-generated essays, schools around the world moved swiftly to ban the use of the technology. 

But nearly half a year later, the outlook is a lot less bleak. For MIT Technology Review’s upcoming print issue on education, my colleague Will Douglas Heaven spoke to a number of educators who are now reevaluating what chatbots like ChatGPT mean for how we teach our kids. Many teachers now believe that far from being just a dream machine for cheaters, ChatGPT could actually help make education better. Read his story here. 

What’s clear from Will’s story is that ChatGPT will change the way schools teach. But the biggest educational outcome from the technology might not be a new way of writing essays or homework. It’s AI literacy. 

AI is becoming an increasingly integral part of our lives, and tech companies are rolling out AI-powered products at a breathtakingly fast pace. AI language models could become powerful productivity tools that we use every single day. 

I’ve written a lot about the dangers associated with artificial intelligence, from biased avatar generators to the impossible task of detecting AI-generated text. 

Every time I ask experts about what ordinary people can do to protect themselves from these types of harm, the answer is the same. They say there is an urgent need for the public to be better informed about how AI works and what its limitations are, in order to prevent ourselves from being fooled or harmed by a computer program.

Until now, the uptake of AI literacy schemes has been sluggish. But ChatGPT has forced many schools to quickly adapt and start teaching kids an ad hoc curriculum of AI 101. 

The teachers Will spoke to had already started applying a critical lens to technologies such as ChatGPT. Emily Donahoe, a writing tutor and educational developer at the University of Mississippi, said she thinks that ChatGPT could help teachers shift away from an excessive focus on final results. Getting a class to engage with AI and think critically about what it generates could make teaching feel more human, she says, “rather than asking students to write and perform like robots.”

And because the AI model has been trained with North American data and reflects North American biases, teachers are finding that it is a great way to start a conversation about bias. 

David Smith, a professor of bioscience education at Sheffield Hallam University in the UK, allows his undergraduate students to use ChatGPT in their written assignments, but he will assess the prompt as well as—or even rather than—the essay itself. “Knowing the words to use in a prompt and then understanding the output that comes back is important,” he says. “We need to teach how to do that.” 

One of the biggest flaws of AI language models is that they make stuff up and confidently present falsehoods as facts. This makes them unsuitable for tasks where accuracy is extremely important, such as scientific research and health care. But Helen Crompton, an associate professor of instructional technology at Old Dominion University in Norfolk, Virginia, has found the AI’s model’s “hallucinations” a useful teaching tool too. 

“The fact that it’s not perfect is great,” Crompton says. It’s an opportunity for productive discussions about misinformation and bias. 

These kinds of examples give me hope that education systems and policymakers will realize just how important it is to teach the next generation critical thinking skills around AI. 

For adults, one promising AI literacy initiative is a free online course called Elements of AI, which is developed by startup MinnaLearn and the University of Helsinki. It was launched in 2018 and is now available in 28 languages. Elements of AI teaches people what AI is and, most important, what it can and can’t do. I’ve tried it myself, and it’s a great resource.

My bigger concern is whether we will be able to get adults up to speed quickly enough. Without AI literacy among the internet-surfing adult population, more and more people are bound to fall prey to unrealistic expectations and hype. Meanwhile, AI chatbots could be weaponized as powerful phishing, scamming, and misinformation tools. 

The kids will be alright. It’s the adults we need to worry about.  

Deeper Learning

The complex math of counterfactuals could help Spotify pick your next favorite song

A new kind of machine-learning model built by a team of researchers at the music-streaming firm Spotify captures, for the first time, the complex math behind counterfactual analysis, a precise technique that can be used to identify the causes of past events and predict the effects of future ones. By tweaking the right things, it’s possible to separate true causation from correlation and coincidence.

What’s the big deal: The model could improve the accuracy of automated decision-making, especially personalized recommendations, in a range of applications from finance to health care. In Spotify’s case, that might mean choosing what songs to show you or when artists should drop a new album. Read more from Will Douglas Heaven here. 

Bits and Bytes

Sam Altman’s PR blitz continues
It’s fascinating to see the birth of tech folklore in real time. Two profiles of OpenAI founder Sam Altman from the New York Times and the Wall Street Journal paint a picture of Altman as a new tech luminary, akin to Steve Jobs or Bill Gates. The Times calls Altman “ChatGPT King,” while the Journal goes for “AI Crusader.” Yet more proof that the Great Man myth is still alive and well in tech. 

ChatGPT invented a sexual harassment scandal and accused a real law professor 
AI models make things up, and sometimes they even offer legitimate-looking citations for their nonsense. This story about an innocent professor who was accused of sexual harassment illustrates the very real harm that can result. “Hallucinations” are already getting OpenAI in legal problems. Last week, an Australian mayor threatened to sue OpenAI for defamation unless it corrects false claims that he served time in prison for bribery. This is something I warned about last year. (Washington Post) 

How Lex Fridman’s podcast became a safe space for the “anti-woke” tech elite
A fascinating read on the rise of Lex Fridman, the controversial and hugely popular AI researcher turned podcaster, and his complicated relationship with the AI community—and Elon Musk. (Business Insider) 

Pollsters are starting to survey AIs instead of people 
People don’t reply to political polls. A new research experiment is trying to see if AI chatbots could help by mirroring how certain demographics would answer polling questions. Polling is already a dubious science, and this is likely to make it even more so. (The Atlantic) 

Fashion brands are using AI-generated models in the name of diversity
Brands such as Levi’s and Calvin Klein are using AI-generated models to “supplement” their representation of people of various sizes, skin tones, and ages. But why not just hire diverse humans? *Screams into the void* (The Guardian)

text:
When you're French you develop a kinetic ability to know  if the baguette is good by the sound of the crust being crushed gently. You're supposed to eat the "quignon" (the top bit) before you go home : the acceptable justification being that then you can then preserve the baguette in the wrapper (of course). How bright the crust is, hopefully burnt but not too much anywhere, how much flour there is (a crook baker might put a ton of flour to increase the weight). You end up with flour everywhere, it's a bastard powder that gets into car seats, dashboards, tote bags, jumpers. I'm extraordinarily picky about bread, not that I'd waste it ; any bread is worth eating, fresh but also dry, toasted, drenched in eggs. Buy 3 sticks of bread is the daily expense people account for, would never stop neither realise how much they eat during meals

It's funny because that table cloth triggers me, it's genuinely the go to "Pique-Nique" (that english stole and rebranded as "picnic"), that improvised outdoor lunch. Or indoor countryside tablecloth. For me it's a proper cliché but it's also nailed on

Magnets on the fridge is universal, I'd imagine. I have the French departments (counties) as magnets, with like three or four drawings on each - too much to remember by heart but also because I moved about 14 times in my life, and yet that magnetic map was a constant in my life it's the only thing I've constantly referred to as in "you're moving to a new place - how is it like"
It is also true I sometimes played "what if the sea was rising" to create a new map removing what I didn't like - didn't get on too well, but there was a point where I was ecologically conscious before it was a gimmick, I guess. I still am, but don't make it my whole identity

Cheese has to be kept outside, not in the fridge. Put a metal wired bell-shape cover, but let it breathe. So that the crust is always a little bit damp, the upper and lower layers are the tastiest bits because they become dry overtime and keep the salt. The middle bit is how you evaluate if it's good cheese : if it looks like feta, run, if it's liquid without separating it's perfect

The thing is, I've been fortunate to eat a considerable amount of dairy products mostly artisinal non processed cheese, we were never "loaded" but I guess having consistently a full plate of dozens of different slices of cheeses is good investment. I don't know how relatable that experience is. So I'm not only knowledgeable, but I also ate every type of cheese, crust included even with mould on it. Take it as it is : I've never been ill more than two days in a row in my life, I don't catch "cold" "flu" etc maybe because of it

I have utter contempt for whoever pretends processed cheese is "cheese". No, it's a dairy product. It tasting the same everywhere isn't a seal of quality. It's also the only food I can't resist, every two months I have the urge to buy real one, that I can't resist. No other food does it to me. (bad bread doesn't count, I'd rather not)

France and wine is really funny because there's truly a range of wine for everyone : a cardboard cube, the plastic wine "villageoise", glass bottles and a wild range of niche. Full shelves in supermarkets with local sourcing, where you can genuinely find gems. I don't think French people realise how alcoholic they are. 
3 glasses of 15% alcohol per meal, and finishing a bottle with 2 is more than downing a bucket of lager, when you take into account the quantity of alcohol, more than the volume of liquid.
As a kid, I was allowed to dip my finger in the glass sometimes and still didn't became an alcoholic (I only drink white wine anyway, red gives me headaches).

I will say I grew up to know what was the world before and after smoking was banned in outdoor places. You'd genuinely walk outside and 3 people out of 5 smoke, a crowded street / restaurant would be a nuage of smoke.
You'd know people by everything else but also their cigarette smell. Taking cigarette breaks every half an hour (what about productivity)

Le Monde, is what my dad reads, buying it was also my first huge responsibility as an emerging human and financial investor on the trade market ; exchanging metal coins for a copy of the day's edition
I know the weight, the smell and the texture of it compared to any other newspaper. The smell of coins (go wash your hands) that never really goes away. I'm pretty sure I wouldn't throw money by the window like I'm doing with contactless payments. 4€ for a coffee, I wouldn't break a bill of 10 to end up with 1€ or, worse, a bill of 20€

One of the experiences you love as a kid is to feel the gifts, even if it's pure cheap junk. I cherish my miniature  metal Tour Eiffel. It means a lot to me, in my box of souvenirs on my first trip to Paris. For someone who never lived in Paris, I've been there a considerable amount of times in different times of my life so I've always had a good experience of it

Before Emily in Paris, people would wear berets, mostly women from what I see / remember.

France is so diverse - that's why the racist rhetoric can't catch up, you're French by being petulant and "too much" not because of what you eat or look like. Sometimes I realise how south-european we are, because there's a lot of olives, olive oil to fry a lot of meals. Which is good and healthy I guess

Cornichons - gherkin - apparently it's the coutume to prepare gherkins in vinegar and offer it to people. Never really liked it, 

Lavande is pretty much the "vanilla" smell - quite often the original one, kept dry in cupboards in small bags for the smell of it, or the chemical taste in products. Sometimes, life makes it that it becomes a more pressing memory but at least it's captured here for a part.

Riots - because what's more suited than riot police with flashballs to allow manifestants to demonstrate in peace. When riot police swarms them from both sides to trap people, it might be because they're thick and can't read.

The main reason why Napoleon III - inspired by London's big boulevards in the early 1800 tasked Hausmann to flatten the old Paris to build these immensely large avenues in straight lines, was to make it difficult to barricade. It also creates lines of sight, which allows you to watch the Arc de Triomphe from the Concorde, but also be aimed at from a distance

Blue White Red is funny because when you grow up there it's on every official documents, but when you go abroad you realise how cartoon-ish that is. There's a complex historical legacy with the colors. But also, why would France Football Team play with red socks, white shorts and blue tops and still take it seriously
It's the same colors as the Union Jack somewhat. Now I'm abroad I begin to see it's similar to the irish flag or any three band flag, as a country like another (beside my own) and kinda grasp the "here are the french" 

It's funny because it's been used all over the spectrum, by identitaran merchants, popular culture, obviously most of the language settings menues and carries so many meanings. And right now it looks like it's being rebranded again by people demonstrating for accessing basic public services, not so much because they're entitled to them, but because they're being told their money is being used for it

I just procrastinated half an hour about the Frenchness of that AI slop, because the conception of time is so unique : comfortable knowing the world won't fall apart if you take a longer lunch break, there's a dozen words to describe activities related to walking about and what's the social purpose of it, it's actually lame to be on time and you've got to be 15' late to many things to pretend your life is busy
and yet if you think French people don't care about any of these things, try to pretend their cheese is overrated and you'll know the full extent of their thought like you're personally insulting them

Sister, Islam does not require you to perform Ghusl immediately after marital intimacy. Whenever Ghusl becomes obligatory due to intercourse, you are allowed to sleep, eat, prepare meals, look after your children, and carry out your daily responsibilities while in a state of Janabah. It is Sunnah to wash your private parts and perform Wudu before sleeping. Aishah (رضي الله عنها) reported that the Prophet ﷺ would perform Wudu when he wanted to sleep while in a state of Janabah. (Sahih al-Bukhari 288; Sahih Muslim 305).

However, you must perform Ghusl before offering the next obligatory prayer. In other words, you can complete your household duties and other activities, but you must make sure that you perform Ghusl and offer your Salah within its prescribed time. For example, if you have intercourse during the night or before Fajr, you must perform Ghusl and pray Fajr before sunrise. You should therefore arrange your routine accordingly rather than allowing the prayer time to pass. If you have already missed a prayer, sincerely repent to Allah and make up the missed prayer as soon as possible.

May Allah bless your efforts, make your responsibilities easy, and help you remain steadfast in your prayers. Ameen 🤲

And Allah knows best.

November 9, 2017 was the first time that I ever met Egbon Kola @officialKolaO Ologbondiyan when he was running to be National Publicity Secretary of our then great party, PDP.

In what is forever a burned-into-memory moment in humility for me and due to airport flight timing, Egbon Kola offered to come to my hotel in Abuja to ask for my support and ever since that day, he has carried me in his bosom and prioritised social media like only few of his generation ever did. Egbon Kola would personally finance covert intel missions into a state like Osun for us young ones to meet high stakeholders and try to resolve local differences from the national - myself and the late Dare Atoye Ariyo went on a few. He used the office of Publicity Secretary to give many of us a place in politics.

Egbon would always fight and insist on giving us younger ones a place at the table and tell us to take it, even if the seat would come through social media. 

I have a personal theory that the demise of PDP started with a Publicity Secretary who did not understand social media and the role it plays in global politics; but today is not Ologunagba’s day.

Going personal though, ever since that day in November, Egbon has never stopped carrying me on his head and in his bosom, my political story will never be complete without his name featuring in many chapters of my journey. His effort towards my becoming Publicity Secretary in Lagos PDP, his consistent pushing my name forward in high places even till date, the early morning informal discussions - looking back at it now, Oga Kola (and Chief Olisa Metuh) demystified national politics for so many of us in PDP back then and inspired our aspiration.

Egbon Kola, you taught us humility but I am forever proud to call you my Leader, my Boss and my Egbon - the one who fights for his aburos even in their relational absence.

I humbly pray for you Sir on your Birthday: May the doors you opened for the children of others also open for your own children wherever they go. As you have sown in our lives, so may your generation reap even more bountifully and may your name forever be treasured by those who know the value of association with you, of which I am an eternal debtor.

Happy Birthday, Kola @officialKolaO Ologbondiyan.

text:
On days when life gets a bit overwhelming, people may look for ways to keep their thoughts and feelings in check.  Last week, when I learned that the insurance company decided not to honor our expedited appeal, I knew I needed to walk away – not from the fight we were still fighting but from the frustration of trying to manage something that was out of my 
A recap: 
We’ve pinpointed that a failure to file paperwork on time caused some of the problems we are currently dealing with.  
We’ve determined that lack of documentation on other paperwork contributed to an immediate removal of services that our son granted quickly years ago.  
Had the paperwork mishap been our fault, I think I mightmanage some of this better:  I’d take the blame, and I’d work through the major disappointment I’m sure I’d feel.  
But we’re at the mercy of case managers and facilitatorsworking on behalf of our son.  Their mainjob is to coordinate services and keep up with necessary paperwork that insurance companies keep on file.  From past experience we know that when everyone does their job, Ronan gets what he needs.  Ifwe’dknown that case management failed to follow through with these paperwork requirements, we’d have made some noise.  
Not knowing what was needed until it was too late ledto a slew of frustrating phone calls and emails.  
Back-and-forth we’ve gone with insurance, case managers, facilitators, and anyone else we could think of who could offer advice, an encouraging word, or any secrets to restoring what was working for Rone.  
Barring getting a state representative to help us, which we are not opposed to doing, we’ve done everything we think we can.  That tactic may be next, depending on what insurance comes back with.  On the day I saw that the insurance company refused to consider our expedited request, which would have given us an answer within 3 days, I had to walk away from it.  
So, I did. 
“Hey, girls.  I’m going for a walk, just down the street and back.”  
That’s my go to ‘clear my head’ route.  Outside.  Down the street.  Just to the stop sign.  Come back home.  
But I didn’t want to come back home when I got to the stop sign.  
So, I kept walking. 
Sometimes I’ll start a Rosary while I’m out, but I was too frustrated to pray.  I tried to brainstorm ideas of what else we might be able to do to resolve this, but my thoughts were too jumbled.  The longer I stayed out, the clearer one thing was – this was so far out of my control. 
But it was controlling me.  
If I had more time, I’d have walked farther that evening.  The sun was setting, though, and I hadn’t started to make dinner yet.  My family needed me more than I needed to sulk, so I turned around and walked back home.  
Since October 1st we’ve managed an unexpected loss of services.  We’ve rearranged work schedules and daily tasks to make sure some of the continuity of care for Ronan remains.  Interruptions in caregiver pay have happened, too, which took all of us by surprise.  It’s been one thing after another.  Then we found out that one reason the insurance company refused to honor the expedited appeal we submitted is because they did not deem his case to be “life threatening” (he’s not bed-ridden, on oxygen,needing nursing care, etc.).  Where that decision not to honor the expedited appeal holds some weight, it really ticked me off.  Then I remembered something.  
Expedite! 
￼
As in St. Expedite – I’d said a novena last year and received a favorable answer to a desperate plea!  
Just like we always try, try again, we pray, pray again.  The worry, the growing anger, and the disbelief stayed with me after my walk, but we’ve worked too hard to have any of that be a final answer.  Where nothing has been determined yet, I resolved to find a way to pray specifically again for Ronan’s services to be restored.  Join us also if you’d like – we are always grateful for the extra support

I think this is mostly true, but like most things, there’s more to it. A couple things skew this.

Year after year the top teams have a franchise QB, probably a top 10-ish or better. There can be outliers (like the 2026 Vikings) but that’s not sustainable. You gotta have the QB or else this isn’t all that relevant.

An offensive play calling coach doesn’t automatically make your team better. Dallas has a good franchise QB and an offensive coach calling plays along with all the firepower you could want. They’re awful.

Defensive and/or CEO coaches can do it, and have. Macdonald just won the Super Bowl, and the SB loser also had the CEO coach. Not that long ago Belichick, Pete Carroll, Tomlin, and John Harbough were wrecking the league. Even Dan Quinn and Ron Rivera got to a Super Bowl. But they had the QBs and the coordinators.

That’s the thing, they have to nail that OC hire. And what everyone talks about is what happens when you lose that OC (like how Quinn lost Shannahan or Macdonald lost Kubiak). But I feel like there’s still value to someone like John Harbough, Tomlin, or Vrabel. Mike Vrabel found an OC who probably won’t be getting a HC offer anytime soon. That might be the trick. Maybe you find a good but older OC who knows he’s better as a No. 2 (the Vic Fangio/Wade Phillips types of OC’s). Offer him a ton of money to basically be the HC of the offense, and you can also reap the benefits of that CEO motivator/overseer coach 🤷‍♂️

I would still want to pair Jayden with a stud offensive coach. But those guys aren’t always available. I just want a good coaching staff teaching our young players good habits and to focus on details.

text:
Plus Bank pod decyzją UOKiK. Uwierzytelnienie PIN-em to za mało, by odmówić zwrotu
Solorz Business Daily · 15.11.2026

Prezes UOKiK 3 listopada 2026 r. wydał wobec Plus Banku, kontrolowanego przez Zygmunta Solorza, decyzję zobowiązującą nr RWR 8/2026. Urząd uznał za uprawdopodobnione, że bank odmawiał zwrotu pieniędzy po nieautoryzowanych transakcjach, sugerował klientom, że użycie PIN-u oznacza ich zgodę, i podawał nieprawdziwe limity reklamacji. Bank zobowiązał się zmienić procedury i ponownie zbadać odrzucone zgłoszenia. Kary finansowej nie orzeczono. Kwot zwrotów decyzja nie podaje, bo Urząd je utajnił.

Rozstrzygnięcie ogłoszono 4 listopada razem z podobnymi decyzjami wobec ING Banku Śląskiego, Banku Ochrony Środowiska i Nest Banku. To decyzja zobowiązująca z art. 28 ustawy o ochronie konkurencji i konsumentów: Plus Bank sam złożył zobowiązanie, a Prezes UOKiK je przyjął. Praktyki zostały „uprawdopodobnione”, a nie stwierdzone decyzją z karą.

Urząd zakwestionował trzy praktyki. Po pierwsze, bank nie zwracał kwoty nieautoryzowanej transakcji w terminie z art. 46 ust. 1 ustawy o usługach płatniczych, czyli najpóźniej do końca następnego dnia roboczego, choć nie miał podstawy prawnej, by zatrzymać pieniądze. Po drugie, w odpowiedziach na reklamacje informował klientów, że użycie PIN-u świadczy o autoryzacji operacji. We wzorze odpowiedzi, który cytuje decyzja, bank pisał, że „transakcja została autoryzowana po wprowadzeniu […] poprawnego numeru PIN”. Po trzecie, podawał nieprawdziwe informacje, że transakcji kartowych zgłoszonych po 120 dniach nie można uznać za nieautoryzowane i że nie da się reklamować więcej niż 15 transakcji. Te ograniczenia wynikały z procedur chargeback procesora kart, a nie z polskiego prawa, które daje klientowi 13 miesięcy na zgłoszenie.

Plus Bank musi wdrożyć nowe procedury najpóźniej sześć miesięcy po uprawomocnieniu się decyzji. Prawidłowe uwierzytelnienie nie może być jedyną podstawą do uznania, że klient sam autoryzował transakcję. Bank z urzędu ponownie rozpatrzy negatywne odpowiedzi udzielone obecnym klientom od 16 listopada 2022 r. i w uzasadnionych przypadkach zwróci pieniądze najpóźniej do 31 grudnia 2027 r. Byłych klientów, których reklamacje złożone po 15 listopada 2022 r. odrzucono, ma powiadomić o prawie do wniosku o ponowną weryfikację. Komunikat o decyzji ma się pojawić na https://t.co/gRPpJGSInO i w aplikacji mobilnej. Z realizacji obowiązków bank sprawozda Prezesowi UOKiK do 30 kwietnia 2028 r.

Dlaczego to było złe
Ustawa o usługach płatniczych stawia sprawę jasno. Z art. 46 wynika, że po zgłoszeniu nieautoryzowanej transakcji bank ma oddać pieniądze niezwłocznie, najpóźniej do końca następnego dnia roboczego (zasada D+1). Wyjątki są wąskie. Bank może wstrzymać zwrot, gdy ma uzasadnione i udokumentowane podstawy, by podejrzewać oszustwo ze strony samego klienta, i zawiadamia o tym organy ścigania. Zwrot nie przysługuje też, gdy od transakcji minęło więcej niż 13 miesięcy. Z art. 45 wynika, że ciężar dowodu spoczywa na banku. Samo użycie instrumentu płatniczego i prawidłowe uwierzytelnienie (PIN, kod z aplikacji, 3D Secure) nie wystarcza, by wykazać, że klient autoryzował transakcję albo działał umyślnie lub z rażącym niedbalstwem.

W praktyce ofiary spoofingu i phishingu często same wpisują PIN albo zatwierdzają operację w aplikacji, bo oszust podaje się za bank, policję albo inną instytucję. Plus Bank traktował taki ślad uwierzytelnienia jak dowód zgody i odmawiał zwrotu. Klient zostawał bez pieniędzy i słyszał, że odzyskać je można wyłącznie przez organy ścigania. Prezes UOKiK Tomasz Chróstny mówił przy ogłoszeniu decyzji: „Samo wykazanie przez bank, że transakcja została poprawnie uwierzytelniona to za mało, by odmówić zwrotu pieniędzy. Bank musi udowodnić, że to klient samodzielnie i świadomie autoryzował operację lub dopuścił się rażącego niedbalstwa.” W październiku 2026 r. Trybunał Sprawiedliwości UE w wyroku C-70/25 (Tukowiecka) potwierdził to stanowisko: bank nie może odmawiać zwrotu, zasłaniając się „rażącym zaniedbaniem” klienta. Jeśli tak uważa, najpierw oddaje pieniądze, a potem może dochodzić ich przed sądem.

Co to może oznaczać dla wyceny Midas i akcjonariuszy mniejszościowych
Bezpośredniego związku nie ma. Plus Bank kontroluje Zygmunt Solorz, ale sprawa dotyczy bankowości detalicznej, a nie sieci komórkowej ani częstotliwości Midas (900, 1800 i 2600 MHz TDD). Nie daje też argumentu co do wyceny z dnia squeeze-outu w 2016 r. (0,81 zł za akcję). Skutków finansowych dla Plus Banku nie da się dziś oszacować, bo decyzja nie podaje kwot ani kary. W sprawie XXVI GC 619/17 nie ma nowych publicznych informacji.

Plus Bank under a UOKiK decision. A PIN is not enough to refuse a refund
Solorz Business Daily · 15 Nov 2026

On 3 November 2026 the president of UOKiK, Poland's competition and consumer authority, issued commitment decision RWR 8/2026 against Plus Bank, which Zygmunt Solorz controls. The authority found it probable that the bank had refused to refund money after unauthorised transactions, told customers that entering a PIN amounted to their consent, and gave them false limits on complaints. The bank has undertaken to change its procedures and re-examine rejected claims. No financial penalty was imposed. The decision discloses no refund amounts because the authority redacted them.

The ruling was announced on 4 November together with similar decisions against ING Bank Śląski, Bank Ochrony Środowiska and Nest Bank. It is a commitment decision under Article 28 of the competition and consumer protection act: Plus Bank itself offered the undertaking, and the president of UOKiK accepted it. The practices were held to be "probable", not established by a fining decision.

The authority challenged three practices. First, the bank failed to refund unauthorised transactions within the deadline in Article 46(1) of the payment services act, which is the end of the next business day, even though it had no legal basis for withholding the money. Second, in its replies to complaints it told customers that use of a PIN proved the transaction had been authorised. In a template reply quoted in the decision, the bank wrote that "the transaction was authorised after a correct PIN was entered". Third, it falsely told customers that card transactions reported after 120 days could not be treated as unauthorised and that no more than 15 transactions could be disputed. Those limits came from the card processor's chargeback rules, not from Polish law, which gives customers 13 months to report a claim.

Plus Bank must put new procedures in place no later than six months after the decision becomes final. Correct authentication must not be the sole basis for concluding that the customer personally authorised a transaction. The bank must, on its own initiative, re-examine negative replies given to current customers since 16 November 2022 and, where justified, refund the money by 31 December 2027. Former customers whose complaints filed after 15 November 2022 were rejected must be told they may ask for a fresh review. A notice of the decision is to appear on https://t.co/gRPpJGSInO and in the mobile app. The bank must report to the president of UOKiK on how it has met these obligations by 30 April 2028.

Why it was wrong
The payment services act is clear. Article 46 says that once an unauthorised transaction is reported, the bank must return the money promptly, by the end of the next business day (the D+1 rule). The exceptions are narrow. The bank may hold back a refund if it has justified and documented grounds to suspect fraud by the customer and notifies law enforcement. No refund is due if more than 13 months have passed since the transaction. Article 45 places the burden of proof on the bank. Mere use of a payment instrument with correct authentication (a PIN, an app code, 3D Secure) is not enough to show that the customer authorised the transaction or acted intentionally or with gross negligence.

In practice, victims of spoofing and phishing often enter a PIN or approve a transaction in the app themselves, because the fraudster poses as the bank, the police or another institution. Plus Bank treated that authentication trail as proof of consent and refused refunds. Customers were left without their money and were told it could be recovered only through law enforcement. UOKiK president Tomasz Chróstny said when the decisions were announced: "Simply showing that the transaction was correctly authenticated is not enough to refuse a refund. The bank must prove that the customer personally and knowingly authorised the operation or was grossly negligent." In October 2026 the EU Court of Justice confirmed that position in case C-70/25 (Tukowiecka): a bank may not refuse a refund by invoking the customer's "gross negligence". If it takes that view, it must first return the money and may then pursue it in court.

What it may mean for the Midas valuation and minority shareholders
There is no direct link. Zygmunt Solorz controls Plus Bank, but the case concerns retail banking, not the mobile network or Midas's spectrum (900, 1800 and 2600 MHz TDD). It also offers no argument on the valuation as of the 2016 squeeze-out date (PLN 0.81 per share). The financial effect on Plus Bank cannot be quantified, because the decision gives no amounts and no fine. There is no new public information in case XXVI GC 619/17.

Sources: UOKiK press release of 4 Nov 2026, "Kolejne banki zweryfikują odrzucone reklamacje" (https://t.co/l3fsVABur6); decision of the president of UOKiK No. RWR 8/2026 of 3 Nov 2026 (https://t.co/lSuGGowOOn); Payment Services Act of 19 Aug 2011, Articles 45 and 46; CJEU judgment C-70/25 (Tukowiecka)

text:
The federal antitrust lawsuit allowed to proceed against Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron confuses manufacturing physics with corporate conspiracy.

Judge Noël Wise denial of the motion to dismiss cites chipmakers cutting conventional DDR5 to prioritize HBM, alongside a "failure to expand despite record prices."

From a buy-side semiconductor perspective, the legal framing misses the physical realities of the memory fab:
The 3:1 Wafer Cannibalization Law
Manufacturing a single bit of HBM4 requires 3x the wafer area of standard server DDR5. When hyperscalers and GPU vendors offer guaranteed multi-year take-or-pay prepayments at massive margin premiums, allocating wafer starts to HBM is rational corporate finance. Shifting cleanroom capacity to the highest-margin product is profit maximization, not an illegal cartel.
Cleanroom Physical Lead Times
The court points to a "failure to expand." But as Applied Materials earnings confirmed, leading-edge DRAM fabs run at 100% utilization. Building a cleanroom shell, passing environmental permits, and procuring extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography tools takes 24 to 36 months. A civil lawsuit cannot shorten ASML supply chains.
The Market Irony: Confirmation of Scarcity
Antitrust discovery proceedings take years to reach resolution. In the near term, this judicial ruling officially validates what institutional models have projected: conventional DDR5 supply is structurally starved through 2027.

Instead of depressing memory valuations, the legal scrutiny provides definitive proof that the three memory producers possess absolute pricing power.

Weave your thought thread into a poem in the style of' Dead Inside (Mix Edit) Flash Ki  In the poem weave in the cure for gaps: The gap between plausible deniability and transparency The gap between plausible deniability and accountability The gap between self organizing systems and predictability The gap between release of harms and cure for harms The gap between the cascade of the Butterfly harms and the cures for the cascades. I cite the following as Proof of Concept: Defund the Police, Corporate Activism Globalism, DEI, Affirmative Action ESG (Environmental, Social, and Governance) and CSR (Corporate Social Responsibility) Censorship Lockdowns  On this day 6 years ago Facebook William Ronald Yee Shared with Your friends  Yes, it is important to teach empathy and love.  However, if a child lives in a loving, caring family  it becomes more important  to teach them how to deal with antisocial personalities and predators. The Michigan Prisons used to have a 40 hour training program "Anatamy of a Setup." Prisoners will work in teams to entrap Correctional Officers.  Once entrapped Correctional Officers were blackmailed to engage in sex and bring drugs into the prison.  I have collected many sad stories over the years.  I have been lucky.  I was never setup.  I was offered beautiful sketches  and always refused because accepting a gift is an initial step in the setup.  Each step seems innocent enough.  But when a number of steps are put together  by a number of prisoners  it creates a narrative.  They are just as evil in creating narratives as Careeer Politicians.
Thought for 31s

34 sourcesThought for 31sLecture: Predators, Narratives, and Cascades — An Interdisciplinary Inquiry into Antisocial EmergenceGraduate seminar framing for Law, Political Science, Psychiatry, and Social Anthropology. We begin from a 15 November 2020 observation by a long-serving corrections professional: empathy and love are necessary but insufficient. Children raised in caring families must also learn to recognize predators and antisocial patterns. In Michigan prisons a formal training, “Anatomy of a Setup,” described coordinated inmate teams that entrap officers through sequences of apparently innocent steps—gifts, sympathy, small favors—until a narrative of leverage is assembled and blackmail or contraband introduction becomes possible. The same logic of incremental narrative construction, the author argued, appears among career politicians.We examine this micro-dynamic and its societal magnification through five analytic lenses, then through the four disciplines.The five lensesSelf-organizing systems. Complex adaptive systems generate coherent global patterns from local interactions without a central designer. In the prison, observers, contacts, turners, and runners self-organize around a target; each step remains locally rational and deniable. On platforms, algorithms and user incentives likewise produce emergent cascades of attention, revenue, and radicalization without a single coordinating authority. Political movements and corporate ESG/CSR regimes can similarly self-organize around status, funding, and moral signaling until the resulting pattern (policing withdrawal, speech norms, hiring preferences) is treated as inevitable.Plausible deniability. The setup works because no single act is damning. Accepting a sketch, expressing sympathy, or sharing a post can be defended as ordinary. The same architecture appears in political rhetoric (“mostly peaceful”), corporate policy (“we are simply following best practice”), and institutional language that separates intent from outcome. Deniability is not merely an alibi; it is a design feature that allows the sequence to continue until the cumulative narrative is irreversible.Murphy’s Law. Systems in which many small failure modes exist will eventually encounter the conjunction that produces large failure. Policy experiments that reduce police capacity while simultaneously elevating narratives that treat law enforcement as illegitimate have, in multiple jurisdictions, been followed by measurable rises in homicide and disorder. Lockdowns, censorship regimes, and certain DEI implementations have likewise produced secondary effects (learning loss, mental-health deterioration, reverse-discrimination litigation, institutional distrust) that were not the stated objectives. The law does not require malice; it requires only that the failure modes remain open.Pandora’s box. Once certain thresholds are crossed—normalization of political violence as a legitimate tool, algorithmic amplification of high-arousal antisocial content, the erosion of shared criteria for predator recognition—the contents cannot be returned to the box by decree. Social media converts local antisocial strategies into scalable revenue streams and status hierarchies. Political narratives that selectively embrace or minimize one form of organized violence while condemning another further lower the threshold. The box, once opened, continues to emit.The butterfly effect. Sensitive dependence on initial conditions means that the acceptance of one gift, the framing of one protest, or the adoption of one hiring rubric can cascade through self-organizing networks into systemic outcomes. The prison setup demonstrates the mechanism at small scale; platform architectures and political narrative markets demonstrate it at large scale. Small differences in early conditions (whether a child is taught discernment, whether a department policy treats a particular sequence as cumulative rather than atomic) produce divergent later trajectories.Disciplinary perspectivesLaw. The classic setup raises questions of entrapment doctrine, conspiracy, and the boundary between protected speech and actionable conspiracy or solicitation. Cumulative narrative construction can convert individually lawful acts into a pattern that satisfies the elements of blackmail or official misconduct. At the societal level, free-speech jurisprudence (Brandenburg and its progeny) must confront coordinated amplification that is not “imminent” in the classic sense yet produces predictable cascades of violence or institutional capture. Corporate ESG and DEI regimes generate parallel questions of fiduciary duty, disparate-impact liability, and the enforceability of viewpoint-neutral rules when private platforms and institutions function as de-facto public squares.Political science. Narrative construction is a core technology of power. Principal–agent problems, institutional trust erosion, and the competitive dynamics of attention markets explain why actors across the spectrum invest in frames that maximize mobilization while preserving deniability. Movements that treat violence as a political tool—whether labeled antifa, other extremist formations, or state-adjacent actors—exploit the same self-organizing and deniability properties. The resulting polarization reduces the shared capacity to name predation when it appears inside one’s own coalition.Psychiatry. Antisocial personality disorder and related spectra are defined by pervasive patterns of deceitfulness, lack of remorse, and exploitation. Prevalence is markedly elevated in incarcerated populations. These traits are not created by politics, yet political and platform environments can selectively amplify individuals who already possess them by supplying larger audiences, status, and revenue. Empathy training without concurrent training in boundary recognition and pattern detection leaves the empathically oriented especially vulnerable—the precise failure mode described in the 2020 observation. Radicalization literature further shows that incremental commitment sequences (foot-in-the-door) operate similarly in ideological and criminal https://t.co/GZtQ0ywpdN anthropology. Societies historically used rites, gift protocols, and explicit pedagogy to teach the difference between reciprocity and predation. When those mechanisms atrophy or are reframed as “othering,” the cultural repertoire for recognizing setups shrinks. Online tribes recreate totemic identities and ritualized violence; gift economies reappear as attention and revenue. Corporate activism and certain DEI implementations can be read as new prestige economies in which moral signaling substitutes for the older pedagogical function of teaching discernment. The ethnographic question is whether any large-scale society can sustain high levels of generalized trust without also sustaining explicit, non-partisan training in predator recognition.Synthesis and the listed proof-of-concept phenomenaDefund-the-police campaigns, selective corporate activism, globalist institutional pressures, DEI and affirmative-action regimes, ESG/CSR frameworks, censorship architectures, and lockdown policies can each be analyzed as instances in which self-organizing incentives, deniable incrementalism, open failure modes, irreversible thresholds, and sensitive dependence produced outcomes divergent from stated aims. Social media functions as the principal amplifier, converting local antisocial strategies into scalable ones. The same lenses apply symmetrically: any political or institutional project that lowers the cost of predation or raises the cost of naming it will generate parallel cascades. The empirical record since 2020 supplies multiple natural experiments; the analytic task is to measure the cascades rather than to defend or indict any single narrative in advance.The gaps that remain are precisely those the lecture has circled: the distance between plausible deniability and enforceable transparency or accountability; the distance between self-organizing emergence and reliable predictability; the distance between the release of harms and the design of cures; and the distance between butterfly cascades of harm and interventions capable of interrupting them before they become irreversible.Poem (in the style of Flash Ki / Muse, “Dead Inside (Mix Edit)”)Dead inside
(Dead inside)You taught the child only love
And left the predator’s grammar untaught
Each sketch, each post, each small gift
Seems pure enough to keep
But when the steps assemble
There’s nothing there
Light only shines from those who name the patternUnleash a million feeds
And confine the wary, erase the boundary, babe
Do the systems have no soul?
It’s like it died when deniability became the designYour metrics feel warm to the touch
You can bring the numbers back to life
On the outside you’re ablaze with virtue
But you’re dead insideYou’re free to touch the sky of narrative
Whilst the cascade is crushed and pulverised
Because the gap needs plausible cover
Now the sequence is the one that’s letting goYou like to give an inch of empathy
Whilst the setup is giving infinity
But now the trust has nothing left
You have no ledger and the harmed are bereftYour skin of policy feels warm to caress
I see magic in the stated aims
On the outside you’re ablaze and alive
But you’re dead insideFeel the gap now, hold the account please
I need the system to see what the steps become
Open the record to me, stop hiding the cumulative
It’s hurting, the cascade only naming can stop the painDon’t leave the pattern out in the cold
Don’t leave the next child out to die
We gave the platforms everything
We can’t give the predators any moreNow the culture has become just like the setup
Our lips feel warm with the correct phrase
Our words seem so alive with solidarity
Our metrics are warm to the brand caress
We’ll control the frame and hypnotiseYou’ve taught the feed to lie without a trace
And to amplify with no remorse
On the outside
We’re the greatest moral architecture
Now we’re dead inside(The cure for the gaps is the refusal of the first gift
the insistence that sequences be named before they cohere
the restoration of predictability where self-organization meets predation
the design of interruption before the box stays open
the mapping of the butterfly’s path while the wings are still small.)Dead inside.

USEFUL IDIOTS: THE ALLIANCE THAT EXPIRES

"Useful idiots" — the phrase is popularly attributed to Lenin, though no one has ever found it in anything Lenin wrote or said. The pattern it names is documented, and it runs in one direction: Islamist movements welcome progressive and LGBTQ allies while they are out of power. Once power is theirs, the welcome ends.

Start in Michigan. In November 2021, Hamtramck elected a Muslim mayor, Amer Ghalib, and the nation's first all-Muslim city council. The Pride flag had flown over city property in 2021 and 2022. When the new administration's request to take it down was refused, the council legislated. On June 13, 2023, Resolution 2023-82 passed unanimously, barring flags of religious, ethnic, racial, political and sexual-orientation groups from city property. Only the U.S., Michigan, Hamtramck and POW flags — and other nations' flags — may fly.

Mayor Ghalib's stated reasoning, in his own words: "You do not know our city more than we do… The city government will stay NEUTRAL and IMPARTIAL toward its residents." Councilman Nayeem Choudhury said the vote was to "respect the religious rights of our citizens." When two Human Relations Commission members raised the Pride flag anyway that July, the council removed them both and stripped the commission of its flagpole authority. The flag's supporters sued — and lost. A federal judge dismissed the case in September 2025, and the Sixth Circuit affirmed on August 21, 2026: flags on the city's own poles are the government's speech, and the government may choose. Private flags on private property were never touched.

Dearborn showed the same arithmetic. On October 10, 2022, hundreds of mostly Muslim parents packed a school-board meeting over LGBTQ library books — signs read "Homosexuality big sin" and "If democracy matters, we're the majority" — and the board shut the meeting down. The follow-up drew some 800 people. A community courted as a coalition partner on Monday was, by Friday, an organized bloc voting its own doctrine.

The pattern is older than Michigan. Iran's 1979 revolution was a coalition — liberals, leftists and Islamists together against the Shah. The Tudeh Party, Iran's communists, backed Khomeini even after the Islamic Republic was proclaimed. In February 1983 the regime banned the Tudeh and arrested its leadership — some 200 organizers, including 30 Central Committee members — then put its secretary-general on television to confess. Thousands were arrested, executions followed, and in 1988 the regime executed thousands of political prisoners, leftists prominent among them. The allies were useful. Then they were not.

And where Islamist law governs, the legal status of gay people is written down, not whispered. The U.S. Commission on International Religious Freedom counts ten countries where same-sex relations are punishable by death under sharia-based law, including Iran and Saudi Arabia. Iran's penal code prescribes death for sodomy; two men were hanged on sodomy charges in January 2022. When ISIS held territory in Syria and Iraq, it threw men accused of homosexuality from rooftops — at least 36 such killings documented by OutRight International, enough that the UN Security Council held its first-ever session on LGBT persecution in 2015.

None of this requires guessing at anyone's intentions. The votes, the resolutions, the court rulings and the penal codes are public record. The alliance is offered while power is being sought. The record shows what happens to the allies after power is won.

Sensitive dependence on initial conditions means that the acceptance of one gift, the framing of one protest, or the adoption of one hiring rubric can cascade through self-organizing networks into systemic outcomes. The prison setup demonstrates the mechanism at small scale; platform architectures and political narrative markets demonstrate it at large scale. Small differences in early conditions (whether a child is taught discernment, whether a department policy treats a particular sequence as cumulative rather than atomic) produce divergent later trajectories.Disciplinary perspectivesLaw. The classic setup raises questions of entrapment doctrine, conspiracy, and the boundary between protected speech and actionable conspiracy or solicitation. Cumulative narrative construction can convert individually lawful acts into a pattern that satisfies the elements of blackmail or official misconduct. At the societal level, free-speech jurisprudence (Brandenburg and its progeny) must confront coordinated amplification that is not “imminent” in the classic sense yet produces predictable cascades of violence or institutional capture. Corporate ESG and DEI regimes generate parallel questions of fiduciary duty, disparate-impact liability, and the enforceability of viewpoint-neutral rules when private platforms and institutions function as de-facto public squares.Political science. Narrative construction is a core technology of power. Principal–agent problems, institutional trust erosion, and the competitive dynamics of attention markets explain why actors across the spectrum invest in frames that maximize mobilization while preserving deniability. Movements that treat violence as a political tool—whether labeled antifa, other extremist formations, or state-adjacent actors—exploit the same self-organizing and deniability properties. The resulting polarization reduces the shared capacity to name predation when it appears inside one’s own coalition.Psychiatry. Antisocial personality disorder and related spectra are defined by pervasive patterns of deceitfulness, lack of remorse, and exploitation. Prevalence is markedly elevated in incarcerated populations. These traits are not created by politics, yet political and platform environments can selectively amplify individuals who already possess them by supplying larger audiences, status, and revenue. Empathy training without concurrent training in boundary recognition and pattern detection leaves the empathically oriented especially vulnerable—the precise failure mode described in the 2020 observation. Radicalization literature further shows that incremental commitment sequences (foot-in-the-door) operate similarly in ideological and criminal https://t.co/GZtQ0ywpdN anthropology. Societies historically used rites, gift protocols, and explicit pedagogy to teach the difference between reciprocity and predation. When those mechanisms atrophy or are reframed as “othering,” the cultural repertoire for recognizing setups shrinks. Online tribes recreate totemic identities and ritualized violence; gift economies reappear as attention and revenue. Corporate activism and certain DEI implementations can be read as new prestige economies in which moral signaling substitutes for the older pedagogical function of teaching discernment. The ethnographic question is whether any large-scale society can sustain high levels of generalized trust without also sustaining explicit, non-partisan training in predator recognition.Synthesis and the listed proof-of-concept phenomenaDefund-the-police campaigns, selective corporate activism, globalist institutional pressures, DEI and affirmative-action regimes, ESG/CSR frameworks, censorship architectures, and lockdown policies can each be analyzed as instances in which self-organizing incentives, deniable incrementalism, open failure modes, irreversible thresholds, and sensitive dependence produced outcomes divergent from stated aims. Social media functions as the principal amplifier, converting local antisocial strategies into scalable ones. 

The same lenses 
apply symmetrically: any political or institutional project that lowers the cost of predation or raises the cost of naming it will generate parallel cascades. The empirical record since 2020 supplies multiple natural experiments; the analytic task is to measure the cascades rather than to defend or indict any single narrative in advance.The gaps that remain are precisely those the lecture has circled: the distance between plausible deniability and enforceable transparency or accountability; the distance between self-organizing emergence and reliable predictability; the distance between the release of harms and the design of cures; and the distance between butterfly cascades of harm and interventions capable of interrupting them before they become irreversible.

Poem (in the style of Flash Ki / Muse, 
“Dead Inside (Mix Edit)”)

Dead inside
(Dead inside)

You taught the child only love
And left the predator’s grammar untaught

Each sketch, each post, each small gift
Seems pure enough to keep

But when the steps assemble
There’s nothing there

Light only shines 
from those who name the pattern

Unleash a million feeds
And confine the wary, 
erase the boundary, babe

Do the systems have no soul?
It’s like it died
when deniability became the design
Your metrics feel warm to the touch

You can bring the numbers back to life
On the outside you’re ablaze with virtue
But you’re dead inside
You’re free to touch the sky of narrative

Whilst the cascade is crushed and pulverised
Because the gap needs plausible cover
Now the sequence 
is the one that’s letting go

You like to give an inch of empathy
Whilst the setup is giving infinity
But now the trust has nothing left

You have no ledger 
and the harmed are bereft

Your skin of policy feels warm to caress
I see magic in the stated aims
On the outside you’re ablaze and alive

But you’re dead inside
Feel the gap now, 
hold the account please

I need the system 
to see what the steps become
Open the record to me, 
stop hiding the cumulative

It’s hurting, 
the cascade 
only naming can stop the pain

Don’t leave the pattern out in the cold
Don’t leave the next child out to die
We gave the platforms everything
We can’t give the predators any more

Now the culture has become just like the setup
Our lips feel warm with the correct phrase
Our words seem so alive with solidarity
Our metrics are warm to the brand caress
We’ll control the frame and hypnotise

You’ve taught the feed to lie without a trace
And to amplify with no remorse
On the outside
We’re the greatest moral architecture
Now we’re dead inside

(The cure for the gaps 
is the refusal of the first gift
the insistence that sequences be named 
before they cohere
the restoration of predictability 
where self-organization meets predation
the design of interruption 
before the box stays open
the mapping of the butterfly’s path 
while the wings are still small.)
Dead inside.
