text:
Every duck in this video is standing on a floor made of holes.

It takes a moment to register, because your eyes go first to the birds. Hundreds of them, dark and glossy, packed across a raised platform of amber-colored grid, their faces flecked red, their heads turning toward the lens one after another like a wave moving through a field. But once you notice the floor, you can't stop seeing it. It is under every foot. It runs to the fences in every direction. There is no mud in this frame, no grass, no reeds, no shoreline. Nothing that the word "duck" has ever taught you to expect.

The clip lasts twenty-seven seconds. Whoever filmed it walks slowly along the edge of the pens, holding the phone upright, and what they capture is less a story than a place. There is a roof overhead, with light coming in at the edges. There are wire partitions, and beyond them more birds, and beyond those still more. There are yellow buckets and small red dishes scattered across the floor, and here and there a little green cone that I could not identify and will not pretend to. In the far background, if you look closely, a strip of white shows up among the dark: a second group of ducks, a different color altogether, sitting in a separate section.

And then, near the end, the camera drops low and the scene closes in. A yellow bucket sits in the middle of a crowd so dense that you cannot see the floor at all. Wings against wings. Red faces tipped up at the phone.

I have watched it perhaps a dozen times now, and I want to be careful about what I say next, because the easy version of this story is already sitting right there, and it is a story the footage cannot actually support. So let me begin with what it can support, and go slowly.

The birds are Muscovy ducks. The file I was given calls them Sudanese ducks, which is a name some people use for them in some places, and which turns out to be the first small crack in the whole picture. Because a Muscovy duck is not from Sudan. It is not from Moscow either, and the second name is the more famous one.

Nobody is entirely sure how the name Muscovy came to be attached to a bird whose home is the other side of the planet. One explanation points to an English trading company that operated between England and Russia in the sixteenth century, and suggests the birds were carried through its networks and the name stuck to the cargo. Another traces the word to an Indigenous people of Colombia. A third, less romantic, points to a faint musky odor that people have noted in the birds. None of these has the kind of certainty you would want from a footnote, and historians of the word tend to say so. What is certain is the geography. Cairina moschata, the species you are looking at, is native to the Americas, from Mexico down through Central America and into the lowland forests of South America. Whoever first called it Muscovy was, at minimum, off by a hemisphere.

So here is a bird with names that point to Russia and to Sudan, filmed in a shed whose location I do not know, standing on a floor that looks nothing like the river forest its ancestors came from. The video does not tell me where it is. It does not give a date, a name, a reason. All it shows me is a great many animals, and the distance between what they are and where they are.

That distance is what I could not stop thinking about. So let me start at the other end of it: with what these birds were before anyone built a floor for them.

In the wild, a Muscovy is a creature of trees.

That sounds like a small fact until you sit with it. Most of the ducks in a child's picture book are surface animals: they paddle, dabble, tip forward with their tails in the air. The wild Muscovy does some of that, but it also does something stranger. It perches. Its feet carry long, sharp claws, and it uses them to grip branches and climb up to roost, high above the water along forested rivers, swamps, and flooded woodland. Hens nest in tree cavities, sometimes far above the ground. When the ducklings hatch, they are said to leap out of the hole and drop to the earth, bounce, and follow their mother into the undergrowth. A duck that nests in a tree has a very different relationship to height, to cover, and to the ground than a duck that nests in the reeds.

The wild birds are mostly black, with a green and blue iridescence that shows when the light hits their feathers, and a patch of white on each wing that flashes in flight. They can fly well. They eat seeds and plants, and also insects, small fish, and other things they find in shallow water and leaf litter. They are not flock animals in the dense way we picture chickens or geese. They live in pairs and small groups, spread along waterways, in forest that gives them somewhere to be out of sight.

Hold that picture against the video.

The birds on the grid floor are, for the most part, the same dark, glossy green-black. In several shots you can see exactly the iridescence I just described, a bottle-green flicker on the shoulders when the camera angle catches it. You can see the white patches on the wings of some of them, tucked against their sides. If you froze the footage and showed it to a naturalist without context, they would tell you without hesitation: those are Muscovy ducks, and they look remarkably close to their wild ancestors.

That is not an accident, and it is the first genuinely surprising thing about this species. Muscovy ducks were domesticated, but they were domesticated by Indigenous peoples in the Americas, long before Europeans arrived, and they have stayed, in appearance, closer to their wild form than almost any other farmed bird. When European travelers reached the Americas, they reported seeing these ducks already living alongside people. They carried them back across the Atlantic in the sixteenth century, and from there the birds spread through Europe, Africa, and Asia along the same sea routes that moved sugar, spices, and a good deal else.

There is something else about them that most people don't know. Nearly every other domestic duck on Earth, from the white Pekin to the Indian Runner to the Khaki Campbell, descends from a single wild species, the mallard. The Muscovy does not. It is an entirely separate animal, in its own genus, more closely related to certain tropical perching ducks than to the mallard. When it is crossed with a mallard-derived duck, the offspring, called mulards, are generally sterile. The two lineages are far enough apart that nature itself has put a lock on the door.

So the dark birds on that floor are not a variation on the duck you drew as a child. They are a different animal that happens to share the word.

Then there is the sound, or rather the lack of one.

I expected what anyone would expect from several hundred ducks in one room: a roar. A wall of quacking. What the recording carries instead is quiet. Measured across the whole clip, the sound sits low and steady, with no sustained din at all. That fits the species. Muscovy ducks are famously poor quackers. The drakes mostly hiss, a breathy rasp closer to a snake than to a pond, and the hens make a soft trilling coo. A crowd of Muscovies is a crowd that mostly murmurs.

It changes the feel of the footage. A noisy flock seems like a place where something is happening. A quiet one seems like a place where something is being endured, or perhaps simply waited out. And I want to be honest that I don't know which of those two readings, if either, would be correct. Silence in ducks does not mean what silence means in people. It is a feature of the species, not a signal of mood.

What I can say is that a great deal of what the viewer feels while watching this clip comes from the viewer. The mind supplies the roar that isn't there, then registers its absence as eerie. It supplies the pond that isn't there, then registers its absence as deprivation. It is worth noticing that kind of thing, because that is where a lot of the pull of this footage actually comes from. It is not telling us anything it doesn't know. It is revealing what we carry in our heads.

So let me look harder at what is actually in front of us.

The red. Every adult Muscovy has it, the bare, bumpy, crimson skin around the eyes and across the base of the bill, called caruncles. It is the species' most recognizable feature, and also its most unfairly mocked: people call it ugly more often than they call it anything else. It is not a wound and it is not a disease. It is simply what the face of a Muscovy is. Drakes tend to carry more of it, and it can swell and flush with color during courtship or aggression. In the video, with so many faces turned toward the camera at once, the effect is almost eerie: a field of small red masks, all tilted at the same angle, all fixed on a single glass eye.

That tilt is worth a second look. Ducks have their eyes on the sides of their heads, which means that to look at something carefully with one eye, a duck turns its head sideways. The birds in this video are doing exactly that. They are not staring blankly. They are inspecting. Some stretch their necks upward, some shift away from the lens, a few step in closer, and in a couple of shots you can see a bird holding its head cocked, watching the phone as it passes. The camera is, for these animals, an event. Something unusual walks along the fence, and a slow ripple of attention follows it.

It's a small thing, but small things are all the footage gives us, so I try to take them seriously. These are animals with curiosity, caution, and preferences about where to stand. They notice. Whatever else is true about this place, it is not populated by objects.

Size is another thing the grid floor makes visible. Muscovy drakes are dramatically larger than hens, often close to twice their weight, with broader shoulders and heavier heads. In the mid-clip shots, where the camera sits low and the birds crowd the foreground, you can pick out the difference without trying: a few big, upright birds standing a head above the rest, and around them a lower, more compact mass of smaller ones. In a species where males can be that much bigger, the arrangement of who stands where is rarely random.

Which brings me back to the floor, because the floor is the real subject of this video, whether or not the person who filmed it meant it to be.

A raised platform of slats or grid is not unusual in poultry housing. It is, in fact, a very common design, and the reasoning behind it is practical and easy to follow. Birds produce a great deal of waste. On solid ground, that waste accumulates around their feet, and with it come moisture, ammonia, bacteria, and parasites that thrive in damp bedding. A raised floor lets droppings fall through to a space below, so the birds stand on a surface that stays comparatively dry and the waste is kept apart from where they eat, rest, and walk. People who run farms this way point to cleaner birds, lower rates of certain diseases, and less labor. Those are real advantages, and anyone writing about this honestly should say so.

But the same design has long drawn criticism, and that criticism is just as real. Birds that evolved on soil, leaf litter, and shallow water do not necessarily find a hard grid comfortable. Some welfare scientists argue that wire or plastic flooring is harder on feet than the surfaces birds are built for, and that it removes the chance to forage, scratch, or root around in the ways that come naturally. And water is its own long-running argument. Ducks, including Muscovies, preen constantly, and they need to be able to clean their eyes and nostrils, which in practice means submerging their heads. Welfare guidance for ducks widely stresses that enough water to do this is important, and that drinking water alone is not the same thing as water to bathe in. Muscovies are known to be somewhat less water-dependent than mallard-type ducks, and farmers who keep them often say so. Critics answer that "less dependent" is not the same as "not at all."

I am not going to settle that argument here, and the video can't settle it either. Looking carefully at the footage, I can see shallow, flat-looking surfaces in the background of some shots, pale and bluish between the pens, that might be channels or troughs of water and might be something else entirely. I can't tell from this angle. Maybe there is a stream of water running behind the grid. Maybe not. Maybe the birds have regular access to it and maybe they do not. The video gives me the floor, and the floor is all I can honestly describe.

What I can say is that this is an environment someone designed on purpose. Every element was chosen. The height of the platform. The mesh of the partitions, close enough to keep a bird from slipping through, open enough for the air to move. The placement of the yellow buckets, the red dishes, the little green cones standing like lawn ornaments on the floor. The roof angled to pour shade over the birds without shutting out the light. Whoever built it spent time thinking about ducks, even if what they were thinking about was how to manage them at scale.

And that, to me, is the odd emotional texture of the clip. It isn't cruelty on display and it isn't kindness. It is competence, aimed at an animal whose original life looked nothing like this. The result is a place that works, by the standards it was built to meet, and that also leaves an observer unsettled for reasons that are hard to name. Both of those things can be true at the same time. I think most of the real world is like that.

Now consider the crowd itself, because a crowd is not just a number of birds. It is a behavior.

Ducks are social animals, but how social depends on the species and the circumstances. Wild Muscovies tend to live in loose pairs and small parties. Put several hundred in a pen and you get something else: a population in which every bird is constantly adjusting to the position of its neighbors. Who is near the feeder. Who is near the edge. Who has room to stretch a wing and who doesn't. Animals in groups sort themselves into hierarchies, and the sorting is mostly invisible unless you know what you are looking for. A drake lifts his head and the bird in front of him steps aside. A hen settles in a corner and the birds around her settle too.

You can see traces of this in the footage. In the open sections of the pen, birds stand scattered at comfortable distances from each other, many of them preening, some resting with their bills tucked into their back feathers. It looks almost relaxed. A few walk slowly across the grid with the unhurried gait of an animal that is not afraid of its surroundings. But as the camera moves toward the far end, the picture tightens. The birds gather. Around one of the yellow buckets they stand so close together that individual outlines blur into a single dark surface, with only the red faces to tell you where one bird ends and the next begins.

I don't know why they gather there. Ducks cluster around food, around shade, around warmth, around whatever the rest of the flock is clustering around. Perhaps the bucket holds feed. Perhaps it is about the time of day. Perhaps something near that corner has just attracted them, the way something near the lens attracted the others. A single clip cannot tell me, and I would rather say that plainly than invent a satisfying reason.

What it does show me is how quickly the density changes, from a space where each bird has a little room to a space where no bird has any. That contrast carries most of the emotional weight of the clip, and I notice that it carries it without anyone raising their voice. There is no soundtrack. There is no narrator. Just a camera moving a few meters along a fence, and the scene shifting from scattered to packed, from calm to something harder to read.

There's an odd fact about ducks that comes to mind here, and I offer it carefully, because it was established in mallards and I don't know that it has been tested in Muscovies. In group-sleeping mallards, birds at the edge of the flock have been found to keep one eye open and half their brain awake while the birds in the middle sleep fully, as if each duck calculated its own exposure to the outside. The edge-sitters watch for danger. The center-sitters rest. Position in the group is not neutral. It changes how an animal sleeps.

If something like that happens in this shed, then the grid floor holds many different experiences at the same moment. The bird by the fence and the bird in the middle of the crush are in the same video, in the same second, in the same place, and may be having entirely different lives.

Look again at the white.

In the background of several shots there is a pale band, a section of pens where the birds are not dark at all but bright white, so many of them together that from a distance they look like a drift of snow along the far fence. One white duck stands in the foreground of a mid-clip shot, alone among the dark birds, its red face the same as everyone else's. It looks like a stray, but I can't say that it is. It may belong to the same pen as its neighbors. It may have wandered. It may simply be a color variant standing in the wrong place at the right moment for the camera.

Muscovies come in many colors once people have spent a few centuries with them: white, black, blue-gray, chocolate, and pied patterns that mix them. The black-and-green form in most of this video is the one closest to the wild bird. The white is the one people breed for, and farmers tend to separate colors into different sections, for reasons that may have to do with record-keeping, with purpose, or with preference. I don't know which applies here.

What interests me is what the color boundary suggests: that the place is organized. Someone has looked at these birds and sorted them. The dark ones go here, the white ones go there, the feeders are spaced at these intervals, the partitions run along these lines. A great deal of attention has been paid to the arrangement of the animals, and almost none of it is visible to a person scrolling past at speed.

That is one of the strange facts of a video like this. It compresses a system into a gesture. The person who filmed it lifted a phone and walked a few steps. The people who built the shed, hauled the grid floors into place, ordered the feeders, decided on the layout, and arranged the daily work of feeding, watering, cleaning, and checking are all absent from the footage, though every one of their decisions is on screen. You can't see them. You can see only what they made.

I find that disorienting in a useful way. We tend to think of animal footage as a window onto animals. This clip is also, quietly, a portrait of human intention. The ducks are the subject. The structure around them is the author.

So what do I actually know?

I know the species, with reasonable confidence, from the shape of the body, the bare red face, the dark iridescent plumage, the white wing patches on some birds, and the upright, heavy-bodied way they stand. I know the setting is a covered, fenced, raised-floor housing with feeders and drinkers inside it. I know the birds are numerous: hundreds, I would say, perhaps more across the whole facility, though I have not counted and I will not pretend to. I know they appear alert and, in the clearest shots, physically intact. I can see no obviously injured bird in the frames I examined, though twenty-seven seconds of vertical video is a poor basis for any kind of health assessment, and I would not claim to read a single one.

I do not know where it is. I do not know who owns it. I do not know what the ducks are being kept for, whether eggs, meat, breeding stock, or something else, and the video offers no hint. I do not know how old they are, how long they have been there, how often they are fed, whether they ever go outside, or whether the strip of pale blue in the background is water.

That list of things I don't know is much longer than the list of things I do. And yet the clip arrives in the world already carrying an interpretation, because every viewer arrives with a story ready to attach to it. Some will see an atrocity. Some will see ordinary agriculture. Some will see a scene of abundance, a large and thriving flock. Some will see an efficient piece of food infrastructure. The footage is compatible with more than one of these readings, and that is exactly why it travels: it invites the viewer to finish it.

I think the right response to that invitation is to decline to finish it too quickly. Not because the questions don't matter. They matter a great deal, and people who care about how animals are kept have good reasons to ask hard ones. But the honest answers live in details this video doesn't contain: stocking density measured in birds per square meter, access to water for bathing, flooring and foot condition, lighting, air quality, how the birds are handled, what the rules in that country require. A person with those facts can say something real about this place. A person with only twenty-seven seconds can say something real only about the seconds.

And the seconds themselves are worth describing precisely. They show a large number of animals that live closely together, in a human-built space, on a surface that is clearly not the forest floor and not the riverbank. They show animals that notice a stranger passing and turn their faces to look. They show a flock that thins into calm and thickens into crowding within the span of a short walk. That is what is on the record. The rest is projection, mine included. It is also worth remembering that the person holding the phone chose where to point it, and for how long. A different twenty-seven seconds, from a different corner of the building, at a different hour of the day, could have shown us a different shed.

Which leaves the question of why a clip this plain should hold a person's attention at all.

I think it's because it does something rare. It makes the animal visible as a population rather than an individual. Almost everything we see of ducks arrives one at a time: the mother with her line of ducklings, the drake on the pond, the single bird rescued from a drain. Those stories work because a single face is easy to love. A hundred faces is something else. A hundred faces asks a different question, which is not "what is this animal feeling?" but "what are we doing with all of them?"

It is an uncomfortable question for another reason too. Ducks, chickens, and the other birds raised in large numbers around the world are the most numerous farmed animals on the planet, and also among the least pictured in the way we picture animals we love. We know them mostly as food, as an item on a menu or a shape in a package. We rarely see them standing in a crowd, tilting their heads at a phone. A video like this closes that gap for twenty-seven seconds, and what comes through the gap is not an argument. It is just a gaze.

The Muscovy is an unusually good animal to carry that gaze. It has a face people find strange, and strange faces hold attention. It has a history that keeps surprising people who learn it: a bird of the American forest that carries a Russian name and sometimes a Sudanese one, domesticated by people whose names most of the world never learned, carried across oceans, bred in a dozen colors, kept on every inhabited continent, and still, under the paint, a tree-climbing river duck with sharp claws and a hiss where its quack should be. It is a bird that has been moved so far from its origins that its origins have almost been erased from its names.

Maybe that's the reason the clip lingers. It shows an animal in a place that has no record of where the animal came from, and an audience that mostly doesn't know either. Everyone is looking at a stranger and calling it by a name that isn't quite right.

I keep returning to the very first thing I noticed: the floor made of holes. At first it seemed like the main fact of the video, the thing that explained everything else. Now I see it as something smaller, and stranger. It is a floor, and the ducks are standing on it, and they are doing what ducks do in whatever space they are given: looking, shifting, settling, adjusting to their neighbors, watching the edges. They are making a life out of the surface under their feet. That is not a verdict on the floor. It is a fact about the ducks.

The last shot is the one I cannot shake. The camera tilts down into the thickest part of the crowd, and for a second or two, one bird near the front lifts its head, turns it sideways, and looks straight into the lens with one dark eye. It does not look afraid. It does not look pleased. It looks the way an animal looks when it is trying to work out what you are.

I can't tell you what it concluded. I only know that it was the one in that room doing the looking, and the rest of us were the ones being studied.

text:
Kimberley A. Martin The First Black Woman
NFL Beat Writer

In a West Indian household in Brooklyn, average was never an option. Kimberley A. Martin took that in early. She grew up a Knicks fan and wrote short stories as a kid.

Wesleyan University gave her a double major in psychology and African American studies. To pay off her loans she took a desk at U.S. Trust in Manhattan, where she filled out her Syracuse application. A master’s in magazine journalism followed, though she has yet to write for a magazine.

Newspapers claimed her instead. An internship at The Record in Hackensack became a staff job. Newsday then sent her to high school field hockey and fencing, covered with the care she gave the Yankees and Mets. In 2011 the National Association of Black Journalists named her its Emerging Journalist of the Year. When her editors insisted on a pro beat, she chose the Jets.

She walked into that locker room with a hard face, determined to be taken seriously. Within a season she found her real strength. The team’s PR director told her to leave the quarterback scrum to the pack and talk to everyone else: when they zig, you zag. She did, and players opened up to a highly qualified reporter who asked about their families as well as their numbers. The NABJ honoured her sports writing again in 2016 and 2017.

The calls kept coming. The Buffalo News created a columnist post for her. Two months later The Washington Post, her dream paper, offered her its Washington beat. Nine months after that, Yahoo Sports made her a national columnist and put her on camera for the first time.

ESPN approached her during Super Bowl week in Miami, and the offer reached her at baggage claim in Newark. She started in March 2020, doing Get Up and First Take over FaceTime from her apartment. Today she reports from one of the week’s biggest games on Sunday NFL Countdown, debates on First Take, and writes and narrates her own features, in Jordans and yellow nails.

Any young woman who walks into a press box with a notebook and a doubt can look to her. Kimberley A. Martin zagged, and the rooms made space for her.

text:
A COW IS NOT JUST A COW: THE AGRICULTURAL QUESTION CANARY MUGUME SHOULD HAVE ASKED

I have been reflecting on Canary Mugume's conversation with former Botswana President Dr Mokgweetsi Masisi and former First Lady Neo Jane Masisi.

Canary reportedly asked why Botswana imports cattle from Texas instead of buying Uganda's famous long-horned Ankole cattle. Dr Masisi reportedly explained that Uganda's persistent foot-and-mouth disease challenges make our cattle less desirable.

That response raises an important issue for Uganda. However, I think the journalist could have pursued a much more informative line of questioning.

Why are we assuming that cattle from Texas and Uganda's Ankole cattle are interchangeable?

In May 2023, Botswana imported 162 breeding animals from the United States, including White Brahman and Beefmaster cattle. Their purpose was genetic improvement through semen and embryo production. By August 2024, Botswana had reported collecting more than 17,000 semen straws from the imported bulls.

This was a specialised breeding intervention, not simply a decision to purchase cattle from one country instead of another.

Consider the differences between livestock production objectives. Someone interested in milk production may prioritise milk yield and butterfat content. A commercial beef producer may prioritise growth rate, feed conversion, carcass quality and reproductive performance. A breeding programme may prioritise genetic merit, fertility and the ability to pass desirable characteristics to subsequent generations.

Then there is environmental adaptation. An animal that performs exceptionally well under one climatic and management system may not necessarily deliver the same results under another.

Uganda's Ankole cattle have distinctive characteristics, including tropical adaptation, hardiness and high milk butterfat content. These deserve serious scientific and commercial attention. But we cannot simply assume that these characteristics make them the ideal replacement for every breed Botswana might want to introduce.

I would have preferred Canary to ask Dr Masisi:

What specific genetic characteristics were you looking for when selecting cattle from Texas? Were you targeting beef production, reproductive technologies, climate resilience or particular market requirements? Did your technical team consider African indigenous breeds, including Uganda's Ankole? What veterinary and certification requirements would Uganda have to satisfy to become a supplier?

Those questions would have opened a much deeper conversation.

The comparison with Cyril Ramaphosa's Ankole cattle business is interesting, but commercial success in one specialised market does not establish suitability for another. We must also distinguish the value of individual breeding animals from actual business profits.

Uganda's foot-and-mouth disease problem deserves attention. So does the commercial potential of our indigenous cattle. But we should not confuse veterinary market-access problems with the genetic quality of the animals.

Journalism should go beyond asking why someone buys elsewhere. It should establish what the buyer needs, what the seller offers and what prevents the transaction.

A cow is not just a cow. A farmer buys genetics, a production system buys performance, and a market buys suitability.

That is the agricultural conversation Uganda needs to have.

text:
G: Federalist No. 10 (Part 2 of 2): The Same Subject Continued — The Union as a Safeguard Against Domestic Faction and Insurrection
by James Madison (as Publius)
Published November 23, 1787, in The New York Packet
Madison continued in the same quiet New York room, the argument now turning from diagnosis to remedy. Having shown that the causes of faction cannot be removed without destroying liberty, he explained how a large republic could control its effects through representation and extended size.
Bulletized summary (Part 2):
• Notes that a minority faction is defeated by the republican principle of majority vote; a majority faction, however, can sacrifice the public good and private rights under popular government.
• Identifies the great object as securing the public good and private rights against majority faction while preserving popular government.
• Contrasts pure democracy (citizens assemble and administer in person), which admits no cure for faction, with a republic (representation and greater extent).
• Explains that representation can refine public views through a chosen body, though it also risks election of factious men.
• Argues that a large republic offers a greater probability of fit choice and makes majority faction harder to form and concert.
• Concludes that the Union supplies a republican remedy for the diseases most incident to republican government.
If a faction is less than a majority, “relief is supplied by the republican principle, which enables the majority to defeat its sinister views by regular vote.” When a majority is included, however, “the form of popular government... enables it to sacrifice to its ruling passion or interest both the public good and the rights of other citizens.” The great object is “to secure the public good and private rights against the danger of such a faction, and at the same time to preserve the spirit and the form of popular government.”
“A pure democracy, by which I mean a society consisting of a small number of citizens, who assemble and administer the government in person, can admit of no cure for the mischiefs of faction... Hence it is that such democracies have ever been spectacles of turbulence and contention; have ever been found incompatible with personal security or the rights of property; and have in general been as short in their lives as they have been violent in their deaths.”
“A republic, by which I mean a government in which the scheme of representation takes place, opens a different prospect... The two great points of difference between a democracy and a republic are: first, the delegation of the government, in the latter, to a small number of citizens elected by the rest; secondly, the greater number of citizens, and greater sphere of country, over which the latter may be extended.” Representation can “refine and enlarge the public views, by passing them through the medium of a chosen body of citizens, whose wisdom may best discern the true interest of their country.” At the same time, “men of factious tempers... may, by intrigue, by corruption, or by other means, first obtain the suffrages, and then betray the interests of the people.” Extensive republics are more favorable to proper choice because they present a greater option of fit characters, and because a majority faction is less likely to form or to concert its schemes across a larger territory and greater variety of interests.
“In the extent and proper structure of the Union, therefore, we behold a republican remedy for the diseases most incident to republican government.”
Contemporary parallels appear whenever large, diverse republics rely on representation and the multiplicity of interests to keep any single faction from dominating. Madison’s remedy remains the structural argument that size and diversity, properly channeled, can protect liberty better than small, homogeneous democracies.
Further reading: Full text— https://t.co/yBVQF7Hq85 or the Library of Congress

text:
An accountant played an online poker qualifier that cost less than $100. He was trying to finish 4th. He won $2.5 million instead and changed poker forever.

Chris Moneymaker, a 27-year-old accountant from Tennessee. 2003. He logged into PokerStars for a cheap qualifier for the World Series of Poker.

The top 3 won seats in the Main Event in Las Vegas. 4th place paid $8,000 in cash.

He wanted the cash. "I want the cash," he says. His friends talked him into going. He finished 1st anyway.

In Vegas he was an amateur among pros. At the end it came down to him and Sam Farha, a pro who looked like he walked out of a movie.

Moneymaker offered to split the money. He says he'd have taken $1.8 million. Farha wanted more.

So they played.

With nothing but king-high, Moneymaker bluffed all-in. Farha folded a pair of nines.

A few hands later it was over. $2.5 million.

An ordinary guy qualified online for pocket money and won the biggest poker event on Earth. Suddenly millions of people thought: I could do that. The press called it the "Moneymaker effect."

In the clip: the bluff and the final hand.

Skill, or the luckiest week in poker history?

Tesla is inviting select customers to buy a Cybercab. The initial offer includes a monthly requirement.

What the first order screen showed
Tesla’s November 13 post showed an estimated $29,990 purchase price before taxes, a $1,000 non-refundable order deposit and a $299/month Autonomy Subscription, with the first month included. The screen estimated December 2026 delivery in Austin, Texas; that is an estimate, not a guarantee.

What owners should check
Tesla’s terms say an active Autonomy Subscription is required to operate the Cybercab. It can operate only in Tesla-supported areas, which may change. Owners are responsible for costs including insurance and charging.

text:
WHEN THE HEAVENS BECOME A WARNING

Strange Lights, Eyewitness Accounts, Spiritual Deception, and the Biblical Signs of the Last Days

Key Scripture — Luke 21:25–26 (KJV)

“And there shall be signs in the sun, and in the moon, and in the stars; and upon the earth distress of nations, with perplexity; the sea and the waves roaring; Men’s hearts failing them for fear, and for looking after those things which are coming on the earth: for the powers of heaven shall be shaken.”

Introduction: Something Is Happening Above Our Heads

On the morning of October 13, 2026, I was driving my children to school in Northeast Florida when something extraordinary appeared in the heavens. There was a brilliant light, an unusual fiery trail, and then an enormous glowing formation that spread across the morning sky. It was unlike anything I had personally witnessed before. I watched it, recorded it, and began investigating what we had seen. The explanation offered was a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket launched from Cape Canaveral, with its exhaust illuminated by the rising sun. There is a sound scientific explanation for how a rocket plume can expand and glow over a tremendous distance, and reports of that particular display came from several states. Nevertheless, seeing such a spectacle with your own eyes is considerably different from watching a news report about it afterward. I was there. I know what I saw, even if I could not have identified its cause without further information. That experience reminded me of something important: a person can witness a genuinely astonishing phenomenon without possessing an immediate explanation for it. And there is nothing foolish, unspiritual, or unreasonable about investigating what appears in the heavens. The Bible does not command Christians to close their eyes, surrender their ability to reason, or pretend that unusual things do not happen simply because somebody else considers the subject uncomfortable.

Exactly one month later, on Friday, November 13, 2026, another remarkable sequence of events captured public attention. The Federal Aviation Administration ordered a nationwide ground stop amid serious disruptions involving air traffic control communications and radar information. Thousands of flights were affected, passengers experienced extensive delays, and questions immediately began circulating about what had happened. Later that afternoon, SpaceX launched its fifteenth Starship flight from Texas, producing the possibility of dramatic luminous displays across portions of the sky. Videos circulated showing glowing formations, bright trails, apparent clusters of lights, and objects that witnesses struggled to identify. Reports came from the United States, the Caribbean, Central America, and other locations, although not every circulated recording has been authenticated or shown to belong to the same event. Since then, I have received photographs, videos, personal testimonies, and accounts from people describing what they believe they witnessed. Some can probably be explained by known technology. Others require additional information before any responsible conclusion can be reached. The aviation disruption and rocket launch were real events, but their occurrence on the same day does not establish that they were connected. We ought to be intelligent enough to recognize that distinction without pretending that the public’s questions are unreasonable.

What concerns me almost as much as the unusual reports themselves is the reaction of some professing Christians who seem to believe that examining anything outside their immediate religious interests is somehow evidence of spiritual compromise. text:
🔥 THE FOURTH REICH 🔥  
        by Randy Ferrell

History should be a warning, not a playbook.  

“THE FOURTH REICH” is a thunderous, unapologetically anti-fascist rock anthem about loving your country enough to refuse the cruelty committed in its name. It turns grief, disbelief, and fury into a declaration that cuts through the noise:  

NOT IN MY NAME. NOT THIS TIME.  

🎹 From dark piano and wounded, intimate vocals to crushing electric guitars, pounding drums, and explosive solos, the song builds around one lone male voice; deep, gritty, and seething one moment; soaring with raw emotion the next.  

Then the chorus opens:  

WEEEEEELCOME TOOO… THE FOOOOOURTH REICH! 

⚡ The soaring warning. The sudden silence. The full-band impact. Then the title returns as a defiant roar.  

That “welcome” is bitter irony. This song is an alarm and a refusal. 

💔 Its anger begins with people, not abstractions: a child’s shoe beside the stairs, a mother pleading, a shuttered clinic, pills counted to stretch through the pain. The lyrics confront authoritarianism, racism, attacks on the press, threats to voting rights, and the human cost of treating power as more important than people.

“You paint your hatred red and white That doesn’t make a fascist right”  

Behind the fury is a question that runs through the entire song: What does patriotism mean when defending your country requires standing against those claiming to speak for it?  

🦅 The answer isn’t blind obedience. It’s dignity, accountability, constitutional freedoms, and the conviction that no bloodline makes one life worth more than another.  

At the bridge, the thunder falls away. Piano, cello, and an exposed voice reveal what all that anger is trying to protect:  

“My father’s flag was never hate 
My sister’s life is not the state’s 
I want my neighbors home tonight 
Not names I sing by candlelight”  

✊ This is a resistance anthem rooted in ballots, peaceful marches, strikes, and song. Its call is to reject fascism, defend democracy, and refuse to let exhaustion become surrender.  

🗳️ “We’ll vote, we’ll march, we’ll hold the line”  The final chorus erupts, but the ending brings everything back to the people behind the protest:  

“Leave the porch light on tonight 
Let the children sleep 
Freedom isn’t what we shout 
It’s the promises we keep”  

🎧 Turn it up. Hear the warning. 
🎸 Let the guitars carry the fury. 
🥁 Feel the thunder beneath the heartbreak. 
❤️ Stay for the ending. That’s what the fight is for.  

If this song hits home:  

👍 LIKE the video and help more listeners discover it. 🔔 SUBSCRIBE and turn on notifications for more original music from Randy Ferrell. 
💬 COMMENT with the lyric that hit hardest—and what “Not in my name” means to you. 
📲 SHARE it on X, Facebook, or with someone who refuses to stay silent. 
🎶 SAVE it to your playlist and keep the message playing.

Defense projects, and specially those related to naval shipbuilding, are political in nature. Internally, they requiere a substantially intelligent dialogue to convince both the public and opposition. It sometimes even requires a huge effort to convince one's own political party and government ministries. Externally, they show the world -and neighbours- the country's strategic goals and the way it sees itself within the larger international security landscape. 

I read this news article on Damen 's offer to the Chilean Navy and could not help but to think of Mexico's ill fated shipbuilding industry. Since December 2019, not a major shipbuilding project has succeeded and it seems the recently-announced Yucatán Class OPV25 is experiencing important delays. After years of abandonment, it is understandable that the Mexican Navy will struggle to get its naval industry back on track.

Two main messages I'd like to share: 

1. I congratulate the MX Navy on its effort to revitalize its naval shipbuilding industry. The OPV25 project is a good start.....but insufficient (and this relates to my second point).

2. Mexico is not a small nation. With 3.5 million square kilometers of ocean domain and an economy that deeply depends on maritime commerce, we should start thinking different. We can't afford to continue viewing our Navy as a purely constabulary one. Developing a minimal but scalable naval defense capability should be a strategic concern (well beyond 2030).

The DAMEN SIGMA POLA PROJECT should be revisited and restarted, ASAP. Focusing solely on OPVs is simply not enough for the geopolitical shifts that are currently taking place. The future will demand us a different naval posture....we better be prepared for that.

🚨NEW🚨 Britain’s nukes are ‘not up for negotiation', Wes Streeting today declared to Russia as he marked the homecoming of a record-breaking nuclear-armed submarine.

Speaking to the Daily Mail as a tired-looking HMS Vengeance sailed into the Clyde on Sunday, the Defence Secretary insisted he would ‘not abandon’ European allies and cave in to ‘delusional’ demands by Vladimir Putin. 

His comments came after it emerged Kremlin negotiators said Russia would only end its war in Ukraine if Britain agreed to stop protecting Europe with its ultimate weapons. 

But Mr Streeting rejected Moscow’s proposed ceasefire ultimatum, insisting the UK’s commitment to defending its allies with nuclear force was ‘unwavering’ and ‘unshakeable’.  

‘The fact that Putin has made these demands demonstrates what the nuclear deterrent is, and the deterrence effect it is having in the Kremlin,’ he said. 

‘At a dangerous time for our continent, our nuclear deterrent is not up for negotiation, and we will not abandon our allies in Nato.’ 

HMS Vengeance finally returned home after a record-breaking 217 days under the waves. 

No other submarine has completed more than seven months under the water continuously, with Vengeance’s 140-strong crew almost entirely cut off from home for it.  

The Vanguard-class bomber, one of four, can carry up to 16 Trident nuclear missiles, capable of delivering multiple warheads that are strong enough to level a city. 

She is Britain's ultimate insurance with one nuclear-armed submarine always on patrol at any time, ready to strike should it be ordered to do so by the Prime Minister. 

But challenges with maintenance have increased the demands on individual boats and their crews, meaning their patrols have increased from about three months to seven. 

And the strain on Vengeance was clear to see, with barnacles, rust and algae coating the boat’s stealth plating as she crept back towards her base in Faslane. 

For the ship’s company, the homecoming was finally a chance to return home after ‘one of the most stressful jobs’ the Navy can offer. 

One senior submariner said the strain crews faced was immense. ‘Anyone who says this would be easy is lying, it is hard,’ they said. ‘But we’re proud to do it.’

When they set off in April, Sir Keir Starmer was still Prime Minister and the World Cup in America was still months away. 

She had been due home last week, but her relief boat needed to return home for spare parts. 

In a message to the crew delivered to the crew, Prime Minister Andy Burnham praised them for their steadfast dedication and for protecting the nation. 

Speaking to Mail as the submarine sailed home, Mr Streeting said he was immensely proud of the crew. 

‘For the time they have been at sea, there is literally no one else, in any part of the country, in the UK or overseas, who has done more to keep our country safe,’ he added. 

‘The nuclear deterrent has been the cornerstone of our national defence and security since its inception, and it is just as - if not more - important today, with the sort of threat environment we have. 

‘So, for the UK, for our country and for our continent, these people can be exceptionally proud of their service.’

• Guests can deposit BTC, ETH or LTC at the casino cage through BurraPay
• They get chips or gaming tickets denominated in U.S. dollars
• BurraPay charges a 5% service fee on deposits
• Only guests 21+ with an Infinity Rewards account, with ID checks
• Crypto can't be bet directly at tables or slots, and crypto isn't offered for cash-out
• It can't be used for hotel rooms, dining or other resort purchases

Give SAHARA its due, since Nevada casinos have been cautious about crypto because of gaming regulation and this is a step past that. With that being said, the bitcoin is converted to dollars at the cage, so nobody is actually spending it, and you pay 5% for the trip.

Fine as a convenience, as long as nobody confuses it with bitcoin becoming money on the Strip.

text:
The key point here is that in the ancient world, kings were directly linked to the Gods, like the Pharaohs in Egypt and rulers in Babylon, where complex scripts kept divine knowledge locked inside the palace and temple elite. When the Israelites adopted the simple Paleo-Hebrew alphabet around the 10th to 9th centuries BCE, it democratized literacy and allowed them to build a direct, "royal-free" covenant with God through a public text. That portable, written law, where even kings were subordinate to the text, is what sits at the origin of the Torah.

A similar disruption happened in the Roman Empire around 110 AD. By then, Roman emperors claimed divine status and controlled access to the Gods through state religion. Non-Jewish converts inside the empire saw how the Jewish scriptures offered a direct line to God without bowing to Caesar, but they couldn't easily join Judaism because it was gated behind strict ethnic and religious laws. So they used Jesus, reframed in late texts like the Gospel of John as the universal Logos ("the Word") and positioned against "the Jews", as a loophole to unlock that written tradition for themselves, breaking the emperor's divine monopoly through scripture rather than royal bloodlines.

Jesus’ Words on the Widow’s Offering
In Mark 12:41–44, Jesus sat opposite the temple treasury and watched the crowd putting money in. Many rich people gave large amounts, but a poor widow came and placed two small copper coins — worth only a few cents. Jesus called His disciples to Him and said, “Truly I tell you, this poor widow has put more into the treasury than all the others. They all gave out of their wealth; but she, out of her poverty, put in everything — all she had to live on”
Meaning and Application
Jesus’ words emphasize that the value of a gift is not measured by the amount given, but by the proportion of one’s resources that is offered. The widow’s offering, though small in monetary terms, represented her entire livelihood, showing complete trust and sacrifice. This contrasts with the rich who gave from surplus, often leaving their needs met.
Chairty, the Willingness to Give to Help Others less fortunate; Why is it important to know this truth?
Because in the life of charity, all growth comes from God, but at the same time he does not will to save us without us (1 Cor 3:6, CCC 1847). In other words, although charity and our growth in this life of friendship with God are his gift to us, God requires of us our cooperation, that we desire and strive to grow in this life and ask him to perfect it within us. “If you knew the gift of God,” Jesus says to the Samaritan woman, “you would have asked him, and he would have given you living water” (John 4:10).
“Do not Cast your Pearls before the Swine”

text:
The White Christian Man arrived to put an end to paganism and the widespread practice of human sacrifice among indigenous peoples—brown, black, and white — around the world.

In Maya and Aztec societies, captives and slaves were routinely dragged up temple pyramids, held down on stone altars, and had their chests cut open with obsidian knives so priests could rip out their still-beating hearts as offerings to the gods. Victims were also decapitated, thrown alive into sacred cenotes, or flayed; their skulls were displayed on racks, and in some cases parts of the bodies were eaten. These were not rare events—major temples could see thousands sacrificed in a single ceremony, and constant warfare was waged largely to capture more victims.

White pagan societies in Europe practiced their own aggressive forms of ritual violence. In the Roman world, human sacrifice was carried out in earlier periods and in moments of crisis, including the live burial of Gauls and Greeks after the Battle of Cannae, while the origins of the gladiatorial games lay in the ritual slaughter of captives as funeral offerings to the dead. Among Germanic tribes, archaeological evidence from bog bodies shows victims who were hanged, throat-cut, bludgeoned, or subjected to multiple forms of killing in overkill rituals; captives and slaves were offered as blood sacrifices to gods such as Odin, often drowned, stabbed, or left hanging from sacred trees, and prisoners taken in war were regularly killed to honor the gods and the dead.

Black pagan societies in Africa also practiced large-scale human sacrifice. In kingdoms such as Dahomey, Ashanti, Benin, and others, captives, slaves, and criminals were regularly killed as offerings to the gods and ancestors—often by beheading, throat-cutting, or live burial during annual festivals and royal ceremonies. Thousands could be sacrificed in a single custom; skulls and body parts were displayed, and warfare was frequently conducted to supply victims for these rituals.

Jews practiced paganism and human sacrifice. Kings Ahaz and Manasseh made their sons pass through the fire. People burned their children in the Valley of Hinnom. Solomon built high places for Chemosh and Molech. The Northern Kingdom set up golden calves at Bethel and Dan. Ahab and Jezebel promoted Baal worship. High places, Asherah poles, and foreign cults were repeatedly established and used. These acts are recorded in 2 Kings 16:3, 21:6, 1 Kings 11, 1 Kings 12, 1 Kings 16–18, Jeremiah 7 and 19, and elsewhere.

Across these cultures, the belief that the gods required human life and blood was widespread, and warfare often supplied the victims. 

With the coming of Jesus Christ, the New Testament, and the spread of Christianity, these sacrificial systems and the pagan practices that sustained them were nullified and destroyed. 

The New Testament declares that the death of Jesus is the final sacrifice that ends every blood offering, and Christian expansion suppressed and replaced these rites wherever it took hold. Christians themselves were also sacrificed and killed for refusing to participate in pagan rites and for working to stop them.

JESUS CHRIST IS KING.

To offer forgiveness when a line has been crossed is one of the highest acts of mastery a soul can perform upon this Earth. Forgiveness is essential to the peace of mind of both vessels involved; it dissolves the heavy, binding tether of resentment so that neither spirit remains chained to the friction of the past.

Yet true forgiveness does not mean leaving the gates of your sanctuary unguarded. As you forgive freely, you must also guard your own heart grail, that sacred, living chalice of your vital essence, peace, and physical well-being. To forgive while firmly tending to your own chalice is not a contradiction; it is the highest wisdom. It allows love to flow unconditionally without permitting the cup itself to be shattered or poured out onto dry ground.

Hold your forgiveness with an open, unburdened spirit, and hold your boundary with the quiet, unshakeable strength of stone. In doing so, you honour both the soul before you and the sacred temple you inhabit.

Abraham Shakespeare won $30 million in the Florida lottery. The woman who offered to manage his money took it, then buried him under a concrete slab in her backyard.

Then she forged a letter in his name to his mother. He couldn't read or write.

In the video below, you hear her talking to him about his money.

Shakespeare washed dishes and worked on garbage trucks in Lakeland, Florida. In November 2006 he won the jackpot and took about $17 million.

He paid off mortgages for family, friends and complete strangers. "I really would like my old life back," he said.

Then DeeDee Moore came into his life and offered to help manage his money. On her own home video she asks him: "Do you get tired of people asking you for money all the time, Abe?"

He was last seen in April 2009. Moore set up a phone call to his mother with a man pretending to be him. "You don't sound like Abraham," his mother said.

"I'm not the one that shot him," Moore told reporters. But the friend she trusted was a police informant, and she asked him to burn the body.

Shakespeare was found on January 28, 2010. His money was almost all gone.

In December 2012 Moore was convicted of first-degree murder and got life without parole.

On a secret police tape she said: "I've never been through nothing like this in my life."

If you won $30 million tomorrow, would you let someone else manage it, or never tell a soul?

text:
Washington can change policy. 

After finding all that fraud they must act. 

Medicaid should be housing for disabled, drug addiction and seniors that have no money for care.

Medicaid recipients should sign in ACA pay something for healthcare. Both of these programs should be flagged for fraud and blatant high cost treatment. Insurance companies should give 3 options for reasonable price policies subsidies only for low income. 
Employers should shop there also for employees. Federal and state employees should sign in ACA. 

Medicare also flagged for fraud and high cost procedures, surgeries and office visits. Online Medicare has no transparency and doesn’t say what was paid by them. 

Medicare Advantage should be paid by the person who wants the coverage, not the insurance company. No one knows what they receives per month or per person. Advantage says it’s all free.

End part D and medigap A-G is a relic has no extra coverage for dental, eyes and hearing coverage. The insurance offered should be for the 20% with levels of deductible for out of pocket. 
A lot of doctors say they are not taking patients on Medicare because in most case they don’t get the reasonable fee they charged.

🇺🇸🇪🇺 Europe is diligently weaning itself off its dependence on Russian gas - only to find itself gravitating toward a new one. According to Forbes, Russia accounted for 45% of the EU’s gas imports before the war. By 2025, that share had dropped to 12%, and Brussels has pledged to phase out Russian gas entirely by the end of 2027. It sounds like a victory - except that Washington has already stepped into the spot once occupied by Moscow.

In the first half of 2026, the U.S. supplied 59% of Europe’s total liquefied natural gas (LNG) imports, a figure that could climb to 80% by 2028. In effect, Europe is simply swapping one supplier for another, all while suffering the consequences of high prices. And this is where things get interesting. While the EU makes a show of turning its back on Russian energy, Trump is moving in the opposite direction, easing sanctions pressure on Moscow. This means that the very leverage Europe worked so hard to wrest from the Kremlin has quietly shifted into the hands of the White House. 

Forbes offers a candid warning: Trump could wield this leverage - not just to pressure allies, but as a bargaining chip in negotiations with Putin. Gas-based blackmail hasn’t disappeared; it has simply changed its address.

MRS. ADWOA SMITH EXTOLS GHANAIAN CULTURE TO SPOUSES OF AMBASSADORS IN USA

WASHINGTON, D.C. — November 5, 2026

Mrs. Adwoa Smith, spouse of Ghana’s Ambassador to the United States, H.E. Victor Emmanuel Smith, hosted a vibrant cultural showcase in Washington, D.C., for spouses of fellow Ambassadors accredited to the United States.

The gathering was organized to deepen bilateral ties through cultural diplomacy by highlighting the beauty, craftsmanship, and rich heritage of Ghana.

Opening the event with a promotional video on Ghanaian tourism, Mrs. Smith set the stage for an immersive exploration of the nation’s diverse traditions. She curated an extensive display of indigenous textiles and accessories, featuring intricate Ashanti kente cloth and Northern fugu, handcrafted bead necklaces and wristlets, and artisanal fans made from traditional printed fabrics and leather, paired with matching handbags and purses.

Addressing her guests, Mrs. Smith celebrated the ingenuity of Ghanaian designers and artisans. Challenging common global perceptions, she boldly declared that while nations like India are famed for their adornments, Ghana’s traditional jewelry pieces are among the most exquisite in the world. She illustrated this richness by pointing to the historic September 2026 Asantehene’s Akwasidae celebration in Washington, D.C., where Otumfuo Osei Tutu II, his entourage, and visiting dignitaries captivated onlookers in resplendent kente, traditional beads, and gold ornaments.

Beyond aesthetics, Mrs. Smith offered an educational breakdown of Ghana’s textile heritage. She explained the distinct weaving techniques and textures unique to the Ashanti, Northern, and Ewe peoples, demonstrating both how these garments were draped in antiquity and how they have evolved into contemporary Ghanaian fashion.

Turning her focus to travel and heritage, Mrs. Smith extended a formal invitation to the diplomatic spouses to plan a trip to Ghana to experience the country’s warmth firsthand. She highlighted key cultural tourism destinations such as Saltpond, Cape Coast, and Elmina, specifically referencing the historic castles and forts that stand as poignant reminders of the transatlantic slave trade. Alongside its deep history, she emphasized Ghana’s reputation as a safe, welcoming destination boasting world-class hotels, friendly hospitality, and a lively nightlife.

The presentation transitioned from visual to experiential as Mrs. Smith demonstrated a few traditional dance moves, showing her guests how effortless and joyful it is to engage with Ghanaian music and rhythm. 

The cultural afternoon concluded with a culinary showcase, where guests were treated to an array of authentic, traditional Ghanaian dishes, including the world famous Ghana jolof.

The school proposed to be erected at the former Cathedral School building is named ‘Fulton Sheen Academy’ and it will offer a Catholic liberal arts education rooted in the great intellectual tradition of the Church, emphasizing the formation of students in faith, virtue, wisdom, and the pursuit of truth.

The proposal has been made in the wake of the interest expressed by families in the Springfield area for having a Catholic classical academy for high school students. Now the Diocese is assessing whether there is sufficient interest and commitment among families to make the school a reality.

Dr. Mark Newcomb, director of the Diocese’s Department for Catholic Education said that families have asked Bishop Thomas John Paprocki and other dignitaries of the diocese to have a Catholic classical academy for high school students. “We have decided that it is time to explore these conversations in earnest to see if there are enough families to commit to the work it would take to make such an academy a reality,” he added.

Fulton Sheen Academy, different from a traditional high school curriculum, would approach learning through the lens of historical periods, integrating literature, mathematics, art, and science into the study of different eras.

Sydney Leathers was 23 when she walked into a gossip website with every text message a candidate for mayor of New York had sent her. Vivid Entertainment then paid her a reported $75,000 to re-enact them on camera. The candidate was Anthony Weiner. His wife worked for Hillary Clinton.

She was a college student from southern Illinois. Weiner had resigned from Congress in 2011 over photos sent to another woman, and in early 2012 she wrote to him on Facebook to say she had defended him. He wrote back.

They spent most of 2012 trading messages, calls and photos. He used the name Carlos Danger. He was 47 and still married to Huma Abedin. She was 22.

In the summer of 2013 he ran for mayor with his wife at his side. On July 23 Sydney took screen captures of the whole thing to a gossip site called The Dirty. She says the site paid her in the low five figures.

Within two weeks Vivid called. Steven Hirsch offered $75,000 and a share of the profits for a parody the studio named Weiner and Me. She signed and flew to Los Angeles for the shoot.

Weiner finished fifth in the primary with about 5% of the vote. In 2017 he pleaded guilty in an unrelated federal case, Huma Abedin filed for divorce the same day, and he got 21 months in prison.

In the video below she says none of it was about fame. "I was outed. And any press stuff I had done really was to try to support myself because I was making money from it. I was not able to work at that time." She went back to college and did p*rn on weekends, "as little as I could to get by."

Thirteen years later she has a degree, a fiancé whose very religious parents heard the whole story and did not care, and a quiet life she calls boring.

The gossip site paid five figures, Vivid paid $75,000, and the man who started it lost the race.

Did a 22-year-old from Illinois knock out a man already caught doing the same thing once, or did a 47-year-old former congressman use a girl who wrote him a single fan message?

I post one star like this every day, on camera and in their own words, about where the money went and who walked away with it.

text:
A concentrated stock position is a sequencing problem before it is a tax problem, and for a corporate insider the first step is permission.

Our one-page map for a low-basis public stock position:

• The gate, insiders only: many companies bar officers, directors, and 10% holders from hedging or pledging, so stock-backed loans, prepaid forwards, and collars need approval; other holders skip it 
• Four coordinated sleeves: borrow, diversify around the stock, hedge, and a fourth sleeve to hold, give, or transfer 
• An exit rail for shares sold on purpose, with an outright sale as the honest benchmark 
• Twenty-two tools rated on liquidity, tax efficiency, downside protection, charitable transfer, and exit timing

The red squares are the point. Borrowing adds leverage and collateral-call risk, an exchange fund gives up liquidity for seven years, holding for a step-up at death leaves shares unhedged, and an outright sale pays the tax today. Every tool solves one problem by creating another, which is why the sleeves are sized against each other.

Twenty-two tools are not the whole list. Also off the grid: Section 351 ETF conversions, kiddie-tax family gifts, life insurance trusts, no-tax-state trusts, installment sales, and Section 1042. Selling a business for the buyer's stock lands here at closing. Check the gate first, then build with your CPA and estate attorney.

text:
Indiana are 29c to beat Philadelphia, but the spread offers a different way to back them

Polymarket has Pacers +7.5 at 50c, with the 76ers at 72c to win

Philadelphia enter at 10-3 and Indiana at 5-8, so the favorite makes sense

Their previous meeting was much closer than those records suggest

The Sixers won 114-109, with Tyrese Maxey scoring 27 points

One five-point game does not settle the rematch, but it gives Indiana a concrete example of staying competitive against this opponent

My preference is Pacers +7.5 at 50c

Indiana can lose another close game and still cover, while the 29c moneyline needs them to turn that competitive performance into a win

The danger is letting Philadelphia build a lead that forces rushed possessions late

Keeping the game within a couple of baskets gives this position a much better finish

text:
Cleveland's home game comes with a pretty rough journey home

The Cavs played in Miami last night, then the flight disruption kept them there until Saturday morning

AP reports they had roughly eight hours between landing and facing Dallas

Polymarket prices the Mavericks at 56c and Cleveland at 45c

That travel matters because the second night of a back-to-back already asks a lot of a team, even before the overnight routine gets disrupted

For Dallas, pushing the pace and making Cleveland defend through multiple actions would be a sensible way to test those legs

The Cavs can still make this a half-court game and keep it close

But at 56c, I favor Dallas with Cleveland coming into this one on such a compressed turnaround

text:

The Pelicans are 4-9 and Polymarket prices their home win at just 16c

Denver at 85c makes sense as the favorite, but the basketball question is how New Orleans keeps this competitive

Let Jokic operate against single coverage and Denver can build its offense through him

Send help and the Pelicans have to recover quickly enough to protect the perimeter and track cutters

For New Orleans, forcing turnovers and getting into transition would reduce the number of possessions spent solving that problem

If this becomes a steady half-court game, I favor Denver

The concern is the entry price

At 85c, a winning share earns just 15c before fees, so I would watch for a cheaper live entryя if New Orleans starts well and Denver's main rotation stays intact

text:
Already in the Express Entry pool? Use Provincial Nominee Programs (PNP) to boost your CRS score by 600 points and almost guarantee an Invitation to Apply.

A provincial nomination through an enhanced (Express Entry-aligned) stream is the single biggest CRS boost available. 
Once you accept it in your profile, IRCC adds 600 points. Most candidates jump well above cut-offs in PNP draws.

Simple process to follow:
1Log into your Express Entry profile and go to Nomination and selection.
2Select the provinces or territories you’re interested in, or choose “all provinces and territories.” This lets them find you when they search the pool.
3Keep your profile accurate (language scores, work experience, education, etc.).
4Watch for a Notification of Interest (NOI) in your account, or apply directly on a province’s website if you meet their stream criteria.
5If invited or interested, apply for the provincial nomination and show genuine intent to live and work there.
6Once nominated, accept the nomination in your Express Entry account. Your CRS score updates with the 600 points.
7Wait for the next Express Entry draw, you’ll almost certainly receive an ITA.

You can express interest in multiple provinces at the same time while in the pool. You can only hold one active nomination, so choose carefully if more than one province offers you a spot.

Quick plain-English notes on provinces
•Ontario: Competitive, often targets specific occupations or French speakers. Job offers help but aren’t always required.
•British Columbia: Strong on tech and healthcare. Usually needs a job offer and uses a points-based registration system.
•Alberta: Good for people with local ties or certain sectors (tech, healthcare, rural). Has an Express Entry stream.
•Saskatchewan & Manitoba: Points-based systems. Connections to the province or in-demand occupations improve chances; some streams don’t need a job offer.
•Atlantic provinces (NS, NB, PEI, NL): Often more accessible with a job offer from a local employer.
•Territories: Smaller programs, usually employer-driven.

Key things to remember: Be honest about where you plan to settle. Rules and open streams change often, so check official provincial sites. Fees are usually non-refundable once processing starts. This strategy works best when your profile matches what a province currently needs. 

Check IRCC and each province’s immigration page for the latest details before applying.
