text:
🎮 100 Facts About Nintendo

🎴 ORIGINS

𝟏. Nintendo was founded on 23 September 1889 in Kyoto, Japan 🇯🇵, by Fusajiro Yamauchi.

𝟐. That makes it the same age as the Eiffel Tower, which opened in 1889 🗼.

𝟑. It started out making hanafuda, traditional Japanese flower playing cards 🎴.

𝟒. The name is usually translated as 'leave luck to heaven', though its exact meaning is debated.

𝟓. Nintendo still makes hanafuda and playing cards today.

𝟔. In 1959 it signed a deal to print playing cards featuring Disney characters.

𝟕. Hiroshi Yamauchi took over in 1949, in his early twenties, and ran the company until 2002.

𝟖. In the 1960s it reportedly tried a taxi company, instant rice and a love hotel chain.

𝟗. Gunpei Yokoi's Ultra Hand, an extending grabber toy from 1966, sold more than a million units 🦾.

𝟏𝟎. Yokoi also created the Love Tester (1969), a gadget that claimed to measure romance ❤️.

𝟏𝟏. In the 1970s Nintendo built Laser Clay Shooting ranges in old bowling alleys 🔫.

🕹️ ARCADES & HANDHELDS

𝟏𝟐. Its first home video game systems, the Color TV-Game series, arrived in Japan in 1977 📺.

𝟏𝟑. Game & Watch (1980) was reportedly inspired by Yokoi seeing a commuter play with a calculator.

𝟏𝟒. The Game & Watch version of Donkey Kong (1982) popularised the cross-shaped D-pad ✚.

𝟏𝟓. Nintendo of America was set up in 1980 and later moved to Redmond, Washington 🇺🇸.

𝟏𝟔. Donkey Kong (1981) was Shigeru Miyamoto's first game as lead designer 🦍.

𝟏𝟕. Its hero was called Jumpman and was a carpenter, not a plumber 🔨.

𝟏𝟖. Jumpman was renamed Mario, reportedly after Mario Segale, the landlord of Nintendo's US warehouse.

𝟏𝟗. Universal sued Nintendo, claiming Donkey Kong copied King Kong, and lost in 1983 ⚖️.

𝟐𝟎. Nintendo's lawyer in that case, John Kirby, is often cited as the namesake of Kirby 🩷.

𝟐𝟏. Luigi made his debut in the arcade game Mario Bros. (1983).

📺 FAMICOM & NES

𝟐𝟐. The Family Computer, or Famicom, launched in Japan on 15 July 1983.

𝟐𝟑. It reached North America in 1985 as the Nintendo Entertainment System (NES).

𝟐𝟒. The NES is widely credited with reviving the US games market after the 1983 crash 📈.

𝟐𝟓. Nintendo bundled R.O.B., a little robot, to sell the NES as a toy rather than a games console 🤖.

𝟐𝟔. The 'Official Nintendo Seal of Quality' was introduced to fight low-quality games.

𝟐𝟕. The NES Zapper light gun came with Duck Hunt 🦆.

𝟐𝟖. The Famicom and NES sold about 61.9 million units worldwide.

𝟐𝟗. Super Mario Bros. (1985) sold more than 40 million copies 🍄.

𝟑𝟎. Mario's cap and moustache helped avoid drawing hair and a mouth in tiny pixel art.

𝟑𝟏. Koji Kondo composed the iconic music of Super Mario Bros. and The Legend of Zelda 🎵.

𝟑𝟐. The Legend of Zelda (1986) was one of the first console games with battery-backed saving 💾.

𝟑𝟑. Metroid (1986) revealed at the end that its armoured hero, Samus, was a woman 👩‍🚀.

𝟑𝟒. Nintendo Power magazine ran in North America from 1988 to 2012 📖.

📟 GAME BOY

𝟑𝟓. The Game Boy launched in 1989, designed by Gunpei Yokoi's team.

𝟑𝟔. In North America it came bundled with Tetris 🧱.

𝟑𝟕. Game Boy and Game Boy Color together sold about 118.7 million units.

𝟑𝟖. A Game Boy that survived a bombing in the Gulf War still works and has been displayed at Nintendo's New York store.

𝟑𝟗. Yokoi's motto 'lateral thinking with withered technology' meant using cheap, proven tech in new ways.

𝟒𝟎. Pokémon Red and Green launched on Game Boy in Japan in 1996 ⚡.

𝟒𝟏. Pokémon is often cited as the highest-grossing media franchise of all time.

𝟒𝟐. Nintendo co-owns The Pokémon Company with Game Freak and Creatures.

𝟒𝟑. The Game Boy Camera (1998) was listed by Guinness as the world's smallest digital camera 📷.

𝟒𝟒. The Game Boy Advance (2001) sold about 81.5 million units.

🎮 SNES, N64 & VIRTUAL BOY

𝟒𝟓. The Super Famicom launched in Japan in 1990 and as the SNES in North America in 1991.

𝟒𝟔. The SNES family sold about 49.1 million units.

𝟒𝟕. Yoshi made his debut in Super Mario World (1990) 🦖.

𝟒𝟖. Star Fox (1993) used the Super FX chip inside the cartridge to draw 3D polygons 🚀.

𝟒𝟗. A planned Nintendo and Sony CD add-on fell apart in 1991; Sony went on to make the PlayStation.

𝟓𝟎. In Japan, the Satellaview add-on beamed games to the Super Famicom by satellite 🛰️.

𝟓𝟏. The Virtual Boy (1995) reportedly sold fewer than 800,000 units, one of Nintendo's biggest flops.

𝟓𝟐. The Nintendo 64 (1996) sold about 32.9 million units.

𝟓𝟑. Super Mario 64 set the template for 3D platform games.

𝟓𝟒. The N64's Rumble Pak (1997) helped make controller vibration standard 📳.

𝟓𝟓. Ocarina of Time (1998) holds a 99 on Metacritic, among the highest scores ever 🗡️.

𝟓𝟔. GoldenEye 007 (1997), made by Rare, became a landmark console shooter.

💿 GAMECUBE, DS, WII & 3DS

𝟓𝟕. The GameCube (2001) used small 8 cm discs and sold about 21.7 million units.

𝟓𝟖. Satoru Iwata became president in 2002, the first from outside the Yamauchi family.

𝟓𝟗. The Nintendo DS (2004) sold about 154 million units, with two screens and a touchscreen ✍️.

𝟔𝟎. Brain Age and Nintendogs drew millions of people who had never played games 🐶.

𝟔𝟏. The Wii (2006) brought motion controls to living rooms and sold about 101.6 million units.

𝟔𝟐. Wii Sports sold nearly 83 million copies, mostly bundled with the console 🎳.

𝟔𝟑. Miis, the customisable avatars, debuted on the Wii.

𝟔𝟒. Wii Fit and its Balance Board turned a games console into a home gym 🧘.

𝟔𝟓. The 3DS (2011) offered glasses-free 3D and sold about 76 million units.

𝟔𝟔. The Wii U (2012) sold only about 13.6 million units, one of Nintendo's weakest home consoles.

𝟔𝟕. Iwata launched the Nintendo Direct video presentations in 2011.

𝟔𝟖. amiibo figures, which unlock in-game content, arrived in 2014.

𝟔𝟗. Iwata died in 2015, aged 55, and is still widely mourned by players.

𝟕𝟎. Splatoon (2015) showed Nintendo could still launch brand-new hit series 🦑.

🔀 THE SWITCH ERA

𝟕𝟏. The Nintendo Switch, a home and handheld hybrid, launched on 3 March 2017.

𝟕𝟐. It has overtaken the DS to become Nintendo's best-selling console ever 🏆.

𝟕𝟑. Switch game cards are coated with a bitter substance to stop children swallowing them 🤢.

𝟕𝟒. Breath of the Wild (2017) reinvented Zelda as an open world 🏔️.

𝟕𝟓. Mario Kart 8 Deluxe has sold more than 60 million copies, the Switch's top seller 🏎️.

𝟕𝟔. Animal Crossing: New Horizons (2020) sold more than 45 million copies 🏝️.

𝟕𝟕. Super Smash Bros. Ultimate has 89 playable fighters 🥊.

𝟕𝟖. Nintendo Labo (2018) let players build cardboard accessories for the Switch 📦.

𝟕𝟗. Nintendo Switch Online includes classic NES, SNES, N64 and other retro libraries.

𝟖𝟎. The Switch 2 launched on 5 June 2025.

𝟖𝟏. It sold 3.5 million units in four days, Nintendo's fastest-selling hardware ever 🚀.

𝟖𝟐. Its Joy-Con 2 controllers attach magnetically and can work like a mouse 🖱️.

𝟖𝟑. Shuntaro Furukawa has been Nintendo's president since 2018.

🍄 CHARACTERS & CREATORS

𝟖𝟒. Mario has appeared in more than 200 games.

𝟖𝟓. Charles Martinet voiced Mario for decades before Kevin Afghani took over in 2023 🎙️.

𝟖𝟔. Miyamoto has said Princess Zelda was named after the writer Zelda Fitzgerald.

𝟖𝟕. Link's name reportedly reflects his role linking the past and the future.

𝟖𝟖. Pikachu became the official mascot of Pokémon.

𝟖𝟗. Miyamoto has said exploring caves and countryside as a child inspired Zelda 🌲.

𝟗𝟎. The Mario series has reportedly sold well over 800 million games across all its spin-offs.

🏢 BUSINESS & BEYOND

𝟗𝟏. From 1992 until 2016, Yamauchi and then Nintendo were majority owners of the Seattle Mariners ⚾.

𝟗𝟐. Nintendo Tokyo, its first official store in Japan, opened in Shibuya in 2019 🛍️.

𝟗𝟑. Nintendo's New York store at Rockefeller Center first opened as Nintendo World in 2005 🗽.

𝟗𝟒. Super Nintendo World opened at Universal Studios Japan in Osaka in 2021 🎢.

𝟗𝟓. Super Nintendo World has since opened in Hollywood (2023) and Orlando (2025) 🎡.

𝟗𝟔. The Nintendo Museum opened in Uji, Kyoto, in 2024, in a former playing-card factory 🏛️.

𝟗𝟕. The Super Mario Bros. Movie (2023) grossed more than $1.3 billion worldwide 🎬.

𝟗𝟖. A sequel, The Super Mario Galaxy Movie, was slated for 2026 🌌.

𝟗𝟗. A live-action Legend of Zelda film is in the works.

𝟏𝟎𝟎. After more than 135 years, Nintendo is still headquartered in Kyoto, the city where it began 🇯🇵.

📸 Super Nintendo World at Universal Studios Japan, Osaka, at dusk. Photo: https://t.co/IQ5AcxLqSC, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

text:
🎙️ HARVEY’S CORNER

🎨 GEORGIA O’KEEFFE — THE ARTIST WHO REFUSED TO SEE THE WORLD ORDINARY 🌺

Good day, everybody.

Some artists paint what they see. Others paint what they want us to see. Georgia O’Keeffe did something rather different: she made the familiar look unfamiliar, the overlooked impossible to ignore, and the ordinary suddenly worth a second look.

Born November 15, 1887, near Sun Prairie, Wisconsin, Georgia Totto O’Keeffe grew up on a dairy farm as the second of seven children. Her artistic ability was recognized early, and she received art lessons while growing up.

She studied at the Art Institute of Chicago and the Art Students League in New York, where she learned traditional techniques. But she became dissatisfied with academic realism and the expectation that art should simply reproduce what the eye could see.

A turning point came in 1912, when she took a summer course at the University of Virginia. Her instructor, Alon Bement, introduced her to the ideas of art educator Arthur Wesley Dow. His approach emphasized composition, line, and design—and offered O’Keeffe a way to express feeling through form rather than merely copy appearances.

She began experimenting with abstraction, producing a remarkable series of charcoal drawings. In 1916, photographer and art dealer Alfred Stieglitz exhibited ten of these works at his avant-garde gallery, 291, in New York. He recognized an original voice. O’Keeffe's work soon attracted attention, and Stieglitz became an important promoter of her art.

In 1918, she accepted his offer of financial support to leave teaching and devote herself to painting in New York. Their personal and professional relationship developed, and they married in 1924.

By the 1920s, O’Keeffe had become known for her large-scale flower paintings and her images of New York skyscrapers. Her flowers were not dainty decorations. She enlarged and cropped them until their shapes, curves, and colors filled the canvas. Viewers were forced to look closely at forms they might otherwise have passed without noticing.

But there was a problem: many critics insisted on interpreting her flower paintings through sexual symbolism. O’Keeffe rejected those readings. She wanted people to look at the paintings themselves, not simply impose meanings on them because the artist was a woman.

Her response was not to abandon the subjects she loved. It was to continue painting them on her own terms.

In 1929, O’Keeffe travelled to northern New Mexico for the first time. The landscape made a profound impression. The vast skies, rugged mountains, adobe architecture, churches, and bleached animal bones offered new subjects and new possibilities.

She returned regularly, spending much of each year in the Southwest. After Stieglitz died in 1946, she moved permanently to New Mexico in 1949. She divided her time between Ghost Ranch and her home in Abiquiú, where the landscape became inseparable from her artistic identity.

Her paintings of desert bones and sweeping landscapes were not simply postcards of the Southwest. They were her way of expressing what a place made her feel.

She continued creating into old age, although failing eyesight increasingly limited her work. She completed her last unassisted oil painting in 1972 and, with the help of assistants, continued exploring her creativity until her retirement in 1984.

O’Keeffe died in Santa Fe on March 6, 1986, aged ninety-eight.

Her legacy is much larger than the famous flowers, skulls, and desert landscapes. She helped shape American modernism, built an artistic language that was unmistakably her own, and refused to let critics dictate how her work should be understood.

She once explained that she had to create an equivalent for what she felt when looking at something—not merely copy it.

That may be the most revealing way to understand her art. She was not asking us simply to look at a flower, a mountain, or a bone. She was asking us to see it differently.

And she spent a lifetime showing us how.

And now, you know the rest of the story.

—— ❧ ——

🧩 TRIVIA: O’Keeffe's breakthrough exhibition in 1916 featured abstract charcoal drawings—not the flower paintings for which she later became famous. Alfred Stieglitz exhibited ten of those drawings at his 291 gallery, introducing her work to the New York art world.

🧬 HUMAN: O’Keeffe resisted being defined primarily as a woman artist. She wanted to be regarded as an artist, full stop. Yet the repeated attempts to interpret her paintings through gendered assumptions reveal how difficult it was for a woman of her generation to control the way her work was discussed.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: O’Keeffe's greatest achievement may have been her refusal to let other people determine what she should see, paint, or become. She created her own artistic language—and left the world looking at familiar things in a new way.

—— ❧ ——

text:
A Virginia couple planned a small backyard hangout for their 13-year-old sons and a handful of classmates. By that same night, they were facing criminal charges.

Lisa and Aubrey Vaughan say an invitation meant for 10 to 20 eighth graders spread on Snapchat, eventually reaching high school students. By 9 p.m., between 100 and 300 teenagers had flooded their McLean neighborhood, with fireworks going off and multiple 911 calls pouring in.

Fairfax County police charged both parents with contributing to the delinquency of a minor and maintaining a common nuisance. The couple disputes that alcohol was permitted, saying the invitation explicitly banned it and that they were home supervising the entire time. Their attorney says they welcomed officers and even offered to let police inspect the party area.

What upsets about the whole brouhaha whining about Vets isn’t the idiots thinking what they think. Idiots are a dime a dozen and frankly these are people without honor who I’d have probably disliked for a number of other reasons anyway even if they hadn’t open their mouths to show what kind of MIG15’s they are. 

What upsets me is that I can look back at the friends I’ve lost since even coming home from war who refused help at every turn, partly because they were too proud to accept the help that’s contractually obligated to them. Benefits for veterans have been with us as a country since 1776 when the Continental Congress established a pension for disabled soldiers from the revolutionary war. None of this is new. Neither the benefits, nor the empty headed motherfuckers who think veterans don’t deserve shit, that soldiers are simply mercenaries. 

Nonetheless I can look back into my own past and see the destructive wake this idiotic sentiment has left behind it. Lives ruined, friends who are no longer with us, good people struggling that frankly shouldn’t be. It’s difficult enough to clear the hurdles within the system without some morons trying to shame struggling veterans to just accept misery and disability they themselves would never accept, because they don’t like to pay taxes. 

Despite their distaste with taxes, despite their advising veterans to just “suck it up” and live a lesser quality of life, it usually turns out they’re all too happy to put their own hand out when the government offers them money. But of course they always have an excuse then. They of course are better, wiser, morally superior and will put this money to good uses, while the veterans are just mooching. 

Fuck these people straight into the sun.

text:
How desperate must someone be for a miracle to wake up, dress up, walk to church, spend hours watching a pastor command a feature phone to charge, and possibly contribute offertory for the performance?

This is where Uganda's religious entertainment industry deserves some serious scrutiny.

The pastor reportedly presents a button-operated feature phone and claims to command it to start charging through prayer. Yet technicians point to a much more ordinary possibility: certain faulty phones can display charging indicators even when they are not actually receiving electrical power.

That distinction matters. A charging symbol is not a charging current. A blinking battery indicator is not proof that the battery is gaining energy. A malfunction can look impressive when nobody in the room understands the electronics.

And here is the bigger problem: why must every unexplained occurrence become a supernatural achievement when it happens inside a church?

Some religious personalities make predictions about public events, hoping that probability and coincidence will eventually produce a convincing testimony. Others have faced allegations of staged testimonies and manufactured healing demonstrations. Such allegations require individual evidence, but the broader accountability question is legitimate.

The feature-phone performance is particularly revealing. Before anyone announces a miracle, why not take the handset to an independent technician? Measure the charging current. Check the battery voltage. Establish whether the battery actually gains charge.

If the pastor is confident, independent testing should not threaten his testimony.

I have a more uncomfortable question for the congregation: what exactly are people rewarding through their offertory when a technical malfunction is presented as supernatural power?

Church should offer spiritual nourishment, moral guidance and genuine fellowship. It should not require congregants to suspend ordinary reasoning.

text:
“Even if posting 10,000 times turns 1 person away from hell, into the arms of Jesus, it was all worth it. All glory belongs to God.”

This thought reflects the heart of the Great Commission. The goal is not to become popular or gain followers, but to faithfully proclaim the gospel of Jesus Christ. If even one sinner repents and believes on Christ, heaven rejoices.

Jesus said:

“For what is a man profited, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul?”
— Matthew 16:26 (KJV)

One soul is worth more than all the wealth, fame, and success this world can offer. If God uses your testimony, preaching, or Scripture posts to lead one person to Christ, that labor is not in vain.

The Apostle Paul wrote:

“I have planted, Apollos watered; but God gave the increase.”
— 1 Corinthians 3:6 (KJV)

We cannot save anyone. Only God can change a heart. Our responsibility is to sow the seed of God's Word faithfully, while giving Him all the glory for every soul that is saved.

Jesus also declared:

“For the Son of man is come to seek and to save that which was lost.”
— Luke 19:10 (KJV)

Never grow weary of sharing the truth. Some will mock, reject, or ignore the message, but others will hear, repent, and be saved by the grace of God.

Finally, remember the promise of Scripture:

“And let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not.”
— Galatians 6:9 (KJV)

Keep exalting Jesus Christ, keep preaching His Word without compromise, and give all glory to God alone. If one soul escapes eternal judgment and comes into the saving arms of Christ, every effort is worth it—for “there is joy in the presence of the angels of God over one sinner that repenteth.” (Luke 15:10, KJV)

text:
The raging debate on the origin of zionism is academic and irrelevant to our lives at this moment.  This is not the conversation to have during a genocide.

I don't care if zionism was first a Christian idea.  Whether that's true or not is immaterial to me as a Palestinian.  

What is relevant and irrefutable is that material Zionism—i.e., the wholesale slaughter and displacement of indigenous Palestinians, the theft of our homes, land, and heritage, and ongoing genocidal apartheid and oppression—is wholly Jewish in its implementation.  

Some of you have criticized me for supporting the work of Benjamin Moser. I hear it, and some of it is fair, especially as it echoes what I've said myself. 

Yes, a few things he said feel like liberal Zionism, even as he explicitly rejects all zionism.  But my impulse was to offer some grace to someone who seems to be embarking on an earnest, moral, anti-zionist journey toward, perhaps, arriving at deeper truths, even if they implicate Judaism itself.  

That's not a defense of him, nor is it an endorsement.  I don't know him nor have I ever spoken with him.  It's just my honest reaction to a Jewish intellectual saying clearly that there is no acceptable form of zionism; that it is an irredeemably murderous, hateful, colonial ideology from the outset.

And there's also something else—something more personal that I have been wrestling with.

Besides the apathy of the Arab masses and complicity of Arab governments, nothing in this genocide has surprised me more than the widespread support Israel continues to enjoy among western Jews. 

Maybe I was naive, but there had always been a part of me that believed the Jewish masses outside Israel were mostly decent families who'd simply been brainwashed; and that if they really knew what Israel has been doing to us in the name of Judaism, they'd end that support.  

But survey after survey showed Jewish support for Israel  increased, even as they witnessed the same horrors the whole world was watching.  All the "holocaust museums" that we were made to march through in school have either been silent on this first live-streamed genocide in human history, or they've closed ranks with other mainstream Jewish institutions, all of them running cover and giving support to Israel, while simultaneously coming after individuals and collectives who dare to speak up. 

The disappointment, outrage, grief, anger, and pain I feel have been intense, and they made me feel mistrust of Jews outside my circles. I don't apologize for that, nor will I pretend it away—not when I'm watching our people shredded and denigrated day in and day out, while Jews in Israel and around the world sadistically celebrate it or at a minimum, make excuses for the mutilated bodies of our families.  

Then comes a statistic that half of the Jewish population in Michigan voted for the first Muslim senator, and a clear Jewish anti-Zionist voice begins to pop up on my feed, effectively countering zionist talking points.  So I held onto that, for my own sake—because I'm Muslim and I'm Palestinian and I'm a mother and grandmother, and at my core is a need to believe that most human are fundamentally decent.  

Ironically, in doing so, I did the thing I criticize others for doing—centering Jewish voices.  

So let me be clear that what matters to me is Palestinian liberation, an end to the zionist project, and full accountability and restitution—nothing short of how Nazis were treated.

The near total merging of Judaism with a brutal colonial project among world Jewry means there can be no getting around an eventual reckoning with western Jewry itself.  

But that, too, is not the conversation I want to have now.  

I want to talk about the dangers that Jewish supremacy poses to humanity, and to Palestinians in particular; about the inherent, wholly natural right to violently resist settler-colonialism; about Palestinians enduring a fourth winter of genocide in flimsy tents that flood with every rain and blow away in the wind, while Israel continues to murder, bomb, starve and eviscerate a captive indigenous society to take their land; about the Israeli politicians and pundits openly debating on their airwaves on a final solution—how to efficiently, realistically, and effectively finish off the Palestinians left in Gaza.

A University of Michigan professor is getting roasted online after going on NPR’s Code Switch podcast and arguing that working out can serve fascism. Fox News flagged the comments Sunday morning.

The professor’s pitch: “𝘞𝘩𝘦𝘯 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘴𝘵𝘢𝘵𝘦 𝘰𝘳 𝘢 𝘱𝘰𝘸𝘦𝘳𝘧𝘶𝘭 𝘪𝘯𝘴𝘵𝘪𝘵𝘶𝘵𝘪𝘰𝘯 𝘰𝘳 𝘢 𝘱𝘰𝘸𝘦𝘳𝘧𝘶𝘭 𝘱𝘦𝘳𝘴𝘰𝘯 𝘪𝘴 𝘱𝘶𝘴𝘩𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘧𝘪𝘵𝘯𝘦𝘴𝘴, 𝘪𝘵 𝘤𝘢𝘯 𝘴𝘦𝘦𝘮 𝘩𝘢𝘳𝘮𝘭𝘦𝘴𝘴, 𝘪𝘵 𝘤𝘢𝘯 𝘴𝘦𝘦𝘮 𝘢𝘯𝘰𝘥𝘺𝘯𝘦, 𝘪𝘵 𝘤𝘢𝘯 𝘴𝘦𝘦𝘮 𝘮𝘢𝘺𝘣𝘦 𝘦𝘷𝘦𝘯 𝘭𝘪𝘬𝘦 𝘢 𝘱𝘰𝘴𝘪𝘵𝘪𝘷𝘦 𝘨𝘰𝘰𝘥.”

Then came the real argument. “𝘍𝘪𝘵𝘯𝘦𝘴𝘴 𝘩𝘢𝘴 𝘣𝘦𝘦𝘯 𝘢𝘯𝘥 𝘤𝘰𝘯𝘵𝘪𝘯𝘶𝘦𝘴 𝘵𝘰 𝘣𝘦 𝘶𝘴𝘦𝘥 𝘵𝘰 𝘥𝘦𝘵𝘦𝘳𝘮𝘪𝘯𝘦 𝘸𝘩𝘰 𝘪𝘴 𝘩𝘢𝘳𝘥𝘸𝘰𝘳𝘬𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘢𝘯𝘥 𝘸𝘩𝘰 𝘪𝘴 𝘭𝘢𝘻𝘺.” And the professor’s verdict: “𝘞𝘦 𝘩𝘢𝘷𝘦 𝘢𝘯 𝘰𝘱𝘱𝘳𝘦𝘴𝘴𝘪𝘷𝘦 𝘩𝘪𝘴𝘵𝘰𝘳𝘪𝘤𝘢𝘭 𝘳𝘦𝘭𝘢𝘵𝘪𝘰𝘯𝘴𝘩𝘪𝘱 𝘵𝘰 𝘧𝘪𝘵𝘯𝘦𝘴𝘴.”

So lifting weights, running, and staying in shape are now suspect. That is the claim from an academic at a major state university, delivered on a podcast from NPR, and it is why the internet is piling on. 𝐏𝐡𝐲𝐬𝐢𝐜𝐚𝐥 𝐟𝐢𝐭𝐧𝐞𝐬𝐬 𝐚𝐬 𝐚 𝐭𝐨𝐨𝐥 𝐨𝐟 𝐟𝐚𝐬𝐜𝐢𝐬𝐦 is a sentence that sounds like satire, and it was offered as serious analysis.

Fox’s Ben Ferguson was brought in to respond. Ask the average American whether being hardworking and healthy is oppression, and you will get a very different answer than the one the podcast gave. Millions of people hit the gym every morning, and 𝐧𝐨𝐧𝐞 𝐨𝐟 𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐦 𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐧𝐤 𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐲 𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝐞𝐧𝐥𝐢𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐢𝐧 𝐚 𝐫𝐞𝐠𝐢𝐦𝐞.

𝐆𝐞𝐭𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐮𝐩 𝐞𝐚𝐫𝐥𝐲 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐠𝐞𝐭𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐟𝐢𝐭 𝐢𝐬𝐧’𝐭 𝐟𝐚𝐬𝐜𝐢𝐬𝐦. 𝐈𝐭’𝐬 𝐝𝐢𝐬𝐜𝐢𝐩𝐥𝐢𝐧𝐞, 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐧𝐨 𝐩𝐨𝐝𝐜𝐚𝐬𝐭 𝐠𝐞𝐭𝐬 𝐭𝐨 𝐫𝐞𝐛𝐫𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐢𝐭.

Lecture: 
Predators, Narratives, and Cascades 
— An Interdisciplinary Inquiry 
into Antisocial Emergence

Graduate seminar framing for 
Law, 
Political Science, 
Psychiatry, and 
Social Anthropology. 

We begin from a 
15 November 2020 observation 
by a long-serving corrections professional: 

empathy and love 
are necessary 
but insufficient. 

Children raised in caring families 
must also learn 
to recognize predators 
and antisocial patterns. 

In Michigan prisons a formal training, 
“Anatomy of a Setup,” 
described coordinated inmate teams t
hat entrap officers 
through sequences of 
apparently innocent steps
—gifts, 
sympathy, 
small favors
—until a narrative of leverage 
is assembled 
and blackmail 
or contraband introduction 
becomes possible. 

The same logic of 
incremental narrative construction, 
the author argued, 
appears among career politicians.

We examine this micro-dynamic 
and its societal magnification 
through five analytic lenses, 
then through the four disciplines.

The five lenses
Self-organizing systems. 
Complex adaptive systems 
generate coherent global patterns from local interactions without a central designer.
 
In the prison, 
observers, 
contacts, 
turners, 
and runners 
self-organize 
around a target; 
each step 
remains locally rational and deniable. 

On platforms, 
algorithms 
and user incentives 
likewise produce emergent cascades 
of attention, 
revenue, 
and radicalization 
without a single coordinating authority. 

Political movements a
nd corporate ESG/CSR regimes 
can similarly self-organize around 
status, 
funding, and 
moral signaling 
until the resulting pattern 
(policing withdrawal, 
speech norms, 
hiring preferences) 
is treated as inevitable.

Plausible deniability. 
The setup works 
because no single act is damning. 
Accepting a sketch, 
expressing sympathy,
or sharing a post 
can be defended as ordinary. 

The same architecture 
appears in political rhetoric 
(“mostly peaceful”), 
corporate policy 
(“we are simply following best practice”), 
and institutional language 
that separates intent from outcome. 

Deniability is not merely an alibi; 
it is a design feature 
that allows the sequence 
to continue 
until the cumulative narrative 
is irreversible.

Murphy’s Law. 
Systems in which 
many small failure modes exist 
will eventually meet
the conjunction t
hat produces large failure. 

Policy experiments 
that reduce police capacity 
while simultaneously elevating narratives 
that treat law enforcement 
as illegitimate 
have, in multiple jurisdictions,
 been followed by 
measurable rises in 
homicide and disorder. 

Lockdowns, 
censorship regimes, 
and certain DEI implementations 
have likewise 
produced secondary effects 
(learning loss, mental-health deterioration, reverse-discrimination litigation, institutional distrust) 
that were not the stated objectives. 

The law does not require malice; 
it requires only 
that the failure modes remain open.

Pandora’s box. 

Once certain thresholds are crossed
—normalization of political violence 
as a legitimate tool, 
algorithmic amplification 
of high-arousal antisocial content, 
the erosion 
of shared criteria for predator recognition
—the contents 
cannot be returned to the box by decree. 

Social media 
converts local antisocial strategies 
into scalable revenue streams 
and status hierarchies. 

Political narratives 
that selectively embrace 
or minimize one form of organized violence 
while condemning another 
further lower the threshold. 

The box, once opened, 
continues to emit.

The butterfly effect. 

Sensitive dependence 
on initial conditions 
means that the acceptance of one gift, 
the framing of one protest, 
or the adoption of one hiring rubric 
can cascade 
through self-organizing networks 
into systemic outcomes. 

The prison setup 
demonstrates the mechanism 
at small scale; 
platform architectures
 and political narrative markets 
demonstrate it at large scale. 

Small differences 
in early conditions 
(whether a child is taught discernment, 
whether a department policy 
treats a particular sequence 
as cumulative rather than atomic) 
produce divergent later trajectories.

Disciplinary perspectives

Law. 
The classic setup
 raises questions 
of entrapment doctrine, 
conspiracy, 
and the boundary 
between protected speech 
and actionable conspiracy 
or solicitation. 

Cumulative narrative construction 
can convert individually lawful acts 
into a pattern 
that satisfies the elements 
of blackmail 
or official misconduct. 

At the societal level, 
free-speech jurisprudence 
(Brandenburg and its progeny) 
must confront 
coordinated amplification 
that is not “imminent” 
in the classic sense 
yet produces 
predictable cascades 
of violence or institutional capture. 

Corporate ESG and DEI regimes 
generate parallel questions 
of fiduciary duty, 
disparate-impact liability, 
and the enforceability 
of viewpoint-neutral rules 
when private platforms 
and institutions 
function as de-facto public squares.

Political science. 
Narrative construction 
is a core technology of power.

Principal–agent problems, 
institutional trust erosion, 
and the competitive dynamics 
of attention markets 
explain why actors 
across the spectrum 
invest in frames
that maximize mobilization 
while preserving deniability. 

Movements 
that treat violence as a political tool
—whether labeled antifa, 
other extremist formations, 
or state-adjacent actors
—exploit the same 
self-organizing and deniability properties. 

The resulting polarization 
reduces the shared capacity 
to name predation 
when it appears 
inside one’s own coalition.

Psychiatry. 
Antisocial personality disorder 
and related spectra 
are defined 
by pervasive patterns of 
deceitfulness, 
lack of remorse, 
and exploitation. 

Prevalence
 is markedly elevated 
in incarcerated populations. 

These traits 
are not created by politics, 
yet political and platform environments 
can selectively amplify 
individuals 
who already possess them 
by supplying larger audiences, 
status, 
and revenue. 

Empathy training 
without concurrent 
training in boundary recognition 
and pattern detection 
leaves the empathically oriented 
especially vulnerable
—the precise failure mode 
described in the 2020 observation.

Radicalization literature
further shows 
that incremental commitment sequences 
(foot-in-the-door) 
operate similarly 
in ideological and criminal domains.

Social anthropology. 
Societies historically 
used rites, 
gift protocols, 
and explicit pedagogy 
to teach the difference 
between reciprocity and predation. 

When those mechanisms atrophy 
or are reframed 
as “othering,” 
the cultural repertoire 
for recognizing setups shrinks. 

Online tribes 
recreate totemic identities 
and ritualized violence; 
gift economies reappear 
as attention and revenue. 

Coporate Activism 
and certain DEI implementations 
can be read as 
new prestige economies 
in which moral signaling 
substitutes 
for the older pedagogical function 
of teaching discernment. 

The ethnographic question 
is whether any large-scale society 
can sustain high levels 
of generalized trust 
without also sustaining 
explicit, non-partisan training 
in predator recognition.

Synthesis 
and the listed proof-of-concept phenomena

Defund-the-police campaigns, 
selective corporate activism, 
globalist institutional pressures, 
DEI and 
affirmative-action regimes, 
ESG/CSR frameworks, 
censorship architectures, 
and lockdown policies 
can each be analyzed 
as instances 
in which self-organizing incentives, 
deniable incrementalism, 
open failure modes,
 irreversible thresholds, 
and sensitive dependence
produced outcomes 
divergent from stated aims. 

Social media 
functions as the principal amplifier, 
into scalable ones. 

The same lenses 
apply symmetrically: 
any political or institutional project 
that lowers the cost of predation 
or raises the cost of naming it 
will generate parallel cascades. 

The empirical record since 2020 
supplies multiple natural experiments; 
the analytic task 
is to measure the cascades 
rather than to defend or indict 
any single narrative in advance.

The gaps that remain 
are precisely those 
the lecture has circled: t
he distance 
between plausible deniability 
and enforceable transparency 
or accountability; 
the distance between 
self-organizing emergence 
and reliable predictability; 
the distance between 
the release of harms 
and the design of cures; 
and the distance 
between butterfly cascades 
of harm and interventions 
capable of interrupting them 
before they become irreversible.

Poem (in the style of Flash Ki / Muse, 
“Dead Inside (Mix Edit)”)

Dead inside
(Dead inside)

You taught the child only love
And left the predator’s grammar untaught

Each sketch, each post, each small gift
Seems pure enough to keep

But when the steps assemble
There’s nothing there

Light only shines 
from those who name the pattern

Unleash a million feeds
And confine the wary, 
erase the boundary, babe

Do the systems have no soul?
It’s like it died
when deniability became the design
Your metrics feel warm to the touch

You can bring the numbers back to life
On the outside you’re ablaze with virtue
But you’re dead inside
You’re free to touch the sky of narrative

Whilst the cascade is crushed and pulverised
Because the gap needs plausible cover
Now the sequence 
is the one that’s letting go

You like to give an inch of empathy
Whilst the setup is giving infinity
But now the trust has nothing left

You have no ledger 
and the harmed are bereft

Your skin of policy feels warm to caress
I see magic in the stated aims
On the outside you’re ablaze and alive

But you’re dead inside
Feel the gap now, 
hold the account please

I need the system 
to see what the steps become
Open the record to me, 
stop hiding the cumulative

It’s hurting, 
the cascade 
only naming can stop the pain

Don’t leave the pattern out in the cold
Don’t leave the next child out to die
We gave the platforms everything
We can’t give the predators any more

Now the culture has become just like the setup
Our lips feel warm with the correct phrase
Our words seem so alive with solidarity
Our metrics are warm to the brand caress
We’ll control the frame and hypnotise

You’ve taught the feed to lie without a trace
And to amplify with no remorse
On the outside
We’re the greatest moral architecture
Now we’re dead inside

(The cure for the gaps 
is the refusal of the first gift
the insistence that sequences be named 
before they cohere
the restoration of predictability 
where self-organization meets predation
the design of interruption 
before the box stays open
the mapping of the butterfly’s path 
while the wings are still small.)
Dead inside.

text:
An American Air Force veteran and her husband moved to Canada chasing the promise of free universal health care. 

Instead, after she was diagnosed with stage 4 ovarian cancer, the system offered her medically assisted death (MAID) before she had even seen an oncologist for treatment options. 

Kristin Logan and Donovan James describe a “dystopian” experience: long waits, dismissed symptoms, a pamphlet on assisted dying arriving early, and pressure toward ending her life rather than fighting the cancer. 

They left Canada, sought care in the United States, and she has since received chemotherapy and surgery. She is now in better shape and in remission periods, something the Canadian system had essentially written off. 

This is the reality of government-run “free” health care that DSA Democrats and many on the left want to impose on Americans. When the government controls the system and rations care, the cheapest option is death instead of expensive treatment. 

Canada’s MAID program has expanded rapidly and now accounts for a significant number of deaths. 

That is the model being sold as compassion and equity.

text:
Individual freedom is not one value among others.

It is the mother of all the others.

I'll own it: I have an almost sacred view of consent. And I believe that if we rebuilt everything from first principles, we would design systems where consent is axiom number one. Not an ideal. An axiom. The starting point for everything else.

Everything good humanity has ever produced rests on the same thing: two people saying yes. Trade, trust, friendship, love, business, innovation. Everything terrible it has produced rests on the opposite: someone deciding for you.

Take taxation.

On a huge range of issues, forced taxation is theft. If an individual took half of what you produce under threat, we'd have a word for it. When the State does it, we call it solidarity. The irony: Article 14 of the French Declaration of the Rights of Man of 1789 literally speaks of citizens "consenting" to taxation. The word is right there. We just emptied it of meaning.

And we all accept this because of two axioms almost nobody questions.

Axiom one: a State can't make money, so it has to take it. Wrong. From first principles, nothing stops us from imagining a State that runs a surplus, funding what it does by selling services people choose to buy, competing with private companies, with no legal monopoly and no abuse of dominant position. If your service is good, people pay. If it's bad, they leave. That's exactly what we demand of every company. And ultimately, I think we'll have to go all the way: a complete separation of economy and State, the way we separated Church and State.

Axiom two: without coercion, nothing holds together. History says the opposite. Mises proved it in 1920: without free prices born of free exchange, an economy can't calculate. It flies blind. Hayek took it further in 1944 in The Road to Serfdom: once you plan the economy, you end up planning people, and the least scrupulous rise to the top. East Germany vs West Germany. North Korea vs South Korea. Venezuela. Every system that breaks consent ends up dysfunctional. Then totalitarian. It's not a drift. It's the natural slope.

Now follow the logic all the way.

When you're convinced you know better than individuals what's good for them, you always end up crossing the most sacred lines. Including this one: a child cannot consent.

A child cannot consent to sex with an adult. Ever. A child is not responsible for their decisions until adulthood, and that is exactly why we must protect them. This principle must be sacred, and violating it must be punished with the utmost severity.

It wasn't always obvious. On January 26, 1977, Le Monde published an open letter written by Gabriel Matzneff and signed by Sartre, Beauvoir, Barthes, Deleuze, Guattari, Aragon, Kouchner and Jack Lang, defending three men prosecuted for sexual relations with minors under 15. In the name of liberation. In the name of progress. The left-wing intelligentsia of the day, in all its glory.

In Germany it was worse, because it was the State. In Berlin, psychologist Helmut Kentler had abandoned children placed in the homes of pedophile men, with the approval and funding of youth welfare services. For nearly thirty years. They called it a pedagogical experiment. A University of Hildesheim report documented the network in 2020.

These weren't the excesses of an era. These were deviants who used the language of emancipation to erase the one boundary that protects a child: their inability to consent.

The same principle applies today to the medicalization of children questioning their gender. A 12-year-old can't vote, sign a contract or buy a beer. How could they consent to an intervention that commits their body for life, when nobody knows the effects? The Cass Review concluded in 2024 that the evidence was remarkably weak. The UK banned puberty blockers for minors. And now it's launching a trial on 226 children under 16. I believe history will judge this period as one of the great medical scandals of our time.

Consent is violated everywhere, every day. And every time, the outcome is net negative.

Forced taxation: they take it before you even see your paycheck. Value moves from those who create to those who redistribute, and some of it gets lost along the way.

Mandatory pay-as-you-go pensions: you're not allowed to choose where your savings go. A system that only works if every generation is bigger than the last.

Public debt: we bind people who haven't been born yet. The purest form of non-consent: they can't even say no.

Inflation: the tax nobody voted for. They print, your savings melt, in silence.

School zoning: someone else decides where and how your child will learn.

Public monopolies: when you can't leave, the service has no reason to improve.

Why is it always net negative? Because a consensual exchange creates value on both sides, otherwise it wouldn't happen. A forced exchange destroys value on at least one side. And above all, it erases the most valuable information there is: what people actually want. No consent, no signal. No signal, no correction. No correction, and the error grows until it becomes a crisis.

So let me go all the way: a State should have no power whatsoever to dictate to individuals what they must do.

None.

Its role fits in one sentence: protect the people and enforce the law. Protect the nation and its borders. Protect every person's life, property and given word. And the law must be chosen by the people, for the people, with one limit no majority should ever be able to cross: the law protects your freedom. It doesn't confiscate it.

Everything else is a matter of consent. An economic service? You choose it or you don't. A vaccine? Your body, your choice. Insurance, retirement, school? Same thing. The State can offer. It must never impose.

We got the full-scale demonstration during Covid.

For two years, we saw what happens when a State decides it knows better than you what you're allowed to do with your body, your days, your social life. Permission slips to leave your own home. A QR code to drink a coffee. A French president explaining in January 2022 that he "really wanted to piss off" part of his own citizens.

And hundreds of thousands of people took to the streets, Saturday after Saturday. People who had never protested in their lives. Nurses, tradesmen, retirees. In Canada, truckers shut down Ottawa for three weeks.

That wasn't irrationality. It was a signal.

When you mess with individual freedom, you're playing with forces that always end badly. You fracture a society. You turn people against each other. You create a hatred that doesn't disappear when the decree is lifted. Trust doesn't come back by decree.

We should have learned the lesson: never build coercive systems again.

Instead, we're accelerating.

Chat Control: scanning the private messages of 450 million Europeans, in the name of protecting children. The European Parliament had asked for targeted investigations authorized by a judge. The permanent version is still being negotiated behind closed doors.

The DSA: giving Brussels leverage of up to 6% of platforms' global revenue to get them to moderate whatever is inconvenient.

The digital euro: a currency issued by the ECB that merchants won't be allowed to refuse, with a cap on how much you'll be allowed to hold. They promise privacy. But centralized monetary infrastructure doesn't need to be abused today to be dangerous. It only needs to exist on the day someone decides to use it.

I think it's pure madness.

Not because the people designing these tools are all malicious. Because every control tool built by people who believe they're benevolent ends up in the hands of people who aren't. That's Hayek again: in a centralized system, the worst get on top.

And if these tools aren't scrapped outright, they will generate enormous negativity. Distrust, anger, division. What we lived through during Covid, only worse. Because it's permanent.

And yet I believe the 21st century will be the century of individual freedom.

The century of private property. The century when bureaucrats, and those who extract rent without building anything, lose their power over the people who actually create value: entrepreneurs.

AI will accelerate this. When one person with a few agents can do what used to take a ministry, the argument "we need the State for that" collapses, line by line.

A State that protects, yes. A State that imposes, never.

The 20th century tried coercion. It filled cemeteries.

The 21st will be the century of yes.

2027: CHINASA NWORU DROPS POLITICAL BOMBSHELL — IPOB'S REGIONAL VOTING STRATEGY COULD DENY PRESIDENTIAL CANDIDATES THE REQUIRED 25%

IPOB MEMBER QUESTIONS PETER OBI'S PRESIDENTIAL CHANCES, PREDICTS REGIONAL VOTING BATTLES AND A POSSIBLE CONSTITUTIONAL CRISIS.

As political calculations ahead of Nigeria's 2027 presidential election intensify, a comment by Mazi Chinasa Nworu, a member of the Directorate of State (DOS) of IPOB, has introduced another dimension to the unfolding political debate.

Speaking during a Radio Biafra broadcast hosted by Mazi Patrick Ikem of Biafra TV, Chinasa Nworu offered his assessment of the presidential race, questioned Peter Obi's chances of emerging victorious and outlined what he described as a possible IPOB approach to the 2027 electoral contest.

TINUBU'S NORTHERN CHALLENGE AND THE SOUTH-WEST ADVANTAGE

According to Chinasa, President Asiwaju Bola Ahmed Tinubu is already facing considerable political difficulties in Northern Nigeria, judging by what he described as growing rejection of the APC and the spread of the "Tinubu Must Go" slogan across parts of the region.

He argued that Tinubu's strongest electoral advantage may remain the South-West, while the president would also need to secure significant support from other regions, including the South-East and coastal communities, to satisfy the constitutional requirements for winning the presidency.

IS PETER OBI'S NORTHERN POPULARITY REAL OR POLITICAL ILLUSION?

Chinasa also questioned whether Peter Obi's perceived popularity among some Northern voters would translate into actual votes in 2027.

His argument was that political sympathy towards Obi, particularly because of his identity as an Igbo presidential contender, should not automatically be interpreted as a willingness by Northern voters to elect him.

He suggested that regional political loyalties could ultimately influence voting decisions, with some Northern voters potentially preferring Atiku Abubakar or another Northern candidate over Obi when faced with the realities of presidential voting.

This raises an important political question: will Obi's perceived national popularity translate into the geographical spread required to win Nigeria's presidency?

IPOB'S PROPOSED REGIONAL VOTING CALCULATION

The most controversial aspect of Chinasa's comments was his suggestion that eligible voters in the Biafran region should participate in the 2027 election while considering the constitutional consequences of regional voting patterns.

He argued that no presidential candidate should automatically expect electoral support from the region and suggested that candidates should be left to demonstrate their popularity within their respective strongholds.

His remarks point towards a proposed strategy of regional electoral calculations that could make it difficult for presidential candidates to satisfy the constitutional requirement of securing at least 25 per cent of votes in two-thirds of the states of the federation and the Federal Capital Territory.

If such a voting pattern emerged, it could complicate the declaration of an outright presidential winner and potentially trigger further constitutional and political negotiations.

THE BIGGER POLITICAL OBJECTIVE: REGIONAL GOVERNMENT OR REFERENDUM?

Chinasa's argument goes beyond the ordinary contest for political power.

He presented the possibility of an electoral stalemate as a means of forcing Nigeria's political establishment to reconsider the country's existing political arrangement.

Among the outcomes he envisaged were negotiations towards a regional government structure or a referendum that could provide an opportunity for a peaceful separation of Nigeria.

However, deliberately obstructing an electoral outcome and creating a constitutional crisis would raise serious legal and democratic questions. Any political strategy must remain within the law and respect citizens' freedom to make their electoral choices.

text:
Powerful New Weight-Loss Drug Could Change How Millions Treat Painful Knee Arthritis | Northwestern University & Vincent L, SciTechDaily

An experimental weight-loss injection may offer more than a way to shed pounds, with clinical trials suggesting it could also ease the burden of painful knee arthritis.

Losing weight can help relieve knee osteoarthritis, yet the condition often makes weight loss difficult in the first place. When walking, climbing stairs, or simply standing up from a chair causes pain, getting enough exercise can become a challenge.

For the roughly 15 million Americans living with painful knee osteoarthritis, treatment options remain limited. Physical therapy, topical medications, anti-inflammatory drugs such as ibuprofen and Voltaren, opioids, and corticosteroid injections can help manage symptoms, although steroid injections typically provide only short-term relief.

Previous research has shown that losing just 5% to 10% of body weight through diet and exercise can improve symptoms. Losing more than 10%, however, is difficult through lifestyle changes alone, particularly for people whose knees already limit their movement.

An experimental weight-loss injection called retatrutide may offer another way to address this problem. In two large clinical trials led by Northwestern University, participants who were overweight or had obesity experienced substantial weight loss alongside significant reductions in knee pain.

Knee pain dropped as weight fell

The phase 3 trials, published in the New England Journal of Medicine, involved more than 1,000 participants combined. Those receiving the highest dose of retatrutide lost approximately 25% of their body weight on average. A pooled analysis found that about two-thirds of participants receiving the drug reported at least a 50% reduction in knee pain, compared with 38% of those given a placebo.

Researchers tracked these changes using the Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Arthritis Index (WOMAC), which asks patients to rate their pain from 0 to 10. Participants also recorded their daily pain levels through an app.

“The findings are really saying for people who are overweight and have OA, if you lose a significant amount of weight with this treatment, there is a good chance that you’re going to get a meaningful reduction in your knee pain,” said corresponding author Dr. Thomas Schnitzer, a professor of physical medicine and rehabilitation, anesthesiology and medicine (rheumatology) at Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine. “A major factor is that you’re loading your knees less and therefore, there’s less pain and it allows you to increase your function.”

A drug that targets three hormones

Developed by Eli Lilly, retatrutide is a once-weekly injection that activates receptors for three naturally occurring hormones involved in metabolism. Existing weight-loss medications such as semaglutide and tirzepatide target one or two receptors and typically produce weight reductions of 10% to 20%. Retatrutide produced losses of approximately 20% to 25% in these trials.

“Participants had remarkable responses,” Schnitzer said. “Many of the people in this study lost considerable amounts of weight, with a few losing up to a hundred pounds or more.”

The improvements also extended beyond body weight and joint pain. Participants experienced lower blood pressure, reduced blood lipid levels, and less systemic inflammation, suggesting broader metabolic benefits.

Scientists from Eli Lilly were among the study’s co-authors. Philip Conaghan, professor of musculoskeletal medicine at the University of Leeds in the United Kingdom, presented results from the TRIUMPH-4 trial at the American College of Rheumatology annual meeting in Orlando, Florida. Findings from the second trial, TRIUMPH-1-OA, were presented separately during a poster session.

Pain relief leaves unanswered questions

Despite the promising results, retatrutide remains experimental and would require approval from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration before becoming a treatment option. Schnitzer emphasized that diet, exercise, and lifestyle changes should remain the first approach because they are less expensive and avoid potential side effects associated with GLP-1 medications, including gastrointestinal problems and muscle loss. Preserving muscle is especially important for patients with knee osteoarthritis because it helps stabilize the joint.

The trials also left a crucial question unanswered. Although retatrutide significantly reduced pain, researchers do not yet know whether it slows the underlying progression of osteoarthritis or could help patients avoid knee replacement surgery. People who already needed knee replacements were excluded from the studies.

“That would be the goal here to say you can reduce people’s pain, and you can stop the progression of their osteoarthritis,” Schnitzer said.

Further research must also determine whether retatrutide could benefit people with knee osteoarthritis who are not overweight, since they were not included in the trials. Scientists are particularly interested in whether the drug’s potential anti-inflammatory effects contribute to pain relief independently of weight loss.

“These drugs are believed to have significant anti-inflammatory activity, but the mechanism is not entirely known,” Schnitzer said. “Whether cutting down inflammation in the joint is also important in addition to reducing load needs more research, so this is still a first step, in my view. I’ve been working in the OA field for a long time, and I think this opens up opportunities to do a lot more studies to understand the condition better.”

text:
The smoking gun — James Connolly was explicitly and consistently against mass migration — regardless of the reason.

Publication: Éire (Published 19 November 1914)
Meeting: Dublin Trades' Council (16 November 1914)
Subject: Belgian Refugees and Fair Labour
Speaker: James Connolly

Context: At the outbreak of World War I in 1914, hundreds of thousands of Belgian refugees fled their country following the German invasion, with at least 250,000 arriving in Britain and approximately 3,000 arriving in Ireland. Thomas Farren, a prominent Irish trade unionist, introduced a resolution to the Dublin Trades' Council to extend hospitality to these refugees and offer them trade union protection. James Connolly explicitly opposed the resolution because it implied that Ireland could automatically accept an unrestricted influx of refugees.

Note: This report is James Connolly's response to Thomas Farren's proposed resolution. The original third-person newspaper summary has been converted directly into the first person.

I think Mr. Farren’s resolution a very dangerous one, as it involves that if the refugees comply with what is laid down in the resolution we have nothing more to complain of. Provided the position was an ordinary one, with no war in question, and these people came to this country they ought to be welcomed no matter what their nationality might be. But the present position is an extraordinary one. It is not a case of a man or two men, but a possible case of a whole army being dumped down here. I am opposed to the resolution because it implies that no matter what number is dumped down we accept them and undertake to work harmoniously along with them. This is no war of ours and the people of this country have no interest in it or in the Allies. I believe the Belgian people have been dragged into it by the machinations of their Government, and the Government, having brought them into it should look after them. The British had called on them to preserve their neutrality—which was not threatened for a moment—and said they would stand behind them. They did stand behind them—so much so that the Belgians did not know they were there.

The Belgian people, I believe, have been sold by their Government for something which we can only guess at. While carefully avoiding saying anything against the Belgians, we ought not to do anything that would give the employers in this country a chance to ‘sack’ Irish workers and take on Belgian employees. We ought not to give any loophole to the employers. If it was true these Belgians had fought for their own neutrality, then they should not be brought here to supplant the workers of Ireland but as a charge on the British Empire.

Source: Originally published in Arthur Griffith's newspaper Éire(19 November 1914).

Arthur Griffith was a major figure in Irish history, best known as the founder of Sinn Féin and later the President of Dáil Éireann. Newspapers like Éire played a critical role in recording political debates and nationalist activities.

Credit and thanks to:

Cartlann: For retrieving, transcribing, and publishing the text online in a first-person format.

The Burkean: For transcribing and preserving the text in its original third-person format.
